# 11. ADR Lifecycle

Every Architecture Decision Record follows this lifecycle:

```text
Draft
   │
   ▼
Review
   │
   ▼
Accepted
   │
   ▼
Implemented
   │
   ▼
Validated
   │
   ▼
Superseded
        or
Deprecated
```

No production-impacting architectural change shall be implemented without an approved ADR.

---

# 12. Technology Governance

New technologies must be evaluated against:

* Business value
* Community maturity
* Vendor support
* Security posture
* Performance
* Licensing
* Cost
* Operational complexity
* Learning curve
* Long-term sustainability

Approved technologies are added to the Enterprise Technology Catalog.

---

# 13. Exception Management

Projects may request temporary exceptions when compliance is not feasible.

Each request must include:

* Business justification
* Architectural impact
* Risk assessment
* Mitigation plan
* Sunset date
* Responsible owner

Exceptions require approval from the Enterprise Architecture Board and are reviewed periodically.

---

# 14. Technical Debt Governance

Technical debt shall be classified as:

### Strategic Debt

Accepted to accelerate delivery with a planned remediation timeline.

### Accidental Debt

Introduced unintentionally and should be addressed promptly.

### Legacy Debt

Inherited from older systems and managed through modernization initiatives.

All technical debt items shall be:

* Documented.
* Prioritized.
* Assigned an owner.
* Reviewed quarterly.
* Tracked to closure.

---

# 15. Architecture Compliance

Compliance shall be validated using:

* Architecture reviews.
* Static code analysis.
* Automated architecture tests (e.g., ArchUnit).
* Security scanning.
* Dependency analysis.
* Infrastructure compliance checks.
* API governance validation.
* Manual audits.

Compliance results become part of release readiness.

---

# 16. Architecture Metrics

The Enterprise Architecture Board shall monitor:

| Category       | Example Metrics                             |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| Architecture   | ADR adoption rate, review completion time   |
| Quality        | Code quality score, architecture violations |
| Security       | Open vulnerabilities, policy compliance     |
| Operations     | Availability, MTTR, deployment frequency    |
| DevOps         | Lead time, change failure rate              |
| Technical Debt | Debt ratio, remediation backlog             |
| Performance    | API latency, throughput, error rate         |
| Governance     | Exception count, audit findings             |

These metrics support continuous improvement and informed decision-making.

---

# 17. Communication and Knowledge Management

Architecture knowledge shall be maintained through:

* Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)
* Reference Architectures
* Technical Standards
* Architecture Diagrams
* Engineering Wiki
* Technology Catalog
* Architecture Community of Practice
* Quarterly Architecture Forums

All approved architectural artifacts shall be version-controlled and accessible to engineering teams.

---

# 18. Consequences

## Positive Consequences

* Consistent architecture across teams.
* Reduced technology sprawl.
* Improved compliance.
* Better knowledge sharing.
* Faster onboarding.
* Lower technical debt.
* Improved engineering quality.
* Stronger alignment with business strategy.

## Negative Consequences

* Additional governance effort.
* Longer approval cycles for major changes.
* Increased documentation requirements.
* Need for ongoing governance participation.

These trade-offs are acceptable given the complexity and criticality of the Mediverse platform.

---

| Outdated standards              | Annual review of governance policies and ADRs                    |
| Limited stakeholder engagement  | Regular architecture forums and cross-functional participation   |

* Improved strategic alignment.
* Reduced long-term costs.
* Better investment decisions.
* Increased stakeholder confidence.

* Reduced architectural drift.
* Better interoperability.

## Operational Impact

# Part II — Technology Stack Decisions

# ADR-011 — Java 21 Selection

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-011
**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-07-30
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)
**Approvers:** CTO, Chief Architect, VP Engineering, Platform Engineering Lead

---

# 1. Executive Summary

This Architecture Decision Record (ADR) establishes **Java 21 (Long-Term Support)** as the primary programming language and runtime for all backend services of the Mediverse Enterprise Healthcare Platform.

Mediverse requires an enterprise-grade programming platform capable of supporting:

* Mission-critical healthcare workloads
* High concurrency
* Long-term maintainability
* Strong security
* Cloud-native deployment
* AI integration
* Large engineering teams
* Mature ecosystem

After evaluating multiple languages and runtime platforms, **Java 21 LTS** has been selected as the enterprise standard.

---

# 2. Decision Statement

**Decision**

All backend services shall be developed using **Java 21 LTS** unless an approved ADR explicitly authorizes another language for a specific use case.

Java shall serve as the foundation for:

* Microservices
* APIs
* Event Processing
* Batch Jobs
* Background Workers
* Integration Services
* AI Orchestration
* Scheduled Tasks

---

# 3. Business Context

The Mediverse platform consists of hundreds of enterprise services handling:

* Patient Records
* Medical Education
* Examination Systems
* Hospital Operations
* Pharmacy
* Laboratory
* Telemedicine
* AI-assisted Diagnostics
* Healthcare Analytics
* Billing
* Notifications

These services require:

* High reliability
* Predictable performance
* Long-term vendor support
* Mature tooling
* Large talent availability

---

# 4. Problem Statement

Selecting the wrong backend language may result in:

* Increased maintenance costs.
* Limited hiring opportunities.
* Reduced ecosystem support.
* Vendor lock-in.
* Lower productivity.
* Security risks.
* Migration challenges.

A strategic programming language decision is therefore required.

---

# 5. Decision Drivers

The decision is driven by:

* Long-Term Support (LTS)
* Enterprise maturity
* Performance
* Stability
* Security
* Ecosystem
* Community support
* Developer productivity
* Framework support
* Cloud-native readiness
* DevOps compatibility

---

# 6. Considered Alternatives

---

## Alternative A — Java 21 LTS

### Advantages

* Long-Term Support
* Mature JVM
* Excellent performance
* Massive ecosystem
* Spring Boot support
* Virtual Threads (Project Loom)
* Strong security
* Enterprise adoption
* Excellent IDE support
* Rich monitoring ecosystem

### Disadvantages

* Higher memory usage than Go
* Slower startup without native compilation
* Verbose compared to Kotlin

**Decision:** ✅ Accepted

---

## Alternative B — Kotlin

### Advantages

* Modern syntax
* Null safety
* Full JVM compatibility
* Spring Boot support
* Concise code

### Disadvantages

* Smaller talent pool
* Smaller enterprise adoption
* Additional learning curve
* Fewer large healthcare deployments

**Decision:** Rejected as primary language.

May be approved for isolated services.

---

## Alternative C — Go

### Advantages

* Small binaries
* Fast startup
* Excellent concurrency
* Low memory footprint

### Disadvantages

* Smaller enterprise ecosystem
* Limited Spring equivalent
* Reduced healthcare library support
* Less suitable for complex domain models

**Decision:** Rejected.

---

## Alternative D — C# (.NET)

### Advantages

* Excellent tooling
* Strong enterprise support
* High performance

### Disadvantages

* Smaller Linux cloud-native adoption compared to Java
* Less alignment with existing platform expertise
* Smaller ecosystem for chosen architecture

**Decision:** Rejected.

---

## Alternative E — Node.js (TypeScript)

### Advantages

* Fast development
* Large package ecosystem
* Good for lightweight APIs

### Disadvantages

* Single-threaded execution model
* Less suitable for CPU-intensive workloads
* Complex large-scale domain modeling

**Decision:** Rejected.

---

# 7. Comparative Analysis

| Criteria             | Java 21 | Kotlin |   Go  |   C#  | Node.js |
| -------------------- | :-----: | :----: | :---: | :---: | :-----: |
| Enterprise Maturity  |  ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐  |  ⭐⭐⭐⭐  |  ⭐⭐⭐  |  ⭐⭐⭐⭐ |   ⭐⭐⭐   |
| Performance          |  ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐  |  ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |   ⭐⭐⭐   |
| LTS Support          |  ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐  |  ⭐⭐⭐⭐  |  ⭐⭐⭐⭐ | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |   ⭐⭐⭐   |
| Healthcare Ecosystem |  ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐  |  ⭐⭐⭐⭐  |  ⭐⭐⭐  |  ⭐⭐⭐  |    ⭐⭐   |
| Cloud Native         |  ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐  |  ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |  ⭐⭐⭐⭐ |   ⭐⭐⭐⭐  |
| Security             |  ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐  |  ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |  ⭐⭐⭐⭐ | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |   ⭐⭐⭐   |
| Tooling              |  ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐  |  ⭐⭐⭐⭐  |  ⭐⭐⭐  | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |   ⭐⭐⭐⭐  |
| Hiring Availability  |  ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐  |   ⭐⭐⭐  |  ⭐⭐⭐  |  ⭐⭐⭐  |   ⭐⭐⭐⭐  |

---

# 8. Why Java 21?

Java 21 introduces enterprise capabilities that significantly improve Mediverse's architecture.

Key features include:

* Long-Term Support (LTS)
* Virtual Threads (Project Loom)
* Record Classes
* Pattern Matching
* Sealed Classes
* Improved Garbage Collection
* Enhanced Performance
* Strong Backward Compatibility
* Mature JVM
* Extensive Monitoring Support

These capabilities align with Mediverse's scalability, maintainability, and operational goals.

---

# 9. Enterprise Technology Stack

Java 21 shall be used together with:

| Component     | Standard                         |
| ------------- | -------------------------------- |
| Language      | Java 21 LTS                      |
| Framework     | Spring Boot                      |
| Build Tool    | Maven                            |
| Testing       | JUnit 5, Mockito, Testcontainers |
| API           | Spring Web                       |
| Security      | Spring Security                  |
| ORM           | Hibernate/JPA                    |
| Messaging     | Kafka, RabbitMQ                  |
| Cache         | Redis                            |
| Search        | Elasticsearch                    |
| Monitoring    | Micrometer                       |
| Observability | OpenTelemetry                    |
| Container     | Docker                           |
| Orchestration | Kubernetes                       |

---

# 10. Coding Standards

Java code shall follow:

* Java Naming Conventions
* SOLID Principles
* Clean Code
* Domain-Driven Design
* Hexagonal Architecture
* Clean Architecture
* Immutable Objects where appropriate
* Constructor Injection
* Dependency Inversion
* Composition over Inheritance

---

# 11. Performance Considerations

Java 21 provides:

* Virtual Threads for high-concurrency I/O workloads.
* Efficient G1, ZGC, and Shenandoah garbage collectors.
* Improved startup and runtime optimizations.
* Mature Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation.
* Excellent scalability on multicore processors.

Performance tuning shall be guided by profiling and production metrics rather than assumptions.

---

# 12. Security Considerations

The Java platform shall support:

* TLS 1.3
* Secure Random APIs
* Strong Cryptography
* Spring Security
* OWASP Compliance
* Dependency Scanning
* Secure Deserialization Practices
* JVM Security Updates
* Secret Management Integration

---

# 13. Operational Considerations

All Java services shall support:

* Containerized deployment
* Health probes
* Graceful shutdown
* JVM metrics
* Distributed tracing
* Structured logging
* Autoscaling
* Rolling deployments

---

# 14. Risks and Mitigations

| Risk                       | Mitigation                                                                          |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| JVM memory consumption     | Tune heap settings and monitor runtime metrics                                      |
| Slow startup               | Optimize application initialization and evaluate AOT/native options where justified |
| Dependency vulnerabilities | Continuous dependency scanning and timely updates                                   |
| Legacy Java versions       | Standardize on Java 21 LTS and define upgrade policies                              |
| Skill variation            | Internal training, coding standards, and peer reviews                               |

---

# 15. Consequences

## Positive Consequences

* Stable long-term platform.
* Mature ecosystem.
* Excellent tooling.
* Large talent pool.
* Strong security.
* Enterprise-grade performance.
* Broad community support.
* Compatibility with existing architectural decisions.

## Negative Consequences

* Larger runtime footprint than some alternatives.
* Requires JVM tuning for specific workloads.
* Native compilation may require additional evaluation for niche use cases.

The long-term benefits outweigh these trade-offs.

---

# 16. Impact Analysis

## Business Impact

* Lower hiring risk.
* Reduced maintenance costs.
* Long-term vendor support.
* Stable technology roadmap.

## Technical Impact

* High-performance runtime.
* Strong framework ecosystem.
* Excellent compatibility with cloud-native architecture.

## Operational Impact

* Mature observability.
* Reliable production operations.
* Predictable upgrade path.

---

# 17. Compliance Considerations

Java 21 supports Mediverse's compliance objectives by enabling secure development practices compatible with:

* HIPAA
* GDPR
* HL7
* FHIR
* ISO/IEC 27001
* SOC 2
* OWASP ASVS
* NIST Cybersecurity Framework

Implementation remains the responsibility of application teams and supporting platform standards.

---

# 18. Success Metrics

This ADR will be considered successful when:

* All new backend services are built using Java 21 LTS.
* Unsupported Java versions are retired according to the platform lifecycle.
* Performance SLOs are consistently achieved.
* Security patches are applied within defined timelines.
* Developer productivity improves through standardized tooling and practices.
* Production incidents attributable to runtime limitations remain minimal.

# ADR-012 — Spring Boot Selection

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-012
**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-07-30
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)
**Approvers:** CTO, Chief Architect, VP Engineering, Platform Engineering Lead

---

# 1. Executive Summary

This Architecture Decision Record (ADR) establishes **Spring Boot** as the standard application framework for all Java-based backend services within the Mediverse Enterprise Healthcare Platform.

Mediverse requires a mature, enterprise-grade application framework capable of supporting:

* Cloud-native microservices
* High-performance REST APIs
* Event-driven architecture
* Enterprise security
* Observability
* Kubernetes deployments
* Distributed systems
* AI integrations
* Long-term maintainability

After evaluating multiple Java frameworks, **Spring Boot** has been selected due to its mature ecosystem, extensive community support, seamless integration with the Spring portfolio, and strong compatibility with enterprise healthcare systems.

---

# 2. Decision Statement

**Decision**

All Java backend services shall use **Spring Boot** as the primary application framework unless an approved ADR authorizes an alternative for a specific use case.

Spring Boot shall provide the foundation for:

* REST APIs
* gRPC Services
* Event Processing
* Background Jobs
* Scheduled Tasks
* Batch Processing
* Integration Services
* Authentication Services

---

# 3. Business Context

Mediverse includes hundreds of services across domains such as:

* Medical Education
* Hospital Management
* Electronic Health Records
* Telemedicine
* Laboratory
* Pharmacy
* AI Services
* Notifications
* Billing
* Analytics

The framework must support rapid development, high reliability, operational consistency, and integration with enterprise tooling.

---

# 4. Problem Statement

Choosing an unsuitable application framework could result in:

* Increased development effort.
* Fragmented technology choices.
* Reduced maintainability.
* Limited ecosystem support.
* Difficult onboarding.
* Operational inconsistency.
* Higher long-term costs.

A standardized framework is therefore required.

---

# 5. Decision Drivers

The decision is based on:

* Enterprise maturity.
* Cloud-native readiness.
* Productivity.
* Security.
* Ecosystem.
* Community support.
* Long-term maintenance.
* Kubernetes compatibility.
* Integration capabilities.
* Observability support.

---

# 6. Considered Alternatives

---

## Alternative A — Spring Boot

### Advantages

* Mature ecosystem
* Auto-configuration
* Dependency Injection
* Spring Security
* Spring Data JPA
* Spring Cloud
* Spring Boot Actuator
* Spring Batch
* Spring Integration
* Excellent Kubernetes support
* Large community

### Disadvantages

* Larger memory footprint
* Slower startup compared to lightweight frameworks
* Extensive ecosystem can increase complexity

**Decision:** ✅ Accepted

---

## Alternative B — Micronaut

### Advantages

* Fast startup
* Low memory usage
* Ahead-of-Time optimizations
* Kubernetes friendly

### Disadvantages

* Smaller ecosystem
* Smaller community
* Fewer enterprise healthcare deployments

**Decision:** Rejected as primary framework.

---

## Alternative C — Quarkus

### Advantages

* Native image support
* Fast startup
* Kubernetes optimized
* Low memory footprint

### Disadvantages

* Smaller ecosystem
* Less mature enterprise tooling
* Limited organizational expertise

**Decision:** Rejected.

---

## Alternative D — Jakarta EE

### Advantages

* Enterprise standard
* Vendor neutrality
* Mature specifications

### Disadvantages

* More configuration
* Lower developer productivity
* Smaller modern cloud-native ecosystem

**Decision:** Rejected.

---

# 8. Why Spring Boot?

Spring Boot aligns with Mediverse because it offers:

* Convention over configuration.
* Comprehensive enterprise ecosystem.
* Rapid application development.
* Mature dependency injection.
* Strong testing support.
* Production-ready monitoring.
* Robust security integration.
* Compatibility with Java 21.

These capabilities accelerate delivery while maintaining enterprise quality.

---

# 9. Spring Ecosystem Standards

The following Spring modules are approved for use:

| Component        | Standard                |
| ---------------- | ----------------------- |
| Core Framework   | Spring Boot             |
| REST APIs        | Spring Web              |
| Security         | Spring Security         |
| Persistence      | Spring Data JPA         |
| Validation       | Spring Validation       |
| Configuration    | Spring Configuration    |
| Batch Processing | Spring Batch            |
| Scheduling       | Spring Scheduler        |
| Messaging        | Spring for Kafka / AMQP |
| Observability    | Spring Boot Actuator    |
| Testing          | Spring Boot Test        |

Additional modules require architectural review if they introduce significant platform dependencies.

---

# 10. Development Standards

All Spring Boot services shall:

* Use constructor injection.
* Prefer immutable configuration objects.
* Avoid field injection.
* Externalize configuration.
* Follow REST standards.
* Use DTOs at API boundaries.
* Implement global exception handling.
* Expose health endpoints.
* Use standardized logging.
* Follow Clean Architecture and DDD.

---

# 11. Cloud-Native Features

Spring Boot services shall support:

* Containerization with Docker.
* Kubernetes deployments.
* Health probes (liveness/readiness).
* Graceful shutdown.
* External configuration.
* Autoscaling compatibility.
* Rolling updates.
* Blue/Green and Canary deployment strategies.

---

# 12. Security Considerations

Spring Boot services shall integrate with:

* Spring Security.
* OAuth2/OpenID Connect.
* JWT authentication.
* Role-Based Access Control (RBAC).
* Method-level authorization.
* CSRF protection where applicable.
* Secure HTTP headers.
* Input validation.
* Secrets management.

---

# 13. Operational Considerations

Every service shall expose:

* Health endpoint
* Readiness endpoint
* Liveness endpoint
* Metrics endpoint
* Prometheus metrics
* Structured logs
* Distributed tracing
* Build information
* Version information

Operational endpoints shall be secured according to platform policies.

---

# 14. Risks and Mitigations

| Risk                     | Mitigation                                                   |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Dependency bloat         | Use approved starters and periodic dependency reviews        |
| Slow startup             | Optimize initialization and evaluate AOT where beneficial    |
| Misconfiguration         | Centralized configuration management and validation          |
| Security vulnerabilities | Regular framework updates and automated dependency scanning  |
| Inconsistent usage       | Shared templates, coding standards, and architecture reviews |

---

# 15. Consequences

## Positive Consequences

* Rapid development.
* Standardized architecture.
* Mature ecosystem.
* Strong security integration.
* Excellent observability.
* Large talent pool.
* Long-term support.
* Reduced operational risk.

## Negative Consequences

* Larger runtime footprint.
* Broad ecosystem requires governance.
* Potential overuse of framework features.

These trade-offs are acceptable given Mediverse's enterprise requirements.

---

# 16. Impact Analysis

## Business Impact

* Faster feature delivery.
* Lower development costs.
* Reduced onboarding effort.
* Improved maintainability.

## Technical Impact

* Consistent application architecture.
* Strong integration with platform services.
* Enhanced testing capabilities.
* Reliable cloud-native deployment.

## Operational Impact

* Simplified monitoring.
* Standardized deployment.
* Improved production support.
* Better operational visibility.

---

# 17. Compliance Considerations

Spring Boot supports compliance objectives by integrating with security, observability, and configuration standards compatible with:

* HIPAA
* GDPR
* HL7
* FHIR
* ISO/IEC 27001
* SOC 2
* OWASP ASVS
* NIST Cybersecurity Framework

Compliance depends on correct implementation and governance rather than framework selection alone.

---

# 18. Success Metrics

This ADR will be considered successful when:

* All Java backend services are implemented using approved Spring Boot versions.
* Platform templates are adopted across engineering teams.
* Security and observability standards are consistently implemented.
* Service startup, deployment, and operational metrics meet platform objectives.
* Framework upgrades are managed within defined support windows.
* Developer productivity improves through standardized practices.

---

# ADR-013 — Spring Cloud Adoption Strategy

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-013
**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-07-30
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)
**Approvers:** CTO, Chief Architect, VP Engineering, Platform Engineering Lead

---

# 1. Executive Summary

This Architecture Decision Record (ADR) establishes the enterprise strategy for adopting **Spring Cloud** within the Mediverse Enterprise Healthcare Platform.

Mediverse is a Kubernetes-first, cloud-native platform built on Java 21 and Spring Boot. As the platform evolves into hundreds of independently deployable microservices, consistent solutions are required for service communication, centralized configuration, resilience, observability, security, and external traffic management.

Spring Cloud provides a comprehensive ecosystem for distributed systems. However, because Kubernetes already provides several infrastructure capabilities, Mediverse adopts a **selective Spring Cloud strategy**, using Kubernetes-native features where appropriate and Spring Cloud components only when they provide clear application-level value.

---

# 2. Decision Statement

**Decision**

Mediverse shall adopt **Spring Cloud selectively**.

The platform will:

* Prefer Kubernetes-native capabilities for infrastructure concerns.
* Use Spring Cloud where application-level functionality is required.
* Avoid overlapping infrastructure responsibilities.
* Standardize approved Spring Cloud modules.
* Prohibit deprecated or redundant components.

---

# 3. Business Context

The Mediverse platform includes:

* Hundreds of microservices
* Kubernetes clusters
* Multi-environment deployments
* External healthcare integrations
* AI services
* Event-driven workflows
* REST APIs
* gRPC APIs
* Kafka messaging
* Multi-region deployments

Managing distributed systems requires standardized tooling.

---

# 4. Problem Statement

Without standardized cloud infrastructure:

* Configuration becomes inconsistent.
* Service communication varies.
* Retry logic is duplicated.
* Traffic management differs across teams.
* Operational complexity increases.
* Observability becomes fragmented.
* Security configurations diverge.

A unified cloud strategy is therefore required.

---

# 5. Decision Drivers

This decision is driven by:

* Cloud-native architecture
* Kubernetes-first philosophy
* Standardization
* Operational simplicity
* Resilience
* Scalability
* Security
* Maintainability
* Developer productivity
* Long-term sustainability

---

# 6. Considered Alternatives

---

## Alternative A — Full Spring Cloud Stack

### Description

Use Spring Cloud for all distributed system concerns.

### Advantages

* Unified programming model
* Mature ecosystem
* Excellent Spring integration

### Disadvantages

* Overlaps with Kubernetes
* Duplicate capabilities
* Increased operational complexity

**Decision:** Rejected.

---

## Alternative B — Kubernetes Only

### Description

Rely exclusively on Kubernetes capabilities.

### Advantages

* Simpler infrastructure
* Reduced dependencies
* Cloud-native

### Disadvantages

* Missing application-level abstractions
* Limited developer convenience
* Increased implementation effort

**Decision:** Rejected.

---

## Alternative C — Hybrid Strategy

### Description

Use Kubernetes for infrastructure responsibilities and Spring Cloud for application-level concerns.

### Advantages

* Best of both worlds
* Minimal duplication
* Flexible
* Scalable
* Easier maintenance

### Disadvantages

* Requires architectural governance
* Teams must understand responsibility boundaries

**Decision:** ✅ Accepted

---

# 7. Approved Spring Cloud Components

| Component                    | Status         | Purpose                                     |
| ---------------------------- | -------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| Spring Cloud Config Client   | ✅ Approved     | External configuration consumption          |
| Spring Cloud OpenFeign       | ✅ Approved     | Declarative REST clients                    |
| Spring Cloud Circuit Breaker | ✅ Approved     | Fault tolerance                             |
| Spring Cloud LoadBalancer    | ✅ Approved     | Client-side load balancing where needed     |
| Spring Cloud Gateway         | ✅ Approved     | API Gateway (non-Kubernetes edge scenarios) |
| Spring Cloud Stream          | ✅ Approved     | Messaging abstraction                       |
| Spring Cloud Sleuth          | ❌ Deprecated   | Replaced by Micrometer/OpenTelemetry        |
| Spring Cloud Netflix Eureka  | ❌ Not Approved | Kubernetes Service Discovery preferred      |
| Ribbon                       | ❌ Deprecated   | Use Spring Cloud LoadBalancer               |
| Hystrix                      | ❌ Deprecated   | Use Resilience4j                            |

---

# 8. Components Replaced by Kubernetes

| Capability         | Kubernetes Standard                        |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------ |
| Service Discovery  | Kubernetes DNS                             |
| Configuration      | ConfigMaps                                 |
| Secrets            | Kubernetes Secrets / External Secret Store |
| Service Registry   | Kubernetes Services                        |
| Health Checks      | Liveness & Readiness Probes                |
| Load Balancing     | Kubernetes Services & Ingress              |
| Horizontal Scaling | HPA                                        |
| Rolling Updates    | Deployment Controller                      |
| Service Networking | Kubernetes Networking                      |

Spring Cloud components shall not duplicate these platform responsibilities.

---

# 9. Service Discovery Strategy

Mediverse shall use:

```text
Service
      │
      ▼
Kubernetes DNS
      │
      ▼
student-service.default.svc.cluster.local
```

Eureka Server shall not be used.

Reasons:

* Native Kubernetes support
* Lower operational overhead
* Better scalability
* Fewer moving parts

---

# 10. Configuration Management

Configuration hierarchy:

```text
Git Repository
        │
        ▼
CI/CD Pipeline
        │
        ▼
ConfigMaps / Secrets
        │
        ▼
Spring Boot Configuration
```

Configuration principles:

* Externalized configuration
* Immutable containers
* Environment-specific values
* Secure secret storage
* Version-controlled configuration

---

# 11. API Gateway Strategy

Primary gateway:

* Kubernetes Ingress Controller

Application gateway (when required):

* Spring Cloud Gateway

Gateway responsibilities:

* Authentication
* Rate limiting
* Request routing
* Header transformation
* API aggregation
* Traffic shaping

Edge routing shall remain consistent across environments.

---

# 12. Resilience Strategy

Approved resilience patterns:

* Retry
* Timeout
* Circuit Breaker
* Bulkhead
* Rate Limiting
* Fallback
* Graceful Degradation

Approved implementation:

* **Resilience4j**
* Spring Cloud Circuit Breaker

Hystrix is prohibited.

---

# 13. Distributed Tracing

Approved observability stack:

* OpenTelemetry
* Micrometer
* Prometheus
* Grafana
* Tempo or Jaeger

Spring Cloud Sleuth shall not be used for new services.

Every request must propagate:

* Trace ID
* Span ID
* Correlation ID

---

# 14. Messaging Integration

Approved messaging:

* Apache Kafka
* RabbitMQ

Spring Cloud Stream may be used when:

* Broker abstraction is beneficial.
* Multiple messaging backends are supported.
* Event contracts remain framework-independent.

Direct Spring Kafka usage is preferred for high-throughput services.

---

# 15. Security Considerations

Spring Cloud integrations shall support:

* OAuth2
* OpenID Connect
* Mutual TLS (mTLS) where required
* JWT propagation
* Secure service-to-service communication
* Secret rotation
* Certificate management
* Zero Trust principles

No sensitive credentials shall be embedded in application binaries.

---

# 16. Operational Considerations

All Spring Cloud-enabled services shall provide:

* Health endpoints
* Metrics
* Distributed tracing
* Structured logging
* Graceful shutdown
* Configuration refresh (where appropriate)
* Version reporting
* Build metadata

Operational behavior shall remain consistent across all environments.

---

# 17. Risks and Mitigations

| Risk                            | Mitigation                                       |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Overlapping Kubernetes features | Prefer Kubernetes-native solutions first         |
| Configuration drift             | GitOps-managed configuration and version control |
| Deprecated Spring Cloud modules | Maintain approved technology catalog             |
| Increased complexity            | Restrict usage to approved components            |
| Vendor lock-in                  | Favor open standards and portable configurations |

---

# 18. Consequences

## Positive Consequences

* Consistent cloud architecture.
* Reduced duplication.
* Better resilience.
* Improved developer productivity.
* Easier operations.
* Standardized distributed system patterns.
* Alignment with Kubernetes.

## Negative Consequences

* Teams must understand both Kubernetes and Spring Cloud.
* Additional governance is required.
* Selective adoption requires architectural discipline.

These trade-offs are acceptable for a cloud-native enterprise platform.

---

# 19. Impact Analysis

## Business Impact

* Faster development.
* Improved platform consistency.
* Reduced operational costs.
* Better scalability.

## Technical Impact

* Simplified distributed system implementation.
* Standardized cloud patterns.
* Reduced framework redundancy.

## Operational Impact

* Lower infrastructure overhead.
* Easier monitoring.
* Simplified troubleshooting.
* Consistent deployment model.

---

# 20. Compliance Considerations

This strategy supports compliance with:

* HIPAA
* GDPR
* HL7
* FHIR
* ISO/IEC 27001
* SOC 2
* NIST Cybersecurity Framework
* OWASP ASVS

through standardized configuration management, secure communication, centralized observability, and governed cloud-native practices.

---

# 21. Success Metrics

This ADR will be considered successful when:

* All services follow the approved Spring Cloud component catalog.
* Deprecated modules (Eureka, Ribbon, Hystrix, Sleuth) are absent from new deployments.
* Kubernetes-native capabilities are consistently used for infrastructure concerns.
* Service resilience objectives meet defined SLOs.
* Configuration management is fully externalized and version-controlled.
* Distributed tracing is implemented across all critical services.

# ADR-014 — PostgreSQL Selection

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-014
**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-07-30
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)
**Approvers:** CTO, Chief Architect, Chief Data Architect, VP Engineering

---

# 1. Executive Summary

This Architecture Decision Record (ADR) establishes **PostgreSQL** as the enterprise-standard relational database management system (RDBMS) for the Mediverse Enterprise Healthcare Platform.

Mediverse requires a highly reliable, ACID-compliant, cloud-native relational database capable of supporting:

* Electronic Health Records (EHR)
* Learning Management
* Hospital Information Systems
* Medical Billing
* Appointment Scheduling
* Pharmacy
* Laboratory
* Clinical Decision Support
* AI Metadata Storage
* Regulatory Audit Logs

After evaluating multiple enterprise database platforms, PostgreSQL has been selected because of its maturity, standards compliance, extensibility, reliability, cloud-native support, and strong ecosystem.

---

# 2. Decision Statement

## Decision

PostgreSQL shall be the **primary transactional relational database** for all Mediverse backend services requiring relational persistence.

Each microservice shall:

* Own its own PostgreSQL database/schema.
* Never directly access another service's database.
* Expose data only through APIs or events.
* Follow enterprise schema governance.
* Use PostgreSQL features according to platform standards.

---

# 3. Business Context

The Mediverse platform manages:

* Patient Information
* Medical Education Records
* Faculty Data
* Clinical Data
* Laboratory Results
* Pharmacy Inventory
* Appointments
* Hospital Operations
* Examination Systems
* Payments
* Audit Logs

These workloads require:

* Strong consistency
* Reliable transactions
* Regulatory compliance
* High availability
* Disaster recovery
* Horizontal scalability at the application layer

---

# 4. Problem Statement

Selecting an unsuitable relational database could lead to:

* Data inconsistency.
* Poor transaction handling.
* Vendor lock-in.
* Expensive licensing.
* Limited scalability.
* Operational challenges.
* Reduced interoperability.
* Higher maintenance costs.

A standardized enterprise RDBMS is therefore required.

---

# 5. Decision Drivers

The decision is based on:

* ACID compliance
* Reliability
* Performance
* SQL standards compliance
* Open-source ecosystem
* High availability
* JSON support
* Extensibility
* Security
* Cloud-native compatibility
* Long-term sustainability

---

# 6. Considered Alternatives

---

## Alternative A — PostgreSQL

### Advantages

* Full ACID compliance
* Advanced indexing
* JSONB support
* Rich SQL features
* Partitioning
* MVCC
* Logical replication
* Strong community
* Open source
* Extensive extensions

### Disadvantages

* Requires tuning for very large deployments.
* More operational expertise than embedded databases.

**Decision:** ✅ Accepted

---

## Alternative B — MySQL

### Advantages

* Mature
* Large community
* High performance
* Easy administration

### Disadvantages

* Less advanced SQL capabilities.
* Weaker JSON functionality.
* Fewer enterprise analytical features.

**Decision:** Rejected.

---

## Alternative C — MariaDB

### Advantages

* Open source
* MySQL compatible
* Good performance

### Disadvantages

* Smaller enterprise ecosystem.
* Less advanced feature set than PostgreSQL.

**Decision:** Rejected.

---

## Alternative D — Oracle Database

### Advantages

* Enterprise maturity
* Advanced clustering
* Comprehensive feature set

### Disadvantages

* High licensing cost.
* Vendor lock-in.
* Operational complexity.

**Decision:** Rejected.

---

## Alternative E — Microsoft SQL Server

### Advantages

* Enterprise tooling
* Strong BI ecosystem
* Mature platform

### Disadvantages

* Licensing costs.
* Less alignment with Linux-first cloud-native environments.

**Decision:** Rejected.

---

# 7. Comparative Analysis

| Criteria          | PostgreSQL | MySQL | MariaDB | Oracle | SQL Server |
| ----------------- | :--------: | :---: | :-----: | :----: | :--------: |
| ACID Compliance   |    ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐   |  ⭐⭐⭐⭐ |   ⭐⭐⭐⭐  |  ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |    ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐   |
| SQL Standards     |    ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐   |  ⭐⭐⭐  |   ⭐⭐⭐   |  ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |    ⭐⭐⭐⭐    |
| JSON Support      |    ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐   |  ⭐⭐⭐  |   ⭐⭐⭐   |  ⭐⭐⭐⭐  |    ⭐⭐⭐⭐    |
| Cloud Native      |    ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐   |  ⭐⭐⭐⭐ |   ⭐⭐⭐⭐  |   ⭐⭐⭐  |    ⭐⭐⭐⭐    |
| High Availability |    ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐   |  ⭐⭐⭐⭐ |   ⭐⭐⭐⭐  |  ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |    ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐   |
| Licensing         |    ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐   | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |  ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐  |    ⭐   |     ⭐⭐     |
| Ecosystem         |    ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐   | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |   ⭐⭐⭐⭐  |  ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |    ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐   |

---

# 8. Why PostgreSQL?

PostgreSQL provides capabilities aligned with Mediverse's long-term architecture:

* ACID transactions
* Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC)
* JSONB support
* Rich indexing
* Declarative partitioning
* Window functions
* Materialized views
* Full-text search
* Logical replication
* Extensive extension ecosystem

These features support transactional integrity, analytical queries, and scalable cloud-native deployments.

---

# 9. Enterprise Database Standards

All PostgreSQL deployments shall follow these standards:

| Component       | Standard              |
| --------------- | --------------------- |
| Database        | PostgreSQL            |
| ORM             | Hibernate/JPA         |
| Migration       | Flyway                |
| Connection Pool | HikariCP              |
| Backup          | Automated             |
| Replication     | Streaming Replication |
| Monitoring      | PostgreSQL Exporter   |
| Security        | TLS Enabled           |

Database versions shall be standardized and centrally governed.

---

# 10. Data Modeling Standards

Database design shall adhere to:

* Third Normal Form (3NF) by default.
* Controlled denormalization only for performance-critical scenarios.
* UUID primary keys where appropriate.
* Foreign keys within service boundaries.
* Explicit constraints.
* Consistent naming conventions.
* Audit columns on business tables.
* Soft delete only when business or regulatory requirements justify it.

---

# 11. Schema Governance

Each microservice:

* Owns its schema.
* Controls schema evolution.
* Uses version-controlled migrations.
* Never performs cross-service joins.
* Publishes business events for data synchronization.

Schema changes shall be backward compatible whenever possible.

---

# 12. Performance Strategy

Approved optimization techniques include:

* B-tree indexes
* Hash indexes (where justified)
* GIN indexes for JSONB
* BRIN indexes for large append-only tables
* Declarative partitioning
* Materialized views
* Query optimization
* Prepared statements
* Connection pooling
* Read replicas for reporting

Performance tuning shall be evidence-based and guided by production metrics.

---

# 13. High Availability Strategy

```text
                Application
                     │
                     ▼
             PostgreSQL Primary
                     │
        ┌────────────┴────────────┐
        ▼                         ▼
 Read Replica 1            Read Replica 2
        │                         │
        └────────────┬────────────┘
                     ▼
               Backup Storage
```

High availability features:

* Streaming replication
* Automatic failover
* Read replicas
* Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR)
* Continuous archiving
* Regular backup validation

---

# 14. Backup and Disaster Recovery

The platform shall implement:

* Daily full backups.
* Continuous WAL archiving.
* Point-in-Time Recovery.
* Cross-region backup replication.
* Periodic restore testing.
* Documented recovery procedures.

Recovery objectives shall align with platform RPO/RTO requirements.

---

# 15. Security Considerations

PostgreSQL deployments shall support:

* TLS encryption.
* Role-Based Access Control.
* Least-privilege access.
* Database auditing.
* Secrets management.
* Encrypted backups.
* Row-Level Security (where appropriate).
* Password rotation.
* Database activity monitoring.

Direct database access shall be restricted to authorized services and administrators.

---

# 16. Operational Considerations

Database operations shall include:

* Automated provisioning.
* Infrastructure as Code.
* Schema migration automation.
* Capacity planning.
* Performance monitoring.
* Query analysis.
* Vacuum management.
* Backup monitoring.
* Replication health checks.

---

# 17. Risks and Mitigations

| Risk                   | Mitigation                                                    |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Poor query performance | Index tuning, execution plan analysis, and query optimization |
| Schema drift           | Version-controlled Flyway migrations and automated validation |
| Storage growth         | Partitioning, retention policies, and capacity planning       |
| Replication lag        | Monitor replica health and scale infrastructure appropriately |
| Backup failure         | Automated verification and scheduled restore testing          |

---

# 18. Consequences

## Positive Consequences

* Strong transactional integrity.
* Mature ecosystem.
* Cloud-native compatibility.
* Rich SQL capabilities.
* Excellent extensibility.
* Cost-effective open-source platform.
* Long-term sustainability.

## Negative Consequences

* Requires operational expertise.
* Periodic tuning for high-volume workloads.
* Replication architecture introduces operational complexity.

These trade-offs are appropriate for an enterprise healthcare platform.

---

# 19. Impact Analysis

## Business Impact

* Lower licensing costs.
* Reliable transactional platform.
* Improved regulatory readiness.
* Long-term vendor independence.

## Technical Impact

* Consistent relational persistence.
* Standardized schema management.
* High-performance transactional processing.

## Operational Impact

* Predictable maintenance.
* Reliable backup and recovery.
* Mature monitoring ecosystem.

---

# 20. Compliance Considerations

PostgreSQL supports Mediverse's compliance objectives with appropriate implementation practices for:

* HIPAA
* GDPR
* HL7
* FHIR
* ISO/IEC 27001
* SOC 2
* OWASP ASVS
* NIST Cybersecurity Framework

Compliance is achieved through secure configuration, auditing, encryption, access controls, and operational governance.

---

# 21. Success Metrics

This ADR will be considered successful when:

* All relational services adopt PostgreSQL.
* Database schemas are managed exclusively through approved migration tools.
* Backup and recovery objectives consistently meet defined RPO/RTO targets.
* Replication health and availability remain within established SLOs.
* Query performance meets application latency requirements.
* Security and audit controls pass compliance assessments.

# ADR-015 — Redis Selection

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-015
**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-07-30
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)
**Approvers:** CTO, Chief Architect, Chief Data Architect, VP Engineering

---

# 1. Executive Summary

This Architecture Decision Record (ADR) establishes **Redis** as the enterprise-standard in-memory data platform for the Mediverse Enterprise Healthcare Platform.

Redis provides ultra-low latency access to frequently used data and supports multiple enterprise use cases beyond caching, including:

* Distributed caching
* Session management
* Distributed locking
* Rate limiting
* Pub/Sub messaging
* Leaderboards
* Token storage
* Temporary workflow state
* Job queues
* Real-time notifications

Redis complements PostgreSQL rather than replacing it. PostgreSQL remains the system of record, while Redis accelerates read-heavy workloads and supports transient application state.

---

# 2. Decision Statement

## Decision

Redis shall be adopted as the enterprise in-memory data platform.

Redis shall be used for:

* Application caching
* Distributed cache
* Session storage
* Rate limiting
* Distributed locks
* Temporary tokens
* Pub/Sub events
* High-speed lookup data

Redis shall **not** be used as the primary persistent database for critical business data.

---

# 3. Business Context

The Mediverse platform serves:

* Millions of API requests
* Student dashboards
* Faculty portals
* Patient portals
* AI recommendation engines
* Real-time notifications
* Authentication services
* Search suggestions
* Frequently accessed reference data

These workloads require response times measured in milliseconds while reducing load on transactional databases.

---

# 4. Problem Statement

Without an enterprise caching layer:

* Database load increases.
* API latency rises.
* Infrastructure costs grow.
* User experience degrades.
* Authentication services become slower.
* Rate limiting becomes difficult.
* Temporary state is inefficiently stored in relational databases.

A dedicated in-memory platform is therefore required.

---

# 5. Decision Drivers

The decision is based on:

* Low latency
* High throughput
* Scalability
* Reliability
* Cloud-native support
* Operational maturity
* Rich data structures
* Distributed capabilities
* Enterprise adoption
* Open-source ecosystem

---

# 6. Considered Alternatives

---

## Alternative A — Redis

### Advantages

* Extremely fast
* Mature ecosystem
* Rich data structures
* Distributed caching
* Pub/Sub
* Cluster support
* Replication
* High availability
* Large community
* Kubernetes support

### Disadvantages

* Memory-intensive
* Limited persistence compared to relational databases
* Requires memory capacity planning

**Decision:** ✅ Accepted

---

## Alternative B — Memcached

### Advantages

* Simple
* Fast
* Lightweight

### Disadvantages

* Limited data structures
* No persistence
* Limited enterprise features
* No Pub/Sub
* No distributed locking

**Decision:** Rejected.

---

## Alternative C — Hazelcast

### Advantages

* Distributed computing
* In-memory grid
* Java integration

### Disadvantages

* Greater operational complexity
* Smaller ecosystem
* Less community adoption

**Decision:** Rejected.

---

## Alternative D — PostgreSQL Only

### Advantages

* Single technology
* Simplified architecture

### Disadvantages

* Higher database load
* Slower response times
* Poor caching capabilities
* Increased infrastructure costs

**Decision:** Rejected.

---

# 7. Comparative Analysis

| Criteria             | Redis | Memcached | Hazelcast | PostgreSQL |
| -------------------- | :---: | :-------: | :-------: | :--------: |
| Performance          | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |   ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐   |    ⭐⭐⭐⭐   |     ⭐⭐⭐    |
| Rich Data Structures | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |     ⭐⭐    |    ⭐⭐⭐⭐   |     ⭐⭐⭐    |
| Persistence          |  ⭐⭐⭐⭐ |     ⭐     |    ⭐⭐⭐    |    ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐   |
| Pub/Sub              | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |     ⭐     |    ⭐⭐⭐⭐   |      ⭐     |
| Distributed Locking  | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |     ⭐     |    ⭐⭐⭐⭐   |     ⭐⭐     |
| Enterprise Adoption  | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |    ⭐⭐⭐    |    ⭐⭐⭐    |    ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐   |
| Kubernetes Support   | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ |    ⭐⭐⭐⭐   |    ⭐⭐⭐    |    ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐   |

---

# 8. Enterprise Redis Use Cases

Redis shall be used for:

### Performance

* API response caching
* Database query caching
* Search result caching
* Frequently accessed reference data

### Authentication

* Session storage
* JWT blacklist
* OAuth temporary state
* Login attempt tracking

### Distributed Systems

* Distributed locks
* Leader election
* Rate limiting
* Idempotency keys

### Real-Time Features

* Notification queues
* Pub/Sub
* Presence information
* Live dashboards

---

# 9. Data Structures

Approved Redis data structures:

| Structure   | Enterprise Use            |
| ----------- | ------------------------- |
| String      | Cache, Tokens             |
| Hash        | User Sessions             |
| List        | Queues                    |
| Set         | Permissions               |
| Sorted Set  | Rankings, Priority Queues |
| Stream      | Event Streams             |
| Bitmap      | Analytics                 |
| HyperLogLog | Approximate Counting      |
| Geo         | Location Services         |

---

# 10. Cache Strategy

The enterprise caching strategy shall include:

```text
Client
   │
   ▼
Redis Cache
   │
 ┌─┴─────────────┐
 │ Cache Hit     │
 ▼               ▼
Response      PostgreSQL
                  │
                  ▼
            Update Cache
```

Cache access pattern:

1. Read Redis.
2. If cache hit → return immediately.
3. If cache miss → query PostgreSQL.
4. Store result in Redis.
5. Return response.

---

# 11. Cache Patterns

Approved caching patterns:

### Cache-Aside

Recommended for most services.

### Read-Through

Allowed for framework-supported integrations.

### Write-Through

Used for selected high-consistency scenarios.

### Write-Behind

Requires architecture approval due to eventual consistency implications.

---

# 12. Cache Expiration Policy

TTL guidelines:

| Data Type             | Recommended TTL                |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| User Sessions         | 30–60 minutes                  |
| Authentication Tokens | Token lifetime                 |
| Reference Data        | 24 hours                       |
| Dashboard Data        | 5–15 minutes                   |
| Search Results        | 5–30 minutes                   |
| Feature Flags         | 5 minutes                      |
| API Responses         | Based on business requirements |

All cached data must define an explicit expiration policy unless there is a documented justification.

---

# 13. High Availability Architecture

```text
                Redis Sentinel
                     │
        ┌────────────┴────────────┐
        ▼                         ▼
   Redis Primary           Redis Replica
        │                         │
        └────────────┬────────────┘
                     ▼
              Kubernetes Cluster
```

Enterprise deployment shall support:

* Replication
* Automatic failover
* Sentinel or Redis Cluster
* Backup
* Monitoring
* Scaling

Deployment mode shall be selected based on workload characteristics.

---

# 14. Persistence Strategy

Redis persistence options:

* RDB Snapshots
* Append Only File (AOF)
* Hybrid Persistence

Mission-critical transient state requiring recovery shall use AOF or hybrid persistence as appropriate.

Persistent business records shall remain in PostgreSQL.

---

# 15. Security Considerations

Redis deployments shall implement:

* TLS encryption
* Authentication (ACLs)
* Network isolation
* Kubernetes Network Policies
* Secret management
* Role-based access
* Encrypted backups
* Audit logging where applicable

Direct internet exposure is prohibited.

---

# 16. Operational Considerations

Platform operations shall include:

* Memory monitoring
* Eviction monitoring
* Replication health
* Cache hit ratio analysis
* Slow command monitoring
* Backup verification
* Capacity planning
* Version management

---

# 17. Risks and Mitigations

| Risk                | Mitigation                                                            |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Memory exhaustion   | Capacity planning, monitoring, and appropriate eviction policies      |
| Cache inconsistency | TTL policies, cache invalidation strategies, and event-driven updates |
| Redis outage        | High availability deployment with failover                            |
| Cache stampede      | Request coalescing, staggered TTLs, and distributed locking           |
| Security exposure   | Private networking, ACLs, TLS, and secret rotation                    |

---

# 18. Consequences

## Positive Consequences

* Reduced database load.
* Faster response times.
* Improved scalability.
* Better user experience.
* Efficient distributed coordination.
* Enhanced support for real-time features.

## Negative Consequences

* Additional infrastructure.
* Cache invalidation complexity.
* Memory cost.
* Operational monitoring requirements.

These trade-offs are justified by the performance and scalability improvements.

---

# 19. Impact Analysis

## Business Impact

* Faster application responsiveness.
* Reduced infrastructure costs through database offloading.
* Improved customer satisfaction.

## Technical Impact

* Standardized caching strategy.
* High-performance data access.
* Consistent distributed coordination mechanisms.

## Operational Impact

* Additional monitoring responsibilities.
* Capacity planning for memory resources.
* High availability management.

---

# 20. Compliance Considerations

Redis supports Mediverse's compliance objectives when configured according to enterprise standards, including:

* HIPAA
* GDPR
* HL7
* FHIR
* ISO/IEC 27001
* SOC 2
* NIST Cybersecurity Framework

Sensitive data stored in Redis shall be minimized, encrypted where appropriate, and governed by defined retention policies.

---

# 21. Success Metrics

This ADR will be considered successful when:

* Cache hit ratios meet or exceed defined service objectives.
* Database read load is significantly reduced for cacheable workloads.
* Redis availability meets platform SLOs.
* Authentication and session management achieve target latency.
* Cache-related incidents remain within acceptable operational thresholds.
* Memory utilization remains within planned capacity limits.

# ADR-016 — Elasticsearch Adoption

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-016
**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-08-01
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)
**Approvers:** CTO, Chief Architect, Chief Data Architect, VP Engineering

> **Sequence correction:** In the original 150-ADR chapter list, **ADR-016 is Elasticsearch Adoption**. Apache Kafka is **ADR-026**. We should keep the canonical numbering rather than allowing the document sequence to drift.

---

# 1. Executive Summary

This Architecture Decision Record establishes **Elasticsearch** as Mediverse's strategic search and indexing technology for use cases requiring capabilities that PostgreSQL alone should not be expected to provide efficiently at enterprise scale.

Mediverse will contain large volumes of searchable information across medical education, healthcare, research, administration, and operational domains.

Representative search workloads include:

* Course and learning-content search
* Medical knowledge search
* Student/faculty directory search
* Patient search where legally and operationally appropriate
* Clinical document discovery
* Research publication search
* Administrative search
* Autocomplete and suggestions
* Faceted filtering
* Relevance-ranked search
* Large-scale text retrieval

Elasticsearch shall operate primarily as a **derived search/read model**, not as Mediverse's transactional system of record.

For authoritative transactional data, PostgreSQL remains the primary relational platform established by ADR-014.

---

# 2. Decision Statement

## Decision

Mediverse shall adopt **Elasticsearch** for advanced search, indexing, and retrieval workloads where justified by measurable requirements.

The standard data responsibility shall be:

```text
PostgreSQL
    │
    │ Authoritative business state
    ▼
Domain / Integration Events
    │
    ▼
Indexing Pipeline
    │
    ▼
Elasticsearch
    │
    ▼
Search APIs
```

Elasticsearch shall **not automatically be introduced into every microservice**.

Services with simple lookup requirements should continue using PostgreSQL.

---

# 3. Architectural Position

The platform data technologies now have clearly separated responsibilities:

| Technology     | Primary Responsibility                       |
| -------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| PostgreSQL     | Transactional system of record               |
| Redis          | Cache and transient high-speed state         |
| Elasticsearch  | Search and retrieval projections             |
| Object Storage | Files and large binary objects               |
| Kafka          | Event streaming and asynchronous integration |

This separation prevents Elasticsearch from becoming an accidental primary database.

---

# 4. Business Context

Mediverse requires sophisticated discovery capabilities across multiple domains.

## Medical Education

Users may search:

* Courses
* Chapters
* Lectures
* Faculty
* Learning resources
* Question banks
* Clinical cases
* Anatomy resources
* Medical terminology

## Healthcare

Authorized users may need to locate:

* Patients
* Appointments
* Clinical documents
* Healthcare providers
* Facilities
* Laboratory records
* Medical resources

## Research

Researchers may search:

* Publications
* Research projects
* Authors
* Medical topics
* Keywords
* Study metadata

These workloads involve more than primary-key or exact-value database lookups.

---

# 5. Problem Statement

Using PostgreSQL for every search requirement would eventually create several problems.

Complex full-text queries can compete with transactional workloads.

Search requirements may require:

* Relevance scoring
* Typo tolerance
* Tokenization
* Autocomplete
* Synonyms
* Faceted navigation
* Complex filtering
* Language-aware analysis
* Highlighting
* Search-specific denormalization

Embedding all of this directly into transactional persistence would increase coupling between operational and search workloads.

A dedicated search architecture is therefore justified.

---

# 6. Decision Drivers

Primary drivers are:

* Search performance
* Full-text search
* Horizontal scalability
* Relevance ranking
* Complex filtering
* Faceted search
* Search analytics
* Near-real-time indexing
* Flexible document models
* Distributed search
* Operational maturity

---

# 7. Considered Alternatives

## Alternative A — PostgreSQL Full-Text Search

### Advantages

* No additional infrastructure
* Strong consistency
* Lower operational complexity
* Excellent for moderate workloads
* Existing PostgreSQL expertise

### Disadvantages

* Search and transactional workloads compete for resources
* Less specialized search functionality
* More difficult to scale search independently

### Decision

**Accepted for simple/moderate search requirements.**

This is important: Elasticsearch should not be deployed merely because a service contains a search box.

---

## Alternative B — Elasticsearch

### Advantages

* Distributed full-text search
* Relevance scoring
* Advanced analyzers
* Faceted search
* Aggregations
* Autocomplete
* Highlighting
* Horizontal scaling
* Near-real-time indexing

### Disadvantages

* Additional infrastructure
* Eventual consistency
* Index lifecycle management
* Cluster operational complexity
* Data synchronization requirements

### Decision

**Accepted for advanced search workloads.**

---

## Alternative C — OpenSearch

OpenSearch provides a technically credible alternative with distributed search, analytics, aggregations, and broad Elasticsearch heritage.

### Advantages

* Open-source ecosystem
* Distributed architecture
* Strong search capabilities
* Cloud deployment options

### Disadvantages

* Creates an additional strategic platform choice
* Requires independent compatibility and operational evaluation

### Decision

**Not selected as the initial Mediverse standard.**

It remains a candidate if licensing, hosting, vendor strategy, or platform requirements change.

---

# 8. Comparative Decision

| Requirement               | PostgreSQL FTS | Elasticsearch | OpenSearch |
| ------------------------- | :------------: | :-----------: | :--------: |
| Transactional consistency |      ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐     |       ⭐⭐      |     ⭐⭐     |
| Full-text search          |      ⭐⭐⭐⭐      |     ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐     |    ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐   |
| Relevance ranking         |       ⭐⭐⭐      |     ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐     |    ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐   |
| Faceted search            |       ⭐⭐⭐      |     ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐     |    ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐   |
| Autocomplete              |       ⭐⭐⭐      |     ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐     |    ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐   |
| Search scalability        |       ⭐⭐⭐      |     ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐     |    ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐   |
| Operational simplicity    |      ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐     |      ⭐⭐⭐      |     ⭐⭐⭐    |
| Transactional storage     |      ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐     |       ⭐⭐      |     ⭐⭐     |
| Search-focused analytics  |       ⭐⭐⭐      |     ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐     |    ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐   |

Therefore:

**PostgreSQL owns truth. Elasticsearch owns optimized search projections.**

---

# 9. Search Architecture

A typical Mediverse search workflow shall follow:

```text
                    ┌─────────────────┐
                    │   PostgreSQL    │
                    │ System of Record│
                    └────────┬────────┘
                             │
                       Business Change
                             │
                             ▼
                    ┌─────────────────┐
                    │ Transactional   │
                    │     Outbox      │
                    └────────┬────────┘
                             │
                             ▼
                    Event Streaming
                             │
                             ▼
                    ┌─────────────────┐
                    │ Search Indexer  │
                    └────────┬────────┘
                             │
                             ▼
                    ┌─────────────────┐
                    │ Elasticsearch   │
                    └────────┬────────┘
                             │
                             ▼
                       Search API
                             │
                             ▼
                     Web / Mobile UI
```

This architecture keeps transactional persistence independent from search infrastructure.

---

# 10. Indexing Strategy

Indexes shall be designed around **search use cases**, not copied mechanically from relational database schemas.

For example, PostgreSQL may contain:

```text
course
faculty
specialization
department
institution
```

The Elasticsearch representation may intentionally create a denormalized search document:

```json
{
  "courseId": "MED-1001",
  "title": "Human Physiology",
  "description": "Foundations of human physiology",
  "faculty": {
    "name": "Faculty Name",
    "specialization": "Physiology"
  },
  "department": "Physiology",
  "level": "MBBS",
  "tags": [
    "physiology",
    "medicine"
  ]
}
```

Search projections may therefore differ substantially from domain aggregates.

---

# 11. Index Ownership

Every Elasticsearch index must have an explicit owning bounded context.

Examples:

```text
education-course-search
education-question-search

clinical-provider-search
clinical-document-search

research-publication-search
```

Teams must not create undocumented shared enterprise indexes.

Cross-domain search should be implemented through deliberate aggregation/search services rather than uncontrolled index sharing.

---

# 12. Synchronization Strategy

Mediverse shall prefer **event-driven indexing**.

Example:

```text
Course Updated
      │
      ▼
CourseUpdatedEvent
      │
      ▼
Kafka
      │
      ▼
Search Projection Consumer
      │
      ▼
Elasticsearch
```

This deliberately introduces eventual consistency between PostgreSQL and Elasticsearch.

---

# 13. Transactional Outbox

A dangerous implementation would be:

```text
Application
   ├── Save PostgreSQL
   └── Update Elasticsearch
```

If PostgreSQL succeeds and Elasticsearch fails, the systems diverge.

Instead:

```text
Transaction
     │
     ├── Business Data
     └── Outbox Event
             │
           COMMIT
             │
             ▼
           Kafka
             │
             ▼
      Elasticsearch Indexer
```

This provides significantly more reliable synchronization.

---

# 14. Consistency Model

Search data shall generally use:

**Eventual Consistency**

Example:

```text
Course Updated
     │
     ▼
PostgreSQL
     │
     │  short synchronization delay
     ▼
Elasticsearch
```

Search results may therefore temporarily lag behind authoritative transactional data.

Business operations requiring immediate authoritative state must query the owning service/system of record rather than trusting a search projection.

---

# 15. Search API Boundary

Clients should generally **not communicate directly with Elasticsearch**.

Use:

```text
React / Mobile
      │
      ▼
API Gateway
      │
      ▼
Search Service
      │
      ▼
Elasticsearch
```

The Search Service controls:

* Authorization
* Query construction
* Filtering
* Data exposure
* Result transformation
* Pagination
* Search analytics

This prevents infrastructure implementation details from leaking into clients.

---

# 16. Query Capabilities

Approved capabilities include:

* Full-text search
* Exact matching
* Boolean queries
* Range queries
* Prefix search
* Fuzzy matching
* Autocomplete
* Synonym matching
* Faceted filtering
* Highlighting
* Aggregations
* Geo queries where justified

Search features should be introduced based on product requirements rather than enabled indiscriminately.

---

# 17. Mapping Standards

Fields must use explicit mappings for production indexes.

Common types include:

```text
keyword
text
date
boolean
integer
long
double
geo_point
object
nested
```

For example:

```json
{
  "properties": {
    "courseId": {
      "type": "keyword"
    },
    "title": {
      "type": "text"
    },
    "department": {
      "type": "keyword"
    },
    "createdAt": {
      "type": "date"
    }
  }
}
```

Uncontrolled dynamic mappings should be avoided for critical production indexes.

---

# 18. `text` vs `keyword`

This distinction must be understood by engineering teams.

### `text`

Used for analyzed full-text content:

```text
"Introduction to Human Physiology"
```

Suitable for:

* Search
* Relevance
* Tokenization

### `keyword`

Used for exact values:

```text
"PHYSIOLOGY"
```

Suitable for:

* Filtering
* Aggregations
* Sorting
* Exact matches

Incorrect mapping choices can significantly damage search correctness and performance.

---

# 19. Index Versioning

Breaking mapping changes shall not mutate critical production indexes recklessly.

Use versioned indexes:

```text
courses-v1
courses-v2
courses-v3
```

with aliases:

```text
courses-search
       │
       ▼
courses-v3
```

Migration:

```text
courses-v2
     │
     ▼
Reindex
     │
     ▼
courses-v3
     │
     ▼
Switch Alias
```

This supports safer zero/low-downtime index evolution.

---

# 20. Reindexing

Mediverse must assume that indexes will occasionally need complete rebuilding.

Sources for reconstruction may include:

* PostgreSQL
* Authoritative APIs
* Event streams
* Historical events where available

An Elasticsearch index must therefore never become the **only surviving copy of critical business information**.

---

# 21. Pagination

Simple pagination may use:

```text
from + size
```

Deep pagination should avoid extremely large offsets.

For large result traversal, prefer mechanisms such as:

* `search_after`
* Point-in-Time search where appropriate

Search APIs shall define maximum result-window policies.

---

# 22. Healthcare Data Security

Search creates a particularly important security problem.

An Elasticsearch index can unintentionally create a broad, denormalized copy of sensitive information.

Therefore:

* PHI/PII must be minimized.
* Only searchable fields should be indexed.
* Sensitive fields require explicit justification.
* Authorization must occur before returning results.
* Search indexes must never become a mechanism for bypassing domain authorization.

For example, a physician being able to search for a patient's name does **not automatically mean they are authorized to view the patient's clinical record**.

Searchability and authorization are separate concerns.

---

# 23. Encryption and Access Control

Production deployments shall enforce:

* TLS
* Authentication
* Role-based access
* Network isolation
* Least privilege
* Secret rotation
* Audit logging
* Encryption at rest where required

Elasticsearch must never be publicly exposed directly to the Internet.

---

# 24. Kubernetes Deployment

Where self-managed deployment is justified:

```text
Kubernetes
   │
   ├── Elasticsearch Nodes
   │      ├── Node 1
   │      ├── Node 2
   │      └── Node 3
   │
   ├── Persistent Volumes
   ├── Services
   ├── Network Policies
   └── Monitoring
```

However, running a stateful distributed search cluster is operationally expensive.

Managed Elasticsearch should be evaluated where it reduces operational risk and satisfies security, residency, cost, and compliance requirements.

---

# 25. High Availability

Production architecture must eliminate single-node dependency.

The deployment strategy shall consider:

* Multiple nodes
* Replica shards
* Failure domains
* Cluster quorum
* Persistent storage
* Snapshot recovery
* Capacity headroom

Cluster topology shall be workload-driven rather than based on a fixed node count.

---

# 26. Backup and Recovery

Elasticsearch snapshots shall be stored outside the cluster.

Recovery procedures must support:

* Index restoration
* Cluster recovery
* Accidental deletion recovery
* Corrupted index recovery
* Disaster recovery

But because Elasticsearch is primarily a derived store, Mediverse must also maintain the ability to rebuild indexes from authoritative systems.

---

# 27. Observability

Required monitoring includes:

* Cluster health
* Node health
* JVM heap
* CPU
* Disk usage
* Search latency
* Indexing latency
* Query rate
* Indexing rate
* Rejected operations
* Shard allocation
* Failed queries
* Cache behavior

Dashboards and alerts shall be integrated into the enterprise observability platform.

---

# 28. Performance Engineering

Search performance depends heavily on:

* Mapping design
* Query design
* Shard strategy
* Document size
* Heap pressure
* Index size
* Aggregation complexity
* Refresh frequency
* Hardware/storage characteristics

Teams shall load-test realistic search workloads before production release.

---

# 29. Anti-Patterns

The following practices are prohibited:

❌ Elasticsearch as the default primary database

❌ Direct frontend → Elasticsearch communication

❌ Indexing every database field automatically

❌ Storing unnecessary PHI/PII

❌ Cross-service ownership of indexes without governance

❌ Assuming Elasticsearch is strongly consistent

❌ Treating Elasticsearch backup as the only copy of business data

❌ Creating an index per user/tenant without demonstrated architectural justification

❌ Unlimited deep pagination

❌ Using Elasticsearch when PostgreSQL search is already sufficient

---

# 30. Risks and Mitigations

| Risk                       | Mitigation                                      |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| Search index becomes stale | Event-driven synchronization and reconciliation |
| Data loss                  | Snapshots + rebuild from authoritative source   |
| PHI leakage                | Data minimization and authorization controls    |
| Mapping explosion          | Explicit mapping governance                     |
| Excessive shard count      | Capacity and shard governance                   |
| Expensive queries          | Query limits and performance testing            |
| Cluster instability        | Monitoring, capacity headroom, HA               |
| Infrastructure complexity  | Managed service evaluation                      |
| Search/database divergence | Outbox + event processing + reconciliation      |

---

# 31. Consequences

## Positive

* Powerful full-text search
* Fast discovery experience
* Independent search scaling
* Better relevance
* Advanced filtering
* Rich aggregations
* Search-specific denormalization
* Reduced transactional database pressure

## Negative

* Additional distributed infrastructure
* Eventual consistency
* Index synchronization complexity
* Operational cost
* Additional security surface
* Requires specialized expertise

Elasticsearch should therefore be introduced only when its capabilities justify this complexity.

---

# 32. Success Metrics

Success shall be evaluated through:

* Search p95/p99 latency
* Search availability
* Indexing latency
* Index freshness
* Query failure rate
* Search relevance quality
* Zero unauthorized search-data exposure
* Successful disaster-recovery tests
* Successful full index reconstruction
* Stable cluster resource utilization

Business-oriented search metrics should additionally measure:

* Search success rate
* Zero-result rate
* Query refinement rate
* Click-through rate

---
