## **ADR-031 — Kubernetes Container Orchestration & Cluster Architecture**

This is the logical next decision. ADR-030 gives Mediverse deployable immutable containers; ADR-031 must define **how those containers actually run, scale, recover, communicate, receive configuration, and survive failures in production**.

ADR-031 should go deep into:

**Kubernetes selection → managed vs self-managed Kubernetes → cluster topology → DEV/UAT/PROD separation → namespace strategy → control plane → worker nodes → node pools → Deployment vs StatefulSet vs DaemonSet vs Job vs CronJob → Pods → Services → ClusterIP/LoadBalancer → DNS → Ingress/Gateway relationship → labels/annotations → selectors → ConfigMaps → Secrets → External Secrets → requests/limits → QoS → JVM container sizing → probes → startup/readiness/liveness → graceful shutdown → replicas → rolling updates → ReplicaSets → HPA → VPA → Cluster Autoscaler → PodDisruptionBudget → topology spread → anti-affinity → node affinity → taints/tolerations → persistent volumes → StorageClass → CSI → StatefulSets → securityContext → RBAC → ServiceAccounts → NetworkPolicy → Pod Security Standards → admission control → image verification → namespaces → quotas → LimitRanges → Secrets encryption → workload identity → mTLS direction → DNS/service discovery → CoreDNS → Jobs → migrations → init containers → sidecars → ephemeral containers → observability → metrics-server → Prometheus → logs → OpenTelemetry → Kubernetes events → failure diagnosis → CrashLoopBackOff → OOMKilled → Pending → ImagePullBackOff → 502/503 scenarios → HA → multi-AZ topology → backup/DR → etcd considerations → GitOps → Argo CD boundary → Helm boundary → Terraform boundary → upgrade strategy → version skew → cluster security → supply-chain enforcement → cost controls → production hardening.**


# Architecture Decision Records (ADR)

---

---

# Part III — Cloud Infrastructure & Deployment Architecture

# ADR-031 — Kubernetes Container Orchestration & Cluster Architecture

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-031
**Status:** Accepted
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)

Mediverse shall adopt **Kubernetes as the standard container orchestration platform** for production-grade application workloads.

ADR-030 established OCI containers as the deployable artifact. ADR-031 establishes how those containers are **scheduled, networked, configured, secured, scaled, upgraded, observed, and recovered**.

> **Containers define the deployable artifact. Kubernetes defines how Mediverse operates those artifacts reliably at scale.**

```text
                         MEDIVERSE
                             │
                             ▼
                    OCI Container Images
                             │
                             ▼
                 ┌─────────────────────┐
                 │     KUBERNETES      │
                 └──────────┬──────────┘
                            │
          ┌─────────────────┼──────────────────┐
          ▼                 ▼                  ▼
       Scheduling        Networking          Storage
          │                 │                  │
          ▼                 ▼                  ▼
       Scaling           Security         Persistence
          │                 │                  │
          └─────────────────┼──────────────────┘
                            ▼
                      Observability
                            │
                            ▼
                       Resilience
```

---

## 1. Problem

Running Mediverse containers manually would eventually require us to build our own orchestration system.

We would need to solve:

```text
Container scheduling
Service discovery
Load balancing
Health checking
Restarting failed workloads
Rolling deployments
Configuration
Secrets
Storage
Autoscaling
Node failures
Network isolation
RBAC
Resource allocation
Observability
High availability
```

That is infrastructure engineering Kubernetes already provides.

---

# 2. Decision

Mediverse shall standardize on:

```text
OCI Containers
      │
      ▼
Kubernetes
      │
      ├── Workload orchestration
      ├── Service discovery
      ├── Configuration
      ├── Secret delivery
      ├── Networking
      ├── Scaling
      ├── Health management
      ├── Storage orchestration
      └── Security controls
```

Kubernetes becomes the primary runtime platform for containerized Mediverse services.

---

# 3. Alternatives Considered

| Technology                       | Decision                   |
| -------------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| Kubernetes                       | ✅ Selected                 |
| Docker Compose production        | ❌ Rejected                 |
| Docker Swarm                     | ❌ Rejected                 |
| Nomad                            | 🟡 Viable but not selected |
| VM-based deployment              | ❌ Rejected                 |
| Raw container runtime management | ❌ Rejected                 |
| Serverless-only architecture     | ❌ Rejected                 |

---

# 4. Managed vs Self-Managed Kubernetes

For production, Mediverse should strongly prefer **managed Kubernetes** when deployed to a major cloud provider.

Examples include managed Kubernetes offerings from AWS, Azure and Google Cloud.

Self-managing the control plane adds responsibility for:

```text
etcd
API server
scheduler
controller manager
control-plane upgrades
control-plane HA
certificates
backups
recovery
```

Unless Mediverse has a concrete reason to own those concerns, that is unnecessary operational burden.

---

# 5. Cluster Environment Strategy

Production isolation should not depend solely on namespaces.

Preferred direction:

```text
DEV
 │
 └── Development Cluster

UAT
 │
 └── UAT / Pre-production Cluster

PROD
 │
 └── Production Cluster
```

At minimum, production should have a strong cluster/account/project isolation boundary from development.

---

# 6. Why Not One Giant Cluster?

A single cluster containing:

```text
dev
uat
prod
```

looks cheaper initially.

It also increases blast radius.

A cluster-level failure, CNI problem, admission-policy mistake, administrator error or upgrade issue could affect every environment.

Namespaces are useful isolation mechanisms.

They are not equivalent to independent infrastructure.

---

# 7. Namespace Strategy

Inside an environment, namespaces provide organizational and security boundaries.

Possible structure:

```text
mediverse-system
mediverse-platform
mediverse-apps
mediverse-observability
mediverse-security
```

For larger environments, workload/domain-specific namespaces may be introduced.

---

# 8. Namespace Per Microservice?

Creating:

```text
content-service
assessment-service
learning-service
notification-service
...
```

as separate namespaces for every tiny service is not automatically good architecture.

Namespace boundaries should reflect meaningful:

```text
Ownership
Security
Resource quotas
Operational isolation
Lifecycle
```

not simply service count.

---

# 9. Kubernetes Control Plane

Conceptually:

```text
                  CONTROL PLANE

             ┌──────────────────┐
             │    API Server    │
             └────────┬─────────┘
                      │
       ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
       ▼              ▼              ▼
   Scheduler      Controllers       etcd
```

Application teams interact primarily through the Kubernetes API.

---

# 10. Worker Nodes

Application workloads execute on worker nodes.

```text
Cluster
   │
   ├── Worker Node A
   │      ├── Pod
   │      ├── Pod
   │      └── Pod
   │
   ├── Worker Node B
   │      ├── Pod
   │      └── Pod
   │
   └── Worker Node C
          ├── Pod
          └── Pod
```

Pods must not be designed around permanent attachment to one node.

---

# 11. Node Pools

Different workloads may justify different node pools.

Example:

```text
General Services
      │
      ▼
General Node Pool

Memory-heavy Search
      │
      ▼
Memory-optimized Pool

AI/GPU Workloads
      │
      ▼
GPU Node Pool
```

Do not run expensive GPU nodes for ordinary REST APIs.

---

# 12. Pod

The Pod is Kubernetes's basic workload scheduling unit.

```text
Pod
 │
 └── Container
```

or occasionally:

```text
Pod
 ├── Application container
 └── tightly coupled sidecar
```

---

# 13. Pods Are Ephemeral

A Pod is not a server.

```text
Pod A
 │
 X deleted
 │
 ▼
Pod B
```

may replace it with:

```text
Different IP
Different Node
Fresh filesystem
```

Application architecture must assume this.

---

# 14. Deployment

Most Mediverse stateless services shall use:

```text
Deployment
```

Example:

```text
Content Deployment
       │
       ▼
   ReplicaSet
       │
   ┌───┼───┐
   ▼   ▼   ▼
 Pod Pod Pod
```

---

# 15. ReplicaSet

Deployments manage ReplicaSets.

Application teams should normally manage Deployments rather than manually creating ReplicaSets.

---

# 16. Desired State

Kubernetes operates around desired state.

```text
Desired replicas = 3
Actual replicas  = 2
        │
        ▼
Kubernetes creates another Pod
```

This reconciliation model is fundamental.

---

# 17. StatefulSet

StatefulSet is intended for workloads requiring stable identities/storage semantics.

```text
database-0
database-1
database-2
```

It should not be used merely because an application writes some temporary files.

---

# 18. Managed Stateful Services

Production databases should generally favor managed services where infrastructure strategy permits.

Running:

```text
PostgreSQL
Kafka
Elasticsearch
```

inside Kubernetes creates substantial operational responsibilities.

Kubernetes can run them.

That does not mean Mediverse should automatically operate them itself.

---

# 19. DaemonSet

DaemonSets run workloads across selected nodes.

Typical infrastructure uses:

```text
Log collector
Security agent
Node monitoring agent
```

Ordinary Mediverse microservices should not use DaemonSets.

---

# 20. Job

Jobs represent bounded work.

Examples:

```text
Data migration
Batch import
One-time processing
Maintenance operation
```

---

# 21. CronJob

Recurring scheduled work may use CronJobs.

Example:

```text
Nightly cleanup
Periodic report
Scheduled synchronization
```

But critical business scheduling may require stronger workflow guarantees than a simple CronJob.

---

# 22. Init Containers

Init containers perform prerequisite work before the main application starts.

```text
Pod
 │
 ├── Init Container
 │       │
 │       ▼
 │     complete
 │
 └── Application
```

They should not become arbitrary startup scripts containing large amounts of business logic.

---

# 23. Database Migrations

Do not let every replica independently race to perform dangerous schema migrations.

Bad:

```text
Pod 1 ─┐
Pod 2 ─┼──► ALTER DATABASE
Pod 3 ─┘
```

Database migration orchestration requires explicit release design.

---

# 24. Sidecars

Sidecars are appropriate when lifecycle and resource coupling genuinely justify sharing a Pod.

Do not introduce sidecars because the pattern is fashionable.

Every sidecar adds:

```text
CPU
Memory
Startup dependency
Failure modes
Upgrade complexity
```

---

# 25. Ephemeral Containers

Ephemeral containers may assist production debugging without permanently adding troubleshooting tools to minimal application images.

This complements ADR-030's minimal-image strategy.

---

# 26. Service

Pods receive ephemeral IP addresses.

Kubernetes Services provide stable discovery.

```text
Client
   │
   ▼
content-service
   │
   ├── Pod A
   ├── Pod B
   └── Pod C
```

---

# 27. ClusterIP

Internal Mediverse services should generally use:

```text
ClusterIP
```

rather than exposing every service externally.

---

# 28. LoadBalancer

`LoadBalancer` should be used when an infrastructure component genuinely requires direct external load-balancer exposure.

It should not be the default for every microservice.

---

# 29. NodePort

Direct NodePort exposure is generally not the preferred production public API architecture.

Ingress/Gateway infrastructure should provide controlled entry.

---

# 30. Service Discovery

Inside Kubernetes:

```text
assessment-service
```

can be resolved through Kubernetes DNS.

Applications should rely on service names rather than Pod IPs.

---

# 31. CoreDNS

CoreDNS provides cluster DNS services.

DNS problems can manifest as widespread application failures even while Pods themselves appear healthy.

Therefore DNS is critical infrastructure.

---

# 32. Never Hardcode Pod IPs

Bad:

```text
http://10.244.3.17:8080
```

Pod IPs are ephemeral.

Use:

```text
http://assessment-service
```

through service discovery.

---

# 33. Gateway Relationship

ADR-029 established:

```text
Internet
   │
   ▼
Ingress
   │
   ▼
Spring Cloud Gateway
   │
   ▼
Kubernetes Services
```

The Kubernetes Service layer remains separate from the application Gateway.

---

# 34. Ingress

Ingress provides controlled HTTP(S) entry into the cluster.

Exact implementation may vary by infrastructure provider.

Ingress should not contain Mediverse business logic.

---

# 35. Gateway API Direction

Kubernetes Gateway API may increasingly provide richer infrastructure traffic management.

Mediverse should avoid unnecessary coupling to legacy Ingress-specific assumptions where future Gateway API adoption is beneficial.

---

# 36. Labels

Labels are fundamental Kubernetes metadata.

Example:

```yaml
app.kubernetes.io/name: content-service
app.kubernetes.io/part-of: mediverse
app.kubernetes.io/component: backend
```

Consistent labels enable:

```text
Selectors
Policies
Observability
Cost allocation
Automation
```

---

# 37. Label Governance

Do not allow every team to invent arbitrary naming conventions.

Mediverse should establish standard Kubernetes labels.

---

# 38. Selectors

Services and workload controllers rely heavily on selectors.

A bad selector can route traffic to the wrong Pods.

Selector changes therefore require care.

---

# 39. Annotations

Annotations may carry non-identifying operational metadata for:

```text
Ingress configuration
Monitoring
GitOps
Secrets integration
Service mesh
```

They should not become an uncontrolled database.

---

# 40. ConfigMaps

Non-sensitive runtime configuration may be stored in ConfigMaps.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
ConfigMap
```

Examples:

```text
Feature configuration
Service URLs
Non-secret limits
Logging configuration
```

---

# 41. Secrets

Sensitive configuration belongs in Kubernetes Secrets or, preferably for stronger production governance, integration with an external secrets-management platform.

---

# 42. Kubernetes Secret Reality

A Kubernetes Secret is not magically secure simply because its resource type is called `Secret`.

Base64 encoding:

```text
password → cGFzc3dvcmQ=
```

is encoding, not encryption.

---

# 43. Secrets Encryption

Production clusters should enable appropriate encryption of Kubernetes secret data at rest where supported.

---

# 44. External Secrets

Preferred production direction:

```text
Vault / Cloud Secret Manager
          │
          ▼
External Secrets Integration
          │
          ▼
Kubernetes Workload
```

rather than storing long-lived production secrets directly in Git.

---

# 45. Secrets in Git

Plaintext production secrets shall not be committed into:

```text
values.yaml
deployment.yaml
application.yml
GitOps repository
```

---

# 46. Secret Rotation

Applications should support credential rotation without rebuilding images.

ADR-030 already establishes externalized runtime configuration.

---

# 47. Resource Requests

Every production Pod should have intentional resource requests.

Example:

```yaml
requests:
  cpu: ...
  memory: ...
```

Requests influence scheduling.

---

# 48. Resource Limits

Limits define resource boundaries.

Memory limits are especially important for preventing one workload from consuming uncontrolled node memory.

---

# 49. Requests Are Not Limits

```text
request
```

means approximately:

> "Reserve/schedule me based on this amount."

```text
limit
```

means:

> "Do not allow me beyond this boundary."

They solve different problems.

---

# 50. CPU Units

Kubernetes CPU:

```text
1000m = 1 CPU
500m  = 0.5 CPU
100m  = 0.1 CPU
```

CPU values should be based on workload measurements.

---

# 51. Memory Units

Memory configuration should be explicit and consistent.

Java services must leave sufficient headroom beyond JVM heap, as ADR-030 established.

---

# 52. JVM Container Sizing

Example:

```text
Pod memory limit
       │
       ├── Java Heap
       ├── Metaspace
       ├── Direct Memory
       ├── Thread Stacks
       ├── Native Memory
       └── JVM Runtime
```

Do not configure heap equal to Pod memory limit.

---

# 53. QoS Classes

Kubernetes derives Pod QoS behavior from resource configuration.

Conceptually:

```text
Guaranteed
Burstable
BestEffort
```

Production critical workloads should not accidentally become BestEffort due to missing resource definitions.

---

# 54. OOMKilled

If a process exceeds its cgroup/container memory boundary:

```text
Pod
 │
 ▼
OOMKilled
```

may occur.

Troubleshooting must inspect:

```text
kubectl describe pod
container status
events
resource limits
JVM metrics
```

rather than assuming an application exception.

---

# 55. CPU Throttling

A Pod can experience poor latency even without high average CPU if CPU limits cause aggressive throttling.

Resource tuning must consider latency, not merely utilization.

---

# 56. ResourceQuota

Namespaces should use ResourceQuota where appropriate to prevent one team/workload from consuming unlimited cluster resources.

---

# 57. LimitRange

LimitRanges may establish namespace defaults and boundaries for:

```text
CPU
Memory
Container resources
```

This prevents completely unbounded workloads.

---

# 58. Startup Probe

Startup probes protect slow-starting applications.

```text
Starting
   │
   ▼
Startup Probe
   │
   ▼
Ready for normal health checks
```

---

# 59. Readiness Probe

Readiness determines whether a Pod receives service traffic.

```text
Pod Running
    │
    ├── Ready     → traffic
    └── Not Ready → no traffic
```

A running Pod is not necessarily ready.

---

# 60. Liveness Probe

Liveness determines whether Kubernetes should restart a stuck application.

It must not fail merely because an external dependency is temporarily unavailable.

---

# 61. Probe Anti-Pattern

Bad:

```text
PostgreSQL down
      │
      ▼
Every Pod liveness fails
      │
      ▼
Every Pod restarts
```

This amplifies the outage.

---

# 62. Spring Boot Actuator

Spring Boot Actuator health groups should support appropriate Kubernetes probe semantics.

The application must distinguish:

```text
Alive
Ready
```

rather than exposing one simplistic health endpoint for everything.

---

# 63. Graceful Termination

Kubernetes termination flow:

```text
Pod selected for termination
          │
          ▼
SIGTERM
          │
          ▼
Stop accepting new work
          │
          ▼
Drain requests
          │
          ▼
Terminate
```

Spring Boot shutdown behavior and Kubernetes termination grace period must align.

---

# 64. Rolling Updates

Deployments should normally use rolling updates.

```text
Version 1 Pods
      │
      ▼
Gradually replaced
      │
      ▼
Version 2 Pods
```

This reduces deployment downtime.

---

# 65. `maxUnavailable`

Rolling update strategy should limit how many replicas can be unavailable simultaneously.

Critical services require conservative values.

---

# 66. `maxSurge`

Kubernetes may temporarily create additional Pods during deployment.

Cluster capacity planning must account for surge.

---

# 67. Zero-Downtime Is Not Automatic

Simply using:

```text
strategy: RollingUpdate
```

does not guarantee zero downtime.

You also need:

```text
Multiple replicas
Correct readiness
Graceful shutdown
Compatible versions
Sufficient capacity
```

---

# 68. Replicas

Critical stateless production services should normally have more than one replica.

```text
replicas: 1
```

creates a workload-level availability weakness.

---

# 69. Horizontal Pod Autoscaler

HPA may scale workloads based on observed metrics.

```text
Load increases
     │
     ▼
HPA
     │
     ▼
Replica count increases
```

---

# 70. CPU-Based HPA

CPU is useful but not universally sufficient.

For some workloads better signals may include:

```text
Request rate
Queue depth
Kafka lag
Latency
Active sessions
```

through custom/external metrics.

---

# 71. AI Autoscaling

AI workloads may require scaling based on:

```text
Queue depth
GPU utilization
Concurrent inference
Token workload
```

rather than ordinary CPU alone.

---

# 72. Kafka Consumer Scaling

Kafka consumers may scale according to consumer lag.

But replicas beyond available partitions do not automatically increase useful parallelism.

Application scaling must understand Kafka semantics.

---

# 73. Vertical Pod Autoscaler

VPA may recommend or adjust resource sizing.

It should be introduced carefully because resource changes may require Pod restarts.

---

# 74. HPA + VPA

Blindly allowing HPA and VPA to control the same resource dimension can create conflicting behavior.

Their responsibilities must be explicitly designed.

---

# 75. Node Autoscaling

When Pods cannot be scheduled because the cluster lacks capacity:

```text
Pending Pods
     │
     ▼
Node Autoscaler
     │
     ▼
Additional Node
```

where the infrastructure supports it.

---

# 76. Autoscaling Delay

Autoscaling is not instantaneous.

Applications must survive the period between:

```text
Traffic spike
```

and:

```text
New capacity ready
```

---

# 77. PodDisruptionBudget

PDBs protect availability during voluntary disruptions.

Example concept:

```text
At least 2 replicas available
```

during maintenance.

---

# 78. PDB Limitation

A PodDisruptionBudget does not protect against:

```text
Node crash
Application crash
Region failure
```

It primarily controls voluntary disruption behavior.

---

# 79. Pod Anti-Affinity

Critical replicas should avoid unnecessary concentration on the same node.

Bad:

```text
Node A
 ├── Gateway 1
 ├── Gateway 2
 └── Gateway 3
```

Node A failure then removes all replicas.

---

# 80. Topology Spread Constraints

Preferred:

```text
Zone A → replicas
Zone B → replicas
Zone C → replicas
```

where infrastructure provides multiple zones.

Topology spreading can improve availability without excessively rigid affinity rules.

---

# 81. Multi-AZ Architecture

Production workloads should distribute critical replicas across failure domains.

```text
                  Production Cluster

       Zone A          Zone B          Zone C
         │               │               │
         ▼               ▼               ▼
       Pods            Pods            Pods
```

---

# 82. Node Affinity

Node affinity can place workloads on appropriate node classes.

Example:

```text
AI workload
    │
    ▼
GPU nodes
```

---

# 83. Anti-Affinity

Anti-affinity can prevent certain workloads from being colocated.

Use it when failure isolation justifies the scheduling restriction.

---

# 84. Taints and Tolerations

Dedicated nodes may use taints.

Example:

```text
GPU Node
  │
  └── taint: workload=ai
```

Only workloads with appropriate toleration can schedule there.

---

# 85. Taints Are Not Security

Taints/tolerations influence scheduling.

They are not a substitute for RBAC or NetworkPolicy.

---

# 86. PersistentVolume

PersistentVolume provides durable storage abstraction.

```text
Pod
 │
 ▼
PVC
 │
 ▼
PV
 │
 ▼
Storage Backend
```

---

# 87. PersistentVolumeClaim

Applications request storage through PVCs rather than hardcoding infrastructure-specific disks.

---

# 88. StorageClass

StorageClass defines storage provisioning characteristics.

Different workloads may require different:

```text
Performance
Durability
Replication
Cost
```

profiles.

---

# 89. CSI

Container Storage Interface drivers connect Kubernetes to storage providers.

Storage architecture should rely on supported CSI integrations.

---

# 90. Stateful Storage Warning

Running a database inside Kubernetes with a PVC does not magically make it highly available.

You still need:

```text
Replication
Backup
Failover
Recovery
Consistency
Monitoring
```

---

# 91. Object Storage

Large Mediverse content remains in object storage per ADR-017.

Do not use Kubernetes PVs as a replacement for scalable object storage for:

```text
Videos
3D models
Images
Large educational assets
```

---

# 92. ServiceAccount

Every workload should use an appropriate Kubernetes ServiceAccount.

Do not give every Pod unnecessary access to the Kubernetes API.

---

# 93. RBAC

Kubernetes RBAC controls access to Kubernetes resources.

```text
Subject
   │
   ▼
Role
   │
   ▼
Permission
```

---

# 94. Least Privilege

A content-service Pod normally does not need permission to:

```text
Delete namespaces
Read every Secret
Create cluster roles
Modify nodes
```

If it does not need Kubernetes API access, grant none.

---

# 95. Default ServiceAccount

Production workloads should not casually depend on an overprivileged default ServiceAccount.

Dedicated identities improve control and auditability.

---

# 96. ClusterRole

Cluster-wide permissions should be rare for ordinary applications.

Most application permissions, when required at all, should be namespace-scoped.

---

# 97. Human RBAC

Human access must also follow least privilege.

```text
Developer
Operator
Platform Engineer
Security Administrator
```

should not all receive unrestricted cluster-admin access.

---

# 98. Production Access

Routine production work should not require:

```text
kubectl as cluster-admin
```

for every engineer.

Privileged access should be exceptional and audited.

---

# 99. Workload Identity

Where cloud infrastructure supports workload identity:

```text
Kubernetes ServiceAccount
          │
          ▼
Cloud Identity
          │
          ▼
Object Storage / Secrets / Services
```

should be preferred over long-lived cloud credentials stored as Secrets.

---

# 100. NetworkPolicy

Default Kubernetes networking may allow broad Pod-to-Pod communication depending on the CNI.

Mediverse should implement NetworkPolicy.

---

# 101. Default-Deny Direction

A mature namespace should move toward:

```text
Default deny
     │
     ▼
Explicitly allow required traffic
```

rather than allowing every Pod to talk to everything.

---

# 102. Example Network Boundary

```text
Gateway
   │
   ├────► Content Service
   ├────► Assessment Service
   └────► Learning Service

Random Pod
   │
   X
Database
```

Network access should reflect architecture.

---

# 103. NetworkPolicy Limitation

NetworkPolicy does not replace application authentication.

A Pod being network-reachable does not mean the caller is authorized.

---

# 104. CNI

NetworkPolicy enforcement depends on the cluster networking implementation.

The selected CNI must support Mediverse's required security/networking features.

---

# 105. Pod Security

Production workloads should align with Kubernetes Pod Security Standards, targeting a restricted posture where feasible.

---

# 106. Security Context

ADR-030 established container requirements such as:

```text
runAsNonRoot
allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
readOnlyRootFilesystem
drop capabilities
```

Kubernetes manifests shall enforce these where practical.

---

# 107. Host Network

Application Pods should not use:

```text
hostNetwork: true
```

without explicit infrastructure justification.

---

# 108. Host PID/IPC

Ordinary application Pods should not access host PID or IPC namespaces.

---

# 109. HostPath

`hostPath` mounts create strong node coupling and security risk.

They should not be used by ordinary Mediverse application workloads.

---

# 110. Privileged Pods

Privileged containers are prohibited for ordinary Mediverse services.

Infrastructure components requiring elevated permissions require explicit security review.

---

# 111. Admission Control

Admission policies should progressively enforce standards before workloads enter the cluster.

Potential rules include:

```text
No privileged containers
Required resource requests
Approved registries
Non-root
Required labels
No production latest tags
```

---

# 112. Signed Image Enforcement

ADR-030 established image-signing direction.

Future admission policy may require:

```text
Unsigned/untrusted image
        │
        X

Approved image
        │
        ▼
Schedule
```

---

# 113. ImagePullPolicy

Production image references should be immutable.

Do not rely on `Always` plus mutable tags as a substitute for proper versioning.

---

# 114. Private Registry

Kubernetes shall pull Mediverse application images from approved registries.

Registry credentials should be managed securely or replaced by workload/platform-native identity where available.

---

# 115. ImagePullBackOff

Typical causes:

```text
Wrong image name
Wrong tag
Registry authentication
Registry unavailable
Network failure
Architecture mismatch
```

Troubleshooting starts with Pod events.

---

# 116. Pending Pods

A Pod in `Pending` may indicate:

```text
Insufficient CPU
Insufficient memory
PVC unavailable
Affinity conflict
Taint mismatch
Node selector mismatch
```

`Pending` does not necessarily mean Kubernetes is broken.

---

# 117. CrashLoopBackOff

Typical causes:

```text
Application crashes
Bad configuration
Missing Secret
Dependency failure
Wrong command
Probe failure
JVM startup failure
```

Use:

```text
kubectl describe pod
kubectl logs
kubectl logs --previous
```

as core diagnostic tools.

---

# 118. OOMKilled Diagnosis

Check:

```text
Container termination reason
Memory limit
JVM heap/native usage
Traffic/load
Recent deployment changes
```

before merely increasing memory.

Increasing limits without understanding the leak or sizing issue can hide the problem temporarily.

---

# 119. 502 Bad Gateway

A Kubernetes-hosted Mediverse application returning repeated `502` errors should be traced through:

```text
Client
  │
  ▼
Ingress
  │
  ▼
Gateway
  │
  ▼
Service
  │
  ▼
Endpoints
  │
  ▼
Pods
```

Likely categories include:

```text
No ready endpoints
Pod restarts
Gateway upstream timeout
Connection resets
Service selector mismatch
Resource exhaustion
Application crash
Ingress/Gateway configuration
```

---

# 120. 503 Service Unavailable

A 503 may indicate:

```text
No available backend
Circuit breaker
Overload
Readiness failure
Intentional temporary unavailability
```

The actual emitting layer must be identified before debugging.

---

# 121. Kubernetes Events

Events are critical troubleshooting evidence.

```text
kubectl get events
```

may reveal:

```text
FailedScheduling
BackOff
Unhealthy
FailedMount
FailedPull
Killing
Evicted
```

---

# 122. Metrics Server

Kubernetes resource metrics support features such as:

```text
kubectl top
HPA
```

through metrics infrastructure such as metrics-server.

This is not a full observability platform.

---

# 123. Prometheus

Application and Kubernetes metrics should feed Prometheus-compatible monitoring according to Mediverse's observability architecture.

---

# 124. Grafana

Grafana should visualize:

```text
Cluster health
Node resources
Pod health
Application SLIs
Gateway metrics
Kafka metrics
Database metrics
```

where appropriate.

---

# 125. Logs

Container logs should flow:

```text
stdout/stderr
      │
      ▼
Node logging agent
      │
      ▼
Central logging platform
```

Do not SSH into nodes to inspect application log files as the normal workflow.

---

# 126. Distributed Tracing

OpenTelemetry context established in ADR-029 should continue through Kubernetes-hosted services.

Kubernetes metadata may enrich telemetry.

---

# 127. Cardinality

Do not turn:

```text
pod UID
request ID
student ID
```

into uncontrolled Prometheus labels.

Observability architecture must control cardinality.

---

# 128. Alerting

Cluster alerts should focus on actionable conditions such as:

```text
Node unavailable
High restart rate
Pods unschedulable
OOMKilled spike
Disk pressure
API availability degradation
Critical workload unavailable
```

---

# 129. Node Failure

When a worker node fails:

```text
Node A
  X
Pods unavailable
      │
      ▼
Kubernetes reschedules workloads
      │
      ▼
Healthy Nodes
```

provided capacity and workload constraints permit it.

---

# 130. Node Capacity Headroom

A three-node cluster running every node at 95% capacity has little failure resilience.

If one node disappears, there may be nowhere to reschedule workloads.

Capacity planning must include failure headroom.

---

# 131. Zone Failure

Critical production architecture should consider losing an entire availability zone.

This requires more than simply having multiple Pods.

---

# 132. Region Failure

Multi-region architecture is substantially more complex than multi-AZ Kubernetes.

It affects:

```text
Databases
Kafka
Object storage
DNS
Identity
Traffic routing
Consistency
```

It should only be adopted when RTO/RPO/business requirements justify it.

---

# 133. Backup

Kubernetes manifests should already be reproducible through GitOps/IaC.

Backup should focus particularly on state not trivially reconstructable from Git.

---

# 134. etcd

For self-managed clusters, etcd backup and recovery are critical.

For managed Kubernetes, control-plane backup responsibilities depend on the provider.

Do not assume a managed control plane automatically backs up application persistent data.

---

# 135. Persistent Volume Backup

PVC-backed state requires explicit backup policy.

A Kubernetes Deployment YAML is not a backup of the data stored by the workload.

---

# 136. Disaster Recovery

DR must answer:

```text
Can we recreate cluster infrastructure?

Can we restore persistent data?

Can we restore secrets?

Can we restore DNS?

Can we restore identity?

Can applications reconnect?

How long will it take?
```

---

# 137. RPO and RTO

Infrastructure decisions should ultimately map to:

```text
RPO
→ acceptable data loss

RTO
→ acceptable recovery time
```

Without these, "high availability" remains vague.

---

# 138. Helm Boundary

Helm should package reusable Kubernetes application configuration.

```text
Application
   │
   ▼
Helm Chart
   │
   ▼
Kubernetes Resources
```

Helm does not provision the cloud network or Kubernetes cluster itself.

---

# 139. Terraform Boundary

Terraform should manage infrastructure such as:

```text
Network
Kubernetes cluster
Node pools
Cloud databases
Object storage
IAM
Load balancers where applicable
```

It should not become the primary application-release engine.

---

# 140. Argo CD Boundary

GitOps architecture:

```text
Git
 │
 ▼
Argo CD
 │
 ▼
Kubernetes
```

Argo CD should reconcile declared application state with cluster state.

---

# 141. CI vs CD

Preferred:

```text
CI
 │
 ├── Build
 ├── Test
 ├── Scan
 └── Publish image

GitOps
 │
 └── Deploy/reconcile
```

CI should not require unrestricted direct production-cluster credentials if GitOps can provide the deployment boundary.

---

# 142. Git as Desired State

Application deployment configuration should be declarative and version controlled.

```text
Git
 │
 ▼
Desired State
 │
 ▼
Argo CD
 │
 ▼
Actual Cluster State
```

---

# 143. Manual `kubectl` Production Changes

Emergency changes may occasionally be necessary.

But routine deployment by:

```text
kubectl edit deployment
```

creates configuration drift.

GitOps should restore Git as the authoritative desired state.

---

# 144. Helm + Argo CD

Preferred relationship:

```text
Helm
→ package/template

Git
→ desired configuration

Argo CD
→ reconciliation

Kubernetes
→ runtime
```

These tools complement rather than replace each other.

---

# 145. Terraform + Argo CD

```text
Terraform
    │
    ▼
Create Cluster
    │
    ▼
Install/Bootstrap Platform
    │
    ▼
Argo CD
    │
    ▼
Deploy Applications
```

Clear ownership prevents Terraform and Argo CD from fighting over the same resources.

---

# 146. Cluster Upgrades

Kubernetes must be upgraded regularly.

Ignoring upgrades indefinitely eventually creates:

```text
Unsupported cluster
Security vulnerabilities
Version incompatibility
Add-on incompatibility
Operational risk
```

---

# 147. Version Skew

Kubernetes components and clients have supported version-skew boundaries.

Upgrade planning must consider:

```text
Control plane
Worker nodes
kubectl
CNI
CSI
Ingress
Monitoring
Admission controllers
```

---

# 148. Upgrade Testing

Production cluster upgrades should first be validated in lower environments.

```text
DEV
 │
 ▼
UAT
 │
 ▼
PROD
```

Production should not be the first place compatibility is discovered.

---

# 149. Node Upgrade

Managed Kubernetes upgrades may replace or drain worker nodes.

Applications must therefore tolerate:

```text
Pod eviction
Rescheduling
Temporary capacity changes
```

This is another reason replicas, PDBs and graceful shutdown matter.

---

# 150. Kubernetes API Deprecation

Kubernetes APIs evolve.

Deprecated manifest API versions must be detected before cluster upgrades.

Old YAML that worked for years can eventually stop being accepted.

---

# 151. Cost Governance

Kubernetes does not automatically reduce infrastructure cost.

Poorly managed Kubernetes can be more expensive than simpler architectures.

Costs come from:

```text
Idle nodes
Oversized requests
Unused load balancers
Persistent disks
Observability
GPU nodes
Cross-zone traffic
Over-replication
```

---

# 152. Resource Right-Sizing

Requests should be adjusted from observed production-like data.

Bad:

```text
Every Java service:
CPU = 2
RAM = 4 GiB
```

simply because one service required it.

---

# 153. GPU Cost Isolation

GPU node pools should scale independently and remain unavailable to workloads that do not need them.

---

# 154. Namespace Cost Attribution

Standard labels/namespaces can support cost attribution by:

```text
Environment
Team
Application
Domain
```

---

# 155. Cluster Autoscaler Cost Risk

Autoscaling without workload limits can convert a runaway application into an automatically expanding cloud bill.

Autoscaling requires quotas and cost controls.

---

# 156. Security Layers

Kubernetes security should be layered:

```text
Cloud IAM
   │
   ▼
Kubernetes RBAC
   │
   ▼
Admission Policy
   │
   ▼
Pod Security
   │
   ▼
NetworkPolicy
   │
   ▼
Workload Identity
   │
   ▼
Application Authentication
   │
   ▼
Domain Authorization
```

No single layer is sufficient.

---

# 157. Cluster Admin

`cluster-admin` is effectively unrestricted cluster authority.

It should be tightly controlled, audited and reserved for justified platform operations.

---

# 158. Kubernetes API Exposure

The Kubernetes API server should not be casually exposed to the entire internet.

Network access, identity and audit controls must reflect its criticality.

---

# 159. Audit Logging

Production clusters should retain appropriate Kubernetes audit records where infrastructure supports them.

Sensitive data must still be protected.

---

# 160. Secret Access Audit

Access to high-value production Secrets should be auditable where possible.

A compromised Kubernetes identity capable of reading all Secrets can compromise much of the platform.

---

# 161. Service Mesh

A service mesh is **not selected by this ADR**.

Potential future capabilities:

```text
mTLS
Traffic policy
Service identity
Telemetry
Retries
```

do not automatically justify adding mesh complexity.

A separate ADR must evaluate it.

---

# 162. Istio Warning

Do not install Istio simply because the architecture uses microservices.

Service meshes add substantial:

```text
Operational complexity
Networking complexity
Resource overhead
Debugging complexity
Upgrade burden
```

There must be a concrete requirement.

---

# 163. Kubernetes Does Not Fix Bad Microservices

Kubernetes can reliably run a badly designed distributed system.

It cannot fix:

```text
Incorrect service boundaries
Chatty synchronous dependencies
Distributed transactions
Poor database design
Bad authorization
Memory leaks
Broken APIs
```

Application architecture remains responsible for those.

---

# 164. Production Hardening Baseline

Every production Mediverse workload should aim to define:

```text
Deployment strategy
Replica count
Resource requests
Resource limits
Startup probe
Readiness probe
Liveness probe
SecurityContext
ServiceAccount
NetworkPolicy
PDB where needed
Topology strategy
Configuration
Secrets
Observability
Graceful shutdown
```

A Deployment with only an image name is not production-ready.

---

# 165. Workload Contract

Each service should document:

```text
Image
Port
Configuration
Secrets
Dependencies
Resources
Health endpoints
Scaling behavior
Storage
Network requirements
Shutdown behavior
Availability requirement
```

This bridges application and platform engineering.

---

# 166. Failure Diagnosis Workflow

When a Mediverse service fails:

```text
1. Is the Pod running?
        │
        ▼
2. Is the Pod ready?
        │
        ▼
3. Is Service selecting the Pod?
        │
        ▼
4. Are endpoints present?
        │
        ▼
5. Can Gateway reach Service?
        │
        ▼
6. Is NetworkPolicy blocking?
        │
        ▼
7. Is application healthy?
        │
        ▼
8. Are dependencies healthy?
        │
        ▼
9. Are resources exhausted?
        │
        ▼
10. What do logs/traces/events show?
```

This systematic approach is far better than randomly restarting Pods.

---

# 167. Kubernetes Anti-Patterns

The following are prohibited or strongly discouraged:

❌ One replica for every critical production service

❌ Production mixed casually with DEV in one namespace

❌ Hardcoded Pod IPs

❌ Every service exposed through LoadBalancer

❌ Production `latest` images

❌ Secrets committed to Git

❌ Unlimited resource consumption

❌ Missing resource requests

❌ Heap equal to container memory limit

❌ Liveness tied to every external dependency

❌ Privileged application Pods

❌ Root containers without justification

❌ `hostNetwork` for ordinary applications

❌ `hostPath` for ordinary application storage

❌ Cluster-admin for routine development

❌ Default-allow networking forever

❌ Database PVC mistaken for database HA

❌ Manual production deployments as normal workflow

❌ StatefulSet used for ordinary stateless services

❌ HPA configured without understanding workload metrics

❌ Autoscaling without quotas/cost controls

❌ Installing service mesh without concrete need

❌ Treating Kubernetes as a substitute for application architecture

---

# 168. Risks and Mitigations

| Risk                   | Mitigation                           |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Cluster failure        | Environment isolation + HA           |
| Node failure           | Replicas + rescheduling              |
| Zone failure           | Topology spreading                   |
| Pod crash              | Deployment reconciliation            |
| OOMKilled              | Correct resource/JVM sizing          |
| Traffic during startup | Readiness/startup probes             |
| Deployment downtime    | Rolling update + replicas            |
| Secret exposure        | External secrets + encryption        |
| Lateral movement       | NetworkPolicy                        |
| Excessive privileges   | RBAC + ServiceAccounts               |
| Supply-chain attack    | Signed images + admission            |
| Capacity exhaustion    | HPA + node autoscaling               |
| Cost explosion         | Quotas + right-sizing                |
| Bad production changes | GitOps                               |
| Storage loss           | Backup + managed stateful services   |
| Upgrade failure        | Lower-env validation                 |
| Cluster drift          | IaC + GitOps                         |
| Gateway 502/503        | Probe/service/endpoint observability |

---

# 169. Consequences

### Positive

* Automated workload recovery
* Horizontal scaling
* Declarative deployments
* Strong service discovery
* Rolling upgrades
* Resource governance
* Standardized configuration
* Security-policy enforcement
* Multi-AZ workload placement
* GitOps compatibility
* Strong observability ecosystem
* Infrastructure portability

### Negative

* Significant operational complexity
* Requires dedicated Kubernetes expertise
* Networking failures become harder to diagnose
* Incorrect probes can cause outages
* Poor resource configuration causes instability
* Security configuration is non-trivial
* Kubernetes can be expensive when poorly managed
* Stateful workload operation remains difficult

---

# 170. Decision Outcome

| Attribute                       | Decision                                     |
| ------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| **ADR**                         | ADR-031                                      |
| **Orchestrator**                | Kubernetes                                   |
| **Production Direction**        | Managed Kubernetes preferred                 |
| **Application Workload**        | Deployment                                   |
| **Stateful Workload**           | StatefulSet only when justified              |
| **Internal Networking**         | ClusterIP                                    |
| **External Entry**              | Ingress → Spring Cloud Gateway               |
| **Service Discovery**           | Kubernetes DNS                               |
| **Configuration**               | ConfigMaps                                   |
| **Secrets**                     | External secrets preferred                   |
| **Autoscaling**                 | HPA + node autoscaling where justified       |
| **Availability**                | Multi-replica + topology distribution        |
| **Resource Governance**         | Requests + limits + quotas                   |
| **Security**                    | RBAC + PSS + NetworkPolicy + securityContext |
| **Identity**                    | Dedicated ServiceAccounts/workload identity  |
| **Deployment Model**            | Declarative GitOps                           |
| **Application Packaging**       | Helm                                         |
| **Infrastructure Provisioning** | Terraform                                    |
| **CD/Reconciliation**           | Argo CD                                      |
| **Production `latest`**         | Prohibited                                   |
| **Service Mesh**                | Deferred to separate ADR                     |
| **Status**                      | Accepted                                     |
| **Priority**                    | Critical                                     |
| **Risk Level**                  | Critical                                     |

---

```text
                              INTERNET

                                  ▼
                         CDN / WAF / DNS
                                  │
                                  ▼
                           Load Balancer
                                  │
                                  ▼

                                  │
                                  ▼
                     Spring Cloud Gateway
                                  │
                                  ▼
              ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐
              │                   │                   │

       Content Service     Learning Service    Assessment Service
              │                   │                   │

                                  │
```

# 172. Environment Architecture

```text
                         MEDIVERSE PLATFORM

          ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
          │              DEV                      │
          │                                       │
          │ Kubernetes Cluster                    │
          │ Lower-cost / developer workloads      │
          └───────────────────┬───────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
          ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
          │              UAT                      │
          │                                       │
          │ Kubernetes Cluster                    │
          │ Production-like validation            │
          └───────────────────┬───────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
          ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
          │             PRODUCTION                │
          │                                       │
          │ Managed Kubernetes                    │
          │ Multi-AZ                              │
          │ HA workloads                          │
          │ Strict RBAC                           │
          │ NetworkPolicy                         │
          │ Admission Controls                    │
          │ GitOps                                │
          └───────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

# 173. Deployment Architecture

```text
Developer
    │
    ▼
Git Repository
    │
    ▼
CI
    │
    ├── Test
    ├── Build
    ├── Scan
    ├── SBOM
    ├── Sign
    └── Push
    │
    ▼
Container Registry
    │
    ▼
GitOps Repository
    │
    ▼
Argo CD
    │
    ▼
Helm
    │
    ▼
Kubernetes API
    │
    ▼
Deployment
    │
    ▼
ReplicaSet
    │
 ┌──┼──┐
 ▼  ▼  ▼
Pod Pod Pod
```

The infrastructure underneath that flow remains:

```text
Terraform
    │
    ▼
Cloud Infrastructure
    │
    ├── Network
    ├── Kubernetes
    ├── Node Pools
    ├── IAM
    ├── Databases
    └── Storage
```

This prevents tool responsibility overlap.

---

# 174. Core Operational Rule

The most important Kubernetes rule for Mediverse is:

```text
                POD FAILED
                    │
                    ▼
             DO NOT PANIC
                    │
                    ▼
          Determine failure layer
                    │
     ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
     ▼              ▼              ▼
 Scheduling      Platform      Application
     │              │              │
     ▼              ▼              ▼
 Events          Network         Logs
 Resources       Storage         Traces
 Placement       DNS             Metrics
```

Random Pod restarts are not troubleshooting.

Kubernetes already restarts workloads. If the same Pod repeatedly fails, the useful question is **why it fails**.

## **ADR-032 — Helm Application Packaging & Kubernetes Configuration Architecture**

Kubernetes tells us **how workloads operate**. The next unresolved problem is how we manage hundreds of Kubernetes manifests without creating copy-pasted YAML chaos.

ADR-032 should establish:

**Helm selection → chart architecture → chart-per-service vs shared/library charts → parent/umbrella chart trade-offs → `Chart.yaml` → `values.yaml` → templates → helpers → naming conventions → labels → annotations → Deployment templates → Service → ConfigMap → Secret references → ServiceAccount → Ingress/Gateway integration → HPA → PDB → NetworkPolicy → probes → resources → securityContext → volumes → Jobs/CronJobs → hooks → why Helm hooks should be minimized → database migration strategy → environment-specific values → DEV/UAT/PROD overrides → secrets prohibition in values files → external secrets → image repository/tag/digest configuration → immutable artifact promotion → values schema validation → `helm lint` → `helm template` → unit testing → chart testing → semantic chart versioning → application versioning → chart registry → OCI Helm registries → dependencies → library charts → avoiding template overengineering → GitOps compatibility → Argo CD + Helm boundary → Helm release ownership → rollback limitations → CRDs → upgrade strategy → backward compatibility → chart documentation → governance and production standards.**
# Architecture Decision Records (ADR)

---

---

# ADR-032 — Helm Application Packaging & Kubernetes Configuration Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — OCI Helm Registry**.

---

# 61. Helm Linting

Every Mediverse Helm chart shall pass:

```bash
helm lint ./content-service
```

before being eligible for deployment.

Linting detects common problems including:

```text
Invalid Chart.yaml
Template syntax errors
Missing required metadata
Invalid chart structure
Dependency problems
```

Linting belongs in CI, not only on developer machines.

---

# 62. Template Rendering Validation

Charts shall be rendered during CI:

```bash
helm template mediverse-content ./content-service \
  -f values-prod.yaml
```

This catches failures before Argo CD attempts deployment.

```text
Helm Chart
    │
    ▼
helm template
    │
    ▼
Rendered Kubernetes YAML
    │
    ▼
Validation
```

---

# 63. Why Rendering Matters

A chart may pass basic linting but still generate incorrect Kubernetes resources because of particular values.

Therefore:

```text
helm lint
     ≠
Complete deployment validation
```

Both chart structure and rendered output must be tested.

---

# 64. Kubernetes Schema Validation

Rendered manifests should be checked against Kubernetes API schemas.

The pipeline should catch:

```text
Invalid API versions
Missing required fields
Wrong field types
Invalid resource structures
Deprecated resources
```

before production.

---

# 65. `values.schema.json`

Important charts should define a values schema.

```text
Chart
 │
 ├── Chart.yaml
 ├── values.yaml
 └── values.schema.json
```

This turns values from loosely structured configuration into a validated contract.

---

# 66. Values Validation

Suppose the chart expects:

```yaml
replicaCount: 3
```

and somebody provides:

```yaml
replicaCount: "three"
```

Schema validation should reject it before deployment.

---

# 67. Required Values

Critical configuration can be marked as required.

Examples include:

```text
Image repository
Application port
Service configuration
Required external endpoints
```

Do not silently deploy broken defaults for mandatory production settings.

---

# 68. Default Values

Defaults should be:

```text
Safe
Predictable
Non-secret
Environment-neutral where practical
```

A default should not accidentally point a development deployment at production infrastructure.

---

# 69. Production Defaults

Dangerous configuration should require explicit production values.

For example:

```text
Public exposure
Privileged capabilities
Persistent storage deletion
Debug mode
Administrative endpoints
```

should not accidentally become enabled.

---

# 70. Helm Unit Testing

Reusable chart logic should be unit-tested where complexity justifies it.

Tests may verify:

```text
Resource names
Labels
Replica count
Container image
Environment variables
Security context
Probes
Resources
Service configuration
```

---

# 71. Template Test Example

Conceptually:

```text
Given:
replicaCount = 3

Expect:
Deployment.spec.replicas = 3
```

Testing templates is particularly useful for shared library charts.

---

# 72. Chart Testing

CI should test chart installation in disposable Kubernetes environments where practical.

Possible environments include:

```text
kind
k3d
Ephemeral CI cluster
Dedicated integration cluster
```

This validates more than YAML syntax.

---

# 73. Installation Test

A meaningful chart test can verify:

```text
Chart installs
Pods start
Readiness succeeds
Service resolves
Application responds
Chart upgrades
Chart uninstalls
```

---

# 74. Upgrade Testing

Installation testing alone is insufficient.

Production systems usually perform:

```text
Version N
   │
   ▼
Upgrade
   │
   ▼
Version N+1
```

Therefore chart upgrade paths must also be tested.

---

# 75. Rollback Testing

Critical services should test rollback scenarios.

```text
v2
 │
 X deployment problem
 │
 ▼
v1
```

But rollback capability has limits.

---

# 76. Helm Rollback Limitation

`helm rollback` cannot automatically reverse:

```text
Database migrations
Kafka schema changes
External API changes
Object-storage transformations
Irreversible business data changes
```

Application rollback and data rollback are separate concerns.

---

# 77. Backward Compatibility

Deployments should favor backward-compatible changes.

For example:

```text
Database schema N
       │
       ├── Application N
       └── Application N+1
```

during rollout.

This supports safer rolling deployments.

---

# 78. Expand-and-Contract Migrations

For database changes, Mediverse should prefer patterns such as:

```text
Step 1
Add new schema

Step 2
Deploy compatible application

Step 3
Migrate usage/data

Step 4
Remove obsolete schema later
```

rather than immediately making destructive changes.

---

# 79. Helm Hooks

Helm supports lifecycle hooks such as:

```text
pre-install
post-install
pre-upgrade
post-upgrade
pre-delete
post-delete
```

These are powerful but must remain exceptional.

---

# 80. Why Minimize Hooks

Hooks introduce hidden lifecycle behavior.

```text
helm upgrade
     │
     ├── Hidden Job
     ├── Application deployment
     └── Cleanup behavior
```

In GitOps, hidden imperative behavior makes desired state harder to understand.

---

# 81. Migration Jobs

Database migrations should preferably use explicit Kubernetes Jobs or release workflows.

```text
Release
   │
   ▼
Migration Job
   │
   ▼
Migration succeeds
   │
   ▼
Application rollout
```

Failure must stop promotion.

---

# 82. Migration Ownership

A migration must have a clearly defined owner.

Do not allow:

```text
Gateway
Content Service
Assessment Service
Learning Service
```

to independently modify the same database schema without governance.

---

# 83. CRDs

Custom Resource Definitions require special treatment.

CRDs extend the Kubernetes API itself.

Examples may come from:

```text
Prometheus Operator
External Secrets
Argo CD
Cert Manager
Service Mesh
```

---

# 84. CRD Lifecycle

Application charts should not casually own shared platform CRDs.

Preferred separation:

```text
Platform Team
     │
     ▼
CRDs / Operators

Application Team
     │
     ▼
Custom Resources
```

---

# 85. Why Separate CRDs?

Removing one application must not accidentally remove a CRD used by twenty other applications.

Shared platform resources require independent lifecycle management.

---

# 86. Argo CD Ownership

ADR-031 established GitOps as the preferred deployment architecture.

Therefore:

```text
Git
 │
 ▼
Argo CD
 │
 ▼
Helm Rendering
 │
 ▼
Kubernetes
```

Argo CD owns reconciliation.

---

# 87. Helm CLI in Production

Routine production deployment should not be:

```bash
helm upgrade --install ...
```

from an engineer's laptop.

That bypasses GitOps governance.

---

# 88. Production Desired State

The authoritative production state should be represented in Git.

```text
Git Commit
     │
     ▼
Desired Configuration
     │
     ▼
Argo CD
```

not someone's terminal history.

---

# 89. Drift Detection

Suppose someone manually changes:

```text
replicas: 3
```

to:

```text
replicas: 10
```

directly in Kubernetes.

Argo CD should detect:

```text
Desired State ≠ Actual State
```

and report or reconcile the drift according to policy.

---

# 90. Self-Healing

For controlled resources, automatic reconciliation may restore Git-defined configuration.

```text
Manual Cluster Change
        │
        ▼
       Drift
        │
        ▼
     Argo CD
        │
        ▼
Desired State Restored
```

---

# 91. GitOps Repository

Application source and deployment configuration may use separate repositories when governance requires it.

Conceptually:

```text
Application Repository
      │
      └── Source

GitOps Repository
      │
      └── Deployment State
```

This provides a clean promotion boundary.

---

# 92. Environment Structure

Example:

```text
gitops/

├── dev/
│   └── mediverse/
│
├── uat/
│   └── mediverse/
│
└── prod/
    └── mediverse/
```

Exact repository structure may evolve, but environment ownership must remain explicit.

---

# 93. Promotion

Production promotion should modify the artifact reference.

```text
UAT
image digest = sha256:ABC
       │
       ▼
Approval
       │
       ▼
PROD
image digest = sha256:ABC
```

The application is not rebuilt.

---

# 94. Git-Based Approval

Production promotion should be reviewable.

Example:

```text
Pull Request
     │
     ▼
Review
     │
     ▼
Approval
     │
     ▼
Merge
     │
     ▼
Argo CD
```

This creates an auditable deployment trail.

---

# 95. CI Responsibility

CI should:

```text
Compile
Test
Build image
Scan
Generate SBOM
Sign
Publish image
Test chart
```

CI should not own continuous production reconciliation.

---

# 96. CD Responsibility

Argo CD should:

```text
Observe Git
Compare desired state
Render Helm configuration
Apply Kubernetes resources
Detect drift
Report synchronization health
```

This creates clear CI/CD separation.

---

# 97. Chart Repository

Released charts should be stored in an approved repository.

Preferred direction:

```text
OCI Registry
   │
   ├── Container Images
   └── Helm Charts
```

where organizational infrastructure supports it.

---

# 98. Chart Immutability

Published chart version:

```text
content-service-chart:2.4.1
```

must not later be replaced with different content.

Released versions are immutable.

---

# 99. Chart Versioning

Helm chart versions shall use semantic versioning.

```text
MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH
```

Examples:

```text
1.0.0
1.1.0
1.1.1
2.0.0
```

---

# 100. Chart Version vs Application Version

These are independent:

```text
Chart Version = 3.2.0

Application Version = 7.4.1
```

A chart can change without application code changing.

---

# 101. Chart Major Version

A major chart version should indicate incompatible packaging/configuration changes.

Example:

```text
values structure changed incompatibly
```

may justify:

```text
2.x → 3.x
```

---

# 102. Chart Minor Version

Backward-compatible chart capabilities generally increment MINOR.

Example:

```text
Added optional NetworkPolicy support
```

---

# 103. Chart Patch Version

Bug fixes that preserve compatibility generally increment PATCH.

Example:

```text
Corrected template annotation
```

---

# 104. `appVersion`

`appVersion` is informational metadata.

Deployment logic should not assume it automatically controls the container image.

Image configuration remains explicit.

---

# 105. Dependency Versioning

Chart dependencies must use controlled versions.

Avoid uncontrolled dependency ranges capable of unexpectedly changing production rendering.

---

# 106. Library Chart Versioning

Shared library charts require particularly careful compatibility management.

A breaking library-chart change can affect many services.

---

# 107. Dependency Blast Radius

Consider:

```text
Shared Library Chart
       │
       ├── 30 Spring Services
       ├── 5 Workers
       └── 4 AI Services
```

One bad change can affect dozens of workloads.

Shared abstraction increases leverage **and blast radius**.

---

# 108. Library Chart Governance

Changes to shared templates require:

```text
Code review
Automated tests
Compatibility analysis
Versioning
Controlled adoption
```

Services should not automatically consume untested latest library versions.

---

# 109. Avoid Universal Chart Syndrome

Do not build one chart containing switches such as:

```text
isJava
isReact
isKafkaConsumer
isAI
isCronJob
isFrontend
isGPU
isStateful
...
```

until the chart effectively becomes a programming framework.

That becomes harder to maintain than Kubernetes itself.

---

# 110. Appropriate Abstraction

Preferred:

```text
Small reusable library
       +
Service-specific chart
```

rather than:

```text
One enormous enterprise super-chart
```

---

# 111. Values Hierarchy

Configuration precedence must remain understandable.

Conceptually:

```text
Chart Defaults
      │
      ▼
Environment Values
      │
      ▼
Service-specific Overrides
```

Avoid ten layers of value files.

---

# 112. Values Documentation

Every important value should document:

```text
Purpose
Type
Default
Required/optional
Security implications
Example
```

Developers should not need to read template internals to understand configuration.

---

# 113. README

Each chart should provide documentation covering:

```text
Installation purpose
Supported configuration
Required dependencies
Values
Upgrade notes
Security requirements
Operational assumptions
```

---

# 114. Generated Values Documentation

Where practical, documentation should be generated or validated against the values schema to prevent documentation drift.

---

# 115. Environment Configuration

Example:

```text
values.yaml
      │
      ├── defaults
      │
values-dev.yaml
      │
      ├── development differences
      │
values-uat.yaml
      │
      ├── pre-production differences
      │
values-prod.yaml
      │
      └── production differences
```

---

# 116. Production Values

Production values typically control:

```text
Replica count
Resources
Autoscaling
Ingress
PDB
Topology
Security
Observability
External endpoints
```

but never plaintext credentials.

---

# 117. Secret Separation

Correct:

```text
values-prod.yaml
       │
       └── secretReference:
               databaseCredentials
```

Incorrect:

```text
values-prod.yaml
       │
       └── password: SuperSecret123
```

---

# 118. Configuration Duplication

If DEV/UAT/PROD values files are 95% identical, the configuration model is poorly structured.

Environment files should primarily express differences.

---

# 119. Feature Flags

Feature flags should not automatically require chart changes.

Dynamic application behavior belongs to the application/configuration architecture where possible.

---

# 120. Security Validation

CI should inspect rendered manifests for violations such as:

```text
Privileged containers
Root execution
Missing resource limits
HostPath
Host networking
Unapproved registry
latest image tag
Missing securityContext
```

---

# 121. Policy-as-Code

Production Helm output should eventually be validated using policy-as-code.

Conceptually:

```text
Helm
 │
 ▼
Rendered YAML
 │
 ▼
Policy Engine
 │
 ├── PASS → eligible
 │
 └── FAIL → pipeline blocked
```

---

# 122. Admission Control

CI policy prevents bad configuration from reaching Git/release.

Kubernetes admission control provides another boundary:

```text
CI Validation
      │
      ▼
GitOps
      │
      ▼
Admission Policy
      │
      ▼
Kubernetes
```

Defense in depth is intentional.

---

# 123. SecurityContext Defaults

Shared charts should default toward secure settings:

```text
runAsNonRoot: true
allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
```

and support read-only root filesystems where workloads permit them.

---

# 124. Privileged Mode

Charts shall not expose an easy:

```yaml
privileged: true
```

switch for ordinary application teams.

Exceptional requirements require security review.

---

# 125. HostPath

General application charts shall not support arbitrary hostPath mounting by default.

This creates node coupling and security risk.

---

# 126. Resource Requirements

Production chart validation should reject workloads without intentional resource configuration unless explicitly exempted.

Kubernetes cannot schedule and govern workloads intelligently if resource expectations are unknown.

---

# 127. Probe Requirements

Production HTTP services should normally define:

```text
startupProbe
readinessProbe
livenessProbe
```

according to ADR-031.

Templates can standardize structure, but application teams must define correct semantics.

---

# 128. Probe Anti-Pattern

A shared Helm chart cannot determine whether:

```text
/database/health
```

is appropriate for liveness.

Infrastructure templating cannot replace application-level health design.

---

# 129. Observability Configuration

Charts should support standardized:

```text
Metrics annotations/resources
OpenTelemetry configuration
Log metadata
ServiceMonitor where applicable
Tracing environment
```

without forcing every team to reinvent integration.

---

# 130. Deployment Metadata

Every workload should expose enough metadata to identify:

```text
Application
Version
Environment
Team
Git revision
Release
```

where practical.

This improves troubleshooting and auditability.

---

# 131. Deployment History

Git + Argo CD + Helm metadata should make it possible to determine:

```text
What changed?

Who approved it?

When was it deployed?

Which image?

Which chart?

Which configuration?
```

---

# 132. Production Rollback

Preferred GitOps rollback:

```text
Bad Git Change
      │
      ▼
Revert Commit
      │
      ▼
Argo CD
      │
      ▼
Previous Desired State
```

This keeps Git authoritative.

---

# 133. `helm rollback` in GitOps

Direct `helm rollback` may temporarily change cluster state without changing Git.

Argo CD may then restore the Git version.

Therefore direct Helm rollback is not the normal Mediverse GitOps rollback mechanism.

---

# 134. Emergency Changes

Emergency production fixes may require manual intervention.

Any emergency change must subsequently be reconciled back into Git.

Otherwise:

```text
Git ≠ Production
```

and the architecture has configuration drift.

---

# 135. Failed Deployment

Deployment failure should not trigger random manual modification.

Investigation should determine:

```text
Rendering failure?
Schema failure?
Admission failure?
Image failure?
Scheduling failure?
Probe failure?
Application failure?
Dependency failure?
```

---

# 136. Helm Debugging

Core commands during development may include:

```bash
helm lint

helm template

helm install --dry-run --debug
```

Production diagnosis should additionally use Kubernetes and Argo CD state.

---

# 137. Rendered Manifest Inspection

When Helm behavior is unclear, inspect the generated Kubernetes YAML.

Debug:

```text
Values
   │
   ▼
Helm Template
   │
   ▼
Rendered Manifest
```

Do not stare indefinitely at template syntax while ignoring what Kubernetes actually receives.

---

# 138. Chart Ownership

Every chart requires an identifiable owner.

Example:

```text
Chart
 │
 ├── Service Team
 │
 └── Platform Standards
```

Unowned deployment code deteriorates quickly.

---

# 139. Platform Team Responsibility

The platform team should own:

```text
Helm standards
Library charts
Security defaults
CI validation
Chart publishing infrastructure
GitOps integration
Documentation conventions
```

---

# 140. Application Team Responsibility

Application teams own:

```text
Application-specific configuration
Resource requirements
Health behavior
Scaling requirements
Dependencies
Service-specific templates
Upgrade compatibility
```

The platform team cannot guess application behavior correctly.

---

# 141. Production Chart Checklist

Every production service chart should be reviewed for:

```text
Chart metadata                 ✅
Versioning                     ✅
Values schema                  ✅
Deployment                     ✅
Service                        ✅
Resources                      ✅
Probes                         ✅
Security context               ✅
ServiceAccount                 ✅
Configuration                  ✅
Secret references              ✅
Autoscaling where required     ✅
PDB where required             ✅
NetworkPolicy                  ✅
Topology                       ✅
Observability                  ✅
Documentation                  ✅
Testing                        ✅
GitOps compatibility           ✅
```

---

# 142. Helm Anti-Patterns

Mediverse shall reject or strongly discourage:

❌ Separate chart for DEV/UAT/PROD

❌ Plaintext secrets in values files

❌ `latest` in production

❌ Manually running production Helm deployments as the standard process

❌ One giant chart for the entire platform

❌ Excessive conditional templating

❌ Environment logic buried inside templates

❌ Unversioned charts

❌ Mutable published chart versions

❌ Hardcoded resource settings

❌ Hardcoded namespaces

❌ Hardcoded environment URLs

❌ Privileged workloads by default

❌ Arbitrary hostPath support

❌ Database migrations hidden everywhere in Helm hooks

❌ CRDs casually owned by application charts

❌ Chart upgrades without testing

❌ Assuming Helm rollback reverses database changes

❌ Shared libraries without compatibility governance

❌ Ten-level values inheritance

❌ Treating Helm as an infrastructure provisioning tool

---

# 143. CI Validation Architecture

```text
Developer
    │
    ▼
Pull Request
    │
    ▼
┌─────────────────────────┐
│       CI PIPELINE       │
├─────────────────────────┤
│ helm lint               │
│ values schema validate  │
│ helm template           │
│ Kubernetes validation   │
│ policy validation       │
│ chart tests             │
│ upgrade tests           │
└────────────┬────────────┘
             │
          PASS
             │
             ▼
           Merge
             │
             ▼
      Publish Chart
```

A syntactically valid chart is not automatically production-ready.

---

# 144. GitOps Architecture

```text
                    APPLICATION SOURCE
                           │
                           ▼
                         CI
                           │
                  ┌────────┴────────┐
                  ▼                 ▼
             OCI Image         Helm Chart
                  │                 │
                  ▼                 ▼
              Registry         OCI Registry
                  │                 │
                  └────────┬────────┘
                           │
                           ▼
                    GitOps Repository
                           │
                    image/chart version
                           │
                           ▼
                        Argo CD
                           │
                           ▼
                    Helm Rendering
                           │
                           ▼
                    Kubernetes API
                           │
                           ▼
                       Workloads
```

---

# 145. Tool Responsibility Architecture

```text
                    MEDIVERSE DELIVERY

Terraform
    │
    ├── Network
    ├── Kubernetes Cluster
    ├── Node Pools
    ├── IAM
    ├── Databases
    └── Cloud Infrastructure
    │
    ▼
Infrastructure Ready


Helm
    │
    ├── Deployment
    ├── Service
    ├── ConfigMap
    ├── HPA
    ├── PDB
    ├── NetworkPolicy
    └── Application K8s Resources
    │
    ▼
Application Package


Git
    │
    ▼
Desired State
    │
    ▼
Argo CD
    │
    ▼
Reconciliation
    │
    ▼
Kubernetes
    │
    ▼
Runtime
```

The ownership boundary is deliberate:

> **Terraform builds the platform. Helm describes application packages. Git declares desired deployment state. Argo CD reconciles it. Kubernetes runs it.**

---

# 146. Risks and Mitigations

| Risk                      | Mitigation                     |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Template complexity       | Keep charts simple             |
| Configuration drift       | GitOps                         |
| Secret exposure           | External Secrets               |
| Broken templates          | Lint + rendering tests         |
| Invalid Kubernetes YAML   | Schema validation              |
| Unsafe manifests          | Policy-as-code                 |
| Breaking chart upgrades   | Semantic versioning            |
| Shared-chart blast radius | Controlled adoption            |
| Environment divergence    | Same chart everywhere          |
| Mutable releases          | Immutable chart versions       |
| Bad rollback assumptions  | Backward-compatible migrations |
| Manual PROD changes       | Argo CD reconciliation         |
| CRD lifecycle conflicts   | Platform ownership             |
| Configuration explosion   | Controlled values hierarchy    |
| Missing resources         | Production validation          |
| Unsafe defaults           | Secure chart defaults          |

---

# 147. Consequences

### Positive

Helm provides:

```text
Reusable Kubernetes packaging
Consistent deployment structure
Environment portability
Configuration standardization
Reduced YAML duplication
Semantic versioning
GitOps compatibility
Security standardization
Automated validation
Reusable platform conventions
```

### Negative

Helm introduces:

```text
Template complexity
Additional tooling
Values-management complexity
Potential over-abstraction
Chart-version governance
Debugging indirection
Shared-library blast radius
```

Helm does not remove Kubernetes complexity.

It organizes it.

---

# 148. Decision Outcome

| Attribute                        | Decision                         |
| -------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| **ADR**                          | ADR-032                          |
| **Technology**                   | Helm                             |
| **Purpose**                      | Kubernetes Application Packaging |
| **Chart Strategy**               | Service-oriented charts          |
| **Shared Logic**                 | Controlled library charts        |
| **Giant Umbrella Chart**         | Avoid                            |
| **Environment Strategy**         | Same chart + different values    |
| **DEV/ UAT/PROD Forked Charts**  | Prohibited                       |
| **Secrets in Values**            | Prohibited                       |
| **Secret Strategy**              | External secret references       |
| **Image Strategy**               | Immutable tag/digest             |
| **Chart Versioning**             | Semantic Versioning              |
| **Chart Distribution**           | OCI Registry preferred           |
| **Validation**                   | Lint + render + schema + policy  |
| **Chart Testing**                | Required for critical charts     |
| **Upgrade Testing**              | Required                         |
| **Production Deployment**        | Argo CD / GitOps                 |
| **Manual Helm PROD Deployments** | Not standard workflow            |
| **Infrastructure Provisioning**  | Terraform                        |
| **Runtime**                      | Kubernetes                       |
| **CRD Ownership**                | Platform-managed                 |
| **Helm Hooks**                   | Minimize                         |
| **Rollback**                     | Git revert preferred             |
| **Status**                       | Accepted                         |
| **Priority**                     | Critical                         |
| **Risk Level**                   | High                             |

---

```text
                         MEDIVERSE
                             │
              ┌──────────────┴──────────────┐
              │                             │
              ▼                             ▼
      Application Source              Helm Charts
              │                             │

             CI                       Chart Validation
              │                             │

     ▼        ▼        ▼          ▼         ▼         ▼

              │                             │
              ▼                             ▼
      Container Registry              OCI Registry
              │                             │
              └──────────────┬──────────────┘
                             │
                             ▼

                             │
                  ┌──────────┼──────────┐
                  ▼          ▼          ▼
                 DEV        UAT        PROD
                  │          │          │
                  └──────────┼──────────┘
                             │
                             ▼
                          Argo CD
                             │

                       Helm Rendering
```
