---

# ADR-036 — CI Platform & Enterprise Software Supply Chain Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing from **Section 60 — Why SBOM Matters**.

---

# 61. Artifact Provenance

Every production artifact should carry evidence describing how it was produced.

Provenance should establish:

```text
Source Repository
       │
       ▼
Source Commit
       │
       ▼
CI Workflow
       │
       ▼
Build Environment
       │
       ▼
Artifact Digest
```

The objective is traceability from running workload back to source.

---

# 62. Why Provenance Matters

Without provenance, possessing an image in ECR does not prove:

```text
Who built it
Which source produced it
Which commit was used
Which workflow produced it
Whether CI controls were executed
Whether the artifact was modified afterward
```

Artifact existence and artifact trust are different things.

---

# 63. SLSA Direction

Mediverse should align its software supply-chain architecture with **SLSA principles**.

The objective is progressive maturity around:

```text
Build integrity
Provenance
Build isolation
Source integrity
Artifact traceability
Tamper resistance
```

This ADR does not mandate chasing a specific SLSA level merely for certification optics.

---

# 64. Build Provenance

Conceptually:

```text
Git Commit
    │
    ▼
GitHub Actions
    │
    ├── Workflow Identity
    ├── Repository Identity
    ├── Commit SHA
    └── Build Metadata
    │
    ▼
OCI Artifact
    │
    ▼
Provenance Attestation
```

---

# 65. Artifact Signing

Production OCI artifacts should be cryptographically signed.

Selected direction:

```text
OCI Image
    │
    ▼
Cosign
    │
    ▼
Signature
```

Signing allows downstream systems to verify artifact identity and provenance.

---

# 66. Cosign

Cosign should be used as the preferred OCI signing technology.

Conceptually:

```text
CI
 │
 ├── Build
 ├── Scan
 ├── SBOM
 └── Sign
      │
      ▼
     ECR
```

---

# 67. Keyless Signing Direction

Where supported by the security model, Mediverse should prefer identity-based/keyless signing over distributing long-lived private signing keys through CI.

```text
GitHub Actions Identity
        │
        ▼
      OIDC
        │
        ▼
Signing Identity
        │
        ▼
OCI Signature
```

This reduces private-key management burden.

---

# 68. Signing Is Not Enough

A signed malicious artifact is still malicious.

Signing proves identity/integrity relationships.

It does not prove software correctness.

Therefore:

```text
Testing
+
Scanning
+
Provenance
+
Signing
+
Admission Policy
```

work together.

---

# 69. Signature Verification

Signing without verification has little security value.

The Kubernetes supply-chain architecture should eventually enforce:

```text
Incoming Image
      │
      ▼
Admission Policy
      │
      ▼
Verify Signature
      │
      ├── Trusted → Admit
      │
      └── Untrusted → Reject
```

---

# 70. Artifact Digest

Every OCI image has a content-addressed digest.

Example:

```text
sha256:7e35...
```

This identifies exact image content.

---

# 71. Tags vs Digests

Tags are human-friendly references.

```text
content-service:1.8.0
```

Digests are immutable content identities.

```text
content-service@sha256:...
```

Production deployment should ultimately resolve to immutable artifact identity.

---

# 72. Mutable Tag Risk

This is dangerous:

```text
content-service:prod
```

if somebody can replace what `prod` points to.

Then Git may remain unchanged while production artifact content changes.

That breaks GitOps traceability.

---

# 73. ECR Publication

Only trusted CI contexts should publish release artifacts to production ECR repositories.

```text
Untrusted PR
    │
    X
    │
Production ECR


Protected Branch
    │
    ▼
Trusted CI
    │
    ▼
Production ECR
```

---

# 74. AWS Authentication

GitHub Actions should authenticate to AWS using short-lived federation.

Preferred:

```text
GitHub Actions
      │
      ▼
     OIDC
      │
      ▼
AWS IAM Trust Policy
      │
      ▼
Temporary Role Session
```

---

# 75. No Permanent AWS Keys

Avoid storing:

```text
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
```

as long-lived GitHub secrets when OIDC federation can replace them.

Long-lived credentials increase rotation and theft risk.

---

# 76. OIDC Trust Policy

AWS trust policies must restrict which GitHub identities can assume sensitive roles.

Do not configure:

```text
Any GitHub repository
      │
      ▼
Production AWS Role
```

Trust should account for repository, organization, branch/environment, and workflow context as appropriate.

---

# 77. AWS Role Separation

CI roles should be separated by responsibility.

Example:

```text
CI Build Role
     │
     └── Limited AWS access

ECR Publisher Role
     │
     └── Push approved artifacts

Terraform Role
     │
     └── Infrastructure operations

PROD Runtime Roles
     │
     └── Workload-specific access
```

---

# 78. CI Does Not Need EKS Admin

Because Argo CD owns deployment:

```text
GitHub Actions
      │
      X
      │
EKS cluster-admin
```

should be the normal architecture.

Removing production Kubernetes credentials from CI materially reduces blast radius.

---

# 79. Maven Repository Architecture

Maven dependencies and internally produced Java artifacts require explicit repository governance.

Potential sources:

```text
Maven Central
Internal Nexus
Approved vendor repositories
```

---

# 80. Nexus Boundary

Nexus may provide:

```text
Maven proxy
Internal Maven releases
Internal snapshots
Dependency caching
Repository governance
```

where Mediverse requires centralized artifact repository management.

It should not duplicate ECR's role for OCI images without a reason.

---

# 81. Artifact Responsibility

Recommended boundary:

```text
Amazon ECR
    │
    └── OCI/container artifacts

Nexus
    │
    └── Maven/internal package artifacts

GitHub
    │
    └── Source + workflow definitions
```

Clear ownership avoids repository sprawl.

---

# 82. Maven Snapshot vs Release

Internal libraries should distinguish:

```text
SNAPSHOT
→ Development artifact

Release
→ Immutable published version
```

Released library versions must not be silently overwritten.

---

# 83. Internal Shared Libraries

Shared Java libraries should be created cautiously.

Excessive shared libraries create tight coupling between microservices.

Good candidates:

```text
Observability conventions
Security integration utilities
Stable platform clients
```

Bad candidate:

```text
One giant mediverse-common.jar
containing every domain model
```

That recreates a distributed monolith.

---

# 84. npm Dependency Governance

Frontend dependencies should follow similar supply-chain controls.

Requirements include:

```text
Committed lockfile
npm ci
Dependency scanning
Controlled registries
Version governance
Minimal package set
```

---

# 85. npm Package Risk

Adding a package is adding executable third-party code to the software supply chain.

Do not install a dependency for functionality that could reasonably be implemented in a few stable lines merely because an npm package exists.

---

# 86. Dependency Update Automation

Automated dependency update tooling may create pull requests for:

```text
Maven dependencies
npm packages
GitHub Actions
Container base images
```

Updates must still pass normal CI and review.

---

# 87. Third-Party GitHub Actions

GitHub Actions themselves are software dependencies.

Example:

```yaml
uses: vendor/action@...
```

A compromised action can compromise CI.

---

# 88. Action Pinning

Security-sensitive workflows should pin third-party actions to immutable commit SHAs where appropriate.

Conceptually:

```text
uses: vendor/action@<commit-sha>
```

rather than blindly trusting a mutable branch reference.

---

# 89. Action Allowlist

Enterprise governance may restrict Actions to:

```text
GitHub-maintained actions
Verified/approved vendors
Internally reviewed actions
```

Unknown Actions should not automatically receive privileged workflow access.

---

# 90. Runner Architecture

GitHub Actions can use:

```text
GitHub-hosted runners
```

or:

```text
Self-hosted runners
```

The choice affects security, networking, cost, and operational complexity.

---

# 91. GitHub-Hosted Runners

Hosted runners are preferred for ordinary CI where they satisfy requirements.

Benefits:

```text
Ephemeral execution
Low operational burden
Managed updates
Elastic capacity
Reduced persistent-runner compromise
```

---

# 92. Self-Hosted Runners

Self-hosted runners may be justified for:

```text
Private network access
Special hardware
Large builds
GPU builds
Custom tooling
Compliance constraints
```

But they create significant security responsibilities.

---

# 93. Persistent Runner Risk

Dangerous architecture:

```text
Untrusted PR
     │
     ▼
Persistent Runner
     │
     ▼
Malicious Persistence
     │
     ▼
Future Trusted Build
     │
     ▼
Credential Theft
```

Persistent self-hosted runners should not casually execute untrusted code.

---

# 94. Ephemeral Self-Hosted Runners

Where self-hosting is required, ephemeral runners are strongly preferred.

```text
Job Requested
     │
     ▼
Create Runner
     │
     ▼
Execute One Job
     │
     ▼
Destroy Runner
```

This reduces persistence opportunities.

---

# 95. Runner Network Access

A CI runner should have only the network access required for its job.

Do not place general-purpose CI runners inside a network from which every production database and internal system is reachable.

---

# 96. CI Secrets

Secrets should be scoped according to:

```text
Repository
Environment
Workflow
Job
```

and exposed only where required.

---

# 97. Environment Secrets

Production-specific credentials should use protected environments and approval controls where applicable.

DEV workflows should not automatically receive PROD secrets.

---

# 98. Secret Masking

Log masking is useful but not a security architecture.

Once arbitrary code receives a secret, that code may exfiltrate it through mechanisms other than plain log output.

The real control is avoiding unnecessary secret exposure.

---

# 99. Cache Poisoning

CI caches create a supply-chain risk when untrusted workflows can populate cache entries later consumed by privileged builds.

Cache keys and trust boundaries must therefore be designed carefully.

---

# 100. Cache Separation

Where necessary:

```text
Untrusted PR Cache
       │
       X
       │
Trusted Release Cache
```

Trusted builds should not blindly consume artifacts produced by untrusted execution contexts.

---

# 101. Build Artifacts

Intermediate build outputs may be stored temporarily for:

```text
Testing
Debugging
Pipeline handoff
Coverage reports
Security reports
```

Artifact retention should match actual operational requirements.

---

# 102. Artifact Retention

Do not retain every intermediate CI artifact forever.

Define retention based on:

```text
Audit requirements
Debugging needs
Release lifecycle
Storage cost
Security sensitivity
```

Production OCI artifacts follow separate registry-retention governance.

---

# 103. Reproducible Builds

The architecture should move toward reproducible builds.

Conceptually:

```text
Same Source
+
Same Dependencies
+
Same Build Configuration
       │
       ▼
Equivalent Artifact
```

Perfect byte-for-byte reproducibility may not always be immediate, but unnecessary nondeterminism should be removed.

---

# 104. Build Metadata

Avoid uncontrolled build inputs such as:

```text
Current timestamp embedded everywhere
Unpinned dependency versions
latest base images
Environment-specific compilation
Random generated content
```

when they undermine reproducibility.

---

# 105. Build Once

Mediverse shall follow:

> **Build once, promote many.**

```text
Commit ABC
    │
    ▼
Build Image
    │
    ▼
sha256:XYZ
    │
    ├── DEV
    ├── UAT
    └── PROD
```

---

# 106. Do Not Rebuild Per Environment

Rejected:

```text
Source
 ├── DEV Build
 ├── UAT Build
 └── PROD Build
```

Those are three different artifacts even when they originate from the same commit.

Testing one does not prove another is identical.

---

# 107. Runtime Configuration

Environment differences belong in runtime configuration.

```text
Same OCI Artifact
       │
       ├── DEV configuration
       ├── UAT configuration
       └── PROD configuration
```

This aligns with Helm + GitOps architecture.

---

# 108. Release Versioning

Mediverse should use clear release identifiers.

For appropriate artifacts:

```text
MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH
```

can provide semantic versioning.

Example:

```text
2.4.1
```

---

# 109. Commit SHA

Every artifact should also retain source commit identity.

Example metadata:

```text
Version:       2.4.1
Commit:        a82f71...
Image Digest:  sha256:...
Build:         GitHub Actions run ...
```

---

# 110. OCI Labels

Container metadata should expose useful provenance such as:

```text
Source repository
Revision
Version
Creation metadata where appropriate
Vendor/project
```

using standardized OCI annotations where practical.

---

# 111. GitOps Update

After publishing an approved artifact, automation may propose a GitOps repository update.

```text
CI
 │
 ▼
New Digest
 │
 ▼
GitOps Pull Request
 │
 ▼
Review / Policy
 │
 ▼
Merge
 │
 ▼
Argo CD
```

---

# 112. CI Should Propose, Not Secretly Deploy

Preferred production flow:

```text
CI
 │
 └──► Creates/updates GitOps PR

Human/Policy
 │
 └──► Approves promotion

Argo CD
 │
 └──► Deploys
```

The exact approval model may vary by environment.

---

# 113. DEV Promotion

DEV may permit highly automated promotion.

Example:

```text
main merged
    │
    ▼
Build + Verify
    │
    ▼
Publish
    │
    ▼
Update DEV GitOps
    │
    ▼
Argo CD
```

Fast feedback is desirable.

---

# 114. UAT Promotion

UAT should promote an artifact already validated in DEV.

```text
sha256:XYZ
    │
    ▼
DEV
    │
    ▼
Promotion
    │
    ▼
UAT
```

No rebuild occurs.

---

# 115. Production Promotion

Production promotion should use the same immutable artifact.

```text
DEV ─────┐
         │
UAT ─────┼──► sha256:XYZ
         │
PROD ────┘
```

Production approval changes deployment authorization, not binary contents.

---

# 116. GitOps Repository Credentials

Automation updating GitOps repositories should receive narrowly scoped credentials.

It does not need unrestricted access to every repository in the organization.

---

# 117. CI-to-Argo Boundary

There should normally be no need for:

```text
GitHub Actions
      │
      ▼
Argo CD Admin API Token
```

CI updates desired state.

Argo CD observes Git.

This decoupling is one of GitOps's strongest properties.

---

# 118. Release Tagging

Release tags should correspond to known source commits.

Protected release workflows should prevent arbitrary users from manufacturing trusted releases from unreviewed code.

---

# 119. Monorepo vs Polyrepo

CI architecture must support both repository models.

Mediverse should not choose repository topology merely because one CI configuration is easier.

---

# 120. Polyrepo

Potential advantages:

```text
Independent ownership
Independent releases
Smaller repository scope
Service-specific permissions
```

Potential disadvantages:

```text
Workflow duplication
Cross-service changes
Dependency coordination
Repository sprawl
```

---

# 121. Monorepo

Potential advantages:

```text
Atomic cross-project changes
Shared tooling
Central visibility
Consistent CI
```

Potential disadvantages:

```text
Larger CI graph
Permission complexity
Repository scale
Unnecessary builds
```

---

# 122. Path Filtering

For monorepos, CI should execute only affected pipelines where reliable.

```text
services/content/**
        │
        ▼
Content Service CI
```

rather than rebuilding 40 unrelated services for every README change.

---

# 123. Path Filtering Risk

Incorrect filtering can skip required builds.

Dependency relationships must be understood before optimizing.

Speed is not worth silently bypassing validation.

---

# 124. Concurrency

CI should control concurrent executions.

Example:

```text
PR Commit A → CI running
PR Commit B → arrives
                │
                ▼
Cancel obsolete A where safe
                │
                ▼
Run B
```

This saves capacity and reduces irrelevant feedback.

---

# 125. Release Concurrency

Release workflows require stricter serialization.

Two concurrent release processes should not race to update the same version or GitOps target.

---

# 126. Flaky Tests

A test that fails randomly is a production engineering defect in the test system.

Repeated:

```text
Re-run
Re-run
Re-run
Finally green
```

is not a valid quality strategy.

---

# 127. Flaky-Test Governance

Flaky tests should be:

```text
Detected
Tracked
Assigned
Fixed
```

Temporary quarantine may be necessary, but permanent quarantine defeats the purpose of the test.

---

# 128. CI Performance Metrics

Mediverse should observe:

```text
Pipeline duration
Queue time
Failure rate
Flaky-test rate
Cache effectiveness
Runner utilization
Build frequency
Security-gate failures
```

CI is production infrastructure for engineering.

---

# 129. Developer Feedback Time

Long pipelines directly reduce development velocity.

Target:

```text
Fast PR checks
        +
Deeper asynchronous/merge validation
        +
Strict release validation
```

rather than putting every possible test into one 90-minute PR pipeline.

---

# 130. CI Logs

CI logs should contain enough information to diagnose failures without exposing:

```text
Secrets
Tokens
Private keys
Sensitive environment values
```

Debug logging must not bypass security.

---

# 131. Auditability

For each release, Mediverse should be able to identify:

```text
Source commit
Pull request
Reviewers
Workflow
Workflow version
Test results
Security results
SBOM
Provenance
Artifact digest
Signature
Registry location
GitOps promotion
```

---

# 132. CI Cost

CI has real cost.

Major drivers include:

```text
Runner minutes
Large runners
Storage
Artifact retention
Container builds
Integration tests
Repeated unnecessary builds
Self-hosted infrastructure
```

Optimization should target waste without weakening validation.

---

# 133. Self-Hosted Runner Cost

Self-hosted does not mean free.

Costs include:

```text
Compute
Scaling
Patching
Security
Monitoring
Networking
Operations
Incident response
```

Hosted runners may be cheaper overall even when per-minute pricing appears higher.

---

# 134. CI Availability

A CI outage should prevent new releases but should not stop existing Mediverse production workloads.

This is another reason CI must not sit inside the runtime request path.

---

# 135. Disaster Recovery

Critical CI configuration already exists in Git:

```text
Workflow definitions
Build scripts
Dockerfiles
Maven configuration
Security configuration
```

External dependencies still require recovery planning.

---

# 136. Supply-Chain Threat Model

Important threats include:

```text
Compromised developer account
Malicious pull request
Compromised dependency
Dependency confusion
Compromised GitHub Action
Compromised runner
Cache poisoning
Credential theft
Malicious base image
Artifact replacement
Registry compromise
Signing identity compromise
GitOps repository compromise
```

---

# 137. Compromise Response

If CI compromise is suspected:

```text
Detect
  │
  ▼
Disable affected workflow/runner
  │
  ▼
Revoke credentials/sessions
  │
  ▼
Identify affected artifacts
  │
  ▼
Invalidate/revoke trust
  │
  ▼
Rebuild from trusted source
  │
  ▼
Re-sign
  │
  ▼
Re-promote
```

Incident response must consider artifacts already produced.

---

# 138. Artifact Trust Revocation

Mediverse must be able to identify which deployed artifacts were built during a compromised window.

This is why provenance, digest tracking, and deployment auditability matter.

---

# 139. Security Governance

```text
Development Teams
      │
      ├── Tests
      ├── Build configuration
      └── Dependency maintenance

Platform Team
      │
      ├── Reusable workflows
      ├── Runner architecture
      ├── Registry integration
      └── GitOps integration

Security Team
      │
      ├── SAST/SCA policy
      ├── Secret scanning
      ├── Signing policy
      ├── Provenance requirements
      └── Vulnerability exceptions

Release Owners
      │
      └── Production promotion governance
```

---

# 140. Reusable Workflows

Common CI behavior should be centralized through reusable workflows where appropriate.

Example:

```text
Reusable Java Workflow
       │
       ├── Service A
       ├── Service B
       ├── Service C
       └── Service D
```

This reduces copy-paste drift.

---

# 141. Reusable Workflow Versioning

Centralized workflows create dependency risk.

A breaking change to one shared workflow could break every repository.

Therefore reusable workflow changes require:

```text
Versioning
Testing
Compatibility management
Controlled rollout
```

---

# 142. CI Anti-Patterns

Mediverse shall reject or strongly discourage:

```text
❌ CI directly deploying production with kubectl
❌ CI with unrestricted EKS cluster-admin
❌ Long-lived AWS keys in GitHub
❌ Secrets available to untrusted PRs
❌ Persistent runners executing arbitrary fork code
❌ Unpinned third-party Actions
❌ Mutable production container tags
❌ Rebuilding separately for DEV/UAT/PROD
❌ Skipping failed security gates
❌ Permanent vulnerability exceptions
❌ Plaintext secrets in workflow YAML
❌ latest container base images for controlled releases
❌ Shared test databases across concurrent builds
❌ npm install instead of deterministic CI installation
❌ Missing dependency lockfiles
❌ Blind cache sharing across trust boundaries
❌ Publishing artifacts from untrusted branches
❌ Giant mediverse-common shared library
❌ Retaining every CI artifact forever
❌ Treating coverage as correctness
❌ Ignoring flaky tests
❌ Running every monorepo pipeline for every trivial change
❌ Giving CI direct Argo CD admin tokens
❌ Signing artifacts without verifying signatures
❌ Generating SBOMs nobody stores or uses
```

---

# 143. Production Quality Gate

A production-candidate artifact should conceptually satisfy:

```text
Source Protected
      │
      ▼
Compilation          ✅
Unit Tests           ✅
Integration Tests    ✅
Frontend Validation  ✅
Quality Gate         ✅
SAST                 ✅
SCA                  ✅
Secret Scan          ✅
OCI Build            ✅
Container Scan       ✅
SBOM                  ✅
Provenance            ✅
Signature             ✅
      │
      ▼
Trusted Artifact
```

Failure of mandatory gates prevents release eligibility.

---

# 144. Release Metadata Contract

Every production artifact should have traceability to:

| Metadata            | Required |
| ------------------- | -------: |
| Application/service |        ✅ |
| Version             |        ✅ |
| Git repository      |        ✅ |
| Git commit SHA      |        ✅ |
| Pull request/change |        ✅ |
| CI workflow         |        ✅ |
| CI run              |        ✅ |
| OCI digest          |        ✅ |
| SBOM                |        ✅ |
| Security scan       |        ✅ |
| Provenance          |        ✅ |
| Signature           |        ✅ |
| Build timestamp     |        ✅ |
| Promotion history   |        ✅ |

---

# 145. CI Security Architecture

```text
                     DEVELOPER
                         │
                         ▼
                    GitHub / Git
                         │
                         ▼
                   Pull Request
                         │
              ┌──────────┴──────────┐
              ▼                     ▼
       Untrusted Context       Trusted Context
              │                     │
              ▼                     ▼
       No Production         Protected Branch
         Credentials                │
                                    ▼
                              GitHub Actions
                                    │
                     ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
                     ▼              ▼              ▼
                   Tests         Security        Build
                                    │              │
                                    ▼              ▼
                                SBOM/Scan      OCI Image
                                                   │
                                                   ▼
                                              Provenance
                                                   │
                                                   ▼
                                                 Sign
                                                   │
                                                   ▼
                                                  ECR
```

---

# 146. Complete CI/CD Architecture

```text
Developer
    │
    ▼
Application Git
    │
    ▼
Pull Request
    │
    ▼
┌──────────────────────────────┐
│        GITHUB ACTIONS        │
├──────────────────────────────┤
│ Compile                      │
│ Unit Tests                   │
│ Integration Tests            │
│ Lint / Type Check            │
│ SonarQube                    │
│ SAST                         │
│ SCA                          │
│ Secret Scan                  │
│ Docker BuildKit              │
│ Container Scan               │
│ SBOM                         │
│ Provenance                   │
│ Cosign                       │
└───────────────┬──────────────┘
                │
                ▼
            Amazon ECR
                │
                ▼
       Immutable OCI Digest
                │
                ▼
         GitOps Update PR
                │
                ▼
        GitOps Repository
                │
                ▼
             Argo CD
                │
                ▼
               Helm
                │
                ▼
              EKS
```

---

# 147. Trust Chain

The final software supply-chain trust path becomes:

```text
Developer Identity
        │
        ▼
Protected Git
        │
        ▼
Reviewed Source
        │
        ▼
Trusted CI Workflow
        │
        ▼
Tests + Security Gates
        │
        ▼
OCI Artifact
        │
        ├── SBOM
        ├── Provenance
        └── Signature
        │
        ▼
Trusted Registry
        │
        ▼
GitOps Promotion
        │
        ▼
Admission Verification
        │
        ▼
Kubernetes Runtime
```

Every major transition introduces an explicit trust decision.

---

# 148. Risks and Mitigations

| Risk                         | Mitigation                        |
| ---------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Developer account compromise | MFA + branch protection           |
| Malicious PR                 | Untrusted execution isolation     |
| AWS credential theft         | OIDC + temporary credentials      |
| Dependency compromise        | SCA + lockfiles + SBOM            |
| GitHub Action compromise     | SHA pinning + allowlist           |
| Runner compromise            | Ephemeral runners                 |
| Cache poisoning              | Trust-aware cache isolation       |
| Malicious base image         | Approved/pinned images            |
| Vulnerable artifact          | Container scanning                |
| Artifact replacement         | Immutable digest                  |
| Registry tampering           | Signing + verification            |
| Build tampering              | Provenance                        |
| Secret leakage               | Scoped secrets + secret scanning  |
| CI→PROD compromise           | No direct cluster credentials     |
| Rebuild inconsistency        | Build once/promote                |
| Flaky tests                  | Tracking + remediation            |
| CI workflow compromise       | CODEOWNERS + protection           |
| Excessive CI cost            | Parallelization + path filtering  |
| Compromised release          | Traceability + revocation/rebuild |

---

# ADR-037 — Observability Platform Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — JSON Logging**.

---

# 61. Log Correlation

Every request should carry sufficient correlation context to connect logs across services.

```text
Request
   │
   ▼
Gateway
   │ trace_id = ABC123
   ▼
Learning Service
   │ trace_id = ABC123
   ▼
Content Service
   │ trace_id = ABC123
   ▼
Database
```

Application logs generated during the request should include the trace identifier automatically where practical.

---

# 62. Trace-Log Correlation

The desired investigation path is:

```text
Grafana
   │
   ▼
Latency Spike
   │
   ▼
Tempo Trace
   │
   ▼
Slow Span
   │
   ▼
Related Loki Logs
```

Operators should not manually search several systems using timestamps alone.

---

# 63. Correlation IDs vs Trace IDs

Legacy correlation IDs may still exist.

For instrumented distributed requests, the OpenTelemetry trace ID should become the primary distributed correlation identifier.

Do not create multiple competing identifiers without a specific requirement.

---

# 64. Logging Context

Useful structured fields may include:

```text
timestamp
severity
service
environment
event
trace_id
span_id
request_method
route
status_code
```

Fields must remain governed to avoid sensitive-data leakage.

---

# 65. Log Levels

Mediverse should standardize:

```text
TRACE
DEBUG
INFO
WARN
ERROR
```

Each level has an operational meaning.

---

# 66. TRACE

TRACE is extremely verbose.

It should normally be disabled in production except during tightly controlled troubleshooting.

---

# 67. DEBUG

DEBUG provides detailed engineering diagnostics.

Persistent DEBUG logging across production microservices can create:

```text
High storage cost
Noise
Performance overhead
Sensitive-data exposure
```

It should therefore not be the normal production level.

---

# 68. INFO

INFO should describe meaningful normal application lifecycle or business-operational events.

Avoid logging every method entry and exit at INFO.

That produces noise rather than observability.

---

# 69. WARN

WARN should indicate unexpected or degraded behavior that does not necessarily cause the current operation to fail.

Examples:

```text
Retry initiated
Fallback activated
Dependency latency elevated
Cache unavailable
```

---

# 70. ERROR

ERROR represents failed operations requiring investigation or meaningful failure accounting.

An ERROR log should provide enough context to diagnose the failure without exposing sensitive information.

---

# 71. Exception Logging

Do not repeatedly log the same exception at every architectural layer.

Bad:

```text
Repository     → ERROR
Service        → ERROR
Controller     → ERROR
Gateway        → ERROR
```

One failure can then appear as four independent incidents.

Log exceptions at the layer where meaningful handling/context exists.

---

# 72. Stack Traces

Stack traces are valuable for unexpected application failures.

They should not be emitted for routine expected business validation failures.

Example:

```text
Invalid quiz answer
```

does not need a Java stack trace.

---

# 73. Sensitive Data Logging

Mediverse shall prohibit logging sensitive user data unless an explicit approved requirement exists.

Examples that should not appear casually in telemetry:

```text
Passwords
Authentication tokens
Refresh tokens
Session secrets
API keys
Private keys
Sensitive profile information
Uploaded confidential content
Sensitive educational/user records
```

---

# 74. Authorization Headers

Authorization headers must never be logged.

```text
Authorization: Bearer eyJ...
```

is credential disclosure.

---

# 75. Request/Response Body Logging

Global request/response body logging is prohibited by default.

It creates serious risks involving:

```text
Credentials
Personal data
Large payloads
Binary data
Security exposure
Storage explosion
```

Specific diagnostic logging requires controlled design.

---

# 76. Data Redaction

Where telemetry fields may contain sensitive values, redaction should occur before storage.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
Telemetry Processing
    │
    ▼
Redaction
    │
    ▼
Backend
```

Do not depend entirely on operators remembering not to query sensitive data.

---

# 77. Loki Label Strategy

Loki labels should represent low-cardinality operational dimensions.

Good candidates:

```text
service
namespace
environment
cluster
level
```

---

# 78. Loki High-Cardinality Anti-Pattern

Do not make fields such as:

```text
trace_id
request_id
user_id
email
session_id
```

Loki index labels.

These belong in structured log content where appropriate, not high-cardinality indexes.

---

# 79. Log Retention

Retention should differ by environment and data class.

Conceptually:

```text
DEV
→ shorter

UAT
→ moderate

PROD
→ operational/compliance requirement
```

Infinite retention is not an observability strategy.

---

# 80. Log Archival

Long-term logs required for audit/compliance may belong in cheaper archival storage rather than the primary interactive logging backend.

```text
Hot Logs
   │
   ▼
Loki
   │
   ▼
Retention Boundary
   │
   ▼
Archive Storage
```

---

# 81. Grafana Tempo

Grafana Tempo shall provide the primary distributed tracing backend.

Reasons include strong integration with:

```text
Grafana
OpenTelemetry
Loki
Prometheus
Object storage
```

---

# 82. Tempo vs Jaeger

Both are valid tracing technologies.

Mediverse selects **Tempo** primarily because the broader observability stack already standardizes on Grafana technologies.

```text
Prometheus → Metrics
Loki       → Logs
Tempo      → Traces
Grafana    → Visualization
```

This reduces unnecessary platform fragmentation.

---

# 83. Tempo Storage

At production scale, trace storage should use scalable object-storage architecture where supported.

On AWS:

```text
Tempo
  │
  ▼
Amazon S3
```

This separates scalable trace storage from compute.

---

# 84. Trace Retention

Trace retention should balance:

```text
Incident investigation
Debugging value
Traffic volume
Storage
Compliance
Cost
```

Retaining every trace forever is unjustified.

---

# 85. Trace Attributes

Useful span attributes may describe:

```text
service
HTTP route
HTTP method
status
database system
messaging system
operation
environment
```

Sensitive or uncontrolled high-cardinality values require governance.

---

# 86. Database Traces

Tracing database operations can reveal where latency occurs.

```text
API
 │ 40 ms
 ▼
Service
 │ 30 ms
 ▼
PostgreSQL
   1.8 sec
```

This immediately changes the investigation direction.

---

# 87. SQL Telemetry Security

Telemetry should not blindly capture:

```text
Raw SQL parameters
Passwords
Tokens
Sensitive field values
```

Database observability must preserve data confidentiality.

---

# 88. Exemplars

Exemplars can connect metric observations to traces.

Conceptually:

```text
Prometheus latency metric
        │
        ▼
p99 spike
        │
        ▼
Trace exemplar
        │
        ▼
Tempo trace
```

This significantly improves investigation speed.

---

# 89. Kubernetes Observability

The Kubernetes platform requires visibility into:

```text
Nodes
Pods
Deployments
StatefulSets
DaemonSets
Jobs
Persistent volumes
Resource requests
Resource limits
Restarts
Scheduling
Autoscaling
```

Application observability alone is insufficient.

---

# 90. kube-state-metrics

kube-state-metrics should expose Kubernetes object-state metrics.

Examples:

```text
Desired replicas
Available replicas
Pod status
Deployment status
Job state
Resource requests
```

---

# 91. Node Exporter

Node-level telemetry should expose infrastructure metrics such as:

```text
CPU
Memory
Filesystem
Network
Load
```

where appropriate to the selected EKS monitoring architecture.

---

# 92. Pod Restart Monitoring

Repeated restarts should be visible.

```text
Pod
 │
 ▼
Crash
 │
 ▼
Restart
 │
 ▼
CrashLoopBackOff
```

An application that eventually answers requests after constant restarts is not healthy.

---

# 93. Kubernetes Resource Saturation

Monitor:

```text
CPU throttling
Memory pressure
OOMKilled
Pending pods
Disk pressure
Node pressure
```

These frequently explain application symptoms that developers incorrectly blame on application code.

---

# 94. Requests and Limits

Observability should compare:

```text
Actual Usage
      │
      versus
      │
Requests / Limits
```

This helps detect severe over-provisioning and under-provisioning.

---

# 95. HPA Observability

Horizontal Pod Autoscaler behavior should be visible.

Monitor:

```text
Current replicas
Desired replicas
Scaling events
Metric values
Maximum replica saturation
```

An HPA stuck at maximum capacity is an important operational signal.

---

# 96. EKS Control Plane

Relevant EKS control-plane logging should be enabled according to security and operational requirements.

Potential categories include:

```text
API
Audit
Authenticator
Controller Manager
Scheduler
```

Retention and cost must be considered.

---

# 97. AWS CloudWatch Integration

CloudWatch remains important for AWS-managed infrastructure.

Examples:

```text
ALB
RDS
ElastiCache
EKS
NAT Gateway
AWS Lambda if introduced
CloudFront
```

Grafana may consume selected CloudWatch data to reduce context switching.

---

# 98. ALB Monitoring

Monitor signals such as:

```text
Request count
Target response time
HTTP 4xx
HTTP 5xx
Healthy targets
Unhealthy targets
Rejected connections where relevant
```

This helps distinguish edge failures from application failures.

---

# 99. 502 Investigation

A `502 Bad Gateway` is a symptom, not a diagnosis.

Investigation should correlate:

```text
ALB 5xx
   │
   ▼
Target health
   │
   ▼
Gateway metrics
   │
   ▼
Pod health/restarts
   │
   ▼
Application traces
   │
   ▼
Dependency saturation
```

Guessing from the HTTP status alone is insufficient.

---

# 100. PostgreSQL Monitoring

Production PostgreSQL observability should include:

```text
CPU
Memory
Connections
Storage
IOPS
Query latency
Locks
Deadlocks
Replication/failover health
```

Application connection-pool metrics should complement RDS metrics.

---

# 101. Connection Pool Monitoring

Spring Boot/HikariCP should expose:

```text
Active connections
Idle connections
Pending threads
Maximum pool size
Acquisition latency
Timeouts
```

This is essential for diagnosing load-related failures.

---

# 102. Database Saturation Pattern

Example:

```text
Traffic rises
    │
    ▼
Connection pool exhausted
    │
    ▼
Requests wait
    │
    ▼
Latency rises
    │
    ▼
Upstream timeout
    │
    ▼
502 / 504
```

Without cross-layer telemetry, the load balancer may incorrectly appear to be the root cause.

---

# 103. Redis Monitoring

Monitor:

```text
Memory
Connections
Evictions
Hit ratio
Miss ratio
Latency
Replication
CPU
```

A cache with constant evictions may increase database load dramatically.

---

# 104. Cache Dependency

Applications should expose whether cache failures are causing:

```text
Fallback
Database load increase
Latency increase
Request failure
```

This is more useful than merely knowing Redis is "up."

---

# 105. Kafka Observability

Kafka requires dedicated operational telemetry.

Important signals:

```text
Broker health
Producer errors
Consumer errors
Throughput
Consumer lag
Partition health
Under-replicated partitions
Message processing latency
```

---

# 106. Consumer Lag

Consumer lag measures how far a consumer is behind produced messages.

```text
Producer
   │
   ▼
Kafka
████████████████████
             ▲
             │
          Consumer
```

Growing lag may indicate insufficient consumer capacity or downstream slowness.

---

# 107. Kafka Application Metrics

Infrastructure metrics alone do not reveal business processing failures.

Consumers should expose meaningful metrics such as:

```text
Messages processed
Messages failed
Retries
Dead-letter events
Processing duration
```

---

# 108. Dead-Letter Monitoring

Dead-letter topics/queues must be monitored.

```text
Failed Message
     │
     ▼
DLQ
     │
     X
 Nobody notices
```

is not a failure-handling strategy.

---

# 109. Argo CD Observability

Monitor:

```text
Application sync state
Health state
Reconciliation failures
OutOfSync applications
Sync duration
Controller health
```

Deployment-system failure can otherwise masquerade as application failure.

---

# 110. GitOps Drift

Important production drift should produce visibility.

```text
Git Desired State
        │
        ≠
Cluster Actual State
        │
        ▼
OutOfSync
```

Persistent unexplained drift requires investigation.

---

# 111. Frontend Observability

Backend telemetry alone cannot show the complete user experience.

React/browser telemetry may measure:

```text
Page-load performance
JavaScript errors
API failures
Core Web Vitals
Frontend route performance
```

subject to privacy requirements.

---

# 112. Browser Trace Propagation

Where appropriate:

```text
Browser
   │ traceparent
   ▼
Gateway
   │
   ▼
Backend
```

can connect frontend operations to backend traces.

Cross-origin and security behavior must be configured intentionally.

---

# 113. Frontend Telemetry Privacy

Browser telemetry has significant privacy risk.

Do not capture:

```text
Form contents
Passwords
Tokens
Sensitive URLs/query values
Sensitive DOM content
```

simply because an observability SDK technically can.

---

# 114. Real User Monitoring

RUM can provide actual user-experience measurements.

Potential signals:

```text
LCP
INP
CLS
Navigation latency
Frontend errors
API timing
```

It should be adopted only with explicit privacy and data-governance controls.

---

# 115. Synthetic Monitoring

Synthetic probes should test critical public journeys independently of real users.

Examples:

```text
Homepage reachable?
Login endpoint reachable?
Content API healthy?
Critical public learning content accessible?
```

---

# 116. Why Synthetic Monitoring?

Internal metrics can say:

```text
Everything healthy
```

while users cannot reach the application because DNS, CDN, TLS or routing is broken.

Synthetic monitoring tests from the user-facing perspective.

---

# 117. Black-Box Monitoring

Black-box probes validate externally observable behavior.

```text
Probe
  │
  ▼
DNS
  │
  ▼
HTTPS
  │
  ▼
Application
```

This complements internal white-box telemetry.

---

# 118. Alertmanager

Alertmanager shall provide alert grouping, routing, inhibition and notification for Prometheus-based alerts.

```text
Prometheus
    │
    ▼
Alertmanager
    │
    ├── Platform
    ├── Application Team
    └── On-call
```

---

# 119. Alert Ownership

Every actionable alert requires an owner.

Bad:

```text
Alert
  │
  ▼
Shared channel
  │
  ▼
Everyone assumes someone else handles it
```

---

# 120. Severity Model

A simple model may include:

```text
Critical
High
Warning
Informational
```

Severity should reflect operational/user impact, not how frightening the metric name sounds.

---

# 121. Critical Alerts

Critical alerts should represent situations requiring immediate response.

Examples may include:

```text
Major production outage
Critical user journey unavailable
Severe sustained error rate
Data-service failure affecting production
```

---

# 122. Warning Alerts

Warnings indicate conditions requiring attention but not necessarily waking somebody immediately.

Examples:

```text
Capacity trending high
Disk growth
Elevated latency
Increasing Kafka lag
Certificate approaching expiry
```

---

# 123. Alert Fatigue

If operators receive hundreds of unactionable alerts, they will ignore alerts.

That is predictable human behavior, not an operator defect.

Alert volume must therefore be engineered.

---

# 124. Symptom-Based Alerting

Prefer alerting on user-visible symptoms.

Example:

```text
High API error rate
```

is generally more actionable than:

```text
CPU > 70% for 30 seconds
```

CPU may be high while the service remains healthy.

---

# 125. Cause-Based Alerts

Cause alerts still have value for conditions requiring action before user impact.

Examples:

```text
Disk nearly full
Certificate expiry
Replication failure
Backup failure
```

Use both approaches intentionally.

---

# 126. SLO Burn-Rate Alerts

For important services, alerts should eventually use error-budget burn rates.

```text
Error Budget
     │
     ▼
Consumption Rate
     │
     ▼
Too Fast?
   │
   ├── Yes → Alert
   └── No
```

This aligns paging with reliability impact.

---

# 127. Multi-Window Burn Rate

Using multiple observation windows can distinguish:

```text
Fast catastrophic burn
```

from:

```text
Slow sustained degradation
```

This is generally more useful than one static threshold.

---

# 128. Alert Grouping

Related alerts should be grouped where practical.

Otherwise one node failure may produce:

```text
50 pod alerts
20 service alerts
10 latency alerts
5 dependency alerts
```

for a single underlying incident.

---

# 129. Alert Inhibition

When a known parent failure explains child failures, downstream alerts may be inhibited.

Example:

```text
Cluster unreachable
      │
      ▼
Suppress redundant pod-level alerts
```

This reduces noise during major incidents.

---

# 130. Runbook Links

Actionable alerts should link to relevant operational guidance.

```text
Alert
  │
  ├── What happened?
  ├── Why does it matter?
  ├── Dashboard
  ├── Logs/trace
  └── Runbook
```

A message saying only `HighLatency=true` is inadequate.

---

# 131. Telemetry Security

Observability infrastructure contains operationally sensitive information.

Access must follow least privilege.

Not every user needs unrestricted access to:

```text
Production logs
Security events
Infrastructure details
Trace payload metadata
Audit information
```

---

# 132. Environment Isolation

At minimum telemetry must be strongly separated logically by:

```text
DEV
UAT
PROD
```

Production access should have stronger authorization.

---

# 133. Tenant Isolation

If future architecture requires stronger organizational/tenant separation, observability backends may require multi-tenancy controls.

This should not be simulated merely with dashboard folders if underlying data access remains unrestricted.

---

# 134. Encryption

Telemetry should be protected:

```text
In transit
→ TLS

At rest
→ Appropriate backend/storage encryption
```

including S3-backed long-term telemetry where applicable.

---

# 135. Telemetry Availability

Observability infrastructure should be highly available enough to remain useful during incidents.

A monitoring system that fails whenever the application is stressed provides little operational value.

---

# 136. Failure Independence

Where practical, observability components should avoid sharing every failure dependency with monitored applications.

For example, do not make the monitoring system dependent on the same overloaded application database it is supposed to diagnose.

---

# 137. Telemetry Backpressure

Collectors and backends can become overloaded.

The architecture should account for:

```text
Batching
Queues
Memory limits
Retry
Backpressure
Dropping policy
Capacity
```

Observability itself is a distributed system.

---

# 138. Telemetry Cost

Major cost drivers include:

```text
Log volume
Trace volume
Metric cardinality
Retention
CloudWatch ingestion
CloudWatch logs
Cross-AZ traffic
Object storage
Collector compute
Grafana capacity
```

Instrumentation decisions directly affect infrastructure cost.

---

# 139. Cost Control Hierarchy

Optimize in this order:

```text
Do we need this telemetry?
        │
        ▼
Can cardinality be reduced?
        │
        ▼
Can noisy logs be removed?
        │
        ▼
Can traces be sampled?
        │
        ▼
Can retention be reduced?
        │
        ▼
Can older data be archived?
```

Buying more storage should not be the first response.

---

# 140. Disaster Recovery

Observability DR requirements should distinguish:

```text
Configuration
Telemetry data
Dashboards
Alert rules
Runbooks
```

Configuration is usually more critical to restore than every historical DEBUG log.

---

# 141. Observability as Code

Critical configuration should live in version control where practical:

```text
Dashboards
Prometheus rules
Alert rules
ServiceMonitors
Collector configuration
Loki configuration
Tempo configuration
```

and should be deployed through the established GitOps process.

---

# 142. Governance

Ownership should be divided clearly.

```text
Application Teams
      │
      ├── Application metrics
      ├── Domain telemetry
      ├── Useful logs
      └── Service dashboards

Platform Team
      │
      ├── Prometheus
      ├── Grafana
      ├── Loki
      ├── Tempo
      ├── OTel Collectors
      └── Platform dashboards

SRE / Operations
      │
      ├── SLOs
      ├── Alerts
      ├── Incident workflows
      └── Runbooks

Security
      │
      ├── Telemetry access
      ├── Sensitive-data policy
      └── Retention requirements
```

---

# 143. Observability Anti-Patterns

Mediverse shall reject or strongly discourage:

```text
❌ Logging passwords/tokens
❌ Logging Authorization headers
❌ Global request-body logging
❌ DEBUG everywhere in production
❌ Every exception logged at every layer
❌ user_id as Prometheus label
❌ trace_id as Prometheus label
❌ request_id as Loki label
❌ Unlimited telemetry retention
❌ Collecting every trace forever
❌ Alerting on every metric
❌ Paging on transient CPU spikes
❌ Alerts without owners
❌ Alerts without actionable context
❌ Dashboards created only manually
❌ One giant dashboard for everything
❌ Metrics without units/meaning
❌ High-cardinality business metrics
❌ Treating CloudWatch as full application observability
❌ Treating logs as the only telemetry source
❌ Treating traces as a replacement for metrics
❌ Assuming "pod running" means application healthy
❌ Ignoring Kafka consumer lag
❌ Ignoring DB connection-pool saturation
❌ Monitoring Redis uptime but not eviction behavior
❌ Exposing Actuator publicly
❌ Sending sensitive browser data to telemetry
❌ Building an observability platform nobody owns
```

---

# 144. Investigation Workflow

A healthy operational investigation should look like:

```text
User Impact
    │
    ▼
SLO / Alert
    │
    ▼
Grafana Service Dashboard
    │
    ▼
RED Metrics
    │
    ▼
Problem Endpoint
    │
    ▼
Tempo Trace
    │
    ▼
Slow / Failed Span
    │
    ├──► Loki Logs
    │
    ├──► PostgreSQL Metrics
    │
    ├──► Redis Metrics
    │
    ├──► Kafka Metrics
    │
    └──► Kubernetes Metrics
             │
             ▼
          Root Cause
```

That is substantially more effective than SSHing into random nodes and running `grep`.

---

# 145. Observability Data Flow

```text
                   APPLICATIONS
                        │
          ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
          ▼             ▼             ▼
       Metrics         Logs         Traces
          │             │             │
          ▼             ▼             ▼
      Micrometer    Structured     OpenTelemetry
          │           Logging           │
          │             │               │
          ▼             ▼               ▼
     Prometheus        Loki        OTel Collector
          │             │               │
          │             │               ▼
          │             │             Tempo
          │             │               │
          └─────────────┼───────────────┘
                        ▼
                     Grafana
                        │
          ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
          ▼             ▼             ▼
      Dashboard      Explore        Alerts
```

---

# 146. AWS + Kubernetes Observability

```text
                         AWS
                          │
       ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐
       ▼                  ▼                  ▼
      ALB                RDS            ElastiCache
       │                  │                  │
       └──────────────────┼──────────────────┘
                          ▼
                     CloudWatch
                          │
                          ▼
                       Grafana


                          EKS
                           │
          ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
          ▼                ▼                ▼
        Nodes             Pods          Kubernetes
          │                │               State
          ▼                ▼                ▼
    Node Exporter      Application    kube-state-metrics
                           │
                           ▼
                       Prometheus
                           │
                           ▼
                        Grafana
```

---

# 147. Complete Mediverse Observability Architecture

```text
Users / Browser
      │
      ▼
Frontend Telemetry
      │
      ▼
OpenTelemetry
      │
      │
CloudFront → ALB → Gateway → Spring Boot Services
                         │
                         ├──── Metrics ───────► Prometheus
                         │
                         ├──── Logs ──────────► Loki
                         │
                         └──── Traces ────────► OTel Collector
                                                   │
                                                   ▼
                                                 Tempo
                                                   │
                     ┌─────────────────────────────┘
                     │
                     ▼
                  Grafana
                     │
        ┌────────────┼─────────────┐
        ▼            ▼             ▼
    Dashboards     Explore       Alerts
                                   │
                                   ▼
                              Alertmanager


Kubernetes ───────────────► Prometheus

Kafka ────────────────────► Prometheus

PostgreSQL ───────────────► Prometheus / CloudWatch

Redis ────────────────────► Prometheus / CloudWatch

AWS Services ─────────────► CloudWatch ─────► Grafana

Argo CD ──────────────────► Prometheus
```

---

# 148. Risks and Mitigations

| Risk                          | Mitigation                            |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| Sensitive data in logs        | Structured logging + redaction policy |
| Credential leakage            | Prohibit token/header logging         |
| Metric explosion              | Cardinality governance                |
| Loki index explosion          | Low-cardinality labels                |
| Trace cost                    | Sampling                              |
| Log cost                      | Levels + retention                    |
| CloudWatch cost               | Selective ingestion/retention         |
| Missing distributed context   | W3C Trace Context                     |
| Kafka trace gaps              | Message context propagation           |
| Alert fatigue                 | SLO/symptom-based alerts              |
| Missed incidents              | Synthetic + internal monitoring       |
| Monitoring outage             | HA architecture                       |
| Collector overload            | Scaling + batching/backpressure       |
| Uncontrolled dashboard drift  | Dashboard-as-code                     |
| Production telemetry exposure | RBAC                                  |
| Browser privacy leakage       | Frontend telemetry governance         |
| Slow incident diagnosis       | Metrics/logs/traces correlation       |
| Hidden DB saturation          | Pool + RDS monitoring                 |
| Hidden async backlog          | Kafka lag monitoring                  |

---
