---

# ADR-038 — Kubernetes Autoscaling, Capacity Management & Performance Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — PDB Limitation**.

---

# 61. Priority Classes

Kubernetes `PriorityClass` should distinguish critical platform workloads from ordinary application workloads.

Conceptually:

```text
Priority
   │
   ├── Critical Platform
   ├── Critical Application
   ├── Standard Application
   └── Batch / Background
```

This helps Kubernetes make scheduling decisions when cluster capacity becomes constrained.

---

# 62. Priority Is Not Free Capacity

Priority does not create resources.

If the cluster has:

```text
CPU available = 0
Memory available = 0
```

assigning everything a higher priority merely creates competing high-priority workloads.

Priority must therefore be selective.

---

# 63. Pod Preemption

When necessary, Kubernetes may evict lower-priority workloads to make room for higher-priority Pods.

```text
Cluster Full
    │
    ▼
Critical Pod Pending
    │
    ▼
Lower-Priority Pod Preempted
    │
    ▼
Critical Pod Scheduled
```

This behavior must be understood before introducing PriorityClasses.

---

# 64. System Workload Isolation

Critical cluster/platform components should not compete indiscriminately with application workloads.

Potential system workloads include:

```text
CoreDNS
Observability
Argo CD
Ingress components
Security agents
OTel Collectors
Controllers
```

A runaway application should not starve the infrastructure required to operate the cluster.

---

# 65. Dedicated System Capacity

Baseline managed node groups may provide stable capacity for critical platform workloads.

```text
EKS
 │
 ├── System Node Group
 │      └── Platform workloads
 │
 └── Karpenter Capacity
        └── Application workloads
```

Taints, tolerations and affinity rules may enforce this boundary.

---

# 66. Taints and Tolerations

Dedicated nodes can use taints.

```text
System Node
    │
    └── Taint: workload=system
```

Only approved workloads receive the matching toleration.

This prevents arbitrary application Pods from consuming reserved system capacity.

---

# 67. Graceful Termination

Applications must tolerate Pod termination correctly.

```text
Termination Requested
        │
        ▼
Pod stops receiving new traffic
        │
        ▼
In-flight requests finish
        │
        ▼
Resources close
        │
        ▼
Process exits
```

Autoscaling depends on safe termination just as much as safe startup.

---

# 68. SIGTERM Handling

Spring Boot services should respond correctly to termination signals.

The application should have enough time to:

```text
Stop accepting work
Finish eligible requests
Commit/rollback transactions
Stop consumers
Close connections
Flush required telemetry
```

before forced termination.

---

# 69. Termination Grace Period

`terminationGracePeriodSeconds` should match actual shutdown behavior.

Setting it arbitrarily low can kill valid in-flight work.

Setting it excessively high can make deployments and scale-down unnecessarily slow.

---

# 70. Connection Draining

Load-balancing behavior must allow terminating Pods to drain connections.

```text
ALB / Service
      │
      X──► Terminating Pod
      │
      └──► Healthy Pods
```

Otherwise users may receive errors during routine scaling or deployments.

---

# 71. Kafka Consumer Shutdown

Kafka consumers should stop gracefully.

```text
Consumer
   │
   ▼
Termination
   │
   ▼
Stop polling
   │
   ▼
Finish/commit eligible work
   │
   ▼
Leave consumer group
```

Abrupt termination can increase duplicate processing and rebalance disruption.

---

# 72. Scale-Up Behavior

Scale-up should normally react faster than scale-down.

```text
Demand ↑
   │
   ▼
Scale quickly

Demand ↓
   │
   ▼
Observe stability
   │
   ▼
Scale cautiously
```

Capacity shortage hurts users faster than temporary excess capacity hurts cost.

---

# 73. Scale-Down Stabilization

A stabilization window can prevent immediate scale-down after a short demand reduction.

Without it:

```text
Load ↑ → Scale Up
Load ↓ → Scale Down
Load ↑ → Scale Up
Load ↓ → Scale Down
```

produces oscillation.

---

# 74. Scaling Thrashing

Repeated scale-up/scale-down cycles waste resources and destabilize applications.

Causes may include:

```text
Noisy metrics
Bad thresholds
Insufficient stabilization
Long startup times
Incorrect requests
Highly bursty traffic
```

Scaling behavior itself must be monitored.

---

# 75. Minimum Capacity as Headroom

Critical services should maintain enough baseline capacity to absorb normal short-term spikes without waiting for:

```text
HPA
+
Scheduler
+
Karpenter
+
EC2 startup
+
Pod startup
```

Autoscaling has latency.

---

# 76. Capacity Headroom

Production should deliberately maintain headroom.

Conceptually:

```text
Available Capacity
████████████████████

Normal Load
████████████

Headroom
            ████████
```

Running permanently at 95–100% utilization leaves little room for failures or spikes.

---

# 77. Headroom Is Workload-Specific

There is no universal rule such as:

```text
Always keep exactly 30% free
```

Appropriate headroom depends on:

```text
Traffic volatility
Scaling latency
SLO
Failure model
Cost
Dependency limits
```

---

# 78. Concurrency Limits

Applications should limit how much concurrent work they accept.

```text
Incoming Requests
       │
       ▼
Concurrency Gate
   ┌───┴────┐
   ▼        ▼
Accept    Reject/Queue
```

Unlimited concurrency usually becomes resource exhaustion.

---

# 79. Little's Law Reality

If request latency increases while arrival rate remains high, the number of concurrent in-flight requests grows.

This means downstream slowness can consume:

```text
Threads
Memory
Connections
Queues
```

even when application CPU remains moderate.

---

# 80. Database Connection Budget

PostgreSQL connections are finite.

Suppose:

```text
20 Pods
×
20 connections per Pod
=
400 potential connections
```

Scaling to 100 Pods would create:

```text
100 × 20 = 2000
```

potential connections.

HPA limits must therefore account for database capacity.

---

# 81. Connection Pool Formula

Capacity planning should explicitly model:

```text
Maximum Application Pods
        ×
Maximum Connections Per Pod
        +
Administrative/System Connections
        <
Database Safe Connection Capacity
```

Do not discover this constraint during a production traffic spike.

---

# 82. HikariCP

Spring Boot's HikariCP pool should be tuned from actual concurrency requirements.

Bigger pools are not automatically faster.

Oversized pools can increase database contention.

---

# 83. Connection Acquisition

Monitor:

```text
Active
Idle
Pending
Timeout
Acquisition duration
```

A growing pending count is often an early saturation signal.

---

# 84. PgBouncer Direction

If connection scalability becomes a genuine constraint, a PostgreSQL connection proxy/pooler such as PgBouncer or an appropriate managed alternative may be evaluated.

It should not be introduced merely to hide fundamentally bad connection management.

---

# 85. Backpressure

When downstream systems cannot keep up, upstream systems must reduce or regulate demand.

```text
Producer
   │
   ▼
Consumer Capacity Reached
   │
   ▼
Backpressure
   │
   ▼
Producer Slows / Queue Builds
```

Without backpressure, overload propagates.

---

# 86. Queue-Based Load Leveling

Kafka can absorb temporary differences between producer and consumer rates.

```text
Traffic Spike
     │
     ▼
Producer
     │
     ▼
Kafka
██████████████
     │
     ▼
Consumers
```

This prevents every workload from needing instantaneous scaling.

---

# 87. Queue Is Not Infinite

Kafka backlog cannot be used as an excuse for permanently insufficient consumer capacity.

Monitor:

```text
Lag size
Lag growth rate
Oldest message age
Recovery time
```

A queue merely moves the overload boundary.

---

# 88. Load Shedding

When capacity is exhausted, intentionally rejecting lower-priority work can protect critical functionality.

```text
Overload
   │
   ▼
Load Shedding
   │
   ├── Critical request → Accept
   └── Non-critical request → Reject/defer
```

Controlled degradation is better than total collapse.

---

# 89. HTTP Overload Response

Where appropriate, overloaded services may return meaningful responses such as:

```text
429 Too Many Requests
503 Service Unavailable
```

rather than accepting work that will inevitably time out.

---

# 90. Retry-After

When the service can reasonably estimate recovery behavior, `Retry-After` may help clients avoid immediate aggressive retries.

Retries without coordination can amplify overload.

---

# 91. Retry Storm

Dangerous sequence:

```text
Service slows
    │
    ▼
Requests timeout
    │
    ▼
Clients retry
    │
    ▼
Traffic doubles
    │
    ▼
Service slows further
```

This can turn degradation into an outage.

---

# 92. Retry Policy

Retries should generally have:

```text
Maximum attempts
Timeout
Exponential backoff
Jitter
Idempotency awareness
```

Infinite or immediate retries are prohibited.

---

# 93. Circuit Breaker

Circuit breakers can prevent repeated calls to a dependency already known to be failing.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
Circuit Breaker
 ┌──┴─────┐
 ▼        ▼
Closed    Open
 │          X
 ▼          │
Dependency  Fast Failure/Fallback
```

---

# 94. Circuit Breaker States

Conceptually:

```text
CLOSED
  │ failures
  ▼
OPEN
  │ wait
  ▼
HALF-OPEN
  │ test
  ├── success → CLOSED
  └── failure → OPEN
```

Thresholds must be tuned from observed behavior.

---

# 95. Bulkhead Pattern

Failures should be isolated so one dependency cannot consume all application capacity.

Example:

```text
Application
   │
   ├── AI Worker Pool
   ├── Content API Pool
   └── Notification Pool
```

A blocked AI integration should not consume every thread required for core learning functionality.

---

# 96. Timeout Architecture

Every remote call should have a finite timeout.

```text
Service A
    │
    ▼
Service B

Timeout = bounded
```

Waiting forever is not resilience.

---

# 97. Timeout Hierarchy

Timeouts should make architectural sense.

Example:

```text
User request timeout        10s
   │
Service A downstream call    5s
   │
Service B DB operation        2s
```

A downstream timeout longer than the entire upstream request budget is often useless.

Exact values require testing.

---

# 98. Graceful Degradation

When non-critical dependencies fail, Mediverse should preserve useful functionality where possible.

Examples:

```text
Recommendation engine unavailable
        │
        ▼
Core learning content still works

Analytics pipeline delayed
        │
        ▼
Assessment submission still works
```

Not every dependency deserves the power to take down the entire platform.

---

# 99. Criticality Classification

Services/workflows should be classified.

Example:

```text
Tier 0 → Platform-critical
Tier 1 → Critical user journey
Tier 2 → Important
Tier 3 → Background / deferrable
```

Capacity, scaling and availability policies can then differ appropriately.

---

# 100. PostgreSQL Capacity

Database scaling requires monitoring and planning around:

```text
CPU
Memory
Connections
Storage
IOPS
Locks
Query latency
Replication
Vacuum behavior
```

Adding application Pods cannot compensate for an overloaded database indefinitely.

---

# 101. Query Optimization Before Scaling

If one query consumes 80% of database resources, increasing RDS size may postpone rather than solve the problem.

The preferred order is:

```text
Identify query
    │
    ▼
Analyze execution plan
    │
    ▼
Fix query/index/schema where appropriate
    │
    ▼
Measure
    │
    ▼
Scale infrastructure if still required
```

---

# 102. Read Scaling

Read-heavy workloads may eventually use:

```text
Primary
   │
   ├── Writes
   │
   └── Replicas → Reads
```

where consistency requirements permit.

Application architecture must explicitly understand replication lag.

---

# 103. Redis Capacity

Redis/ElastiCache capacity planning should consider:

```text
Memory
Evictions
Connections
CPU
Network
Hit ratio
Key distribution
TTL behavior
```

A cache at its memory boundary can create cascading database load.

---

# 104. Cache Stampede

When a popular cached object expires:

```text
Cache Entry Expires
       │
       ▼
1000 Requests
       │
       ▼
1000 DB Queries
```

This is a cache stampede.

Mitigation may involve:

```text
Request coalescing
TTL jitter
Background refresh
Stale-while-revalidate patterns
```

where appropriate.

---

# 105. Kafka Capacity

Kafka/MSK capacity planning should account for:

```text
Partitions
Replication
Broker CPU
Disk
Network
Producer throughput
Consumer throughput
Retention
Consumer lag
```

Partition count is both a scalability and operational design decision.

---

# 106. Partition Planning

Too few partitions restrict parallelism.

Too many partitions create additional metadata and operational overhead.

Partition count should reflect:

```text
Expected throughput
Consumer parallelism
Ordering requirements
Future growth
```

---

# 107. AI Workload Capacity

AI workloads may have fundamentally different resource characteristics:

```text
High CPU
High memory
GPU
Long-running requests
Large model memory
Batch processing
External model APIs
```

They should not be mixed blindly with ordinary Spring Boot capacity policies.

---

# 108. Dedicated AI Node Pools

GPU or specialized AI workloads should use dedicated node capacity.

```text
EKS
 │
 ├── General Application Nodes
 │
 └── AI/GPU Nodes
          │
          └── AI workloads
```

Taints/tolerations and node affinity should enforce placement.

---

# 109. GPU Scheduling

GPU workloads should request explicit GPU resources.

Conceptually:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    nvidia.com/gpu: 1
```

A GPU is a scarce and expensive schedulable resource.

---

# 110. GPU Scale-to-Zero

Where startup latency permits, non-interactive GPU workloads may scale aggressively down or to zero.

Keeping expensive GPU nodes idle continuously without a latency requirement is wasteful.

---

# 111. AI Concurrency

AI endpoints require explicit concurrency control.

One model instance may only support a limited number of concurrent operations before:

```text
Memory exhaustion
Latency explosion
GPU saturation
External API throttling
```

HPA alone cannot infer all of these constraints.

---

# 112. External AI APIs

If Mediverse uses external AI providers, local autoscaling cannot increase provider quota.

Capacity planning must include:

```text
Rate limits
Token limits
Concurrent request limits
Provider latency
Provider availability
Cost
```

---

# 113. Performance Testing

No production scaling policy should be considered mature without performance testing.

The primary test classes are:

```text
Load
Stress
Spike
Soak
```

Each answers a different question.

---

# 114. Load Testing

Load testing validates expected workload.

Question:

> Can Mediverse satisfy its performance objectives at anticipated traffic levels?

Example:

```text
Expected peak = X requests/sec
```

The actual target must come from product usage assumptions and measurement.

---

# 115. Stress Testing

Stress testing intentionally exceeds expected capacity.

Question:

> Where does Mediverse break, and how does it fail?

The goal is to identify the bottleneck and failure behavior.

---

# 116. Spike Testing

Spike testing applies sudden demand.

```text
100 RPS
   │
   │ sudden
   ▼
5000 RPS
```

This evaluates whether:

```text
HPA reacts
Karpenter reacts
Queues absorb load
Dependencies survive
```

---

# 117. Soak Testing

Soak testing maintains sustained load over an extended period.

It can expose:

```text
Memory leaks
Connection leaks
GC degradation
Disk growth
Queue accumulation
Resource fragmentation
```

that short tests miss.

---

# 118. Performance Test Environment

A tiny DEV environment does not accurately predict production behavior.

Meaningful tests require sufficiently production-like:

```text
Topology
Resource ratios
Dependencies
Data volumes
Configuration
```

without requiring every test environment to equal full production scale.

---

# 119. Test Data

Performance tests require realistic data characteristics.

Testing a database with 100 rows does not prove performance against millions of records.

Data volume and distribution matter.

---

# 120. Performance Budgets

Critical operations should have explicit performance objectives.

Examples:

```text
API latency
Frontend load performance
Database query latency
Kafka processing delay
AI response latency
```

Exact numbers belong to service SLOs and product requirements.

---

# 121. SLO-Driven Capacity

Capacity should ultimately be tied to user-visible objectives.

```text
Traffic
   │
   ▼
Capacity
   │
   ▼
Latency / Availability
   │
   ▼
SLI
   │
   ▼
SLO
```

A system with low CPU but failing latency SLOs is not sufficiently provisioned or designed.

---

# 122. Capacity Forecasting

Autoscaling handles short-term elasticity.

Forecasting handles longer-term growth.

Forecast:

```text
Users
Traffic
Storage
Kafka volume
Database growth
AI consumption
Network
```

over appropriate planning horizons.

---

# 123. Autoscaling Cannot Solve Everything

If traffic doubles every quarter, autoscaling does not eliminate the need for:

```text
Database planning
Partition planning
Quota increases
Architecture changes
Cost forecasting
Capacity reservations
```

Elasticity and capacity planning are complementary.

---

# 124. Rightsizing

Resources should periodically be compared against actual usage.

```text
Requested CPU: 4 cores
Observed p95:   0.3 cores
```

may indicate severe over-provisioning.

Conversely:

```text
Requested CPU: 0.2 cores
Observed:      constantly throttled
```

indicates under-provisioning.

---

# 125. Rightsizing Is Not Minimization

The objective is not:

```text
Use the smallest possible resources
```

The objective is:

```text
Meet reliability/performance targets
at economically reasonable capacity
```

Aggressive cost cutting that creates outages is not optimization.

---

# 126. FinOps Integration

Capacity telemetry should inform:

```text
Cost per environment
Cost per workload
Idle capacity
Spot usage
Node utilization
GPU utilization
Rightsizing opportunities
```

Engineering and cost decisions should use the same underlying capacity data.

---

# 127. Resource Ownership

Every workload should have identifiable ownership.

Without ownership, nobody is accountable for:

```text
Bad requests/limits
Waste
Scaling failures
Unbounded replicas
Performance regressions
```

---

# 128. Namespace Quotas

ResourceQuota may prevent one namespace/team from consuming unbounded cluster capacity.

Conceptually:

```text
Namespace
   │
   ├── CPU budget
   ├── Memory budget
   └── Object limits
```

Quotas should protect shared infrastructure without preventing legitimate scaling.

---

# 129. LimitRange

LimitRange may provide namespace-level defaults/bounds for resource configuration.

It should act as a guardrail, not replace explicit workload sizing.

---

# 130. Capacity Failure Scenario

Consider:

```text
Traffic × 10
    │
    ▼
HPA scales Pods
    │
    ▼
Nodes full
    │
    ▼
Karpenter adds nodes
    │
    ▼
Pods start
    │
    ▼
DB connections explode
    │
    ▼
PostgreSQL saturates
    │
    ▼
Latency rises
    │
    ▼
Retries increase
    │
    ▼
System collapses
```

This demonstrates why "enable autoscaling" is not a complete architecture.

---

# 131. Corrected Failure Architecture

A resilient version introduces:

```text
Traffic Spike
    │
    ▼
Rate / Concurrency Controls
    │
    ▼
HPA / KEDA
    │
    ▼
Bounded Replica Count
    │
    ▼
Connection Budget
    │
    ▼
Queue / Backpressure
    │
    ▼
Dependency Protection
    │
    ▼
Graceful Degradation
```

---

# 132. Availability During Node Loss

Capacity planning must assume node failure.

If normal operation consumes virtually all cluster capacity, losing one node can immediately cause service degradation.

This is why failure headroom matters.

---

# 133. Availability During AZ Loss

For high-criticality services, capacity design should consider whether remaining Availability Zones can carry required traffic after an AZ failure.

```text
AZ-A  X

AZ-B + AZ-C
     │
     ▼
Can they sustain required service?
```

Multi-AZ placement alone does not answer that question.

---

# 134. Scaling During Incident

Autoscaling systems should remain observable during incidents.

ADR-037 should expose:

```text
HPA desired/current replicas
KEDA activity
Pending Pods
Karpenter provisioning
Node capacity
CPU throttling
OOM events
DB saturation
Kafka lag
```

Otherwise operators cannot tell whether scaling is helping.

---

# 135. Scaling Alerts

Useful alerts may include:

```text
HPA at maximum replicas
Pods unschedulable
Karpenter provisioning failures
Persistent CPU throttling
Repeated OOMKilled
DB connection exhaustion
Kafka lag continuously growing
Node capacity shortage
GPU capacity unavailable
```

These should be actionable, not noisy.

---

# 136. Scaling Auditability

Important scaling configuration belongs in Git.

```text
Deployment resources
HPA
KEDA ScaledObject
PDB
PriorityClass
Topology constraints
NodePool
NodeClass
```

Changes therefore flow through review and GitOps.

---

# 137. Capacity Governance

```text
Application Teams
      │
      ├── Application performance
      ├── Requests/limits
      ├── HPA policy
      └── Concurrency behavior

Platform Team
      │
      ├── Karpenter
      ├── Node pools
      ├── Quotas
      ├── Scheduling policy
      └── Cluster capacity

Database Team / Platform
      │
      ├── PostgreSQL capacity
      ├── Connection budgets
      └── Storage/IOPS

SRE
      │
      ├── SLOs
      ├── Headroom
      ├── Performance testing
      └── Capacity forecasting

FinOps
      │
      └── Cost efficiency
```

---

# 138. Capacity Review

Critical services should periodically review:

```text
Peak demand
Resource utilization
HPA behavior
Startup latency
DB connection usage
Dependency saturation
Error budget
Cost
Forecast growth
```

Autoscaling configurations should not be written once and forgotten.

---

# 139. Performance Regression

CI/release processes should eventually detect major performance regressions for critical workloads.

A release that passes unit tests but doubles API latency is still defective.

Performance validation should be proportionate to service criticality.

---

# 140. Capacity Anti-Patterns

Mediverse shall reject or strongly discourage:

```text
❌ No CPU/memory requests
❌ Copying identical resources to every service
❌ Setting JVM heap equal to container memory
❌ Treating CPU limits as harmless
❌ HPA without maxReplicas
❌ Scaling APIs without DB connection budgets
❌ Scaling solely on latency without dependency analysis
❌ KEDA consumers beyond useful Kafka partition concurrency
❌ Scale-to-zero for latency-critical APIs without justification
❌ One replica for critical production services
❌ All replicas on one node/AZ
❌ Missing PDBs for critical workloads
❌ Making every workload highest priority
❌ No graceful shutdown
❌ Immediate scale-down after traffic drops
❌ Unlimited application concurrency
❌ Infinite retries
❌ No timeout on remote calls
❌ Treating Kafka as infinite storage for overload
❌ Increasing DB size before investigating pathological queries
❌ Unbounded database connection pools
❌ Mixing expensive GPU workloads with general nodes
❌ Idle GPU fleets without latency justification
❌ Performance testing only after production incidents
❌ Testing with unrealistic data
❌ Running cluster capacity permanently near exhaustion
❌ Assuming autoscaling replaces forecasting
❌ Optimizing cost at the expense of SLOs
```

---

# 141. Scaling Decision Hierarchy

When load increases:

```text
                 Demand
                    │
                    ▼
          Is service healthy?
                    │
          ┌─────────┴─────────┐
          ▼                   ▼
         YES                  NO
          │                   │
          ▼                   ▼
Is demand signal valid?   Find bottleneck
          │                   │
          ▼                   ▼
      Scale Pods       DB / Cache / Kafka /
          │            external dependency?
          ▼                   │
Enough nodes?                 ▼
    │                    Protect dependency
 ┌──┴──┐                 │
 ▼     ▼                  ▼
YES    NO             Backpressure /
 │      │             load shedding
 ▼      ▼
Serve Karpenter
        │
        ▼
      Nodes
```

---

# 142. Application Scaling Architecture

```text
                   HTTP TRAFFIC
                        │
                        ▼
                       ALB
                        │
                        ▼
                  API / Gateway
                        │
                        ▼
                 Spring Services
                        │
              ┌─────────┴─────────┐
              ▼                   ▼
          Prometheus          Dependencies
              │                   │
              ▼                   ├── PostgreSQL
             HPA                  ├── Redis
              │                   └── External APIs
              ▼
        Desired Replicas
              │
              ▼
       Kubernetes Scheduler
              │
              ▼
          Karpenter
              │
              ▼
           EC2 Nodes
```

---

# 143. Event-Driven Scaling Architecture

```text
Producer
   │
   ▼
 Kafka
   │
   ├──────────────► Prometheus
   │
   │                   │
   │                   ▼
   │                  KEDA
   │                   │
   ▼                   ▼
Backlog           Consumer Replicas
                       │
                       ▼
                    Workers
```

Scaling is based on work waiting to be processed.

---

# 144. Resource Management Architecture

```text
                    WORKLOAD
                       │
            ┌──────────┼──────────┐
            ▼          ▼          ▼
          CPU        Memory    Concurrency
            │          │          │
            ▼          ▼          ▼
        Requests     Limits      Pools
            │          │          │
            └──────────┼──────────┘
                       ▼
                   Kubernetes
                       │
             ┌─────────┴─────────┐
             ▼                   ▼
            HPA                 VPA
             │             Recommendations
             ▼
          Replicas
```

---

# 145. Dependency Protection Architecture

```text
Incoming Traffic
       │
       ▼
Rate / Concurrency Limit
       │
       ▼
Application
       │
       ├── Timeout
       ├── Retry + Backoff
       ├── Circuit Breaker
       ├── Bulkhead
       └── Backpressure
             │
             ▼
        Dependencies
       ┌─────┼─────┐
       ▼     ▼     ▼
      DB    Redis Kafka
```

This boundary is critical. Horizontal scaling without it can turn application elasticity into dependency overload.

---

# 146. Complete Capacity Control Loop

```text
                    USER DEMAND
                         │
                         ▼
                      MEDIVERSE
                         │
                         ▼
                   TELEMETRY
                         │
             ┌───────────┼───────────┐
             ▼           ▼           ▼
            CPU      Request Rate   Queue Lag
             │           │           │
             ▼           ▼           ▼
            HPA         HPA         KEDA
             │           │           │
             └───────────┼───────────┘
                         ▼
                  Desired Pods
                         │
                         ▼
                    Scheduler
                         │
                 Capacity exists?
                   ┌─────┴─────┐
                   ▼           ▼
                  YES          NO
                   │           │
                   ▼           ▼
                Schedule   Karpenter
                               │
                               ▼
                           EC2 Nodes
                               │
                               ▼
                         New Capacity
```

---

# 147. Full Mediverse Performance Architecture

```text
Users
  │
  ▼
CloudFront
  │
  ▼
ALB
  │
  ▼
Gateway
  │
  ├── Rate Limiting
  ├── Concurrency Control
  └── Load Shedding
  │
  ▼
Spring Boot Services
  │
  ├──────────── HPA ───────────────┐
  │                                │
  ├──────────── KEDA ────────┐     │
  │                          │     │
  ▼                          ▼     ▼
Kafka                     Workers Pods
  │                                │
  │                                ▼
  │                           Kubernetes
  │                                │
  │                                ▼
  │                           Karpenter
  │                                │
  │                                ▼
  │                             EC2
  │
  ├────────► PostgreSQL
  ├────────► Redis
  └────────► Search / AI

          ▲
          │
Prometheus + OpenTelemetry
          │
          ▼
Capacity / SLO Decisions
```

---

# 148. Risks and Mitigations

| Risk                       | Mitigation                                 |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Pod resource starvation    | Requests + rightsizing                     |
| OOMKilled                  | JVM/container memory budgeting             |
| CPU throttling             | Measure before enforcing aggressive limits |
| Insufficient replicas      | HPA                                        |
| Event backlog              | KEDA                                       |
| No node capacity           | Karpenter                                  |
| Spot interruption          | Diversification + graceful rescheduling    |
| AZ/node concentration      | Topology spread                            |
| Maintenance outage         | PDB                                        |
| System workload starvation | Dedicated system capacity                  |
| Scaling oscillation        | Stabilization                              |
| Cold-start latency         | Minimum replicas + startup optimization    |
| DB overload from HPA       | Connection budget + max replicas           |
| Retry storm                | Backoff + jitter + bounded attempts        |
| Dependency cascade         | Circuit breakers + bulkheads               |
| Overload collapse          | Backpressure + load shedding               |
| Kafka backlog              | Lag monitoring + consumer scaling          |
| Cache stampede             | TTL/request-coalescing strategies          |
| GPU waste                  | Dedicated elastic GPU capacity             |
| Unknown breaking point     | Stress testing                             |
| Long-term degradation      | Soak testing                               |
| Traffic spike failure      | Spike testing                              |
| Cost waste                 | Rightsizing + FinOps                       |
| Capacity exhaustion        | Forecasting + headroom                     |

---

# ADR-039 — Backup, Disaster Recovery, Business Continuity & Multi-Region Resilience Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Backup Isolation**.

---

# 61. AWS Backup Architecture

AWS Backup should provide centralized backup policy management for supported AWS resources where it adds operational value.

```text
Production Resources
        │
        ▼
    AWS Backup
        │
        ▼
   Backup Plan
        │
        ▼
   Backup Vault
        │
        ├── Local Copy
        ├── Cross-Account Copy
        └── Cross-Region Copy
```

It should complement service-native recovery capabilities rather than blindly replace them.

---

# 62. Backup Plans

Backup policies should define:

```text
Schedule
Retention
Lifecycle
Resource scope
Vault destination
Cross-region copies
Cross-account copies
```

Different workload tiers should receive different policies.

---

# 63. Tag-Based Backup Assignment

Resources can be assigned to backup policies using controlled tags where appropriate.

Example conceptually:

```text
backup-tier = critical
backup-tier = standard
backup-tier = none
```

Tag governance must prevent critical resources from silently escaping backup coverage.

---

# 64. Backup Vaults

Backup vaults provide controlled storage boundaries for recovery points.

Recommended logical separation:

```text
AWS Backup
    │
    ├── Production Vault
    ├── Long-Term Vault
    └── Isolated Recovery Vault
```

Access should follow least privilege.

---

# 65. Vault Access

Application deployment roles should not automatically have permission to delete backups.

```text
Application Role
      │
      X
Delete Recovery Points
```

Compromising an application should not automatically compromise its recovery mechanism.

---

# 66. Backup Immutability

Critical recovery assets should use immutable controls where justified.

The objective is:

```text
Attacker compromises production
           │
           ▼
Deletes production
           │
           ▼
Attempts to delete backups
           │
           X
      Immutable Vault
```

---

# 67. Vault Lock

AWS Backup Vault Lock should be evaluated for critical backup vaults requiring stronger retention enforcement.

This can protect recovery points against unauthorized or accidental deletion.

---

# 68. Immutability Warning

Immutability is powerful precisely because administrators cannot casually override it.

Incorrect retention configuration can therefore create:

```text
Unexpected storage cost
Compliance problems
Operational constraints
```

Vault Lock policies must be reviewed carefully before enforcement.

---

# 69. Cross-Account Backup

Critical backups should be copied to a dedicated backup/security account where supported.

```text
Production Account
       │
       ▼
    Backup
       │
       ▼
Backup Account
```

This reduces the blast radius of production-account compromise.

---

# 70. Cross-Region Backup

Critical recovery points should also exist outside the primary region where RTO/RPO requires regional disaster protection.

```text
Primary Region
      │
      ▼
Backup Copy
      │
      ▼
DR Region
```

---

# 71. Combined Isolation

For the highest-value recovery assets:

```text
Production Account
Primary Region
       │
       ▼
Cross-Account
+
Cross-Region
       │
       ▼
Backup Account
DR Region
```

provides stronger failure-domain separation.

---

# 72. Ransomware Resilience

DR design must assume destructive credentials may be used intentionally.

Controls should include:

```text
Least privilege
MFA
Immutable backups
Cross-account isolation
Versioning
Restricted deletion
Audit logging
Credential separation
Restore testing
```

Backups accessible to the same compromised administrator are weaker than they appear.

---

# 73. Recovery Credentials

Emergency recovery access must itself be recoverable.

If the organization loses:

```text
Identity provider
Primary account access
Normal administrative path
```

there must still be a controlled emergency access mechanism.

---

# 74. Break-Glass Access

A tightly controlled break-glass process should exist for catastrophic identity/access failures.

Requirements include:

```text
Strong authentication
Restricted membership
Auditability
Secure credential custody
Periodic testing
Documented activation
Post-use credential rotation
```

It should not become a convenient alternative to normal access.

---

# 75. KMS Dependency

Encryption introduces a critical recovery dependency:

> **Backups are useless if the required decryption keys cannot be used during recovery.**

KMS architecture must therefore be included in DR planning.

---

# 76. KMS Key Recovery

Recovery planning should document which data depends on which KMS keys.

```text
RDS Backup ──────► KMS Key
S3 Objects ──────► KMS Key
EBS Snapshot ────► KMS Key
Secrets ─────────► KMS Key
```

Key deletion or inaccessible key policy can make otherwise valid backups unusable.

---

# 77. Cross-Region Encryption

Cross-region recovery must use encryption architecture compatible with the destination region.

The recovery procedure should not assume that a primary-region encryption dependency automatically exists in Region B.

---

# 78. KMS Deletion Protection

Destructive key operations require strong governance.

Key deletion should involve:

```text
Restricted IAM
Approval
Waiting period
Audit trail
Monitoring
```

Critical encryption keys are part of the recoverability boundary.

---

# 79. ECR Recovery

Container images are required to reconstruct applications.

```text
GitOps
  │
  ▼
Deployment
  │
  ▼
Image: mediverse/content-service:v5
```

If that image no longer exists, Git alone may not reproduce the exact historical deployment immediately.

---

# 80. ECR Cross-Region Replication

Critical production repositories should support replication to the DR region where appropriate.

```text
ECR Region A
     │
     ▼
Replication
     │
     ▼
ECR Region B
```

This accelerates regional recovery.

---

# 81. Immutable Image References

Production deployments should use immutable artifact references.

Preferred:

```text
image digest
```

or controlled immutable version tags.

Avoid depending on mutable tags such as:

```text
latest
```

during disaster reconstruction.

---

# 82. Artifact Retention

ECR lifecycle policies must not delete artifacts still required for:

```text
Rollback
DR
Audit
Supported releases
```

Storage cleanup must understand release-retention requirements.

---

# 83. Secrets Manager Recovery

Applications depend on secrets such as:

```text
Database credentials
External API credentials
Signing material
Integration secrets
```

Secret availability must therefore be part of regional recovery planning.

---

# 84. Secrets Are Not GitOps Data

Plaintext secrets must not be recovered by storing them directly in Git.

GitOps should reference approved secret-management mechanisms.

---

# 85. Regional Secrets

Where the DR region requires equivalent secrets, the design must establish how they are:

```text
Replicated
Recreated
Rotated
Validated
```

without insecure manual copying during an incident.

---

# 86. Secret Rotation During Disaster

If compromise caused the disaster, restoring old secrets may restore the compromise.

Recovery may require:

```text
Restore infrastructure
       │
       ▼
Rotate credentials
       │
       ▼
Update dependencies
       │
       ▼
Activate workloads
```

Recovery and credential rotation must therefore be coordinated.

---

# 87. EBS Snapshots

EBS-backed persistent workloads requiring recovery should use appropriate snapshot strategies.

However, Mediverse should avoid accumulating critical application state on unmanaged Kubernetes volumes when managed durable services are more appropriate.

---

# 88. EFS Recovery

If EFS is introduced for shared persistent files, its recovery requirements must include:

```text
Backup
Restore
Cross-region requirement
Permissions
Encryption
Application consistency
```

A shared filesystem can become a hidden Tier-1 dependency.

---

# 89. Application-Consistent Backups

Storage-level snapshots are not automatically application-consistent.

For some workloads, recovery may require coordination with:

```text
Transactions
Filesystem writes
Database state
Application quiescing
```

The recovery guarantee must be understood per technology.

---

# 90. Observability Recovery

During a disaster, operators need observability more than usual.

Recovery planning should include:

```text
Grafana configuration
Prometheus rules
Alert definitions
OTel configuration
Dashboards
Runbooks
Critical historical telemetry where required
```

---

# 91. Observability Configuration Recovery

ADR-037 already established observability-as-code.

Therefore:

```text
Git
 │
 ▼
Dashboards
Alerts
Collectors
ServiceMonitors
 │
 ▼
Recovered Observability Stack
```

should be possible without recreating everything manually.

---

# 92. Historical Telemetry

Not every historical metric or trace needs immediate DR restoration.

Priority should generally be:

```text
Current operational visibility
        │
        ▼
Alerting
        │
        ▼
Recent incident context
        │
        ▼
Historical telemetry
```

unless compliance requirements dictate otherwise.

---

# 93. DR Networking

The secondary region requires a predesigned network topology.

Potential foundation:

```text
DR Region
   │
   └── VPC
       ├── Public Subnets
       ├── Private Application Subnets
       ├── Data Subnets
       ├── Route Tables
       ├── NAT/egress
       ├── Security Groups
       └── VPC Endpoints
```

Do not design this during the outage.

---

# 94. CIDR Planning

Primary and DR network ranges should avoid unnecessary overlap.

Overlapping CIDRs can complicate:

```text
Inter-region connectivity
VPN
Transit Gateway
Recovery tooling
Hybrid connectivity
```

Network address planning is therefore part of DR.

---

# 95. Security Parity

The DR region must not become a weaker security environment.

Recovery infrastructure should preserve:

```text
IAM controls
Encryption
Network segmentation
Logging
Secrets management
Security policies
```

A disaster is not justification for abandoning security architecture.

---

# 96. Route 53

Route 53 should provide DNS-level regional routing/failover where applicable.

Conceptually:

```text
Users
  │
  ▼
Route 53
  │
  ├── Primary healthy ──► Region A
  │
  └── Primary failed ───► Region B
```

---

# 97. Health Checks

Failover decisions require meaningful health signals.

A health check should not merely verify:

```text
TCP port 443 accepts connection
```

if the application cannot actually serve critical workflows.

---

# 98. Deep Health Checks

A regional readiness endpoint may validate enough dependencies to determine whether the region can safely receive traffic.

But it should avoid becoming so deep that one non-critical dependency marks the entire region unavailable.

---

# 99. Automatic vs Manual Failover

Not every regional failover should be fully automatic.

For stateful systems, automatic routing before database authority is established can create severe data problems.

Preferred critical sequence may be:

```text
Detect disaster
      │
      ▼
Validate condition
      │
      ▼
Establish data authority
      │
      ▼
Activate applications
      │
      ▼
Validate
      │
      ▼
Shift traffic
```

---

# 100. DNS TTL

DNS TTL affects failover speed.

```text
High TTL
→ slower propagation
→ lower DNS query load

Low TTL
→ faster change visibility
→ higher query activity
```

TTL should reflect actual recovery requirements.

---

# 101. CloudFront

CloudFront can remain a global entry layer while origins change during regional recovery.

```text
Users
   │
   ▼
CloudFront
   │
   ▼
Regional Origin
```

Origin failover behavior must match application/data architecture.

---

# 102. CDN Does Not Solve Backend DR

CloudFront may continue serving cached static content while the transactional backend is unavailable.

That can improve degraded-mode experience, but it does not recover:

```text
Authentication
Assessment submission
User progress
Dynamic APIs
Database writes
```

---

# 103. TLS Certificates

DR must account for certificate availability and validation.

A recovered region that cannot terminate HTTPS is not operational.

Certificate dependencies should be provisioned before disaster where required.

---

# 104. External DNS Dependencies

Regional recovery may also depend on:

```text
Domain registrar
DNS provider
Certificate validation
External identity provider
Email provider
AI provider
Payment/integration providers
```

These dependencies belong in recovery planning.

---

# 105. Dependency Recovery Graph

Services should have an explicit dependency graph.

```text
Network
  │
  ▼
Security / IAM / KMS
  │
  ▼
Database / Kafka / Redis
  │
  ▼
EKS
  │
  ▼
Platform Services
  │
  ▼
Applications
  │
  ▼
Ingress
  │
  ▼
DNS Traffic
```

Recovery order matters.

---

# 106. Recovery Sequencing

Starting every service simultaneously is usually wrong.

For example:

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
Database unavailable
    │
    ▼
Crash / Retry Storm
```

Dependencies should become ready before dependent workloads are allowed to generate uncontrolled load.

---

# 107. EKS Bootstrap

A reconstructed cluster should follow a documented bootstrap sequence.

Conceptually:

```text
Terraform
   │
   ▼
EKS
   │
   ▼
Core Add-ons
   │
   ▼
Networking
   │
   ▼
Storage Drivers
   │
   ▼
Secrets Integration
   │
   ▼
Observability
   │
   ▼
Argo CD
   │
   ▼
Applications
```

---

# 108. Argo CD Bootstrap

Argo CD itself cannot be recovered by saying:

> "Argo CD will restore everything."

Something must first restore Argo CD.

The bootstrap mechanism must therefore exist outside the Argo-managed dependency loop.

---

# 109. GitOps Application Waves

Argo CD sync waves or equivalent dependency controls may restore components in stages.

Example:

```text
Wave 0 → Cluster foundations
Wave 1 → Security / secrets
Wave 2 → Data integrations
Wave 3 → Platform services
Wave 4 → Applications
Wave 5 → Ingress / exposure
```

Exact ordering depends on actual dependencies.

---

# 110. DR Configuration

Region-specific configuration should be explicit.

Avoid hidden assumptions such as:

```text
region = us-east-1
```

hardcoded throughout application or deployment code.

Regional parameters belong in controlled configuration.

---

# 111. DR Application Validation

Before routing users, validate:

```text
Authentication
Database connectivity
Redis connectivity
Kafka
Critical APIs
Content access
Object storage
Critical external integrations
Observability
```

A successful Kubernetes deployment does not prove service recovery.

---

# 112. Smoke Tests

Automated smoke tests should run during DR activation.

```text
DR Environment
      │
      ▼
Smoke Tests
      │
      ├── Login
      ├── Read content
      ├── API call
      ├── DB operation
      └── Critical workflow
```

Traffic should shift only after defined gates pass.

---

# 113. Data Validation

Recovered data should be validated for:

```text
Expected timestamp
Schema
Integrity
Record availability
Replication state
Application compatibility
```

A database being `available` does not prove correct recovery.

---

# 114. Degraded Mode

Business continuity may allow partial functionality.

Example:

```text
Full Mediverse
      │
      ▼
Regional Disaster
      │
      ▼
Degraded Mediverse
      │
      ├── Learning content available
      ├── Read-only functionality
      └── Some non-critical features disabled
```

This may provide much better continuity than waiting for every subsystem.

---

# 115. Read-Only Mode

In some failure scenarios, safe read-only operation may be preferable to risky writes.

```text
Database authority uncertain
        │
        ▼
Disable writes
        │
        ▼
Preserve safe reads
```

This requires application support and explicit business approval.

---

# 116. Feature Flags During DR

Feature flags can disable non-critical functionality.

Examples:

```text
AI generation       OFF
Recommendations     OFF
Analytics           DELAYED
Core learning       ON
Authentication      ON
```

This reduces dependencies and resource requirements during recovery.

---

# 117. Third-Party Failure

Business continuity must account for providers outside AWS.

Examples:

```text
Identity provider
Email/SMS
AI provider
External APIs
CDN/DNS
Payment provider if introduced
```

Multi-region AWS architecture does nothing if the only identity provider is unavailable globally.

---

# 118. Third-Party Degradation

For each important external provider determine:

```text
Can the feature degrade?
Can requests queue?
Is there an alternative provider?
Can cached data be used?
Should the feature fail closed?
Should the feature fail open?
```

Security-sensitive functions should not fail open casually.

---

# 119. Disaster Declaration

DR activation should have defined authority.

A regional failover is a major operational action.

Define:

```text
Who can declare disaster?
Who approves failover?
Who leads recovery?
Who owns database promotion?
Who controls DNS?
Who communicates externally?
```

---

# 120. Incident Command

Major disasters require clear command structure.

Conceptually:

```text
Incident Commander
      │
      ├── Infrastructure Lead
      ├── Application Lead
      ├── Data Lead
      ├── Security Lead
      └── Communications Lead
```

Ten engineers independently changing production is not an incident-management strategy.

---

# 121. Communication

Business continuity includes communication.

Stakeholders may include:

```text
Engineering
Operations
Security
Leadership
Faculty
Students
Support teams
External partners
```

Communication templates should exist before incidents.

---

# 122. Status Communication

During a major outage, updates should communicate:

```text
Impact
Known scope
Current mitigation
Workaround if available
Recovery status
Next update time
```

Avoid unsupported recovery-time promises.

---

# 123. DR Runbook

The operational runbook should specify executable steps.

Example:

```text
1. Confirm disaster criteria
2. Freeze risky production changes
3. Establish incident command
4. Validate backup/replica
5. Activate DR data layer
6. Scale DR infrastructure
7. Bootstrap applications
8. Execute smoke tests
9. Shift traffic
10. Validate SLOs
11. Communicate recovery
```

The actual runbook must contain concrete commands, owners and validation criteria.

---

# 124. Runbook Automation

Repeatable recovery steps should be automated where safe.

But automation must not remove critical stateful decision gates.

Good automation:

```text
Provision infrastructure
Deploy applications
Run validation
Generate status
```

Potentially dangerous blind automation:

```text
Automatically promote database
Automatically redirect all users
```

without confirming disaster state.

---

# 125. DR Testing

A DR plan that exists only as documentation is unproven.

Testing should include:

```text
Backup restore tests
Component recovery
Cluster rebuild
Regional failover simulation
Failback
Business workflow validation
```

---

# 126. Game Days

Scheduled DR game days should exercise realistic failure scenarios.

Example:

```text
Scenario:
Primary region considered unavailable.

Team must:
→ activate DR
→ recover dependencies
→ validate application
→ shift test traffic
→ measure recovery time
```

---

# 127. Game-Day Objective

The objective is not to prove the architecture is perfect.

It is to discover:

```text
Missing permissions
Broken Terraform
Expired secrets
Incorrect documentation
Unexpected dependencies
Slow restores
DNS problems
Human coordination problems
```

before a real disaster does.

---

# 128. Chaos Engineering

Controlled failure injection can test resilience below full DR scale.

Examples:

```text
Kill Pods
Terminate nodes
Block dependency
Increase latency
Simulate AZ capacity loss
Break network path
```

Chaos experiments require safety boundaries and rollback mechanisms.

---

# 129. Chaos Is Not Random Destruction

Good chaos engineering begins with a hypothesis.

Example:

> If one application node fails, critical API availability remains within the SLO.

Then the failure is introduced and measured.

Randomly breaking production resources proves little.

---

# 130. Backup Monitoring

Backup jobs must be monitored.

Alerts should cover:

```text
Backup failure
Missed backup
Copy failure
Vault problems
Retention anomalies
Replication failure
Restore-test failure
```

Silent backup failure is unacceptable.

---

# 131. Recovery Evidence

Critical recovery tests should record:

```text
Backup used
Recovery point
Start time
Restore completion
Application validation
Measured RTO
Measured RPO
Failures encountered
Corrective actions
```

This converts DR from belief into evidence.

---

# 132. RTO Measurement

Actual RTO should be measured:

```text
Disaster declaration
        │
        ▼
Recovery starts
        │
        ▼
Service validated
        │
        ▼
Traffic restored
```

If target RTO is one hour but repeated exercises take five hours, the architecture does not meet its stated objective.

---

# 133. RPO Measurement

Actual recoverable data position should also be measured.

```text
Disaster Time
     │
     ▼
Latest Valid Recovery Point
```

The difference represents actual data-loss exposure.

---

# 134. Failback Testing

Failback deserves explicit testing.

```text
Region A
   X
   │
   ▼
Region B ACTIVE
   │
   ▼
Region A recovered
   │
   ▼
Data synchronization
   │
   ▼
Controlled failback
```

Failback can be more dangerous than failover because data has changed while the secondary region was active.

---

# 135. Backup Retention

Retention should reflect:

```text
Operational recovery
Compliance
Data classification
Cost
Legal requirements
Historical recovery needs
```

Keeping everything forever is neither cheap nor automatically compliant.

---

# 136. Data Deletion Requirements

Backup retention must be reconciled with legitimate data-deletion requirements.

Immutable retention and privacy/deletion obligations must be designed together.

This requires governance rather than ad-hoc engineering decisions.

---

# 137. DR Cost

Increasing resilience usually increases cost.

Conceptually:

```text
Backup/Restore
      $
      │
Pilot Light
      $$
      │
Warm Standby
      $$$
      │
Active/Passive high capacity
      $$$$
      │
Active/Active
      $$$$$ + complexity
```

The cheapest architecture is not necessarily sufficient; the most expensive is not automatically justified.

---

# 138. Resilience Economics

The decision should compare:

```text
Expected business impact of downtime
              versus
Cost of reducing downtime
```

A background analytics service does not need the same regional architecture as authentication or core learning workflows.

---

# 139. DR Ownership

Responsibilities should be explicit.

```text
Application Teams
      ├── Application recovery
      ├── Smoke tests
      └── Degraded mode

Platform Team
      ├── EKS
      ├── Networking
      ├── Terraform
      └── GitOps bootstrap

Data Team
      ├── PostgreSQL
      ├── Kafka
      └── Data validation

Security
      ├── Backup isolation
      ├── KMS
      ├── Emergency access
      └── Compromise recovery

SRE / Operations
      ├── RTO/RPO
      ├── Runbooks
      ├── Game days
      └── Incident command
```

---

# 140. DR Anti-Patterns

Mediverse shall reject or strongly discourage:

```text
❌ Calling Multi-AZ "disaster recovery"
❌ Calling replication "backup"
❌ Backups only in production account
❌ Backups only in primary region for critical data
❌ Never testing restores
❌ Assuming successful backup job means usable recovery
❌ Storing critical state only in Pods
❌ Manual console-only DR
❌ Terraform without state recovery
❌ GitOps without Argo CD bootstrap strategy
❌ Mutable image tags for DR
❌ Deleting historical release images too aggressively
❌ Plaintext secrets in Git
❌ Forgetting KMS dependencies
❌ Automatic regional traffic shift before data authority
❌ Ignoring split-brain
❌ Designing failover but not failback
❌ Hardcoded primary-region configuration
❌ Restoring compromised credentials after security incidents
❌ Treating Redis cache as durable source of truth
❌ Assuming Kafka is automatically a backup
❌ No external dependency strategy
❌ No degraded operating mode
❌ No incident commander
❌ Runbooks with no owners
❌ RTO/RPO never measured
❌ Active/active solely for architectural prestige
```

---

# 141. Regional Failover Sequence

```text
               DISASTER DETECTED
                       │
                       ▼
                Confirm Impact
                       │
                       ▼
              Declare Disaster?
                  ┌────┴────┐
                  ▼         ▼
                 NO        YES
                  │         │
                  ▼         ▼
              Continue   Incident
             Mitigation   Command
                            │
                            ▼
                    Establish Data
                       Authority
                            │
                            ▼
                     Activate DR
                       Data Layer
                            │
                            ▼
                     Scale / Build
                       DR EKS
                            │
                            ▼
                       Argo CD
                            │
                            ▼
                    Applications
                            │
                            ▼
                      Smoke Tests
                            │
                            ▼
                    Security Checks
                            │
                            ▼
                     Shift Traffic
                            │
                            ▼
                       Monitor
```

---

# 142. Backup Architecture

```text
                    PRODUCTION ACCOUNT
                           │
            ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
            ▼              ▼              ▼
           RDS            EBS             EFS
            │              │              │
            └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                           ▼
                       AWS Backup
                           │
                ┌──────────┴──────────┐
                ▼                     ▼
          Local Recovery        Cross-Account Copy
                                      │
                                      ▼
                               BACKUP ACCOUNT
                                      │
                                      ▼
                              Immutable Vault
                                      │
                                      ▼
                                DR REGION
```

---

# 143. Data Resilience Architecture

```text
                         DATA
                          │
       ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐
       ▼                  ▼                  ▼
   PostgreSQL            S3                Kafka
       │                  │                  │
       ▼                  ▼                  ▼
 Backup + PITR       Versioning        Retention /
       │             + Replication       Recovery
       │                  │                  │
       └──────────────────┼──────────────────┘
                          ▼
                   Recovery Strategy
                          │
                          ▼
                      DR Region
```

---

# 144. EKS Reconstruction Architecture

```text
Git Repositories
      │
      ├── Terraform
      ├── Helm
      ├── GitOps
      └── Policies
      │
      ▼
Terraform
      │
      ▼
DR AWS Foundation
      │
      ▼
EKS Cluster
      │
      ▼
Core Add-ons
      │
      ▼
Argo CD Bootstrap
      │
      ▼
Git Reconciliation
      │
      ▼
Mediverse Workloads
```

The Kubernetes environment is reconstructed from authoritative code rather than treated as an irreplaceable pet cluster.

---

# 145. Multi-Region Architecture

```text
                              USERS
                                │
                                ▼
                           CloudFront
                                │
                                ▼
                            Route 53
                                │
                  ┌─────────────┴─────────────┐
                  ▼                           ▼
          PRIMARY REGION                 DR REGION
             ACTIVE                       PASSIVE
                │                            │
                ▼                            ▼
               ALB                          ALB
                │                            │
                ▼                            ▼
               EKS                          EKS
                │                            │
       ┌────────┼────────┐          ┌────────┼────────┐
       ▼        ▼        ▼          ▼        ▼        ▼
      RDS     Redis    Kafka       RDS     Redis    Kafka
       │                  │          ▲                  ▲
       │                  │          │                  │
       └──── Replication / Recovery ─┴──────────────────┘

              S3 Region A ───────► S3 Region B
              ECR Region A ──────► ECR Region B
```

The exact secondary-region data-service topology depends on each service's approved RTO/RPO.

---

# 146. Security Recovery Architecture

```text
                 SECURITY FAILURE
                       │
                       ▼
                Incident Command
                       │
            ┌──────────┼──────────┐
            ▼          ▼          ▼
        Isolate     Preserve    Revoke
        Accounts    Evidence   Credentials
            │                     │
            └──────────┬──────────┘
                       ▼
                Clean Recovery
                       │
                       ▼
             Isolated Backups
                       │
                       ▼
                Rotate Secrets
                       │
                       ▼
                 Rebuild IaC
                       │
                       ▼
                Validate Security
                       │
                       ▼
                Restore Service
```

A security disaster may require a **clean-room recovery**, not merely restoring infrastructure into the compromised environment.

---

                            │

# 148. Risks and Mitigations

| Risk                          | Mitigation                        |
| ----------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| AZ failure                    | Multi-AZ                          |
| Region failure                | Secondary-region DR               |
| Accidental DB deletion        | PITR                              |
| Database corruption           | Historical recovery points        |
| Backup deletion               | Vault isolation/immutability      |
| Production-account compromise | Cross-account backup              |
| Regional backup loss          | Cross-region copies               |
| Ransomware                    | Immutable isolated backups        |
| KMS key loss                  | Key governance/recovery design    |
| Git loss                      | Repository recovery strategy      |
| EKS loss                      | Terraform + GitOps reconstruction |
| Image unavailable             | ECR retention/replication         |
| Secret loss                   | Managed secret recovery           |
| Split-brain                   | Controlled data authority         |
| Bad automatic failover        | Human/stateful validation gates   |
| Stale DR database             | RPO monitoring/data validation    |
| DR configuration drift        | IaC/GitOps                        |
| Unknown restore duration      | Regular recovery testing          |
| External provider outage      | Dependency continuity strategy    |
| Failback corruption           | Controlled synchronization        |
| Security compromise           | Clean-room recovery capability    |
| Unusable runbook              | Game days                         |
| Unrealistic RTO               | Measured recovery exercises       |

---

| --------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |

| **DR Mode**                 | Tier-dependent pilot light / warm standby       |
| **Active/Active**           | Separate justification required                 |
| **Backup Management**       | AWS Backup + native mechanisms                  |
| **Database Recovery**       | Backup + PITR + regional strategy               |

| **Backup Isolation**        | Cross-account for critical assets               |

| **Immutability**            | Required/evaluated for critical recovery assets |
| **Infrastructure Recovery** | Terraform                                       |
| **Application Recovery**    | GitOps + Helm                                   |
| **EKS**                     | Reconstructable                                 |
| **Artifact Recovery**       | ECR retention + replication                     |
