# ADR-040 — Enterprise API Gateway, Traffic Management, Rate Limiting & Resilience Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Concurrency Gate**.

---

# 61. HTTP 429 Semantics

When a client exceeds an enforced rate limit, the gateway should normally return:

```http
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
```

This communicates that the request is valid, but the caller has exceeded the permitted request rate.

---

# 62. Rate-Limit Response

Where useful, the response should provide enough information for well-behaved clients to react correctly.

Conceptually:

```text
HTTP 429
   │
   ├── Retry-After
   ├── Correlation ID
   └── Standard error body
```

Avoid exposing sensitive internal capacity information.

---

# 63. Retry-After

Where recovery timing is meaningful:

```http
Retry-After: 30
```

can instruct the client not to immediately retry.

This helps reduce retry storms.

---

# 64. Standard Error Contract

Gateway-generated failures should follow Mediverse's standardized API error model.

Example conceptually:

```json
{
  "code": "RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED",
  "message": "Request limit exceeded.",
  "correlationId": "..."
}
```

Clients should not need completely different parsing logic for gateway and service errors.

---

# 65. Retry Architecture

Retries are appropriate only for failures likely to be transient.

Potential candidates:

```text
Connection reset
Temporary service unavailability
Selected 5xx responses
Transient network failure
```

Retries should never be blindly applied to every failure.

---

# 66. Retry Boundaries

A request may cross several components:

```text
Client
  │
  ▼
Gateway
  │
  ▼
Service A
  │
  ▼
Service B
  │
  ▼
Database
```

If every layer independently retries three times, one user request can multiply into a large number of downstream operations.

Retry ownership must therefore be explicit.

---

# 67. Retry Storm

```text
Dependency slows
      │
      ▼
Requests fail
      │
      ▼
Clients retry
      │
      ▼
Gateway retries
      │
      ▼
Services retry
      │
      ▼
Dependency receives MORE traffic
      │
      ▼
Dependency collapses
```

This is one of the most dangerous resilience anti-patterns.

---

# 68. Bounded Retries

Retries must have a maximum attempt count.

Conceptually:

```text
Attempt 1
   │ failure
   ▼
Attempt 2
   │ failure
   ▼
Attempt 3
   │ failure
   ▼
STOP
```

Infinite retries are prohibited.

---

# 69. Exponential Backoff

Retry delays should generally increase between attempts.

```text
Retry 1 → 100 ms
Retry 2 → 200 ms
Retry 3 → 400 ms
```

Exact values depend on workload requirements.

---

# 70. Jitter

Randomized jitter should be introduced where large numbers of clients could retry simultaneously.

Without jitter:

```text
10,000 clients fail
      │
      ▼
All wait 1 second
      │
      ▼
All retry together
      │
      ▼
Another traffic spike
```

With jitter, retries become distributed over time.

---

# 71. Retry Safety

A retry must consider whether the operation is safe to repeat.

Generally:

```text
GET
→ commonly retryable

POST
→ may create duplicate state
```

HTTP method alone is not enough; actual operation semantics matter.

---

# 72. Idempotency

An idempotent operation produces the same intended business outcome when repeated.

This is critical for operations such as:

```text
Assessment submission
Payment-like operations
Content creation
AI job creation
File-processing requests
```

where duplicate execution could be harmful.

---

# 73. Idempotency Keys

For appropriate APIs:

```text
Client
   │
   │ Idempotency-Key: abc123
   ▼
Gateway / Service
   │
   ▼
Has abc123 already completed?
   │
 ┌─┴────────────┐
 ▼              ▼
NO             YES
 │              │
 ▼              ▼
Process       Return previous
request       result
```

The business service should normally own durable idempotency semantics.

---

# 74. Gateway Idempotency Boundary

The gateway may propagate and validate an idempotency key.

It should not automatically become the authoritative database for every business operation.

Business-level duplicate prevention belongs near the business transaction.

---

# 75. Circuit Breakers

Circuit breakers should protect services from repeatedly calling dependencies known to be unhealthy.

```text
Service
   │
   ▼
Circuit Breaker
   │
 ┌─┴──────────┐
 ▼            ▼
CLOSED       OPEN
 │            │
 ▼            X
Dependency   Fast failure
```

---

# 76. Circuit Breaker States

```text
CLOSED
   │
   │ failure threshold reached
   ▼
OPEN
   │
   │ recovery interval
   ▼
HALF-OPEN
   │
   ├── success → CLOSED
   └── failure → OPEN
```

Thresholds must be tuned rather than copied blindly between services.

---

# 77. Gateway Circuit Breaker

Gateway-level circuit breakers may protect external routing paths.

However, downstream services still need resilience for their own dependencies.

```text
Gateway
   │
   ▼
Service A
   │
   ▼
Service B
```

The gateway cannot protect `Service A → Service B` if it never sees that call.

---

# 78. Fallbacks

Fallbacks should only be used when a meaningful degraded response exists.

Good candidate:

```text
Recommendation service unavailable
        │
        ▼
Return learning page without recommendations
```

Bad candidate:

```text
Assessment submission failed
        │
        ▼
Pretend submission succeeded
```

Fallbacks must preserve correctness.

---

# 79. Bulkheads

Independent traffic/resource pools should prevent one workload from consuming everything.

```text
Gateway / Service
       │
 ┌─────┼─────────┐
 ▼     ▼         ▼
Core   AI      Background
Pool   Pool       Pool
```

An overloaded AI feature should not consume all capacity needed for authentication.

---

# 80. Load Shedding

When capacity is exhausted, the platform should reject lower-value work deliberately.

```text
Incoming Load
      │
      ▼
Capacity Boundary
      │
 ┌────┴────┐
 ▼         ▼
Critical   Non-critical
 │         │
 ▼         X
Serve     Shed
```

Controlled rejection is preferable to uncontrolled system collapse.

---

# 81. Load-Shedding Priority

Potential priority order:

```text
Authentication
Core learning
Assessment operations
Content retrieval
Recommendations
Analytics
Background work
```

Actual business criticality must determine final policy.

---

# 82. HTTP 503

When the platform cannot temporarily serve an otherwise valid request:

```http
503 Service Unavailable
```

may be appropriate.

This differs from:

```text
429 → Caller exceeded allowed rate
503 → Service currently unable to serve
```

---

# 83. Graceful Degradation

Mediverse should preserve critical workflows when optional dependencies fail.

```text
AI Service ✕
     │
     ▼
Core Learning Platform
     │
     └── Still Available
```

Architecture should explicitly identify optional dependencies.

---

# 84. Gateway Failure

The gateway itself is critical infrastructure.

If there is only one gateway Pod:

```text
Gateway Pod
    X
    │
    ▼
Entire API unavailable
```

Therefore production requires redundant gateway replicas.

---

# 85. Gateway High Availability

```text
ALB
 │
 ├──► Gateway Pod A
 ├──► Gateway Pod B
 └──► Gateway Pod C
```

Replicas should be distributed across nodes and Availability Zones where practical.

---

# 86. Gateway HPA

Spring Cloud Gateway should scale horizontally according to measured demand.

Potential signals include:

```text
CPU
Request rate
Concurrent connections
Event-loop pressure
Latency
```

CPU alone may not represent gateway saturation.

---

# 87. Gateway Resource Requests

Gateway Pods require explicit:

```text
CPU requests
Memory requests
Validated limits
```

Because every API request may pass through them, resource starvation here has platform-wide impact.

---

# 88. Gateway Readiness

A gateway Pod should receive traffic only after:

```text
Application initialized
Routes loaded
Required configuration available
Critical dependencies ready
```

Readiness must not simply mean that the JVM process exists.

---

# 89. Gateway Liveness

Liveness should answer:

> Can this gateway process recover only by restarting it?

It should not restart every gateway Pod simply because one downstream service is unavailable.

---

# 90. WebSocket Traffic

WebSockets have different characteristics from ordinary request/response APIs.

```text
Client
  │
  │ persistent connection
  ▼
Gateway
  │
  ▼
Realtime Service
```

Connections may remain open for long periods.

---

# 91. WebSocket Capacity

Capacity planning should consider:

```text
Concurrent connections
Connection lifetime
Memory per connection
Heartbeat traffic
Reconnect storms
Node draining
Gateway scaling
```

RPS alone is a poor capacity metric for WebSockets.

---

# 92. WebSocket Reconnect Storm

If a gateway node fails:

```text
10,000 connections lost
        │
        ▼
10,000 clients reconnect
        │
        ▼
Sudden traffic spike
```

Clients should use reconnect backoff and jitter.

---

# 93. Server-Sent Events

SSE may be used for server-to-client streaming where full bidirectional WebSocket communication is unnecessary.

SSE also creates long-lived HTTP connections and therefore requires separate capacity consideration.

---

# 94. Long-Running HTTP Requests

Long-running operations such as AI generation should not automatically keep gateway requests open indefinitely.

Where appropriate:

```text
POST /ai/jobs
      │
      ▼
202 Accepted
      │
      ▼
Background Processing
      │
      ▼
Job Status / SSE / WebSocket
```

may be more resilient.

---

# 95. API Versioning

Externally consumed APIs require explicit version management.

Preferred initial pattern:

```text
/api/v1/...
```

Future incompatible contracts may use:

```text
/api/v2/...
```

---

# 96. Versioning Is Not for Every Change

Adding a backward-compatible optional field does not necessarily require `/v2`.

Version changes should correspond to meaningful incompatible contract changes.

---

# 97. Backward Compatibility

During migration:

```text
Clients v1
   │
   ▼
API v1

Clients v2
   │
   ▼
API v2
```

Both may need to coexist for a defined transition period.

---

# 98. API Deprecation

Deprecated APIs should have:

```text
Owner
Replacement
Deprecation date
Usage telemetry
Migration plan
Removal date
```

"Deprecated forever" creates permanent maintenance cost.

---

# 99. API Consumer Visibility

Before removing an API version, Mediverse should know who still uses it.

Gateway telemetry should help identify:

```text
Endpoint
Version
Client
Traffic volume
Error rate
```

where identity/privacy policies permit.

---

# 100. Canary Traffic

The traffic layer may support gradual rollout.

```text
Users
  │
  ▼
Gateway / Routing
  │
  ├── 95% → Version A
  └──  5% → Version B
```

This limits blast radius during releases.

---

# 101. Canary Progression

Example conceptually:

```text
1%
 │
 ▼
5%
 │
 ▼
25%
 │
 ▼
50%
 │
 ▼
100%
```

Promotion should depend on health signals rather than elapsed time alone.

---

# 102. Canary Metrics

Important comparison signals include:

```text
Error rate
Latency
Resource consumption
Business failures
Dependency errors
SLO impact
```

A technically healthy canary can still contain business defects.

---

# 103. Canary Rollback

If the new version violates defined thresholds:

```text
Canary
  │
  ▼
Regression detected
  │
  ▼
Traffic → Stable Version
```

Rollback should be fast and controlled.

---

# 104. Blue/Green Routing

Another deployment model:

```text
BLUE
Current production

GREEN
New release
```

Traffic switches only after GREEN is validated.

---

# 105. Blue/Green Trade-Off

Advantages:

```text
Fast rollback
Clear environment separation
```

Costs:

```text
Temporary duplicate capacity
Database compatibility challenges
Operational complexity
```

It should not be forced onto every service.

---

# 106. Database Compatibility

Traffic switching cannot fix incompatible database migrations.

During progressive delivery:

```text
Old App
   │
   ├──► Database
   │
New App
   └──► Same Database
```

schema changes must often remain compatible with both versions during transition.

---

# 107. Expand-Contract Migration

Preferred approach for many schema changes:

```text
EXPAND
Add backward-compatible schema
        │
        ▼
DEPLOY
Old + new applications coexist
        │
        ▼
MIGRATE
Move data/usage
        │
        ▼
CONTRACT
Remove obsolete schema
```

This reduces deployment coupling.

---

# 108. Header-Based Routing

Selected test traffic may route according to trusted headers.

```text
X-Mediverse-Canary: true
        │
        ▼
Canary Service
```

External clients must not be allowed to abuse privileged routing headers.

---

# 109. Cookie-Based Routing

Controlled cookies may support preview or session-affinity scenarios where justified.

Sticky routing should not be introduced without understanding its effect on scaling and failure recovery.

---

# 110. Internal APIs

Not every API should be exposed through the public gateway.

```text
Public APIs
   │
   ▼
External Gateway

Internal APIs
   │
   ▼
Private Kubernetes Network
```

Internal-only interfaces should remain private.

---

# 111. Service-to-Service Calls

Internal communication should use stable service identities.

```text
assessment-service
       │
       ▼
user-service
```

rather than calling public internet endpoints for routine internal communication.

---

# 112. Public Hairpinning

Bad:

```text
Service A
   │
   ▼
Public CloudFront/WAF/ALB
   │
   ▼
Service B
```

for ordinary internal service communication.

This adds unnecessary:

```text
Latency
Cost
Failure points
External exposure
```

---

# 113. Internal Authentication

Private network location alone is not sufficient authorization.

Internal services should authenticate/authorize calls according to the security architecture.

A future ADR may introduce workload identity and mTLS.

---

# 114. East-West Resilience

Service-to-service calls still require:

```text
Timeouts
Retries where safe
Circuit breakers
Concurrency limits
Observability
```

The public gateway does not solve east-west resilience.

---

# 115. Correlation IDs

Every incoming request should receive or carry a correlation identifier.

```text
Client
   │
   ▼
Gateway
   │ correlation-id
   ▼
Service A
   │
   ▼
Service B
```

This helps trace failures across distributed systems.

---

# 116. Trace Context

ADR-037 established OpenTelemetry.

The gateway should propagate standard distributed tracing context across downstream requests.

```text
Browser
   │
   ▼
Gateway
   │
   ▼
Service A
   │
   ▼
Service B
   │
   ▼
Database
```

The trace should reveal the end-to-end request path.

---

# 117. Request Logging

Gateway access logs should capture useful metadata such as:

```text
Timestamp
Route
Method
Status
Latency
Correlation ID
Client/application identity where appropriate
Response size
```

Sensitive request bodies or credentials should not be logged indiscriminately.

---

# 118. Sensitive Headers

Logs must avoid exposing:

```text
Authorization tokens
Cookies
API keys
Secrets
Sensitive personal data
```

Observability cannot be allowed to become a credential-leak mechanism.

---

# 119. RED Metrics

Gateway monitoring should include RED metrics:

```text
Rate
Errors
Duration
```

broken down by useful dimensions such as:

```text
Route
Status class
API version
Upstream service
```

while controlling metric-cardinality growth.

---

# 120. Gateway Saturation

Additional signals include:

```text
CPU
Memory
Active connections
Connection-pool utilization
Pending requests
Event-loop saturation
Rate-limit rejections
Circuit-breaker state
```

These help distinguish gateway saturation from backend saturation.

---

# 121. Rate-Limit Metrics

Monitor:

```text
Allowed requests
Rejected requests
Limit policy
Endpoint
Client class
```

A sudden increase in 429 responses may indicate:

```text
Attack
Bad client
Incorrect policy
Unexpected product usage
Capacity problem
```

---

# 122. Security Telemetry

Traffic architecture should expose relevant events from:

```text
CloudFront
WAF
ALB
Gateway
Authentication
```

into the broader security/observability architecture.

---

# 123. WAF vs Gateway Metrics

WAF blocking and gateway rejection are different signals.

```text
WAF Block
→ Request never reaches application boundary

Gateway 429
→ Valid traffic boundary reached but policy rejected request
```

Dashboards should preserve this distinction.

---

# 124. Health Endpoints

Health endpoints should be separated appropriately.

Potential concepts:

```text
/actuator/health/liveness
/actuator/health/readiness
```

They should not expose unnecessary internal details publicly.

---

# 125. Actuator Exposure

Bad:

```text
Internet
   │
   ▼
/actuator/**
```

with unrestricted access.

Only explicitly required operational endpoints should be exposed, and sensitive management endpoints should remain private/protected.

---

# 126. Gateway Configuration

Routes and policies should be version controlled.

```text
Git
 │
 ▼
Gateway Configuration
 │
 ▼
CI validation
 │
 ▼
GitOps
 │
 ▼
Gateway
```

Manual production route editing should not be the normal operating model.

---

# 127. Configuration Validation

Gateway configuration should be tested before deployment.

Examples:

```text
Duplicate routes
Invalid predicates
Broken filters
Missing upstream services
Unsafe CORS
Invalid timeout values
```

A malformed gateway configuration can affect the entire platform.

---

# 128. Route Ownership

Every externally exposed API route should have:

```text
Owning team
Backend service
API version
Security classification
Rate-limit policy
SLO
Lifecycle status
```

Unowned public APIs become permanent liabilities.

---

# 129. API Catalog

Mediverse should maintain an API inventory/catalog containing at least:

```text
API
Owner
Purpose
Consumers
Authentication
Version
Lifecycle
Documentation
```

This complements OpenAPI specifications.

---

# 130. OpenAPI

Externally consumed REST APIs should maintain OpenAPI contracts.

```text
Service Code
   │
   ▼
OpenAPI Contract
   │
   ├── Documentation
   ├── Testing
   ├── Client integration
   └── Governance
```

The API contract should not drift silently from implementation.

---

# 131. Contract Testing

Service/gateway changes should eventually include automated contract validation.

This can detect:

```text
Removed fields
Changed types
Removed endpoints
Breaking status-code changes
```

before production deployment.

---

# 132. Gateway SLO

Because the gateway sits on critical request paths, it requires its own availability and latency objectives.

A gateway that adds significant latency to every API call becomes a systemic performance problem.

---

# 133. Failure Scenario — Gateway Saturation

```text
Traffic Spike
    │
    ▼
Gateway CPU/Connections saturated
    │
    ▼
Latency rises
    │
    ▼
Client retries
    │
    ▼
More traffic
```

Mitigation:

```text
Rate limiting
Concurrency controls
HPA
Capacity headroom
Retry governance
```

---

# 134. Failure Scenario — Redis Rate Limiter

```text
Redis unavailable
      │
      ▼
Distributed limiter unavailable
      │
      ▼
Endpoint policy
   ┌────┴────┐
   ▼         ▼
Fail Open   Fail Closed
```

The behavior must be deliberate per traffic class.

---

# 135. Failure Scenario — Backend Down

```text
Gateway
   │
   ▼
content-service ✕
   │
   ▼
Timeout / Circuit Breaker
   │
   ▼
Controlled 5xx / Fallback
```

The gateway should not queue unbounded requests waiting for recovery.

---

# 136. Failure Scenario — Authentication Service

If authentication requires synchronous introspection on every request:

```text
Auth Service ✕
      │
      ▼
Entire Platform ✕
```

This is a major availability dependency.

Self-contained JWT validation can reduce that dependency where consistent with the security design.

---

# 137. Failure Scenario — Bad Client

```text
Buggy Client
    │
    ▼
Infinite request loop
    │
    ▼
Rate Limit
    │
    X
Backend overload
```

Traffic governance protects the platform from accidental abuse as well as attackers.

---

# 138. Failure Scenario — AI Endpoint

```text
10,000 AI Requests
       │
       ▼
Rate Limit
       │
       ▼
Concurrency Limit
       │
       ▼
Job Queue
       │
       ▼
AI Workers
```

Allowing all 10,000 requests to synchronously occupy gateway and backend resources would be poor architecture.

---

# 139. Traffic Governance Ownership

```text
Platform Team
   │
   ├── CloudFront
   ├── WAF
   ├── ALB
   ├── Kubernetes entry
   └── Gateway platform

Application Teams
   │
   ├── API contracts
   ├── Domain authorization
   ├── Idempotency
   └── Service resilience

Security
   │
   ├── WAF policy
   ├── Authentication requirements
   └── Exposure governance

SRE
   │
   ├── Gateway SLO
   ├── Capacity
   ├── Alerts
   └── Failure testing
```

---

# 140. Traffic Architecture Anti-Patterns

Mediverse shall reject or strongly discourage:

```text
❌ Exposing every microservice publicly
❌ Public databases, Redis or Kafka
❌ Business logic inside gateway filters
❌ Treating gateway authentication as complete domain authorization
❌ Blind trust of client-supplied identity headers
❌ Wildcard production CORS without justification
❌ Unlimited request bodies
❌ Proxying every large S3 upload through Spring Boot
❌ Missing network timeouts
❌ Retrying every failure
❌ Retries at every architectural layer
❌ Retries without backoff/jitter
❌ Retrying non-idempotent operations blindly
❌ Infinite concurrency
❌ One rate limit for every endpoint
❌ IP address as the only authenticated-user identity
❌ Unlimited expensive AI requests
❌ One gateway replica
❌ Liveness dependent on every backend
❌ Long synchronous AI operations without justification
❌ Mutable API contracts without version governance
❌ Public hairpinning for internal calls
❌ Public Actuator exposure
❌ Logging JWTs/API keys
❌ Manual production route configuration
❌ Removing API versions without usage telemetry
❌ Canary rollout without rollback criteria
❌ Assuming private network = trusted caller
```

---

# 141. Request Decision Pipeline

```text
                     REQUEST
                        │
                        ▼
                   CloudFront
                        │
                        ▼
                       WAF
                        │
                 Allowed request?
                  ┌─────┴─────┐
                  ▼           ▼
                 NO          YES
                  │           │
                  X           ▼
                             ALB
                              │
                              ▼
                           Gateway
                              │
                    ┌─────────┼─────────┐
                    ▼         ▼         ▼
                  Auth     Rate Limit   Size
                    │         │         │
                    └─────────┼─────────┘
                              ▼
                       Concurrency
                              │
                              ▼
                           Routing
                              │
                              ▼
                        Circuit Breaker
                              │
                              ▼
                         Microservice
```

---

# 142. External Traffic Architecture

```text
                          INTERNET
                              │
                              ▼
                         CloudFront
                              │
                              ▼
                           AWS WAF
                              │
                              ▼
                             ALB
                              │
                              ▼
                    Kubernetes Entry
                              │
                              ▼
                   Spring Cloud Gateway
                              │
        ┌─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┐
        ▼                     ▼                     ▼
 Authentication          Traffic Policy         Routing
        │                     │                     │
        ├─ JWT                ├─ Rate limit         ├─ /auth
        ├─ CORS               ├─ Quotas             ├─ /content
        └─ AuthZ              ├─ Concurrency        ├─ /assessment
                              └─ Size limits         └─ /ai
                                      │
                                      ▼
                               Microservices
```

---

# 143. Internal Traffic Architecture

```text
                  EKS PRIVATE NETWORK
                         │
        ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
        ▼                ▼                ▼
   Service A         Service B        Service C
        │                │                │
        └────────────────┼────────────────┘
                         │
                         ▼
                Kubernetes Services
                         │
             ┌───────────┼───────────┐
             ▼           ▼           ▼
          Timeout      Retry       Circuit
                       Policy      Breaker
```

East-west traffic remains private but not implicitly trusted.

---

# 144. Media Traffic Architecture

```text
                     USER
                      │
              ┌───────┴────────┐
              ▼                ▼
         API Request        Media Download
              │                │
              ▼                ▼
           Gateway         CloudFront
              │                │
              ▼                ▼
       Media Metadata          S3
              │
              ▼
     Presigned Upload URL
              │
              ▼
USER ───────────────────────► S3
```

This prevents application infrastructure from becoming a bulk-media transfer layer.

---

# 145. AI Traffic Architecture

```text
User
 │
 ▼
Gateway
 │
 ├── Authentication
 ├── AI-specific quota
 ├── Rate limit
 └── Concurrency policy
 │
 ▼
AI API
 │
 ▼
Job Queue / Kafka
 │
 ▼
AI Workers
 │
 ├── External Model API
 │
 └── GPU Model
 │
 ▼
Result
```

This isolates expensive AI workloads from ordinary synchronous API capacity.

---

# 146. Progressive Delivery Traffic

```text
                         USERS
                           │
                           ▼
                     Traffic Layer
                           │
               ┌───────────┴───────────┐
               ▼                       ▼
          Stable Version            Canary
               │                       │
               │ 95%               5%  │
               └───────────┬───────────┘
                           ▼
                    Observability
                           │
                ┌──────────┴──────────┐
                ▼                     ▼
              Healthy              Regression
                │                     │
                ▼                     ▼
             Promote               Rollback
```

Traffic management and ADR-037 observability therefore operate together.

---

# 147. Complete Mediverse Traffic Control Plane

```text
                              USERS
                                │
                                ▼
                           CloudFront
                                │
                                ▼
                              WAF
                                │
                                ▼
                              ALB
                                │
                                ▼
                      Kubernetes Entry
                                │
                                ▼
                     SPRING CLOUD GATEWAY
                                │
         ┌──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┐
         ▼                      ▼                      ▼
      SECURITY               CONTROL               RESILIENCE
         │                      │                      │
         ├─ JWT                 ├─ Rate Limit          ├─ Timeout
         ├─ CORS                ├─ Quota               ├─ Retry
         ├─ AuthZ               ├─ Burst               ├─ Circuit Breaker
         └─ Headers             ├─ Concurrency         ├─ Bulkhead
                                └─ Request Size        └─ Load Shedding
         │                      │                      │
         └──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┘
                                ▼
                             ROUTING
                                │
          ┌─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┐
          ▼                     ▼                     ▼
      Auth Service        Content Service      Assessment Service
          │                     │                     │
          └─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┘
                                ▼
                       Internal Services
                                │
              ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
              ▼                 ▼                 ▼
          PostgreSQL           Redis             Kafka
```

---

# 148. Risks and Mitigations

| Risk                        | Mitigation                           |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Malicious edge traffic      | WAF + AWS edge protection            |
| Direct service exposure     | Controlled gateway boundary          |
| Invalid authentication load | Early JWT validation                 |
| Header spoofing             | Gateway-controlled trusted headers   |
| Browser CORS failure        | Centralized explicit CORS            |
| Oversized payloads          | Request-size limits                  |
| Large media overhead        | S3 presigned uploads + CloudFront    |
| Runaway clients             | Rate limiting                        |
| Expensive AI abuse          | Dedicated quota/concurrency policies |
| Gateway overload            | HPA + headroom                       |
| Retry storm                 | Bounded retries + backoff + jitter   |
| Duplicate writes            | Idempotency                          |
| Dependency collapse         | Circuit breakers                     |
| Resource starvation         | Bulkheads                            |
| Platform overload           | Load shedding                        |
| Optional dependency failure | Graceful degradation                 |
| Gateway failure             | Multi-replica HA                     |
| WebSocket reconnect storm   | Backoff + jitter                     |
| API breaking change         | Versioning + contract testing        |
| Bad release                 | Canary/blue-green rollback           |
| Internal service exposure   | Private east-west traffic            |
| Debugging difficulty        | Correlation + tracing                |
| Sensitive log leakage       | Logging controls                     |
| Configuration drift         | GitOps                               |

---

# 149. Decision Outcome

| Attribute                   | Decision                                 |
| --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| **ADR**                     | ADR-040                                  |
| **Global Edge**             | CloudFront                               |
| **HTTP Security Edge**      | AWS WAF                                  |
| **AWS Load Balancing**      | ALB                                      |
| **Kubernetes Entry**        | Ingress/Gateway abstraction              |
| **Application Gateway**     | Spring Cloud Gateway                     |
| **Public Service Exposure** | Gateway-controlled only                  |
| **Authentication**          | JWT validation                           |
| **Domain Authorization**    | Backend services                         |
| **CORS**                    | Centrally governed                       |
| **Request Limits**          | Required                                 |
| **Large Uploads**           | Presigned S3                             |
| **Large Downloads**         | CloudFront/S3                            |
| **Timeouts**                | Bounded and hierarchical                 |
| **Rate Limiting**           | Required                                 |
| **Distributed Limiting**    | Redis where justified                    |
| **AI Quotas**               | Dedicated                                |
| **Concurrency Limits**      | Required where appropriate               |
| **Retries**                 | Bounded + backoff + jitter               |
| **Idempotency**             | Required for applicable write operations |
| **Circuit Breakers**        | Dependency-specific                      |
| **Bulkheads**               | Critical workload isolation              |
| **Load Shedding**           | Overload protection                      |
| **Gateway HA**              | Multi-replica                            |
| **Gateway Scaling**         | HPA                                      |
| **WebSockets/SSE**          | Supported with separate capacity policy  |
| **API Versioning**          | `/api/vN` initial convention             |
| **Progressive Delivery**    | Canary/blue-green where justified        |
| **Internal Traffic**        | Private service discovery                |
| **Tracing**                 | OpenTelemetry context propagation        |
| **API Contracts**           | OpenAPI                                  |
| **Configuration**           | GitOps                                   |
| **Status**                  | Accepted                                 |
| **Priority**                | Critical                                 |
| **Risk Level**              | Critical                                 |

---

# 150. Relationship With Previous ADRs

```text
ADR-033 — Argo CD / GitOps
      │
      ├── Deploy gateway configuration
      ▼
ADR-035 — AWS Architecture
      │
      ├── CloudFront / WAF / ALB / Route 53
      ▼
ADR-037 — Observability
      │
      ├── Gateway metrics / logs / traces
      ▼
ADR-038 — Capacity
      │
      ├── HPA / concurrency / load protection
      ▼
ADR-039 — DR
      │
      ├── Regional traffic failover
      ▼
ADR-040 — API Gateway & Traffic Architecture
```

The complete request lifecycle is now:

```text
                         CLIENT
                           │
                           ▼
                    DNS / CloudFront
                           │
                           ▼
                          WAF
                           │
                           ▼
                          ALB
                           │
                           ▼
                         GATEWAY
                           │
        ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐
        ▼                  ▼                  ▼
     SECURITY          GOVERNANCE         RESILIENCE
        │                  │                  │
        ▼                  ▼                  ▼
       JWT             Rate Limits          Timeout
      AuthZ              Quotas             Retry
      CORS             Concurrency          Circuit
        │                  │                Breaker
        └──────────────────┼──────────────────┘
                           ▼
                         ROUTE
                           │
                           ▼
                     MICROSERVICE
                           │
                           ▼
                      DEPENDENCIES
                           │
                           ▼
                      OBSERVABILITY
                           │
                           ▼
                     SLO / SCALING
```

---

---

# Part IV — Data Platform & Storage Architecture

# ADR-041 — Service-to-Service Communication, Service Discovery, Workload Identity & Service Mesh Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Least-Privilege AWS Access**.

---

# 61. Service-to-Service Authentication

Mediverse services must be able to establish **which workload is calling them**.

```text
Assessment Service
        │
        │ authenticated workload identity
        ▼
Progress Service
```

Being inside the EKS cluster is not sufficient proof of identity.

---

# 62. User Identity vs Workload Identity

These are separate security concepts.

```text
User Identity
     │
     ▼
"Student 123 initiated this request"

Workload Identity
     │
     ▼
"Assessment Service made this network call"
```

Both may be relevant to the same request.

---

# 63. Identity Chain

A typical request may contain:

```text
Student
   │
   ▼
Gateway
   │
   ▼
Assessment Service
   │
   ▼
Progress Service
```

Progress Service may need to know:

```text
WHO is the workload?
→ Assessment Service

WHO initiated the operation?
→ Student 123
```

These identities must not be conflated.

---

# 64. Zero-Trust Principle

Mediverse shall follow the principle:

> **Network location does not automatically imply trust.**

Bad assumption:

```text
Inside EKS
   =
Trusted
```

Preferred:

```text
Request
   │
   ▼
Authenticate caller
   │
   ▼
Authorize operation
   │
   ▼
Process
```

---

# 65. Service Authorization

Authentication answers:

```text
Who are you?
```

Authorization answers:

```text
What are you allowed to do?
```

Example:

```text
analytics-service
        │
        ├── Read assessment events      ✓
        └── Modify student assessment   ✕
```

---

# 66. Least-Privilege Service Access

Service permissions should reflect actual dependency requirements.

Bad:

```text
Every Service
     │
     ▼
Can call every API
```

Preferred:

```text
Assessment Service
     │
     ├──► User read API
     └──► Progress update API
```

Nothing more unless justified.

---

# 67. Authorization at Destination

The receiving service must ultimately protect its own resources.

Do not rely entirely on:

```text
Gateway
NetworkPolicy
Service Mesh
```

to replace domain authorization.

These are additional enforcement layers.

---

# 68. User Context Propagation

When downstream services require end-user context:

```text
Gateway
   │
   ▼
Service A
   │
   ▼
Service B
```

the identity context must be propagated using a controlled mechanism.

Services should not manufacture user identity arbitrarily.

---

# 69. Token Propagation

Blindly forwarding the original external access token through ten internal services increases exposure.

The security design should minimize token propagation and use workload identity where user identity is unnecessary.

---

# 70. Identity Confusion

Avoid situations where Service B cannot distinguish:

```text
User directly calling B
```

from:

```text
Service A calling B on user's behalf
```

Caller identity and delegated user context should remain distinguishable.

---

# 71. mTLS

Mutual TLS provides:

```text
Encryption
+
Server authentication
+
Client/workload authentication
```

Conceptually:

```text
Service A
   │
   │ certificate A
   ▼
mTLS
   ▲
   │ certificate B
Service B
```

Both sides authenticate each other.

---

# 72. TLS vs mTLS

Ordinary TLS:

```text
Client → verifies server
```

mTLS:

```text
Client verifies server
+
Server verifies client
```

This makes mTLS useful for workload-to-workload trust.

---

# 73. Certificate Lifecycle

mTLS requires management of:

```text
Certificate issuance
Private keys
Certificate rotation
Expiration
Revocation
Trust roots
Identity mapping
```

Manual certificate management across dozens of services is not acceptable.

---

# 74. Automatic Rotation

If mTLS is adopted, workload certificates must be short-lived and automatically rotated.

```text
Workload starts
      │
      ▼
Identity verified
      │
      ▼
Certificate issued
      │
      ▼
Certificate expires soon
      │
      ▼
Automatic rotation
```

---

# 75. Service Mesh Problem

As Mediverse grows, every service independently implementing:

```text
mTLS
Retries
Telemetry
Traffic policy
Identity
Authorization
```

creates duplicated infrastructure logic.

A service mesh can centralize some of these concerns.

---

# 76. What a Service Mesh Does

Conceptually:

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
Mesh Data Plane
    │
    ▼
Network
    │
    ▼
Mesh Data Plane
    │
    ▼
Application
```

The mesh can provide infrastructure-level controls without embedding all network logic into business code.

---

# 77. What a Service Mesh Does Not Do

A mesh does **not** solve:

```text
Business authorization
Bad domain boundaries
Shared databases
Poor API design
Broken Kafka contracts
Distributed transactions
Bad application code
```

Installing Istio does not make an architecture "microservices-ready."

---

# 78. Service Mesh Candidates

The primary options considered are:

```text
Option A — No service mesh
Option B — Linkerd
Option C — Istio
```

Each has different operational and capability trade-offs.

---

# 79. Option A — No Mesh

Architecture:

```text
Service A
   │
   ▼
Kubernetes Network
   │
   ▼
Service B
```

Application/platform libraries handle resilience and telemetry.

Advantages:

```text
Lowest complexity
Lower resource overhead
Simpler debugging
Fewer platform components
```

---

# 80. No-Mesh Disadvantages

Challenges include:

```text
mTLS implementation
Certificate lifecycle
Consistent workload authorization
Traffic policies
Telemetry standardization
```

As service count grows, application-level duplication can increase.

---

# 81. Option B — Linkerd

Linkerd provides a relatively focused service-mesh capability.

Strengths generally include:

```text
mTLS
Workload identity
Traffic metrics
Relatively simpler operational model
```

It can be attractive where the organization wants a narrower mesh feature set.

---

# 82. Linkerd Trade-Off

Its narrower scope can be an advantage or limitation depending on Mediverse's eventual requirements.

Selecting a simpler mesh and later demanding significantly more advanced traffic/security capabilities can create migration cost.

---

# 83. Option C — Istio

Istio provides a broader service-mesh platform.

Capabilities include concepts such as:

```text
mTLS
Workload identity
Authorization policies
Traffic management
Telemetry integration
Gateways
Advanced routing
```

This provides substantial control but also increases platform complexity.

---

# 84. Istio Complexity

Istio introduces additional:

```text
Control-plane components
Configuration
Policies
Operational knowledge
Debugging requirements
Resource consumption
Upgrade responsibilities
```

It should not be introduced merely because it is popular.

---

# 85. Sidecar Architecture

Traditional mesh architecture places a proxy beside application containers.

```text
Pod
┌───────────────────────────┐
│                           │
│  Spring Boot   Envoy      │
│      App   →   Proxy      │
│                           │
└───────────────────────────┘
```

Traffic is intercepted through the proxy.

---

# 86. Sidecar Advantages

Sidecars provide workload-local traffic enforcement.

Potential benefits:

```text
Fine-grained control
Mature model
Strong workload isolation
Rich telemetry
```

---

# 87. Sidecar Cost

If Mediverse runs:

```text
500 application Pods
```

and each receives a proxy, the platform also operates approximately:

```text
500 additional proxies
```

This affects:

```text
Memory
CPU
Startup
Upgrades
Operational debugging
```

---

# 88. Ambient Mesh

Modern Istio architecture also provides an ambient model that can move parts of mesh functionality outside individual application Pods.

Conceptually:

```text
Application Pods
      │
      ▼
Node-Level Secure Data Plane
      │
      ▼
Optional L7 Policy Layer
```

This can reduce sidecar-related operational overhead.

---

# 89. Ambient Trade-Off

Ambient architecture should not automatically be selected merely because it is newer.

Mediverse must evaluate:

```text
Required features
Operational maturity
Version support
Team expertise
Performance
Troubleshooting
Upgrade strategy
```

before production adoption.

---

# 90. Selected Mesh Direction

Mediverse shall **not require a service mesh during the earliest microservice stage**.

Initial architecture:

```text
Kubernetes Services
+
NetworkPolicy
+
Application resilience
+
OpenTelemetry
+
Workload identity
```

This avoids paying substantial mesh complexity before the system actually requires it.

---

# 91. Mesh Adoption Trigger

Istio should be evaluated for production adoption when requirements justify capabilities such as:

```text
Mandatory east-west mTLS
Fine-grained workload authorization
Consistent identity-based traffic policy
Complex service traffic governance
Large microservice count
Cross-cluster communication
```

This is a deliberate adoption gate.

---

# 92. Why Not Istio Immediately?

Because:

```text
Microservices
+
Kafka
+
EKS
+
Argo CD
+
Observability
+
Istio
+
Complex security policies
```

all introduced simultaneously creates unnecessary operational risk.

Architecture maturity should be incremental.

---

# 93. Future Mesh Preference

If Mediverse reaches the mesh-adoption threshold, **Istio shall be the primary candidate**, subject to a dedicated proof of concept and architecture review.

The deployment mode—sidecar or ambient—must be decided based on the capabilities and operational maturity available at that time.

---

# 94. Mesh Migration Strategy

Potential progression:

```text
Stage 1
Kubernetes networking

        │
        ▼

Stage 2
Selected namespace mesh pilot

        │
        ▼

Stage 3
Non-critical production workloads

        │
        ▼

Stage 4
Critical workloads

        │
        ▼

Stage 5
Strict mTLS/policy enforcement
```

Do not enable strict mesh security across the entire platform in one uncontrolled change.

---

# 95. Permissive mTLS Migration

During transition:

```text
Mesh Workload
    │
    ├── mTLS callers
    └── temporary non-mTLS callers
```

may coexist.

After migration is verified:

```text
STRICT mTLS
```

can be enforced.

The transition period should not become permanent.

---

# 96. NetworkPolicy

Regardless of service-mesh adoption, Kubernetes NetworkPolicy should restrict unnecessary network paths.

Default unrestricted networking means:

```text
Every Pod
   │
   └──► Potentially every Pod
```

which creates excessive blast radius.

---

# 97. Default-Deny Direction

Sensitive namespaces should move toward:

```text
Default deny
     │
     ▼
Explicitly allow required communication
```

rather than relying indefinitely on allow-all networking.

---

# 98. Network Policy Example

```text
Assessment Service
       │
       ├──► PostgreSQL      ✓
       ├──► Kafka           ✓
       ├──► User Service    ✓
       ├──► Progress        ✓
       └──► Random Service  ✕
```

Actual policies should reflect dependency architecture.

---

# 99. NetworkPolicy Is Not Authorization

NetworkPolicy can answer roughly:

```text
Can network traffic flow?
```

It does not answer:

```text
Can this caller update Student 123's assessment?
```

Domain authorization remains an application responsibility.

---

# 100. Namespace Isolation

Namespaces can provide useful operational/security boundaries.

Potential structure:

```text
mediverse-platform
mediverse-apps
mediverse-observability
mediverse-security
```

or domain-oriented namespaces where justified.

Namespace count should not explode without purpose.

---

# 101. Namespace Is Not a Hard Security Boundary

Kubernetes namespaces help organize and scope policy.

They should not be treated as equivalent to separate AWS accounts or physically isolated clusters.

Threat models must recognize this distinction.

---

# 102. East-West Gateway

Not every internal service call should be forced through the public Spring Cloud Gateway.

Bad:

```text
Service A
   │
   ▼
Public Gateway
   │
   ▼
Service B
```

Routine east-west traffic should remain direct/private.

---

# 103. Mesh East-West Gateway

If Mediverse later spans multiple clusters or regions, a mesh east-west gateway may provide controlled cross-cluster communication.

```text
EKS Cluster A
      │
      ▼
East-West Gateway
      │
      ▼
East-West Gateway
      │
      ▼
EKS Cluster B
```

This is a future requirement, not an immediate default.

---

# 104. Cross-Region Synchronous Calls

Avoid architectures where normal user requests require synchronous calls across AWS regions.

```text
Region A Service
      │
      ▼
Region B Service
```

This introduces:

```text
Higher latency
Regional coupling
Network cost
Failure propagation
```

Regional autonomy should be preferred.

---

# 105. Service Dependency Graph

Mediverse shall maintain visibility into service dependencies.

Example:

```text
Assessment
   │
   ├──► User
   ├──► Progress
   └──► Kafka

Progress
   │
   └──► PostgreSQL
```

Unknown dependencies are operational liabilities.

---

# 106. Dependency Classification

Dependencies should be classified:

```text
Critical synchronous
Optional synchronous
Asynchronous
Infrastructure
External
```

This helps determine failure behavior.

---

# 107. Optional Dependency

Example:

```text
Learning Service
      │
      ├── Content Service       CRITICAL
      └── Recommendation        OPTIONAL
```

If recommendations fail, learning content should remain available.

---

# 108. Dependency Budget

Teams should challenge every new synchronous dependency.

Before adding:

```text
Service A → Service B
```

ask:

```text
Does A truly need B synchronously?

Could data be local/read-model based?

Could an event update A asynchronously?

What happens when B is unavailable?
```

---

# 109. Local Read Models

For high-volume read scenarios, services may maintain local projections from events.

Instead of:

```text
Progress Service
      │
      ▼
User Service
```

for every request:

```text
UserUpdated
     │
     ▼
Kafka
     │
     ▼
Progress Local Projection
```

may reduce synchronous coupling.

---

# 110. Read-Model Trade-Off

Local projections improve autonomy but introduce:

```text
Eventual consistency
Duplicate data
Synchronization logic
Schema evolution concerns
```

They should be introduced where their benefits justify that complexity.

---

# 111. Distributed Transactions

Mediverse shall avoid distributed two-phase transactions across microservices as the default consistency mechanism.

```text
Service A DB
      │
      ├── Global Transaction
      │
Service B DB
```

This introduces tight coupling and difficult failure behavior.

---

# 112. Saga Pattern

Multi-service business workflows requiring coordinated state changes should use Saga-style patterns where appropriate.

```text
Step A
  │
  ▼
Step B
  │
  ▼
Step C
```

Failures may require compensating actions rather than global rollback.

---

# 113. Compensation

Example:

```text
Create Enrollment
      │
      ▼
Reserve Resource
      │
      ▼
Send downstream command
      │
      X failure
      │
      ▼
Compensate Reservation
```

Compensation is a business operation, not equivalent to database rollback.

---

# 114. Saga Choreography

```text
Service A
   │
   ▼
Event A
   │
   ▼
Service B
   │
   ▼
Event B
   │
   ▼
Service C
```

Each service reacts to events.

Advantages:

```text
Loose runtime coupling
No central coordinator
```

---

# 115. Choreography Risk

Large choreography chains can become difficult to understand.

```text
Event A
 ├──► B
 │     └──► Event B
 │             ├──► C
 │             └──► D
 └──► E
```

The business workflow can disappear into dozens of event handlers.

---

# 116. Saga Orchestration

An orchestrator explicitly coordinates the workflow.

```text
              Orchestrator
             /     |      \
            ▼      ▼       ▼
        Service A Service B Service C
```

This improves workflow visibility but introduces a coordinator.

---

# 117. Orchestration Decision

Use orchestration when:

```text
Workflow is long
Many ordered steps exist
Compensation is complex
Central workflow visibility is valuable
```

Use choreography when:

```text
Reactions are naturally independent
Workflow is simple
Event ownership is clear
```

Neither approach should be treated as universally superior.

---

# 118. Workflow State

Long-running orchestration requires durable workflow state.

Do not keep critical workflow progress only in application memory.

```text
Orchestrator Pod dies
        │
        X
Workflow knowledge
```

must not occur.

---

# 119. Kafka Consumer Failure

```text
Producer
   │
   ▼
Kafka
   │
   ▼
Consumer ✕
```

Kafka allows the event to remain available according to retention while the consumer recovers.

This is a key advantage over synchronous coupling.

---

# 120. Consumer Retry

Consumer retries should distinguish:

```text
Transient failure
     │
     ▼
Retry

Permanent malformed/problem event
     │
     ▼
Do not retry forever
```

Infinite retry loops can block partition progress.

---

# 121. Dead-Letter Handling

Where justified:

```text
Kafka Topic
    │
    ▼
Consumer
    │
    X
Repeated failure
    │
    ▼
DLT / Recovery Topic
```

Operators can then investigate problematic messages without permanently blocking normal processing.

---

# 122. Dead-Letter Warning

A dead-letter topic must not become:

```text
A graveyard nobody monitors.
```

It requires:

```text
Alerting
Ownership
Investigation
Replay procedure
Retention
```

---

# 123. Event Replay

Kafka replay can rebuild derived state where event history and semantics permit.

```text
Historical Events
       │
       ▼
Consumer
       │
       ▼
Rebuilt Projection
```

Consumers should therefore be designed with replay/idempotency considerations.

---

# 124. Event Ordering

Kafka ordering is normally scoped to a partition.

If events for one business entity require ordering, partition-key strategy must reflect that.

Example:

```text
key = assessmentId
```

may keep related events together.

---

# 125. Global Ordering

Requiring global ordering across every event dramatically limits scalability and is rarely necessary.

Ordering requirements should be defined at the smallest business scope possible.

---

# 126. Kafka Backpressure

If producers outpace consumers:

```text
Producer Rate
     >
Consumer Rate
```

consumer lag increases.

This is preferable to immediately crashing synchronous callers, but lag still requires capacity management.

---

# 127. Consumer Lag

ADR-037 observability should monitor:

```text
Consumer lag
Processing latency
Failure rate
Retry rate
DLT volume
```

Lag is one of the key health signals for asynchronous workflows.

---

# 128. Service Metrics

For synchronous dependencies monitor:

```text
Request rate
Error rate
Latency
Timeouts
Retries
Circuit-breaker state
Connection-pool saturation
```

broken down by dependency where practical.

---

# 129. Distributed Tracing

Trace context should propagate across synchronous service calls.

```text
Gateway
   │
   ▼
Service A
   │
   ▼
Service B
   │
   ▼
Database
```

ADR-037's OpenTelemetry architecture should expose the dependency chain.

---

# 130. Async Trace Correlation

Asynchronous workflows should also propagate useful tracing/correlation context.

```text
HTTP Request
     │
     ▼
Service A
     │
     ▼
Kafka Event
     │
     ▼
Service B
```

Operators should be able to connect the original operation with downstream processing where practical.

---

# 131. Service Dependency Dashboard

Operational dashboards should answer:

```text
What does this service call?

Who calls this service?

Which dependency is slow?

Which dependency is failing?

Which Kafka consumer is lagging?
```

This is more useful than isolated CPU graphs.

---

# 132. Contract Testing

Synchronous API contracts should be tested.

Changes such as:

```text
Endpoint removal
Field removal
Type change
Status-code change
Required-field change
```

can break downstream services even if the changed service passes its own unit tests.

---

# 133. Event Contract Testing

Kafka producers and consumers also require compatibility testing.

CI should detect incompatible event schema changes before deployment.

---

# 134. Integration Testing

Critical communication paths should be tested with realistic infrastructure where practical.

Examples:

```text
Service → PostgreSQL
Service → Kafka
Service → Redis
Service → Service
Outbox → Kafka
Consumer → DB
```

Mocks alone do not prove distributed integration behavior.

---

# 135. Failure Testing

Tests should deliberately include:

```text
Dependency unavailable
Dependency slow
DNS failure
Connection reset
Kafka unavailable
Duplicate event
Out-of-order event
Consumer restart
Timeout
Partial workflow failure
```

Happy-path-only integration tests are inadequate.

---

# 136. Local Development

Developers should be able to run selected services without booting the entire production architecture.

Potential approach:

```text
Application
+
Docker Compose dependencies
+
Selected local services
```

Requiring all microservices to start for every local change is a sign of excessive coupling.

---

# 137. Local Kafka

Local Kafka-compatible development infrastructure may be provided through containerized tooling.

Local environments should preserve production semantics where important without attempting to reproduce the entire AWS platform.

---

# 138. Performance Overhead

Every network abstraction has cost.

```text
HTTP serialization
TLS/mTLS
Proxy
Tracing
Retries
Mesh
```

all consume some:

```text
CPU
Memory
Latency
Network bandwidth
```

Architecture should measure rather than assume the overhead is negligible.

---

# 139. Service Granularity

If two services:

```text
Always deploy together
Always call each other
Share the same data
Cannot function independently
Change together
```

then they may not deserve to be separate microservices.

Splitting code into more repositories and Pods is not automatically better architecture.

---

# 140. East-West Anti-Patterns

Mediverse shall reject or strongly discourage:

```text
❌ Service chains A → B → C → D → E for routine requests
❌ Chatty network APIs
❌ Shared-table ownership
❌ Direct Pod-IP calls
❌ Eureka duplicated inside Kubernetes without justification
❌ Unlimited HTTP connection pools
❌ Missing east-west timeouts
❌ Retries at every layer
❌ Blind retries of non-idempotent operations
❌ Static AWS access keys in Pods
❌ One privileged ServiceAccount for everything
❌ Trusting all traffic because it is inside EKS
❌ Using NetworkPolicy as business authorization
❌ Passing external JWTs everywhere unnecessarily
❌ Installing Istio merely to look enterprise
❌ Mesh policies without operational ownership
❌ Manual workload certificate management
❌ Synchronous calls where events are sufficient
❌ Dual writes to DB and Kafka without reliability pattern
❌ Assuming exactly-once solves business idempotency
❌ Non-versioned event contracts
❌ Infinite Kafka consumer retries
❌ Unmonitored dead-letter topics
❌ Global event ordering without business justification
❌ Distributed 2PC as default microservice consistency
❌ Saga choreography so complex nobody understands the workflow
❌ Critical workflow state stored only in memory
❌ Cross-region synchronous calls for normal workflows
❌ Splitting services that cannot actually operate independently
```

---

                SERVICE NEEDS SOMETHING
                         │
                         ▼

            │            │      ▼
         Fallback/    Reconsider
         degrade      dependency
                               │

                         Consumers
                               │
                               ▼
                        Idempotent
                        Processing
```

                        │
                ┌───────┼───────┐
                ▼       ▼       ▼
              Pod A   Pod B   Pod C
```

                        ▼

No static AWS access key should be required for normal workload operation.

| Dependency collapse                | Circuit breakers                   |

# ADR-042 — Distributed Data Consistency, Transactions, Saga, Outbox & Event-Driven Reliability Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Saga Failure**.

---

# 61. Compensation Semantics

A Saga cannot rely on database rollback after another service has already committed.

Instead, it performs a new business operation that compensates for the previous one.

```text
Local Transaction A
        │
        ✓
        ▼
Local Transaction B
        │
        ✕
        ▼
Compensating Transaction A
```

Compensation is **not rollback**. It is another committed business action.

---

# 62. Compensation Example

Consider enrollment:

```text
1. Create Enrollment        ✓
2. Grant Course Access      ✓
3. Initialize Progress      ✕
```

Possible compensation:

```text
Revoke Course Access
        │
        ▼
Cancel Enrollment
```

The original operations still happened historically; new operations restore an acceptable business state.

---

# 63. Compensatable Operations

Some operations are relatively easy to compensate.

Examples:

```text
Reserve resource
→ Release resource

Create provisional enrollment
→ Cancel enrollment

Allocate entitlement
→ Revoke entitlement
```

These workflows are strong Saga candidates.

---

# 64. Irreversible Operations

Some actions cannot truly be undone.

Examples:

```text
Email sent
Push notification delivered
External webhook delivered
Certificate downloaded
User viewed information
External AI request consumed
```

You cannot "unsend" an email by changing a database row.

---

# 65. Irreversible Action Ordering

Where possible, irreversible side effects should happen after critical reversible state transitions succeed.

Preferred:

```text
Critical State Changes
        │
        ▼
Workflow Confirmed
        │
        ▼
Notification
```

rather than:

```text
Send Notification
        │
        ▼
Critical State Change ✕
```

---

# 66. Semantic Compensation

Sometimes compensation means acknowledging reality rather than pretending the original action disappeared.

Example:

```text
CertificateIssued
        │
        ▼
Later invalidated
        │
        ▼
CertificateRevoked
```

The historical record remains.

This is especially important for auditability.

---

# 67. Compensation Failure

Compensation itself can fail.

```text
Step A                ✓
Step B                ✕
Compensate A          ✕
```

Therefore Saga design needs more than:

```text
try
catch
rollbackEverything()
```

---

# 68. Compensation Retry

Transient compensation failures may be retried.

```text
Compensation
     │
     ✕
     ▼
Backoff
     │
     ▼
Retry
```

Retries must remain bounded and idempotent.

---

# 69. Compensation Escalation

If automatic recovery cannot restore a valid state:

```text
Automatic Recovery
        │
        ✕
        ▼
Manual Intervention
```

The workflow should enter an explicit operational state such as:

```text
COMPENSATION_FAILED
REQUIRES_REVIEW
```

rather than disappearing silently.

---

# 70. Saga State Machine

Complex Sagas should be represented explicitly as state machines.

```text
STARTED
   │
   ▼
ENROLLMENT_CREATED
   │
   ▼
ACCESS_GRANTED
   │
   ▼
PROGRESS_INITIALIZED
   │
   ▼
COMPLETED
```

Failure transitions must also be represented.

---

# 71. Failure States

Example:

```text
ACCESS_GRANTED
      │
      ✕ Progress initialization
      ▼
COMPENSATING
      │
      ▼
ACCESS_REVOKED
      │
      ▼
ENROLLMENT_CANCELLED
```

Explicit states make recovery and observability substantially easier.

---

# 72. Saga Choreography

Choreography coordinates through events.

```text
Enrollment Service
       │
       ▼
EnrollmentCreated
       │
       ▼
Kafka
       │
       ▼
Access Service
       │
       ▼
AccessGranted
       │
       ▼
Progress Service
```

There is no central workflow controller.

---

# 73. Choreography Advantages

Advantages include:

```text
Loose runtime coupling
Natural event-driven model
Independent consumers
No central coordinator
```

This works well for relatively simple workflows.

---

# 74. Choreography Complexity

The problem emerges when:

```text
Event A
 ├──► Service B
 │      └──► Event B
 │             ├──► Service C
 │             │      └──► Event C
 │             └──► Service D
 └──► Service E
```

Understanding one business workflow may require tracing many services and topics.

---

# 75. Event Spaghetti

Mediverse shall avoid uncontrolled choreography where business flow exists only implicitly across event handlers.

Symptoms:

```text
Nobody owns the complete workflow
Unknown event dependencies
Difficult compensation
Difficult debugging
Unclear completion state
```

This is event-driven coupling, not architectural independence.

---

# 76. Saga Orchestration

For complex workflows, an orchestrator may explicitly coordinate Saga steps.

```text
                 Saga Orchestrator
                 /      |       \
                ▼       ▼        ▼
          Enrollment  Access   Progress
```

The orchestrator knows workflow state and required transitions.

---

# 77. Orchestration Commands

Conceptually:

```text
Orchestrator
    │
    ├──► CreateEnrollment
    │
    ◄── EnrollmentCreated
    │
    ├──► GrantAccess
    │
    ◄── AccessGranted
    │
    └──► InitializeProgress
```

If a step fails, the orchestrator determines the next recovery action.

---

# 78. Orchestration Advantages

Orchestration provides:

```text
Explicit workflow
Central state visibility
Clear timeout handling
Clear compensation
Operational observability
Easier reasoning for complex workflows
```

---

# 79. Orchestration Trade-Off

The orchestrator itself creates coordination coupling.

It must not become a new business monolith controlling every internal decision.

Domain services remain owners of their domain rules.

---

# 80. Choreography vs Orchestration Decision

Use choreography when:

```text
Few steps
Independent reactions
Simple compensation
No complex sequencing
```

Use orchestration when:

```text
Many ordered steps
Long-running workflow
Complex compensation
Timeouts matter
Human intervention possible
Workflow visibility matters
```

---

# 81. Durable Workflow State

Long-running Saga state must survive process failure.

Bad:

```text
Map<String, SagaState> sagas;
```

stored only in JVM memory.

If the Pod disappears:

```text
Pod ✕
 │
 └── Saga state ✕
```

That is unacceptable.

---

# 82. Durable Saga Persistence

Workflow state should be durably persisted.

```text
Saga ID
Workflow Type
Current State
Business Reference
Started At
Updated At
Retry Count
Failure Reason
```

This allows processing to resume after restart.

---

# 83. Workflow Engine Evaluation

As workflow complexity grows, Mediverse should evaluate whether implementing custom Saga orchestration remains sensible.

Candidates may include workflow engines such as:

```text
Temporal
Camunda
```

but introducing one immediately is not automatically justified.

---

# 84. Workflow Engine Adoption Trigger

A dedicated workflow engine becomes more attractive when Mediverse has:

```text
Many long-running workflows
Complex timers
Human approval steps
Complex compensation
Durable retries
Workflow versioning
Operational workflow inspection
```

Before that point, a simpler Saga implementation may be preferable.

---

# 85. Avoid Infrastructure Inflation

Do not introduce:

```text
Kafka
Debezium
Kafka Connect
Schema Registry
Temporal
Istio
Redis
```

simultaneously simply because each solves a legitimate distributed-systems problem.

Every component creates another system that must be:

```text
Deployed
Secured
Monitored
Backed up
Upgraded
Debugged
Operated
```

Complexity must be earned by requirements.

---

# 86. Saga Timeout

Long-running workflows need explicit deadlines.

```text
Saga Started
     │
     ▼
Waiting for Step B
     │
     │ timeout exceeded
     ▼
Recovery Policy
```

Waiting forever is not a valid state-management strategy.

---

# 87. Timeout State

Example:

```text
WAITING_FOR_PROGRESS
        │
        │ 10 minutes
        ▼
TIMED_OUT
        │
        ▼
Retry / Compensate / Escalate
```

Exact durations are business-specific.

---

# 88. Retry State Machine

Retries should be represented explicitly for critical workflows.

```text
PROCESSING
    │
    ✕
    ▼
RETRY_PENDING
    │
    ▼
PROCESSING
    │
    ✕
    ▼
RETRY_PENDING
    │
    ▼
FAILED
```

This makes operational behavior inspectable.

---

# 89. Human Intervention

Some consistency failures cannot safely be resolved automatically.

Examples:

```text
Ambiguous external system result
Repeated compensation failure
Conflicting authoritative records
Irreversible side effect
```

Mediverse should support controlled operational resolution.

---

# 90. Manual Recovery Audit

Manual changes must be auditable.

Record:

```text
Who performed recovery
When
Why
Previous state
New state
Related incident
Saga/event ID
```

Production consistency should not be repaired through undocumented SQL commands.

---

# 91. Reconciliation

Even well-designed distributed systems need reconciliation.

```text
Authoritative State
        │
        ▼
Compare
        │
        ▼
Derived State
```

Discrepancies can then be detected and repaired.

---

# 92. Reconciliation Example

Suppose:

```text
Assessment Service
Completed assessments = 100

Progress Service
Recorded completions = 99
```

A reconciliation process should identify the missing derived state.

---

# 93. Reconciliation Is Defense in Depth

Transactional Outbox and idempotency dramatically reduce inconsistency.

They do not justify assuming inconsistency can never occur.

Failures can still arise from:

```text
Software bugs
Bad deployments
Operator mistakes
Corrupted messages
Incorrect migrations
Expired retention
```

Reconciliation provides another recovery layer.

---

# 94. Self-Healing Reconciliation

Where correction is deterministic:

```text
Mismatch detected
       │
       ▼
Generate repair action
       │
       ▼
Derived state corrected
```

may be automated.

Critical ambiguous discrepancies should instead be escalated.

---

# 95. Read-Your-Writes Problem

Eventual consistency creates a UX issue.

```text
User updates profile
      │
      ▼
Authoritative Service ✓
      │
      ▼
Event
      │
      ▼
Read Model not updated yet
      │
      ▼
User refreshes
      │
      ▼
Old data appears
```

Technically correct eventual consistency can still create a poor product experience.

---

# 96. Read-Your-Writes Strategies

Depending on workflow, options include:

```text
Read authoritative service temporarily
Return updated representation from write
Client optimistic state
Version-aware reads
Wait for projection where justified
```

The choice must match business and latency requirements.

---

# 97. CQRS

For domains with materially different read and write requirements, Mediverse may use CQRS-style separation.

```text
                COMMAND
                   │
                   ▼
              Write Model
                   │
                   ▼
                 Event
                   │
                   ▼
               Read Model
                   │
                   ▼
                 QUERY
```

CQRS is not required for every CRUD service.

---

# 98. CQRS Warning

Turning every simple entity into:

```text
Command Handler
Event Store
Projection
Read Database
Write Database
```

without a real scaling/domain reason is architecture theater.

Use CQRS where the separation creates measurable value.

---

# 99. Materialized Projection

A consumer may maintain query-optimized local data.

```text
AssessmentCompleted
        │
        ▼
Progress Projection
        │
        ▼
Student Dashboard
```

This reduces synchronous cross-service queries.

---

# 100. Projection Rebuild

A projection should ideally be rebuildable when sufficient event history or authoritative source data exists.

```text
Delete/Recreate Projection
          │
          ▼
Replay
          │
          ▼
Reconstructed State
```

This is valuable for recovery and schema evolution.

---

# 101. Cache Consistency

Redis introduces another consistency boundary.

```text
Database
   │
   ▼
Redis
```

The database remains authoritative unless a specific architecture says otherwise.

---

# 102. Cache-Aside

Typical model:

```text
Read
 │
 ▼
Redis
 │
 ├── HIT → return
 │
 └── MISS
       │
       ▼
    Database
       │
       ▼
     Cache
```

Write behavior must explicitly address stale cache entries.

---

# 103. Cache Invalidation

Possible strategy:

```text
Update Database
      │
      ▼
Invalidate Cache
```

But this is another multi-system operation.

Temporary cache staleness must be considered.

---

# 104. Cache TTL

TTL provides a bounded staleness/recovery mechanism.

A cache entry that cannot be reliably invalidated should not remain valid indefinitely.

Critical authorization or authoritative state should not rely casually on stale cache data.

---

# 105. Kafka Producer Reliability

Kafka producers should use reliability settings appropriate to the event criticality.

Relevant concepts include:

```text
Acknowledgements
Idempotent producer
Retries
Delivery timeout
Ordering
```

Exact configuration should be standardized by the platform team.

---

# 106. Kafka Transactions

Kafka transactions can provide useful atomicity within Kafka workflows.

For example:

```text
Consume Kafka
     │
     ▼
Process
     │
     ▼
Produce Kafka
```

may use Kafka-specific transactional capabilities.

But this does not automatically include PostgreSQL or external systems.

---

# 107. Kafka + Database Boundary

This remains distributed:

```text
Kafka Transaction
       │
       X
PostgreSQL Transaction
```

Do not assume Kafka transaction configuration eliminates the need for outbox/inbox/idempotency patterns.

---

# 108. Poison Event

A poison event repeatedly fails because of content or logic rather than transient infrastructure.

```text
Event
  │
  ▼
Consumer
  │
  ✕
Retry
  │
  ✕
Retry
  │
  ✕
```

Retrying forever is destructive.

---

# 109. Retry Classification

Failures should be classified.

```text
Transient
→ retry

Rate limited
→ retry with appropriate backoff

Permanent validation failure
→ don't blindly retry

Unknown
→ bounded retry then escalation
```

---

# 110. Dead-Letter Topic

After bounded failure:

```text
Main Topic
    │
    ▼
Consumer
    │
    ✕
    ▼
Retry
    │
    ✕
    ▼
DLT
```

The normal partition can continue processing.

---

# 111. DLT Metadata

Recovery records should preserve useful context:

```text
Original topic
Partition
Offset
Event ID
Event type
Failure reason
Attempt count
Failure timestamp
```

without leaking sensitive payload data unnecessarily.

---

# 112. DLT Ownership

Every DLT requires an owner.

A DLT with 50,000 messages and no alert is not a recovery strategy.

It is hidden data loss.

---

# 113. Replay

After fixing the underlying problem:

```text
DLT
 │
 ▼
Validated Replay
 │
 ▼
Original/Recovery Processing
```

Consumers must remain idempotent because replay can encounter previously processed events.

---

# 114. Blind Replay

Never replay thousands of failed production events merely because the code was redeployed.

Before replay:

```text
Understand failure
Validate fix
Estimate side effects
Verify idempotency
Control throughput
Monitor result
```

---

# 115. Event Retention

Kafka event retention must reflect recovery and replay requirements.

If recovery requires seven days of history but events are retained for one day, the architecture contradicts itself.

---

# 116. Retention Is Not Backup

Kafka retention should not automatically be treated as permanent archival or business backup.

Long-term audit requirements may require separate durable storage.

---

# 117. Tombstones

Where compacted Kafka topics are used, tombstone records may represent key deletion.

Consumers must understand their semantics.

```text
key = student-123
value = null
```

should not be treated as an ordinary malformed event if the topic contract defines it as deletion.

---

# 118. Schema Evolution

Event schemas must evolve compatibly.

Preferred evolution:

```text
Add optional field
Consumers ignore unknown fields
Producer maintains existing semantics
```

Breaking semantic changes require deliberate migration.

---

# 119. Semantic Compatibility

Schema compatibility alone is insufficient.

Suppose:

```text
status = "COMPLETED"
```

used to mean "student submitted assessment" but later means "faculty graded assessment."

The JSON schema may remain identical while business semantics break every consumer.

Contracts include meaning, not just field types.

---

# 120. Data Migration

Database migrations must consider:

```text
Current application
Previous application
Events in flight
Old consumers
New consumers
Projection rebuild
Rollback strategy
```

Distributed deployments make schema evolution a system-wide concern.

---

# 121. Expand-Contract

Prefer backward-compatible migrations:

```text
EXPAND
Add new structure
      │
      ▼
DEPLOY
Old + new versions coexist
      │
      ▼
MIGRATE
Data/consumers move
      │
      ▼
CONTRACT
Remove obsolete structure
```

This aligns with ADR-040 progressive delivery.

---

# 122. Failure Matrix

Critical workflows should explicitly document failure points.

Example:

| Step                 | Failure             | Recovery         |
| -------------------- | ------------------- | ---------------- |
| DB update            | Rollback            | Retry request    |
| Outbox insert        | Rollback with DB    | Retry request    |
| Kafka unavailable    | Outbox retained     | Publisher retry  |
| Duplicate event      | Consumer dedup      | Ignore/reconcile |
| Consumer unavailable | Kafka retains event | Resume           |
| Poison event         | Repeated failure    | DLT              |
| Saga step fails      | Workflow state      | Retry/compensate |
| Compensation fails   | Saga failure        | Escalation       |
| Projection drift     | Reconciliation      | Repair           |

---

# 123. Crash Before Commit

```text
Business update
Outbox insert
      │
      ▼
Process crashes before COMMIT
```

Database transaction rolls back.

Result:

```text
Business state ✕
Event ✕
```

Correct.

---

# 124. Crash After Commit

```text
COMMIT ✓
    │
    ▼
Process crashes
```

Business data and outbox event remain durable.

The publisher can continue later.

This is precisely why the outbox exists.

---

# 125. Consumer Crash Before Commit

```text
Receive Event
     │
     ▼
Begin DB Transaction
     │
     ▼
Consumer crashes
```

Local transaction rolls back.

Kafka may redeliver the event.

Idempotent processing handles this safely.

---

# 126. Consumer Crash After Commit

Harder case:

```text
Database COMMIT ✓
        │
        ▼
Crash before offset acknowledged
```

Kafka may redeliver.

Again:

```text
Idempotency
```

is the protection.

---

# 127. Disaster Recovery

ADR-039 disaster recovery must consider distributed consistency state including:

```text
Business databases
Outbox records
Kafka topics
Consumer offsets
Saga state
Inbox/dedup records
Projections
```

Restoring only PostgreSQL while ignoring related event state can create inconsistency.

---

# 128. Recovery Point Alignment

If:

```text
PostgreSQL restored to T0
Kafka restored/retained to T1
```

events may describe changes no longer present in the restored database.

Recovery procedures must account for cross-system timeline alignment.

---

# 129. Recovery Reconciliation

After major recovery:

```text
Restore
   │
   ▼
Validate authoritative state
   │
   ▼
Validate event processing
   │
   ▼
Reconcile projections
   │
   ▼
Resume normal traffic
```

Recovery is not complete merely because Pods are running.

---
