# 130. Consistency Observability

Distributed consistency needs observable signals.

Monitor:

```text
Outbox backlog
Oldest unpublished event
Publish failure rate
Consumer lag
Consumer failures
DLT volume
Saga failures
Saga age
Compensation failures
Reconciliation mismatches
```

---

# 131. Outbox Backlog

A growing outbox backlog indicates:

```text
Kafka unavailable
Publisher failure
Insufficient publisher throughput
Database contention
Bad deployment
```

It should trigger operational attention.

---

# 132. Event Age

Count alone is insufficient.

```text
100 queued events
```

could be harmless if they are 200 ms old.

But:

```text
1 event
```

stuck for six hours may indicate a serious correctness problem.

Track oldest event age.

---

# 133. Saga Observability

Operators should be able to answer:

```text
How many Sagas are running?
How many failed?
Which step failed?
How long have they been running?
Which compensations failed?
Which require intervention?
```

Without this, distributed workflows become operational black boxes.

---

# 134. Business Invariant Monitoring

Technical metrics may all look healthy while business state is wrong.

Monitor important invariants where feasible.

Example:

```text
Completed assessment
        │
        ▼
Eventually must have
progress representation
```

Violations can trigger reconciliation or alerts.

---

# 135. Data Drift Detection

Conceptually:

```text
Authoritative Data
        │
        ▼
Expected Derived State
        │
        ▼
Compare
        │
   ┌────┴────┐
   ▼         ▼
MATCH      DRIFT
             │
             ▼
        Repair/Alert
```

This is particularly valuable for critical derived models.

---

# 136. Testing Local Transactions

Tests should verify:

```text
All writes commit together
Failure rolls back
Constraints hold
Optimistic locking works
Outbox insertion is atomic
```

Do not rely only on mocked repositories for transaction correctness.

---

# 137. Testing Outbox

Required scenarios include:

```text
Business update + outbox commit
Business failure rolls back outbox
Kafka unavailable
Publisher restart
Duplicate publication
Backlog recovery
```

---

# 138. Testing Consumers

Consumers should be tested against:

```text
Duplicate events
Out-of-order events
Unknown optional fields
Old event versions
Transient failures
Permanent failures
Restart after processing
Replay
```

---

# 139. Saga Testing

Test:

```text
Every step succeeds
Each individual step fails
Retry succeeds
Retry exhausts
Compensation succeeds
Compensation fails
Timeout occurs
Orchestrator restarts
Duplicate response arrives
```

Testing only the successful Saga path proves very little.

---

# 140. Distributed Consistency Anti-Patterns

Mediverse shall reject or strongly discourage:

```text
❌ Assuming @Transactional spans microservices
❌ DB + Kafka dual writes without reliability design
❌ Global 2PC as default architecture
❌ Holding DB transactions open during remote calls
❌ Assuming Kafka means exactly-once business processing
❌ Consumers that cannot tolerate duplicates
❌ Events without stable IDs
❌ Unversioned event contracts
❌ Serializing JPA entities directly as public events
❌ Global event ordering without justification
❌ Infinite consumer retries
❌ DLTs without ownership
❌ Blind production replay
❌ Compensation treated as database rollback
❌ Assuming every operation is compensatable
❌ Saga state stored only in memory
❌ Unbounded Saga execution
❌ Event choreography with no workflow owner
❌ Workflow engines introduced without workflow complexity
❌ CQRS applied to every CRUD operation
❌ Cache treated as authoritative accidentally
❌ Kafka retention treated as permanent backup
❌ Ignoring events-in-flight during schema migration
❌ Restoring DB without considering Kafka/Saga state
❌ No reconciliation because "outbox guarantees consistency"
❌ Manual production data fixes without audit
```

---

# 141. Consistency Decision Tree

```text
                 BUSINESS STATE CHANGE
                          │
                          ▼
               One service/database?
                   ┌──────┴──────┐
                   ▼             ▼
                  YES            NO
                   │             │
                   ▼             ▼
              Local ACID     Cross-Service
              Transaction       Workflow
                                   │
                       ┌───────────┴───────────┐
                       ▼                       ▼
                Immediate response?      Async acceptable?
                       │                       │
                       ▼                       ▼
                 Controlled REST             Kafka
                                               │
                                               ▼
                                      Reliable publication
                                               │
                                               ▼
                                            Outbox
                                               │
                                               ▼
                                       Idempotent Consumer
                                               │
                                               ▼
                                 Multiple coordinated changes?
                                               │
                                        ┌──────┴──────┐
                                        ▼             ▼
                                       YES            NO
                                        │             │
                                        ▼             ▼
                                      Saga         Complete
```

---

# 142. Reliable Publication Architecture

```text
                    DOMAIN SERVICE
                         │
                         ▼
                   LOCAL ACID TX
                  ┌──────┴──────┐
                  ▼             ▼
             Domain Data     Outbox
                                 │
                                 ▼
                            COMMITTED
                                 │
                                 ▼
                         Outbox Publisher
                                 │
                         ┌───────┴───────┐
                         ▼               ▼
                       Kafka           Failure
                         │               │
                         │               ▼
                         │             Retry
                         │
                         ▼
                     Consumer
                         │
                         ▼
                    Idempotency
                         │
                         ▼
                   LOCAL ACID TX
```

---

# 143. Saga Reference Architecture

```text
                       BUSINESS WORKFLOW
                              │
                              ▼
                       Saga Coordinator
                              │
              ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
              ▼               ▼               ▼
          Service A       Service B       Service C
              │               │               │
              ▼               ▼               ▼
          Local Tx        Local Tx        Local Tx
              │               │               │
              └───────────────┼───────────────┘
                              ▼
                        Saga State Store
                              │
                   ┌──────────┴──────────┐
                   ▼                     ▼
                SUCCESS                FAILURE
                   │                     │
                   ▼                     ▼
               Complete          Retry / Compensate
                                         │
                                         ▼
                                    Escalation
```

---

# 144. CQRS / Projection Architecture

```text
                    AUTHORITATIVE SERVICE
                            │
                            ▼
                         Write DB
                            │
                            ▼
                          Outbox
                            │
                            ▼
                           Kafka
                            │
              ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
              ▼             ▼             ▼
          Progress       Search       Analytics
          Projection     Index        Projection
              │             │             │
              ▼             ▼             ▼
           Queries       Search        Reports
```

The source domain remains authoritative; projections are derived.

---

# 145. Recovery Architecture

```text
                         FAILURE
                            │
             ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
             ▼              ▼              ▼
         Transient        Poison        Data Drift
             │              │              │
             ▼              ▼              ▼
           Retry           DLT        Reconciliation
             │              │              │
             ▼              ▼              ▼
          Success       Investigation     Repair
                            │
                            ▼
                         Replay
                            │
                            ▼
                       Idempotency
```

---

# 146. Complete Mediverse Consistency Architecture

```text
                        USER / SYSTEM ACTION
                               │
                               ▼
                         DOMAIN SERVICE
                               │
                               ▼
                         LOCAL ACID TX
                     ┌─────────┴─────────┐
                     ▼                   ▼
                Domain State          Outbox
                                         │
                                         ▼
                                   Event Publisher
                                         │
                                         ▼
                                       Kafka
                                         │
                    ┌────────────────────┼────────────────────┐
                    ▼                    ▼                    ▼
                Consumer A           Consumer B           Consumer C
                    │                    │                    │
                    ▼                    ▼                    ▼
               Inbox/Idempotency   Inbox/Idempotency   Inbox/Idempotency
                    │                    │                    │
                    ▼                    ▼                    ▼
                Local DB             Projection           Side Effect
                    │
                    └────────────────────┬────────────────────┘
                                         │
                                         ▼
                                  Saga / Workflow
                                         │
                          ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
                          ▼              ▼              ▼
                        Retry       Compensation    Escalation
                                         │
                                         ▼
                                  Reconciliation
                                         │
                                         ▼
                               Business Invariants
```

---

# 147. Reliability Layers

The architecture deliberately uses multiple layers:

```text
Layer 1
Database constraints
        │
        ▼
Layer 2
Local ACID transactions
        │
        ▼
Layer 3
Transactional Outbox
        │
        ▼
Layer 4
Kafka durability
        │
        ▼
Layer 5
Idempotent consumers
        │
        ▼
Layer 6
Saga recovery
        │
        ▼
Layer 7
Reconciliation
        │
        ▼
Layer 8
Operational intervention
```

No single pattern is expected to solve every distributed failure.

---

# 148. Risks and Mitigations

| Risk                              | Primary Mitigation                 |
| --------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| Partial cross-service failure     | Saga                               |
| DB/Kafka dual write               | Transactional Outbox               |
| Duplicate event                   | Idempotency/Inbox                  |
| Lost event publication            | Persistent outbox                  |
| Out-of-order processing           | Partitioning + version checks      |
| Concurrent modification           | Optimistic locking                 |
| Long DB transactions              | Short local transaction boundaries |
| Poison event                      | Bounded retry + DLT                |
| Consumer outage                   | Kafka retention                    |
| DLT accumulation                  | Ownership + alerting               |
| Complex workflow                  | Saga orchestration                 |
| Compensation failure              | Durable state + escalation         |
| Projection drift                  | Reconciliation                     |
| Stale user read                   | Read-your-writes strategy          |
| Cache inconsistency               | Invalidation + TTL                 |
| Breaking event contract           | Schema/version governance          |
| Bad replay                        | Controlled replay + idempotency    |
| DR inconsistency                  | Cross-system recovery planning     |
| Hidden business corruption        | Invariant monitoring               |
| Excessive architecture complexity | Requirement-driven adoption        |

---

# 149. Decision Outcome

| Attribute                        | Decision                                   |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| **ADR**                          | ADR-042                                    |
| Local consistency                | ACID transactions                          |
| Cross-service global transaction | Not used by default                        |
| 2PC                              | Avoid                                      |
| Event publication                | Transactional Outbox                       |
| Initial outbox transport         | Controlled publisher                       |
| Future high-scale option         | CDC/Debezium                               |
| Event delivery assumption        | At least once                              |
| Consumer requirement             | Idempotent                                 |
| Critical deduplication           | Inbox/processed-event pattern              |
| Event identity                   | Stable unique ID                           |
| Ordering                         | Business-key/partition scoped              |
| Concurrency                      | Optimistic locking by default where needed |
| Long-running consistency         | Saga                                       |
| Simple Saga                      | Choreography where appropriate             |
| Complex Saga                     | Orchestration                              |
| Workflow engine                  | Adoption-gated                             |
| Compensation                     | Explicit business operation                |
| Failed compensation              | Retry + escalation                         |
| Poison messages                  | DLT                                        |
| Replay                           | Controlled + idempotent                    |
| CQRS                             | Requirement-driven                         |
| Projections                      | Eventually consistent                      |
| Cache                            | Non-authoritative by default               |
| Reconciliation                   | Required for critical derived state        |
| Consistency observability        | Required                                   |
| DR                               | Cross-system consistency aware             |
| Status                           | **Accepted**                               |
| Priority                         | **Critical**                               |

---

# 150. Relationship With the Architecture

ADR-042 completes an important chain:

```text
ADR-040
North-South Traffic
      │
      ▼
ADR-041
Service-to-Service Communication
      │
      ▼
ADR-042
Distributed Consistency & Reliability
```

The architecture now answers three different questions:

```text
How does traffic ENTER Mediverse?
        │
        ▼
ADR-040

How do services COMMUNICATE?
        │
        ▼
ADR-041

How does distributed DATA remain CORRECT?
        │
        ▼
ADR-042
```

Combined:

```text
                       CLIENT
                         │
                         ▼
                    API GATEWAY
                      ADR-040
                         │
                         ▼
                    SERVICE A
                         │
             ┌───────────┴───────────┐
             ▼                       ▼
          REST                     OUTBOX
        ADR-041                       │
             │                        ▼
             ▼                      KAFKA
         SERVICE B                  ADR-041
             │                        │
             │                        ▼
             │                    SERVICE C
             │                        │
             └───────────┬────────────┘
                         ▼
                  CONSISTENCY LAYER
                      ADR-042
                         │
          ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
          ▼              ▼              ▼
       Local TX        Saga        Idempotency
          │              │              │
          └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                         ▼
                  Reconciliation
                         │
                         ▼
                 CORRECT BUSINESS
                      STATE
```

---

---

# ADR-043 — Enterprise Caching, Redis, Distributed Cache & Data Access Performance Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — AI Response Caching**.

---

# 61. AI Cache Key Design

AI caching cannot safely use only the raw user prompt as the cache key.

```text
"Explain cardiac cycle"
```

may produce different valid results depending on:

```text
Model
Model version
System prompt
Temperature
Language
Student level
Content version
Output format
```

Therefore these dimensions must be considered when determining cache identity.

---

# 62. Model-Aware Cache Keys

Conceptually:

```text
ai:<model>:<model-version>:<prompt-hash>:<context-version>
```

For example:

```text
mediverse:ai:v1:model-x:prompt-hash:content-v17
```

Changing the model or educational context should prevent accidental reuse of obsolete output.

---

# 63. Prompt Hashing

Large prompts should generally not become literal Redis keys.

Instead:

```text
Normalized Input
      │
      ▼
Canonical Representation
      │
      ▼
Cryptographic Hash
      │
      ▼
Redis Key
```

This keeps keys bounded and predictable.

---

# 64. AI Context Versioning

Suppose a cached explanation was generated from:

```text
Physiology Content v12
```

and faculty later publishes:

```text
Physiology Content v13
```

The old AI result may now be outdated.

The content/version dimension should therefore participate in cache validity.

---

# 65. Nondeterministic AI Outputs

Generative AI is often nondeterministic.

Two identical prompts can legitimately produce different responses.

Therefore caching changes semantics from:

```text
Generate new answer
```

to:

```text
Reuse previous answer
```

That should be a deliberate product decision.

---

# 66. AI Cache Eligibility

Good candidates may include:

```text
Generated summaries of immutable content
Repeated deterministic transformations
Pre-generated explanations
Structured extraction
Expensive embeddings
Stable educational metadata
```

Poor candidates include highly personalized or rapidly changing responses.

---

# 67. Personalized AI Responses

If output depends on:

```text
Student history
Learning level
Previous answers
Preferences
Progress
```

then sharing a generic cached response may produce incorrect personalization.

Cache identity must include the relevant personalization dimensions—or caching should be avoided.

---

# 68. AI Cache Privacy

Never allow:

```text
Student A personalized prompt
        │
        ▼
Shared cache
        │
        ▼
Student B receives Student A data
```

Tenant/user isolation must be explicit where cached data contains personalized information.

---

# 69. Semantic Caching

A future optimization may identify semantically similar requests.

```text
"What is cardiac output?"

"Explain cardiac output."

"Define cardiac output."
```

could potentially reuse related computation.

This is **semantic caching**.

---

# 70. Semantic Cache Risk

Semantic similarity does not prove equivalent intent.

In medical education, subtle wording differences can matter.

Therefore semantic caching shall **not** initially replace exact/context-aware caching for authoritative educational responses.

It requires dedicated quality evaluation.

---

# 71. Embedding Cache

Embedding generation is a stronger caching candidate.

```text
Content
   │
   ▼
Content Hash
   │
   ▼
Embedding Cache
```

If the exact content and embedding model/version are unchanged, regeneration is often unnecessary.

---

# 72. Redis Data Structures

Redis provides several structures:

```text
String
Hash
Set
Sorted Set
List
Stream
Bitmap
HyperLogLog
```

Architecture should select the simplest structure that matches the use case.

Do not use complex Redis structures simply because they exist.

---

# 73. Redis Strings

Strings are suitable for many cache entries.

```text
key
 │
 ▼
serialized value
```

Examples:

```text
JSON
small binary representation
counter
token-like temporary value
```

---

# 74. Redis Hashes

Hashes can represent grouped fields.

```text
course:123
   │
   ├── title
   ├── faculty
   ├── status
   └── version
```

But domain models should not be forced into Redis hashes merely to mimic relational tables.

---

# 75. Sorted Sets

Sorted sets can support workloads such as:

```text
Leaderboards
Rankings
Priority queues
Time-ordered scores
```

where Redis semantics genuinely fit.

---

# 76. Redis Streams

Redis Streams provide event-stream capabilities.

However, Mediverse has already selected:

```text
Kafka
```

as the primary enterprise event backbone.

Redis Streams should therefore not become a second competing general-purpose event platform.

---

# 77. Kafka vs Redis Streams

Architecture remains:

```text
Enterprise domain events
        │
        ▼
       Kafka

Cache / ephemeral fast state
        │
        ▼
       Redis
```

A separate ADR would be required to change that boundary.

---

# 78. Serialization

Objects stored in Redis require serialization.

Potential formats include:

```text
JSON
Binary serialization
MessagePack-like formats
Protobuf
```

Selection should balance:

```text
Size
Performance
Debuggability
Compatibility
Security
Schema evolution
```

---

# 79. Java Native Serialization

Java native object serialization should not be the default distributed cache format.

It creates:

```text
Tight Java coupling
Versioning problems
Poor interoperability
Security concerns
Opaque debugging
```

Explicit serialization formats are preferable.

---

# 80. JSON

JSON is easy to inspect:

```json
{
  "courseId": 123,
  "title": "Human Physiology"
}
```

Advantages:

```text
Readable
Debuggable
Language-neutral
```

Trade-off:

```text
Larger payload
More serialization overhead
```

---

# 81. Schema Evolution

Cached serialized objects can outlive a deployment.

Suppose:

```text
Application v1
→ caches object schema v1

Application v2
→ expects schema v2
```

Deployments must tolerate old cache entries or invalidate/version them.

---

# 82. Cache Schema Version

Key namespaces can include cache format versions:

```text
mediverse:v2:content:course:123
```

This makes incompatible migrations easier than attempting to mutate millions of existing cache entries.

---

# 83. Compression

Large cache values may be compressed where measurement proves worthwhile.

```text
Object
  │
  ▼
Serialize
  │
  ▼
Compress
  │
  ▼
Redis
```

But compression trades memory/network savings for CPU.

---

# 84. Compression Threshold

Compressing every 100-byte value is pointless.

Compression should only be considered above a measured payload threshold where savings justify CPU overhead.

---

# 85. Big Keys

A Redis key containing enormous data can cause:

```text
Network latency
CPU spikes
Memory pressure
Deletion latency
Replication overhead
```

Example of poor design:

```text
student:all-data
→ 100 MB
```

Cache objects should remain appropriately bounded.

---

# 86. Hot Keys

A hot key receives disproportionately high traffic.

```text
              course:popular
                    ▲
          ┌─────────┼─────────┐
          │         │         │
       Pod A      Pod B      Pod C
```

Even a distributed Redis cluster can bottleneck if nearly all traffic targets one shard/key.

---

# 87. Hot-Key Mitigation

Potential strategies include:

```text
L1 local caching
Request coalescing
Replica reads where semantics permit
Key decomposition
CDN caching
Application-level distribution
```

The correct approach depends on the workload.

---

# 88. Memory Sizing

Redis capacity should not be estimated only from raw business payload size.

Memory includes:

```text
Keys
Values
Redis object overhead
Allocator overhead
Replication
Fragmentation
Operational headroom
```

Therefore:

```text
10 GB raw JSON
```

does not imply:

```text
10 GB Redis memory required.
```

---

# 89. Capacity Headroom

Running Redis continuously near 100% memory usage is bad capacity planning.

Operational headroom is required for:

```text
Traffic spikes
Replication
Failover
Fragmentation
Temporary growth
Rebalancing
```

---

# 90. Eviction

When Redis reaches configured memory limits, eviction policy determines what happens.

Possible conceptual policies include:

```text
LRU-like
LFU-like
TTL-oriented
No eviction
```

The correct choice depends on whether the Redis deployment contains disposable cache data or correctness-sensitive state.

---

# 91. Cache Eviction Policy

For a dedicated disposable application cache, an LFU/LRU-style eviction strategy may be appropriate.

For correctness-sensitive Redis workloads:

```text
Idempotency
Coordination
Security controls
```

silent eviction may be unacceptable.

This reinforces the need for workload isolation.

---

# 92. Eviction Monitoring

Unexpected evictions should be monitored.

```text
evictions increasing
       │
       ▼
Memory pressure
       │
       ▼
Hit ratio falls
       │
       ▼
DB traffic rises
```

Cache problems can therefore propagate into database problems.

---

# 93. Managed Redis Architecture

Production Mediverse should prefer AWS-managed Redis-compatible infrastructure over self-hosting Redis Pods inside EKS.

Conceptually:

```text
EKS
 │
 ▼
Private Network
 │
 ▼
Managed Redis
```

This reduces operational responsibility for node replacement and high-availability mechanics.

---

# 94. Self-Hosted Redis in Kubernetes

Running Redis in EKS means Mediverse owns:

```text
StatefulSets
Persistent storage
Failover
Backups
Replication
Upgrades
Recovery
Capacity
Redis operations
```

There needs to be a compelling reason to accept that burden.

---

# 95. High Availability

Production Redis should avoid a single-instance architecture.

Bad:

```text
Applications
     │
     ▼
 Redis Node
     │
     X
Entire cache unavailable
```

High availability should include replicas/failover where required.

---

# 96. Primary/Replica

Conceptually:

```text
             Primary
               │
        ┌──────┴──────┐
        ▼             ▼
    Replica A      Replica B
```

If the primary fails, managed failover can promote an appropriate replica.

---

# 97. Multi-AZ

Production cache infrastructure should span availability zones where availability requirements justify it.

```text
AZ-A              AZ-B
 │                  │
 ▼                  ▼
Primary          Replica
```

This protects against more than a single-node failure.

---

# 98. Failover Is Not Zero Impact

During failover, applications may experience:

```text
Connection failures
Timeouts
Short unavailability
Topology changes
Retries
```

Applications must be designed to tolerate this.

---

# 99. Redis Cluster / Sharding

As data or throughput exceeds a single primary's practical capacity:

```text
Keyspace
   │
   ├── Shard A
   ├── Shard B
   └── Shard C
```

horizontal sharding may be required.

---

# 100. Do Not Start With Excessive Sharding

A tiny workload does not need a large Redis cluster.

Sharding introduces:

```text
Operational complexity
Cross-slot restrictions
Rebalancing
More nodes
Higher cost
```

Start according to measured capacity requirements.

---

# 101. Key Distribution

Good key design should distribute workload across shards.

Poor design can create:

```text
Shard A = 90% traffic
Shard B = 5%
Shard C = 5%
```

despite having three shards.

---

# 102. Multi-Key Operations

In sharded Redis architectures, operations involving several keys may have constraints depending on key placement.

Application design should not assume every multi-key operation behaves like a single-node Redis instance.

---

# 103. Spring Data Redis

Spring Boot services should standardize Redis access using supported Spring integrations such as:

```text
Spring Data Redis
```

rather than every service building custom Redis clients and conventions independently.

---

# 104. Lettuce

Lettuce is a common Redis client in the Spring ecosystem.

It supports capabilities such as:

```text
Async operations
Reactive operations
Connection management
Cluster awareness
```

Platform configuration should standardize appropriate client behavior.

---

# 105. Redis Connection Pooling

More connections are not automatically better.

```text
500 Pods
×
100 connections
=
50,000 Redis connections
```

can create unnecessary infrastructure pressure.

Connection strategy must be capacity-aware.

---

# 106. Redis Timeout

Redis calls require short, explicit timeouts.

Bad:

```text
Application waits indefinitely
        │
        ▼
Request threads exhausted
```

A cache dependency should not freeze the application.

---

# 107. Cache Latency Budget

If PostgreSQL normally responds in:

```text
20 ms
```

waiting:

```text
5 seconds
```

for a broken cache before falling back is absurd.

Cache timeout budgets should reflect the fact that caching exists to make operations faster.

---

# 108. Redis Retry

Blind retries can worsen an outage.

```text
Redis overloaded
     │
     ▼
Requests fail
     │
     ▼
Every Pod retries
     │
     ▼
Redis receives more traffic
```

Retries should be bounded and used only where safe.

---

# 109. Circuit Breaker

For suitable cache interactions:

```text
Application
     │
     ▼
Circuit Breaker
     │
     ▼
Redis
```

can prevent repeatedly waiting on an unhealthy cache.

The fallback path must still be capacity-controlled.

---

# 110. Database Protection During Cache Failure

The dangerous failure:

```text
Redis fails
    │
    ▼
100% requests
    │
    ▼
PostgreSQL
    │
    X
```

turns a cache outage into a database outage.

Fallback needs protection.

---

# 111. Controlled Degradation

Potential mechanisms include:

```text
Rate limiting
Concurrency limits
Serve stale values
Request coalescing
Circuit breakers
Partial feature degradation
```

depending on the endpoint.

---

# 112. TLS

Redis network communication containing sensitive Mediverse data should use encryption in transit.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
   TLS
    │
    ▼
Redis
```

---

# 113. Authentication

Redis access must be authenticated using the capabilities of the selected managed platform.

Do not deploy a production cache that accepts arbitrary unauthenticated cluster connections.

---

# 114. Network Isolation

Redis should reside in private network boundaries.

```text
Internet
   │
   X
Redis

EKS Workloads
   │
   ▼
Private Network
   │
   ▼
Redis
```

It should not require public internet exposure.

---

# 115. Security Groups

AWS network controls should restrict Redis connectivity to authorized application/platform workloads.

"Inside the VPC" is too broad as a security policy.

---

# 116. Secret Management

If Redis credentials/tokens are required, they should follow ADR-034's secrets architecture.

Avoid:

```text
application.yml
password: production-secret
```

committed into Git.

---

# 117. Sensitive Cached Data

Before caching sensitive data, evaluate:

```text
Is caching actually necessary?

What fields are needed?

Can data be minimized?

How long should it live?

Who can access Redis?

Will logs expose it?
```

Performance does not justify indiscriminate duplication of sensitive information.

---

# 118. Redis Persistence

Redis supports persistence mechanisms, but cache workloads should not automatically depend on them for correctness.

For disposable cache:

```text
Redis lost
    │
    ▼
Cache rebuilt
```

should remain a valid architecture.

---

# 119. Critical Redis State

If Redis stores something whose loss breaks correctness:

```text
Idempotency state
Certain rate-limit state
Coordination state
```

then that workload has different persistence/DR requirements from ordinary caching.

It should be treated explicitly rather than pretending all Redis data is disposable.

---

# 120. Backup Strategy

Ordinary reconstructable cache data may not justify expensive backup requirements.

Critical Redis-backed state may.

Backup policy must therefore be workload-specific.

---

# 121. Disaster Recovery

ADR-039 applies.

After regional recovery:

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
Cache Empty
```

should generally be survivable for normal caching workloads.

However, cache warm-up can create a large database spike.

---

# 122. Cold Cache

After cache loss:

```text
0% hit ratio
     │
     ▼
Every request misses
     │
     ▼
Database load spikes
```

This is the **cold-cache problem**.

---

# 123. Cache Warm-Up

For highly predictable hot datasets, controlled warm-up may be appropriate.

```text
Deployment / Recovery
        │
        ▼
Load selected hot keys
        │
        ▼
Open normal traffic
```

Do not preload the entire database blindly.

---

# 124. Observability

Redis observability should include:

```text
Hit ratio
Miss ratio
Latency
Connections
Memory usage
Evictions
Expired keys
CPU
Network
Replication health
Failover
Errors
Timeouts
Hot keys where available
```

---

# 125. Cache Hit Ratio

Conceptually:

```text
hit ratio =
cache hits /
(cache hits + cache misses)
```

But a high hit ratio alone does not prove the cache is useful.

---

# 126. Hit Ratio Context

A cache with:

```text
99% hit ratio
```

saving 1 ms on an irrelevant endpoint may have less value than:

```text
70% hit ratio
```

preventing thousands of expensive AI requests.

Measure business and infrastructure impact.

---

# 127. Application Metrics

Each service should expose cache metrics by logical cache where practical:

```text
courseMetadata
studentProgress
referenceData
aiResponse
```

rather than one meaningless global cache number.

---

# 128. Cache Latency

Monitor percentile latency:

```text
p50
p95
p99
```

A Redis average of 1 ms can hide severe tail latency.

---

# 129. Cache Miss Cost

Observability should understand what happens after a miss.

```text
Cache MISS
    │
    ├── DB query
    ├── external API
    └── AI inference
```

Not all misses have equal cost.

---

# 130. Memory Fragmentation

Redis memory consumption can exceed logical dataset size due to allocator behavior and fragmentation.

Capacity planning should therefore use actual runtime metrics, not only serialized payload estimates.

---

# 131. Rate Limiting State

Redis is a strong candidate for distributed rate-limit counters.

```text
Gateway replicas
      │
      ▼
Shared Redis
      │
      ▼
Rate-limit state
```

This provides consistent counters across multiple gateway instances.

---

# 132. Rate-Limit Isolation

Rate limiting should not compete uncontrolled with disposable cache entries.

A massive content-cache workload should not evict security-sensitive rate-limit state.

Isolation should reflect criticality.

---

# 133. Idempotency Keys

Redis can store short-lived idempotency records for APIs where the required durability window permits.

```text
Idempotency-Key
      │
      ▼
Redis
      │
 ┌────┴────┐
 ▼         ▼
NEW      EXISTS
 │         │
 ▼         ▼
Process  Return prior outcome
```

For critical durable workflows, ADR-042's database-backed idempotency/inbox patterns may be more appropriate.

---

# 134. Distributed Locking

Redis can provide coordination primitives for narrowly defined cases.

But a lock requires careful handling of:

```text
Lease expiry
Client crash
Clock assumptions
Fencing
Duplicate execution
Network partitions
```

A lock alone does not prove exclusive business execution.

---

# 135. Fencing Tokens

For high-risk distributed coordination, fencing/version tokens may be needed.

```text
Worker A lock token = 41
Worker B lock token = 42
```

Downstream state can reject stale token `41` after `42` becomes current.

This is stronger than trusting lock ownership indefinitely.

---

# 136. L1/L2 Coherence

With:

```text
Caffeine
   +
Redis
```

invalidating Redis does not automatically invalidate every JVM's Caffeine cache.

```text
Redis = new
Pod A L1 = old
Pod B L1 = old
```

This is the central cost of two-level caching.

---

# 137. L1 Strategy

If L1 is used, Mediverse should rely on:

```text
Very short TTL
+
Versioning
+
Optional invalidation events
```

depending on data criticality.

Do not attempt complex global L1 coherence unless the business requirement truly demands it.

---

# 138. Cache Testing

Tests should cover:

```text
Cache hit
Cache miss
Expired entry
Redis unavailable
Redis timeout
Invalidation
Concurrent miss
Serialization failure
Old cache schema
Eviction
```

Caching tests should not only prove that `@Cacheable` returns something.

---

# 139. Load Testing

Performance testing should compare:

```text
Warm cache
Cold cache
Partial cache
Redis degraded
Redis unavailable
```

A system that performs well only with a perfect warm cache is fragile.

---

# 140. Cache Anti-Patterns

Mediverse shall reject or strongly discourage:

```text
❌ Redis as default source of truth
❌ Cache everything
❌ Infinite TTL everywhere
❌ Same TTL for every domain
❌ Missing tenant dimension in keys
❌ Giant cache values
❌ Unbounded key growth
❌ Java native serialization by default
❌ Cache schema without versioning
❌ Authorization cached indefinitely
❌ Assessment transactional state blindly cached
❌ Large media stored in Redis
❌ No protection against stampede
❌ Every Pod rebuilding same missing key
❌ Redis locks used as global transactions
❌ Cache failure immediately flooding PostgreSQL
❌ Redis calls without timeouts
❌ Unlimited retries
❌ One Redis deployment for every criticality level
❌ Critical state using an eviction policy designed for disposable cache
❌ Redis Streams competing with Kafka without justification
❌ Self-hosted production Redis in EKS without a strong reason
❌ Hit ratio treated as the only success metric
❌ Two-level caching everywhere
❌ Personalized AI cache shared across users
❌ Semantic AI cache without quality validation
```

---

# 141. Cache Decision Tree

```text
                  DATA / COMPUTATION
                         │
                         ▼
                  Expensive/frequent?
                    ┌────┴────┐
                    ▼         ▼
                   NO        YES
                    │         │
                    ▼         ▼
                Don't cache  Can tolerate
                              staleness?
                             ┌────┴────┐
                             ▼         ▼
                            NO        YES
                             │         │
                             ▼         ▼
                       Avoid generic  Redis
                          caching      │
                                      ▼
                                Cache-Aside
                                      │
                                      ▼
                              Select TTL
                                      │
                                      ▼
                         Need ultra-low latency?
                               ┌──────┴──────┐
                               ▼             ▼
                              YES            NO
                               │             │
                               ▼             ▼
                          Consider L1       L2 only
                               │
                               ▼
                        Define coherence
```

---

# 142. Read Path

```text
                       REQUEST
                          │
                          ▼
                     Spring Boot
                          │
                          ▼
                  Optional Caffeine
                          │
                  ┌───────┴───────┐
                  ▼               ▼
                 HIT             MISS
                  │               │
                  │               ▼
                  │             Redis
                  │       ┌───────┴───────┐
                  │       ▼               ▼
                  │      HIT             MISS
                  │       │               │
                  │       │               ▼
                  │       │           PostgreSQL
                  │       │               │
                  │       │               ▼
                  │       │          Populate Redis
                  │       │               │
                  │       └───────┬───────┘
                  │               ▼
                  │          Populate L1
                  │               │
                  └───────────────┼───────────────
                                  ▼
                              RESPONSE
```

---

# 143. Write Path

```text
                       WRITE REQUEST
                            │
                            ▼
                       Domain Service
                            │
                            ▼
                    PostgreSQL Transaction
                            │
                            ▼
                          COMMIT
                            │
                            ▼
                    Cache Invalidation
                      ┌─────┴─────┐
                      ▼           ▼
                    Redis      Local L1
                      │
                      ▼
                  TTL remains
                safety boundary
```

Where distributed invalidation is justified:

```text
Domain Change
     │
     ▼
Transactional Outbox
     │
     ▼
Kafka
     │
     ▼
Cache Invalidation Consumer
```

---

# 144. Redis Infrastructure Architecture

```text
                         AWS
                          │
                          ▼
                         VPC
                          │
             ┌────────────┴────────────┐
             ▼                         ▼
           EKS                    Managed Redis
             │                         │
      ┌──────┼──────┐          ┌──────┴──────┐
      ▼      ▼      ▼          ▼             ▼
    Pod A  Pod B  Pod C      Primary       Replica
             │                  │             │
             └──────── TLS ─────┼─────────────┘
                                │
                                ▼
                         Multi-AZ Failover
```

Redis remains privately accessible.

---

# 145. Workload Separation

```text
                    REDIS PLATFORM
                          │
          ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
          ▼               ▼               ▼
     Disposable       Rate-Limit      Idempotency /
       Cache             State        Coordination
          │               │               │
          ▼               ▼               ▼
      Evictable       Security       Stronger
       Policy          semantics      retention
```

These may use logical or physical separation depending on scale, blast radius and criticality.

---

# 146. Complete Mediverse Caching Architecture

```text
                         STUDENT
                            │
                            ▼
                      CloudFront/CDN
                            │
                            ▼
                       API Gateway
                            │
                            ▼
                     Spring Boot
                            │
                ┌───────────┴───────────┐
                ▼                       ▼
          L1 Caffeine              L2 Redis
           Optional                    │
                │                      │
                └───────────┬──────────┘
                            │ MISS
                            ▼
                       PostgreSQL
                            │
                            ▼
                     Authoritative Data
                            │
                            ▼
                         Outbox
                            │
                            ▼
                          Kafka
                            │
                            ▼
                    Cache Invalidation
```

For media:

```text
S3 → CloudFront → Client
```

For AI:

```text
AI Request
   │
   ▼
Privacy + Eligibility Check
   │
   ▼
Model/Context-Aware Cache Key
   │
   ├── HIT → Cached Result
   │
   └── MISS → AI Provider → Cache
```

---

# 147. Reliability Model

```text
Cache healthy
    │
    ▼
Fast response

Cache slow
    │
    ▼
Short timeout
    │
    ▼
Controlled fallback

Cache unavailable
    │
    ▼
Circuit / degradation
    │
    ▼
Protect PostgreSQL

Cache recovered
    │
    ▼
Gradual warm-up
```

The objective is not merely "Redis HA."

The objective is preventing Redis failure from becoming a Mediverse outage.

---

# 148. Risks and Mitigations

| Risk                          | Mitigation                           |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Stale cache                   | TTL + invalidation                   |
| Cache stampede                | Jitter + coalescing                  |
| Cache avalanche               | Controlled fallback                  |
| Cache penetration             | Validation + rate limiting           |
| Redis outage overloads DB     | Circuit breaker + concurrency limits |
| Hot key                       | L1/CDN/key strategy                  |
| Big key                       | Size governance                      |
| Memory exhaustion             | Capacity + eviction                  |
| Tenant leakage                | Tenant-aware keys                    |
| Authorization staleness       | Short TTL/revalidation               |
| Serialization incompatibility | Versioned schema                     |
| Cold-cache spike              | Controlled warm-up                   |
| L1/L2 disagreement            | Short L1 TTL/versioning              |
| AI data leakage               | User/tenant-aware caching            |
| AI stale output               | Model/context versioning             |
| Redis lock correctness        | Narrow use + fencing where required  |
| Redis becomes database        | Explicit source-of-truth governance  |
| Critical state eviction       | Workload isolation                   |
| Cache observability gaps      | Metrics + tracing                    |

---

# 149. Decision Outcome

| Attribute                 | Decision                                   |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| **ADR**                   | ADR-043                                    |
| Distributed cache         | Redis-compatible managed service           |
| Production deployment     | AWS-managed                                |
| Self-hosted Redis in EKS  | Avoid by default                           |
| Default pattern           | Cache-Aside                                |
| Source of truth           | PostgreSQL/domain owner                    |
| L1 cache                  | Caffeine, targeted only                    |
| L2 cache                  | Redis                                      |
| CDN                       | CloudFront for appropriate assets          |
| Media cache               | CDN/object storage, not Redis blobs        |
| TTL                       | Domain-specific                            |
| TTL jitter                | Required for large cache populations       |
| Invalidation              | TTL + explicit/event-driven where needed   |
| Key naming                | Namespaced/versioned                       |
| Tenant isolation          | Mandatory                                  |
| Serialization             | Explicit portable format                   |
| Java native serialization | Avoid                                      |
| Cache schema versioning   | Required                                   |
| AI caching                | Context/model/privacy aware                |
| Semantic AI cache         | Adoption-gated                             |
| Redis Streams             | Not general event backbone                 |
| Enterprise events         | Kafka                                      |
| Distributed locking       | Narrowly scoped                            |
| Rate limiting             | Redis candidate                            |
| Idempotency               | Redis only where durability window permits |
| Security                  | Private network + TLS + authentication     |
| High availability         | Multi-AZ/replication according to tier     |
| Sharding                  | Capacity-driven                            |
| Redis timeout             | Short and explicit                         |
| Retry                     | Bounded                                    |
| DB fallback               | Controlled                                 |
| Observability             | Mandatory                                  |
| Status                    | **Accepted**                               |
| Priority                  | **High**                                   |

---

# 150. Relationship With Existing ADRs

The architecture now forms another clear chain:

```text
ADR-038
Capacity & Performance
      │
      ▼
ADR-041
Service Communication
      │
      ▼
ADR-042
Distributed Consistency
      │
      ▼
ADR-043
Caching & Redis
```

The order matters.

We first established:

```text
Who owns data?
        │
        ▼
What is authoritative?
        │
        ▼
How is distributed consistency achieved?
        │
        ▼
THEN
        │
        ▼
What can safely be cached?
```

Reversing that sequence is how Redis accidentally becomes an undocumented second database.

The resulting Mediverse data path is:

```text
                       REQUEST
                          │
                          ▼
                    CDN / Gateway
                          │
                          ▼
                    Application
                          │
             ┌────────────┴────────────┐
             ▼                         ▼
          Caffeine                   Redis
             │                         │
             └────────────┬────────────┘
                          │
                          ▼
                     PostgreSQL
                          │
                          ▼
                 AUTHORITATIVE STATE
                          │
                          ▼
                         Outbox
                          │
                          ▼
                         Kafka
                          │
              ┌───────────┼───────────┐
              ▼           ▼           ▼
          Projection   Cache       Analytics
                       Invalidation
```

---

---

# ADR-044 — Enterprise Search, OpenSearch, Indexing, Relevance, Semantic Search & RAG Retrieval Architecture

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-044
**Status:** Accepted
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)

ADR-043 established caching and Redis as optimization infrastructure. ADR-044 addresses a different problem: **searchable derived data**.

The central question is:

> **How should Mediverse provide fast, relevant, secure, multilingual, typo-tolerant, semantic and eventually AI/RAG-ready search without turning the search engine into another source of truth?**

---

# 1. Search Is Not Database Lookup

A database lookup answers questions such as:

```text
Find course where id = 123
```

Search answers questions such as:

```text
"cardiac cycle"
"heart sounds"
"renal physiology"
"action potential"
```

and must consider:

```text
Tokenization
Relevance
Spelling
Synonyms
Language
Ranking
Filters
Semantic similarity
Permissions
```

---

# 2. Mediverse Search Requirements

Users may need to search:

```text
Courses
Subjects
Chapters
Topics
Learning resources
Faculty content
Questions
Assessments
Medical terminology
3D learning modules
```

Eventually:

```text
Natural-language questions
Conceptually related material
AI/RAG knowledge retrieval
```

---

# 3. Core Decision

Mediverse shall use:

```text
PostgreSQL
     │
     │ Authoritative data
     ▼
Transactional Outbox
     │
     ▼
Kafka
     │
     ▼
Search Indexer
     │
     ▼
Amazon OpenSearch
     │
     ▼
Search API
```

The search index shall be a **derived projection**.

---

# 4. Source of Truth

The fundamental rule:

```text
PostgreSQL / Owning Service
          =
   AUTHORITATIVE STATE

OpenSearch
          =
    SEARCH PROJECTION
```

Search data must be reconstructable from authoritative sources.

---

# 5. Why This Matters

Suppose:

```text
PostgreSQL:
course.status = ARCHIVED

OpenSearch:
course.status = ACTIVE
```

PostgreSQL wins.

The index must eventually be corrected.

Never change PostgreSQL business state simply because OpenSearch disagrees.

---

# 6. PostgreSQL Search

PostgreSQL already provides useful search capabilities including:

```text
LIKE / ILIKE
Full-text search
GIN indexes
Trigram-based matching
```

A dedicated search platform is not automatically necessary for every query.

---

# 7. When PostgreSQL Is Enough

PostgreSQL remains appropriate for:

```text
Small datasets
Simple filtering
Exact lookups
Admin searches
Limited full-text requirements
Strongly transactional queries
```

Do not route every query through OpenSearch merely because OpenSearch exists.

---

# 8. Why Dedicated Search

A dedicated search engine becomes useful when Mediverse requires combinations of:

```text
Full-text relevance
Typo tolerance
Autocomplete
Synonyms
Faceting
Highlighting
Multilingual analysis
Large-scale search
Complex ranking
Vector search
Hybrid retrieval
```

---

# 9. Elasticsearch vs OpenSearch

Both ecosystems provide strong search capabilities.

For Mediverse's AWS-oriented architecture, the default managed search platform shall be:

```text
Amazon OpenSearch Service
```

rather than self-managing an Elasticsearch/OpenSearch cluster inside Kubernetes.

---

# 10. Why Managed OpenSearch

Operating search clusters requires handling:

```text
Cluster membership
Node failure
Shard allocation
Storage
Snapshots
Upgrades
Security
Capacity
JVM pressure
Recovery
```

These are specialized operational responsibilities.

Managed infrastructure reduces—but does not eliminate—the burden.

---

# 11. Search Architecture

```text
                  PostgreSQL
                      │
                      ▼
                 Domain Service
                      │
                      ▼
                    Outbox
                      │
                      ▼
                    Kafka
                      │
                      ▼
               Search Indexer
                      │
                      ▼
                  OpenSearch
                      │
                      ▼
                 Search API
                      │
                      ▼
                    Client
```

---

# 12. Why Kafka-Based Indexing

Bad architecture:

```text
Business Transaction
      │
      ├── Update PostgreSQL
      │
      └── Update OpenSearch
```

This recreates ADR-042's dual-write problem.

---

# 13. Search Dual-Write Failure

Example:

```text
PostgreSQL UPDATE    ✓
OpenSearch UPDATE    ✕
```

The business operation succeeded but the search index did not change.

The API should not pretend both writes were one transaction.

---

# 14. Outbox-Based Search Projection

Preferred:

```text
BEGIN

UPDATE course

INSERT outbox_event

COMMIT
```

Then:

```text
Outbox
  │
  ▼
Kafka
  │
  ▼
Search Indexer
  │
  ▼
OpenSearch
```

ADR-042's reliability model therefore extends naturally into search.

---

# 15. Event Example

Conceptually:

```json
{
  "eventId": "evt-123",
  "eventType": "CourseUpdated",
  "aggregateId": "course-456",
  "version": 7
}
```

The search consumer updates the corresponding search projection.

---

# 16. Indexing Must Be Idempotent

Kafka may redeliver events.

```text
CourseUpdated v7
       │
       ├──► Indexer
       └──► Indexer again
```

Repeated processing must not corrupt the search index.

---

# 17. Entity Versioning

Search documents should contain appropriate source/version information.

Conceptually:

```json
{
  "courseId": "456",
  "sourceVersion": 7
}
```

If an older update arrives after a newer one, the indexer can avoid overwriting newer state where the workflow requires such protection.

---

# 18. Out-of-Order Event Example

```text
CourseUpdated v8
      │
      ▼
OpenSearch = v8

CourseUpdated v7 arrives late
      │
      ▼
DO NOT regress to v7
```

Version-aware indexing protects against stale updates.

---

# 19. Delete Propagation

Deletion must also reach search.

```text
CourseDeleted
      │
      ▼
Kafka
      │
      ▼
Indexer
      │
      ▼
DELETE search document
```

Otherwise users may discover content that no longer exists.

---

# 20. Soft Deletion

Where business records use:

```text
status = ARCHIVED
```

rather than physical deletion, search behavior must explicitly decide whether archived content should:

```text
Disappear
Remain searchable to faculty
Remain accessible by direct link
```

This is a product/security decision.

---

# 21. Search Document

Search documents should be designed for retrieval.

They do **not** need to mirror normalized relational entities.

Example:

```json
{
  "courseId": "123",
  "title": "Human Physiology",
  "subject": "Physiology",
  "facultyName": "Faculty Name",
  "chapterNames": [
    "Cardiovascular Physiology",
    "Renal Physiology"
  ]
}
```

---

# 22. Denormalization

Search commonly benefits from denormalization.

Relational model:

```text
course
  │
  ├── subject
  ├── faculty
  └── chapters
```

Search projection:

```text
Course Search Document
 ├── course fields
 ├── subject fields
 ├── faculty searchable fields
 └── relevant classification fields
```

This avoids relational joins during every search query.

---

# 23. Denormalization Cost

If faculty name changes:

```text
Faculty
  │
  ├── Course A document
  ├── Course B document
  ├── Course C document
  └── Course D document
```

multiple search documents may need updating.

Denormalization trades update complexity for query performance.

---

# 24. Index Boundaries

Do not create one giant index containing every Mediverse object without considering lifecycle and query behavior.

Possible logical boundaries include:

```text
Learning content
Assessments
Users/faculty
Reference terminology
AI retrieval corpus
```

Actual physical index boundaries should be driven by:

```text
Scale
Security
Mappings
Lifecycle
Query patterns
```

---

# 25. Index Naming

Use versioned index names.

Example:

```text
mediverse-content-v1
mediverse-content-v2
```

Applications should generally query through aliases rather than hard-coded physical index names.

---

# 26. Search Alias

```text
Application
     │
     ▼
mediverse-content
     │
     ▼
mediverse-content-v3
```

The application knows the logical alias.

Infrastructure manages the underlying physical index.

---

# 27. Why Aliases Matter

Suppose mappings need a breaking change.

Instead of modifying production search destructively:

```text
Create v4
   │
   ▼
Reindex
   │
   ▼
Validate
   │
   ▼
Switch alias
```

This supports safer migration.

---

# 28. Zero-Downtime Reindex

```text
               Current
                  │
                  ▼
        mediverse-content-v3
                  ▲
                  │
              Alias
```

Build:

```text
mediverse-content-v4
```

Then:

```text
Backfill
Validate
Catch up events
Switch alias
```

Users continue searching during migration.

---

# 29. Full Reindexing

Mediverse must be able to rebuild search from authoritative state.

```text
PostgreSQL
     │
     ▼
Reindex Pipeline
     │
     ▼
New OpenSearch Index
```

Search correctness must not depend on preserving one irreplaceable index forever.

---

# 30. Reindex Triggers

Full or partial reindexing may be required after:

```text
Mapping change
Analyzer change
Document redesign
Indexer bug
Search corruption
New derived fields
Major ranking changes
```

---

# 31. Reindex and Live Updates

A subtle problem:

```text
Reindex starts at 10:00

Course changes at 10:15

Reindex finishes at 11:00
```

The new index must not lose the 10:15 update.

Backfill and live-event synchronization must therefore be coordinated.

---

# 32. Mapping

Mappings define field behavior.

Conceptually:

```text
title        → text
courseId     → keyword
status       → keyword
publishedAt  → date
rating       → numeric
```

Incorrect mappings can severely limit future search behavior.

---

# 33. Text vs Keyword

A critical distinction:

```text
text
→ analyzed full-text search

keyword
→ exact matching / filtering / aggregation
```

Example:

```text
title = text
status = keyword
tenantId = keyword
```

---

# 34. Multi-Fields

Sometimes the same value needs both behaviors.

Example:

```text
title
 ├── text representation
 └── keyword representation
```

This can support both relevance search and exact sorting/filtering.

---

# 35. Dynamic Mapping Risk

Allowing arbitrary application payloads to generate uncontrolled mappings can cause:

```text
Mapping explosion
Incorrect field types
Memory overhead
Operational instability
```

Important production indexes should use controlled mappings.

---

# 36. Analyzer

An analyzer transforms searchable text.

Conceptually:

```text
"Cardiac Cycle"
      │
      ▼
Tokenizer
      │
      ▼
cardiac
cycle
```

Additional filters can normalize the resulting terms.

---

# 37. Tokenization

Input:

```text
Cardiac output regulation
```

might become:

```text
cardiac
output
regulation
```

Search relevance then operates on these terms rather than only exact full strings.

---

# 38. Lowercase Normalization

Users may search:

```text
CARDIAC
Cardiac
cardiac
```

Search should generally normalize case appropriately.

---

# 39. Stop Words

Common words such as:

```text
the
a
of
```

may carry little search value in some contexts.

But medical terminology and educational phrases require caution.

Aggressive stop-word removal can destroy meaning.

---

# 40. Stemming

Stemming attempts to normalize related word forms.

Conceptually:

```text
regulate
regulating
regulation
```

may be treated as related terms.

However, medical terminology requires quality testing before aggressive linguistic transformations.

---

# 41. Medical Search Is Different

Generic e-commerce search assumptions cannot simply be copied into Mediverse.

Medical terminology contains:

```text
Acronyms
Latin-derived terminology
Drug names
Anatomical terms
Abbreviations
Similar spellings with different meanings
```

Search normalization must preserve clinical/educational meaning.

---

# 42. Synonyms

Users may search:

```text
heart attack
```

while educational content uses:

```text
myocardial infarction
```

Synonym support can bridge terminology.

---

# 43. Medical Synonym Governance

Synonym dictionaries must be curated.

Blindly generated synonyms can produce medically incorrect retrieval.

For example, "related concepts" are not automatically interchangeable synonyms.

This is a content-governance problem, not merely an OpenSearch configuration problem.

---

# 44. Acronyms

Search should understand appropriate domain abbreviations.

Examples:

```text
ECG
BP
CNS
ANS
```

But acronym expansion must consider ambiguity.

One acronym can have multiple meanings depending on context.

---

# 45. Typo Tolerance

Users will make spelling mistakes.

Example:

```text
physiolgy
```

should potentially discover:

```text
physiology
```

Fuzzy matching can help.

---

# 46. Fuzzy Search Risk

Excessive fuzziness may retrieve unrelated medical terms.

Therefore:

```text
More fuzzy
≠
Better search
```

Fuzziness must be tuned and relevance-tested.

---

# 47. Autocomplete

Users may type:

```text
card...
```

and receive suggestions such as:

```text
Cardiac Cycle
Cardiac Output
Cardiac Muscle
Cardiovascular Physiology
```

Autocomplete should use a dedicated query/indexing strategy rather than expensive wildcard searches across everything.

---

# 48. Prefix Search

Prefix matching may support:

```text
neph
```

→

```text
nephron
nephrology
```

but prefix strategies need careful index design to avoid excessive index growth.

---

# 49. Wildcard Anti-Pattern

Queries such as:

```text
*cardiac*
```

across large fields can become expensive.

Do not use unrestricted wildcard search as the primary autocomplete architecture.

---

# 50. Search Relevance

Search is not simply:

```text
MATCH / NO MATCH
```

It must rank results.

```text
Query
  │
  ▼
Result A score 12.4
Result B score 8.7
Result C score 4.2
```

Ranking quality directly affects product usability.

---

# 51. BM25

OpenSearch commonly uses BM25-style lexical relevance.

It considers factors such as:

```text
Term frequency
Document frequency
Document length
```

This provides a strong baseline for text retrieval.

---

# 52. Field Boosting

Matches in some fields should matter more.

Example:

```text
Title match          × high boost
Chapter title        × medium boost
Description          × normal
Body text            × lower
```

A query matching the exact topic title should usually outrank a document that mentions the phrase once deep in its body.

---

# 53. Exact Match Boost

If the user searches:

```text
Cardiac Cycle
```

an exact title:

```text
Cardiac Cycle
```

should generally rank above:

```text
Introduction to Cardiovascular Physiology
```

that merely mentions cardiac cycle.

---

# 54. Phrase Matching

Word order can matter.

```text
cardiac output
```

should often receive stronger relevance than documents independently containing:

```text
cardiac
...
output
```

far apart.

---

# 55. Freshness

Recently updated content may deserve a ranking boost in some contexts.

But:

```text
Newest
≠
Most educationally relevant
```

Freshness should be one ranking signal, not the universal ranking rule.

---

# 56. Popularity

Signals such as:

```text
Views
Enrollments
Completion
Faculty curation
Student engagement
```

could influence ranking.

But blindly ranking by popularity creates feedback loops where popular content becomes permanently dominant.

---

# 57. Ranking Governance

Mediverse should distinguish:

```text
Lexical relevance
Content quality
Curriculum relevance
Freshness
Popularity
Personalization
```

rather than mixing them into undocumented scoring logic.

---

# 58. Filters

Users may filter search results by:

```text
Subject
Year
Course
Content type
Faculty
Difficulty
Language
Publication status
```

Filter fields should generally use exact/non-analyzed representations.

---

# 59. Facets

Search can expose result distributions:

```text
Subject
 ├── Physiology (120)
 ├── Anatomy (96)
 └── Biochemistry (75)
```

This improves navigation and discovery.

---

# 60. Security Filters

Search results must never rely on the frontend to hide unauthorized documents.

Authorization constraints must participate in server-side search.

```text
Search Query
     │
     +
Authorization Context
     │
     ▼
OpenSearch Query
     │
     ▼
Authorized Results Only
```

---

## ADR-044 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

The core search architecture is now:

```text
                    AUTHORITATIVE DATA
                           │
                           ▼
                       PostgreSQL
                           │
                           ▼
                         Outbox
                           │
                           ▼
                          Kafka
                           │
                           ▼
                     Search Indexer
                           │
                           ▼
                      OpenSearch
                           │
                           ▼
                       Search API
                           │
                           ▼
                         User
```

with index lifecycle:

```text
Current Index v3
      │
      ▼
Create Index v4
      │
      ▼
Backfill
      │
      ▼
Process live changes
      │
      ▼
Validate
      │
      ▼
Atomic Alias Switch
      │
      ▼
Retire v3
```

and retrieval:

```text
User Query
    │
    ▼
Normalization
    │
    ▼
Lexical Search
    │
    ├── Title
    ├── Chapter
    ├── Description
    ├── Medical synonyms
    ├── Typo tolerance
    └── Filters
          │
          ▼
       Ranking
          │
          ▼
Security Filtering
          │
          ▼
Results
```

The most important rule established so far is:

> **OpenSearch is not Mediverse's database. PostgreSQL/domain services own business truth; OpenSearch owns search-optimized projections that must be disposable and rebuildable.**

This prevents the same architectural mistake ADR-043 prevented with Redis: creating another hidden source of truth.

**Part 2** should continue from **Section 61 — Tenant & ACL-Aware Search**, then cover document-level authorization, permission changes and stale indexes, pagination, deep pagination, `search_after`, sorting, highlighting, multilingual search, English/Hindi/Marathi analysis, transliteration, language detection, medical terminology dictionaries, query understanding, zero-result recovery, query suggestions, semantic search, embeddings, vector indexing, approximate nearest-neighbor search, embedding model/version lifecycle, chunking, hybrid lexical + vector retrieval, reciprocal rank fusion, reranking, RAG retrieval, metadata filtering, citations/source traceability, hallucination boundaries, personalized search, search analytics, click signals, relevance evaluation, offline test sets, NDCG/MRR/Recall@K, A/B testing, bulk indexing, backpressure, Kafka lag, indexing failures, DLT/replay, shard strategy, replicas, hot shards, Multi-AZ, capacity planning, query timeouts, circuit breakers, degraded search, snapshots, DR, security, encryption, observability, cost governance, testing, anti-patterns and the final Mediverse enterprise search + semantic retrieval architecture.

---

---

# ADR-045 — Enterprise AI Platform, LLM Gateway, RAG, Prompt Orchestration, AI Safety & Agent Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Output Controls**.

---

# 61. AI Privacy Boundary

Every AI request crosses a new data-processing boundary.

```text
Mediverse Data
      │
      ▼
AI Platform
      │
      ▼
Model Provider
```

Before data crosses that boundary, Mediverse must determine:

```text
What data is being sent?
Why is it required?
Which provider/model receives it?
How long can it be retained?
Can less data accomplish the same task?
```

---

# 62. Data Minimization

Do not send an entire student profile when the model only needs:

```text
Course
Topic
Difficulty level
Question
```

Preferred:

```text
Minimum Required Context
        │
        ▼
      Model
```

not:

```text
Entire User Record
        │
        ▼
      Model
```

---

# 63. PII Handling

AI prompts may accidentally contain:

```text
Names
Email addresses
Student identifiers
Institution identifiers
Free-text personal information
```

AI integrations must therefore follow Mediverse privacy and data-classification policies.

---

# 64. Redaction Layer

Where appropriate:

```text
Raw Input
    │
    ▼
PII Detection
    │
    ▼
Redaction / Tokenization
    │
    ▼
LLM Request
```

Example:

```text
"Explain this to student John Smith"
```

may become:

```text
"Explain this to the student"
```

when identity is irrelevant.

---

# 65. Provider Data Policy

Provider selection must evaluate more than model quality.

Evaluate:

```text
Data retention
Training usage
Enterprise privacy terms
Regional processing
Security controls
Compliance
Deletion mechanisms
Logging behavior
```

A technically strong model with unacceptable data handling is not an acceptable Mediverse provider.

---

# 66. Data Residency

Where contractual or regulatory requirements impose residency constraints:

```text
Student Data
     │
     ▼
Approved Region
     │
     ▼
Approved AI Endpoint
```

Model routing must respect those constraints.

---

# 67. Prompt Logging

Logging full prompts is dangerous.

Prompts may contain:

```text
Personal information
Assessment content
Student answers
Retrieved educational material
Internal system instructions
```

Therefore production AI logs should default toward metadata rather than indiscriminate raw content.

---

# 68. AI Log Metadata

Useful metadata includes:

```text
Request ID
User/tenant pseudonymous reference
Feature
Prompt version
Model
Model version
Token count
Latency
Cost
Retrieval IDs
Safety result
Outcome
```

Raw prompts and responses require explicit retention policy.

---

# 69. AI Credentials

Provider API keys must follow Mediverse secrets-management architecture.

Never:

```text
frontend.js
   │
   ▼
LLM API key
```

Clients should never receive privileged provider credentials.

---

# 70. Tenant Isolation

AI processing must preserve tenant boundaries across:

```text
Prompt construction
RAG retrieval
Conversation memory
Caching
Logs
Vector search
Agent state
```

Tenant leakage in AI context is a serious security incident.

---

# 71. Authorization Before AI

Authorization happens **before** retrieval and model invocation.

```text
User
 │
 ▼
Authentication
 │
 ▼
Authorization
 │
 ▼
AI Workflow
```

The LLM must not decide whether a user is permitted to access protected content.

---

# 72. AI Cannot Expand Permissions

If a student cannot access:

```text
Faculty-only assessment answers
```

the RAG system cannot retrieve them merely because the student asks:

```text
"Tell me the faculty answer key."
```

Search and tool access must enforce existing authorization.

---

# 73. Token Budget

Tokens are simultaneously:

```text
Capacity
Latency
Cost
```

Therefore every AI feature should have a defined token budget.

---

# 74. Token Budget Components

```text
System Prompt
      +
Conversation
      +
Retrieved Context
      +
User Input
      +
Tool Results
      +
Output Budget
```

must fit within the approved model context.

---

# 75. Context Is Not Free

Sending 100,000 tokens because the model supports them is poor architecture.

Large contexts can increase:

```text
Cost
Latency
Noise
Retrieval dilution
```

Context size should be intentionally controlled.

---

# 76. AI Rate Limiting

AI endpoints require dedicated rate limits.

```text
User
 │
 ▼
API Gateway
 │
 ▼
AI Rate Limit
 │
 ▼
AI Platform
```

This protects both infrastructure and budget.

---

# 77. AI Quotas

Mediverse may define quotas by:

```text
Tenant
User
Feature
Model class
Subscription tier
Time period
```

For example, expensive AI tutoring should not necessarily have the same quota as lightweight classification.

---

# 78. Cost Attribution

Every AI request should be attributable to:

```text
Tenant
Feature
Model
Environment
```

where practical.

Without attribution, AI spend becomes an unexplained infrastructure bill.

---

# 79. AI Cost Formula

Conceptually:

```text
AI Cost
   =
Input Tokens
   +
Output Tokens
   +
Embedding Cost
   +
Reranking Cost
   +
Tool/Infrastructure Cost
```

RAG itself is not free simply because retrieval is internal.

---

# 80. Budget Guardrails

Controls should support:

```text
Daily limits
Monthly limits
Tenant budgets
Feature budgets
Unexpected-spend alerts
```

A software bug must not be able to generate unlimited model calls.

---

# 81. Semantic Caching

ADR-043 established AI caching boundaries.

For suitable workloads:

```text
AI Request
    │
    ▼
Eligibility
    │
    ▼
Cache
 ┌──┴──┐
 ▼     ▼
HIT   MISS
 │     │
 ▼     ▼
Return Model
```

Cache identity must remain model/context/version aware.

---

# 82. AI Cache Safety

Do not cache personalized outputs globally.

Cache scope may need:

```text
Global
Tenant
User
Conversation
```

depending on data sensitivity and semantics.

---

# 83. Streaming Responses

AI tutoring benefits from streaming:

```text
LLM
 │
 ▼
Token Stream
 │
 ▼
Backend
 │
 ▼
Student UI
```

Users see output before full generation completes.

---

# 84. Streaming Does Not Bypass Safety

A major complication:

```text
Token generated
      │
      ▼
Immediately displayed
```

means post-generation validation becomes harder.

High-risk features may require buffering or incremental safety controls.

---

# 85. AI Timeout

Model calls require explicit deadlines.

```text
Request
  │
  ▼
LLM
  │
  ...
  │ timeout
  ▼
Controlled Failure
```

A model provider must not consume application resources indefinitely.

---

# 86. Retry Policy

Retries are appropriate only for transient failures.

```text
Timeout
429
Temporary 5xx
```

may justify bounded retries.

Invalid requests or safety rejections generally do not.

---

# 87. Duplicate Generation

Retrying after an ambiguous timeout may generate twice.

Therefore workflows involving cost or downstream actions require idempotency awareness.

---

# 88. Provider Circuit Breaker

```text
AI Platform
    │
    ▼
Circuit Breaker
    │
    ▼
Provider
```

Repeated provider failures should stop causing every request to wait for the same unhealthy dependency.

---

# 89. Provider Fallback

```text
Model A
   │
   ✕
   ▼
Routing Policy
   │
   ▼
Model B
```

Fallback is allowed only when Model B is approved for the same workload/risk class.

---

# 90. Graceful AI Degradation

AI failure should not necessarily break Mediverse.

Example:

```text
AI Tutor unavailable
       │
       ▼
Traditional Search
       │
       ▼
Learning Content
```

Core educational navigation should remain usable where possible.

---

# 91. Hallucination Measurement

"Hallucination" must become measurable rather than anecdotal.

Evaluate:

```text
Unsupported claims
Contradictions
Incorrect citations
Incorrect medical facts
Missing evidence
```

against curated evaluation datasets.

---

# 92. Groundedness

A grounded response should be supported by retrieved evidence.

Conceptually:

```text
Claim
 │
 ▼
Evidence exists?
 ├── YES → supported
 └── NO  → unsupported
```

Groundedness is separate from writing quality.

---

# 93. Correctness vs Groundedness

A statement can be:

```text
Factually correct
but
```
