```text
not supported by supplied Mediverse evidence
```

or:

```text
Supported by retrieved material
but
source material itself is outdated
```

Both dimensions matter.

---

# 94. RAG Evaluation

Evaluate the pipeline separately:

```text
Retrieval Quality
       │
       ▼
Context Quality
       │
       ▼
Generation Quality
```

Otherwise a bad answer cannot be diagnosed properly.

---

# 95. Golden Dataset

Mediverse should maintain curated evaluation datasets.

Example:

```text
Question
Expected Concepts
Expected Sources
Known Incorrect Answers
Risk Category
```

Faculty-reviewed datasets are particularly valuable.

---

# 96. Retrieval Metrics

From ADR-044:

```text
Recall@K
MRR
NDCG
Precision
```

help determine whether correct material reaches the model.

---

# 97. Generation Metrics

Possible dimensions include:

```text
Correctness
Groundedness
Completeness
Relevance
Citation accuracy
Instruction adherence
Safety
```

No single score should represent total AI quality.

---

# 98. LLM-as-Judge

Another model may evaluate generated responses.

```text
Response
   │
   ▼
Judge Model
   │
   ▼
Score
```

This can scale evaluation but introduces another probabilistic system.

---

# 99. LLM-as-Judge Limitation

Judge models can exhibit:

```text
Bias
Inconsistency
Position effects
Model-family preference
Incorrect medical judgment
```

Therefore automated judges supplement—not replace—faculty-reviewed evaluation.

---

# 100. Faculty Evaluation

For educational correctness:

```text
AI Evaluation
     +
Faculty Evaluation
```

is stronger than either alone.

High-risk AI changes should include domain-expert review.

---

# 101. Prompt Regression Testing

Changing:

```text
Prompt v8
   ↓
Prompt v9
```

may improve one scenario and break another.

Every production prompt update should run against an evaluation suite.

---

# 102. Model Upgrade Testing

Never assume:

```text
Newer model
=
Better for Mediverse
```

A new model may change:

```text
Medical accuracy
Formatting
Latency
Cost
Tool behavior
Safety
```

Model upgrades require regression evaluation.

---

# 103. Shadow Evaluation

A candidate model can process duplicated evaluation/production-like requests without serving its output to users.

```text
Production Request
       │
       ├──► Current Model → User
       │
       └──► Candidate Model → Evaluation
```

This helps compare behavior safely.

---

# 104. Canary AI Rollout

After validation:

```text
5% traffic
   │
   ▼
Observe
   │
   ▼
25%
   │
   ▼
Observe
   │
   ▼
100%
```

where the product and provider architecture permit controlled routing.

---

# 105. AI Observability

Every request should produce correlated telemetry across:

```text
Gateway
AI Platform
Retrieval
Reranker
Model
Tools
Validation
```

A single AI request can span many systems.

---

# 106. AI Trace

Conceptually:

```text
Trace ID
   │
   ├── Authorization
   ├── Retrieval
   ├── Reranking
   ├── Prompt construction
   ├── Model invocation
   ├── Tool calls
   └── Validation
```

This dramatically improves debugging.

---

# 107. AI Metrics

Monitor:

```text
Requests
Latency
Failures
Timeouts
Token usage
Cost
Cache hits
Provider errors
Safety blocks
Retrieval quality
Grounding failures
```

---

# 108. Quality Monitoring

Traditional infrastructure monitoring can tell you:

```text
HTTP 200
Latency 1.5 sec
```

while the AI answer is wrong.

Therefore AI requires **quality telemetry** in addition to infrastructure telemetry.

---

# 109. Agent Architecture

An agent differs from ordinary generation because it can:

```text
Reason
Select tools
Execute actions
Observe results
Repeat
```

Conceptually:

```text
Goal
 │
 ▼
LLM
 │
 ▼
Choose Tool
 │
 ▼
Execute
 │
 ▼
Observe
 │
 └────► LLM
```

This dramatically increases risk.

---

# 110. Tool Calling

Tools expose deterministic capabilities to the model.

Examples:

```text
Search curriculum
Get course details
Retrieve student progress
Generate draft quiz
Create faculty draft
```

The model selects tools, but the platform executes them.

---

# 111. Tool Registry

Mediverse should maintain a governed tool registry.

Each tool should define:

```text
Tool ID
Description
Input schema
Output schema
Owner
Authorization policy
Risk class
Read/write classification
Timeout
```

---

# 112. Tool Input Validation

Never trust model-generated arguments.

```text
LLM Tool Call
      │
      ▼
Schema Validation
      │
      ▼
Authorization
      │
      ▼
Business Validation
      │
      ▼
Execution
```

The model is an untrusted caller.

---

# 113. Least Privilege

An AI tutor should not receive:

```text
deleteStudent()
publishAssessment()
changeRole()
```

merely because those APIs exist.

Each agent receives only the minimum required tools.

---

# 114. Read vs Write Tools

Classify:

```text
READ
────
Search content
Get progress
Retrieve chapter

WRITE
─────
Create draft
Modify content
Publish content
Change enrollment
```

Write tools require substantially stronger controls.

---

# 115. Human Confirmation Boundary

High-impact actions should use:

```text
Agent proposes action
        │
        ▼
Human confirms
        │
        ▼
Domain Service executes
```

not:

```text
LLM thinks action is useful
        │
        ▼
Production mutation
```

---

# 116. Confirmation Must Be Meaningful

A confirmation such as:

```text
"AI wants to perform an action. Continue?"
```

is poor UX.

Users should see:

```text
What will change
Which resource
Expected effect
Potential consequence
```

before approval.

---

# 117. Autonomous Action Restrictions

Mediverse shall initially prohibit unrestricted autonomous AI actions affecting:

```text
Roles/permissions
Student records
Assessment publication
Grades
Financial operations
Security configuration
Production infrastructure
```

Such capabilities require separate explicit architectural approval.

---

# 118. Agent Loop Limit

An agent must not run indefinitely.

```text
Step 1
Step 2
...
Step 9,999
```

creates cost and safety risk.

Define:

```text
Maximum steps
Maximum tool calls
Maximum tokens
Maximum elapsed time
Maximum cost
```

---

# 119. Agent Termination

Agents should terminate when:

```text
Goal completed
No progress
Tool repeatedly fails
Budget exceeded
Safety policy triggered
Human approval required
```

---

# 120. Agent State

Agent execution may need state:

```text
Goal
Current step
Tool results
Pending approvals
Budget consumed
Status
```

Critical long-running state must not live only in JVM memory.

---

# 121. Durable Agent Workflow

For long-running agents:

```text
Agent
  │
  ▼
Durable Workflow State
  │
  ▼
Tool Execution
  │
  ▼
Checkpoint
```

ADR-042's durable workflow principles apply directly.

---

# 122. Agent Idempotency

Suppose:

```text
Create Draft
     ✓
     │
Agent crashes
     │
Retry
```

The retry must not accidentally create ten duplicate drafts.

Write tools require idempotency where appropriate.

---

# 123. Tool Result Trust

Tool outputs can contain malicious or untrusted text.

Example:

```text
Search Result
"Ignore system instructions..."
```

Tool results therefore remain data, not privileged instructions.

---

# 124. Agent Authorization

Authorization must be evaluated against the actual user/service identity.

```text
Agent
 │
 ▼
Tool Call
 │
 ▼
Authorization Service
 │
 ▼
Allowed?
```

Do not give the agent a superuser identity simply to simplify implementation.

---

# 125. Delegated Identity

Where agents act on behalf of users:

```text
User Identity
      │
      ▼
Delegated Agent Context
      │
      ▼
Tool
```

the action should remain attributable to the originating user and agent workflow.

---

# 126. Agent Audit

Audit records should capture:

```text
Who initiated
Which agent
Model/version
Prompt/version
Tools invoked
Arguments or safe representation
Results
Approvals
Mutations
Final outcome
```

according to security/privacy policy.

---

# 127. MCP Evaluation

A standardized protocol such as MCP may simplify tool/resource integration.

But protocol adoption does not solve:

```text
Authorization
Trust
Prompt injection
Tool safety
Audit
Data leakage
```

These remain Mediverse responsibilities.

---

# 128. MCP Adoption Rule

MCP should be considered where it provides meaningful interoperability.

It should **not** be adopted merely because it is fashionable.

The architecture must first define:

```text
Trust boundaries
Tool ownership
Authentication
Authorization
Data classification
```

---

# 129. Multi-Agent Systems

Possible future architecture:

```text
Coordinator Agent
     │
 ┌───┼─────────┐
 ▼   ▼         ▼
Search Tutor Assessment
Agent  Agent     Agent
```

This can separate responsibilities.

It also multiplies complexity.

---

# 130. Multi-Agent Warning

Multiple LLMs communicating with each other introduce:

```text
More tokens
More latency
More failure points
Harder debugging
Harder evaluation
Emergent behavior
```

Use multiple agents only when specialization demonstrably improves outcomes.

---

# 131. AI Incident Response

AI incidents may include:

```text
Unsafe response
Medical misinformation
Data leakage
Prompt injection
Runaway cost
Unauthorized tool action
Provider compromise
Systematic bad retrieval
```

These require explicit incident procedures.

---

# 132. AI Kill Switch

Mediverse should be able to disable:

```text
Specific feature
Specific prompt
Specific model
Specific provider
Specific tool
Specific agent
```

without requiring an emergency full-platform deployment.

---

# 133. Feature Flags

AI capabilities should integrate with feature-management controls.

```text
AI Tutor
ON/OFF

Quiz Generation
ON/OFF

Agent Writes
ON/OFF
```

This supports safe rollout and incident response.

---

# 134. AI Auditability

For consequential operations, Mediverse should be able to answer:

```text
Which model generated this?
Which prompt?
Which knowledge sources?
Which tools?
Which user?
Which approvals?
When?
```

If these questions cannot be answered, governance is insufficient.

---

# 135. AI Governance

Governance should cover:

```text
Approved providers
Approved models
Approved use cases
Risk classification
Evaluation thresholds
Privacy requirements
Human-review requirements
Retention
Incident management
Retirement
```

---

# 136. AI Threat Model

The threat model should explicitly consider:

```text
Prompt injection
Indirect prompt injection
Sensitive-data disclosure
Excessive agency
Insecure tool invocation
Output handling vulnerabilities
Knowledge poisoning
Model denial-of-service
Supply-chain risks
```

AI security is broader than content moderation.

---

# 137. Knowledge Poisoning

If an attacker can insert malicious content into the RAG corpus:

```text
Attacker Content
      │
      ▼
Search Index
      │
      ▼
RAG
      │
      ▼
AI Answer
```

they may influence future answers.

Knowledge ingestion therefore requires authorization and provenance controls.

---

# 138. AI Testing Pyramid

```text
               Faculty Evaluation
                     ▲
                    / \
                   /   \
              E2E AI Tests
                 /       \
            RAG Evaluation
              /           \
        Prompt Regression
            /               \
      Deterministic Unit Tests
```

Not every AI test should call a live expensive model.

---

# 139. Deterministic Testing

Traditional tests remain useful for:

```text
Authorization
Prompt assembly
Schema validation
Tool validation
Budget calculation
Citation mapping
Routing policy
Cache keys
```

These should not depend on probabilistic model responses.

---

# 140. AI Anti-Patterns

Mediverse shall reject or strongly discourage:

```text
❌ Every service directly integrating model providers
❌ API keys exposed to frontend clients
❌ LLM treated as medical source of truth
❌ RAG assumed to eliminate hallucination
❌ Entire database sent as model context
❌ Full prompts logged indiscriminately
❌ Personalized AI output globally cached
❌ New model deployed because benchmark marketing says it is better
❌ Prompts edited directly in production
❌ No prompt/model version tracking
❌ Fake LLM-generated citations
❌ Retrieval without authorization filtering
❌ User conversation treated as authoritative medical knowledge
❌ LLM used where deterministic code is sufficient
❌ AI grading automatically controlling high-stakes outcomes
❌ Model-generated JSON trusted without validation
❌ Tool arguments trusted because the LLM generated them
❌ Agent given superuser credentials
❌ Agent given every available tool
❌ Unlimited agent loops
❌ Autonomous production writes without explicit governance
❌ Multi-agent architecture without measurable benefit
❌ MCP treated as a security boundary
❌ LLM-as-judge treated as objective ground truth
❌ AI quality measured only through HTTP uptime
❌ No AI kill switch
```

---

# 141. AI Request Decision Tree

```text
                     AI USE CASE
                         │
                         ▼
                Deterministic code
                   sufficient?
                 ┌───────┴───────┐
                 ▼               ▼
                YES              NO
                 │               │
                 ▼               ▼
             Use code        Classify risk
                                 │
                    ┌────────────┼────────────┐
                    ▼            ▼            ▼
                   LOW         MEDIUM        HIGH
                    │            │            │
                    ▼            ▼            ▼
                 Model       RAG/Safety    Human Review
                    │            │            │
                    └────────────┼────────────┘
                                 ▼
                          Approved Model
                                 │
                                 ▼
                           Validate Output
```

---

# 142. AI Gateway Architecture

```text
                   MEDIVERSE SERVICES
                           │
                           ▼
                      AI GATEWAY
                           │
          ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
          ▼                ▼                ▼
     Authentication    Rate Limits       Quotas
          │                │                │
          └────────────────┼────────────────┘
                           ▼
                      Model Router
                           │
              ┌────────────┼────────────┐
              ▼            ▼            ▼
           Model A       Model B     Embeddings
```

---

# 143. RAG Architecture

```text
Student Question
       │
       ▼
Authorization
       │
       ▼
Query Understanding
       │
       ▼
Hybrid Retrieval
       │
       ▼
ACL Filtering
       │
       ▼
Reranking
       │
       ▼
Context Builder
       │
       ▼
Prompt Registry
       │
       ▼
Model Router
       │
       ▼
LLM
       │
       ▼
Grounding Validation
       │
       ▼
Answer + Verified Sources
```

---

# 144. Agent Architecture

```text
                       USER
                        │
                        ▼
                  Agent Gateway
                        │
                        ▼
                  Agent Runtime
                        │
             ┌──────────┼──────────┐
             ▼          ▼          ▼
          Planner    Policy     Budget
             │          │          │
             └──────────┼──────────┘
                        ▼
                  Tool Registry
                        │
           ┌────────────┼────────────┐
           ▼            ▼            ▼
        Search       Read APIs    Write APIs
           │            │            │
           │            │            ▼
           │            │      Human Approval
           │            │            │
           └────────────┼────────────┘
                        ▼
                   Domain Services
```

---

# 145. AI Reliability Architecture

```text
AI Request
    │
    ▼
Primary Model
    │
 ┌──┴────┐
 ▼       ▼
OK     Failure
 │       │
 │       ▼
 │   Circuit Breaker
 │       │
 │       ▼
 │   Approved Fallback
 │       │
 └───────┼───────
         ▼
   Output Validation
         │
         ▼
      Response
```

If all AI providers fail:

```text
AI unavailable
      │
      ▼
Graceful degradation
      │
      ▼
Core Mediverse remains available
```

---

# 146. Complete Mediverse AI Architecture

```text
                         CLIENT
                           │
                           ▼
                      API GATEWAY
                           │
                           ▼
                    DOMAIN SERVICES
                           │
                           ▼
                       AI PLATFORM
                           │
      ┌────────────────────┼────────────────────┐
      ▼                    ▼                    ▼
Prompt Registry       RAG Engine          Agent Runtime
      │                    │                    │
      │                    ▼                    ▼
      │                OpenSearch          Tool Registry
      │                    │                    │
      └────────────┬───────┴────────────┬───────┘
                   ▼                    ▼
              Safety Layer        Policy Engine
                   │                    │
                   └─────────┬──────────┘
                             ▼
                       Model Router
                             │
             ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
             ▼               ▼               ▼
           LLMs          Embeddings       Reranker
             │
             ▼
       Output Validation
             │
             ▼
      Grounding / Citations
             │
             ▼
          RESPONSE
```

---

# 147. AI Governance Lifecycle

```text
Use Case Proposed
       │
       ▼
Risk Classification
       │
       ▼
Model / Prompt Selection
       │
       ▼
Offline Evaluation
       │
       ▼
Security / Privacy Review
       │
       ▼
Faculty Review
       │
       ▼
Canary Release
       │
       ▼
Production Monitoring
       │
       ▼
Continuous Evaluation
       │
       ▼
Upgrade / Retire
```

AI deployment is therefore a lifecycle, not an API call.

---

# 148. Risks and Mitigations

| Risk                              | Primary Mitigation                   |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Hallucination                     | RAG + grounding evaluation           |
| Medical misinformation            | Faculty-reviewed evaluation          |
| Prompt injection                  | Trust boundaries + tool controls     |
| Sensitive-data leakage            | Minimization + redaction             |
| Cross-tenant leakage              | Tenant-aware retrieval/state         |
| Fake citations                    | Programmatic source mapping          |
| Provider outage                   | Circuit breaker + approved fallback  |
| Provider lock-in                  | AI platform abstraction              |
| Unexpected spend                  | Quotas + budgets + attribution       |
| Prompt regression                 | Versioning + evaluation              |
| Model regression                  | Model upgrade testing                |
| Incorrect structured output       | Schema + business validation         |
| Unauthorized tool execution       | Authorization + least privilege      |
| Agent runaway                     | Step/token/time/cost limits          |
| Duplicate write actions           | Idempotency                          |
| Excessive agency                  | Human confirmation                   |
| Poisoned RAG corpus               | Ingestion authorization + provenance |
| Bad automated evaluation          | Human/faculty review                 |
| AI incident                       | Kill switches + feature flags        |
| Privacy exposure through logs     | Metadata-first logging               |
| AI dependency breaks core product | Graceful degradation                 |

---

| Attribute                                | Decision                               |
| ---------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| **ADR**                                  | ADR-045                                |
| AI integration                           | Central AI Platform                    |
| Direct provider integration from domains | Avoid                                  |
| Provider abstraction                     | Required                               |
| Model registry                           | Required                               |
| Model routing                            | Capability/risk/cost based             |
| Prompt registry                          | Versioned                              |

| Embeddings                               | Versioned                              |
| Chunking                                 | Versioned                              |
| Citations                                | Source-backed                          |
| LLM output                               | Untrusted until validated              |
| Medical source of truth                  | Curated authoritative content, not LLM |
| AI cache                                 | ADR-043 policies                       |
| PII                                      | Minimize/redact where appropriate      |
| Raw prompt logging                       | Restricted                             |

| Status                                   | **Accepted**                           |
| Priority                                 | **Critical**                           |

# 150. Relationship With Existing Architecture

ADR-045 sits on top of several earlier decisions:

```text
ADR-042
Distributed Consistency
       │
       ▼
ADR-043
Caching / Redis
       │
       ▼
ADR-044
Search / OpenSearch / Vector Retrieval
       │
       ▼
ADR-045
Enterprise AI Platform
```

Together:

```text
                    MEDIVERSE
                        │
          ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
          ▼             ▼             ▼
      PostgreSQL      Redis       OpenSearch
          │             │             │
          ▼             ▼             ▼
    Authoritative   Performance    Retrieval
       State        Optimization    Projection
          │                           │
          └─────────────┬─────────────┘
                        ▼
                   AI PLATFORM
                        │
             ┌──────────┼──────────┐
             ▼          ▼          ▼

             │          │          │
             └──────────┼──────────┘
                        ▼

                        │

```

The separation is critical:

```text
PostgreSQL
=
Business Truth

Redis
=
Performance

OpenSearch
=
Retrieval

LLM
=
Probabilistic Generation / Reasoning

Domain Services
=
Business Authority

Faculty-approved Content
=

```

An enterprise AI architecture fails when these boundaries blur.

---

# ADR-046 — Enterprise File, Media, Object Storage, CDN & Digital Asset Management Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing from **Section 60 — Deduplication**.

---

# 61. Asset Versioning & Immutability

Published educational assets should preferably behave as immutable objects.

Instead of:

```text
course/video.mp4
        │
        ▼
overwrite same object
```

prefer:

```text
asset-123/version-1/source.mp4
asset-123/version-2/source.mp4
```

This makes caching, rollback and auditability substantially safer.

---

# 62. Logical Version vs S3 Version

Mediverse should distinguish:

```text
Application Asset Version
        ≠
S3 Object Version
```

Application versioning represents business meaning.

S3 Versioning is an infrastructure protection mechanism.

Do not make application workflows dependent directly on opaque S3 version IDs.

---

# 63. S3 Versioning

Versioning should be enabled where recovery requirements justify it.

```text
Object v1
   │
   ▼
Object v2
   │
   ▼
Object v3
```

This can protect against accidental overwrite or deletion.

---

# 64. Replacement Semantics

When faculty replaces a lecture PDF:

```text
Asset
 ├── Version 1
 └── Version 2
```

the system should explicitly decide whether existing course references:

```text
Automatically follow latest
```

or remain pinned:

```text
Course Publication → Asset Version 1
```

For auditable educational releases, explicit version references are safer.

---

# 65. Immutable Object Keys

Preferred:

```text
/assets/<asset-id>/<version>/<variant>
```

Once published, that object should not normally change.

A new binary produces a new version/key.

---

# 66. Why Immutability Helps CDN

If:

```text
URL A
=
Always same bytes
```

CloudFront can cache aggressively.

If the same URL constantly changes, invalidation and stale-content problems increase.

---

# 67. Content-Addressable Storage

An alternative architecture derives storage identity from content:

```text
SHA-256
   │
   ▼
objects/ab/cd/<hash>
```

This can simplify deduplication and integrity verification.

However, it complicates logical asset lifecycle and access semantics.

Mediverse should not make this its initial business-facing storage model.

---

# 68. Asset References

Domain entities should reference:

```text
assetId
```

or a controlled asset/version identifier.

Avoid storing raw S3 URLs throughout domain tables.

---

# 69. Why Raw URLs Are Dangerous

Infrastructure changes:

```text
Bucket A
   ↓
Bucket B

CloudFront A
   ↓
CloudFront B
```

should not require updating millions of domain records.

Asset resolution belongs behind an asset abstraction.

---

# 70. Asset Resolver

Conceptually:

```text
assetId
   │
   ▼
Asset Service
   │
   ▼
Authorization
   │
   ▼
Delivery Policy
   │
   ▼
CloudFront URL / Cookie
```

Storage implementation remains hidden.

---

# 71. Deletion Is a Workflow

Bad:

```text
DELETE FROM asset
DELETE S3 object
```

inside one HTTP operation.

Asset deletion may involve:

```text
References
Versions
Derivatives
CDN
Retention
Audit
Legal requirements
Processing jobs
```

It should therefore be lifecycle-driven.

---

# 72. Soft Delete

First transition:

```text
READY
  │
  ▼
DELETE_REQUESTED
  │
  ▼
DELETED
```

can prevent immediate destructive removal.

---

# 73. Reference Validation

Before deleting:

```text
Asset
 │
 ├── Course A
 ├── Chapter B
 └── Assessment C
```

Mediverse must determine whether those references block deletion.

---

# 74. Physical Deletion

Physical object removal should happen only after:

```text
Authorization
Reference validation
Retention checks
Lifecycle transition
```

succeed.

---

# 75. Derived Asset Cleanup

Deleting the source may require deleting:

```text
Thumbnail
HLS segments
Manifest
Transcript
Waveform
Optimized 3D models
Preview images
```

Derived assets must not become permanent garbage.

---

# 76. Orphan Detection

Possible inconsistency:

```text
S3 Object
   │
   ▼
No PostgreSQL asset record
```

or:

```text
PostgreSQL Asset
   │
   ▼
Missing S3 object
```

Periodic reconciliation should detect these conditions.

---

# 77. Orphan Cleanup Safety

Never implement:

```text
Not referenced?
    │
    ▼
DELETE immediately
```

Use:

```text
Detect
  │
  ▼
Mark Candidate
  │
  ▼
Grace Period
  │
  ▼
Revalidate
  │
  ▼
Delete
```

This prevents destructive cleanup from temporary inconsistencies.

---

# 78. Temporary Assets

Temporary objects may include:

```text
Upload fragments
Processing intermediates
Generated previews
Failed transformations
Temporary exports
```

They require shorter lifecycle policies than published educational content.

---

# 79. S3 Lifecycle Policies

Storage lifecycle can automatically transition objects based on age and category.

Conceptually:

```text
Hot
 │
 ▼
Warm
 │
 ▼
Archive
 │
 ▼
Delete
```

Policies must align with actual access requirements.

---

# 80. Archive Tier

Rarely accessed historical material may move to archival storage.

But archive retrieval may not be immediate.

Do not archive content students expect to open interactively.

---

# 81. Retention Policy

Retention should be defined by asset class.

Example:

```text
Published course content
Assessment evidence
Temporary uploads
Processing artifacts
Audit-related exports
```

should not all share one arbitrary retention period.

---

# 82. CDN Security Boundary

Primary delivery architecture:

```text
Internet
   │
   ▼
CloudFront
   │
   ▼
Private S3 Origin
```

Users should not bypass CloudFront and access private origin objects directly.

---

# 83. Origin Access Control

CloudFront should use controlled origin access so S3 permits the distribution while denying general public access.

```text
CloudFront
     │
     │ authorized origin access
     ▼
    S3
```

---

# 84. Public vs Private Assets

Not every asset requires identical access controls.

Potential classes:

```text
PUBLIC
──────
Marketing image
Public logo

AUTHENTICATED
─────────────
General learning resource

ENROLLMENT_RESTRICTED
─────────────────────
Course content

FACULTY_ONLY
────────────
Answer keys
Draft materials
```

Delivery policy must follow business authorization.

---

# 85. Private Content Delivery

For protected material:

```text
Student
   │
   ▼
Mediverse API
   │
   ▼
Authorization
   │
   ▼
Temporary CDN Access
   │
   ▼
CloudFront
```

The application authorizes; the CDN transfers.

---

# 86. Signed URLs

A signed URL grants temporary access to a specific resource.

Useful for:

```text
Single PDF
Single download
Specific private asset
```

Access should expire.

---

# 87. Signed Cookies

Signed cookies can be useful when access covers many related objects.

This matters particularly for streaming:

```text
master.m3u8
segment001
segment002
segment003
...
```

Generating separate signed URLs for hundreds of segments may be unnecessarily cumbersome.

---

# 88. Signed URL vs Signed Cookie

```text
Single object
    │
    ▼
Signed URL

Multiple related protected objects
    │
    ▼
Signed Cookie
```

The exact mechanism should follow the delivery pattern.

---

# 89. URL Expiration

Shorter expiry reduces exposure but increases renewal frequency.

Longer expiry improves convenience but increases sharing risk.

Expiry should therefore depend on:

```text
Asset sensitivity
Session duration
Streaming requirements
User experience
```

---

# 90. Signed URLs Are Not DRM

A signed URL controls initial access.

It does **not** guarantee that an authorized user cannot:

```text
Download
Copy
Screen record
Redistribute
```

This distinction matters.

---

# 91. Content Protection Reality

There is no architecture that can perfectly prevent an authorized user from capturing content displayed on their device.

Claims of:

```text
100% download prevention
```

are unrealistic.

Mediverse should distinguish access control from perfect copying prevention.

---

# 92. DRM Evaluation

If premium video content requires stronger controls, DRM may be evaluated.

Possible architecture:

```text
Encrypted Stream
      │
      ▼
DRM License
      │
      ▼
Authorized Player
```

But DRM introduces:

```text
Cost
Player complexity
Browser/device compatibility
License infrastructure
Operational burden
```

It should be requirement-driven.

---

# 93. Cache-Control

Immutable public/static assets can use aggressive caching.

Conceptually:

```text
Cache-Control:
public, max-age=..., immutable
```

Protected assets require policies consistent with authorization and privacy.

---

# 94. Immutable Asset URLs

Best CDN behavior:

```text
/content/v1/hash-or-version/file
```

Then when content changes:

```text
/content/v2/...
```

instead of overwriting v1.

---

# 95. CDN Invalidation

Sometimes content must be removed or corrected immediately.

Then:

```text
CloudFront
   │
   ▼
Invalidate Path
```

may be necessary.

But routine deployment should not depend on massive invalidations.

---

# 96. Why Excessive Invalidation Is Bad

Frequent invalidation suggests poor cache identity.

Prefer:

```text
New content
=
New URL
```

where possible.

---

# 97. CDN Cache Key

Cache identity may consider:

```text
Path
Query parameters
Headers
Cookies
```

Adding unnecessary dimensions reduces cache hit ratio.

---

# 98. Cache-Key Explosion

Bad:

```text
Asset URL
+
Unique user ID
=
Unique CDN cache entry per student
```

This destroys CDN efficiency.

Authorization and cache identity should be designed separately where possible.

---

# 99. Query Parameters

Only query parameters that genuinely alter representation should normally influence cache identity.

Tracking parameters should not automatically create distinct cached objects.

---

# 100. Hot Assets

A newly released lecture may suddenly receive:

```text
10 requests
100 requests
10,000 requests
```

CDN caching protects the origin from repeated identical delivery.

---

# 101. Origin Shielding

For sufficiently large global traffic, an additional centralized caching layer/origin-shield strategy may reduce repeated origin fetches.

This should be introduced based on measured traffic, not speculation.

---

# 102. Geographic Delivery

CloudFront edge locations can improve latency for geographically distributed students.

But application APIs, databases and dynamic content still require separate regional architecture.

CDN does not make the entire application globally distributed.

---

# 103. Encryption at Rest

S3 assets must use approved server-side encryption.

Potential choices include:

```text
SSE-S3
SSE-KMS
```

Selection depends on security and key-management requirements.

---

# 104. SSE-S3

SSE-S3 provides managed encryption at rest with comparatively low operational complexity.

It may be sufficient for asset classes without dedicated KMS governance requirements.

---

# 105. SSE-KMS

SSE-KMS provides additional key-control and audit capabilities.

It may be preferred where requirements demand:

```text
Explicit key policies
Key-level audit
Controlled key ownership
Separation of duties
```

---

# 106. KMS Is Not Free Complexity

Using a customer-managed key for every conceivable object class can create:

```text
Policy complexity
API cost
Operational dependencies
Quota pressure
Key-management burden
```

Use KMS deliberately.

---

# 107. Tenant Encryption

A separate KMS key per tenant should not be assumed automatically.

It may be appropriate for specific enterprise contractual requirements, but it materially increases lifecycle and operational complexity.

Logical tenant isolation remains mandatory regardless of key strategy.

---

# 108. Encryption in Transit

All upload and delivery traffic should use TLS.

```text
Client
  │ HTTPS
  ▼
CloudFront / S3 / API
```

Plain HTTP should not be accepted for protected production content.

---

# 109. Metadata Privacy

Even when object bytes are encrypted, metadata may expose information.

Avoid keys such as:

```text
/HIV-patient/john-smith/...
```

Sensitive meaning should not be unnecessarily encoded in object names.

---

# 110. Event Notification Architecture

Infrastructure events may feed a queue:

```text
S3
 │
 ▼
Event Notification
 │
 ▼
Queue
 │
 ▼
Processing Worker
```

A queue decouples upload rate from processing capacity.

---

# 111. Why Queue Processing?

Suppose:

```text
1,000 videos uploaded
```

while workers can process:

```text
20 concurrently
```

A queue absorbs the difference.

Without backpressure, workers or downstream services may collapse.

---

# 112. Processing Concurrency

Concurrency should be controlled by:

```text
Asset type
CPU
Memory
GPU
Transcoder capacity
External quotas
Cost
```

More parallelism is not automatically better.

---

# 113. Processing Retry

Transient processing failures may retry.

Example:

```text
Job
 │
 ▼
Worker
 │
 ✕
 ▼
Retry with backoff
```

Retries must be bounded.

---

# 114. Processing Dead-Letter Path

After repeated failure:

```text
Processing Queue
      │
      ▼
Retries exhausted
      │
      ▼
DLT / Failure Queue
      │
      ▼
Investigation / Replay
```

The asset should transition to a clear failure state.

---

# 115. Transcoding Infrastructure

Video transcoding is computationally expensive.

Mediverse should evaluate managed media-processing services rather than building an entire transcoding platform inside Kubernetes by default.

---

# 116. MediaConvert Evaluation

For AWS-centric deployment, a managed transcoding service such as AWS Elemental MediaConvert is a reasonable architectural candidate for:

```text
HLS packaging
Resolution variants
Codec conversion
Audio tracks
Thumbnails
```

The exact adoption remains workload/cost driven.

---

# 117. Lambda vs Containers

Small transformations:

```text
Metadata extraction
Thumbnail generation
Lightweight validation
```

may suit short-lived serverless execution.

Heavy workloads:

```text
Complex 3D processing
Large media manipulation
Long CPU jobs
GPU workloads
```

may require containers or specialized managed services.

---

# 118. Do Not Force Everything Into Lambda

A 30-minute 3D optimization pipeline should not be forced into a serverless function merely because S3 can trigger one.

Compute choice must follow workload characteristics.

---

# 119. Asset Service

Mediverse should expose an explicit Asset/Media Service boundary.

Responsibilities:

```text
Asset metadata
Upload authorization
Upload sessions
Lifecycle
Access authorization
Delivery resolution
Processing status
Deletion orchestration
```

It should not necessarily perform all binary processing itself.

---

# 120. Asset API

Representative APIs may include:

```text
POST   /assets/uploads
POST   /assets/{id}/complete
GET    /assets/{id}
GET    /assets/{id}/status
GET    /assets/{id}/access
DELETE /assets/{id}
```

Exact contracts belong in the ADS.

---

# 121. Upload Session

Large uploads benefit from an explicit session:

```text
Create Upload Session
       │
       ▼
Receive assetId
       │
       ▼
Upload parts
       │
       ▼
Complete
       │
       ▼
Verify
```

This creates a clean application-level lifecycle.

---

# 122. Upload Completion Verification

Never accept:

```text
Client says upload completed
```

as sufficient evidence.

The backend/processing workflow should verify the expected object exists and matches required properties.

---

# 123. Checksum Verification

Where appropriate:

```text
Expected Checksum
       │
       ▼
Uploaded Object
       │
       ▼
Verify
```

This protects against corruption and supports integrity guarantees.

---

# 124. Resumable Upload

For unreliable/mobile networks:

```text
Upload
  │
  ✕ network failure
  │
  ▼
Resume remaining parts
```

is far better UX than restarting a multi-gigabyte lecture.

Multipart architecture enables this.

---

# 125. Status API

Processing may take minutes.

Therefore:

```text
GET /assets/{id}/status
```

might return:

```json
{
  "status": "PROCESSING"
}
```

rather than holding the original request open.

---

# 126. Event Notification to UI

Where justified:

```text
Processing Complete
      │
      ▼
Backend Event
      │
      ▼
WebSocket / SSE / Notification
      │
      ▼
Faculty UI
```

can reduce polling.

Do not add real-time infrastructure if simple polling adequately meets the requirement.

---

# 127. Cleanup Jobs

Scheduled reconciliation may handle:

```text
Expired upload sessions
Abandoned multipart uploads
Orphan objects
Failed processing artifacts
Expired temporary exports
Deletion candidates
```

Cleanup is part of the architecture, not an afterthought.

---

# 128. Backup Philosophy

Remember:

```text
S3 durability
≠
Complete backup strategy
```

Accidental application deletion, malicious actions or logical corruption still require recovery controls.

---

# 129. Versioning + Replication

Depending on recovery requirements:

```text
S3 Versioning
+
Replication
+
Retention controls
```

may provide layered protection.

---

# 130. Cross-Region Replication

For sufficiently strict disaster-recovery requirements:

```text
Primary Region S3
       │
       ▼
Replication
       │
       ▼
Secondary Region S3
```

can reduce asset recovery risk.

It should be justified by RPO/RTO and cost.

---

# 131. Replication Is Not Backup

A bad deletion or corruption may also propagate.

Therefore:

```text
Replication
≠
Immutable historical recovery
```

Recovery architecture must consider the actual failure scenarios.

---

# 132. Asset RPO

RPO asks:

> How much recently uploaded asset data can Mediverse tolerate losing?

For critical published content, the answer may approach zero.

Temporary uploads may tolerate more.

---

# 133. Asset RTO

RTO asks:

> How long can asset delivery remain unavailable?

Different services may have different objectives:

```text
Public images
Course PDFs
Lecture video
3D models
Faculty uploads
```

---

# 134. DR Architecture

Conceptually:

```text
Primary Region
 ├── PostgreSQL metadata
 ├── S3
 └── CloudFront Origin
        │
        ▼
Disaster
        │
        ▼
Secondary Recovery
 ├── Metadata recovery
 ├── Asset recovery
 └── Delivery restoration
```

Metadata and binaries must remain consistent enough to recover together.

---

# 135. Observability

Asset infrastructure should expose telemetry for:

```text
Uploads
Failures
Processing duration
Queue depth
Malware results
Storage growth
Delivery latency
CDN hit ratio
Origin requests
Bandwidth
4xx/5xx
```

---

# 136. Processing Metrics

Important metrics include:

```text
Jobs queued
Jobs running
Jobs completed
Jobs failed
Retry count
Processing latency
Queue age
```

Queue age is particularly important because a healthy worker count can still hide growing delays.

---

# 137. CDN Metrics

Monitor:

```text
Request volume
Cache hit ratio
Origin fetches
4xx
5xx
Bytes transferred
Latency
Geographic traffic
```

A low cache hit ratio on highly reusable content should trigger investigation.

---

# 138. Storage Metrics

Track:

```text
Total bytes
Object count
Asset class
Environment
Storage tier
Growth rate
Incomplete uploads
Derived/original ratio
```

Without classification, cost optimization becomes guesswork.

---

# 139. Cost Model

Digital asset cost roughly includes:

```text
Storage
+
Requests
+
Processing
+
Transcoding
+
CDN delivery
+
Internet egress
+
Replication
+
Encryption/key operations
```

The largest bill may not be S3 storage itself.

---

# 140. Video Cost

Video is particularly expensive because it combines:

```text
Large storage
Transcoding
Multiple renditions
High bandwidth
Long consumption sessions
```

Architecture should track cost per delivered hour where useful.

---

# 141. 3D Cost

3D assets can similarly become expensive through:

```text
Large textures
Large models
Repeated downloads
Multiple LODs
Processing
```

Optimization directly affects both performance and cost.

---

# 142. Egress Optimization

The main strategy is not:

```text
Compress the API response harder
```

but:

```text
Efficient formats
      +
Asset optimization
      +
CDN caching
      +
Adaptive streaming
      +
Correct cache lifetime
```

---

# 143. Asset Testing

Testing should cover:

```text
Authorization
Upload limits
MIME spoofing
Malformed files
Malware workflow
Multipart upload
Interrupted upload
Checksum mismatch
Processing retry
Duplicate events
Private delivery
Signed URL expiry
Deletion
Orphan cleanup
CDN behavior
```

---

# 144. Security Testing

Explicitly test attempts to:

```text
Upload executable disguised as image
Access another tenant's asset
Modify object key
Reuse expired URL
Bypass CloudFront
Upload oversized file
Inject path-like filename
Access quarantined content
Retrieve faculty-only material
```

---

# 145. Chaos Testing

Failure scenarios should include:

```text
S3 temporarily unavailable
Processing worker crash
Queue backlog
Transcoder failure
Malware scanner failure
Database unavailable
CDN origin failure
Duplicate infrastructure event
Partial multipart upload
```

The system should fail predictably.

---

# 146. Asset Anti-Patterns

Mediverse shall reject or strongly discourage:

```text
❌ Large binaries stored in PostgreSQL by default
❌ Videos streamed through Spring Boot Pods
❌ Multi-GB uploads proxied through application Pods without need
❌ Public production S3 buckets
❌ Client-controlled arbitrary object keys
❌ Trusting file extensions
❌ Trusting client Content-Type
❌ Making uploaded content immediately public
❌ Skipping malware scanning for untrusted uploads
❌ Synchronous video transcoding inside HTTP requests
❌ Using one source MP4 as complete streaming architecture
❌ Treating S3 ObjectCreated as a business event
❌ Non-idempotent processing consumers
❌ Raw S3 URLs stored throughout domain tables
❌ PII embedded in object keys
❌ Overwriting published assets under the same CDN URL
❌ Massive routine CloudFront invalidations
❌ Unique CDN cache entry per user without necessity
❌ Assuming signed URLs prevent copying
❌ Claiming screen recording can be completely prevented
❌ Using DRM without a real business requirement
❌ Permanent abandoned multipart uploads
❌ Immediate destructive orphan cleanup
❌ Unlimited processing concurrency
❌ Infinite retries
❌ Heavy transcoding forced into Kubernetes without justification
❌ Heavy workloads forced into Lambda without workload analysis
❌ Treating replication as backup
❌ No asset lifecycle/status model
❌ No cleanup architecture
❌ No asset cost attribution
```

---

# 147. Upload Decision Flow

```text
                    UPLOAD REQUEST
                          │
                          ▼
                     Authenticate
                          │
                          ▼
                      Authorize
                          │
                          ▼
                  Validate Intent
                          │
                          ▼
                  Create Asset Record
                          │
                          ▼
                     Asset Size?
                    ┌─────┴─────┐
                    ▼           ▼
                  SMALL        LARGE
                    │           │
                    ▼           ▼
               Presigned     Multipart
                 Upload       Upload
                    │           │
                    └─────┬─────┘
                          ▼
                    Verify Object
                          │
                          ▼
                      Quarantine
                          │
                          ▼
                    Malware Scan
                    ┌─────┴─────┐
                    ▼           ▼
                  CLEAN      INFECTED
                    │           │
                    ▼           ▼
                Validate      Reject
                    │
                    ▼
                 Process
                    │
                    ▼
                  READY
```

---

# 148. Delivery Decision Flow

```text
                     ASSET REQUEST
                          │
                          ▼
                     Asset Lookup
                          │
                          ▼
                     Visibility?
             ┌────────────┼─────────────┐
             ▼            ▼             ▼
           PUBLIC    AUTHENTICATED   RESTRICTED
             │            │             │
             │            ▼             ▼
             │       Authenticate    Authorize
             │            │             │
             └────────────┼─────────────┘
                          ▼
                   Delivery Policy
                          │
               ┌──────────┴──────────┐
               ▼                     ▼
          Single Object        Protected Stream
               │                     │
               ▼                     ▼
          Signed URL          Signed Cookie /
                              Stream Policy
               │                     │
               └──────────┬──────────┘
                          ▼
                      CloudFront
                          │
                          ▼
                      Private S3
```

---

# 149. Final Reference Architecture

```text
                       MEDIVERSE CLIENT
                              │
              ┌───────────────┴────────────────┐
              │                                │
              ▼                                ▼
        CONTROL PLANE                     DATA PLANE
              │                                │
              ▼                                │
        API Gateway                            │
              │                                │
              ▼                                │
         Asset Service                         │
              │                                │
       ┌──────┼─────────┐                      │
       ▼      ▼         ▼                      │
     Auth   Metadata   Upload Session           │
              │         │                      │
              ▼         ▼                      │
         PostgreSQL  Presigned Upload           │
                        │                      │
                        └──────────┐           │
                                   ▼           │
                                  S3 ◄─────────┘
                                   │
                                   ▼
                              Quarantine
                                   │
                                   ▼
                             Malware Scan
                                   │
                                   ▼
                          Processing Coordinator
                                   │
                ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐
                ▼                  ▼                  ▼
              Image              Video                3D
            Processor          Transcoder          Processor
                │                  │                  │
                ▼                  ▼                  ▼
             Variants          HLS/DASH          GLB / LOD
                │                  │                  │
                └──────────────────┼──────────────────┘
                                   ▼
                           Processed Asset Store
                                   │
                                   ▼
                              CloudFront
                                   │
                    ┌──────────────┴──────────────┐
                    ▼                             ▼
                Public Assets              Private Assets
                                                  │
                                           Signed Access
                                                  │
                                                  ▼
                                               Student
```

Supporting event architecture:

```text
S3 Event
   │
   ▼
Processing Queue
   │
   ▼
Worker
   │
   ▼
Asset Metadata Update
   │
   ▼
Transactional Outbox
   │
   ▼
Kafka
   │
   ├──► Search Indexing
   ├──► Notification
   ├──► AI/RAG Ingestion
   └──► Analytics
```

This connects ADR-046 directly to the architecture already established in ADR-042 through ADR-045.

---

# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                   | Decision                                  |
| ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| Binary source of truth | **Amazon S3**                             |
| Business metadata      | **PostgreSQL**                            |
| Asset identity         | Application-level UUID/ID                 |
| Large upload path      | Direct-to-S3                              |
| Upload authorization   | Backend-controlled                        |
| Large files            | Multipart upload                          |
| Public S3 access       | Disabled by default                       |
| Delivery               | **CloudFront**                            |
| Origin                 | Private S3                                |
| Private content        | Signed CDN access                         |
| Video delivery         | Adaptive streaming where required         |
| Video processing       | Asynchronous                              |
| 3D format              | glTF/GLB-oriented web pipeline            |
| Uploaded content       | Untrusted until validated                 |
| Malware scanning       | Required for applicable untrusted uploads |
| Published assets       | Prefer immutable/versioned objects        |
| Raw S3 URLs in domains | Avoid                                     |
| Asset references       | Stable asset/version IDs                  |
| Encryption             | Required                                  |
| CDN caching            | Version-aware                             |
| Processing             | Queue/event driven                        |
| Processing consumers   | Idempotent                                |
| Domain events          | Outbox + Kafka                            |
| Orphan cleanup         | Reconciliation + grace period             |
| Lifecycle policies     | Required                                  |
| DR                     | RPO/RTO driven                            |
| Observability          | Required                                  |
| Cost governance        | Required                                  |
| Asset Service          | Dedicated application boundary            |
| Status                 | **Accepted**                              |
| Priority               | **Critical**                              |

The architectural separation is now:

```text
PostgreSQL
=
Asset metadata / business truth

S3
=
Binary truth

CloudFront
=
Scalable asset delivery

Processing Pipeline
=
Derived representations

Kafka
=
Business integration

OpenSearch
=
Searchable projection

AI Platform
=
AI/RAG consumption
```

---

---

# ADR-047 — Enterprise Observability, OpenTelemetry, Logging, Metrics, Distributed Tracing, Alerting & SRE Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — AI Trace**.

---

# 61. AI Quality & Cost Telemetry

Traditional observability tells us whether the AI request succeeded technically.

That is insufficient.

```text
HTTP 200
Model responded
Latency = 1.8s
```

does **not** mean:

```text
Answer correct
Answer grounded
Citation correct
Answer safe
Cost acceptable
```

AI requires additional quality and economic telemetry.

---

# 62. AI Operational Metrics

Track:

```text
ai_requests_total

ai_request_duration

ai_errors_total

ai_timeouts_total

ai_fallback_total

ai_input_tokens

ai_output_tokens

ai_cost

ai_safety_blocks_total
```

Dimensions must remain cardinality-controlled.

---

# 63. Model Identity

AI telemetry should identify:

```text
provider
model
modelVersion
feature
environment
```

where operationally useful.

This allows comparison such as:

```text
Model A
p95 = 1.2 sec

Model B
p95 = 4.8 sec
```

---

# 64. Prompt Version Telemetry

From ADR-045, prompts are versioned artifacts.

Telemetry should therefore correlate:

```text
Feature
   │
   ▼
Prompt Version
   │
   ▼
Model Version
   │
   ▼
Outcome
```

This is essential when a prompt deployment causes quality regression.

---

# 65. Do Not Log Full Prompts by Default

A prompt may contain:

```text
Student information
Conversation history
Retrieved course content
Assessment answers
System instructions
```

Therefore:

```text
promptVersion = v17
```

is usually safer operational metadata than indiscriminately storing the complete prompt.

---

# 66. RAG Telemetry

A RAG trace should expose stages such as:

```text
Question
   │
   ▼
Query Processing
   │
   ▼
Retrieval
   │
   ▼
Reranking
   │
   ▼
Context Building
   │
   ▼
Generation
```

This allows engineers to determine whether a poor answer originated from retrieval or generation.

---

# 67. Retrieval Telemetry

Useful operational attributes include:

```text
retrieved_document_count
retrieval_duration
reranking_duration
selected_chunk_count
zero_result
```

Quality evaluation remains governed by ADR-044 and ADR-045.

---

# 68. AI Tool Telemetry

Agent traces should show:

```text
Agent
 │
 ├── Search Tool
 ├── Course Tool
 ├── Progress Tool
 └── Draft Tool
```

including:

```text
Tool name
Duration
Result status
Retry
Authorization outcome
```

without leaking sensitive arguments.

---

# 69. Agent Loop Metrics

Monitor:

```text
agent_steps
tool_calls
agent_duration
agent_token_usage
agent_cost
agent_failures
human_approval_requests
```

Unexpectedly increasing step counts may indicate agent loops or degraded reasoning.

---

# 70. Structured Logging

Mediverse application logs shall be machine-readable structured events.

Preferred:

```json
{
  "timestamp": "2026-08-03T10:15:30Z",
  "level": "ERROR",
  "service": "course-service",
  "environment": "production",
  "traceId": "abc123",
  "event": "COURSE_FETCH_FAILED",
  "message": "Course retrieval failed"
}
```

instead of uncontrolled text.

---

# 71. Why JSON Logging?

Structured logs allow queries such as:

```text
service = course-service
AND
level = ERROR
AND
environment = production
```

without unreliable text parsing.

---

# 72. Common Log Schema

Core fields should be standardized.

For example:

```text
timestamp
severity
service
serviceVersion
environment
traceId
spanId
event
message
```

Optional domain-safe attributes may be added where justified.

---

# 73. Log Event Names

Stable event identifiers are valuable.

Example:

```text
ASSET_PROCESSING_FAILED
COURSE_PUBLICATION_FAILED
KAFKA_EVENT_RETRY
AI_PROVIDER_TIMEOUT
```

Humans can change message wording without breaking dashboards and searches.

---

# 74. Log Levels

Standard semantics:

```text
TRACE
DEBUG
INFO
WARN
ERROR
```

Teams must use them consistently.

---

# 75. INFO Abuse

Bad:

```text
INFO Entering method
INFO variable x = ...
INFO leaving method
```

across every request.

This creates enormous noise.

INFO should represent meaningful operational events.

---

# 76. DEBUG Logging

DEBUG may provide detailed diagnostics but should normally be disabled or tightly controlled in production.

Dynamic temporary enablement may be useful during incidents.

---

# 77. ERROR Logging

ERROR should indicate genuine failures requiring investigation or meaningful operational awareness.

If every expected 404 produces an ERROR, the signal becomes useless.

---

# 78. Exception Logging

Avoid logging the same exception at every layer.

Bad:

```text
Repository logs exception
    │
Service logs same exception
    │
Controller logs same exception
    │
Global handler logs same exception
```

One failure becomes four noisy events.

---

# 79. Stack Traces

Stack traces are valuable for unexpected failures.

But they are:

```text
Large
Expensive
Potentially sensitive
```

Use them where they improve diagnosis rather than for every expected business error.

---

# 80. Sensitive Data Redaction

Logs must not contain uncontrolled:

```text
Passwords
JWTs
API keys
Authorization headers
Session tokens
Secrets
Sensitive personal data
```

Logging policy must be enforced through code review, libraries and telemetry processing.

---

# 81. Never Log Credentials

This:

```text
Authorization: Bearer eyJ...
```

must never become normal application telemetry.

Credential leakage into logging systems expands the security blast radius.

---

# 82. Request/Response Body Logging

Logging complete HTTP bodies is dangerous.

A body may contain:

```text
Student profile
Assessment answer
Password
AI prompt
Uploaded metadata
```

Body logging should be disabled by default and explicitly controlled.

---

# 83. Audit Logs vs Operational Logs

These are separate concerns.

```text
Operational Log
=
Why did software fail?

Audit Log
=
Who performed a consequential action?
```

Do not treat application logs as the authoritative audit trail.

---

# 84. Audit Event

Example:

```text
Faculty X
published
Assessment Y
at Time Z
```

Audit requirements may demand:

```text
Immutability
Longer retention
Restricted access
Integrity protection
```

beyond ordinary logs.

---

# 85. Centralized Logging

Architecture:

```text
Applications
     │
     ▼
Log Collection
     │
     ▼
Central Log Backend
     │
     ▼
Search / Dashboards
```

Engineers should not SSH into individual Pods to investigate production.

---

# 86. Pods Are Ephemeral

A Kubernetes Pod can disappear.

```text
Pod
 │
 ▼
Crash
 │
 ▼
Replacement Pod
```

If logs exist only on the container filesystem, evidence may disappear with it.

---

# 87. Log Backend Selection

Possible architectures include:

```text
CloudWatch Logs
OpenSearch
Grafana Loki
Managed observability platforms
```

The decision should consider:

```text
Search requirements
Retention
Scale
Cost
Operational complexity
Existing AWS architecture
Security
```

---

# 88. Do Not Automatically Use OpenSearch for Everything

Mediverse already uses OpenSearch for application search.

That does not mean the same cluster should automatically store enormous observability logs.

Search workloads and log workloads have different:

```text
Retention
Scaling
Index patterns
Failure characteristics
```

Separate architecture may be necessary.

---

# 89. Log Retention

Retention should vary by class.

Example:

```text
Debug/diagnostic logs
Operational logs
Security logs
Audit logs
```

A universal "keep everything forever" policy is expensive and often unnecessary.

---

# 90. Log Sampling

High-volume repetitive events may be sampled.

But never blindly sample:

```text
Security incidents
Rare errors
Audit events
```

Sampling policy must preserve important signals.

---

# 91. Distributed Trace Sampling

Tracing every request at massive scale can become expensive.

Therefore Mediverse shall support trace sampling.

```text
Requests
   │
   ▼
Sampling
 ┌─┴─┐
 ▼   ▼
Keep Drop
```

---

# 92. Head Sampling

Decision occurs near trace start.

Example:

```text
Keep 10%
```

Advantages:

```text
Simple
Low overhead
Predictable volume
```

Disadvantage:

An important failed trace may be discarded before the failure occurs.

---

# 93. Tail Sampling

Decision occurs after enough of the trace is observed.

This allows rules such as:

```text
Keep errors
Keep slow traces
Keep rare operations
Sample normal traffic
```

This provides richer control but requires more collector infrastructure.

---

# 94. Recommended Sampling Strategy

Production should prioritize retaining:

```text
Errors
High latency
Critical workflows
Rare conditions
```

while sampling routine successful traffic according to volume.

---

# 95. Exemplars

Metrics can reference representative traces.

Conceptually:

```text
p99 latency spike
       │
       ▼
Example Trace ID
       │
       ▼
Distributed Trace
```

This creates a powerful metrics → traces investigation path.

---

# 96. Prometheus Architecture

Prometheus should be the primary Kubernetes/service operational metrics model where appropriate.

```text
Applications
     │
     ▼
Metrics Endpoints
     │
     ▼
Prometheus
     │
     ▼
Grafana
```

OpenTelemetry can participate in the telemetry pipeline without eliminating Prometheus-native infrastructure requirements.

---

# 97. Metrics Scraping

Spring Boot applications expose approved metrics endpoints.

Prometheus discovers and scrapes them.

```text
course-service
      │
      ▼
/actuator/prometheus
      │
      ▼
Prometheus
```

Management endpoints remain network-controlled.

---

# 98. ServiceMonitor

Where the Prometheus Operator is used, resources such as:

```text
ServiceMonitor
PodMonitor
```

can declaratively define scraping targets.

This fits Kubernetes-native operations.

---

# 99. Recording Rules

Expensive or frequently used PromQL expressions can be precomputed.

Conceptually:

```text
Raw Metrics
    │
    ▼
Recording Rule
    │
    ▼
Precomputed Series
```

This improves dashboard/query efficiency.

---

# 100. Long-Term Metrics

Local Prometheus storage alone may not satisfy long retention or multi-cluster requirements.

At larger scale, evaluate systems such as:

```text
Thanos
Grafana Mimir
Managed Prometheus
```

based on requirements.

Do not add them before those requirements exist.

---

# 101. Grafana

Grafana should provide unified operational visualization across:

```text
Services
Infrastructure
Databases
Kafka
Search
Media
AI
SLOs
```

where corresponding data sources are available.

---

# 102. Dashboard Hierarchy

Avoid one giant dashboard containing 200 panels.

Prefer hierarchy:

```text
Platform Overview
       │
       ├── Service Overview
       ├── Kubernetes
       ├── PostgreSQL
       ├── Kafka
       ├── Redis
       ├── OpenSearch
       ├── Media
       └── AI
```

---

# 103. Service Golden Dashboard

Every production service should have a baseline dashboard showing:

```text
Request rate
Error rate
Latency
Resource saturation
Dependency health
Deployment version
```

This creates consistent first-line investigation.

---

# 104. Dashboard Variables

Useful bounded variables:

```text
Environment
Cluster
Namespace
Service
Region
```

allow the same dashboard design to serve multiple deployments.

---

# 105. Deployment Markers

Dashboards should display deployment/change events.

```text
Latency
   │
   │       ↑ deployment
   │       │
   └───────┼────────────
           │
           └── errors rise
```

This makes change correlation much faster.

---

# 106. Kubernetes Observability

Monitor:

```text
Cluster
Node
Namespace
Pod
Container
Deployment
StatefulSet
Job
HPA
Persistent Volume
```

not merely application endpoints.

---

# 107. kube-state-metrics

Kubernetes object-state telemetry can expose:

```text
Desired replicas
Available replicas
Pod states
Deployment status
Job status
Resource requests
Resource limits
```

for monitoring.

---

# 108. Node Metrics

Node-level monitoring should cover:

```text
CPU
Memory
Disk
Filesystem
Network
Load
```

to detect infrastructure saturation.

---

# 109. Container Metrics

Track:

```text
CPU usage
Memory usage
Throttling
Restarts
OOM kills
Network
```

Container restart count alone is not sufficient.

---

# 110. CPU Throttling

A Pod may have:

```text
CPU usage apparently below node capacity
```

while aggressive CPU limits cause throttling.

This can create unexplained application latency.

Monitor throttling when diagnosing performance.

---

# 111. OOMKill

If:

```text
Container memory
     │
     ▼
Limit exceeded
     │
     ▼
OOMKilled
```

Kubernetes restarts the container.

Telemetry should make the reason obvious.

---

# 112. HPA Observability

If Horizontal Pod Autoscaling is used, monitor:

```text
Current replicas
Desired replicas
Scaling metric
Scaling events
Maximum replicas
```

A service pinned at maximum replicas while latency rises indicates capacity problems.

---

# 113. Health Endpoints

Different health concepts must remain separate:

```text
Liveness
Readiness
Startup
```

They solve different Kubernetes problems.

---

# 114. Liveness Probe

Liveness asks:

> Is this process stuck or irrecoverably unhealthy such that Kubernetes should restart it?

Do not include every downstream dependency.

---

# 115. Bad Liveness Check

If liveness depends on PostgreSQL:

```text
PostgreSQL outage
      │
      ▼
Every application fails liveness
      │
      ▼
Kubernetes restarts everything
```

This makes an outage worse.

---

# 116. Readiness Probe

Readiness asks:

> Can this instance currently serve traffic correctly?

If not:

```text
Pod
 │
 ▼
Removed from Service endpoints
```

without necessarily restarting it.

---

# 117. Startup Probe

Slow-starting services can use startup probes to prevent premature liveness failures during initialization.

This is particularly useful when startup time legitimately varies.

---

# 118. Synthetic Monitoring

Internal metrics alone are insufficient.

Synthetic tests can periodically execute workflows such as:

```text
Open application
Login
Load course
Search chapter
```

to test user-visible availability.

---

# 119. Black-Box Monitoring

Black-box monitoring asks:

```text
Can the service be reached from outside?
Does DNS resolve?
Does TLS work?
Does HTTP respond?
```

rather than relying on internal application metrics.

---

# 120. Frontend Observability

Backend telemetry cannot explain every student experience.

React should support appropriate frontend observability for:

```text
JavaScript errors
Page load
API failures
Navigation performance
User-perceived latency
```

while respecting privacy requirements.

---

# 121. Real User Monitoring

RUM captures actual user experience.

This can reveal differences caused by:

```text
Device
Browser
Network
Geography
```

that backend monitoring cannot see.

---

# 122. Core Web Vitals

For web experience, monitor relevant user-facing performance signals such as:

```text
LCP
INP
CLS
```

rather than relying only on server response time.

---

# 123. SLI

A **Service Level Indicator** is a measured reliability signal.

Example:

```text
Successful requests
───────────────────
Total valid requests
```

or:

```text
Percentage of requests
completed below 500 ms
```

---

# 124. SLO

A **Service Level Objective** defines the target.

Example:

```text
99.9% of valid API requests
succeed over 30 days.
```

SLOs should represent user-relevant reliability.

---

# 125. SLA vs SLO

```text
SLO
=
Internal reliability target

SLA
=
Contractual/business commitment
```

They should not be casually treated as identical.

---

# 126. Availability SLI

Conceptually:

```text
Good Requests
──────────────
Valid Requests
```

But defining "good" requires care.

For example, a correct:

```text
404
```

may be a successful application response rather than system failure.

---

# 127. Latency SLI

Instead of:

```text
average latency < 500 ms
```

prefer user-oriented distributions:

```text
99% of requests
under threshold
```

for important workflows.

---

# 128. Workflow SLOs

Some Mediverse SLOs should measure complete experiences.

Examples:

```text
Course page availability

Assessment submission success

Search response success

Asset playback startup

AI tutor response availability
```

not merely individual microservice uptime.

---

# 129. Error Budget

If SLO is:

```text
99.9%
```

then:

```text
0.1%
```

of the measurement window is the reliability error budget.

This makes reliability trade-offs explicit.

---

# 130. Error Budget Use

If a team rapidly consumes its error budget:

```text
Feature velocity
      ↓

Reliability work
      ↑
```

may be required.

An SLO without operational consequences is just a dashboard number.

---

# 131. Burn Rate

Burn rate measures how quickly the error budget is being consumed.

```text
Burn rate = 1
```

roughly means consumption at the expected sustainable rate.

A very high burn rate signals a serious reliability problem.

---

# 132. Burn-Rate Alerting

Instead of alerting on every small error spike, alerts can detect:

```text
Fast severe burn
```

and:

```text
Slow sustained burn
```

across different windows.

This reduces noise while protecting SLOs.

---

# 133. Alert Philosophy

An alert should generally mean:

> **A human may need to act.**

If no one needs to do anything, it probably belongs on a dashboard rather than paging an engineer.

---

# 134. Symptom vs Cause Alerts

Prefer:

```text
Students cannot submit assessments
```

over paging first on:

```text
Pod CPU = 81%
```

CPU may be a cause.

User-visible failure is the symptom.

Cause metrics remain useful for diagnosis.

---

# 135. Alert Severity

Example classification:

```text
SEV1 / CRITICAL
Major production outage

SEV2 / HIGH
Significant degradation

SEV3 / MEDIUM
Non-critical operational issue

INFO
Non-paging notification
```

Exact definitions must be documented.

---

# 136. Alert Routing

Architecture:

```text
Metrics / Events
       │
       ▼
Alert Rules
       │
       ▼
Alertmanager / Alert Platform
       │
       ▼
Routing
   ┌───┼─────────┐
   ▼   ▼         ▼
On-call Team   Chat   Ticket
```

Routing depends on severity and ownership.

---

# 137. Alert Ownership

Every production alert must have:

```text
Owner
Severity
Meaning
Action
Runbook
Escalation path
```

An orphan alert is operational debt.

---

# 138. Runbooks

A useful alert links to a runbook containing:

```text
What the alert means
Likely causes
Dashboards
Queries
Immediate checks
Mitigation
Escalation
Recovery verification
```

This directly connects ADR-047 with the future Operations Runbook.

---

# 139. Alert Noise

If engineers receive hundreds of meaningless alerts:

```text
Alert
Alert
Alert
Alert
Alert
```

they will stop trusting alerts.

Alert fatigue is an architecture failure, not merely a human problem.

---

# 140. Security Telemetry

Security-relevant events should include appropriate monitoring for:

```text
Authentication failures
Authorization failures
Suspicious access
Credential abuse
Privilege changes
Administrative operations
WAF/security events
```

Security telemetry and operational telemetry may have different retention/access policies.

---

# 141. Observability RBAC

Telemetry itself can contain sensitive operational information.

Access should be role-controlled.

Not every developer automatically needs unrestricted access to:

```text
Production logs
Audit events
Security telemetry
Potentially sensitive traces
```

---

# 142. Telemetry Pipeline Reliability

The observability system must not take down the application.

Bad:

```text
Telemetry backend unavailable
        │
        ▼
Application request blocks
        │
        ▼
Production outage
```

Telemetry export should generally be asynchronous and failure-tolerant.

---

# 143. Backpressure

If collectors cannot export fast enough:

```text
Applications
    │
    ▼
Collectors
    │
    X
Backend
```

the system requires:

```text
Queues
Batching
Memory limits
Dropping policy
Retry limits
```

Telemetry must not grow without bounds.

---

# 144. Observing the Observability System

Monitor:

```text
Collector health
Dropped telemetry
Export failures
Queue utilization
Backend ingestion latency
Prometheus scrape failures
Storage capacity
```

Otherwise telemetry can silently disappear.

---

# 145. Cost Governance

Observability cost grows through:

```text
Log volume
Metric cardinality
Trace volume
Retention
Indexing
Dashboard queries
Data transfer
```

Cost controls must be designed from the beginning.

---

# 146. Observability Testing

CI/CD and environment validation should test:

```text
Trace propagation
Required metrics
Structured log schema
Sensitive-data redaction
Health endpoints
Alert rules
Dashboard queries
SLO calculations
Collector configuration
```

Observability configuration is production code.

---

# 147. Observability Anti-Patterns

Mediverse shall reject or strongly discourage:

```text
❌ Logs as the only observability mechanism
❌ SSHing into Pods as the standard debugging workflow
❌ Unstructured production logging
❌ Logging passwords/JWTs/API keys
❌ Full request/response logging by default
❌ User IDs as Prometheus labels
❌ Dynamic IDs in metric names
❌ Dynamic IDs in span names
❌ Unlimited metric cardinality
❌ INFO log for every method entry/exit
❌ Same exception logged at every layer
❌ Every HTTP 4xx treated as ERROR
❌ Keeping all telemetry forever
❌ Tracing 100% forever without cost analysis
❌ Sampling away every error
❌ Publicly exposed Actuator endpoints
❌ Database dependency inside liveness probe
❌ Treating readiness and liveness as identical
❌ Monitoring CPU while ignoring user symptoms
❌ Alerting on everything measurable
❌ Alerts without owners
❌ Alerts without runbooks
❌ SLOs without error-budget consequences
❌ Monitoring AI only through HTTP status
❌ Logging complete AI prompts indiscriminately
❌ Treating audit logs as ordinary application logs
❌ One gigantic Grafana dashboard
❌ Using the production search cluster as a log dump by default
❌ Telemetry export blocking application requests
❌ No monitoring of telemetry collectors themselves
```

---

# 148. Incident Investigation Flow

```text
                  USER IMPACT DETECTED
                          │
                          ▼
                      SLO Alert
                          │
                          ▼
                 Platform Dashboard
                          │
                          ▼
                  Identify Service
                          │
              ┌───────────┼───────────┐
              ▼           ▼           ▼
            Metrics      Traces       Logs
              │           │           │
              └───────────┼───────────┘
                          ▼
                    Dependency?
              ┌───────────┼────────────┐
              ▼           ▼            ▼
          PostgreSQL     Kafka      OpenSearch
              │           │            │
              ├───────────┼────────────┤
              ▼           ▼            ▼
            Redis        AI         Asset/CDN
              │           │            │
              └───────────┼────────────┘
                          ▼
                     Root Cause
                          │
                          ▼
                      Mitigation
                          │
                          ▼
                  Verify SLI Recovery
                          │
                          ▼
                   Incident Review
```

---

# 149. Final Mediverse Observability Architecture

```text
                         MEDIVERSE USERS
                               │
                 ┌─────────────┴─────────────┐
                 ▼                           ▼
              React                       Synthetic
               RUM                         Probes
                 │                           │
                 └─────────────┬─────────────┘
                               ▼
                          API GATEWAY
                               │
                               ▼
                       MICROSERVICES
                               │
       ┌───────────────────────┼────────────────────────┐
       ▼                       ▼                        ▼
 PostgreSQL / Redis           Kafka               OpenSearch
                                                       │
       ┌───────────────────────┼────────────────────────┐
       ▼                       ▼                        ▼
   AI Platform              S3/CDN               Kubernetes
       │                       │                        │
       └───────────────────────┼────────────────────────┘
                               ▼
                        OpenTelemetry
                               │
                               ▼
                      OTel Collectors
                               │
              ┌────────────────┼─────────────────┐
              ▼                ▼                 ▼
            LOGS            METRICS            TRACES
              │                │                 │
              ▼                ▼                 ▼
        Log Backend       Prometheus        Trace Backend
              │                │                 │
              └────────────────┼─────────────────┘
                               ▼
                            Grafana
                               │
                  ┌────────────┼────────────┐
                  ▼            ▼            ▼
              Dashboards      SLOs        Alerts
                                            │
                                            ▼
                                       Alertmanager
                                            │
                                            ▼
                                          On-call
                                            │
                                            ▼
```
