```text
                                         Runbook
```

The operational correlation model becomes:

```text
Deployment Version
        +
Trace ID
        +
Service
        +
Environment
        +
Metrics
        +
Logs
        +
Distributed Trace
        +
SLO State
        =
Investigable Production System
```

---

# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                       | Decision                                   |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Observability standard     | **OpenTelemetry**                          |
| Primary signals            | Logs + Metrics + Traces                    |
| Spring instrumentation     | Actuator + Micrometer + OTel               |
| Trace propagation          | W3C Trace Context                          |
| Telemetry transport        | OTLP where appropriate                     |
| Telemetry processing       | OpenTelemetry Collector                    |
| Metrics model              | Prometheus-compatible                      |
| Visualization              | Grafana                                    |
| Logging                    | Structured JSON                            |
| Central logging            | Required                                   |
| Audit vs operational logs  | Separate concerns                          |
| Sensitive data             | Redact / prohibit                          |
| Metric cardinality         | Strictly controlled                        |
| User IDs as metric labels  | Prohibited                                 |
| Trace sampling             | Required at scale                          |
| Error/slow traces          | Preferential retention                     |
| Kubernetes metrics         | Required                                   |
| Liveness/readiness/startup | Separate semantics                         |
| Synthetic monitoring       | Required for critical workflows            |
| Frontend RUM               | Recommended                                |
| Reliability model          | SLI + SLO + Error Budget                   |
| Alert model                | User-impact/action oriented                |
| Burn-rate alerts           | Preferred for SLOs                         |
| Alert ownership            | Mandatory                                  |
| Runbook association        | Mandatory for actionable production alerts |
| AI observability           | Operational + cost + quality               |
| Telemetry RBAC             | Required                                   |
| Collector resilience       | Required                                   |
| Cost governance            | Required                                   |
| Status                     | **Accepted**                               |
| Priority                   | **Critical**                               |

The architecture now establishes an important distinction:

```text
LOGS
=
Detailed events

METRICS
=
System behavior over time

TRACES
=
Request causality

AUDIT
=
Accountability

RUM
=
Actual user experience

SYNTHETICS
=
Externally tested experience

SLIs
=
Measured reliability

SLOs
=
Reliability targets

ERROR BUDGET
=
Allowed unreliability

ALERTS
=
Human action required
```

---

---

# ADR-048 — Enterprise Identity, Authentication, Authorization, RBAC/ABAC, OAuth 2.0, OIDC & Zero-Trust Security Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing from **Section 60 — Resource-Level Authorization**.

---

# 61. Authorization Policy Enforcement Points

Authorization must happen at explicit enforcement points.

```text
Request
   │
   ▼
API Gateway
   │
   ▼
Service
   │
   ▼
Domain Operation
```

Possible enforcement exists at multiple layers, but those layers have different responsibilities.

---

# 62. Gateway Authorization

The gateway can enforce coarse-grained controls such as:

```text
Valid access token?
Correct issuer?
Correct audience?
Required broad scope?
Known client?
```

Example:

```text
GET /admin/*
      │
      ▼
Require authenticated request
```

This reduces obviously unauthorized traffic reaching backend services.

---

# 63. Gateway Authorization Is Not Enough

The gateway usually cannot safely determine:

```text
Does Faculty A own Course 123?

Is Student B enrolled in Course 123?

Can Admin C modify Institution X?

Is Assessment 42 currently editable?
```

These require domain knowledge.

Therefore:

> Gateway authentication/authorization must never replace service-level resource authorization.

---

# 64. Defense in Depth

Preferred:

```text
                   Request
                      │
                      ▼
                 API Gateway
                      │
              Token Validation
                      │
                      ▼
               Resource Service
                      │
               Authorization
                      │
                      ▼
                Domain Policy
                      │
                      ▼
                  Resource
```

Security does not depend on one perimeter.

---

# 65. Spring Security

Spring Boot services shall use Spring Security as the standard application security framework.

Responsibilities may include:

```text
JWT validation
Security context
Authority mapping
Endpoint rules
Method authorization
Authentication integration
```

Teams should not implement custom token parsers and authorization frameworks independently.

---

# 66. Resource Server

Spring Boot APIs act as OAuth resource servers.

Conceptually:

```text
Access Token
     │
     ▼
Spring Security
     │
     ├── Verify signature
     ├── Verify issuer
     ├── Verify audience
     ├── Verify expiry
     └── Map authorities
            │
            ▼
        Controller
```

---

# 67. Method-Level Authorization

Sensitive service operations may use method authorization.

Conceptually:

```java
@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('course:create')")
public Course createCourse(...) {
    ...
}
```

But annotations alone do not solve resource ownership.

---

# 68. Domain Authorization

Example:

```text
Faculty has:
course:update

             +
Course belongs to faculty's tenant

             +
Faculty owns/manages course

             +
Course state permits editing

             =
ALLOW
```

This logic belongs near the domain boundary.

---

# 69. IDOR / BOLA

One of the most important API authorization risks is:

```text
GET /students/1001
```

changing to:

```text
GET /students/1002
```

and receiving another user's protected resource.

This is an authorization failure, not an authentication failure.

---

# 70. Never Trust Resource IDs

An authenticated caller supplying:

```text
courseId
studentId
tenantId
assessmentId
```

does not prove they are authorized to access that resource.

Every protected object reference requires authorization.

---

# 71. Tenant Isolation

Tenant isolation must be enforced systematically.

Conceptually:

```text
User
 │
 ▼
Membership
 │
 ▼
Tenant
 │
 ▼
Resource
```

The resource must belong to an authorized tenant context.

---

# 72. Never Trust Client Tenant ID

Bad:

```json
{
  "tenantId": "institution-B",
  "courseId": "123"
}
```

followed by:

```text
Use tenantId directly
```

The server must derive or validate tenant context against authenticated membership.

---

# 73. Tenant Context

A request may resolve:

```text
Authenticated User
       │
       ▼
Selected Tenant
       │
       ▼
Membership Validation
       │
       ▼
Authorized Tenant Context
```

Only then should tenant-scoped operations proceed.

---

# 74. Database Isolation

Application authorization should be reinforced by data-access patterns.

Bad:

```text
SELECT *
FROM course
WHERE id = ?
```

when tenant isolation is required.

Safer conceptual query:

```text
SELECT *
FROM course
WHERE id = ?
AND tenant_id = ?
```

Authorization should be difficult to accidentally bypass.

---

# 75. Global Administrators

Platform administrators may legitimately operate across tenants.

This must be an explicit privileged capability.

Do not implement:

```text
if admin
   skip all security
```

Administrative actions still require:

```text
Authentication
Authorization
Audit
Scope
```

---

# 76. Policy Decision Architecture

Complex authorization can be conceptualized as:

```text
PEP
Policy Enforcement Point

PDP
Policy Decision Point

PIP
Policy Information Point
```

Flow:

```text
Request
   │
   ▼
PEP
   │
   ▼
PDP
   │
   ├── Identity
   ├── Resource
   ├── Environment
   └── Attributes
         │
         ▼
      ALLOW / DENY
```

---

# 77. Policy Engine Evaluation

External policy engines such as OPA may be evaluated when authorization rules become sufficiently complex.

Potential advantages:

```text
Central policy language
Policy-as-code
Consistent evaluation
Independent testing
```

But introducing one too early can create unnecessary architecture.

---

# 78. Do Not Centralize All Authorization Blindly

A global policy engine cannot magically understand every business invariant.

For example:

```text
Assessment can be modified
only before publication
unless revision workflow active
```

may belong directly in the assessment domain.

External policy systems should complement domain authorization, not replace domain modeling.

---

# 79. Default Deny

Authorization should follow:

```text
No explicit permission
        │
        ▼
       DENY
```

not:

```text
No rule found
     │
     ▼
Probably allow
```

Default-deny is fundamental.

---

# 80. Authorization Decision Logging

Important authorization outcomes should produce appropriate telemetry.

Examples:

```text
Denied administrative action
Cross-tenant access attempt
Privilege escalation attempt
Policy evaluation failure
```

But logging every successful authorization check at high volume may create useless noise.

---

# 81. Authorization Caching

Some authorization information may be cached.

Examples:

```text
Role mappings
Tenant membership
Static permission mappings
```

But caching introduces stale-authorization risk.

---

# 82. Permission Revocation vs Cache

Suppose:

```text
Faculty permission removed
        │
        ▼
Authorization cache still says ALLOW
```

The cache TTL determines how long the stale privilege remains.

Security-sensitive permissions therefore require carefully bounded caching.

---

# 83. Workload Identity

Humans are not the only callers.

```text
Course Service
Search Indexer
Media Worker
Notification Worker
AI Platform
```

also require identities.

Using shared passwords between services is unacceptable.

---

# 84. Service Identity

Each workload should have its own identity.

```text
course-service
      │
      ▼
Identity A

asset-service
      │
      ▼
Identity B
```

not:

```text
all-backend-services
      │
      ▼
Shared Credential
```

This enables least privilege and attribution.

---

# 85. Kubernetes ServiceAccount

Within Kubernetes:

```text
Pod
 │
 ▼
ServiceAccount
 │
 ▼
Workload Identity
```

should form part of the workload identity architecture.

Avoid distributing static cloud credentials into Pods.

---

# 86. Cloud Workload Identity

In AWS-oriented Kubernetes deployments:

```text
Pod
 │
 ▼
Kubernetes ServiceAccount
 │
 ▼
AWS Workload Identity Mechanism
 │
 ▼
IAM Role
```

can grant narrowly scoped cloud access without embedding long-lived AWS access keys.

---

# 87. Least-Privilege IAM

Example:

```text
asset-service
```

may need access to:

```text
specific S3 asset resources
specific KMS operations
```

It does not therefore need:

```text
s3:*
kms:*
*
```

across the AWS account.

---

# 88. Client Credentials

For appropriate machine-to-machine OAuth scenarios:

```text
Service A
    │
    ▼
Authorization Server
    │
    ▼
Access Token
    │
    ▼
Service B
```

OAuth client-credentials flow may be used.

This represents the service itself, not an end user.

---

# 89. User Context vs Service Context

Suppose:

```text
Student
   │
   ▼
Course Service
   │
   ▼
Progress Service
```

Progress Service may need to know:

```text
Student identity
```

while also knowing:

```text
Course Service is the caller
```

These are different security contexts.

---

# 90. Token Propagation

Simple architecture:

```text
User Token
   │
   ▼
Service A
   │
   ▼
Service B
```

Service A forwards the original token.

This preserves user identity but can create excessive token reach.

---

# 91. Token Reach

Suppose the user's token permits:

```text
Course API
Assessment API
Profile API
```

but Service A only needs to call:

```text
Profile API
```

forwarding the broad original token gives Service A more delegated capability than necessary.

---

# 92. Token Exchange

For higher-security workflows:

```text
User Token
    │
    ▼
Service A
    │
    ▼
Token Exchange
    │
    ▼
Narrow Token
    │
    ▼
Service B
```

can reduce downstream privilege.

This should be introduced where threat/risk justifies the complexity.

---

# 93. Confused Deputy Problem

Suppose:

```text
User
 │
 ▼
Service A
 │
 ▼
Privileged Service B
```

Service A must not accidentally use its own broad privilege to perform an operation the user was never allowed to request.

Authorization must consider:

```text
Caller identity
+
Delegated user authority
+
Requested operation
```

where applicable.

---

# 94. mTLS

Mutual TLS can authenticate both sides of a service connection.

```text
Service A
   │
   │ mTLS
   ▼
Service B
```

Both endpoints establish cryptographic workload identity.

---

# 95. mTLS Does Not Replace Authorization

mTLS proves something like:

```text
This connection came from course-service.
```

It does not prove:

```text
course-service may delete assessment 123.
```

Authentication and authorization remain separate.

---

# 96. Service Mesh Identity

If ADR-041 adopts a service mesh, workload certificates and mTLS can provide:

```text
Workload identity
Encrypted east-west traffic
Service authentication
Policy enforcement
```

But the mesh does not understand all Mediverse business authorization.

---

# 97. Zero Trust

Mediverse shall follow zero-trust principles.

The simplified principle is:

> **Network location is not sufficient evidence of trust.**

Being:

```text
inside Kubernetes
inside VPC
inside corporate network
```

does not automatically authorize access.

---

# 98. Zero Trust Request

Conceptually:

```text
Request
   │
   ▼
Authenticate identity
   │
   ▼
Evaluate authorization
   │
   ▼
Evaluate context
   │
   ▼
Apply least privilege
   │
   ▼
Allow / Deny
```

for sensitive boundaries.

---

# 99. AI Agent Identity

ADR-045 introduced agents capable of calling tools.

An AI agent must not receive magical unrestricted system access.

```text
AI Agent
   │
   ▼
Delegated Identity
   │
   ▼
Authorized Tools
```

Agent capabilities must remain bounded.

---

# 100. Agent Delegation

If a student asks:

```text
"Show my progress."
```

the AI system may call the Progress API using authority derived from that student's permitted context.

It must not call:

```text
GET /students/*
```

with unrestricted backend privilege simply because the AI service itself is trusted.

---

# 101. Agent Tool Authorization

Every tool call remains subject to authorization.

```text
LLM Decision
    │
    ▼
Tool Invocation
    │
    ▼
Authorization
    │
    ├── ALLOW
    └── DENY
```

The LLM is never the authorization authority.

---

# 102. Privileged AI Actions

High-impact actions such as:

```text
Publishing content
Changing grades
Deleting course material
Changing permissions
Sending institutional communication
```

should not automatically execute merely because an agent generated the request.

ADR-045's human-approval architecture remains applicable.

---

# 103. Administrative Privileges

Privileged accounts require stronger controls.

Examples:

```text
Platform Admin
Security Admin
Institution Admin
Support Admin
```

Avoid one universal:

```text
SUPER_ADMIN
```

role with unrestricted permanent access whenever finer separation is practical.

---

# 104. Separation of Duties

Sensitive operations may require distinct privileges.

For example:

```text
Identity Administration
Infrastructure Administration
Security Administration
Content Administration
```

should not automatically collapse into one role.

---

# 105. Just-in-Time Privilege

Where operational maturity supports it:

```text
Normal Account
     │
     ▼
Request Elevation
     │
     ▼
Approval / Verification
     │
     ▼
Temporary Privilege
     │
     ▼
Expiry
```

is safer than permanent privileged access.

---

# 106. Break-Glass Access

Emergency access may be required during severe incidents.

A break-glass mechanism should be:

```text
Rare
Strongly authenticated
Time-limited
Audited
Alert-generating
Reviewed afterward
```

It should not become the normal administrative workflow.

---

# 107. Support Access

Support personnel may need to investigate user issues.

Bad:

```text
Support employee
=
Can access every student's account whenever desired
```

Support access requires explicit scope and auditing.

---

# 108. Impersonation

If user impersonation is required:

```text
Support Identity
      │
      ▼
Impersonation Session
      │
      ▼
User Context
```

the system must preserve both:

```text
Actual actor
Impersonated subject
```

in audit records.

---

# 109. Impersonation UI

The UI should make impersonation obvious.

```text
YOU ARE IMPERSONATING:
Student 123
```

Silent impersonation creates severe security and audit risks.

---

# 110. Secrets Management

Secrets include:

```text
Database credentials
API keys
OAuth client secrets
Signing material
Third-party credentials
```

They should be managed through an approved secrets-management architecture.

---

# 111. Secrets Are Not Configuration

This:

```text
application-prod.yml

database.password=...
```

committed to Git is unacceptable.

Git history makes secret removal difficult even after deleting the visible line.

---

# 112. Kubernetes Secrets

Kubernetes Secrets alone should not automatically be treated as a complete enterprise secrets-management solution.

The architecture must consider:

```text
Encryption at rest
RBAC
Secret distribution
Rotation
Audit
External secret stores
```

---

# 113. External Secrets

An architecture may use:

```text
AWS Secrets Manager
        │
        ▼
External Secrets mechanism
        │
        ▼
Kubernetes workload
```

where appropriate.

The source of truth should remain controlled.

---

# 114. Secret Rotation

Credentials should be rotatable without:

```text
manual editing across 40 services
```

Rotation architecture should support:

```text
New credential
      │
      ▼
Controlled overlap
      │
      ▼
Workloads refresh
      │
      ▼
Old credential revoked
```

where the credential type permits it.

---

# 115. Browser Cookies

For BFF sessions, cookies should use appropriate controls such as:

```text
Secure
HttpOnly
SameSite
```

according to the deployment architecture.

---

# 116. HttpOnly

`HttpOnly` prevents normal JavaScript access to the cookie.

This reduces session theft through XSS.

It does not eliminate XSS itself.

---

# 117. Secure Cookie

`Secure` ensures the browser sends the cookie only over HTTPS.

Production authentication must not rely on plaintext HTTP.

---

# 118. SameSite

`SameSite` can reduce cross-site request risks.

But the correct mode depends on:

```text
Frontend domain
BFF domain
Federated login flow
Cross-site requirements
```

Do not set it blindly.

---

# 119. CSRF

Cookie-based authentication creates CSRF considerations because browsers may automatically attach cookies.

Therefore state-changing requests require an appropriate CSRF defense.

---

# 120. CSRF Protection

Possible architecture:

```text
Browser
   │
   ├── Session Cookie
   │
   └── CSRF Token
          │
          ▼
         BFF
```

Combined with:

```text
SameSite
Origin validation
CSRF tokens
```

as appropriate.

---

# 121. XSS

XSS can allow attacker-controlled JavaScript to execute in the Mediverse frontend.

Potential consequences include:

```text
Act as user
Read page data
Call APIs
Steal non-HttpOnly credentials
Manipulate content
```

Frontend security is therefore part of identity security.

---

# 122. localStorage Token Risk

Storing long-lived authentication tokens in:

```text
localStorage
```

makes them directly accessible to JavaScript.

An XSS vulnerability can therefore extract them.

This is one major reason the BFF architecture is preferred for sensitive browser sessions.

---

# 123. CSP

Content Security Policy can reduce some XSS attack paths.

A production CSP should be deliberately designed rather than:

```text
script-src *
unsafe-inline
unsafe-eval
```

which destroys much of its protection.

---

# 124. CORS

CORS controls which browser origins can access APIs.

It is **not authentication**.

Bad assumption:

```text
CORS allows only mediverse.com
therefore API is secure
```

Non-browser attackers are not constrained by browser CORS enforcement.

---

# 125. CORS Policy

Production should explicitly allow required origins.

Avoid:

```text
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
```

for credentialed sensitive APIs.

---

# 126. Rate Limiting

Identity endpoints require dedicated abuse protection.

Examples:

```text
/login
/password-reset
/token
/MFA verification
/account recovery
```

These should not necessarily use the same limits as ordinary course APIs.

---

# 127. Authentication Telemetry

ADR-047 observability should monitor:

```text
Login success/failure
MFA challenges
Token failures
Suspicious refresh activity
Account recovery
Authorization denials
Administrative elevation
Break-glass use
```

with privacy-aware telemetry.

---

# 128. Audit Trail

Security-sensitive actions require durable audit events.

Conceptually:

```text
Actor
Action
Resource
Tenant
Timestamp
Outcome
Relevant Context
```

Examples:

```text
Role changed
Course published
Grade modified
User impersonated
Admin privilege elevated
Break-glass activated
```

---

# 129. Audit Integrity

Audit data should be protected against unauthorized modification or deletion.

An administrator capable of performing an action should not automatically have unrestricted ability to erase evidence of that action.

---

# 130. Security Event Correlation

From ADR-047:

```text
Authentication Event
        │
        ▼
Trace / Request
        │
        ▼
Authorization Event
        │
        ▼
Domain Action
        │
        ▼
Audit Event
```

should be correlatable where appropriate.

---

# 131. Threat Modeling

Security architecture must be threat-driven.

For important workflows, evaluate:

```text
Who is the attacker?

What asset are they targeting?

What trust boundary is crossed?

What privilege is required?

What happens if compromised?
```

rather than simply adding security products.

---

# 132. STRIDE

A threat-modeling framework such as STRIDE can help evaluate:

```text
Spoofing
Tampering
Repudiation
Information Disclosure
Denial of Service
Elevation of Privilege
```

across major Mediverse trust boundaries.

---

# 133. Identity Threat Example

```text
Attacker
   │
   ▼
Steals refresh token
   │
   ▼
Obtains access tokens
   │
   ▼
Acts as student
```

Controls:

```text
Secure token storage
Rotation
Reuse detection
Session revocation
Short access-token lifetime
Telemetry
```

---

# 134. Authorization Threat Example

```text
Student A
   │
   ▼
GET /assessment/123
   │
   ▼
Changes ID to 124
   │
   ▼
Receives restricted assessment
```

Control:

```text
Resource-level authorization
```

not simply JWT validation.

---

# 135. Tenant Threat Example

```text
Institution A Admin
        │
        ▼
Changes tenantId
        │
        ▼
Institution B data
```

Controls:

```text
Server-derived tenant context
Membership validation
Tenant-scoped queries
Audit
Security testing
```

---

# 136. Service Compromise

Assume eventually a workload may be compromised.

If:

```text
notification-service
```

is compromised, it should not automatically have credentials allowing:

```text
Database administration
S3 deletion
User-role changes
Assessment modification
```

Least privilege limits blast radius.

---

# 137. Key Compromise

Security design must answer:

> What happens if a signing key, API key, client secret or workload credential is compromised?

Required capabilities include:

```text
Detection
Revocation
Rotation
Replacement
Audit
Blast-radius analysis
```

---

# 138. Security Testing

Testing should include:

```text
Authentication bypass
Expired tokens
Wrong issuer
Wrong audience
Invalid signature
Role escalation
IDOR/BOLA
Cross-tenant access
CSRF
CORS misconfiguration
Session fixation
Refresh-token reuse
Privilege revocation
Admin workflows
```

---

# 139. Automated Authorization Tests

Every sensitive endpoint should have negative tests.

Example:

```text
Student → Student resource     ALLOW
Student → Other private user   DENY
Faculty → Own course           ALLOW
Faculty → Other tenant course  DENY
Admin A → Tenant B             DENY
```

Testing only happy paths is inadequate.

---

# 140. Dependency Security

Identity/security libraries require active patching.

Critical dependencies include:

```text
Spring Security
OAuth/OIDC libraries
JWT libraries
IdP
Ingress/Gateway
Service Mesh
Secrets tooling
```

Security architecture degrades if dependencies remain unpatched.

---

# 141. Zero-Trust Decision Flow

```text
                     REQUEST
                        │
                        ▼
                  Establish Identity
                        │
                        ▼
                  Validate Credential
                        │
                        ▼
                  Resolve Tenant
                        │
                        ▼
                  Resolve Resource
                        │
                        ▼
                  Evaluate RBAC
                        │
                        ▼
                  Evaluate ABAC
                        │
                        ▼
                 Domain Constraints
                        │
               ┌────────┴────────┐
               ▼                 ▼
             ALLOW              DENY
               │                 │
               ▼                 ▼
          Execute Action     Security/Audit
               │
               ▼
             Audit
```

---

# 142. Human Identity Flow

```text
                       USER
                        │
                        ▼
                 Identity Provider
                        │
              ┌─────────┴─────────┐
              ▼                   ▼
          Password /            External
          Passkey/MFA             IdP
              │                   │
              └─────────┬─────────┘
                        ▼
                 OIDC Authorization
                        │
                        ▼
                       BFF
                        │
                Secure Session
                        │
                        ▼
                     Browser
```

Backend interaction:

```text
Browser
   │
   ▼
BFF
   │ Access Token
   ▼
API Gateway
   │
   ▼
Spring Boot Resource Server
   │
   ▼
RBAC + ABAC + Domain Policy
```

---

# 143. Workload Identity Flow

```text
                   Kubernetes Pod
                         │
                         ▼
                  ServiceAccount
                         │
             ┌───────────┴───────────┐
             ▼                       ▼
      Cloud Workload Identity   Service Identity
             │                       │
             ▼                       ▼
           AWS APIs              Service APIs
             │                       │
             ▼                       ▼
         IAM Policy          OAuth / mTLS Policy
```

No static universal backend credential is required.

---

# 144. AI Agent Security Flow

```text
                      STUDENT
                         │
                         ▼
                     AI Tutor
                         │
                  User Context
                         │
                         ▼
                     AI Agent
                         │
                         ▼
                   Tool Request
                         │
                         ▼
                    Tool Gateway
                         │
                         ▼
                    Authorization
                  ┌──────┴──────┐
                  ▼             ▼
                ALLOW          DENY
                  │
                  ▼
             Domain Service
                  │
                  ▼
              Audit / Trace
```

The rule is:

```text
AI reasoning
≠
authorization decision
```

---

# 145. Identity & Security Anti-Patterns

Mediverse shall reject:

```text
❌ Authentication implemented independently by every microservice
❌ Custom OAuth server without compelling reason
❌ Passwords stored by domain services
❌ Plaintext passwords
❌ Email used as immutable user ID
❌ JWT decoded without signature validation
❌ ID token used blindly as API access token
❌ Sensitive data stored inside JWT claims
❌ 30-day bearer access tokens
❌ Long-lived browser tokens in localStorage by default
❌ Shared service credentials
❌ Static AWS keys inside Pods
❌ One universal SUPER_ADMIN for everything
❌ Global role=FACULTY without tenant context
❌ Gateway-only authorization
❌ Checking role without resource ownership
❌ Trusting tenantId supplied by client
❌ Cross-tenant queries without tenant constraints
❌ mTLS treated as business authorization
❌ Internal network treated as trusted
❌ AI agents given unrestricted backend credentials
❌ LLM allowed to decide authorization
❌ Secrets committed to Git
❌ Secrets stored in application.yml
❌ Logging JWTs/passwords/API keys
❌ CORS treated as authentication
❌ Wildcard credentialed CORS
❌ Cookie sessions without CSRF consideration
❌ Support impersonation without audit
❌ Permanent unrestricted break-glass accounts
❌ Authorization tests covering only successful cases
```

---

# 146. Security Boundaries

The Mediverse security architecture now contains explicit trust boundaries:

```text
Internet
   │
   ▼
────────────────────────
Edge Boundary
────────────────────────
   │
API Gateway / BFF
   │
   ▼
────────────────────────
Application Boundary
────────────────────────
   │
Microservices
   │
   ▼
────────────────────────
Data Boundary
────────────────────────
   │
PostgreSQL / Redis /
Kafka / OpenSearch / S3

Separate:

────────────────────────
Identity Boundary
────────────────────────
Identity Provider

────────────────────────
Administration Boundary
────────────────────────
Privileged Operations

────────────────────────
Cloud Boundary
────────────────────────
IAM / KMS / Secrets
```

Crossing a boundary requires explicit trust evaluation.

---

# 147. Authorization Responsibility Matrix

| Layer                 | Responsibility                                    |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| Identity Provider     | Authenticate identity                             |
| BFF                   | Browser session and token handling                |
| API Gateway           | Coarse authentication/access controls             |
| Spring Security       | Token validation and application security context |
| Domain Service        | Resource/business authorization                   |
| RBAC                  | Broad capability                                  |
| ABAC                  | Contextual authorization                          |
| Database access layer | Tenant-aware data constraints                     |
| Service Mesh          | Workload transport identity/mTLS                  |
| IAM                   | AWS resource authorization                        |
| Kubernetes RBAC       | Kubernetes API authorization                      |
| Secrets Manager       | Credential protection                             |
| Audit Platform        | Accountability                                    |
| AI Tool Gateway       | Agent capability enforcement                      |

No single layer replaces the others.

---

# 148. Final Identity Reference Architecture

```text
                       ┌─────────────────┐
                       │     USERS       │
                       │ Student/Faculty │
                       │ Admin/Support   │
                       └────────┬────────┘
                                │
                                ▼
                       ┌─────────────────┐
                       │ IDENTITY        │
                       │ PROVIDER        │
                       │ OIDC/OAuth/MFA  │
                       │ Federation      │
                       └────────┬────────┘
                                │
                                ▼
                       ┌─────────────────┐
                       │       BFF       │
                       │ Secure Session  │
                       └────────┬────────┘
                                │
                                ▼
                       ┌─────────────────┐
                       │   API GATEWAY   │
                       │ Authentication  │
                       │ Coarse Policy   │
                       └────────┬────────┘
                                │
                                ▼
                  ┌──────────────────────────┐
                  │   SPRING BOOT SERVICES  │
                  │                          │
                  │ JWT Validation           │
                  │ RBAC                     │
                  │ ABAC                     │
                  │ Resource Authorization   │
                  │ Tenant Isolation         │
                  └────────────┬─────────────┘
                               │
             ┌─────────────────┼──────────────────┐
             ▼                 ▼                  ▼
        PostgreSQL           Redis              Kafka
             │                                    │
             ▼                                    ▼
        Tenant Data                           Consumers
             │                                    │
             └─────────────────┬──────────────────┘
                               ▼
                         Domain Resources


                    WORKLOAD SECURITY

                     Kubernetes Pod
                           │
                           ▼
                    ServiceAccount
                           │
             ┌─────────────┴──────────────┐
             ▼                            ▼
       Workload Identity              mTLS/OAuth
             │                            │
             ▼                            ▼
           AWS IAM                   Other Services
             │
      ┌──────┼─────────┐
      ▼      ▼         ▼
     S3     KMS     Secrets Manager


                     AI SECURITY

                        User
                         │
                         ▼
                     AI Agent
                         │
                         ▼
                    Tool Gateway
                         │
                         ▼
                    Authorization
                         │
                         ▼
                    Domain APIs
                         │
                         ▼
                   Audit + Trace
```

---

# 149. Core Security Invariants

These invariants should remain true regardless of future implementation changes:

```text
1. Every human and workload has an identifiable security principal.

2. Authentication does not imply authorization.

3. Protected resources require resource-level authorization.

4. Tenant context is validated server-side.

5. Authorization defaults to DENY.

6. Services receive only necessary privileges.

7. Browser JavaScript does not receive long-lived powerful credentials by default.

8. Tokens are short-lived and scoped appropriately.

9. Secrets are never committed to source control.

10. Internal network location does not imply trust.

11. AI agents cannot bypass ordinary authorization.

12. Privileged actions are auditable.

13. Emergency privilege is exceptional and temporary.

14. Authentication and authorization failures are observable.

15. Identity infrastructure itself is treated as critical production infrastructure.
```

---

# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                            | Decision                                              |
| ------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| Identity architecture           | Centralized IdP                                       |
| Primary authentication standard | **OpenID Connect**                                    |
| Delegated authorization         | **OAuth**                                             |
| SPA flow                        | Authorization Code + PKCE                             |
| Browser architecture            | **BFF preferred**                                     |
| Browser session                 | Secure HttpOnly cookie                                |
| Access tokens                   | Short-lived                                           |
| Distributed API token           | Signed JWT reasonable default                         |
| Token verification              | Signature + issuer + audience + expiry                |
| Signing-key discovery           | JWKS                                                  |
| Refresh tokens                  | Controlled + rotation where applicable                |
| User identity                   | Stable internal ID                                    |
| Federation                      | OIDC preferred; SAML supported where required         |
| Authorization                   | **RBAC + ABAC + domain policy**                       |
| Resource authorization          | Mandatory                                             |
| Tenant isolation                | Mandatory                                             |
| Client tenant IDs               | Never blindly trusted                                 |
| Gateway authorization           | Coarse only                                           |
| Service authorization           | Mandatory                                             |
| Spring security framework       | Spring Security                                       |
| Policy engine                   | Evaluate when complexity justifies                    |
| Default authorization           | DENY                                                  |
| Service identity                | Per-workload                                          |
| Kubernetes identity             | ServiceAccount-based                                  |
| AWS access                      | Workload identity + IAM                               |
| Static cloud keys in Pods       | Prohibited                                            |
| East-west authentication        | OAuth/mTLS according to use case                      |
| Service mesh                    | Transport/workload identity, not domain authorization |
| Zero trust                      | Adopted                                               |
| AI authorization                | Same domain policies as other callers                 |
| LLM as authorization authority  | Prohibited                                            |
| Privileged access               | Least privilege + strong authentication               |
| Break-glass                     | Temporary + audited                                   |
| Support impersonation           | Explicit + audited                                    |
| Secrets                         | Centralized secret management                         |
| Frontend token storage          | Avoid long-lived localStorage tokens                  |
| CSRF                            | Required consideration for cookie auth                |
| CORS                            | Browser control, not security identity                |
| Security telemetry              | Integrated with ADR-047                               |
| Audit                           | Required for sensitive operations                     |
| Threat modeling                 | Required                                              |
| Negative authorization testing  | Required                                              |
| Status                          | **Accepted**                                          |
| Priority                        | **Critical**                                          |

---

---

# ADR-049 — Enterprise Secrets, PKI, Cryptography, KMS, Certificate & Key Lifecycle Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing from **Section 60 — Do Not Encrypt Every Database Column**.

---

# 61. Data Classification Drives Encryption

Encryption decisions must follow data classification.

```text
PUBLIC
INTERNAL
CONFIDENTIAL
RESTRICTED
```

A single encryption policy for every byte of Mediverse data would either be insufficient for sensitive information or unnecessarily complex for low-risk information.

---

# 62. Encryption Layers

Mediverse can protect data at several layers:

```text
Application Encryption
        │
        ▼
Database / Storage Encryption
        │
        ▼
Volume / Disk Encryption
        │
        ▼
Infrastructure Encryption
```

These layers protect against different threats.

---

# 63. Encryption at Rest

Persistent production data should use encryption at rest where supported.

This includes:

```text
PostgreSQL
S3
OpenSearch
Redis persistence
Kafka storage
EBS volumes
Backups
Snapshots
Logs
```

Encryption should be enabled by architecture rather than manually remembered by individual teams.

---

# 64. PostgreSQL Encryption

PostgreSQL protection consists of multiple controls:

```text
Storage encryption
        +
TLS connections
        +
Database authorization
        +
Application authorization
        +
Selective field encryption
```

Disk encryption alone does not protect against an application using valid database credentials.

---

# 65. Managed PostgreSQL

For AWS-managed PostgreSQL deployments, storage encryption should integrate with KMS where appropriate.

Conceptually:

```text
Application
    │ TLS
    ▼
PostgreSQL
    │
    ▼
Encrypted Storage
    │
    ▼
KMS
```

---

# 66. Database Backup Encryption

Encryption policy must extend to:

```text
Automated backups
Manual snapshots
Cross-region copies
Exported backups
DR replicas
```

Protecting the primary database while leaving backups unencrypted defeats the security boundary.

---

# 67. Database Field Encryption

Restricted fields may justify:

```text
Application
     │
     ▼
Envelope Encryption
     │
     ▼
Ciphertext
     │
     ▼
PostgreSQL
```

The decision must account for query requirements and operational complexity.

---

# 68. S3 Encryption

ADR-046 established S3 as the object-storage foundation.

Objects should use approved server-side encryption.

Possible models include:

```text
SSE-S3
SSE-KMS
```

SSE-KMS should be used where KMS-level control, auditability or key separation is required.

---

# 69. SSE-KMS

Conceptually:

```text
Asset
  │
  ▼
S3
  │
  ▼
Data Encryption Key
  │
  ▼
KMS Key
```

Applications should normally rely on the storage platform's managed envelope-encryption implementation rather than implementing custom object cryptography.

---

# 70. S3 Bucket Keys

At very high object/request volumes, KMS request patterns can affect cost.

S3 Bucket Keys may reduce KMS request costs for appropriate SSE-KMS workloads.

Cost optimization must not silently weaken required security boundaries.

---

# 71. Object Key Separation

Different classes of objects may justify separate encryption boundaries.

Example:

```text
Public educational assets
Restricted faculty assets
Private student submissions
Audit exports
```

But creating a dedicated KMS key for every individual object would be unnecessary operational complexity.

---

# 72. Kafka Encryption

Kafka requires protection both:

```text
At Rest
+
In Transit
```

Broker storage encryption alone does not protect messages crossing the network.

---

# 73. Kafka TLS

Connections such as:

```text
Producer → Broker
Consumer → Broker
Broker → Broker
```

should use TLS according to deployment architecture.

Authentication and authorization remain separate concerns.

---

# 74. Kafka Payload Encryption

Do not automatically encrypt every Kafka message at the application layer.

That complicates:

```text
Debugging
Schema evolution
Stream processing
Replay
Consumer interoperability
```

Use application-level payload encryption only where data classification requires protection beyond broker/storage controls.

---

# 75. Redis Encryption

Redis security should include:

```text
Network isolation
TLS where applicable
Authentication
Authorization
Encryption of persistent storage
```

from ADR-043.

Do not treat Redis as safe merely because it is "internal."

---

# 76. OpenSearch Encryption

ADR-044's OpenSearch architecture should protect:

```text
Node storage
Snapshots
Client connections
Node-to-node communication
```

according to deployment capabilities.

Search indices may contain derived sensitive information and must follow data-classification policy.

---

# 77. Logs Are Data

Observability storage from ADR-047 may contain:

```text
User identifiers
Resource identifiers
Error context
Infrastructure metadata
Security events
```

Therefore logs, traces and audit stores require encryption policies too.

---

# 78. Encryption in Transit

Mediverse shall protect sensitive network communication using TLS.

Primary paths include:

```text
Browser → Edge
Edge → Application
Service → Service
Application → Database
Application → Kafka
Application → Redis
Application → OpenSearch
Application → AWS/External APIs
```

---

# 79. TLS Policy

Production should support modern TLS configurations.

Conceptually:

```text
TLS 1.3
TLS 1.2 where compatibility requires
```

Legacy protocol versions and weak cipher suites should be disabled unless an explicitly documented compatibility requirement exists.

---

# 80. TLS Provides Multiple Properties

TLS can provide:

```text
Confidentiality
Integrity
Server authentication
```

and with mutual TLS:

```text
Client authentication
```

It does not provide application-level authorization.

---

# 81. Public TLS

Public Mediverse endpoints require publicly trusted certificates.

```text
Browser
   │
   ▼
HTTPS
   │
   ▼
CloudFront / Load Balancer / Gateway
```

Certificates should be issued and renewed automatically where practical.

---

# 82. AWS Certificate Manager

For AWS-managed public endpoints, AWS Certificate Manager should be preferred where supported.

ACM can manage certificates used by services such as:

```text
CloudFront
Application Load Balancer
API endpoints
```

depending on the architecture.

---

# 83. Certificate Lifecycle

Certificates have a lifecycle:

```text
Request
  │
  ▼
Validate
  │
  ▼
Issue
  │
  ▼
Deploy
  │
  ▼
Monitor
  │
  ▼
Renew
  │
  ▼
Replace
  │
  ▼
Revoke / Expire
```

Certificate architecture must cover the entire chain.

---

# 84. Manual Certificate Renewal Is Operational Debt

A production process such as:

```text
Engineer remembers certificate expiry
        │
        ▼
Downloads certificate
        │
        ▼
Manually installs it
```

will eventually fail.

Renewal should be automated.

---

# 85. Certificate Expiry Monitoring

Even automated systems can fail.

ADR-047 should alert before certificate expiry.

Example windows might include escalating warnings such as:

```text
30 days
14 days
7 days
1 day
```

according to certificate lifetime and renewal design.

---

# 86. Internal PKI

Internal service identities may require a private PKI.

```text
Root CA
   │
   ▼
Intermediate CA
   │
   ▼
Workload Certificate
```

The root should not routinely sign workload certificates directly.

---

# 87. Root CA

The root CA represents the highest cryptographic trust anchor.

Compromise can undermine the entire certificate hierarchy.

Therefore root-key custody requires especially strong controls.

---

# 88. Intermediate CA

Preferred:

```text
Root CA
   │
   ▼
Intermediate CA
   │
   ▼
Service Certificates
```

If an intermediate is compromised, it can potentially be replaced without replacing the entire root trust architecture.

---

# 89. Certificate Subject Identity

Certificates should identify workloads through stable identities rather than ephemeral infrastructure details.

Bad:

```text
pod-7f8d99c5-x2abc
```

Better:

```text
course-service
```

within an appropriate namespace/trust-domain model.

---

# 90. Subject Alternative Names

Modern TLS identity validation relies on SANs rather than assumptions about legacy certificate fields.

SANs may represent:

```text
DNS identities
URI identities
```

according to the PKI architecture.

---

# 91. cert-manager

For Kubernetes certificate automation, cert-manager may manage:

```text
Certificate requests
Issuance
Renewal
Kubernetes certificate resources
```

against supported issuers.

It should not be confused with the CA itself.

---

# 92. ACME

ACME automates certificate issuance and renewal.

Conceptually:

```text
cert-manager
     │
     ▼
ACME Server
     │
     ▼
Challenge
     │
     ▼
Certificate
```

It is particularly useful for publicly trusted TLS certificate automation where appropriate.

---

# 93. Internal Certificates

Internal workload certificates may instead be issued by:

```text
Private CA
Service Mesh CA
SPIFFE-compatible infrastructure
```

depending on ADR-041's service-mesh decision.

---

# 94. Service Mesh Certificates

A service mesh may automate:

```text
Workload certificate issuance
Short certificate lifetime
Rotation
mTLS
Identity verification
```

This is preferable to manually provisioning static TLS certificates into every Pod.

---

# 95. Short-Lived Certificates

Short-lived workload certificates reduce the usefulness of stolen credentials.

```text
Certificate
   │
   ▼
Hours / Days
   │
   ▼
Automatic Rotation
```

This is stronger than distributing multi-year private keys to containers.

---

# 96. SPIFFE

SPIFFE provides a standardized workload-identity model.

A workload may receive an identity conceptually like:

```text
spiffe://mediverse.example/prod/course-service
```

This identifies the workload independent of IP address.

---

# 97. SPIRE Evaluation

SPIRE can implement SPIFFE workload identities and automated credential issuance.

Potential advantages:

```text
Strong workload identity
Short-lived credentials
Environment-independent identity
mTLS integration
```

Trade-off:

```text
Additional security infrastructure
Operational complexity
```

If the service mesh already provides sufficient workload identity, adding SPIRE separately may be redundant.

---

# 98. Certificate Private Keys

Private keys must not be:

```text
Committed to Git
Baked into container images
Shared across services
Copied manually between environments
```

Private-key access must be restricted to the workload that requires it.

---

# 99. Certificate Rotation

Rotation should support overlapping trust where necessary:

```text
Certificate A
      │
      ▼
Issue Certificate B
      │
      ▼
Deploy B
      │
      ▼
Verify
      │
      ▼
A expires/revoked
```

Automation should handle this without application outages.

---

# 100. Certificate Revocation

Revocation requirements depend on certificate architecture.

Possible mechanisms include:

```text
CRL
OCSP
Short certificate lifetime
Trust-bundle changes
```

Short-lived workload certificates can reduce dependence on complex revocation mechanisms.

---

# 101. JWT Signing Keys

ADR-048 established signed JWT access tokens.

The IdP signing private key is therefore critical cryptographic material.

```text
IdP
 │
 │ Private Key
 ▼
JWT Signature

Services
 │
 │ Public Key
 ▼
Verification
```

---

# 102. Signing-Key Custody

Only the component responsible for signing should require access to signing capability.

Resource services should receive:

```text
Public verification key
```

not:

```text
Private signing key
```

---

# 103. JWKS Rotation

A safe signing-key rotation may look like:

```text
JWKS:
Key A

      ↓

JWKS:
Key A
Key B

      ↓

New tokens signed with B

      ↓

Old A tokens expire

      ↓

Remove A
```

This avoids invalidating every active token immediately.

---

# 104. `kid`

JWT headers can identify the signing key using:

```text
kid
```

Resource servers use it to select the corresponding public verification key.

Services must not blindly trust attacker-controlled key references outside the trusted issuer/JWKS model.

---

# 105. Signing vs Encryption Keys

Do not casually reuse one key for unrelated purposes.

```text
JWT signing
Database field encryption
Backup encryption
Webhook signing
```

have different cryptographic roles and lifecycle requirements.

Key separation reduces blast radius.

---

# 106. HSM

A Hardware Security Module provides hardened cryptographic-key protection and operations.

Conceptually:

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
HSM
    │
    ├── Key never exported
    └── Crypto operation
```

---

# 107. CloudHSM Evaluation

AWS CloudHSM may be appropriate when requirements demand:

```text
Dedicated HSM control
Specific compliance requirements
Custom cryptographic integration
Direct HSM ownership/control
```

But using CloudHSM simply because it sounds more secure would add substantial cost and operational complexity.

---

# 108. KMS vs CloudHSM

Default:

```text
AWS KMS
```

for most managed encryption/key-management requirements.

Evaluate:

```text
CloudHSM
```

only when requirements exceed KMS capabilities or demand dedicated HSM control.

---

# 109. Password Hashing

Passwords must not use reversible encryption.

Correct model:

```text
Password
   │
   ▼
Password Hash Function
   │
   ▼
Stored Hash
```

The original password should not be recoverable.

---

# 110. Password Hashing Algorithms

Use modern password-hashing algorithms supported by the identity platform, such as:

```text
Argon2id
bcrypt
scrypt
PBKDF2
```

according to current platform/security requirements.

Do not use fast general-purpose hashes such as plain SHA-256 for password storage.

---

# 111. Salt

Each password should use a unique random salt.

```text
Password + Salt
       │
       ▼
Password Hash
```

Salts protect against precomputed hash attacks and identical-password hash equality.

Salts do not need to be secret.

---

# 112. Pepper

A system may additionally use a secret pepper protected separately from the password database.

```text
Password
+
Salt
+
Pepper
```

But pepper management adds complexity.

It should not compensate for weak password hashing.

---

# 113. Secure Randomness

Security-sensitive values require cryptographically secure randomness.

Examples:

```text
Tokens
Nonces
Password reset codes
Session IDs
Cryptographic keys
```

Do not use ordinary pseudo-random functions intended for simulations or UI behavior.

---

# 114. Nonces and IVs

Cryptographic modes have specific requirements for:

```text
Nonce
IV
```

including uniqueness and/or unpredictability.

Developers should use established cryptographic libraries and safe high-level APIs rather than inventing nonce-generation schemes.

---

# 115. Do Not Build Custom Cryptography

Prohibited architecture:

```text
Developer
   │
   ▼
"Simple encryption algorithm"
   │
   ▼
Production
```

Use established protocols, libraries and managed cryptographic services.

Cryptography is not an appropriate area for clever custom implementations.

---

# 116. Algorithm Governance

Mediverse should maintain an approved cryptographic baseline covering:

```text
TLS versions
Cipher suites
Encryption algorithms
Signature algorithms
Password hashing
Key sizes
Certificate parameters
```

This avoids each team making independent cryptographic decisions.

---

# 117. Deprecated Cryptography

Legacy or broken algorithms should not be introduced into new systems.

Examples requiring rejection or strong legacy justification include:

```text
MD5
SHA-1 signatures
DES
3DES
RC4
```

and obsolete TLS configurations.

---

# 118. Crypto Agility

Algorithms and key sizes change over time.

Applications should avoid hard-wiring assumptions such as:

```text
RSA forever
one exact certificate algorithm
one fixed key identifier
```

Architecture should permit controlled migration.

---

# 119. Key Versioning

Encrypted records may need metadata indicating which key/version protected them.

Conceptually:

```text
ciphertext
keyReference
algorithmVersion
```

This supports migration and rotation without guessing how historical data was encrypted.

---

# 120. Key Rotation vs Data Re-Encryption

Rotating a KMS key does not automatically mean every historical ciphertext must immediately be rewritten.

These are different operations:

```text
Key Rotation

vs

Data Re-encryption
```

Requirements determine whether historical data must be re-encrypted.

---

# 121. Key Deletion

Deleting a cryptographic key can permanently destroy access to encrypted data.

Therefore key deletion requires:

```text
Strong authorization
Waiting period
Impact analysis
Audit
Recovery verification
```

This is not a routine cleanup operation.

---

# 122. KMS Deletion Protection

Production controls should prevent accidental destructive key operations.

A command equivalent to:

```text
delete encryption key
```

must not be casually available to ordinary application operators.

---

# 123. Backup Key Dependency

A backup is useless if its decryption key is unavailable during disaster recovery.

DR planning must preserve:

```text
Backup
+
Required cryptographic keys
+
Required policies
+
Recovery identities
```

---

# 124. Cross-Region DR

If ADR-040/DR architecture requires another region:

```text
Primary Region
      │
      ▼
Encrypted Backup
      │
      ▼
DR Region
```

the DR environment must have an intentional key-access strategy.

Do not discover during an outage that the backup exists but cannot be decrypted.

---

# 125. Multi-Region KMS

AWS KMS multi-Region keys may be evaluated where:

```text
Cross-region cryptographic interoperability
DR
Application architecture
```

requires them.

They should not be enabled automatically for every key.

Regional isolation can itself be a useful security boundary.

---

# 126. Key Compromise Response

If a key is suspected compromised:

```text
Detect
  │
  ▼
Determine affected key
  │
  ▼
Identify protected assets
  │
  ▼
Disable / Restrict
  │
  ▼
Create replacement
  │
  ▼
Rotate dependents
  │
  ▼
Re-encrypt if required
  │
  ▼
Investigate
```

This procedure must exist before an incident occurs.

---

# 127. Secret Compromise Response

For a leaked API/database credential:

```text
Revoke
Rotate
Redeploy/refresh
Search usage logs
Determine blast radius
Verify attacker access
Fix leakage source
```

Merely deleting the secret from Git is not remediation.

---

# 128. Certificate Compromise

If a TLS/workload private key is compromised:

```text
Revoke / invalidate
Issue replacement
Deploy replacement
Update trust where necessary
Investigate impersonation
```

Short-lived automated certificates materially simplify this response.

---

# 129. JWT Signing-Key Compromise

This is severe.

An attacker possessing an active signing key may forge tokens.

Response may require:

```text
Stop use of compromised key
Generate replacement
Publish trusted replacement
Remove compromised trust
Invalidate affected sessions/tokens
Investigate forged-token activity
```

Token lifetime directly affects the response strategy.

---

# 130. Cryptographic Audit

Security-sensitive operations should be auditable.

Examples:

```text
Secret read
Secret update
KMS decrypt
Key policy change
Key disablement
Key deletion request
Certificate issuance
Privileged secret access
```

ADR-047 should ingest relevant security telemetry.

---

# 131. CloudTrail

AWS control-plane/API activity should be captured through appropriate CloudTrail architecture.

This can help answer:

```text
Who requested Decrypt?

Who changed this key policy?

Who retrieved this secret?

Who scheduled key deletion?
```

subject to service-specific logging behavior.

---

# 132. High-Volume Decrypt Telemetry

Do not create a paging alert for every normal KMS decrypt operation.

Instead detect anomalies such as:

```text
Unexpected principal
Unexpected region
Sudden volume spike
Access outside expected workload
Repeated denied decrypt attempts
```

Security telemetry needs signal, not noise.

---

# 133. Secret Inventory

Mediverse should maintain ownership metadata for secrets.

Every important secret should have:

```text
Owner
Purpose
Environment
Consumer
Rotation strategy
Expiration if applicable
```

Unknown secrets become permanent liabilities.

---

# 134. Key Inventory

Likewise every KMS/signing key should have:

```text
Owner
Purpose
Data classification
Consumers
Rotation policy
Deletion policy
DR requirement
```

A key nobody understands cannot be safely rotated or deleted.

---

# 135. Developer Workflow

Developers need a usable local secret workflow.

Bad security that developers cannot practically use leads to:

```text
.env files shared in chat
Secrets pasted into tickets
Passwords committed temporarily
Production credentials reused locally
```

Local development should use non-production credentials and documented retrieval/bootstrap mechanisms.

---

# 136. Local Environment Isolation

Developers should not need production secrets to run Mediverse locally.

Preferred:

```text
Local PostgreSQL
Local Redis
Local Kafka
Sandbox external accounts
Mock services
DEV secrets
```

Production credentials should remain inaccessible unless a specific operational role requires them.

---

# 137. `.env`

Local `.env` files may be convenient for development but:

```text
.env
```

must be excluded from source control when containing secrets.

Provide:

```text
.env.example
```

containing variable names and safe placeholders instead.

---

# 138. CI Secret Scanning

Pipeline controls should detect secrets before deployment.

Conceptually:

```text
Commit
  │
  ▼
Secret Scan
  │
 ┌┴──────────┐
 ▼           ▼
Clean      Secret Found
 │           │
 ▼           X
Continue    Block / Investigate
```

Pre-commit scanning can provide an additional earlier layer.

---

# 139. Container Image Scanning

Secret scanning should also inspect relevant build artifacts/images where practical.

A credential copied into an image during an intermediate build can remain exposed even if the final application configuration looks clean.

---

# 140. Build Arguments

Do not assume Docker build arguments are a safe secret store.

Bad:

```text
docker build --build-arg PASSWORD=...
```

Secrets can leak through:

```text
Build history
Layers
Logs
Caching
```

Use secure build-secret mechanisms when a build genuinely requires temporary secret access.

---

# 141. Kubernetes RBAC

Access to Kubernetes Secret resources must be tightly controlled.

A principal able to:

```text
get secrets
list secrets
```

across production namespaces may effectively possess credentials for many workloads.

This is a highly privileged permission.

---

# 142. Namespace Isolation

Secrets should normally follow workload/environment boundaries.

```text
prod/course-service
prod/assessment-service
uat/course-service
```

Broad cross-namespace secret access should require explicit justification.

---

# 143. Threat Model

Primary threats include:

```text
Secret committed to Git
Developer laptop compromise
CI/CD credential theft
Compromised Pod
Overprivileged IAM
Kubernetes Secret exposure
KMS policy misconfiguration
Private-key theft
Expired certificates
Signing-key compromise
Backup/key mismatch
Insider misuse
```

ADR-049 controls must reduce both probability and blast radius.

---

# 144. Post-Quantum Readiness

Mediverse does not need to prematurely replace established cryptography with experimental algorithms.

But long-lived architecture should support crypto agility.

```text
Today's Algorithm
       │
       ▼
Future Migration
       │
       ▼
New Approved Algorithm
```

Protocol/library abstraction and key versioning matter more today than speculative custom post-quantum implementations.

---

# 145. Cryptographic Anti-Patterns

Mediverse shall reject:

```text
❌ Plaintext production secrets in Git
❌ Secrets baked into container images
❌ Base64 treated as encryption
❌ Shared production credentials across services
❌ Static AWS access keys in Pods
❌ Production credentials on developer laptops by default
❌ React applications containing client secrets
❌ Root DB credentials used by applications
❌ Secrets fetched remotely on every HTTP request
❌ Manual secret rotation as the standard model
❌ Permanent secrets without ownership
❌ One KMS key for everything without threat analysis
❌ One KMS key per tiny resource without justification
❌ Private signing keys distributed to verifiers
❌ TLS private keys committed to Git
❌ Multi-year static workload certificates
❌ Manual certificate renewal
❌ Missing certificate-expiry monitoring
❌ Custom cryptographic algorithms
❌ Plain SHA-256 password storage
❌ Password encryption instead of password hashing
❌ Hard-coded IVs/nonces
❌ Weak/deprecated cryptography
❌ Uncontrolled KMS key deletion
❌ Backups without recoverable keys
❌ DR architecture without key-access testing
❌ Secret leakage considered fixed merely by deleting the source line
❌ Unrestricted Kubernetes `get secrets`
❌ CI/CD using permanent administrator cloud credentials
```

---

# 146. Secret Lifecycle Architecture

```text
                    SECRET CREATED
                          │
                          ▼
                    Secret Manager
                          │
                          ▼
                  Access Policy / IAM
                          │
                          ▼
                    Workload Identity
                          │
                          ▼
                       Workload
                          │
                          ▼
                       Usage
                          │
                          ▼
                      Rotation
                          │
                          ▼
                     Revocation
                          │
                          ▼
                      Deletion
```

Every transition should be controlled and, where security-relevant, auditable.

---

# 147. Cryptographic Trust Hierarchy

```text
                       TRUST ROOTS
                           │
            ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
            ▼              ▼              ▼
          KMS            Root CA       IdP Signing
           │               │              Keys
           ▼               ▼               │
      Data Keys      Intermediate CA       ▼
           │               │              JWT
           ▼               ▼               │
     Encrypted Data   Certificates          ▼
                           │             Services
                           ▼
                     Workload Identity
```

The hierarchy makes trust dependencies explicit.

---

# 148. Final Mediverse Cryptographic Architecture

```text
                           MEDIVERSE
                               │
           ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐
           ▼                   ▼                   ▼
        Humans             Workloads             CI/CD
           │                   │                   │
           ▼                   ▼                   ▼
       OIDC/MFA          ServiceAccount       Federation
           │                   │                   │
           └───────────────────┼───────────────────┘
                               ▼
                        IDENTITY / IAM
                               │
              ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
              ▼                ▼                ▼
      Secrets Manager         KMS             PKI
              │                │                │
              ▼                ▼                ▼
        Credentials       Key Hierarchy    Certificates
              │                │                │
              │                ▼                │
              │         Envelope Encryption     │
              │                │                │
              └────────────────┼────────────────┘
                               ▼
                         APPLICATIONS
                               │
       ┌───────────────┬───────┼────────┬───────────────┐
       ▼               ▼       ▼        ▼               ▼
   PostgreSQL         Redis    Kafka  OpenSearch         S3
       │               │       │        │               │
       └───────────────┴───────┼────────┴───────────────┘
                               ▼
                      ENCRYPTED STORAGE

                 NETWORK TRUST ARCHITECTURE

Browser ──TLS──► Edge ──TLS──► Gateway
                                │
                                ▼
                           Microservice
                                │
                           mTLS / TLS
               ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
               ▼                ▼                ▼
           Services         Databases          Kafka


                  CERTIFICATE ARCHITECTURE

                       Root CA
                          │
                          ▼
                    Intermediate CA
                          │
                          ▼
                Automated Certificate
                     Issuance
                          │
                          ▼
                    Workload Identity
                          │
                          ▼
                         mTLS


                   OBSERVABILITY / AUDIT

Secrets Manager ─┐
KMS ──────────────┤
PKI ──────────────┼──► Security Telemetry
IAM ──────────────┤          │
Kubernetes ───────┘          ▼
                       ADR-047 Platform
```

---

# 149. Core Cryptographic Invariants

These must remain true regardless of future implementation changes:

```text
1. Production secrets never exist as plaintext in source control.

2. Workloads authenticate using identity rather than embedded
   long-lived cloud credentials wherever possible.

3. Every workload receives only required secret/key permissions.

4. Cryptographic private keys are accessible only to components
   requiring private-key operations.

5. Encryption keys and signing keys are separate by purpose.

6. Sensitive persistent data is encrypted at rest.

7. Sensitive communication is protected in transit.

8. Base64 is never considered encryption.

9. Passwords are hashed using dedicated password-hashing algorithms.

10. Key, secret and certificate rotation is automatable.

11. Certificate renewal does not depend on human memory.

12. Compromised credentials can be rapidly revoked and replaced.

13. Backups cannot outlive access to required recovery keys.

14. Key deletion is treated as a destructive privileged operation.

15. Cryptographic operations and administrative changes are auditable.

16. Production secrets are isolated from non-production environments.

17. Applications do not implement custom cryptographic algorithms.

18. Cryptographic architecture remains agile enough for future
    algorithm migration.
```

---

# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                                | Decision                                          |
| ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| Production secret source            | **AWS Secrets Manager** where appropriate         |
| Cryptographic key management        | **AWS KMS**                                       |
| Public AWS certificates             | **AWS ACM**                                       |
| Kubernetes secret synchronization   | External Secrets pattern                          |
| Plaintext Git secrets               | **Prohibited**                                    |
| Base64 as security                  | **Rejected**                                      |
| Workload authentication             | ServiceAccount + workload identity                |
| Static AWS keys in Pods             | **Prohibited**                                    |
| Secret access                       | Least privilege                                   |
| Environment isolation               | Mandatory                                         |
| Secret injection                    | File/env/runtime based on requirement             |
| Per-request secret retrieval        | Avoid                                             |
| Secret rotation                     | Automated                                         |
| Emergency rotation                  | Mandatory capability                              |
| Database credentials                | Per-service, least privilege                      |
| Root DB credentials in applications | Prohibited                                        |
| CI/CD cloud credentials             | Short-lived federation preferred                  |
| GitOps encrypted secrets            | SOPS/alternative where justified                  |
| Storage encryption                  | Mandatory for sensitive production storage        |
| S3                                  | SSE-KMS where KMS control is required             |
| Envelope encryption                 | Standard model for application encryption         |
| Field encryption                    | Selective, classification-driven                  |
| TLS                                 | Modern TLS required                               |
| Public TLS                          | Automated managed certificates                    |
| Internal PKI                        | Automated hierarchy                               |
| Kubernetes certificate automation   | cert-manager where appropriate                    |
| Workload certificates               | Short-lived + automatically rotated               |
| SPIFFE/SPIRE                        | Evaluate based on mesh/workload identity needs    |
| JWT signing keys                    | Private signing custody + JWKS verification       |
| Signing-key rotation                | Overlapping controlled rotation                   |
| HSM                                 | KMS-backed defaults; CloudHSM only when justified |
| Password storage                    | Dedicated password hashing                        |
| Secure randomness                   | Cryptographically secure RNG                      |
| Custom cryptography                 | Prohibited                                        |
| Algorithm governance                | Central baseline                                  |
| Crypto agility                      | Required                                          |
| Backup encryption                   | Required                                          |
| DR key availability                 | Must be tested                                    |
| Key deletion                        | Restricted + audited                              |
| Secret/key inventory                | Required                                          |
| Security audit                      | Integrated with ADR-047                           |
| Secret scanning                     | CI/CD + repository controls                       |
| Status                              | **Accepted**                                      |
| Priority                            | **Critical**                                      |

---

---

# ADR-050 — Enterprise Kubernetes Platform, EKS, Multi-Environment, Namespace, Autoscaling, Scheduling & Cluster Governance Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Karpenter**.

---

# 61. Karpenter vs Cluster Autoscaler Decision

Both solve node-capacity scaling, but differently.

```text
Cluster Autoscaler
      │
      ▼
Existing Node Groups
      │
      ▼
Scale Group Capacity
```

Karpenter is more workload-driven:

```text
Pending Pods
     │
     ▼
Scheduling Requirements
     │
     ▼
Karpenter
     │
     ▼
Select EC2 Capacity
     │
     ▼
Launch Node
```

For Mediverse, **Karpenter is the preferred strategic node autoscaler**, subject to production validation.

---

# 62. Why Karpenter?

Mediverse has heterogeneous workloads:

```text
Spring Boot APIs
Kafka consumers
Media workers
AI workloads
Batch jobs
Platform services
```

Karpenter can provision capacity matching actual Pod requirements rather than forcing every workload through a small fixed set of node groups.

---

# 63. Do Not Remove All Stable Capacity

Dynamic provisioning does not mean:

```text
Cluster starts with zero reliable nodes
```

Critical platform components need dependable baseline capacity.

Preferred:

```text
Stable System Capacity
        +
Dynamic Application Capacity
```

---

# 64. Spot Instances

Spot capacity can substantially reduce compute cost.

Suitable candidates include:

```text
Stateless workers
Fault-tolerant consumers
Batch jobs
Media processing
Horizontally scalable services
```

provided interruption is handled correctly.

---

# 65. Spot Is Interruptible

Spot instances can disappear.

Therefore:

```text
Cheap
≠
Reliable
```

A workload using Spot must tolerate node termination.

---

# 66. Critical Workload Strategy

Do not place all replicas of a critical API exclusively on one Spot capacity type.

Preferred:

```text
Critical Service
     │
     ├── On-Demand baseline
     └── Spot burst capacity
```

where economics justify it.

---

# 67. Capacity Diversification

Spot reliability improves when capacity requirements are flexible across:

```text
Instance families
Instance sizes
Availability Zones
```

Over-constraining:

```text
exact-instance-type = X
exact-AZ = Y
```

reduces Karpenter's options.

---

# 68. Interruption Handling

Node interruption should trigger:

```text
Interruption Notice
      │
      ▼
Cordon / Drain
      │
      ▼
Pods rescheduled
      │
      ▼
Replacement capacity
```

Applications must already support graceful termination.

---

# 69. Consolidation

Karpenter can potentially consolidate inefficient nodes.

```text
Node A → 20% utilized
Node B → 25% utilized
Node C → 15% utilized
```

may become:

```text
Fewer better-utilized nodes
```

when scheduling constraints permit.

---

# 70. Consolidation Safety

Aggressive consolidation can create unnecessary Pod churn.

Critical workloads require:

```text
PDB
Graceful shutdown
Topology controls
Correct readiness
```

before aggressive optimization.

Cost optimization must not destroy reliability.

---

# 71. Persistent Storage

Kubernetes Pods are ephemeral.

Persistent data therefore requires separate storage.

Primary AWS options:

```text
EBS
EFS
S3
Managed databases
```

These solve different problems.

---

# 72. EBS

EBS provides block storage.

Typical:

```text
Pod
 │
 ▼
PersistentVolumeClaim
 │
 ▼
EBS CSI
 │
 ▼
EBS Volume
```

Suitable for workloads requiring persistent block devices.

---

# 73. EBS Availability-Zone Constraint

An EBS volume exists in an Availability Zone.

Therefore:

```text
EBS Volume in AZ-A
       │
       ▼
Pod must attach appropriately in AZ-A
```

This matters during scheduling and failure recovery.

---

# 74. EFS

EFS provides shared network filesystem capabilities.

```text
Pod A ─┐
Pod B ─┼──► EFS
Pod C ─┘
```

Useful where multiple Pods genuinely need shared POSIX filesystem access.

Do not use EFS simply because persistent storage is required.

---

# 75. S3 Is Not a Filesystem Replacement

ADR-046 established S3 for object storage.

Use:

```text
S3
```
