Low-value history should be summarized or discarded.

---

# 111. AI Caching

Deterministic or sufficiently reusable AI results may be cached where semantics permit.

```text
Request
 │
 ▼
Cache
 │
 ├── Hit → Return
 └── Miss → Model
```

Caching user-specific or sensitive output requires careful isolation.

---

# 112. Semantic Caching

Semantically similar queries may reuse previous answers.

This can reduce:

```text
Cost
Latency
Provider traffic
```

but introduces risks of:

```text
Incorrect equivalence
Stale answers
Authorization leakage
Personalization mismatch
```

Use selectively.

---

# 113. Rate Limiting

AI endpoints require explicit rate controls.

```text
User
 │
 ▼
Rate Limit
 │
 ▼
AI Gateway
```

This protects capacity and cost.

---

# 114. Quotas

Quota dimensions may include:

```text
User
Tenant
Feature
Model
Token count
Time period
```

A flat request count may be inadequate because AI requests can vary dramatically in cost.

---

# 115. Cost Attribution

Every model invocation should be attributable where practical.

```text
Request
 │
 ├── Application
 ├── Feature
 ├── Tenant/User category
 ├── Model
 ├── Tokens
 └── Estimated Cost
```

Without attribution, AI spending becomes difficult to govern.

---

# 116. AI Cost Optimization

Optimize in this order:

```text
Do we need AI?
       │
       ▼
Do we need this much context?
       │
       ▼
Do we need this model?
       │
       ▼
Can result be cached?
       │
       ▼
Can work be asynchronous/batched?
```

Do not start by degrading answer quality blindly.

---

# 117. Latency

AI latency includes more than inference.

```text
Request
 │
 ▼
Authorization
 │
 ▼
Retrieval
 │
 ▼
Reranking
 │
 ▼
Model Queue
 │
 ▼
Inference
 │
 ▼
Validation
```

End-to-end latency should be measured.

---

# 118. Streaming Responses

For long generation:

```text
Model
 │
 ▼
Token Stream
 │
 ▼
Client
```

can improve perceived responsiveness.

Streaming does not reduce total inference time.

---

# 119. Asynchronous AI Jobs

Long-running workloads such as:

```text
Large document summarization
Question-bank generation
Bulk embeddings
Transcription
Content processing
```

should often run asynchronously.

```text
API
 │
 ▼
Job Queue
 │
 ▼
Worker
 │
 ▼
AI
 │
 ▼
Result Store
```

---

# 120. AI Retries

Model calls may fail transiently.

Retry only appropriate failures using:

```text
Bounded attempts
Exponential backoff
Jitter
Timeouts
```

Do not retry every 4xx or policy rejection.

---

# 121. AI Fallback

Fallback may operate across:

```text
Model
Region
Provider
Capability mode
```

Example:

```text
Premium Model unavailable
        │
        ▼
Approved Secondary Model
```

Only if secondary behavior remains acceptable.

---

# 122. AI Circuit Breaker

Repeated provider failure should trigger protective behavior.

```text
Calls
 │
 ▼
Failures
 │
 ▼
Circuit Open
 │
 ▼
Fallback / Degraded Experience
```

This prevents retry storms.

---

# 123. AI Observability

Monitor:

```text
Request volume
Model latency
Time to first token
Total latency
Input tokens
Output tokens
Cost
Error rate
Rate-limit events
Fallback rate
Retrieval latency
Tool failures
Safety interventions
```

---

# 124. AI Tracing

A single AI interaction may span:

```text
API
 │
 ▼
Retriever
 │
 ▼
Vector Store
 │
 ▼
Reranker
 │
 ▼
LLM
 │
 ▼
Tool
 │
 ▼
LLM
```

Distributed tracing should expose these stages without logging sensitive raw content indiscriminately.

---

# 125. RAG Telemetry

Record metrics such as:

```text
Chunks retrieved
Retrieval scores
Reranking scores
Context size
Source IDs
Citation count
Retrieval latency
```

This helps diagnose whether failures originate from retrieval or generation.

---

# 126. AI SLOs

AI capabilities require explicit objectives.

Example:

```text
Tutor availability ≥ target
p95 first-token latency ≤ target
p95 completion latency ≤ target
Grounded-answer score ≥ target
Unsafe-response rate ≤ target
```

AI SLOs may include quality as well as infrastructure reliability.

---

# 127. Model Registry

Models used by Mediverse should be cataloged.

```text
Model
 │
 ├── Provider
 ├── Version
 ├── Purpose
 ├── Owner
 ├── Evaluation
 ├── Risk classification
 └── Approval status
```

Unknown models should not quietly appear in production.

---

# 128. Model Lifecycle

```text
Evaluate
   │
   ▼
Approve
   │
   ▼
Deploy
   │
   ▼
Observe
   │
   ▼
Re-evaluate
   │
   ▼
Deprecate
```

Model lifecycle is continuous because model/provider behavior changes.

---

# 129. Fine-Tuning Decision

Fine-tuning should not be the first response to poor AI quality.

Evaluate first:

```text
Prompt improvement
Retrieval improvement
Better context
Better model
Tool use
```

Fine-tune only when evidence indicates it solves the actual problem.

---

# 130. Fine-Tuning Use Cases

Fine-tuning may be useful for:

```text
Stable output behavior
Specialized style
Classification
Domain-specific patterns
Repeated structured tasks
```

It is generally not the preferred mechanism for injecting frequently changing factual knowledge.

RAG is usually more appropriate for that.

---

# 131. Training Data Governance

Fine-tuning/training datasets require:

```text
Provenance
Usage rights
Quality
Classification
PII review
Retention
Versioning
Approval
```

"You found the dataset online" is not sufficient governance.

---

# 132. Traditional ML Boundary

Not every AI capability requires an LLM.

Examples:

```text
Risk prediction
Recommendation ranking
Dropout prediction
Difficulty estimation
Classification
```

may be better served by conventional ML.

---

# 133. MLOps

Traditional/self-hosted ML requires lifecycle management:

```text
Data
 │
 ▼
Training
 │
 ▼
Evaluation
 │
 ▼
Model Registry
 │
 ▼
Deployment
 │
 ▼
Monitoring
 │
 ▼
Retraining
```

---

# 134. Feature Store

A feature store should only be introduced when Mediverse operates enough reusable ML features to justify it.

```text
User mastery score
Course engagement
Assessment history
```

may eventually become shared features.

Premature feature-store infrastructure is rejected.

---

# 135. Online vs Batch Inference

Online:

```text
Request
 │
 ▼
Model
 │
 ▼
Immediate prediction
```

Batch:

```text
Dataset
 │
 ▼
Model
 │
 ▼
Bulk predictions
```

Use batch processing where immediate inference is unnecessary.

---

# 136. GPU Infrastructure

Self-hosted generative models may require GPU infrastructure.

Potential architecture:

```text
Kubernetes
    │
    ▼
GPU Node Pool
    │
    ▼
Inference Runtime
    │
    ▼
Model
```

GPU capacity must not be introduced merely for architectural prestige.

---

# 137. Inference Autoscaling

Self-hosted inference scaling should consider:

```text
Request concurrency
Queue depth
Tokens/sec
GPU utilization
Model memory
Startup/model-loading time
```

CPU-based HPA alone may be meaningless for GPU inference.

---

# 138. Model Loading

Large models may require significant startup time.

```text
Pod starts
   │
   ▼
Load model
   │
   ▼
Allocate GPU memory
   │
   ▼
Warm up
   │
   ▼
Ready
```

Autoscaling design must account for this delay.

---

# 139. Model Rollout

Model changes should use progressive validation.

```text
Current Model
      │
      ├──────────────┐
      ▼              ▼
Most Traffic     Candidate
                     │
                     ▼
                 Evaluation
```

---

# 140. Shadow Evaluation

A candidate model can receive copied production requests without serving its responses.

```text
Request
   │
   ├──► Production Model → User
   │
   └──► Candidate Model → Evaluation only
```

This enables realistic comparison with reduced user risk.

---

# 141. AI Canary

After offline/shadow validation:

```text
1%
 │
 ▼
5%
 │
 ▼
25%
 │
 ▼
100%
```

traffic may progressively move to the candidate when metrics remain acceptable.

---

# 142. Educational & Medical Content Governance

Mediverse's educational domain requires stricter treatment of medically relevant generated content.

AI-generated educational explanations should distinguish:

```text
Educational information
        vs
Authoritative clinical guidance
```

The platform must not imply that probabilistic generation is equivalent to verified medical instruction or patient-specific clinical advice.

---

# 143. Human-in-the-Loop

High-impact generated content may require expert approval.

```text
AI Generates
    │
    ▼
Draft
    │
    ▼
Expert Review
    │
    ├── Approve
    ├── Edit
    └── Reject
```

Human review should occur before publication when risk warrants it.

---

# 144. AI Incident Response

AI incidents may include:

```text
Unsafe output
Cross-user data leakage
Prompt injection
Tool misuse
Cost runaway
Model degradation
Incorrect educational content
Provider outage
Retrieval corruption
```

Incident procedures should capture AI-specific evidence.

---

# 145. AI Supply-Chain Security

AI dependencies include:

```text
Models
Model providers
Embedding models
Python packages
Inference containers
Datasets
Prompt libraries
Agent tools
Vector infrastructure
```

All require provenance and security governance appropriate to their risk.

---

# 146. AI Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ LLM for every problem
❌ Direct provider SDK calls scattered across services
❌ Largest model for every request
❌ Provider lock-in without deliberate decision
❌ Prompts edited manually in production
❌ Secrets inside prompts
❌ Treating retrieved documents as trusted instructions
❌ Using the model as an authorization engine
❌ Retrieving unauthorized data then asking the model not to reveal it
❌ Assuming RAG eliminates hallucination
❌ Vector database introduced without workload justification
❌ Arbitrary chunk size copied from tutorials
❌ Embeddings without source/version metadata
❌ Stale indexes after source changes
❌ AI evaluation based on a few demo prompts
❌ LLM-as-judge treated as objective truth
❌ Agent with unrestricted tools
❌ Agent running as platform administrator
❌ Arbitrary SQL/shell exposed as general-purpose agent tools
❌ Irreversible actions without approval
❌ Unlimited agent loops
❌ Unlimited token budgets
❌ Persisting every conversation as long-term memory
❌ Cross-user memory/context leakage
❌ Blind trust in tool output
❌ Raw AI output directly causing privileged side effects
❌ Sending unnecessary PII to model providers
❌ No provider privacy/residency review
❌ No AI cost attribution
❌ Retrying policy failures
❌ No fallback/degradation strategy
❌ Logging every raw prompt containing sensitive information
❌ Fine-tuning before diagnosing retrieval/prompt problems
❌ Training on datasets without provenance
❌ GPU clusters before workload justification
❌ Model rollout directly from 0% to 100%
❌ AI-generated medical educational content treated as automatically authoritative
```

---

# 147. AI Ownership Model

```text
Application Teams
      │
      ├── AI feature behavior
      ├── Business integration
      ├── Feature evaluation
      └── User experience

AI Platform Team
      │
      ├── AI Gateway
      ├── Model integrations
      ├── Prompt infrastructure
      ├── RAG platform
      ├── Evaluation platform
      ├── Model registry
      └── AI observability

Data Platform Team
      │
      ├── Knowledge pipelines
      ├── Data quality
      ├── Vector/index lifecycle
      └── Training datasets

Security Team
      │
      ├── Threat model
      ├── Prompt-injection testing
      ├── Tool security
      ├── Privacy
      └── AI red teaming

Domain Experts
      │
      ├── Educational correctness
      ├── Golden datasets
      ├── Content review
      └── High-risk approvals

SRE / Platform
      │
      ├── Reliability
      ├── Capacity
      ├── GPU infrastructure
      └── Incident response
```

---

# 148. Final Mediverse Enterprise AI Platform Architecture

```text
                              USERS
                                │
                                ▼
                         MEDIVERSE APIs
                                │
                                ▼
                      AI ORCHESTRATION LAYER
                                │
          ┌─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┐
          ▼                     ▼                     ▼
       POLICY                 RAG                  AGENTS
          │                     │                     │
          │              AUTHORIZED RETRIEVAL         │
          │                     │                     │
          │        ┌────────────┼────────────┐        │
          │        ▼            ▼            ▼        │
          │     Lexical       Vector      Metadata    │
          │        │            │          Filters    │
          │        └────────────┼────────────┘        │
          │                     ▼                     │
          │                  Reranker                 │
          │                     │                     │
          │                     ▼                     │
          │               Context Builder             │
          │                     │                     │
          └──────────────┬──────┴──────────────┬─────┘
                         ▼                     ▼
                    AI GATEWAY            TOOL GATEWAY
                         │                     │
             ┌───────────┼───────────┐         ▼
             ▼           ▼           ▼    Authorization
         Primary      Secondary   Self-hosted      │
          Model         Model       Model          ▼
             │           │           │       Business Tools
             └───────────┼───────────┘
                         ▼
                  OUTPUT VALIDATION
                         │
             ┌───────────┼────────────┐
             ▼           ▼            ▼
          Schema       Safety      Grounding
             │           │            │
             └───────────┼────────────┘
                         ▼
                      RESPONSE


                 KNOWLEDGE / DATA PLANE

 Approved Content ─► Parse ─► Chunk ─► Metadata
                                      │
                                      ▼
                                  Embeddings
                                      │
                           ┌──────────┴─────────┐
                           ▼                    ▼
                       pgvector            OpenSearch


                    GOVERNANCE PLANE

       ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
       │ Prompt Registry                             │
       │ Model Registry                              │
       │ Golden Evaluation Datasets                  │
       │ Offline Evaluation                          │
       │ Human Evaluation                            │
       │ AI Red Teaming                              │
       │ Privacy / Data Residency                    │
       │ Cost Governance                             │
       │ Audit                                       │
       │ Model / Prompt / Retrieval Traceability     │
       └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘


                    OPERATIONS PLANE

       ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
       │ AI Metrics / Tracing                        │
       │ Token / Cost Monitoring                     │
       │ Retrieval Telemetry                         │
       │ Quality Metrics                             │
       │ SLOs                                        │
       │ Rate Limits / Quotas                        │
       │ Circuit Breakers                            │
       │ Fallback                                    │
       │ Shadow / Canary Rollout                     │
       │ Incident Response                           │
       └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

# 149. Core AI Invariants

Regardless of future providers, models or frameworks:

```text
1. AI never becomes the authorization boundary.

2. Deterministic rules remain deterministic where correctness demands it.

3. AI capabilities are isolated behind governed platform interfaces.

4. Models, prompts, retrieval configuration and datasets are versioned.

5. Prompt changes are production changes.

6. Retrieved content is untrusted input.

7. Authorization occurs before knowledge reaches the model.

8. RAG does not guarantee factuality.

9. Retrieval quality and generation quality are evaluated independently.

10. AI quality is measured against representative evaluation datasets.

11. LLM judges are evidence, not ground truth.

12. High-risk outputs receive appropriate human oversight.

13. Agent tools are narrow, typed and independently authorized.

14. Agents operate with delegated least privilege.

15. Irreversible actions require stronger controls.

16. Agent execution is bounded by steps, time, tokens and cost.

17. AI memory is minimized, scoped and governed.

18. Model-generated tool arguments are untrusted input.

19. Sensitive data is minimized before model invocation.

20. Provider privacy and residency are architecture concerns.

21. AI usage has explicit rate, token and cost budgets.

22. AI telemetry measures retrieval, inference, tools, quality and cost.

23. Models undergo evaluation before production rollout.

24. Model changes use progressive delivery.

25. Fine-tuning is introduced only when evidence justifies it.

26. Training data has provenance and governance.

27. Self-hosted GPU infrastructure requires demonstrated need.

28. Educational/medical AI content is not automatically authoritative.

29. AI incidents are observable, auditable and recoverable.

30. Humans remain accountable for the system's behavior.
```

---

# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                                  | Decision                                              |
| ------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| AI architecture                       | **Central governed AI platform**                      |
| AI vs deterministic logic             | Requirement-driven                                    |
| Direct provider calls across services | Rejected                                              |
| Provider abstraction                  | AI Gateway                                            |
| Multi-model strategy                  | Supported                                             |
| Model routing                         | Capability/cost/quality aware                         |
| Model fallback                        | Controlled                                            |
| Prompt management                     | Version-controlled                                    |
| Prompt registry                       | Required at scale                                     |
| Structured output                     | Preferred for machine consumption                     |
| Output validation                     | Mandatory before side effects                         |
| RAG                                   | Strategic knowledge-grounding pattern                 |
| RAG authorization                     | Before retrieval                                      |
| Retrieval                             | Hybrid where justified                                |
| Vector platform                       | pgvector/OpenSearch evaluation                        |
| Vector DB proliferation               | Rejected without justification                        |
| Reranking                             | Selective                                             |
| Knowledge versioning                  | Required                                              |
| Citation support                      | Required for appropriate grounded educational answers |
| RAG evaluation                        | Retrieval + generation                                |
| Golden datasets                       | Required                                              |
| Human evaluation                      | Required for high-risk/domain-critical use cases      |
| LLM-as-judge                          | Supporting signal only                                |
| AI red teaming                        | Required risk-based capability                        |
| Prompt injection                      | Architectural defense                                 |
| Agent architecture                    | Bounded agents                                        |
| Deterministic workflow                | Preferred when workflow is known                      |
| Agent tool permissions                | Least privilege                                       |
| Tool authorization                    | Independent of model                                  |
| Human approval                        | High-impact/irreversible actions                      |
| Agent execution limits                | Mandatory                                             |
| AI memory                             | Purpose-limited                                       |
| Cross-user memory                     | Prohibited                                            |
| PII minimization                      | Mandatory                                             |
| Provider privacy review               | Mandatory                                             |
| Data residency                        | Classification-driven                                 |
| AI audit trail                        | Required for high-value interactions                  |
| Token budgets                         | Required                                              |
| Rate limits / quotas                  | Required                                              |
| Cost attribution                      | Required                                              |
| Streaming                             | User-experience optimization                          |
| Long AI workloads                     | Async jobs                                            |
| Retries                               | Bounded + backoff                                     |
| Circuit breaker                       | Required where dependency criticality warrants        |
| AI observability                      | Required                                              |
| AI SLOs                               | Reliability + quality                                 |
| Model registry                        | Required                                              |
| Fine-tuning                           | Evidence-driven                                       |
| Training-data governance              | Mandatory                                             |
| Traditional ML                        | Preferred when problem fits                           |
| Feature store                         | Only when justified                                   |
| GPU platform                          | Only when self-hosting justified                      |
| Model autoscaling                     | AI-specific signals                                   |
| Model rollout                         | Shadow/canary/progressive                             |
| Medical educational content           | Governed + human oversight where risk requires        |
| Status                                | **Accepted**                                          |
| Priority                              | **Critical**                                          |

---

# ADR-056 — Enterprise Identity, Authentication, Authorization, IAM, Zero Trust & Digital Identity Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Defense in Depth**.

---

# 61. Authorization Architecture

Authentication produces an identity.

Authorization determines whether that identity can perform a particular action.

```text
Principal
   │
   ▼
Action + Resource + Context
   │
   ▼
Authorization Decision
   │
   ├── ALLOW
   └── DENY
```

Authorization must default to **deny** when no explicit permission exists.

---

# 62. Authorization Decision Model

Every meaningful decision should conceptually answer:

```text
WHO
 │
 ▼
wants to perform WHAT
 │
 ▼
on WHICH RESOURCE
 │
 ▼
under WHICH CONTEXT?
```

Example:

```text
Student 123
   │
   ▼
READ
   │
   ▼
Assessment Result 987
   │
   ▼
owns result?
course relationship?
tenant matches?
```

---

# 63. RBAC

Role-Based Access Control maps permissions through roles.

```text
User
 │
 ▼
Role
 │
 ▼
Permissions
 │
 ▼
Resources
```

Example:

```text
STUDENT
INSTRUCTOR
COURSE_ADMIN
PLATFORM_ADMIN
```

RBAC should remain understandable enough that engineers can reason about permissions.

---

# 64. Permissions

Roles should map to explicit capabilities.

```text
COURSE_VIEW
COURSE_EDIT
ASSESSMENT_CREATE
ASSESSMENT_SUBMIT
RESULT_VIEW
USER_ADMIN
```

Avoid authorization logic based entirely on vague role names.

---

# 65. Role Explosion

This architecture is dangerous:

```text
STUDENT
PREMIUM_STUDENT
PREMIUM_STUDENT_INDIA
PREMIUM_STUDENT_INDIA_CARDIOLOGY
PREMIUM_STUDENT_INDIA_CARDIOLOGY_ADMIN
...
```

When roles encode every contextual combination, RBAC becomes unmanageable.

Use attributes or relationships for contextual decisions.

---

# 66. Role Hierarchy

Limited hierarchy may be useful:

```text
PLATFORM_ADMIN
      │
      ▼
COURSE_ADMIN
      │
      ▼
INSTRUCTOR
```

But inheritance must be explicit.

Do not assume senior organizational roles automatically require every lower-level application permission.

---

# 67. ABAC

Attribute-Based Access Control evaluates attributes.

```text
Subject Attributes
        +
Resource Attributes
        +
Environment
        +
Action
        │
        ▼
Policy
        │
        ▼
ALLOW / DENY
```

Example:

```text
subject.tenant == resource.tenant
AND
subject.department == resource.department
```

---

# 68. Resource Ownership

Many Mediverse authorization decisions require ownership.

```text
Student
   │
   ▼
Assessment Attempt
   │
   ▼
attempt.studentId == authenticatedUser.id
```

Possessing the attempt ID is not sufficient authorization.

---

# 69. ReBAC

Relationship-Based Access Control evaluates relationships.

```text
User
 │
 ├── enrolled-in ──► Course
 │
 └── instructor-of ► Course
```

ReBAC should be evaluated if Mediverse authorization becomes relationship-heavy.

Do not introduce a dedicated graph authorization system prematurely.

---

# 70. Hybrid Authorization

Mediverse will likely require combinations of:

```text
RBAC
 +
ABAC
 +
Ownership
 +
Relationships
```

Example:

```text
ALLOW assessment:view
IF

role == INSTRUCTOR
AND
instructor teaches assessment.course
AND
tenant matches
```

---

# 71. Policy Decision Point

A Policy Decision Point evaluates authorization policy.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
PDP
    │
    ├── ALLOW
    └── DENY
```

The PDP may be embedded or external depending on architecture.

---

# 72. Policy Enforcement Point

A Policy Enforcement Point prevents unauthorized execution.

```text
Request
   │
   ▼
PEP
   │
   ▼
PDP Decision
   │
   ├── ALLOW → Resource
   └── DENY  → Reject
```

An authorization decision that is not enforced is worthless.

---

# 73. Centralized vs Distributed Authorization

Fully centralized authorization can provide:

```text
Consistency
Central governance
Policy visibility
```

but introduces:

```text
Latency
Availability dependency
Complex resource context
```

Fully distributed authorization provides autonomy but risks inconsistent policy.

Mediverse should use a hybrid architecture.

---

# 74. Domain Authorization Ownership

Domain services should own authorization requiring domain knowledge.

Example:

```text
Assessment Service
       │
       ▼
"May instructor X modify assessment Y?"
```

The gateway cannot know every domain relationship reliably.

---

# 75. Policy Engine

A policy engine may be introduced where authorization complexity warrants it.

Candidates may include architectures based on:

```text
OPA/Rego
Cedar-style policies
Custom domain policy libraries
```

Selection should follow actual authorization requirements.

---

# 76. Policy as Code

Authorization policies should be:

```text
Version-controlled
Reviewed
Tested
Auditable
Deployable
Rollback-capable
```

Production authorization rules should not exist only as undocumented admin-console configuration.

---

# 77. Policy Testing

Policies require positive and negative tests.

```text
Student accesses own result
→ ALLOW

Student accesses another student's result
→ DENY

Instructor accesses own course
→ ALLOW

Instructor accesses unrelated course
→ DENY
```

Negative tests are mandatory.

---

# 78. Policy Versioning

Authorization decisions should be attributable to a policy version where practical.

```text
Decision
 │
 ├── Policy ID
 ├── Version
 ├── Principal
 ├── Action
 └── Resource
```

This improves incident investigation.

---

# 79. Tenant Isolation

If Mediverse becomes multi-tenant:

```text
Tenant A
   │
   X
Tenant B Resources
```

must remain a hard invariant.

Tenant identity must propagate through relevant authorization boundaries.

---

# 80. Tenant ID Is Not User Input

Dangerous:

```text
GET /api/data?tenantId=B
```

and trusting the supplied tenant ID.

Tenant context must be derived from authenticated/authorized identity and validated relationships.

---

# 81. Object-Level Authorization

Every endpoint accessing user-controlled object identifiers requires resource authorization.

```text
/api/attempts/{attemptId}
/api/files/{fileId}
/api/users/{userId}
/api/courses/{courseId}
```

This directly addresses BOLA/IDOR classes of vulnerabilities.

---

# 82. BOLA / IDOR Defense

Correct architecture:

```text
Request object 987
      │
      ▼
Load resource
      │
      ▼
Evaluate caller relationship
      │
      ├── Authorized → Continue
      └── Unauthorized → Reject
```

Never rely on unpredictable UUIDs as authorization.

---

# 83. Data-Layer Defense

Where risk warrants, authorization can extend into data access.

```text
API Authorization
      │
      ▼
Repository Query
      │
      ▼
WHERE user_id = authenticated_user
```

This reduces accidental cross-user retrieval.

---

# 84. PostgreSQL Row-Level Security

PostgreSQL RLS may be evaluated for strong tenant/data isolation.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
PostgreSQL
    │
    ▼
RLS Policy
    │
    ▼
Permitted Rows
```

RLS can provide defense in depth but introduces operational and connection-context complexity.

It should not be added casually.

---

# 85. Least Privilege

Every identity receives only the permissions necessary.

```text
Human
Service
Pipeline
Pod
Agent
```

all follow the same principle.

---

# 86. Separation of Duties

Critical operations should avoid excessive concentration of privilege.

Example:

```text
Developer
   │
   X
Unreviewed production deployment
+
Audit deletion
+
Database administrator
```

No individual identity should automatically possess every control-plane capability.

---

# 87. Administrative Privilege

Platform administrators represent high-value identities.

Controls should include:

```text
Strong authentication
Short sessions
Explicit privileged roles
Detailed audit
Access reviews
Restricted environments
```

---

# 88. Just-In-Time Privilege

Privileged access should preferably be temporary.

```text
Engineer
   │
   ▼
Request Privilege
   │
   ▼
Approval / Policy
   │
   ▼
Temporary Role
   │
   ▼
Automatic Expiration
```

Standing privilege increases compromise impact.

---

# 89. Privileged Access Management

PAM-style controls should be considered for high-risk administrative access.

Capabilities may include:

```text
Approval
Temporary elevation
Session recording
Credential protection
Audit
```

depending on platform requirements.

---

# 90. Break-Glass Access

Emergency access must exist for scenarios where normal identity systems fail.

```text
Emergency
   │
   ▼
Break Glass
   │
   ▼
Strongly Protected Credential
   │
   ▼
Privileged Access
   │
   ▼
Immediate Audit + Review
```

Break-glass access should be rarely used and continuously monitored.

---

# 91. Impersonation

Support personnel may sometimes need to reproduce user experiences.

Do not give them user passwords.

If impersonation is required:

```text
Support Identity
      │
      ▼
Explicit Impersonation Grant
      │
      ▼
User Context
      │
      ▼
Prominent Audit Trail
```

---

# 92. Impersonation Restrictions

Impersonation should prohibit or strongly control:

```text
Credential changes
Security settings
Payments
Privilege escalation
Sensitive exports
Irreversible operations
```

depending on use case.

---

# 93. Delegated Access

A user may explicitly delegate limited authority.

```text
User A
 │
 ▼
Delegate
 │
 ▼
User B
 │
 ▼
Specific Resource + Scope + Time
```

Delegation should never become invisible permanent privilege.

---

# 94. AI Agent Identity

ADR-055 established bounded agents.

Every AI agent invocation requiring tools must have an identity context.

```text
User
 │
 ▼
AI Agent
 │
 ▼
Delegated Identity
 │
 ▼
Authorized Tools
```

The model itself is not the identity.

---

# 95. Agent Delegation

An AI agent acting for a student should receive:

```text
Student-authorized capabilities
```

not:

```text
AI platform service's full backend privileges
```

This is essential to prevent confused-deputy failures.

---

# 96. Agent Tool Authorization

Every agent tool call must independently validate:

```text
User
Agent
Action
Resource
Arguments
Policy
```

Prompt instructions are not authorization.

---

# 97. Service-to-Service Authorization

Internal traffic is not automatically trusted.

```text
Course Service
      │
      ▼
Assessment Service
```

Assessment Service should know whether Course Service is authorized to invoke the requested capability.

---

# 98. Kubernetes RBAC

Kubernetes API access should follow least privilege.

```text
ServiceAccount
      │
      ▼
Role / ClusterRole
      │
      ▼
RoleBinding
      │
      ▼
Allowed Kubernetes Resources
```

Avoid unnecessary `cluster-admin`.

---

# 99. Namespace-Scoped Permissions

Prefer namespace-scoped Roles when cluster-wide authority is unnecessary.

```text
UAT1 ServiceAccount
      │
      X
Production resources
```

Environment boundaries should be enforced technically.

---

# 100. AWS IAM Architecture

AWS authorization should use explicit roles aligned with workload responsibility.

```text
Identity
   │
   ▼
IAM Role
   │
   ▼
Policy
   │
   ▼
AWS Resource
```

Avoid giant shared roles.

---

# 101. IAM Policy Design

Policies should constrain:

```text
Actions
Resources
Conditions
Region
Tags
Account
Network/context where applicable
```

`Action: "*"` and `Resource: "*"` should be exceptional, not default.

---

# 102. IAM Permission Boundaries

Permission boundaries may restrict maximum effective permissions for delegated role creation.

```text
Identity Policy
      ∩
Permission Boundary
      =
Effective Maximum
```

Useful where teams can create or manage IAM roles.

---

# 103. AWS Organizations SCP

Service Control Policies can establish account-level guardrails.

```text
Organization
    │
    ▼
SCP
    │
    ▼
Account
    │
    ▼
IAM Permissions
```

SCPs constrain possible permissions; they do not themselves grant access.

---

# 104. Resource Policies

Some AWS resources support resource-based authorization.

Examples include policies attached to:

```text
S3
KMS
SQS
SNS
Secrets Manager
```

Identity and resource policies must be reasoned about together.

---

# 105. Cross-Account Access

Cross-account access should prefer role assumption.

```text
Account A
   │
   ▼
AssumeRole
   │
   ▼
Account B Role
   │
   ▼
Resource
```

Avoid copying long-lived credentials between accounts.

---

# 106. Zero Trust

Zero trust means:

> **Do not grant trust solely because a request originates from an internal network.**

Every request should be evaluated using relevant identity and policy context.

---

# 107. Internal Network Is Not Identity

This is rejected:

```text
10.x.x.x
   │
   ▼
Must be trusted
```

Network location can be a contextual signal, but it does not prove principal identity or authorization.

---

# 108. Zero-Trust Request

Conceptually:

```text
Request
 │
 ▼
Identity
 │
 ▼
Device / Workload
 │
 ▼
Context
 │
 ▼
Policy
 │
 ▼
Resource
```

Trust is continuously established at access boundaries.

---

# 109. Context-Aware Access

Authorization may consider:

```text
Authentication strength
Device state
Location/risk signal
Network
Time
Resource sensitivity
Session age
```

where the identity platform supports reliable signals.

---

# 110. Risk-Based Authentication

Suspicious behavior may trigger:

```text
Additional MFA
Reauthentication
Session restriction
Account protection
```

rather than treating every authentication event identically.

---

# 111. Brute-Force Defense

Authentication endpoints require:

```text
Rate limiting
Progressive controls
Monitoring
Account protection
Bot detection where justified
```

Naive unlimited password attempts are unacceptable.

---

# 112. Credential Stuffing

Attackers may reuse credentials leaked from unrelated systems.

Controls include:

```text
MFA/passkeys
Rate controls
Compromised-credential detection where available
Risk signals
User notification
```

Strong password hashing alone does not stop credential stuffing.

---

# 113. Account Enumeration

Authentication and recovery interfaces should avoid unnecessary disclosure such as:

```text
"This email exists."
```

where doing so materially aids attackers.

Operational/user-experience trade-offs should be deliberate.

---

# 114. CSRF

Cookie-authenticated browser applications require CSRF protection for state-changing requests.

```text
Victim Browser
     │
     ▼
Malicious Site
     │
     ▼
Authenticated Request
```

SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens and architecture-specific controls should be applied appropriately.

---

# 115. CORS

CORS controls which browser origins may interact with APIs.

It is **not an authentication or authorization mechanism**.

```text
CORS ≠ Access Control
```

Non-browser clients do not obey browser CORS policy.

---

# 116. Token Theft

Token theft can occur through:

```text
XSS
Logs
Browser storage
Malware
URLs
Telemetry
Compromised extensions
```

Token storage architecture must consider the client threat model.

---

# 117. Browser Token Storage

Do not automatically put long-lived sensitive tokens in `localStorage` simply because it is convenient.

Depending on architecture, secure HttpOnly cookies or BFF-style approaches may reduce direct JavaScript exposure.

The choice must consider CSRF and deployment architecture.

---

# 118. Backend-for-Frontend

A BFF can keep certain OAuth tokens server-side.

```text
Browser
   │
   ▼
BFF Session
   │
   ▼
BFF
   │
   ▼
OAuth Tokens
   │
   ▼
Backend APIs
```

This can reduce token exposure in browser JavaScript but adds infrastructure and session complexity.

---

# 119. Replay Protection

Short token lifetimes, nonce/state validation, PKCE and protocol-specific sender-constrained mechanisms reduce replay opportunities.

Bearer tokens remain replayable while valid if stolen.

---

# 120. Session Fixation

Authentication should establish a fresh authenticated session rather than allowing attacker-controlled session identifiers to persist through login.

---

# 121. Credential Compromise Response

When compromise is suspected:

```text
Detect
 │
 ▼
Revoke
 │
 ▼
Rotate
 │
 ▼
Terminate Sessions
 │
 ▼
Investigate
 │
 ▼
Recover
```

Response procedures should exist before an incident.

---

# 122. Secret Rotation

Machine credentials that cannot yet be replaced by workload identity require rotation.

Rotation must avoid:

```text
New secret deployed
Old secret removed too early
Application outage
```

Use overlap where the target system supports it.

---

# 123. Identity Lifecycle

Human identity follows:

```text
Create
 │
 ▼
Provision
 │
 ▼
Change
 │
 ▼
Review
 │
 ▼
Disable
 │
 ▼
Delete / Archive
```

Access must evolve with the identity.

---

# 124. Joiner-Mover-Leaver

Workforce access should address:

```text
JOINER
→ Grant required baseline access

MOVER
→ Recalculate permissions

LEAVER
→ Revoke promptly
```

Mover events are frequently overlooked and cause privilege accumulation.

---

# 125. Provisioning

Provisioning should be automated where scale justifies it.

Identity creation should not depend on undocumented manual steps across many platforms.

---

# 126. SCIM

SCIM may be used for standardized identity provisioning/deprovisioning with compatible enterprise identity systems.

```text
Enterprise IdP
      │
      ▼
SCIM
      │
      ▼
Mediverse
```

Authentication federation and lifecycle provisioning solve different problems.

---

# 127. Deprovisioning

Disabling a user should trigger removal/revocation of relevant:

```text
Sessions
Refresh tokens
Roles
API access
Cloud access
Administrative privileges
```

Leaving active secondary credentials defeats account disablement.

---

# 128. Dormant Accounts

Inactive accounts should be identified according to policy.

Dormant privileged accounts deserve particularly strong scrutiny.

---

# 129. Identity Reconciliation

Periodically compare:

```text
Expected identities
        vs
Actual identities and entitlements
```

This detects orphaned accounts and unauthorized privilege drift.

---

# 130. Access Reviews

Sensitive privileges should undergo periodic review.

```text
Identity
 │
 ▼
Current Entitlements
 │
 ▼
Owner / Manager Review
 │
 ├── Retain
 └── Remove
```

Reviews should produce actual revocation when access is unnecessary.

---

# 131. Entitlement Governance

Mediverse should know:

```text
Who has access?
Why?
Who approved it?
To what?
Since when?
Until when?
```

If these questions cannot be answered for privileged access, governance is inadequate.

---

# 132. Identity Audit Events

Important events include:

```text
Login success/failure
MFA changes
Password/recovery changes
Role grants
Role removals
Privilege elevation
Impersonation
Token revocation
Account disablement
Break-glass use
Authorization denial
```

---

# 133. Authorization Decision Logging

High-value authorization decisions should produce useful evidence.

```text
principal
action
resource
decision
policy/version
reason
timestamp
correlation ID
```

Avoid logging sensitive token contents.

---

# 134. Identity Observability

Monitor:

```text
Authentication failure rate
MFA failure
Token validation failures
Authorization denials
Privilege changes
Suspicious login patterns
Break-glass activity
Dormant privileged accounts
```

Identity systems require operational telemetry like any other critical platform.

---

# 135. Alerting

High-value alerts may include:

```text
Repeated admin login failures
Unexpected privilege escalation
Cross-tenant access attempts
Break-glass activation
Mass role changes
Token validation anomalies
```

Alerts must be tuned enough to remain actionable.

---

# 136. Authorization Testing

ADR-054 quality architecture must include identity-specific tests.

```text
Authentication
Authorization
Resource ownership
Role boundaries
Tenant isolation
Token validation
Privilege revocation
```

---

# 137. Negative Authorization Tests

For every critical allowed path, ask:

```text
Who must NOT be able to do this?
```

Example:

```text
Instructor edits own course
→ ALLOW

Different instructor
→ DENY

Student
→ DENY

Unauthenticated caller
→ DENY
```

---

# 138. Tenant Isolation Testing

Automated tests should deliberately attempt:

```text
Tenant A API → Tenant B resource
Tenant A search → Tenant B content
Tenant A export → Tenant B data
Tenant A AI retrieval → Tenant B knowledge
```

A single successful cross-tenant test is a critical defect.

---

# 139. Token Security Testing

Test:

```text
Expired token
Wrong issuer
Wrong audience
Invalid signature
Unknown key
Malformed token
Missing token
Revoked session
Insufficient scope
```

Do not test only valid tokens.

---

# 140. Identity Incident Response

Identity incidents may involve:

```text
Account takeover
Token theft
Signing-key compromise
Privilege escalation
Cross-tenant access
Compromised workload identity
Compromised CI identity
Break-glass misuse
```

Each requires specific containment procedures.

---

# 141. Signing-Key Compromise

Response may require:

```text
Revoke compromised key
Publish replacement key
Stop token issuance
Invalidate affected sessions/tokens where possible
Investigate forged access
Rotate dependent trust
```

Key compromise should be rehearsed for critical identity infrastructure.

---

# 142. Authorization Failure Philosophy

When authorization cannot confidently establish permission:

```text
DENY
```

not:

```text
Probably okay.
```

Fail closed for protected operations unless a deliberately documented availability trade-off says otherwise.

---

# 143. Identity Ownership Model

```text
Identity Platform Team
   ├── IdP
   ├── Federation
   ├── Authentication standards
   └── Token architecture

Application Teams
   ├── Domain permissions
   ├── Resource authorization
   └── Negative tests

Platform Team
   ├── Workload identity
   ├── Kubernetes RBAC
   └── CI federation

Cloud/Security Team
   ├── AWS IAM guardrails
   ├── SCPs
   ├── Privileged access
   └── Security monitoring

Data Teams
   └── Data-layer isolation

AI Platform Team
   └── Agent delegation/tool authorization
```

---

# 144. Identity Architecture Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ Authentication implemented independently by every service
❌ Home-grown password system without compelling requirement
❌ Password grant for modern browser applications
❌ ID tokens used as universal API access tokens
❌ JWT decoding without cryptographic validation
❌ Tokens accepted without issuer/audience validation
❌ Very long-lived bearer access tokens
❌ Refresh tokens without lifecycle controls
❌ Secrets/tokens written to logs
❌ Authorization based on hidden frontend buttons
❌ Authorization based on possession of resource ID
❌ UUID unpredictability treated as access control
❌ Gateway authentication treated as complete authorization
❌ Giant role containing every privilege
❌ Role explosion for contextual permissions
❌ Tenant ID blindly trusted from request parameters
❌ Cross-tenant retrieval followed by application filtering
❌ Permanent admin privileges for ordinary engineering work
❌ Shared administrator accounts
❌ Unmonitored break-glass credentials
❌ Static AWS keys in Pods
❌ Static cloud credentials in CI when OIDC is available
❌ One Kubernetes ServiceAccount shared by every workload
❌ cluster-admin granted for convenience
❌ One giant AWS IAM role for all applications
❌ Internal network treated as trusted identity
❌ Blind propagation of broad user tokens across services
❌ Client credentials used to impersonate users
❌ CORS treated as API security
❌ Long-lived tokens casually stored in browser localStorage
❌ AI agent running with platform administrator privilege
❌ Model deciding whether its own tool call is authorized
❌ Disabled user retaining refresh/API credentials
❌ No entitlement reviews
❌ Authorization failures not audited
```

---

# 145. Mediverse Identity Trust Chain

```text
                     PRINCIPAL
                         │
                         ▼
                 AUTHENTICATION
                         │
                         ▼
                VERIFIED IDENTITY
                         │
                         ▼
               TEMPORARY CREDENTIAL
                         │
                         ▼
                REQUEST CONTEXT
                         │
          ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
          ▼              ▼              ▼
        ROLE         ATTRIBUTES    RELATIONSHIPS
          │              │              │
          └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                         ▼
                POLICY DECISION
                         │
                         ▼
                POLICY ENFORCEMENT
                         │
                         ▼
                     RESOURCE
                         │
                         ▼
                       AUDIT
```

---

# 146. Zero-Trust Architecture

```text
                 INTERNET / CORPORATE / VPC
                           │
                           ▼
                    NO IMPLICIT TRUST
                           │
                           ▼
                       IDENTITY
                           │
              ┌────────────┼────────────┐
              ▼            ▼            ▼
            Human       Workload      Agent
              │            │            │
              └────────────┼────────────┘
                           ▼
                    AUTHENTICATION
                           │
                           ▼
                    POLICY CONTEXT
                           │
          ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
          ▼                ▼                ▼
        Action          Resource         Context
          │                │                │
          └────────────────┼────────────────┘
                           ▼
                    AUTHORIZATION
                           │
                   ┌───────┴───────┐
                   ▼               ▼
                 ALLOW            DENY
                   │
                   ▼
                RESOURCE
                   │
                   ▼
                  AUDIT
```

---

# 147. Enterprise Identity Quality Gates

Identity-related changes should pass:

```text
Source Change
     │
     ▼
Policy Static Validation
     │
     ▼
Unit Tests
     │
     ▼
Authentication Tests
     │
     ▼
Positive Authorization
     │
     ▼
Negative Authorization
     │
     ▼
Tenant Isolation
     │
     ▼
Token Validation
     │
     ▼
Integration Tests
     │
     ▼
Security Regression
     │
     ▼
Deployment
     │
     ▼
Production Identity Monitoring
```

Authorization policy changes deserve the same engineering discipline as application code.

---

# 148. Final Mediverse Enterprise Identity Reference Architecture

```text
                         HUMAN IDENTITIES
              ┌────────────────────────────────┐
              │ Student / Instructor / Admin   │
              │ Developer / SRE / Security     │
              └───────────────┬────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
                       IDENTITY PROVIDER
                              │
              ┌───────────────┼────────────────┐
              ▼               ▼                ▼
            OIDC          MFA/Passkeys      Federation
              │               │                │
              └───────────────┼────────────────┘
                              ▼
                    SHORT-LIVED IDENTITY
                              │
                              ▼
                         API / BFF
                              │
                              ▼
                    AUTHORIZATION LAYER
                              │
             ┌────────────────┼─────────────────┐
             ▼                ▼                 ▼
           RBAC             ABAC              ReBAC/
                                             Ownership
             │                │                 │
             └────────────────┼─────────────────┘
                              ▼
                      DOMAIN SERVICES
                              │
                              ▼
                         DATA LAYER
                              │
                              ▼
                            AUDIT


                       WORKLOAD IDENTITIES

 Kubernetes Pod ─► ServiceAccount ─► EKS Pod Identity/IRSA ─► AWS Role

 CI/CD ─► OIDC Federation ─► Temporary Deployment Role

 Service A ─► Workload Identity / OAuth ─► Service B

 AI Agent ─► Delegated User Identity ─► Tool Authorization


                      GOVERNANCE PLANE

 ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ Policy as Code                                            │
 │ Identity Lifecycle                                        │
 │ Access Reviews                                            │
 │ JIT Privilege                                             │
 │ Break Glass                                               │
 │ Federation                                                │
 │ SCIM                                                      │
 │ Entitlement Governance                                    │
 │ Audit                                                     │
 │ Security Monitoring                                       │
 └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

# 149. Core Identity Invariants

Regardless of future IdP, cloud provider or policy engine:

```text
1. Every protected action is attributable to a principal.

2. Authentication never implies unrestricted authorization.

3. Authorization defaults to deny.

4. Identity standards are centralized.

5. Access tokens are scoped, audience-bound and short-lived.

6. JWTs are cryptographically validated.

7. Signing keys support controlled rotation.

8. Higher-risk identities use stronger authentication.

9. Authorization is enforced server-side.

10. Resource IDs never constitute authorization.

11. Tenant boundaries are explicit security boundaries.

12. Domain services own domain-level authorization.

13. Negative authorization tests are mandatory.

14. Human cloud access uses federation where possible.

15. Workloads use workload identity instead of static secrets.

16. CI/CD uses temporary federated credentials where possible.

17. Internal network location does not establish trust.

18. Service identity remains distinguishable from user identity.

19. User tokens are not propagated indiscriminately.

20. Privileged access follows least privilege.

21. Standing privilege is minimized.

22. Break-glass access is protected and audited.

23. AI agents operate through delegated identities.

24. Agent tool calls are independently authorized.

25. Identity lifecycle includes timely deprovisioning.

26. Dormant and excessive entitlements are reviewed.

27. Critical authorization decisions are auditable.

28. Identity infrastructure is observable.

29. Credential compromise has defined containment procedures.

30. When permission cannot be established, access is denied.
```

---

# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                       | Decision                                                  |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| Identity architecture      | **Centralized standards + distributed enforcement**       |
| Application authentication | OIDC/OAuth                                                |
| Browser OAuth              | Authorization Code + PKCE                                 |
| Password grant             | Rejected                                                  |
| Access tokens              | Short-lived + scoped + audience-bound                     |
| ID token as API token      | Rejected                                                  |
| Refresh tokens             | Controlled + rotation where supported                     |
| JWT                        | Selective                                                 |
| JWT validation             | Signature + issuer + audience + lifetime                  |
| Opaque tokens              | Supported where centralized control warrants              |
| Signing keys               | JWKS + rotation                                           |
| MFA                        | Risk-based requirement                                    |
| Passkeys                   | Strategic preference where supported                      |
| Admin authentication       | Strong/phishing-resistant preferred                       |
| Workforce identity         | Federation                                                |
| Human AWS access           | Temporary federated roles                                 |
| Kubernetes workloads       | ServiceAccount-based identity                             |
| AWS workloads              | EKS Pod Identity/IRSA-style workload identity             |
| Static AWS keys in Pods    | Rejected                                                  |
| CI/CD AWS access           | OIDC federation                                           |
| Machine-to-machine         | Workload identity/OAuth as appropriate                    |
| Blind token propagation    | Rejected                                                  |
| Token exchange             | Evaluate where delegation requires                        |
| Service authorization      | Required                                                  |
| API gateway                | Authentication/coarse policy—not sole authorization layer |
| Primary authorization      | RBAC + ABAC + ownership                                   |
| ReBAC                      | Evaluate when relationship complexity justifies           |
| Policy engine              | Introduce when complexity warrants                        |
| Policy as code             | Required for centralized policy                           |
| Authorization default      | **Deny**                                                  |
| Resource authorization     | Mandatory                                                 |
| UUID as authorization      | Rejected                                                  |
| Tenant isolation           | Hard security invariant                                   |
| PostgreSQL RLS             | Evaluate for high-value isolation                         |
| Administrative privilege   | Least privilege                                           |
| JIT access                 | Preferred                                                 |
| PAM                        | Risk-based                                                |
| Break glass                | Required + audited                                        |
| Impersonation              | Explicit + restricted + audited                           |
| Kubernetes RBAC            | Least privilege                                           |
| `cluster-admin`            | Exceptional                                               |
| AWS IAM                    | Role-based least privilege                                |
| Permission boundaries      | Use where delegated IAM requires                          |
| SCP                        | Organization guardrails                                   |
| Cross-account access       | AssumeRole                                                |
| Zero trust                 | **No implicit network trust**                             |
| CSRF                       | Required where cookie architecture requires               |
| CORS                       | Browser policy, not authorization                         |
| Browser token architecture | Threat-model driven                                       |
| BFF                        | Evaluate for sensitive browser applications               |
| Identity lifecycle         | Automated where practical                                 |
| SCIM                       | Enterprise provisioning where required                    |
| Access reviews             | Required for sensitive entitlements                       |
| Authorization testing      | Positive + negative                                       |
| Tenant security testing    | Mandatory if multi-tenant                                 |
| Agent identity             | Delegated principal                                       |
| Agent authorization        | Independent tool authorization                            |
| Audit                      | Authentication + privilege + critical authorization       |
| Status                     | **Accepted**                                              |
| Priority                   | **Critical**                                              |

---

---

# ADR-057 — Enterprise API Architecture, API Gateway, REST, GraphQL, gRPC, WebSockets, Versioning & API Governance

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — RED Method**.

---

# 61. GraphQL Architecture

GraphQL should be introduced when consumer-driven data composition provides measurable value.

```text
Client
  │
  ▼
GraphQL API
  │
  ▼
Schema
  │
  ▼
Resolvers
  │
  ├── Course Service
  ├── User Service
  └── Assessment Service
```

GraphQL is **not automatically superior to REST**.

---

# 62. GraphQL Schema

The schema is the GraphQL contract.

```graphql
type Course {
  id: ID!
  title: String!
  description: String
  instructor: Instructor!
}
```

Schema design should model consumer-facing domain concepts rather than database tables.

---

# 63. Queries

Queries represent read operations.

```graphql
query {
  course(id: "123") {
    title
    description
  }
}
```

Queries should not secretly perform destructive operations.

---

# 64. Mutations

State-changing operations belong in mutations.

```graphql
mutation {
  enroll(courseId: "123") {
    enrollmentId
    status
  }
}
```

Mutation names should express domain intent.

---

# 65. GraphQL Over-Fetching Advantage

REST may require:

```text
GET /courses/123
GET /courses/123/instructor
GET /courses/123/progress
```

GraphQL can potentially retrieve the required shape through one client operation.

This can benefit complex frontend experiences.

---

# 66. GraphQL Is Not One Database Query

This misconception is rejected:

```text
One GraphQL request
       =
One backend query
```

One request may trigger dozens or hundreds of resolver operations if poorly implemented.

---

# 67. N+1 Problem

Example:

```text
1 query → 100 courses

Then:

100 queries → instructor for each course
```

Total:

```text
101 backend operations
```

This is a classic GraphQL performance failure.

---

# 68. DataLoader / Batching

Resolvers should batch compatible lookups.

```text
100 instructor requests
        │
        ▼
      Batch
        │
        ▼
getInstructors(ids[])
```

Batching and caching can dramatically reduce N+1 behavior.

---

# 69. Query Depth

Clients can construct deeply nested queries.

```text
course
 └── instructor
      └── courses
           └── students
                └── courses
                     └── ...
```

Unbounded depth creates resource-exhaustion risk.

---

# 70. Query Complexity

Depth alone is insufficient.

A shallow query returning huge collections can still be expensive.

GraphQL gateways should evaluate:

```text
Depth
Field cost
Collection cardinality
Resolver cost
Overall complexity
```

---

# 71. GraphQL Pagination

Large collections must remain paginated.

GraphQL does not justify returning an entire dataset.

Connection/cursor patterns are appropriate where stable traversal is required.

---

# 72. GraphQL Authorization

Authorization must occur at the correct resource/domain boundary.

```text
Resolver
  │
  ▼
Load Resource
  │
  ▼
Authorization
  │
  ├── ALLOW
  └── DENY
```

A valid GraphQL query does not imply permission to access every requested field.

---

# 73. Field-Level Authorization

Some fields may require stronger privileges.

```text
User
 ├── displayName
 ├── avatar
 └── administrativeMetadata
```

The final field may require administrative authorization.

Do not assume object-level authorization automatically covers every field.

---

# 74. GraphQL Introspection

Introspection is valuable for tooling and development.

Whether it remains available publicly in production should follow the threat model.

Disabling introspection alone is not meaningful API security.

---

# 75. Persisted Queries

For controlled clients:

```text
Client
  │
  ▼
Known Query ID
  │
  ▼
GraphQL Gateway
```

persisted queries can improve:

```text
Governance
Caching
Security controls
Traffic predictability
```

They are especially useful for first-party clients.

---

# 76. GraphQL Federation

Federation may allow multiple domains to contribute to a larger graph.

```text
                GraphQL Router
                      │
       ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
       ▼              ▼              ▼
     Course        Student       Assessment
    Subgraph       Subgraph        Subgraph
```

This should only be introduced when organizational/domain scale justifies its operational complexity.

---

# 77. GraphQL Federation Boundary

Federation must not erase bounded contexts.

Each domain remains responsible for:

```text
Data ownership
Authorization
Schema ownership
Performance
Compatibility
```

A unified graph is not a unified database.

---

# 78. REST vs GraphQL

Use REST when:

```text
Resource operations are straightforward
HTTP caching matters
Simple integrations dominate
API consumers need conventional contracts
```

Consider GraphQL when:

```text
Frontend data requirements vary significantly
Many related resources must be composed
Consumer-controlled projections provide clear value
```

---

# 79. GraphQL Decision

Mediverse will **not replace REST globally with GraphQL**.

Preferred architecture:

```text
REST
→ Primary service/public API style

GraphQL
→ Selective consumer-facing composition layer
```

---

# 80. gRPC Architecture

gRPC should primarily target controlled service-to-service communication requiring:

```text
Strong contracts
Low overhead
High throughput
Streaming
Generated clients
```

---

# 81. Protocol Buffers

gRPC contracts should use Protobuf schemas.

```protobuf
message CourseRequest {
  string course_id = 1;
}
```

The `.proto` file is a production contract.

---

# 82. Protobuf Field Numbers

Field numbers are part of wire compatibility.

```protobuf
string course_id = 1;
```

Once published, numbers should not be casually reused for different meanings.

---

# 83. Protobuf Evolution

Prefer additive changes.

```text
Add new field
→ Usually compatible

Remove/reuse field number
→ Dangerous
```

Removed fields should be reserved when appropriate.

---

# 84. gRPC Unary Calls

Unary RPC:

```text
Client
  │
  ▼
One Request
  │
  ▼
Server
  │
  ▼
One Response
```

This resembles conventional synchronous request/response communication.

---

# 85. Server Streaming

```text
Client Request
      │
      ▼
Server
      │
      ├── Response 1
      ├── Response 2
      └── Response N
```

Useful where one request naturally produces a stream of results.

---

# 86. Client Streaming

```text
Client
  ├── Message 1
  ├── Message 2
  └── Message N
       │
       ▼
     Server
       │
       ▼
    Response
```

Use only where the domain naturally benefits from streamed input.

---

# 87. Bidirectional Streaming

```text
Client ◄════════════► Server
```

Both sides communicate through a persistent stream.

This adds lifecycle, backpressure and failure-handling complexity.

---

# 88. gRPC Deadlines

Every synchronous gRPC request should have a deadline.

```text
Client
  │
  ▼
Deadline
  │
  ▼
Service
```

Without deadlines, failed downstream calls can consume resources indefinitely.

---

# 89. Deadline Propagation

Downstream calls should respect the remaining upstream deadline.

```text
3s original budget
      │
      ▼
1.8s remaining
      │
      ▼
Downstream must not wait 10s
```

---

# 90. REST vs gRPC

Use REST when:

```text
Browser/external interoperability dominates
Human-readable debugging matters
HTTP ecosystem is valuable
```

Consider gRPC when:

```text
Internal high-throughput communication
Strong generated contracts
Low serialization overhead
Streaming
```

Mediverse should not convert every internal API to gRPC without evidence.

---

# 91. WebSocket Architecture

WebSockets support persistent bidirectional communication.

```text
Client
  │
  ▼
HTTP Upgrade
  │
  ▼
Persistent Connection
  │
  ⇅
Server
```

Potential Mediverse uses include real-time notifications and collaborative experiences.

---

# 92. WebSocket Authentication

Authentication must occur when establishing the connection using a secure architecture appropriate to the client.

```text
Connection
    │
    ▼
Authenticate
    │
    ▼
Authorize
    │
    ▼
Accept
```

A connected client is not automatically authorized for every channel.

---

# 93. WebSocket Authorization

Subscription authorization must be resource-aware.

```text
User
 │
 ▼
Subscribe course:123
 │
 ▼
Is user authorized for course 123?
```

Channel names are not authorization.

---

# 94. Connection Lifetime

Long-lived connections introduce:

```text
Authentication expiration
Network interruption
Server restart
Load balancer timeout
Client sleep
Deployment
```

Connection lifecycle must explicitly handle these events.

---

# 95. Heartbeats

Heartbeat/ping mechanisms can detect dead connections.

```text
Client ◄── ping/pong ──► Server
```

Timeout values must avoid excessive traffic.

---

# 96. Reconnection

Clients should use bounded reconnection with:

```text
Backoff
Jitter
Maximum delay
State recovery
```

Immediate reconnection loops during outages can overload the platform.

---

# 97. Backpressure

If:

```text
Producer rate
   >
Consumer rate
```

the architecture needs a policy.

Possible responses include:

```text
Buffer
Drop
Aggregate
Throttle
Disconnect
```

Unlimited memory buffering is not acceptable.

---

# 98. Horizontal WebSocket Scaling

Persistent connections complicate scaling.

```text
Client A ─► Pod 1
Client B ─► Pod 2
Client C ─► Pod 3
```

Events may require a shared messaging backbone so the correct connected client can receive them.

---

# 99. Real-Time Backbone

Conceptually:

```text
Domain Event
    │
    ▼
Kafka / Messaging
    │
    ▼
Realtime Service
    │
    ▼
Connected Clients
```

WebSocket servers should not become the authoritative source of domain state.

---

# 100. SSE

Server-Sent Events provide server-to-client streaming over HTTP.

```text
Client
  │
  ▼
HTTP Connection
  │
  ◄──── Events ─── Server
```

SSE can be simpler than WebSockets when communication is primarily one-directional.

---

# 101. SSE vs WebSocket

Use SSE when:

```text
Server → client dominates
Browser support fits
Simple event streaming is sufficient
```

Use WebSockets when:

```text
Frequent bidirectional communication is required
```

Do not choose WebSockets merely because "real-time" appears in the requirement.

---

# 102. Webhooks

Webhooks notify external systems.

```text
Mediverse
    │
    ▼
HTTPS POST
    │
    ▼
External Consumer
```

Unlike normal APIs, Mediverse becomes the caller.

---

# 103. Webhook Signing

Webhook payloads should be cryptographically authenticated.

Conceptually:

```text
Payload
 +
Secret/Key
   │
   ▼
Signature
```

The receiver verifies authenticity before processing.

---

# 104. Webhook Replay Protection

Signed payloads alone may still be replayed.

Include appropriate:

```text
Timestamp
Event ID
Signature context
Acceptance window
```

and receiver-side duplicate detection.

---

# 105. Webhook Delivery

Webhook delivery should generally be asynchronous.

```text
Domain Event
    │
    ▼
Webhook Queue
    │
    ▼
Delivery Worker
    │
    ▼
Consumer
```

A slow external webhook endpoint must not block the core business transaction.

---

# 106. Webhook Retries

Transient failures should use:

```text
Bounded retries
Exponential backoff
Jitter
Dead-letter handling
```

Permanent failures must not retry forever.

---

# 107. Webhook Idempotency

Consumers may receive duplicate events.

```text
eventId = evt_123
```

should allow duplicate detection.

Webhook architecture should assume **at-least-once delivery** unless a stronger guarantee is explicitly implemented.

---

# 108. Synchronous Communication

Synchronous calls are appropriate when the caller needs an immediate result.

```text
Service A
    │
    ▼
Service B
    │
    ▼
Response required now
```

But synchronous chains increase temporal coupling.

---

# 109. Long Synchronous Chains

Avoid:

```text
Gateway
  ▼
A
  ▼
B
  ▼
C
  ▼
D
  ▼
E
```

for ordinary user requests when the architecture can avoid it.

Latency and failure probability compound across the chain.

---

# 110. Asynchronous Communication

Use events/messages when immediate completion is unnecessary.

```text
Producer
   │
   ▼
Broker
   │
   ▼
Consumer
```

ADR-052 messaging architecture remains authoritative for delivery semantics.

---

# 111. API vs Event

Use API:

```text
"I need this answer now."
```

Use event:

```text
"This happened; interested consumers may react."
```

Do not model every integration as synchronous REST.

---

# 112. API Composition

A consumer may require data owned by several services.

```text
Client
  │
  ▼
Composition Layer
  │
  ├── User Service
  ├── Course Service
  └── Progress Service
```

Composition should avoid leaking backend topology directly to clients.

---

# 113. Backend-for-Frontend

A BFF may provide client-specific orchestration.

```text
Web
 │
 ▼
Web BFF
 │
 ├── Course
 ├── User
 └── Assessment
```

A mobile BFF may expose a different optimized contract.

---

# 114. BFF Boundary

BFFs may handle:

```text
Aggregation
Client-specific shaping
Session/token handling
Protocol adaptation
```

They should not become the new home of core domain business rules.

---

# 115. Mobile Contracts

Mobile clients may remain deployed for months.

Breaking API changes therefore have longer compatibility implications than web clients that can be updated immediately.

Version/deprecation policy must account for this.

---

# 116. API Versioning

Versioning exists to manage incompatible contract evolution.

The goal is not:

```text
Create v2 every month.
```

The goal is:

```text
Avoid unnecessary breaking changes.
```

---

# 117. URI Versioning

Example:

```text
/api/v1/courses
/api/v2/courses
```

Advantages:

```text
Visible
Simple
Easy to route
```

Disadvantages include URL proliferation.

---

# 118. Header Versioning

Version information can instead be negotiated through headers.

This can keep resource URIs stable but is less visible during debugging and consumer usage.

---

# 119. Media-Type Versioning

Custom media types can encode versions.

This provides sophisticated negotiation but often adds unnecessary complexity for ordinary application APIs.

---

# 120. Mediverse Versioning Strategy

Preferred:

```text
Additive evolution first
        │
        ▼
Avoid version bump
        │
        ▼
Breaking change unavoidable?
        │
        ▼
Introduce explicit major API version
```

URI major versioning is acceptable for externally consumed REST APIs where clarity is valuable.

---

# 121. Breaking Changes

Examples include:

```text
Removing field
Renaming field
Changing type
Changing requiredness
Changing status semantics
Changing enum semantics
Removing endpoint
Changing authorization assumptions
```

A syntactically compatible change can still be behaviorally breaking.

---

# 122. Additive Changes

Usually safer:

```text
New optional field
New endpoint
New optional query parameter
New operation
```

But consumers must tolerate unknown fields where contract conventions require it.

---

# 123. Enum Evolution

Adding a new enum value can break clients that assume exhaustive known values.

Therefore even apparently additive schema changes require consumer-awareness.

---

# 124. Breaking-Change Detection

CI should compare API contracts.

```text
Current OpenAPI
      │
      ▼
Candidate OpenAPI
      │
      ▼
Compatibility Check
      │
      ├── Compatible
      └── Breaking
```

The same principle applies to Protobuf and GraphQL schemas.

---

# 125. Consumer Inventory

Providers should know important consumers.

```text
API
 │
 ├── Web
 ├── Mobile
 ├── Internal Service
 ├── Partner
 └── External Integration
```

Deprecation without knowing consumers is operational gambling.

---

# 126. Deprecation

Deprecation should define:

```text
Deprecated capability
Replacement
Migration guidance
Timeline
Owner
```

"Deprecated" without removal planning is meaningless.

---

# 127. Sunset

A removal lifecycle should resemble:

```text
Announce
  │
  ▼
Deprecate
  │
  ▼
Measure Usage
  │
  ▼
Migrate Consumers
  │
  ▼
Sunset
  │
  ▼
Remove
```

Do not silently remove active APIs.

---

# 128. Contract Testing

Provider/consumer contracts should be validated automatically where useful.

```text
Consumer expectation
       │
       ▼
Contract Test
       │
       ▼
Provider Build
```

This catches compatibility failures before deployment.

---

# 129. API Mocking

Contract-based mocks can enable frontend/mobile development before backend completion.

Mocks must derive from the actual API contract, otherwise they create false confidence.

---

# 130. Generated SDKs

For stable externally consumed APIs, generated clients may reduce repetitive integration work.

```text
OpenAPI / Protobuf
       │
       ▼
Code Generation
       │
       ├── Java
       ├── TypeScript
       └── Other approved clients
```

Generated code still requires lifecycle/version governance.

---

# 131. API Documentation

Documentation should include:

```text
Purpose
Authentication
Endpoints/operations
Schemas
Errors
Examples
Rate limits
Pagination
Versioning
Deprecation
```

A Swagger page alone is not always sufficient developer documentation.

---

# 132. Developer Portal

If Mediverse exposes significant partner/public APIs, a developer portal should eventually provide:

```text
Documentation
Credentials/onboarding
API catalog
Examples
SDKs
Changelog
Deprecation notices
Status
```

Do not build a portal before there is a real external developer ecosystem.

---

# 133. API Security

Every API should be reviewed for:

```text
Authentication
Object authorization
Function authorization
Input validation
Mass assignment
Rate limits
Resource exhaustion
Sensitive-data exposure
Injection
Logging
```

ADR-056 remains authoritative for identity.

---

# 134. Excessive Data Exposure

Do not return entire internal objects and expect the frontend to hide sensitive fields.

Bad:

```text
Database Entity
      │
      ▼
Huge JSON
      │
      ▼
Frontend displays only 3 fields
```

The API should expose only necessary data.

---

# 135. Injection

User-controlled values must never become trusted query/code fragments.

Applies to:

```text
SQL
Search queries
GraphQL resolver backends
Shell commands
Template engines
NoSQL queries
```

Parameterized and constrained interfaces remain mandatory.

---

# 136. API Caching

Caching can reduce latency and backend load.

```text
Client
 │
 ▼
Cache
 │
 ├── HIT
 │
 └── MISS → Origin
```

Only cache responses whose authorization and freshness semantics permit it.

---

# 137. Cache-Control

HTTP caching directives should explicitly describe intended caching behavior.

Sensitive/private responses should not accidentally become shared-cache content.

---

# 138. ETag

ETags enable conditional retrieval.

```text
Client
 │
 ▼
If-None-Match
 │
 ▼
Server
 │
 ├── Changed → 200
 └── Same    → 304
```

This reduces unnecessary payload transfer.

---

# 139. Optimistic Concurrency

ETag/version concepts may also protect updates.

```text
Client reads version 5
       │
       ▼
Update requires version 5
       │
       ▼
Current version 6?
       │
       ▼
Reject conflict
```

This prevents silent lost updates.

---

# 140. CDN

Static/publicly cacheable API responses may benefit from edge caching.

Do not place personalized authenticated content into shared CDN caches without correct cache-key and privacy controls.

---

# 141. Compression

Compression can reduce network transfer for sufficiently large textual payloads.

Trade-offs include:

```text
CPU
Latency
Payload size
Security context
```

Tiny responses do not need aggressive compression.

---

# 142. API Performance Budget

Critical APIs should define targets such as:

```text
p50 latency
p95 latency
p99 latency
```
