
---

# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                     | Decision                                 |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------- |
| Native mobile framework  | **React Native + TypeScript**            |
| Development platform     | **Expo preferred/evaluated**             |
| Responsive web/PWA       | Retained alongside native                |
| Web/mobile sharing       | Contracts/domain logic selectively       |
| 100% UI sharing          | Rejected                                 |
| Mobile structure         | Feature/domain-oriented                  |
| API contracts            | ADR-057 governed                         |
| Generated clients        | Preferred where practical                |
| Authentication           | OAuth/OIDC Authorization Code + PKCE     |
| Embedded client secrets  | Rejected                                 |
| Sensitive token storage  | Keychain/Keystore-backed                 |
| Biometrics               | Local protection / step-up UX            |
| Local structured storage | SQLite/appropriate mobile DB             |
| Offline learning         | **First-class capability**               |
| Binary downloads         | Managed filesystem                       |
| Large downloads          | Network-aware + resumable                |
| Content integrity        | Verified                                 |
| Content versioning       | Required                                 |
| Mobile 3D                | Adaptive quality                         |
| Low-capability devices   | Accessible fallback                      |
| Offline mutations        | Durable sync queue                       |
| Synchronization          | Central sync engine                      |
| Delta sync               | Preferred                                |
| Sync cursor              | Opaque server-controlled                 |
| Deletions                | Tombstones/defined equivalent            |
| Multi-device             | Explicitly supported                     |
| Conflict strategy        | Domain-specific                          |
| Retryable mutations      | Idempotent                               |
| Background execution     | Opportunistic                            |
| Push                     | FCM + APNs                               |
| Push token               | Installation endpoint, not identity      |
| Sensitive push content   | Minimized                                |
| Push payload             | Signal where freshness matters           |
| Deep links               | Verified links preferred                 |
| Mobile server state      | TanStack Query selectively               |
| Persistent state         | Local DB                                 |
| Global client state      | Redux Toolkit selectively                |
| Accessibility            | Required                                 |
| Tablet UX                | Adaptive, not stretched phone UI         |
| Observability            | Crashes + hangs + performance + sync     |
| Certificate pinning      | **Not default**                          |
| Root/jailbreak detection | Risk signal only                         |
| Device attestation       | Selective risk control                   |
| WebViews                 | Minimized/restricted                     |
| Permissions              | Least privilege/contextual               |
| Physical-device testing  | Required                                 |
| Offline/network testing  | Required                                 |
| Migration testing        | Required                                 |
| Release signing          | Controlled CI infrastructure             |
| Production artifacts     | Immutable/traceable                      |
| Distribution             | Play Store + App Store                   |
| Rollout                  | Staged/phased                            |
| Feature flags            | Governed                                 |
| Minimum version          | Supported                                |
| Forced updates           | Exceptional                              |
| API compatibility        | Multiple mobile generations              |
| OTA updates              | Native-runtime compatibility constrained |
| Rollback                 | Layer-specific                           |
| Status                   | **Accepted**                             |
| Priority                 | **Critical**                             |

---

---

# ADR-060 — Enterprise Cloud & AWS Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — AWS Identity for Pods**.

---

# 61. IAM & Human Access Architecture

Human access to AWS should be centralized rather than based on individually created IAM users across accounts.

```text
Human User
    │
    ▼
Corporate Identity Provider
    │
    ▼
IAM Identity Center
    │
    ▼
Permission Set
    │
    ▼
AWS Account / Role
```

Long-lived IAM users should be exceptional.

---

# 62. IAM Identity Center

IAM Identity Center should provide centralized workforce access across Mediverse AWS accounts.

It should govern:

```text
User/group assignment
Account access
Permission sets
Federated sessions
Central access lifecycle
```

---

# 63. Federation

Where an enterprise identity provider exists:

```text
Enterprise IdP
      │
      ▼
IAM Identity Center
      │
      ▼
AWS Accounts
```

should be preferred over maintaining a separate AWS identity lifecycle.

---

# 64. Permission Sets

Access should be based on job responsibilities.

Examples:

```text
Developer
ReadOnly
PlatformEngineer
SecurityAuditor
ProductionOperator
BillingAdministrator
```

Do not create unique permissions manually for every individual.

---

# 65. Least Privilege

Permissions should answer:

```text
Who?
Can perform what action?
Against which resource?
Under what conditions?
```

Avoid:

```text
Action: *
Resource: *
```

except where explicitly justified for tightly controlled administration.

---

# 66. Production Human Access

Routine developer workflows should not require unrestricted production console access.

Preferred:

```text
Developer
   │
   ▼
CI/CD / GitOps
   │
   ▼
Production
```

Direct production access should be controlled and auditable.

---

# 67. Break-Glass Access

Emergency privileged access should exist for scenarios where normal identity or deployment paths fail.

```text
Normal Access Fails
       │
       ▼
Break-Glass Procedure
       │
       ▼
Strong Authentication
       │
       ▼
Temporary Privileged Access
       │
       ▼
Audit + Review
```

Break-glass credentials must not become everyday administrator credentials.

---

# 68. Temporary Credentials

Prefer short-lived AWS credentials.

```text
Federation
   │
   ▼
STS
   │
   ▼
Temporary Session
```

Long-lived access keys create unnecessary credential exposure.

---

# 69. Access Keys

Human IAM access keys should be minimized.

Workloads should use IAM roles/workload identity rather than static AWS keys stored in:

```text
GitHub secrets
Kubernetes Secrets
application.yml
developer laptops
```

unless an unavoidable integration requires them.

---

# 70. Cross-Account Roles

Cross-account operations should use explicit IAM roles.

```text
CI Account
    │
    ▼
AssumeRole
    │
    ▼
Production Deployment Role
```

Trust policy and permissions policy should remain independently understandable.

---

# 71. Permission Boundaries

Permission boundaries may be used where delegated IAM creation is necessary.

They constrain the maximum permissions delegated identities can grant.

They do not grant permissions themselves.

---

# 72. IAM Policy Governance

IAM policies should be:

```text
Version controlled
Reviewed
Tested
Least privilege
Traceable to ownership
```

Security-critical permissions should not be manually edited without auditability.

---

# 73. KMS Architecture

AWS KMS should provide centralized cryptographic key management for supported AWS workloads.

```text
Application/Data
      │
      ▼
AWS Service
      │
      ▼
KMS Key
```

Encryption architecture should distinguish AWS-managed and customer-managed keys based on governance requirements.

---

# 74. Envelope Encryption

Large data should not normally be directly encrypted by repeatedly sending entire payloads to KMS.

Conceptually:

```text
KMS Key
   │
   ▼
Data Encryption Key
   │
   ▼
Encrypt Data
```

The encrypted data key can accompany encrypted content.

---

# 75. KMS Key Policies

Key policies are a critical authorization boundary.

A principal having access to an AWS resource does not automatically imply permission to use every KMS key.

---

# 76. Key Separation

Separate keys should be considered when required by:

```text
Environment
Data classification
Administrative boundary
Service ownership
Compliance
Blast radius
```

Do not create one KMS key per object or one universal key for the entire organization.

---

# 77. Key Rotation

Rotation policy should follow key type and governance requirements.

Rotation does not eliminate the need to:

```text
Control key access
Audit usage
Protect key policies
Plan key deletion
```

---

# 78. Key Deletion

KMS key deletion is potentially destructive.

```text
Delete Key
    │
    ▼
Encrypted Data
    │
    X
Cannot decrypt
```

Deletion requires waiting periods, approval and impact analysis.

---

# 79. Secrets Manager

Secrets Manager should be preferred for secrets requiring managed lifecycle capabilities.

Examples:

```text
Database credentials
External API credentials
Rotatable application secrets
```

---

# 80. Parameter Store

Systems Manager Parameter Store may hold non-secret configuration and selected protected parameters where its capabilities are sufficient.

Do not force every configuration value into Secrets Manager.

---

# 81. Secret Separation

```text
Configuration
      ≠
Secret
```

Example:

```text
DATABASE_HOST
→ configuration

DATABASE_PASSWORD
→ secret
```

This distinction improves lifecycle management.

---

# 82. Secret Rotation

Where supported and operationally safe:

```text
Old Secret
    │
    ▼
Generate New
    │
    ▼
Update Dependency
    │
    ▼
Validate
    │
    ▼
Retire Old
```

Applications must tolerate the chosen rotation strategy.

---

# 83. Secrets in Kubernetes

AWS secrets should be integrated into Kubernetes using an approved mechanism rather than manually copying long-lived credentials into manifests.

```text
Secrets Manager
      │
      ▼
Approved Integration
      │
      ▼
Pod
```

Git remains prohibited as secret storage.

---

# 84. RDS PostgreSQL

Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL should remain the primary managed relational database platform for Mediverse where PostgreSQL semantics are required.

```text
EKS Services
     │
     ▼
RDS PostgreSQL
```

Self-hosting PostgreSQL inside EKS is rejected for the primary production relational database unless a future requirement fundamentally changes the trade-off.

---

# 85. RDS Multi-AZ

Production databases should use Multi-AZ deployment where availability requirements demand it.

```text
AZ-A
Primary
   │
   │ synchronous managed replication
   ▼
AZ-B
Standby
```

Multi-AZ primarily improves availability—not read scaling.

---

# 86. Database Failover

Applications must tolerate database failover.

Expect:

```text
Existing connections break
Transient errors occur
Endpoint remains logically stable
New connections required
```

A Multi-AZ checkbox does not make applications failure-proof.

---

# 87. Read Replicas

Read replicas may support:

```text
Read scaling
Analytics-style workloads
Reporting
Selected read-heavy services
```

They introduce replication lag.

Do not use replicas where immediate read-after-write consistency is required unless the application handles the semantics.

---

# 88. Database Connections

Microservices can create a connection explosion.

```text
50 services
×
20 pods
×
20 connections

= 20,000 potential connections
```

Connection pools must be intentionally sized.

---

# 89. RDS Proxy

RDS Proxy should be evaluated where connection pooling/multiplexing provides meaningful benefit.

Potential cases:

```text
Highly elastic workloads
Large numbers of application instances
Connection churn
Serverless workloads
```

It is not automatically required for every Spring Boot service.

---

# 90. PostgreSQL Connection Pools

Application pools such as HikariCP should use bounded configurations based on:

```text
Database capacity
Replica count
Pod count
Workload behavior
Query duration
```

Increasing pool size is not automatically a performance improvement.

---

# 91. Database Encryption

RDS storage encryption should use KMS according to the platform encryption standard.

Encryption in transit should also be enforced for application connections where required.

---

# 92. RDS Backups

Production RDS should enable automated backups and point-in-time recovery according to defined retention requirements.

```text
Database
   │
   ├── Automated Backups
   ├── Transaction Logs
   └── Snapshots
```

---

# 93. Backup Is Not High Availability

These concepts solve different problems:

```text
Multi-AZ
→ Infrastructure availability

Backup
→ Historical recovery

Read Replica
→ Read scaling / selected DR capability
```

None replaces the others.

---

# 94. Backup Restore Testing

A backup that has never been restored is an assumption.

Regular exercises should validate:

```text
Backup exists
Backup is readable
Restore works
Application connects
Data is usable
Recovery time is acceptable
```

---

# 95. ElastiCache Redis

Amazon ElastiCache should host Redis workloads where managed Redis-compatible infrastructure fits Mediverse requirements.

Use cases may include:

```text
Caching
Distributed coordination
Rate-limit state
Ephemeral application data
```

Redis should not become the accidental authoritative database for critical durable business state.

---

# 96. Redis High Availability

Production Redis architecture should use appropriate replication and Multi-AZ failover where required.

Applications must still tolerate transient connection failures during failover.

---

# 97. Redis Cache Failure

Cache architecture should assume Redis can become unavailable.

Where Redis is genuinely a cache:

```text
Redis Down
    │
    ▼
Performance degradation
```

should be preferred over:

```text
Redis Down
    │
    ▼
Entire platform unusable
```

unless the feature fundamentally depends on Redis.

---

# 98. MSK / Kafka

Amazon MSK should be evaluated as the managed Kafka platform where ADR-052 Kafka requirements remain valid.

```text
Producer Services
       │
       ▼
      MSK
       │
       ▼
Consumer Services
```

---

# 99. Kafka AZ Architecture

Kafka brokers should span availability zones.

```text
Broker 1 → AZ-A
Broker 2 → AZ-B
Broker 3 → AZ-C
```

Topic replication must align with failure tolerance.

---

# 100. Kafka Durability

Production topics should define:

```text
Replication factor
min.insync.replicas
Producer acknowledgements
Retention
Partition strategy
```

These settings must align with ADR-052 delivery guarantees.

---

# 101. MSK Connectivity

MSK should remain privately reachable from authorized workloads.

Public Kafka brokers should not be the default architecture.

---

# 102. OpenSearch

Amazon OpenSearch Service should be evaluated for ADR-053 search workloads where its operational model fits.

It should remain a derived/search system.

```text
PostgreSQL
→ authoritative data

Events / indexing
→ OpenSearch

OpenSearch
→ search projection
```

---

# 103. Search Failure

Loss of OpenSearch should not corrupt authoritative business data.

Search may degrade while transactional systems remain available where product requirements allow it.

---

# 104. S3 Architecture

Amazon S3 should provide durable object storage for appropriate content such as:

```text
Images
Documents
Audio
Video source assets
3D assets
Exports
Backups where applicable
Logs
```

Buckets should be purpose-oriented rather than one universal bucket for everything.

---

# 105. S3 Public Access

S3 Block Public Access should remain enabled unless a narrowly justified architecture requires otherwise.

Public delivery should generally occur through controlled mechanisms such as CloudFront.

---

# 106. S3 Bucket Policies

Bucket policies should constrain:

```text
Allowed principals
Allowed actions
Transport security
Expected access paths
Cross-account access
```

Broad wildcard access should be rejected.

---

# 107. S3 Encryption

S3 objects should use appropriate server-side encryption.

Customer-managed KMS keys should be used where access governance requires them.

---

# 108. S3 Versioning

Versioning should be enabled for buckets where accidental overwrite/deletion recovery matters.

```text
Object v1
Object v2
Object v3
```

Versioning increases storage usage, so lifecycle policy must account for old versions.

---

# 109. S3 Lifecycle

Lifecycle rules should move or expire data based on actual access patterns.

Conceptually:

```text
Frequently Accessed
      │
      ▼
Less Frequent
      │
      ▼
Archive
      │
      ▼
Expiration
```

Do not archive data without considering retrieval latency and cost.

---

# 110. Multipart Upload

Large media uploads should use multipart/resumable mechanisms.

```text
Large Video
   │
   ├── Part 1
   ├── Part 2
   ├── Part 3
   └── ...
```

Failed abandoned multipart uploads should be cleaned through lifecycle policy.

---

# 111. Direct Client Upload

Where security requirements permit:

```text
Mobile/Web
    │
    ▼
Request Upload Authorization
    │
    ▼
Backend
    │
    ▼
Short-Lived Upload URL
    │
    ▼
Client ─────────► S3
```

can avoid proxying large binaries through application pods.

Authorization must occur before upload capability is issued.

---

# 112. Media Processing

Uploaded media should follow an asynchronous pipeline.

```text
Upload
  │
  ▼
S3
  │
  ▼
Event
  │
  ▼
Processing
  │
  ├── Validation
  ├── Transcoding
  ├── Optimization
  ├── Metadata
  └── Security checks
        │
        ▼
Published Asset
```

User-uploaded files should not automatically become trusted/public content.

---

# 113. CloudFront Media Delivery

Processed public/authorized media should use CDN delivery where appropriate.

For protected content, signed URLs/cookies or equivalent controlled access mechanisms should be evaluated.

---

# 114. Backup Architecture

Backup policy should classify workloads by recoverability.

```text
Workload
   │
   ▼
RPO / RTO
   │
   ▼
Backup Policy
```

Not every dataset requires identical retention.

---

# 115. AWS Backup

AWS Backup should be evaluated for centralized policy-driven backup of supported resources.

Potential benefits:

```text
Central policy
Cross-account backup
Retention
Vault management
Compliance visibility
```

---

# 116. Backup Isolation

Critical backups should be isolated from workload administrators where practical.

```text
Production Account
      │
      ▼
Cross-Account Backup
      │
      ▼
Backup/Security Account
```

This reduces the blast radius of destructive compromise.

---

# 117. Immutable Backups

Backup Vault Lock or equivalent immutability controls should be evaluated for critical recovery datasets.

The purpose is to resist:

```text
Accidental deletion
Malicious deletion
Ransomware-style destruction
```

---

# 118. Cross-Region Backups

Cross-region copies should be driven by regional disaster requirements.

A backup stored only in the failed region does not satisfy every regional disaster scenario.

---

# 119. CloudTrail

Organization-level CloudTrail should capture supported management activity centrally.

```text
AWS Activity
    │
    ▼
CloudTrail
    │
    ▼
Central Log Archive
```

Security-sensitive trails should be protected from workload administrators.

---

# 120. AWS Config

AWS Config should be evaluated for resource configuration history and compliance checks.

Questions it can help answer include:

```text
Was this bucket public?
When did this security group change?
Which resources violate policy?
```

---

# 121. GuardDuty

GuardDuty should provide managed threat detection across governed accounts.

Findings should enter a centralized security workflow rather than being ignored inside individual accounts.

---

# 122. Security Hub

Security Hub should aggregate supported security findings and posture signals.

```text
GuardDuty
Config
Inspector
Other supported findings
      │
      ▼
Security Hub
      │
      ▼
Triage / Automation
```

A dashboard full of unowned findings is not a security program.

---

# 123. Vulnerability Management

Vulnerability signals may originate from:

```text
Container scanning
Dependency scanning
Host/node scanning
AWS Inspector
Application testing
```

Findings require severity, ownership, remediation SLA and exception processes.

---

# 124. Centralized Observability

AWS telemetry should integrate with the broader Mediverse observability architecture.

```text
Applications
EKS
AWS Services
Databases
Network
     │
     ▼
Metrics / Logs / Traces
     │
     ▼
Central Observability
```

---

# 125. CloudWatch

CloudWatch should collect appropriate AWS-native:

```text
Metrics
Logs
Alarms
Service telemetry
```

It may coexist with Prometheus/Grafana/OpenTelemetry rather than forcing one monitoring system to solve every problem.

---

# 126. OpenTelemetry

Application telemetry should remain vendor-neutral where practical.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
OpenTelemetry
    │
    ├── Metrics
    ├── Traces
    └── Logs/context
```

This reduces unnecessary coupling between application instrumentation and a single backend.

---

# 127. Prometheus & Grafana

Kubernetes/application metrics may continue using Prometheus-compatible collection and Grafana dashboards.

Managed AWS offerings may be evaluated when they reduce operational burden without violating platform requirements.

---

# 128. Log Architecture

Logs should be:

```text
Structured
Timestamped
Environment-aware
Service-aware
Trace-correlated
Retention-governed
```

Do not log secrets merely because centralized logging exists.

---

# 129. Alerting

Alerts should represent actionable conditions.

Bad:

```text
CPU > 50%
```

with no operational meaning.

Better signals include:

```text
SLO burn
Sustained error rate
Critical dependency unavailable
Queue lag beyond threshold
Database capacity risk
```

---

# 130. RTO & RPO

Disaster recovery begins with explicit business requirements.

```text
RTO
→ Maximum acceptable recovery time

RPO
→ Maximum acceptable data loss window
```

Architecture cannot rationally select a DR strategy before these are defined.

---

# 131. DR Tiering

Different services may have different recovery requirements.

Example:

```text
Identity / Core Learning
→ High priority

Transactional database
→ High priority

Recommendation cache
→ Lower priority

Rebuildable search index
→ Lower data-recovery priority
```

Do not assign expensive active-active architecture to every component.

---

# 132. Backup-and-Restore DR

Lowest infrastructure cost:

```text
Primary Region
      │
      X
Regional Failure
      │
      ▼
Provision DR Infrastructure
      │
      ▼
Restore Backups
```

Recovery time is relatively high.

---

# 133. Pilot Light

Critical foundational services remain prepared in the secondary region.

```text
Primary
→ Full capacity

DR
→ Minimal critical foundation
```

During disaster, DR capacity is expanded.

---

# 134. Warm Standby

A reduced but functioning environment runs in the secondary region.

```text
Primary
→ 100%

Secondary
→ Reduced capacity
```

Failover scales the standby environment.

This costs more but reduces recovery time.

---

# 135. Active-Active

Both regions actively serve production traffic.

```text
Users
  │
  ├── Region A
  └── Region B
```

This creates major complexity around:

```text
Data consistency
Routing
State
Messaging
Deployments
Operations
Cost
```

Mediverse should **not adopt active-active multi-region by default**.

---

# 136. Mediverse DR Decision

Initial preferred model:

```text
Primary Region
→ Multi-AZ production

Secondary Region
→ Backup/pilot-light or warm-standby capability
   according to validated RTO/RPO
```

Active-active requires a separate future ADR and business justification.

---

# 137. Route 53 Failover

For multi-region DR:

```text
Route 53
   │
   ├── Primary healthy → Primary Region
   │
   └── Primary failed  → DR Region
```

DNS failover alone does not make the application recoverable.

Data, secrets, images, infrastructure and dependencies must also exist or be recoverable.

---

# 138. DR Data Replication

Each datastore requires its own DR strategy.

```text
PostgreSQL
→ backup / cross-region replica strategy

S3
→ replication / backup

Kafka
→ replication/recovery strategy

Redis
→ usually rebuild or replication depending on role

OpenSearch
→ snapshot/rebuild strategy
```

There is no single "replicate AWS" button.

---

# 139. DR Exercises

Disaster recovery must be tested.

```text
Declare Scenario
      │
      ▼
Recover
      │
      ▼
Measure RTO
      │
      ▼
Measure Data Loss
      │
      ▼
Validate Application
      │
      ▼
Record Gaps
```

A DR document that has never been executed is not evidence of recoverability.

---

# 140. Terraform Architecture

AWS infrastructure should be managed through Terraform according to the established IaC strategy.

Conceptually:

```text
modules/
├── network/
├── eks/
├── rds/
├── redis/
├── kafka/
├── storage/
└── security/

environments/
├── dev/
├── staging/
└── prod/
```

Modules should represent reusable infrastructure capabilities, not hide the entire AWS account behind one enormous module.

---

# 141. Terraform State

Terraform state must be remote, encrypted and access-controlled.

```text
Terraform
    │
    ▼
Remote State Backend
    │
    ├── Encryption
    ├── Locking
    ├── Versioning
    └── Restricted Access
```

State may contain sensitive infrastructure information.

---

# 142. Terraform State Separation

Production and non-production should not share one giant Terraform state.

Prefer boundaries aligned with:

```text
Account
Environment
Platform component
Blast radius
Ownership
```

One corrupted state file should not endanger the entire organization.

---

# 143. Terraform Execution

Production Terraform should run through controlled CI/CD workflows.

```text
Pull Request
    │
    ▼
terraform plan
    │
    ▼
Review
    │
    ▼
Approval
    │
    ▼
terraform apply
```

Routine production infrastructure changes from individual laptops should be minimized.

---

# 144. GitOps Boundary

Terraform and GitOps should have clear ownership.

```text
Terraform
→ AWS infrastructure
→ EKS cluster
→ foundational cloud resources

GitOps
→ Kubernetes applications
→ application configuration
→ platform workloads
```

Do not allow both systems to fight over the same resource.

---

# 145. Drift Detection

Infrastructure drift should be detected.

```text
Desired State
     │
     ▼
Actual AWS State
     │
     ▼
Difference?
```

Emergency manual changes must be reconciled back into IaC.

---

# 146. Tagging & Cost Allocation

Required resource metadata should include appropriate:

```text
Environment
Application
Owner
Cost center/team
Managed-by
Data classification where useful
```

Tagging standards should be enforced automatically where possible.

---

# 147. FinOps Architecture

Cost should be treated as an operational signal.

```text
AWS Usage
   │
   ▼
Cost Allocation
   │
   ▼
Budgets / Anomalies
   │
   ▼
Team Visibility
   │
   ▼
Optimization
```

Cost optimization without ownership usually becomes a periodic cleanup exercise rather than engineering discipline.

Key areas include:

```text
Compute rightsizing
Savings Plans
Reserved capacity where appropriate
Spot workloads
Graviton evaluation
S3 lifecycle
Idle resources
NAT Gateway traffic
Cross-AZ transfer
Cross-region transfer
Log retention
Oversized databases
Unused EBS volumes
Overprovisioned Kubernetes
```

---

# 148. AWS Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ Entire enterprise in one AWS account
❌ Production workloads in the Organizations management account
❌ Developers permanently holding AdministratorAccess in production
❌ Long-lived human AWS access keys
❌ Static AWS credentials inside Kubernetes manifests
❌ One giant node IAM role used by every pod
❌ Production databases exposed publicly
❌ 0.0.0.0/0 database security groups
❌ Overlapping VPC CIDRs selected without planning
❌ Public EKS nodes merely for convenience
❌ Every private AWS API call routed through NAT without analysis
❌ VPC endpoints created blindly without cost analysis
❌ One EKS cluster per microservice
❌ latest container tags in production
❌ Kubernetes namespaces treated as network isolation
❌ One universal KMS key for everything
❌ Secrets committed to Git
❌ Secrets treated as normal configuration
❌ Self-hosted primary PostgreSQL in EKS without strong justification
❌ Huge DB connection pools used as a performance fix
❌ Read replicas assumed to be strongly consistent
❌ Redis used as accidental durable system of record
❌ Kafka deployed without replication/failure planning
❌ OpenSearch treated as authoritative data
❌ Public S3 buckets used simply to make CloudFront work
❌ Large uploads proxied unnecessarily through application pods
❌ Backups existing without restore tests
❌ Backups controlled only by the same compromised workload account
❌ CloudTrail logs deletable by ordinary workload administrators
❌ Security Hub deployed with nobody owning findings
❌ Alerting on every metric fluctuation
❌ Multi-AZ described as disaster recovery from region failure
❌ Multi-region active-active introduced without RTO/RPO justification
❌ DNS failover treated as complete disaster recovery
❌ DR documentation never exercised
❌ One Terraform state for the entire organization
❌ Production Terraform routinely applied from laptops
❌ Terraform and GitOps managing the same resources
❌ Manual AWS changes never reconciled into IaC
❌ No cost allocation tags
❌ NAT/data-transfer costs ignored
❌ Kubernetes overprovisioning accepted indefinitely
❌ Cost optimization performed without reliability context
```

---

# 149. Final Mediverse AWS Reference Architecture

```text
                              USERS
                                │
                                ▼
                            Route 53
                                │
                                ▼
                    ┌─────────────────────┐
                    │ CloudFront + WAF    │
                    └──────────┬──────────┘
                               │
                  ┌────────────┴────────────┐
                  ▼                         ▼
             Static/Media                  ALB
                  │                         │
                  ▼                         ▼
                 S3                   ┌───────────┐
                                     │    EKS    │
                                     └─────┬─────┘
                                           │
                    ┌──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┐
                    ▼                      ▼                      ▼
                Services                Workers             Realtime
                    │                      │                      │
       ┌────────────┼────────────┬─────────┼───────────┐          │
       ▼            ▼            ▼         ▼           ▼          │
      RDS       ElastiCache     MSK    OpenSearch      S3 ◄───────┘
  PostgreSQL       Redis       Kafka
       │            │            │         │
       └────────────┴────────────┴─────────┘
                         │
                         ▼
                    KMS / BACKUP


               ───────── IDENTITY PLANE ─────────

             Enterprise Identity Provider
                         │
                         ▼
                 IAM Identity Center
                         │
              ┌──────────┼──────────┐
              ▼          ▼          ▼
           NonProd     Production  Security

                    Workload Identity
                         │
                         ▼
                 EKS Pod Identity/IRSA


               ───────── SECURITY PLANE ─────────

      Organizations / SCPs / IAM / KMS / Secrets
                         │
                         ▼
     CloudTrail / Config / GuardDuty / Security Hub
                         │
                         ▼
                Central Security Account


               ───────── NETWORK PLANE ─────────

                         VPC
                          │
          ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
          ▼               ▼               ▼
        AZ-A             AZ-B            AZ-C
          │               │               │
       Public          Public          Public
       Private         Private         Private
       Isolated        Isolated        Isolated
          │               │               │
          └───────────────┼───────────────┘
                          ▼
                   VPC Endpoints / NAT


               ───────── OPERATIONS PLANE ─────────

        OpenTelemetry / CloudWatch / Prometheus
                         │
                         ▼
                       Grafana
                         │
                         ▼
                 SLOs / Alerting


               ───────── DELIVERY PLANE ─────────

                         Git
                          │
              ┌───────────┴───────────┐
              ▼                       ▼
          Terraform                 GitOps
              │                       │
              ▼                       ▼
        AWS Infrastructure      Kubernetes State
              │                       │
              └───────────┬───────────┘
                          ▼
                    Production


               ───────── RECOVERY PLANE ─────────

                  PRIMARY REGION
                        │
              Multi-AZ Production
                        │
        ┌───────────────┼────────────────┐
        ▼               ▼                ▼
    Backups        Replication       IaC State
        │               │                │

                        ▼

                        ▼
```

---

# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                     | Decision                               |
| ------------------------ | -------------------------------------- |
| Cloud provider           | **AWS**                                |
| Account model            | **Multi-account**                      |
| Production isolation     | Separate AWS account                   |
| Security account         | Required                               |
| Log archive              | Centralized                            |
| Landing zone             | Control Tower evaluated                |
| Workforce access         | IAM Identity Center                    |
| Human credentials        | Short-lived/federated                  |
| Production admin         | Restricted + auditable                 |
| Break-glass              | Controlled emergency mechanism         |
| Workload AWS access      | EKS Pod Identity / IRSA                |
| Static AWS keys          | Avoided                                |
| Region baseline          | Single primary region                  |
| Availability             | Multi-AZ                               |
| Multi-region             | RTO/RPO-driven                         |
| Network                  | VPC with public/private/data tiers     |
| EKS nodes                | Private                                |
| Databases                | Private                                |
| VPC endpoints            | Cost/security evaluated                |
| Kubernetes               | Amazon EKS                             |
| Worker capacity          | Managed node groups                    |
| Dynamic provisioning     | Karpenter evaluated                    |
| Container registry       | ECR                                    |
| Image deployment         | Immutable                              |
| Primary relational DB    | RDS PostgreSQL                         |
| DB availability          | Multi-AZ                               |
| DB scaling               | Read replicas selectively              |
| Connection proxy         | RDS Proxy selectively                  |
| Cache                    | ElastiCache Redis                      |
| Event streaming          | MSK/Kafka                              |
| Search                   | OpenSearch                             |
| Object storage           | S3                                     |
| CDN                      | CloudFront                             |
| Edge protection          | WAF + AWS DDoS baseline                |
| Encryption               | KMS governed                           |
| Secret storage           | Secrets Manager                        |
| Configuration            | Parameter Store where appropriate      |
| Audit                    | Organization CloudTrail                |
| Threat detection         | GuardDuty                              |
| Security posture         | Security Hub                           |
| Configuration history    | AWS Config                             |
| Observability            | OpenTelemetry + AWS/platform telemetry |
| Backups                  | Policy-driven                          |
| Backup isolation         | Cross-account for critical data        |
| Immutable backup         | Evaluated/required by data class       |
| DR baseline              | Backup/pilot-light or warm standby     |
| Active-active            | **Rejected by default**                |
| DR testing               | Mandatory                              |
| Infrastructure as Code   | Terraform                              |
| Terraform state          | Remote + encrypted + separated         |
| Kubernetes desired state | GitOps                                 |
| Terraform/GitOps overlap | Prohibited                             |
| Drift detection          | Required                               |
| Tagging                  | Mandatory                              |
| FinOps                   | Continuous engineering discipline      |
| Production rollout       | Controlled                             |
| Status                   | **Accepted**                           |
| Priority                 | **Critical**                           |

---

# Part VI — Security, Identity & Compliance Architecture

# ADR-061 — Enterprise Infrastructure as Code & GitOps

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Argo CD RBAC**.

---

# 61. Argo CD AppProjects

AppProjects should provide security and organizational boundaries around groups of applications.

```text
Argo CD
   │
   ├── mediverse-nonprod
   ├── mediverse-prod
   └── platform
```

Projects should constrain:

```text
Allowed repositories
Allowed destination clusters
Allowed namespaces
Permitted resource kinds
Deployment permissions
```

An AppProject is a security boundary, not merely a folder.

# 62. Argo CD Applications

An Argo CD Application represents the relationship between:

```text
Git Source
    │
    ▼
Desired Kubernetes State
    │
    ▼
Destination Cluster/Namespace
```

Applications should have clear ownership.

# 63. ApplicationSets

ApplicationSets should generate Applications when environments, clusters or services follow repeatable patterns.

```text
ApplicationSet
     │
     ├── service-a-dev
     ├── service-a-uat
     ├── service-a-prod
     ├── service-b-dev
     └── service-b-prod
```

Avoid manually duplicating dozens of nearly identical Application definitions.

# 64. ApplicationSet Generators

Potential generators include:

```text
Git directories/files
Cluster inventory
Lists
Matrices
Pull requests where justified
```

Generator choice should remain understandable to operators.

# 65. Repository Boundaries

Mediverse should distinguish source repositories from deployment-state repositories.

```text
Application Repository
        │
        ▼
Source + Tests + Dockerfile
        │
        ▼
CI
        │
        ▼
Immutable Artifact


Environment Repository
        │
        ▼
Deployment Configuration
        │
        ▼
Argo CD
```

This separation supports controlled promotion.

# 66. Cluster Registration

Argo CD should receive only the cluster permissions required to reconcile its assigned workloads.

Registering a cluster must not automatically imply unrestricted cluster-admin privileges.

# 67. Destination Restrictions

AppProjects should restrict where applications can deploy.

Example:

```text
NonProd Project
      │
      X
Production Namespace
```

Repository content alone should not be sufficient to escape deployment boundaries.

# 68. Automated Synchronization

Automated synchronization may be enabled for appropriate environments.

```text
Git Change
    │
    ▼
Argo CD Detects
    │
    ▼
Automatic Sync
```

Production automation requires stronger validation and promotion controls upstream.

# 69. Self-Heal

Self-heal should restore managed resources that have drifted from Git.

```text
Git:
replicas = 3

Manual kubectl:
replicas = 8

        │
        ▼
Argo CD
        │
        ▼
replicas = 3
```

This is intentional reconciliation.

# 70. Pruning

Pruning removes managed resources deleted from desired state.

```text
Git Resource Removed
       │
       ▼
Argo CD
       │
       ▼
Kubernetes Resource Removed
```

Production pruning requires safeguards because a mistaken Git deletion can become a real deletion.

# 71. Manual kubectl Changes

Routine:

```text
kubectl edit deployment
```

against GitOps-managed production resources is rejected.

Emergency mutation may occur, but Git must subsequently be reconciled.

# 72. Sync Windows

Sync windows may restrict production changes during:

```text
Critical business periods
Known events
Maintenance freezes
Regulated change windows
```

They should not become permanent obstacles to emergency remediation.

# 73. Sync Waves

Resources with ordering requirements may use synchronization waves.

```text
Wave -2 → Namespace
Wave -1 → Configuration
Wave  0 → Database migration
Wave  1 → Application
Wave  2 → Supporting jobs
```

Ordering should be used only where a real dependency exists.

# 74. Resource Hooks

Hooks may support controlled lifecycle actions:

```text
PreSync
Sync
PostSync
SyncFail
```

Typical use:

```text
PreSync
   │
   ▼
Migration Job
   │
   ▼
Application Deployment
```

# 75. Hook Idempotency

Deployment hooks must tolerate retries.

A failed synchronization followed by another attempt should not corrupt the environment.

# 76. Health Checks

Argo CD should understand meaningful workload health.

```text
Synced
   ≠
Healthy
```

A Deployment existing in Kubernetes does not prove that the application works.

# 77. Custom Health Checks

Custom resources may require custom health interpretation when default Argo CD behavior cannot determine readiness correctly.

# 78. Orphaned Resources

Argo CD should detect resources within managed boundaries that are no longer associated with desired Git state where practical.

This helps expose unmanaged cluster drift.

# 79. GitOps Drift

The operational question should be:

```text
Why is the cluster different from Git?
```

rather than:

```text
Which engineer remembers what was changed manually?
```

# 80. Helm Architecture

Helm should remain the primary packaging mechanism for configurable Mediverse Kubernetes applications.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
Helm Chart
    │
    ├── Templates
    ├── Values
    ├── Schema
    └── Metadata
```

# 81. Helm Chart Structure

A conventional chart should remain understandable.

```text
chart/
├── Chart.yaml
├── values.yaml
├── values.schema.json
├── templates/
└── charts/
```

Avoid excessive abstraction that makes rendered Kubernetes resources impossible to reason about.

# 82. Chart Ownership

Every production chart requires an owning team.

Ownership includes:

```text
Versioning
Security updates
Compatibility
Documentation
Testing
Deprecation
```

# 83. Chart Versioning

Charts should use meaningful versioning.

Application version and chart version are distinct concepts.

```text
Chart version
→ packaging/configuration change

Application version
→ deployed software release
```

# 84. Values Hierarchy

Prefer a predictable hierarchy.

```text
Chart Defaults
      │
      ▼
Environment Defaults
      │
      ▼
Service Configuration
      │
      ▼
Explicit Overrides
```

Avoid five layers of undocumented values files.

# 85. Production Values

Production-specific values belong in governed deployment configuration.

Examples:

```text
Replica counts
Resource requests
Autoscaling
Domain names
Observability settings
Feature configuration
```

Secrets do not belong there in plaintext.

# 86. Helm Schema Validation

`values.schema.json` should validate important chart inputs.

It can catch:

```text
Wrong data types
Missing required values
Invalid enumerations
Malformed configuration
```

before deployment.

# 87. Library Charts

Library charts may encapsulate genuinely repeated template behavior.

They should not create an internal templating framework more complicated than Kubernetes itself.

# 88. Chart Dependencies

Dependencies should be explicit and version constrained.

Do not silently pull arbitrary latest dependency charts during production deployment.

# 89. Umbrella Charts

Large umbrella charts should be used cautiously.

Coupling every microservice release into one chart destroys independent deployment capability.

# 90. Configuration Governance

Configuration should be classified.

```text
Application defaults
Environment configuration
Runtime configuration
Secret configuration
Feature flags
Infrastructure configuration
```

Different categories require different ownership and lifecycle.

# 91. ConfigMaps

Non-sensitive Kubernetes configuration may use ConfigMaps.

```text
ConfigMap
   │
   ▼
Pod
```

ConfigMaps must never be treated as secret stores.

# 92. Configuration Versioning

Configuration affecting application behavior should normally be version controlled.

A production incident should be traceable to both:

```text
Code version
+
Configuration version
```

# 93. Immutable Configuration

Where practical, deployment configuration should produce a new workload revision rather than silently changing state underneath running applications.

# 94. Configuration Reloading

If applications support runtime configuration reload:

```text
Configuration Changes
        │
        ▼
Validate
        │
        ▼
Reload
```

behavior must be explicitly designed and tested.

Do not assume every Spring Boot property is safely hot-reloadable.

# 95. External Secrets

External Secrets Operator or an equivalent approved integration should be preferred for retrieving secrets from AWS Secrets Manager.

```text
AWS Secrets Manager
        │
        ▼
External Secrets
        │
        ▼
Kubernetes Secret
        │
        ▼
Pod
```

# 96. Secret Source of Truth

The source of truth for governed production secrets should remain the approved secret-management platform.

Not:

```text
Git
```

and not:

```text
developer laptop
```

# 97. Secret Rotation

Secret rotation must propagate safely to consumers.

```text
Secrets Manager
      │
      ▼
Rotate
      │
      ▼
Kubernetes Secret Updated
      │
      ▼
Application Reload / Restart
```

The final step must be intentionally designed.

# 98. Sealed Secrets Evaluation

Sealed Secrets can safely represent encrypted Kubernetes secret material in Git under appropriate controls.

However, if AWS Secrets Manager already provides centralized secret lifecycle management, introducing Sealed Secrets as another secret authority may create unnecessary duplication.

For Mediverse:

> **External secret retrieval from Secrets Manager is preferred over making Sealed Secrets the primary enterprise secret architecture.**

# 99. Git Repository Architecture

A possible model:

```text
mediverse-service/
├── src/
├── tests/
├── Dockerfile
└── helm/

mediverse-environments/
├── dev/
├── uat/
├── staging/
└── production/
```

Repository boundaries may evolve with organizational scale.

# 100. Application Repository

Application repositories own:

```text
Source code
Unit tests
Integration tests
Build definition
Dockerfile
Application-specific chart
```

They should not grant themselves uncontrolled production deployment simply because they produce an artifact.

# 101. Environment Repository

The environment repository represents what should be running.

```text
production/
└── course-service/
    ├── image digest
    ├── chart version
    └── configuration
```

Argo CD reconciles this state.

# 102. Build Once, Promote Many

A production artifact should not be rebuilt separately for each environment.

Preferred:

```text
Source
  │
  ▼
BUILD ONCE
  │
  ▼
Artifact A
  │
  ├── Dev
  ├── UAT
  ├── Staging
  └── Production
```

This preserves artifact identity.

# 103. Rebuild Per Environment — Rejected

This is rejected:

```text
Dev build
UAT build
Staging build
Prod build
```

from the same source revision.

Those are technically different artifacts.

Testing one does not prove another is identical.

# 104. Image Digest Promotion

Prefer immutable digest promotion.

```text
course-service
sha256:7ac...
```

rather than relying only on mutable tags.

# 105. Environment Promotion

The logical promotion path remains:

```text
DEV
 │
 ▼
UAT
 │
 ▼
STAGING
 │
 ▼
PRODUCTION
```

Promotion advances a verified artifact, not source code that gets rebuilt.

# 106. Promotion Gates

Each stage may require different evidence.

```text
DEV
→ automated tests

UAT
→ acceptance validation

STAGING
→ production-like validation

PRODUCTION
→ approval + policy + release criteria
```

# 107. Promotion Pull Request

Production promotion should normally be visible as a Git change.

```text
image:
- sha256:old
+ sha256:new
```

This provides reviewable deployment intent.

# 108. Database Migration Architecture

Database migration must be coordinated with application promotion.

Preferred principle:

> **Schema changes should remain backward compatible across the deployment transition whenever practical.**

# 109. Expand-and-Contract Migration

For risky schema changes:

```text
1. EXPAND
   Add new schema

2. DEPLOY
   Application supports old + new

3. MIGRATE
   Move/backfill data

4. SWITCH
   New schema becomes authoritative

5. CONTRACT
   Remove obsolete schema later
```

This is safer than destructive one-step migration.

# 110. Migration Rollback

Application rollback does not automatically reverse a database migration.

Therefore migration design must answer:

```text
Can old application code still operate?
```

before production deployment.

# 111. Feature Flags

Feature flags may decouple:

```text
Deployment
     │
     X
Feature Exposure
```

Code can be deployed while a feature remains disabled.

# 112. Feature Flag Governance

Flags require:

```text
Owner
Purpose
Default
Expiration/removal plan
Auditability
```

Permanent forgotten flags become technical debt.

# 113. Progressive Delivery

High-risk application releases should support gradual exposure where justified.

```text
New Version
    │
    ▼
Small Traffic %
    │
    ▼
Observe
    │
    ▼
Increase
```

# 114. Argo Rollouts

Argo Rollouts should be evaluated/adopted for workloads requiring advanced progressive delivery beyond standard Kubernetes Deployment behavior.

# 115. Canary Deployment

Conceptually:

```text
Traffic
   │
   ├──────── 95% → Stable
   │
   └────────  5% → Canary
```

Then:

```text
5%
→ 10%
→ 25%
→ 50%
→ 100%
```

based on validated health.

# 116. Canary Analysis

Promotion should evaluate meaningful metrics.

Examples:

```text
HTTP error rate
Latency
SLO burn
Crash/error signals
Business transaction failures
```

CPU usage alone is insufficient evidence of release correctness.

# 117. Automated Analysis

Where telemetry quality is strong:

```text
Canary
  │
  ▼
Metrics
  │
  ▼
Analysis
  │
 ┌┴────────────┐
 ▼             ▼
Healthy      Regression
 │             │
Promote      Abort
```

# 118. Blue/Green Deployment

Blue/green may be appropriate when two complete revisions can coexist.

```text
BLUE
Current Production

GREEN
Candidate
```

Traffic switches after validation.

# 119. Blue/Green Cost

Blue/green temporarily requires duplicate capacity.

It should not be selected merely because it sounds safer.

# 120. Rollback

Rollback should distinguish:

```text
Application rollback
Configuration rollback
Feature-flag disable
Database recovery
Infrastructure rollback
```

They are not equivalent operations.

# 121. Kubernetes Policy-as-Code

Cluster security rules should be enforced through admission policy where valuable.

```text
Deployment Request
       │
       ▼
Admission Control
       │
       ├── Allowed → Kubernetes
       └── Denied
```

# 122. Kyverno vs Gatekeeper

Mediverse should avoid running multiple overlapping admission-policy frameworks without need.

A practical default is:

> **Prefer Kyverno for Kubernetes-native policy authoring unless organizational OPA/Rego standardization makes Gatekeeper strategically preferable.**

The final choice should be standardized platform-wide.

# 123. Policy Enforcement Lifecycle

New policies should often move through:

```text
Audit
  │
  ▼
Observe violations
  │
  ▼
Remediate workloads
  │
  ▼
Enforce
```

Immediately enforcing an untested policy can break production deployments.

# 124. Namespace Policy

Namespaces should receive baseline governance for:

```text
Resource quotas
Limit ranges
Network policies
RBAC
Pod security
Required labels
```

# 125. Pod Security Standards

Mediverse workloads should align with Kubernetes Pod Security Standards at an appropriate level.

Production applications should avoid unnecessary:

```text
Privileged containers
Host networking
Host PID
Host filesystem mounts
Root execution
Excess Linux capabilities
```

# 126. Image Registry Restrictions

Admission policy should restrict production workloads to approved registries where practical.

```text
Production Pod
      │
      X
random-user/image:latest
```

# 127. Image Signature Verification

Container signing should be evaluated/adopted as the software supply-chain architecture matures.

Conceptually:

```text
CI
 │
 ▼
Build Image
 │
 ▼
Sign
 │
 ▼
Registry
 │
 ▼
Admission Verification
 │
 ▼
EKS
```

# 128. SBOM

Build pipelines should generate a Software Bill of Materials for production artifacts.

```text
Artifact
  │
  ├── Application
  ├── Libraries
  ├── OS packages
  └── Dependency metadata
```

This improves vulnerability and incident response.

# 129. Provenance

Artifact provenance should answer:

```text
Which source commit?
Which pipeline?
Which dependencies?
Which builder?
Which artifact digest?
```

Production trust should increasingly depend on verifiable provenance rather than artifact names.

# 130. Deployment Attestation

Higher-assurance environments may require evidence that:

```text
Source reviewed
Tests passed
Security scans passed
Artifact signed
Artifact originated from trusted CI
```

before admission.

# 131. Git Branch Protection

Critical repositories require branch protection.

Controls should include appropriate:

```text
Pull request review
Status checks
Restricted direct pushes
Required approvals
Protected branches
```

# 132. CODEOWNERS

CODEOWNERS should route high-risk changes to appropriate reviewers.

Examples:

```text
/prod/
→ Platform + Production owners

/security/
→ Security owners

/terraform/modules/iam/
→ Platform + Security
```

# 133. Signed Commits/Tags

Signed commits or tags may improve provenance where the organization can manage identity and keys correctly.

They should be evaluated as part of broader supply-chain assurance rather than treated as sufficient security by themselves.

# 134. GitOps Disaster Recovery

Argo CD itself must be recoverable.

The desired-state repository should contain enough information to reconstruct application deployment state.

```text
Git
 │
 ▼
Rebuild Argo CD
 │
 ▼
Register Cluster
 │
 ▼
Bootstrap Projects/Applications
 │
 ▼
Reconcile
```

# 135. Argo CD Backup

Persistent Argo CD configuration not declaratively stored elsewhere should be backed up.

But the preferred architecture minimizes irreplaceable control-plane state.

# 136. Repository Recovery

Git repositories are critical production infrastructure.

They require:

```text
Protected hosting
Access controls
Backup/recovery
Audit logs
Branch protection
Incident procedures
```

Losing GitOps source-of-truth repositories is a serious platform incident.

# 137. Cluster Bootstrap

A new cluster should follow an automated bootstrap path.

```text
Terraform
   │
   ▼
EKS
   │
   ▼
Bootstrap GitOps
   │
   ▼
Argo CD
   │
   ▼
Platform Applications
   │
   ▼
Mediverse Workloads
```

# 138. Bootstrap Minimalism

Terraform should bootstrap only enough Kubernetes capability to establish GitOps.

After that point, GitOps should own its designated Kubernetes resources.

This prevents permanent dual ownership.

# 139. Platform Self-Service

Platform engineering should eventually expose approved self-service capabilities.

Example:

```text
Developer requests new service
        │
        ▼
Golden Path
        │
        ├── Repository
        ├── CI pipeline
        ├── Helm chart
        ├── Namespace
        ├── Observability
        └── GitOps registration
```

# 140. Golden Paths

A golden path is an opinionated supported route.

It should make the secure/reliable option easier than inventing infrastructure from scratch.

Golden paths should not prohibit justified exceptions.

# 141. Developer Portal

A developer portal such as Backstage may be evaluated once service/platform scale justifies it.

Potential capabilities:

```text
Service catalog
Ownership
Documentation
Templates
Deployment visibility
Operational links
```

Introducing Backstage before there is meaningful platform complexity creates another platform to maintain.

# 142. Ownership Matrix

A clear ownership model is required.

| Resource                          | Primary Owner           |
| --------------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| AWS Organizations                 | Cloud Platform          |
| VPC/EKS/RDS                       | Terraform / Platform    |
| EKS cluster bootstrap             | Terraform               |
| Kubernetes applications           | Argo CD                 |
| Application Helm charts           | Service teams           |
| Platform Helm charts              | Platform team           |
| Production secrets                | Secrets Manager         |
| Kubernetes secret synchronization | External Secrets        |
| Container artifacts               | CI/ECR                  |
| Environment desired state         | GitOps repository       |
| Admission policy                  | Platform/Security       |
| Application feature flags         | Product/service teams   |
| Database migrations               | Service/database owners |
| Release promotion                 | Delivery workflow       |

# 143. Deployment Observability

Every production deployment should emit or expose:

```text
Application
Version
Artifact digest
Environment
Timestamp
Deployment ID
Git revision
Result
```

This allows telemetry to correlate failures with releases.

# 144. Deployment Metrics

Track at minimum:

```text
Deployment frequency
Deployment success rate
Failed deployment rate
Rollback rate
Lead time
Time to recovery
Change failure rate
```

These metrics reveal delivery-system quality.

# 145. GitOps SLO

The platform should eventually define objectives such as:

```text
Git commit accepted
      │
      ▼
Argo CD observes
      │
      ▼
Cluster converges
```

Excessive reconciliation delays should be observable.

# 146. Policy Metrics

Track:

```text
Policy violations
Denied deployments
Audit-only violations
Exceptions
Expired exceptions
```

A policy system that nobody measures becomes either ineffective or obstructive.

# 147. Configuration Drift Metrics

Track persistent:

```text
OutOfSync applications
Unmanaged resources
Failed reconciliation
Manually modified resources
```

rather than relying solely on dashboard inspection.

# 148. IaC/GitOps Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ Production infrastructure created manually by default
❌ One Terraform state for the whole enterprise
❌ Terraform state stored on laptops
❌ Secrets hard-coded into Terraform
❌ Assuming Terraform sensitive values disappear from state
❌ Unpinned providers
❌ Shared modules consumed from uncontrolled latest versions
❌ Giant Terraform modules managing everything
❌ Terraform and Argo CD controlling the same resource
❌ Routine production terraform apply from developer laptops
❌ Long-lived AWS keys in CI
❌ Plans applied without review
❌ Security scanners treated as proof of security
❌ ignore_changes used to hide drift
❌ Manual infrastructure changes never reconciled
❌ Infrastructure cost ignored during review
❌ CI directly using unrestricted kubectl against production
❌ Shared Argo CD admin credentials
❌ AppProjects without destination/repository restrictions
❌ Automated prune enabled blindly
❌ Manual kubectl edits used as configuration management
❌ Helm charts with undocumented override layers
❌ One giant umbrella chart for every microservice
❌ Plaintext secrets in values.yaml
❌ ConfigMaps used for credentials
❌ Git treated as production secret storage
❌ Multiple competing secret authorities
❌ Rebuilding application artifacts for each environment
❌ Mutable latest tags promoted to production
❌ Database migrations assumed to rollback with application code
❌ Feature flags without owners/removal dates
❌ Canary rollout based only on CPU
❌ Blue/green used without considering duplicate capacity
❌ Multiple overlapping Kubernetes policy engines
❌ Admission policies moved directly to enforce without validation
❌ Privileged containers accepted by default
❌ Production allowed to pull arbitrary registries
❌ Artifact names treated as supply-chain provenance
❌ Git repositories treated as non-critical infrastructure
❌ Cluster bootstrap requiring undocumented manual steps
❌ Platform self-service without security guardrails
❌ Developer portal introduced merely because it is fashionable
```

# 149. Final Mediverse IaC/GitOps Reference Architecture

```text
                           ENGINEER
                              │
                              ▼
                             Git
                              │
             ┌────────────────┴────────────────┐
             ▼                                 ▼
      APPLICATION REPO                  INFRASTRUCTURE REPO
             │                                 │
             ▼                                 ▼
             CI                            Terraform
             │                                 │
      ┌──────┼────────┐                        ▼
      ▼      ▼        ▼                 Validate / Plan
    Tests   Scan    Build                       │
                      │                         ▼
                      ▼                    Policy Gate
                     ECR                        │
                      │                         ▼
                 Immutable Image             Review
                      │                         │
                      ▼                         ▼
               Sign / SBOM                  AWS Apply
                      │                         │
                      │                         ▼
                      │                 AWS Infrastructure
                      │                         │
                      │                    ┌────┴────┐
                      │                    ▼         ▼
                      │                   EKS       Data
                      │                    │
                      ▼                    │
               ENVIRONMENT REPO            │
                      │                    │
              ┌───────┼────────┐           │
              ▼       ▼        ▼           │
             DEV     UAT    STAGING         │
                       \       │            │
                        \      ▼            │
                         └──► PROD           │
                              │             │
                              ▼             │
                           Argo CD ◄─────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
                        AppProjects
                              │
                              ▼
                    Applications/ApplicationSets
                              │
                              ▼
                           Helm
                              │
                              ▼
                    Admission Policies
                              │
                    ┌─────────┼──────────┐
                    ▼         ▼          ▼
                  PSS      Registry    Signature
                           Policy      Verification
                    │         │          │
                    └─────────┼──────────┘
                              ▼
                             EKS
                              │
               ┌──────────────┼───────────────┐
               ▼              ▼               ▼
           Services       Platform         Policies
               │
               ▼
        External Secrets
               │
               ▼
       AWS Secrets Manager


        ───────── PROMOTION PLANE ─────────

        Source Commit
             │
             ▼
          Build Once
             │
             ▼
       Immutable Digest
             │
             ▼
            DEV
             │
             ▼
            UAT
             │
             ▼
          STAGING
             │
             ▼
         PRODUCTION


        ───── PROGRESSIVE DELIVERY ─────

         Production Candidate
                  │
                  ▼
             Argo Rollouts
                  │
          ┌───────┴────────┐
          ▼                ▼
        Canary          Blue/Green
          │                │
          ▼                ▼
      Telemetry         Validation
          │                │
          └───────┬────────┘
                  ▼
            Promote / Abort


        ───────── GOVERNANCE PLANE ─────────

          Pull Request
               │
               ▼
        Static Validation
               │
               ▼
          Policy-as-Code
               │
               ▼
        Security / Cost
               │
               ▼
             Review
               │
               ▼

        ───── SOFTWARE SUPPLY CHAIN ─────

               │

               │
        ┌──────┼────────┐
        ▼      ▼        ▼

                       Scan

               │

               │

              +
        Git Repositories
              +
        Artifact Registry
              +
        Secret Authority
              │

              │
```
