
# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                          | Decision                                                 |
| ----------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| AWS infrastructure            | **Terraform**                                            |
| Kubernetes desired state      | **GitOps / Argo CD**                                     |
| Terraform/Argo overlap        | **Prohibited**                                           |
| Terraform modules             | Reusable + versioned                                     |
| Terraform state               | Remote, encrypted, segmented                             |
| State locking                 | Required                                                 |
| Production Terraform          | CI-controlled                                            |
| CI AWS credentials            | Federated/short-lived                                    |
| Terraform plans               | PR-visible                                               |
| Infrastructure policy         | Policy-as-code                                           |
| IaC security scanning         | Required                                                 |
| Drift detection               | Required                                                 |
| Manual production changes     | Emergency only + reconcile                               |
| GitOps model                  | Pull-based                                               |
| Argo CD                       | Primary reconciler                                       |
| Argo AppProjects              | Security boundary                                        |
| ApplicationSets               | Preferred for repeated patterns                          |
| Automated sync                | Supported                                                |
| Self-heal                     | Supported                                                |
| Production prune              | Controlled                                               |
| Helm                          | Kubernetes application packaging                         |
| Helm schemas                  | Required for important inputs                            |
| Secrets authority             | AWS Secrets Manager                                      |
| Kubernetes secret integration | External Secrets preferred                               |
| Sealed Secrets                | Secondary/not primary                                    |
| Artifact strategy             | **Build once, promote many**                             |
| Container identity            | Immutable digest                                         |
| Environment flow              | Dev → UAT → Staging → Prod                               |
| Production promotion          | Git-controlled                                           |
| DB migration                  | Backward-compatible / expand-contract                    |
| Feature flags                 | Governed                                                 |
| Progressive delivery          | Argo Rollouts                                            |
| Canary                        | Supported                                                |
| Blue/green                    | Selectively supported                                    |
| Automated analysis            | Telemetry-driven                                         |
| Admission policy              | Kyverno preferred unless OPA standard dictates otherwise |
| Pod security                  | Kubernetes PSS                                           |
| Registry restriction          | Enforced                                                 |
| Container signing             | Adopt/evaluate                                           |
| SBOM                          | Required for production artifacts                        |
| Provenance                    | Traceable                                                |
| Git protection                | Required                                                 |
| CODEOWNERS                    | Required for critical areas                              |
| GitOps recovery               | Declarative reconstruction                               |
| Cluster bootstrap             | Automated                                                |
| Platform self-service         | Golden paths                                             |
| Developer portal              | Backstage evaluated when scale justifies                 |
| Deployment telemetry          | Required                                                 |
| Status                        | **Accepted**                                             |
| Priority                      | **Critical**                                             |

---

---

# ADR-062 — Enterprise CI/CD & Software Supply Chain Security

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing from **Section 60 — Vulnerability Exceptions**.

---

# 61. SBOM Architecture

Every production software artifact should have an associated **Software Bill of Materials**.

```text
Source
  │
  ▼
Build
  │
  ├── Application Artifact
  │
  └── SBOM
        │
        ├── Components
        ├── Versions
        ├── Package identifiers
        └── Dependency relationships
```

An SBOM answers:

> **What exactly is inside this software?**

---

# 62. SBOM Scope

SBOM generation should cover relevant artifact types:

```text
Spring Boot JAR
Container image
Frontend application
Mobile application
Internal libraries
```

Container SBOMs are particularly important because the final image contains dependencies beyond application package managers.

---

# 63. CycloneDX

CycloneDX should be the preferred SBOM format where Mediverse security tooling supports it well.

It is designed around software-component and dependency analysis.

---

# 64. SPDX

SPDX should remain supported where ecosystem, compliance or external integration requirements demand it.

Mediverse does not need to generate multiple formats merely to claim support for more standards.

---

# 65. SBOM Generation Timing

SBOM generation should occur from the artifact actually being released.

Preferred:

```text
Final Artifact
     │
     ▼
SBOM Generation
```

rather than generating an SBOM from source assumptions that differ from the final package.

---

# 66. SBOM Identity

The SBOM should be correlated with immutable artifact identity.

```text
Artifact Digest
      │
      ├── SBOM
      ├── Provenance
      ├── Signature
      └── Scan Results
```

This creates an evidence bundle around a specific artifact.

---

# 67. SBOM Storage

SBOMs should be retained as release evidence.

They may be stored as OCI artifacts or in another governed artifact/evidence repository.

They should not exist only as temporary CI files that disappear after the job.

---

# 68. Vulnerability Correlation

SBOMs enable later vulnerability analysis.

```text
New CVE
  │
  ▼
Affected Component
  │
  ▼
Search SBOM Inventory
  │
  ▼
Affected Mediverse Artifacts
```

This matters because vulnerabilities are often disclosed **after** software reaches production.

---

# 69. Vulnerability Re-evaluation

An artifact that passed scanning on release day is not permanently secure.

```text
Day 1
Artifact → No known critical CVE

Day 30
New CVE published

Same artifact
→ Now vulnerable
```

Artifact inventories should therefore support continuous re-evaluation.

---

# 70. VEX

Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange should be evaluated as Mediverse vulnerability-management maturity grows.

VEX can communicate that a known vulnerable component is:

```text
Affected
Not affected
Under investigation
Fixed
```

according to supported standards and evidence.

---

# 71. VEX Limitation

VEX must not become a mechanism for suppressing inconvenient CVEs without technical justification.

A `not affected` assertion requires defensible reasoning.

---

# 72. Build Provenance

Production artifacts require provenance.

Provenance should answer:

```text
Which source repository?
Which commit?
Which workflow?
Which builder?
Which dependencies/build inputs?
When?
Which artifact digest?
```

---

# 73. Provenance Architecture

```text
Git Commit
    │
    ▼
Trusted CI
    │
    ▼
Build
    │
    ├── Artifact
    └── Provenance
           │
           ▼
      Attestation
```

The provenance belongs to the artifact identity, not merely its human-readable version.

---

# 74. SLSA

SLSA should provide the conceptual maturity model for Mediverse software supply-chain assurance.

The goal is progressively stronger guarantees around:

```text
Source integrity
Build integrity
Provenance
Build isolation
Tamper resistance
```

---

# 75. SLSA Adoption

Do not chase a SLSA level as a vanity certification exercise.

Controls should be implemented because they reduce real supply-chain risk.

---

# 76. Trusted Builders

Production artifacts should originate only from approved build infrastructure.

```text
Developer Laptop
      │
      X
Production Release


Trusted CI
      │
      ▼
Production Artifact
```

Locally compiled production binaries are rejected.

---

# 77. Build Isolation

Build jobs should be isolated sufficiently to prevent one build from contaminating another.

Ephemeral runners provide a strong baseline.

---

# 78. Runner Persistence Risk

Persistent runners can accumulate:

```text
Credentials
Repository files
Build artifacts
Malicious modifications
Caches
Environment state
```

A compromised job can potentially influence later jobs.

---

# 79. GitHub Actions Hardening

Production workflows should apply controls including:

```text
Minimal permissions
Protected environments
OIDC
Restricted secrets
Pinned Actions
Branch protection
Review requirements
Trusted runners
```

---

# 80. Third-Party Actions

Third-party GitHub Actions execute code inside the CI environment.

Therefore:

```text
uses: random/action@main
```

should not be considered trustworthy merely because it exists in the marketplace.

---

# 81. Action Pinning

Security-sensitive workflows should pin third-party actions to immutable references where practical.

```text
Action
   │
   ▼
Immutable Commit SHA
```

Mutable tags can move.

---

# 82. Action Review

High-privilege third-party Actions should be:

```text
Reputable
Reviewed
Version controlled
Minimized
```

Writing a few lines of shell may sometimes be safer than importing an unnecessary privileged dependency.

---

# 83. Workflow Modification Protection

Changes to:

```text
.github/workflows/
```

should require appropriate review.

A workflow change can be equivalent to changing production infrastructure permissions.

---

# 84. Dependency Provenance

Dependency security must consider more than CVEs.

Questions include:

```text
Who published it?
From which registry?
Was the package expected?
Has ownership changed?
Is the version authentic?
```

---

# 85. Package Pinning

Production builds should avoid uncontrolled floating dependency versions.

Lockfiles and version constraints form part of supply-chain integrity.

---

# 86. Registry Governance

Approved package sources should be explicitly configured.

```text
CI
 │
 ▼
Approved Proxy / Registry
 │
 ▼
External Ecosystem
```

This reduces uncontrolled dependency retrieval.

---

# 87. Sigstore

Sigstore should be adopted/evaluated for modern artifact-signing workflows.

It provides an ecosystem for signing and verifying software artifacts.

---

# 88. Cosign

Cosign should be the preferred tool for signing OCI/container artifacts where compatible with the Mediverse platform.

```text
Container Image
      │
      ▼
Cosign
      │
      ▼
Signature
```

---

# 89. Keyless Signing

Keyless signing should be preferred where organizational and platform requirements support it.

Conceptually:

```text
Trusted CI Identity
       │
       ▼
OIDC
       │
       ▼
Short-lived Signing Identity
       │
       ▼
Artifact Signature
```

This avoids long-lived private signing keys in CI.

---

# 90. Signing Identity

A valid signature is useful only if the verifier knows which identity is trusted.

Policy should validate:

```text
Expected issuer
Expected repository
Expected workflow/build identity
Artifact digest
```

not simply:

```text
"some signature exists"
```

---

# 91. OCI Signatures

Container signatures should be associated with immutable OCI image digests.

```text
Image Digest
    │
    ├── Signature
    ├── SBOM
    └── Provenance
```

---

# 92. Attestations

Attestations should represent claims about an artifact.

Examples:

```text
Built by trusted CI
SBOM generated
Tests passed
Security scan performed
Provenance generated
```

Claims should be machine-verifiable where practical.

---

# 93. Admission Verification

ADR-061 established Kubernetes admission policy.

ADR-062 supplies the evidence it verifies.

```text
ECR Image
   │
   ▼
Deployment Request
   │
   ▼
Admission Policy
   │
   ├── Trusted signature?
   ├── Trusted provenance?
   ├── Approved registry?
   └── Allowed artifact?
          │
      ┌───┴───┐
      ▼       ▼
    Admit    Reject
```

---

# 94. Verification Failure

If a production artifact lacks required trust evidence:

```text
Deployment
    │
    X
Production
```

The correct response is not to disable verification casually.

---

# 95. Helm OCI Artifacts

Helm charts should be distributed through OCI-compatible registries where this simplifies artifact governance.

```text
Helm Chart
    │
    ▼
Package
    │
    ▼
OCI Registry
```

---

# 96. Helm Provenance

Critical Helm packages should eventually receive equivalent provenance/signing controls.

Application security is undermined if a trusted container is deployed through a malicious chart.

---

# 97. Nexus Boundary

Nexus should primarily serve dependency/artifact repository functions where needed:

```text
Maven proxy
npm proxy
Internal libraries
Selected generic artifacts
```

---

# 98. ECR Boundary

ECR should primarily serve:

```text
Container images
OCI artifacts
Helm OCI artifacts
Associated supply-chain metadata
```

Do not deploy multiple repositories simply because they overlap slightly.

---

# 99. Artifact Retention

Retention should distinguish:

```text
Temporary CI artifact
Snapshot
Release candidate
Production release
Security evidence
```

Production evidence generally requires longer retention than temporary build outputs.

---

# 100. ECR Lifecycle

ECR lifecycle policy should clean:

```text
Old unreferenced images
Temporary builds
Stale development artifacts
```

without deleting artifacts required for production rollback or investigation.

---

# 101. Release Manifest

Each production release should produce a release manifest.

Example:

```text
Release: 2026.08.15

course-service:
  digest: sha256:...

auth-service:
  digest: sha256:...

frontend:
  digest: sha256:...

chart:
  version: ...

database:
  migration: ...

git:
  revision: ...
```

This gives the release an exact machine-readable identity.

---

# 102. Release Evidence

Production release evidence should connect:

```text
Source
  │
  ▼
Build
  │
  ▼
Tests
  │
  ▼
Security Results
  │
  ▼
Artifact
  │
  ▼
Approval
  │
  ▼
Deployment
```

---

# 103. Artifact Promotion

ADR-061's rule remains:

> **Build once, promote many.**

```text
Build
  │
  ▼
sha256:ABC
  │
  ├── DEV
  ├── UAT
  ├── STAGING
  └── PROD
```

---

# 104. Artifact Rebuild Prohibition

Do not:

```text
git checkout v1.5
build-for-dev
build-for-uat
build-for-prod
```

and pretend these are the same artifact.

They are different build outputs.

---

# 105. Promotion Evidence

Promotion should reference:

```text
Artifact digest
SBOM
Provenance
Security status
Test status
Environment validation
```

rather than only a semantic version string.

---

# 106. Separation of Duties

Production release permissions should be separated where organizational scale/risk requires it.

Example:

```text
Developer
→ produces change

CI
→ produces artifact

Release workflow
→ proposes promotion

Authorized reviewer
→ approves production

Argo CD
→ deploys
```

---

# 107. Production Environments

GitHub protected environments or equivalent controls should gate production-capable workflows.

Controls may include:

```text
Required reviewers
Branch restrictions
Environment secrets
Deployment protection
```

---

# 108. Production Approval

Approval should authorize a **specific release candidate**.

It should not grant an indefinite permission to deploy arbitrary future artifacts.

---

# 109. Emergency Release

Emergency release paths are necessary.

They should be:

```text
Fast
Controlled
Audited
Restricted
Post-reviewed
```

Emergency does not mean bypassing all security.

---

# 110. Emergency Workflow

```text
Critical Incident
      │
      ▼
Emergency Change
      │
      ▼
Minimum Required Validation
      │
      ▼
Authorized Approval
      │
      ▼
Deploy
      │
      ▼
Observe
      │
      ▼
Post-Incident Review
```

---

# 111. Rollback Artifact

Rollback should deploy a previously trusted immutable artifact.

```text
Current:
sha256:NEW

Rollback:
sha256:PREVIOUS
```

Do not rebuild the old commit during an incident.

---

# 112. Rollback Evidence

Rollback candidates must remain available with their:

```text
Image
Chart
Configuration
SBOM
Provenance
Migration compatibility
```

---

# 113. Database Migration Gate

Before production release, CI/CD should determine whether database migrations exist.

```text
Release
   │
   ▼
Migration?
   │
 ┌─┴─────┐
 ▼       ▼
No      Yes
 │       │
 │       ▼
 │   Compatibility Gate
 │       │
 └───────┴──► Deploy
```

---

# 114. Destructive Migration

Operations such as:

```text
DROP COLUMN
DROP TABLE
ALTER incompatible type
```

require stronger review.

Prefer ADR-061's expand-and-contract strategy.

---

# 115. Migration Testing

Database migrations should be tested against realistic PostgreSQL behavior.

Using H2 as the only migration validation environment is insufficient for a PostgreSQL production platform.

---

# 116. Mobile Signing

Mobile release pipelines introduce another high-value trust boundary.

```text
Source
 │
 ▼
Trusted Mobile Build
 │
 ▼
Signed APK/AAB/IPA
 │
 ▼
Store
```

Signing assets require strict access controls.

---

# 117. Android Signing

Android production signing keys should not be exposed to normal development or PR workflows.

Use controlled release infrastructure and supported Play signing mechanisms where appropriate.

---

# 118. iOS Signing

iOS certificates/profiles and App Store credentials should similarly remain restricted to trusted release workflows.

---

# 119. Mobile Artifact Identity

Mobile releases should retain:

```text
Source revision
Build number
Version
Signing identity
SBOM
Release evidence
```

---

# 120. Store Promotion

Mobile release is not identical to backend deployment.

```text
CI
 │
 ▼
Signed Artifact
 │
 ▼
Internal Testing
 │
 ▼
Beta/Test Track
 │
 ▼
Store Review
 │
 ▼
Production Rollout
```

Store-controlled lifecycle must be represented in release architecture.

---

# 121. Progressive Mobile Rollout

Where supported, mobile releases should use staged rollout.

```text
1%
 ↓
5%
 ↓
20%
 ↓
50%
 ↓
100%
```

when risk justifies gradual exposure.

---

# 122. Mobile Rollback Reality

Backend rollback can often occur quickly.

Mobile rollback is harder because users retain installed binaries.

Therefore mobile architecture must heavily emphasize:

```text
Backward-compatible APIs
Feature flags
Server-side kill switches
Version compatibility
```

---

# 123. CI Observability

The CI platform itself requires observability.

Track:

```text
Queue time
Build duration
Failure rate
Runner utilization
Cache performance
Artifact publication failures
```

---

# 124. Pipeline Telemetry

A pipeline should produce structured telemetry.

```text
Pipeline
   │
   ├── Repository
   ├── Commit
   ├── Workflow
   ├── Duration
   ├── Result
   └── Artifact
```

---

# 125. DORA Metrics

Mediverse should measure:

```text
Deployment frequency
Lead time for changes
Change failure rate
Time to restore service
```

These should inform improvement, not become targets teams game.

---

# 126. Pipeline SLO

Example objective:

```text
PR accepted
   │
   ▼
Required CI result
```

should complete within a defined target for the majority of normal changes.

A 45-minute mandatory pipeline for every one-line change destroys developer feedback loops.

---

# 127. Pipeline Stage Budget

Each stage should justify its execution cost.

```text
Fast checks
→ every PR

Expensive integration
→ appropriate changes

Full E2E
→ controlled stage

DAST
→ deployed test environment
```

Not every test belongs in every pipeline invocation.

---

# 128. Runner Autoscaling

Ephemeral runners should scale according to workload.

```text
Queue ↑
   │
   ▼
Runner Capacity ↑

Queue ↓
   │
   ▼
Runner Capacity ↓
```

Capacity policy must prevent uncontrolled cost explosions.

---

# 129. Build Cost

CI cost includes:

```text
Runner compute
Artifact storage
Network transfer
Container builds
Security tooling
Test infrastructure
Cache storage
```

Pipeline efficiency is a FinOps concern.

---

# 130. Cache Optimization

Cache hit rate should be measured.

Gigabytes of rarely reused cache can cost more than it saves.

---

# 131. Parallelization

Independent pipeline stages should run concurrently where this reduces feedback time without creating excessive compute waste.

```text
          ┌── Unit Tests
Checkout ─┼── SAST
          ├── SCA
          └── Lint
```

---

# 132. CI Concurrency

Redundant builds for obsolete commits should be cancelled where safe.

If five new commits arrive rapidly, spending resources fully validating four obsolete intermediate PR states may provide little value.

---

# 133. CI Disaster Recovery

CI configuration should be reproducible.

```text
Git repositories
Workflow definitions
Runner IaC
IAM configuration
Artifact registries
Secret references
```

should allow reconstruction of the software factory.

---

# 134. CI Provider Outage

The organization needs an operational response for CI provider outages.

Not every outage requires immediately maintaining an entire second CI platform.

Dual CI platforms can cost more operationally than the resilience they provide.

---

# 135. Artifact Registry Availability

Already-built production artifacts should remain available even when CI is unavailable.

CI failure must not prevent rollback to a known-good artifact.

---

# 136. Compromised Runner

If a privileged runner is suspected compromised:

```text
Isolate runner
     │
     ▼
Terminate
     │
     ▼
Revoke sessions/credentials
     │
     ▼
Identify executed workflows
     │
     ▼
Inspect produced artifacts
     │
     ▼
Invalidate untrusted releases
```

Ephemeral runners reduce persistence but do not eliminate incident response.

---

# 137. Compromised Dependency

When a dependency is compromised:

```text
Identify package/version
       │
       ▼
Search SBOM inventory
       │
       ▼
Identify affected artifacts
       │
       ▼
Determine production exposure
       │
       ▼
Patch / rebuild
       │
       ▼
Redeploy
```

This is one of the strongest practical reasons for maintaining SBOM inventory.

---

# 138. Signing-Key Compromise

If long-lived signing keys exist and are compromised:

```text
Revoke trust
Rotate keys
Identify signed artifacts
Re-establish trusted identity
Re-sign/rebuild where required
Investigate releases
```

This operational burden strengthens the case for keyless signing where feasible.

---

# 139. Malicious Release

A suspected malicious production artifact requires:

```text
Stop promotion
      │
      ▼
Identify artifact digest
      │
      ▼
Contain affected environments
      │
      ▼
Rollback
      │
      ▼
Revoke artifact trust
      │
      ▼
Investigate provenance
```

Artifact digest identity is critical during this process.

---

# 140. Supply-Chain Incident Response

Incident procedures should connect:

```text
Source Control
CI
Dependencies
Artifact Registry
Signing
GitOps
Runtime
Observability
```

Supply-chain incidents cross normal team boundaries.

---

# 141. Evidence Preservation

Security incidents require preservation of:

```text
Workflow logs
Audit logs
OIDC activity
Artifact digests
Provenance
Signatures
SBOMs
Deployment history
Repository changes
```

Retention policies must support investigation.

---

# 142. Release Audit Trail

For any production workload, Mediverse should eventually answer:

```text
What is running?
Who approved it?
Which source created it?
Which pipeline built it?
What tests passed?
What dependencies are inside?
What vulnerabilities were known?
Who signed it?
When was it deployed?
What configuration accompanied it?
```

If these questions require manually searching five systems for hours, release governance is weak.

---

# 143. Software Factory Ownership

The platform team should own common CI foundations.

Service teams own application-specific correctness.

Security owns/defines appropriate security policy.

Release governance should avoid turning the platform team into a manual deployment ticket desk.

---

# 144. Golden Pipelines

Supported templates should exist for major workload classes.

```text
Spring Boot Service
React Web Application
React Native Application
Terraform
Helm/Kubernetes
Internal Java Library
```

Developers should start from a secure pipeline rather than assembling one from random internet snippets.

---

# 145. Pipeline Evolution

Golden pipelines should be versioned and evolve deliberately.

Security improvements should be distributable across services without silently breaking every repository.

---

# 146. Release Engineering Metrics

Beyond DORA, track:

```text
Build success rate
Median PR feedback time
Flaky-test rate
Vulnerability remediation time
Rollback frequency
Artifact promotion time
Runner utilization
Security gate failure reasons
```

These expose software-factory bottlenecks.

---

# 147. Maturity Path

Do not attempt every advanced supply-chain control on day one.

A sensible progression is:

```text
LEVEL 1
CI + tests + immutable artifacts

        ↓

LEVEL 2
SAST + SCA + container scanning

        ↓

LEVEL 3
SBOM + secret scanning + IaC scanning

        ↓

LEVEL 4
Signing + provenance + attestations

        ↓

LEVEL 5
Admission verification + advanced SLSA controls

        ↓

LEVEL 6
Continuous artifact/vulnerability intelligence
```

This avoids building a security bureaucracy that the team cannot operate.

---

# 148. CI/CD & Supply-Chain Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ Production artifacts built on developer laptops

❌ Separate rebuilds for dev, UAT, staging and production

❌ Mutable release artifacts

❌ :latest as production artifact identity

❌ Long-lived AWS credentials inside CI

❌ Production credentials exposed to untrusted PRs

❌ Every CI job receiving every secret

❌ Persistent privileged runners without isolation

❌ Third-party Actions referenced blindly by @main

❌ Workflow files modifiable without review

❌ Dependency lockfiles ignored

❌ Random package registries used directly

❌ Dependency proxy treated as proof a package is safe

❌ Build secrets copied into Docker layers

❌ Huge runtime containers containing build toolchains

❌ H2 assumed to perfectly validate PostgreSQL behavior

❌ E2E tests used to replace unit/integration tests

❌ Flaky tests solved by infinite retries

❌ Coverage percentage treated as software quality

❌ SAST treated as complete application security

❌ Every CVE blindly blocking every release

❌ Critical CVEs blindly ignored because fixing them is inconvenient

❌ Security exceptions without expiry

❌ SBOM generated but discarded after CI

❌ SBOM unrelated to final artifact digest

❌ Artifact scanned only once and considered permanently safe

❌ SLSA levels pursued as vanity badges

❌ "Signed" accepted without validating signer identity

❌ Long-lived signing keys stored casually in CI secrets

❌ Provenance existing without verification

❌ Trusted container deployed through untrusted deployment metadata

❌ Production approval granting arbitrary future deployment power

❌ Emergency release meaning "disable every control"

❌ Rollback rebuilding an old commit during an incident

❌ Application rollback assumed to reverse database changes

❌ Mobile signing keys exposed to ordinary PR builds

❌ Mobile deployment treated like backend deployment

❌ Pipeline runtime allowed to grow indefinitely

❌ CI costs ignored

❌ Obsolete commits consuming unlimited runner capacity

❌ CI outage making existing production rollback impossible

❌ Compromised dependencies investigated without SBOM inventory

❌ Supply-chain evidence deleted before incident-retention requirements

❌ Golden pipelines becoming unversioned magic

❌ Security tooling added without ownership or remediation workflows
```

---

# 149. Final Mediverse Enterprise Software Factory Architecture

```text
                         DEVELOPER
                             │
                             ▼
                       SOURCE CONTROL
                             │
                             ▼
                       PULL REQUEST
                             │
        ┌────────────────────┼────────────────────┐
        ▼                    ▼                    ▼
      REVIEW             FAST TESTS          SECURITY
                             │                    │
                       ┌─────┼─────┐       ┌─────┼─────┐
                       ▼     ▼     ▼       ▼     ▼     ▼
                     Unit   Lint Contract  SAST  SCA  Secret
                                                     Scan
                       │     │     │       │     │     │
                       └─────┴─────┴───────┴─────┴─────┘
                                     │
                                     ▼

                                     │
                                     ▼
                              TRUSTED BUILDER
                                     │
                   ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
                   ▼                 ▼                 ▼
              Spring Boot          React          React Native
                   │                 │                 │
```

---

# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                          | Decision                                |
| ----------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Primary repository CI         | **GitHub Actions preferred**            |
| Jenkins                       | Retained only where justified           |
| CI runners                    | Ephemeral preferred                     |
| Production builds             | Trusted CI only                         |
| AWS authentication            | OIDC/STSv2-style short-lived federation |
| Long-lived AWS CI keys        | **Rejected**                            |
| Pipeline model                | Reusable golden workflows               |
| Java build                    | Maven/Gradle with pinned tooling        |
| Maven Wrapper                 | Preferred                               |
| React dependency installation | Lockfile-controlled                     |
| Dependency proxy              | Nexus evaluated/adopted where justified |
| Container builds              | BuildKit/buildx                         |
| Container pattern             | Multi-stage                             |
| Runtime images                | Minimal/non-root where practical        |
| Artifact strategy             | **Build once, promote many**            |
| Artifact identity             | Immutable digest                        |
| Source identity               | Git SHA                                 |
| Branch model                  | Short-lived/trunk-oriented              |
| Test strategy                 | Test pyramid                            |
| Integration infrastructure    | Testcontainers preferred                |
| PostgreSQL testing            | Real PostgreSQL behavior                |
| Quality platform              | SonarQube                               |
| SAST                          | Required                                |
| SCA                           | Required                                |
| Secret scanning               | Required                                |
| IaC scanning                  | Required                                |
| Container scanning            | Required                                |
| DAST                          | Risk-based                              |
| License checks                | Requirement-driven                      |
| SBOM                          | **Required for production artifacts**   |
| Preferred SBOM                | CycloneDX                               |
| SPDX                          | Supported where required                |
| SBOM retention                | Persistent release evidence             |
| Vulnerability re-evaluation   | Continuous                              |
| VEX                           | Evaluated                               |
| Provenance                    | Required                                |
| Supply-chain framework        | SLSA-aligned maturity                   |
| Signing                       | Sigstore/Cosign preferred               |
| Signing model                 | Keyless preferred where feasible        |
| Signature verification        | Production admission                    |
| Attestations                  | Machine-verifiable where practical      |
| Helm distribution             | OCI preferred                           |
| Container/OCI registry        | ECR                                     |
| Dependency repository         | Nexus where required                    |
| Production approval           | Specific release candidate              |
| Emergency release             | Controlled + audited                    |
| Rollback                      | Previous immutable artifact             |
| DB migrations                 | Compatibility-gated                     |
| Mobile signing                | Isolated trusted workflow               |
| Mobile rollout                | Staged where supported                  |
| CI observability              | Required                                |
| DORA metrics                  | Required                                |
| Pipeline SLOs                 | Required                                |
| Runner scaling                | Autoscaled                              |
| CI cost management            | Required                                |
| CI recovery                   | Declaratively reconstructable           |
| Supply-chain IR               | Required                                |
| Status                        | **Accepted**                            |
| Priority                      | **Critical**                            |

---

---

# ADR-063 — Enterprise Observability, SRE & Production Operations

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Dashboard Anti-Pattern**.

---

# 61. Business Observability

Technical health must connect to actual Mediverse outcomes.

```text
Infrastructure
     │
     ▼
Application
     │
     ▼
Business Workflow
     │
     ▼
User Outcome
```

Examples of business-level signals:

```text
Successful logins
Course launches
Lesson completions
Quiz submissions
Video playback starts
Search success
Payment completion
Notification delivery
```

A platform can have healthy CPU and still be failing users.

---

# 62. Business Metrics vs Technical Metrics

These answer different questions.

```text
Technical:
HTTP error rate = 0.2%

Business:
Course-start success = 82%
```

The first does not prove the second.

Business observability must complement technical telemetry.

---

# 63. Business Metric Cardinality

Business metrics must still obey telemetry-cardinality rules.

Good:

```text
course_start_total{
  result="success"
}
```

Bad:

```text
course_start_total{
  user_id="..."
  email="..."
}
```

Per-user identifiers do not belong in Prometheus labels.

---

# 64. Synthetic Monitoring

Synthetic probes should continuously test critical workflows.

```text
Synthetic Client
      │
      ▼
Route 53 / CDN
      │
      ▼
Application
      │
      ▼
Dependency
```

This validates the platform from an external perspective.

---

# 65. Synthetic Checks

Potential checks include:

```text
Homepage available
Authentication endpoint reachable
Course catalogue loads
API responds correctly
Critical static assets load
Health endpoints reachable
```

Complex synthetic transactions should be used selectively.

---

# 66. Synthetic Monitoring Limitation

A `/health` endpoint returning `200` proves very little about the complete user journey.

```text
GET /health
→ 200 OK

Student
→ cannot authenticate
```

is entirely possible.

---

# 67. Real User Monitoring

Frontend applications should capture real-user performance where privacy requirements permit.

RUM can reveal:

```text
Actual page latency
Browser-specific failures
Geographic performance
JavaScript errors
Resource loading failures
User experience degradation
```

---

# 68. React Telemetry

React telemetry should correlate frontend operations with backend traces where practical.

```text
Browser
   │
   │ trace context
   ▼
API Gateway / ALB
   │
   ▼
Backend Service
```

This allows investigation from browser interaction through distributed backend execution.

---

# 69. Core Web Vitals

Relevant web applications should observe user-experience signals such as:

```text
LCP
INP
CLS
```

where applicable.

Infrastructure latency alone cannot describe browser experience.

---

# 70. JavaScript Errors

Unhandled frontend errors should be captured with sufficient context to identify:

```text
Application version
Route
Browser
Error type
Release
```

without leaking sensitive user information.

---

# 71. Mobile Telemetry

Mobile applications require separate observability because deployed binaries remain on user devices.

Track relevant:

```text
App version
Crash rate
Startup performance
Network failures
API compatibility
Device/OS class
```

---

# 72. Mobile Crash Reporting

Crash-free sessions/users can provide a useful release-health signal.

A backend may be perfectly healthy while a new mobile build crashes during startup.

---

# 73. Mobile Version Distribution

Observe active application versions.

```text
v5.4 → 72%
v5.3 → 20%
v5.2 → 7%
older → 1%
```

Backend compatibility decisions must account for real version distribution.

---

# 74. Centralized Logging

Production logs should flow into a centralized logging architecture.

```text
Applications
Kubernetes
AWS Services
Platform Components
      │
      ▼
Log Pipeline
      │
      ▼
Central Log Backend
```

Engineers should not SSH into machines searching local files.

---

# 75. Structured Logging

Application logs should preferably use structured output.

```json
{
  "timestamp": "...",
  "level": "ERROR",
  "service": "course-service",
  "trace_id": "...",
  "event": "course_start_failed"
}
```

Structured logs enable reliable querying and correlation.

---

# 76. Log Schema

Standard fields should include appropriate:

```text
timestamp
severity
service
environment
version
trace_id
span_id
event
message
```

Consistency matters more than every team inventing its own "perfect" schema.

---

# 77. Log Severity

Severity should have defined semantics.

```text
DEBUG
→ diagnostic development detail

INFO
→ normal meaningful operation

WARN
→ abnormal but recoverable condition

ERROR
→ failed operation requiring investigation

FATAL
→ process/service cannot continue
```

Do not log every routine event as `ERROR`.

---

# 78. Trace Correlation

Logs should include trace context where available.

```text
Alert
  │
  ▼
Metric
  │
  ▼
Trace
  │
  ▼
trace_id
  │
  ▼
Related Logs
```

This is one of the highest-value observability integrations.

---

# 79. Sensitive Logging

Logs must not contain secrets.

Never intentionally log:

```text
Passwords
Access tokens
Refresh tokens
API keys
Private keys
Session secrets
Database credentials
```

---

# 80. PII/PHI Logging

Because Mediverse can process sensitive educational/medical-domain information, logging requires strict data minimization.

Do not casually log:

```text
Patient/student personal details
Medical information
Full request bodies
Authorization headers
Uploaded document contents
```

Observability does not justify uncontrolled data collection.

---

# 81. Redaction

Sensitive fields should be redacted before telemetry reaches centralized storage.

```text
Incoming telemetry
      │
      ▼
Filter / Processor
      │
      ▼
Redaction
      │
      ▼
Telemetry Backend
```

Redaction after sensitive data has already been widely replicated is weaker.

---

# 82. Logging Allowlist

For sensitive services, an allowlist approach can be safer than trying to blacklist every dangerous field.

```text
Explicitly approved fields
        │
        ▼
Structured Log
```

Unknown payload content should not automatically be serialized.

---

# 83. Log Retention

Retention should depend on log class.

```text
Debug/application logs
→ shorter

Operational logs
→ medium

Security/audit logs
→ longer according to policy
```

Keeping everything forever is expensive and creates additional security exposure.

---

# 84. Log Tiers

A useful model is:

```text
Hot
 │
 ▼
Fast interactive search
 │
 ▼
Warm
 │
 ▼
Lower-cost retention
 │
 ▼
Archive
```

The exact architecture should follow investigation requirements.

---

# 85. Loki vs OpenSearch

For Kubernetes/application operational logs, **Loki should be preferred when the primary requirement is cost-efficient log aggregation tightly integrated with Grafana**.

OpenSearch should remain appropriate where richer full-text search/indexing requirements justify it.

Do not operate both for identical logs without a reason.

---

# 86. Loki Architecture

Conceptually:

```text
Pods
 │
 ▼
Log Agent
 │
 ▼
Loki
 │
 ▼
Grafana
```

Loki's label model requires the same cardinality discipline as metrics systems.

---

# 87. Log Label Cardinality

Never create labels from uncontrolled identifiers such as:

```text
request_id
trace_id
user_id
session_id
full URL
```

Trace IDs belong in log content/structured fields, not high-cardinality index labels.

---

# 88. Audit Logs

Audit logs differ from normal application debugging logs.

They should capture security/business-sensitive events such as:

```text
Authentication changes
Privilege changes
Administrative actions
Sensitive configuration changes
Security policy changes
Critical data operations
```

according to requirements.

---

# 89. Audit Log Integrity

Audit logs should be protected against unauthorized modification/deletion.

```text
Workload
   │
   ▼
Audit Event
   │
   ▼
Protected Central Storage
```

The actor being audited should not trivially erase the evidence.

---

# 90. Alert Architecture

Alerts should detect conditions requiring human or automated action.

```text
Telemetry
   │
   ▼
Alert Rule
   │
   ▼
Routing
   │
   ▼
Owner
   │
   ▼
Action
```

An alert without a defined action should be questioned.

---

# 91. Alertmanager

Prometheus Alertmanager or equivalent should provide:

```text
Grouping
Routing
Deduplication
Inhibition
Silencing
Notification
```

for Prometheus-derived alerts.

---

# 92. Alert Grouping

Related alerts should be grouped.

Bad:

```text
course-service pod-1 down
course-service pod-2 down
course-service pod-3 down
course-service pod-4 down
...
```

Better:

```text
Course service availability degraded
```

with diagnostic detail attached.

---

# 93. Deduplication

Multiple telemetry sources may detect the same incident.

Operators should not receive twenty pages for one underlying failure.

---

# 94. Alert Inhibition

Secondary alerts should be suppressed when a known parent failure explains them.

Example:

```text
EKS Node Failure
      │
      ├── Pod unavailable
      ├── scrape failed
      ├── service degraded
      └── workload restart
```

Paging independently on all symptoms creates noise.

---

# 95. Paging vs Ticketing

Not every alert deserves a page.

```text
PAGE
→ immediate human action required

TICKET
→ action required but not immediately

DASHBOARD
→ informational/diagnostic
```

If nobody should wake up at 3 AM for it, it probably should not page at 3 AM.

---

# 96. Actionable Alerts

Every paging alert should ideally answer:

```text
What failed?
What is the user impact?
Who owns it?
Where is the dashboard?
Where is the runbook?
```

---

# 97. Alert Thresholds

Static infrastructure thresholds should not dominate alerting.

Instead of:

```text
CPU > 80%
```

prefer user-impact or saturation signals when possible.

High CPU can represent efficient utilization rather than failure.

---

# 98. SLI Architecture

A Service Level Indicator measures an aspect of user-visible reliability.

```text
Good Events
────────────
Total Events
```

is a common pattern.

---

# 99. SLO

A Service Level Objective defines the target reliability.

Example:

```text
99.9% successful course-start requests
over 30 days
```

SLOs should reflect meaningful user experience.

---

# 100. SLA vs SLO

```text
SLI
→ measurement

SLO
→ internal reliability objective

SLA
→ external/business agreement with consequences
```

These terms should not be used interchangeably.

---

# 101. Availability SLI

Example:

```text
Successful eligible requests
────────────────────────────
Total eligible requests
```

Defining "eligible" and "successful" correctly matters.

---

# 102. Latency SLI

Example:

```text
Requests completed < 500 ms
────────────────────────────
Total valid requests
```

This is often more meaningful than average latency.

---

# 103. Correctness SLI

Some systems can respond successfully but return wrong results.

Therefore critical workflows may need correctness indicators.

```text
Correct successful operations
─────────────────────────────
Total operations
```

---

# 104. Freshness SLI

Asynchronous systems may require freshness.

Example:

```text
Notification generated
      │
      ▼
Delivered within 60 sec?
```

Availability alone cannot represent delayed processing.

---

# 105. Kafka Lag SLI

For event-driven workflows:

```text
Events processed within target delay
────────────────────────────────────
Total relevant events
```

can be more user-centric than raw broker availability.

---

# 106. Composite Journey SLO

Critical journeys may cross multiple services.

```text
Login
  │
  ▼
Find Course
  │
  ▼
Open Lesson
  │
  ▼
Start Playback
```

A user-journey SLO can reveal reliability failures hidden by individual service SLOs.

---

# 107. Dependency SLO

Services should understand dependency reliability.

However:

> A downstream provider's SLO does not automatically become your service's SLO.

Your architecture may need caching, retries, redundancy or graceful degradation.

---

# 108. Error Budget

For a 99.9% SLO:

```text
Allowed unreliability
= 0.1%
```

This allowance is the error budget.

It converts reliability from vague aspiration into measurable engineering capacity.

---

# 109. Error Budget Consumption

```text
Healthy system
→ budget consumed slowly

Major incident
→ budget consumed rapidly
```

Teams should monitor consumption rather than waiting until the end of the month.

---

# 110. Error Budget Policy

When a service burns excessive budget:

```text
Feature velocity
      ↓

Reliability work
      ↑
```

may be appropriate.

SLOs without consequences for repeated violation are just dashboard decorations.

---

# 111. Burn Rate

Burn rate measures how quickly the error budget is being consumed.

```text
Burn rate = 1
→ budget consumed at expected maximum rate

Burn rate >> 1
→ reliability deteriorating too quickly
```

---

# 112. Multi-Window Burn Alerts

SLO alerting should use multiple windows where practical.

```text
Fast burn
→ severe current incident

Slow burn
→ persistent degradation
```

This reduces both missed incidents and noisy transient alerts.

---

# 113. Service Ownership Registry

Every service should expose ownership metadata.

```text
course-service
Owner: Learning Platform Team
Runbook: ...
Dashboard: ...
Repository: ...
SLO: ...
```

This may later integrate with the developer portal defined in ADR-061.

---

# 114. On-Call

Critical production services require a defined response mechanism.

On-call responsibilities must align with actual service ownership.

Do not page teams for systems they cannot diagnose or change.

---

# 115. Incident Severity

Mediverse should define a severity model.

Example:

```text
SEV-1
Critical widespread outage/security impact

SEV-2
Major degradation

SEV-3
Limited production impact

SEV-4
Minor operational issue
```

Exact criteria should be documented.

---

# 116. Incident Declaration

An incident should be declared based on impact and risk, not embarrassment.

Early declaration improves coordination during significant failures.

---

# 117. Incident Commander

Major incidents should assign an Incident Commander.

The IC coordinates:

```text
Priorities
People
Communication
Decision flow
Escalation
```

The IC does not need to personally debug every component.

---

# 118. Incident Roles

For larger incidents:

```text
Incident Commander
      │
      ├── Technical Lead
      ├── Communications
      ├── Scribe
      └── Subject-Matter Experts
```

Roles prevent everyone from simultaneously debugging while nobody coordinates.

---

# 119. Incident Timeline

Important events should be recorded:

```text
21:04 Alert fired
21:07 Incident declared
21:10 DB saturation identified
21:14 traffic reduced
21:21 service recovered
```

Accurate timelines dramatically improve later analysis.

---

# 120. Incident Communication

Communication should state:

```text
Impact
Current status
Mitigation
Next update
```

Do not publish speculative root causes during active response as established facts.

---

# 121. Runbooks

A runbook provides actionable response steps for known operational conditions.

Example:

```text
Alert:
Kafka consumer lag high

Runbook:
1. Confirm affected consumer group
2. Check processing rate
3. Check consumer errors
4. Check partition assignment
5. Check dependency latency
6. Evaluate safe scaling
```

---

# 122. Runbook Quality

Bad runbook:

```text
"Investigate Kafka."
```

That adds almost no value.

A useful runbook shortens diagnosis or mitigation.

---

# 123. Playbooks

Playbooks address broader scenarios.

Examples:

```text
Regional outage
Database corruption
Credential compromise
Kafka outage
Massive traffic spike
Bad deployment
```

They coordinate multiple systems and teams.

---

# 124. Safe Production Debugging

Production diagnostics should prefer:

```text
Metrics
Logs
Traces
Profiling
Read-only queries
Controlled ephemeral debugging
```

before invasive changes.

---

# 125. Debug Containers

Kubernetes ephemeral debugging capabilities may be used under controlled access.

They must not become a way to bypass:

```text
RBAC
Image policy
Audit
Production access governance
```

---

# 126. Production SQL

Direct production SQL requires strict controls.

Diagnostic queries should be:

```text
Read-only where possible
Bounded
Reviewed for expensive scans
Audited
```

A "quick query" can become the production incident.

---

# 127. Postmortems

Significant incidents should produce postmortems covering:

```text
Impact
Timeline
Detection
Contributing factors
Root causes
Mitigation
Recovery
What worked
What failed
Actions
Owners
Deadlines
```

---

# 128. Blameless Does Not Mean Accountability-Free

A useful postmortem avoids personal blame while still identifying:

```text
Bad decisions
Missing controls
Incorrect assumptions
Process failures
Technical defects
Unowned risks
```

Calling everything a "system issue" to avoid difficult conclusions defeats the purpose.

---

# 129. Root Cause

Complex incidents often have multiple contributing causes.

Avoid simplistic:

```text
"Engineer deployed bad code."
```

Better analysis asks:

```text
Why could the change pass CI?
Why did canary detection miss it?
Why was blast radius large?
Why did rollback take 40 minutes?
```

---

# 130. Corrective Actions

Postmortem actions must be:

```text
Specific
Owned
Prioritized
Trackable
Time-bound where appropriate
```

"Improve monitoring" is not an adequate corrective action.

---

# 131. Recurring Problem Management

Repeated incidents should be grouped into systemic reliability work.

If the same service fails every month, repeatedly improving the runbook is not enough.

The underlying architecture must be fixed.

---

# 132. Capacity Planning

Capacity management should use historical and forecast signals.

```text
Current demand
      │
      ▼
Growth trend
      │
      ▼
Peak multiplier
      │
      ▼
Failure headroom
      │
      ▼
Capacity requirement
```

---

# 133. Headroom

Running every critical resource continuously at 99% capacity is not efficient architecture.

It removes failure and traffic-spike tolerance.

---

# 134. Load Testing

Critical services should undergo representative load testing before major scale events or architectural changes.

Test:

```text
Normal load
Peak load
Burst load
Sustained load
Overload
Recovery
```

---

# 135. Load Test Realism

A test generating 100,000 requests to one trivial endpoint does not prove the application handles 100,000 real users.

Realistic workload mixes matter.

---

# 136. Performance Baselines

Maintain known baselines for:

```text
Throughput
p50 latency
p95 latency
p99 latency
Error rate
Resource consumption
Dependency load
```

Performance regression should be detectable between releases.

---

# 137. Chaos Engineering

Chaos engineering should validate known resilience assumptions.

Examples:

```text
Kill pod
Terminate node
Introduce dependency latency
Remove Redis
Interrupt Kafka consumer
Simulate AZ-related failure
```

It should not mean randomly breaking production.

---

# 138. Chaos Hypothesis

Every experiment needs a hypothesis.

```text
Given:
one course-service pod fails

We expect:
no meaningful user-visible availability loss
```

Then test whether reality matches architecture.

---

# 139. Blast Radius

Chaos experiments should start with bounded blast radius.

```text
Development
   ↓
Staging
   ↓
Controlled production
```

Production chaos should occur only when maturity and safeguards justify it.

---

# 140. Game Days

Game days simulate coordinated failure scenarios.

Example:

```text
Scenario:
Primary database failover

Validate:
Detection
Alerting
Application retry
Connection recovery
Communication
Runbook
SLO impact
```

They test people and processes as well as technology.

---

# 141. Operational Readiness Review

Before a critical service reaches production, verify:

```text
Owner exists
Dashboard exists
SLO defined
Alerts configured
Runbook available
Capacity understood
Dependencies known
Backup/recovery defined
Security reviewed
Deployment/rollback tested
```

---

# 142. Production Readiness

"Works on staging" is insufficient.

A production-ready service must be:

```text
Deployable
Observable
Supportable
Recoverable
Scalable
Secure
Owned
```

---

# 143. Deployment Markers

Dashboards should show deployments.

```text
Latency
  │
  │       ▲ Release 5.8.1
  │       │
  │       │    ╭──────
  │───────┴────╯
```

This makes release-related regressions obvious.

---

# 144. DORA Integration

ADR-062's DORA metrics should integrate with operational telemetry.

```text
Deployment
    │
    ▼
Production behavior
    │
    ▼
Incident?
Rollback?
SLO impact?
```

Deployment frequency without change-failure context is incomplete.

---

# 145. Cost Observability

Operational dashboards should expose relevant cost drivers.

Examples:

```text
EKS compute
RDS capacity
Kafka storage
OpenSearch
Telemetry ingestion
Log retention
Cross-AZ traffic
NAT traffic
```

Reliability and cost must be analyzed together.

---

# 146. Observability Platform SLO

The observability platform itself requires reliability objectives.

During an incident, losing:

```text
Metrics
Logs
Traces
Alerts
```

simultaneously is extremely damaging.

Monitor the monitoring system.

---

# 147. Telemetry Pipeline Failure

Applications should tolerate telemetry backend failure.

The pipeline should detect:

```text
Dropped telemetry
Collector queue growth
Export failures
Backend ingestion failures
Sampling anomalies
```

Observability must itself be observable.

---

# 148. Observability & SRE Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ "Install Prometheus and Grafana" treated as an observability strategy
❌ Infrastructure health treated as user health
❌ Every application inventing unrelated telemetry conventions
❌ Metrics, logs and traces impossible to correlate
❌ user_id/email/request_id used as Prometheus labels
❌ Unbounded metric cardinality
❌ Average latency used as the only latency measure
❌ Histograms created with meaningless buckets
❌ Every trace stored forever
❌ Sampling errors away
❌ OpenTelemetry Collector failure crashing applications
❌ Database CPU treated as complete DB observability
❌ Kafka broker uptime treated as proof consumers are healthy
❌ Redis hit-rate changes ignored while DB load explodes
❌ 80-chart dashboards nobody can interpret
❌ /health returning 200 treated as proof user journeys work
❌ Frontend/mobile failures invisible to backend monitoring
❌ Plaintext secrets written to logs
❌ Authorization headers logged
❌ Sensitive request bodies logged "for debugging"
❌ Infinite log retention
❌ Trace IDs used as Loki/Prometheus high-cardinality labels
❌ Every warning generating a page
❌ CPU > 80% waking engineers without user impact
❌ Alert storms for one root failure
❌ Paging teams that do not own the service
❌ Alerts without runbooks
❌ SLOs chosen because 99.99% sounds professional
❌ SLIs based on infrastructure rather than user outcomes
❌ Error budgets calculated but never used
❌ Every incident labeled SEV-1
❌ Ten engineers debugging while nobody coordinates
❌ Speculative root cause communicated during active incident
❌ Runbooks saying only "investigate"
❌ Uncontrolled production SQL during incidents
❌ Blameless postmortems used to avoid accountability
❌ Postmortem actions without owners
❌ Repeated incidents accepted as normal
❌ Capacity planning based only on average traffic
❌ Load testing unrealistic endpoints
❌ Chaos engineering interpreted as random destruction
❌ Production chaos without blast-radius controls
❌ Services launched without owners
❌ Services launched without rollback procedures
❌ Monitoring platform not monitoring itself
❌ Telemetry cost treated as unlimited
```

---

# 149. Final Mediverse Enterprise SRE Reference Architecture

```text
                              USERS
                                │
              ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
              ▼                 ▼                 ▼

                                ▼
                         MEDIVERSE EDGE

                                ▼
```

---

# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                           | Decision                                 |
| ------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------- |
| Observability framework        | **OpenTelemetry**                        |
| Application metrics            | Prometheus-compatible                    |
| Visualization                  | Grafana                                  |
| Operational logging            | Loki preferred where suitable            |
| Search-heavy logs              | OpenSearch selectively                   |
| Telemetry signals              | Metrics + logs + traces                  |
| Request monitoring             | RED                                      |
| Resource monitoring            | USE                                      |
| User monitoring                | Business SLIs + RUM + synthetics         |
| Trace propagation              | Required                                 |
| Log/trace correlation          | Required                                 |
| High-cardinality metric labels | Prohibited                               |
| Histogram strategy             | Required for critical latency            |
| Exemplars                      | Preferred                                |
| Kubernetes state               | kube-state-metrics                       |
| Node telemetry                 | Required                                 |
| AWS telemetry                  | Integrated                               |
| RDS monitoring                 | DB + query + connection level            |
| Redis monitoring               | Required                                 |
| Kafka monitoring               | Broker + consumer lag                    |
| Frontend observability         | RUM                                      |
| Mobile observability           | Crash/performance/version telemetry      |
| Logging                        | Structured                               |
| Sensitive logging              | Restricted/redacted                      |
| Log retention                  | Tiered                                   |
| Audit logs                     | Protected                                |
| Alert manager                  | Alertmanager/equivalent                  |
| Paging                         | User-impact/action-driven                |
| Alert deduplication            | Required                                 |
| SLI                            | User-centric                             |
| SLO                            | Required for critical services           |
| Error budgets                  | Required                                 |
| Burn-rate alerts               | Preferred                                |
| Composite journey SLOs         | Supported                                |
| Ownership                      | Mandatory                                |
| On-call                        | Critical services                        |
| Incident severity              | Standardized                             |
| Incident command               | Major incidents                          |
| Runbooks                       | Required for paging alerts               |
| Postmortems                    | Significant incidents                    |
| Corrective actions             | Owned + tracked                          |
| Capacity planning              | Required                                 |
| Load testing                   | Required for critical workloads          |
| Performance baseline           | Maintained                               |
| Chaos engineering              | Controlled/hypothesis-driven             |
| Game days                      | Required for critical recovery scenarios |
| Operational readiness review   | Required                                 |
| Deployment markers             | Required                                 |
| DORA correlation               | Required                                 |
| Cost observability             | Required                                 |
| Observability platform SLO     | Required                                 |
| Telemetry pipeline monitoring  | Required                                 |
| Status                         | **Accepted**                             |
| Priority                       | **Critical**                             |
