---

# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                       | Decision                                        |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| Primary OLTP               | **PostgreSQL**                                  |
| AWS relational default     | **RDS PostgreSQL**                              |
| Aurora PostgreSQL          | Requirement-driven evaluation                   |
| Service data ownership     | Mandatory                                       |
| Database-per-service       | Logical ownership                               |
| Shared-table microservices | **Rejected**                                    |
| Schema design              | Domain/invariant driven                         |
| Referential integrity      | DB constraints within domain boundary           |
| IDs                        | Sequence/UUID based on requirements             |
| Indexing                   | Query-driven                                    |
| ORM fetch strategy         | Explicit                                        |
| Transaction boundaries     | Business-operation aligned                      |
| Default isolation          | Workload-driven                                 |
| Optimistic locking         | Preferred for normal low-contention concurrency |
| Pessimistic locking        | Selective                                       |
| Connection pool            | HikariCP                                        |
| Connection budget          | Required                                        |
| PgBouncer                  | Scale-driven evaluation                         |
| Multi-AZ                   | Critical production DBs                         |
| PITR                       | Required                                        |
| Restore testing            | Required                                        |
| Cache                      | **Redis**                                       |
| Cache model                | Cache-aside default                             |
| Cache TTL                  | Mandatory/bounded                               |
| Cache invalidation         | Explicit                                        |
| Stampede protection        | Required for high-volume keys                   |
| Redis as authoritative DB  | Generally **rejected**                          |
| Sessions                   | Redis where architecture requires               |
| Event backbone             | **Kafka**                                       |
| Event model                | Domain facts                                    |
| Delivery assumption        | At least once                                   |
| Consumers                  | Idempotent                                      |
| Ordering                   | Partition scoped                                |
| Retry                      | Bounded/backoff                                 |
| DLQ                        | Owned + monitored                               |
| Event schemas              | Governed                                        |
| Schema Registry            | Required where structured contracts justify it  |
| Dual-write solution        | **Transactional Outbox**                        |
| CDC                        | Requirement-driven                              |
| CDC technology             | Debezium preferred evaluation                   |
| Search                     | **OpenSearch**                                  |
| OpenSearch role            | Derived search projection                       |
| Search consistency         | Eventual                                        |
| Reindexing                 | Alias-based replacement                         |
| Object storage             | **Amazon S3**                                   |
| Upload model               | Authorized presigned upload                     |
| Upload security            | Quarantine + validation/scanning                |
| Data lineage               | Required for critical data                      |
| Data quality               | Measured                                        |
| Retention                  | Technology-wide                                 |
| Deletion                   | End-to-end                                      |
| RPO/RTO                    | Defined per critical data service               |
| DR                         | Requirement-driven                              |
| Schema migration           | Version-controlled automation                   |
| Zero-downtime migration    | Expand → migrate → contract                     |
| Analytics                  | Separated from production OLTP                  |
| Lake/lakehouse             | Scale/use-case driven                           |
| Status                     | **Accepted**                                    |
| Priority                   | **Critical**                                    |

---

---

# ADR-066 — Enterprise Resilience, High Availability, Disaster Recovery & Failure Engineering

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Capacity for Failure**.

---

# 61. Node Failure

Kubernetes nodes must be treated as disposable infrastructure.

```text
Node Failure
     │
     ▼
Pods become unavailable
     │
     ▼
Kubernetes reschedules
     │
     ▼
Healthy nodes
```

Applications must not depend on local node state for durable business data.

---

# 62. Node Replacement

Failed/unhealthy nodes should normally be replaced rather than manually repaired.

```text
Immutable infrastructure
        >
SSH + manual repair
```

This aligns with ADR-061.

---

# 63. Node Drain

Planned maintenance should use controlled draining.

```text
Node
 │
 ▼
Cordon
 │
 ▼
Drain
 │
 ▼
PDB evaluation
 │
 ▼
Pods rescheduled
```

Maintenance procedures should verify remaining capacity before disruption.

---

# 64. Availability-Zone Failure

Production architecture should assume an entire AZ can become unavailable.

```text
             Region
                │
      ┌─────────┼─────────┐
      ▼         ▼         ▼
     AZ-A      AZ-B      AZ-C
      X         │         │
                ▼         ▼
             Continue Operation
```

Critical workloads should not depend on one AZ.

---

# 65. AZ-Aware Scheduling

Application replicas should be distributed across availability zones.

The architecture should prevent accidental concentration caused by:

```text
Insufficient nodes
Poor scheduling constraints
Capacity imbalance
Single-AZ node groups
Persistent-volume topology
```

---

# 66. AZ Failure Capacity

The remaining AZs must have enough capacity to absorb critical workloads.

For three AZs, planning should consider:

```text
Normal:
A + B + C

Failure:
B + C
```

not only normal-state efficiency.

---

# 67. Cluster Autoscaler During Failure

Autoscaling may provision replacement capacity after failure.

But autoscaling is not instantaneous.

Therefore:

```text
Spare capacity
      +
Autoscaling
```

is stronger than relying exclusively on emergency provisioning.

---

# 68. Karpenter

Karpenter may provide dynamic EKS node provisioning where adopted by ADR-061.

Failure architecture must consider:

```text
Instance availability
AZ capacity
Instance-family diversity
Provisioning latency
AWS API dependencies
Disruption policies
```

---

# 69. Instance Diversification

Critical workloads should avoid unnecessary dependence on one EC2 instance type.

Flexible node requirements improve recovery during regional capacity constraints.

---

# 70. Spot Instances

Spot capacity should primarily host interruption-tolerant workloads.

Critical capacity must not depend entirely on Spot.

```text
Critical baseline
→ On-Demand

Elastic/fault-tolerant capacity
→ Spot where appropriate
```

---

# 71. EKS Control Plane

EKS provides a managed Kubernetes control plane, but workloads must still tolerate temporary Kubernetes API unavailability.

Existing application traffic should not require continuous control-plane access to function.

---

# 72. Control-Plane Dependency

Applications should not unnecessarily make business requests depend on live Kubernetes API access.

```text
User Request
     │
     X
kubectl/Kubernetes API
```

should not be a normal application dependency.

---

# 73. ALB Architecture

Internet-facing traffic should use redundant AWS-managed load-balancing capabilities.

```text
Internet
   │
   ▼
  ALB
   │
 ┌─┼───────────────┐
 ▼ ▼               ▼
AZ-A              AZ-B              AZ-C
```

Backends must expose meaningful health signals.

---

# 74. Load-Balancer Health

ALB target health should align with application readiness.

A process being alive does not necessarily mean it can safely receive traffic.

---

# 75. Deregistration Draining

During deployment or termination, existing connections should receive appropriate time to complete where protocol/workload permits.

```text
Pod termination
      │
      ▼
Stop new traffic
      │
      ▼
Drain requests
      │
      ▼
Terminate
```

---

# 76. Graceful Shutdown

Spring Boot applications should support graceful shutdown.

Shutdown sequence should coordinate:

```text
Readiness removal
Request draining
Consumer shutdown
Background work
Connection closure
Process exit
```

---

# 77. Termination Grace Period

Kubernetes termination grace periods must reflect actual shutdown requirements.

Too short:

```text
Request processing
      │
      X SIGKILL
```

Too long can unnecessarily delay deployments/recovery.

---

# 78. DNS Resilience

DNS is a critical dependency.

Architecture should consider:

```text
Resolver availability
Caching
TTL
Failover records
Propagation delay
Application DNS caching
```

DNS changes are not instantaneous global switches.

---

# 79. DNS TTL

TTL determines a trade-off:

```text
Short TTL
→ faster endpoint change
→ more DNS queries

Long TTL
→ better caching
→ slower failover
```

TTL should match failover requirements.

---

# 80. Application DNS Caching

JVM/application DNS caching behavior must be understood.

A 30-second Route 53 TTL is useless for rapid failover if the application retains an obsolete address much longer.

---

# 81. RDS Failure

Applications must expect database connection loss during RDS failover.

```text
Application
     │
     X
Primary DB
     │
     ▼
Failover
     │
     ▼
New Primary
```

Existing connections may become invalid.

---

# 82. Database Connection Recovery

Connection pools should discard broken connections and establish new ones after failover.

Applications must not require restart merely because the database endpoint changed behind DNS.

---

# 83. Transaction Failure During Failover

A transaction interrupted by database failover may have uncertain outcome.

Applications must not assume:

```text
connection lost
=
transaction definitely failed
```

Idempotency and reconciliation may be required.

---

# 84. RDS Multi-AZ

Critical relational workloads should use Multi-AZ deployment as the primary HA mechanism.

This protects against infrastructure failure but not:

```text
Bad DELETE
Schema corruption
Application bug
Malicious modification
Logical data corruption
```

Those require recovery mechanisms.

---

# 85. Read Replica Failure

Loss of a read replica should degrade read capacity rather than destroy write availability.

Applications should have routing/fallback behavior appropriate to consistency requirements.

---

# 86. Redis Failure

Redis failure should be evaluated according to Redis's role.

For cache:

```text
Redis unavailable
      │
      ▼
Controlled fallback
      │
      ▼
PostgreSQL
```

But this can create a database traffic surge.

---

# 87. Cache Failure Storm

If Redis disappears:

```text
100k cached requests
       │
       ▼
PostgreSQL
```

may overload the authoritative database.

Fallback therefore requires:

```text
Rate limiting
Load shedding
Request coalescing
Database capacity protection
```

---

# 88. Redis Failover

Managed Redis replication/failover should be used for critical Redis workloads.

Clients must tolerate:

```text
Connection reset
Endpoint transition
Temporary errors
Replica promotion
```

---

# 89. Kafka Broker Failure

Kafka should tolerate individual broker failures when replication is configured correctly.

```text
Partition
   │
   ├── Leader Broker A  X
   ├── Replica Broker B
   └── Replica Broker C

             │
             ▼
       New leader elected
```

---

# 90. Kafka Replication

Critical topics should use appropriate replication factors across failure domains.

A replication factor of three is useful only if replicas are actually distributed appropriately.

---

# 91. Kafka In-Sync Replicas

Producer durability settings should consider:

```text
acks
min.insync.replicas
replication factor
```

These determine the trade-off between availability and durability during broker failures.

---

# 92. Kafka Consumer Recovery

Consumers must survive:

```text
Broker restart
Partition reassignment
Rebalancing
Transient network loss
Consumer restart
```

without corrupting business state.

---

# 93. Kafka Backlog Recovery

After consumer outage:

```text
Producer continues
       │
       ▼
Kafka backlog
       │
       ▼
Consumer restored
       │
       ▼
Catch-up
```

Capacity must support recovery faster than ongoing production.

Otherwise backlog never disappears.

---

# 94. OpenSearch Failure

Search should be treated as a secondary capability where possible.

```text
OpenSearch unavailable
       │
       ▼
Search degraded
       │
       ▼
Core transactional workflows continue
```

This prevents search failure from becoming platform failure.

---

# 95. OpenSearch Replica Recovery

Production search indexes should use appropriate replicas and multi-AZ placement.

Shard recovery capacity must be considered during node failure.

---

# 96. Search Rebuild

Because OpenSearch is derived state:

```text
Catastrophic Search Loss
        │
        ▼
Authoritative Data / Events
        │
        ▼
Reindex
        │
        ▼
Search Restored
```

Rebuild procedures must be tested.

---

# 97. S3 Failure Behavior

Applications should handle S3 failures explicitly.

For noncritical media:

```text
Object unavailable
→ placeholder / retry later
```

For critical upload:

```text
Storage unavailable
→ operation fails safely
```

Never report durable upload success before durability is established.

---

# 98. Asynchronous Dependency Isolation

Nonessential external side effects should be moved out of synchronous request paths where possible.

```text
Enrollment
    │
    ▼
DB Commit
    │
    ▼
Event
    │
    ├── Email
    ├── Analytics
    └── Notification
```

Email-provider failure should not roll back a valid enrollment.

---

# 99. Multi-AZ Baseline

Mediverse production should use multi-AZ architecture as its standard HA baseline for critical components.

```text
               REGION
                  │
       ┌──────────┼──────────┐
       ▼          ▼          ▼
      AZ-A       AZ-B       AZ-C
       │          │          │
       └──────────┼──────────┘
                  ▼
             APPLICATION
                  │
                  ▼
             DATA SERVICES
```

---

# 100. Multi-Region Is Not Default

Multi-region architecture is substantially more difficult than multi-AZ.

It introduces:

```text
Data replication
Consistency problems
Failover orchestration
DNS complexity
Higher cost
Operational duplication
Testing requirements
Security duplication
```

Mediverse should not adopt it without business justification.

---

# 101. Regional Failure

Regional DR begins with a scenario:

```text
Primary AWS Region
       X
       │
       ▼
Can Mediverse recover elsewhere?
```

The answer depends on RTO/RPO.

---

# 102. Multi-Region Decision Framework

Adoption should consider:

```text
Required RTO
Required RPO
Revenue/business impact
Regulatory requirements
Regional outage tolerance
Operational maturity
Data consistency requirements
Cost
```

---

# 103. Backup and Restore Strategy

Lowest-complexity regional DR:

```text
Primary Region
      │
      ▼
Cross-Region Backup
      │
      ▼
Disaster
      │
      ▼
Provision Secondary
      │
      ▼
Restore
```

Cost is relatively low.

RTO is relatively high.

---

# 104. Pilot Light

Pilot light maintains critical foundational components in the DR region.

```text
DR Region

Data replication ✓
Core infrastructure ✓
Full compute scale ✗
```

During disaster, compute capacity is expanded.

---

# 105. Warm Standby

Warm standby maintains a reduced but functioning secondary environment.

```text
Primary
100% capacity

Secondary
20–40% capacity
```

During failover, secondary capacity scales up.

---

# 106. Active/Passive

One region serves traffic while another is prepared to take over.

```text
Region A
 ACTIVE

Region B
 PASSIVE
```

This simplifies write consistency compared with active/active.

---

# 107. Active/Active

Both regions simultaneously serve production traffic.

```text
          USERS
            │
      ┌─────┴─────┐
      ▼           ▼
 Region A       Region B
 ACTIVE         ACTIVE
```

This is the most complex option.

---

# 108. Active/Active Warning

Active/active requires explicit answers for:

```text
Where are writes accepted?
How are conflicts resolved?
How is identity synchronized?
How is Kafka coordinated?
How is cache consistency handled?
What happens during network partition?
```

If these answers do not exist, the architecture is not truly active/active.

---

# 109. Recommended Mediverse DR Direction

Until business requirements prove otherwise:

```text
Production HA
→ Multi-AZ

Regional DR
→ Backup/Restore initially

Evolution
→ Pilot Light / Warm Standby
   when RTO requires it
```

Active/active is rejected as the default.

---

# 110. Route 53 Failover

For regional active/passive DR, Route 53 may direct users toward the healthy region.

```text
               Route 53
                  │
          ┌───────┴───────┐
          ▼               ▼
      Primary          Secondary
       Region            Region
```

Health checks must represent actual service readiness.

---

# 111. Health-Check Design

A DR health check should not declare a region healthy merely because one load balancer returns HTTP 200.

It should reflect critical dependencies sufficiently to determine whether the region can serve the intended journey.

---

# 112. False Failover

Over-sensitive health checks can cause unnecessary regional failover.

Failover itself carries risk.

Therefore:

```text
Temporary degradation
≠
automatic regional disaster
```

---

# 113. Failover Automation

Automation should be used where it reduces recovery time safely.

But destructive/high-risk decisions may require controlled human approval depending on architecture and maturity.

"Fully automatic" is not automatically superior.

---

# 114. Data Replication

Regional DR requires independent replication decisions for:

```text
PostgreSQL
S3
Kafka
Redis
OpenSearch
Secrets
Container images
Configuration
Infrastructure state
```

There is no single "replicate region" switch.

---

# 115. Authoritative vs Derived DR

Prioritize authoritative state.

```text
PostgreSQL
S3 authoritative objects
Secrets/configuration
        │
        ▼
      RECOVER
        │
        ▼
Kafka/projections as required
        │
        ▼
Redis/OpenSearch rebuild
```

Derived systems may often be reconstructed.

---

# 116. Consistency During DR

Regional failover can create:

```text
Replication lag
Lost recent writes
Duplicate processing
Out-of-order events
Stale caches
```

Applications must operate according to declared RPO and consistency semantics.

---

# 117. Split Brain

A severe risk is both regions believing they are primary writers.

```text
Region A ── writes
      X network
Region B ── writes
```

Without conflict strategy, data diverges.

Single-writer DR is simpler and preferred unless active/active is explicitly justified.

---

# 118. RPO Hierarchy

Recovery Point Objectives should be defined by business capability/data class.

Example:

```text
Tier 0 transactional data
→ very low acceptable loss

Tier 1 learning progress
→ low acceptable loss

Derived search indexes
→ reconstructable

Cache
→ zero recovery requirement
```

Exact numbers require business agreement.

---

# 119. RTO Hierarchy

Recovery Time Objectives should similarly vary.

```text
Authentication
→ fastest

Core learning
→ fast

Search
→ slower acceptable

Analytics
→ substantially slower acceptable
```

Do not assign identical RTOs to every component.

---

# 120. Dependency Recovery Order

Recovery should follow dependencies.

```text
1. AWS/network foundation
        │
2. Identity/secrets
        │
3. Authoritative databases
        │
4. Messaging
        │
5. Core services
        │
6. Edge/API
        │
7. Search/cache
        │
8. Secondary systems
```

Starting frontend pods before the database exists achieves little.

---

# 121. DR Runbook

Every critical system requires executable recovery documentation.

A runbook should contain:

```text
Trigger conditions
Roles
Dependencies
Commands/automation
Validation
Decision points
Rollback/failback
Communication
Evidence
```

---

# 122. Recovery Orchestration

Infrastructure-as-code and GitOps should reconstruct environments rather than relying on manual recreation.

```text
Terraform
   │
   ▼
AWS Infrastructure
   │
   ▼
EKS
   │
   ▼
Argo CD
   │
   ▼
Applications
```

ADR-061 becomes a DR dependency.

---

# 123. DR Infrastructure Drift

The secondary region must not exist only as outdated Terraform that has never successfully deployed.

Recovery code must be exercised.

---

# 124. Failover Procedure

A controlled regional failover may conceptually follow:

```text
Declare disaster
      │
      ▼
Freeze/confirm primary writes
      │
      ▼
Validate replicated data
      │
      ▼
Promote secondary data systems
      │
      ▼
Start/scale workloads
      │
      ▼
Validate critical journeys
      │
      ▼
Shift traffic
      │
      ▼
Monitor
```

Exact steps depend on selected technologies.

---

# 125. Failback

Returning to the original region can be harder than failing over.

```text
Secondary now contains newer writes
          │
          ▼
Original region restored
          │
          ▼
How does data return?
```

Failback must be designed before the first disaster.

---

# 126. Failback Strategy

Failback should consider:

```text
Data synchronization
Write freeze requirements
DNS transition
Validation
Rollback
Customer impact
```

Never improvise this during recovery.

---

# 127. Backup Isolation

Backups should be protected from the same administrative failure that destroys production.

Potential controls:

```text
Separate account
Restricted IAM
Independent encryption controls
Cross-region copies
Retention controls
```

---

# 128. Immutable Backups

Critical recovery data should use immutability mechanisms where justified.

The objective:

```text
Compromised production admin
          │
          X
Cannot immediately destroy
all recovery points
```

---

# 129. Backup Deletion Protection

Backup deletion should require stronger controls than ordinary application data modification.

A ransomware attacker should not be able to erase both production and recovery with one credential.

---

# 130. Ransomware Recovery

Recovery architecture should assume:

```text
Production compromised
Credentials compromised
Some backups targeted
Configuration potentially malicious
```

Recovery therefore requires trusted recovery points and clean infrastructure—not merely restarting existing servers.

---

# 131. Clean-Room Recovery

Severe security incidents may require:

```text
Trusted IaC
   │
   ▼
Clean AWS environment
   │
   ▼
Trusted artifacts
   │
   ▼
Verified backup
   │
   ▼
Restore
```

rather than reusing compromised infrastructure.

---

# 132. Business Continuity

DR restores technology.

Business continuity answers:

> How does the organization continue critical operations while technology is degraded or unavailable?

This requires coordination beyond engineering.

---

# 133. Business Impact Analysis

Critical capabilities should undergo BIA to determine:

```text
Maximum tolerable downtime
Business impact
Data-loss tolerance
Dependencies
Manual alternatives
Recovery priority
```

Technical RTO/RPO should follow business requirements.

---

# 134. Crisis Roles

Major incidents should establish explicit roles such as:

```text
Incident Commander
Technical Lead
Security Lead
Communications Lead
Business Representative
Scribe
```

One person should not attempt to perform every function.

---

# 135. Crisis Communication

Communication plans should define:

```text
Internal stakeholders
Leadership
Support
Customers/users
Vendors
Regulators where applicable
```

including who is authorized to communicate.

---

# 136. Status Communication

During major outages, updates should communicate:

```text
Known impact
Current mitigation
What is unknown
Next update time
```

Avoid unsupported recovery estimates.

---

# 137. Degraded Business Modes

Mediverse should identify operations that can continue during partial outages.

Example:

```text
Search unavailable
→ direct course navigation

Recommendation unavailable
→ default catalogue

Analytics unavailable
→ no user-facing impact

Notification unavailable
→ queue and deliver later
```

---

# 138. Chaos Engineering

Chaos engineering should validate resilience assumptions through controlled failure.

```text
Hypothesis
    │
    ▼
Inject Failure
    │
    ▼
Observe
    │
    ▼
Compare Expected vs Actual
    │
    ▼
Improve
```

Randomly breaking production without a hypothesis is not chaos engineering.

---

# 139. Chaos Preconditions

Before production chaos experiments:

```text
Observability exists
Rollback exists
Blast radius is bounded
Owners are present
Steady-state metric is defined
Experiment has stop conditions
```

---

# 140. AWS Fault Injection Service

AWS Fault Injection Service should be evaluated for controlled experiments such as:

```text
EC2 interruption
Network impairment
Resource stress
Selected AWS service faults
```

where supported and useful.

---

# 141. Kubernetes Failure Experiments

Game days should test scenarios including:

```text
Kill pod
Kill node
Drain node
Lose AZ capacity
Break DNS
Increase latency
Block dependency
Terminate consumer
Force DB failover
Disable Redis
```

in controlled environments.

---

# 142. Game Days

Regular game days should validate cross-team operational readiness.

A successful game day is not one where nothing fails.

It is one where assumptions are tested and weaknesses are discovered safely.

---

# 143. DR Exercises

At least periodically, teams should execute realistic recovery exercises:

```text
Backup restore
Regional infrastructure creation
Database recovery
Application deployment
Traffic failover
Critical journey validation
Failback
```

Paper runbooks alone are insufficient.

---

# 144. Resilience in CI/CD

Some failure properties should be continuously tested.

Examples:

```text
Timeout behavior
Retry limits
Idempotency
Dependency unavailability
Graceful shutdown
Startup/readiness behavior
Schema compatibility
```

Not every resilience test requires production chaos.

---

# 145. Capacity Testing

Load tests should evaluate:

```text
Normal capacity
Peak capacity
One-pod loss
One-node loss
One-AZ loss
Dependency slowdown
Recovery catch-up
```

Testing only healthy steady state gives misleading capacity numbers.

---

# 146. Resilience Scorecard

Critical services should maintain a scorecard covering:

```text
SLO defined?
Timeouts configured?
Retries bounded?
Circuit breaker?
Bulkhead?
Graceful degradation?
Multi-replica?
Multi-AZ?
PDB?
RPO/RTO?
Backup?
Restore tested?
DR runbook?
Chaos tested?
Owner?
```

This converts resilience from architectural rhetoric into measurable engineering work.

---

# 147. Operational Readiness Review

Before a critical service reaches production, verify:

```text
Failure modes understood
Dependencies documented
SLOs established
Alerts operational
Capacity known
Runbooks available
Backup/recovery proven
Security controls operational
Deployment rollback tested
Ownership established
```

Production should not be the first resilience test.

---

# 148. Resilience Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ "Kubernetes makes us highly available"

❌ Single replica for critical services

❌ All replicas scheduled on one node/AZ

❌ 100% normal-state infrastructure utilization

❌ Critical workloads entirely dependent on Spot

❌ Durable state stored on pod/node filesystem

❌ Liveness probe checking every downstream dependency

❌ Readiness and liveness treated identically

❌ No graceful shutdown

❌ Arbitrary five-minute termination periods

❌ Remote calls without timeouts

❌ Every layer independently retrying

❌ Infinite retries

❌ Retry without idempotency analysis

❌ Retry storms without jitter

❌ Circuit breaker configured globally with identical settings

❌ Unlimited thread pools

❌ Unlimited connection pools

❌ Queue buffering treated as infinite capacity

❌ Kafka backlog ignored because brokers are healthy

❌ Fallback that violates security/correctness

❌ Redis outage allowed to DDoS PostgreSQL

❌ Database failover assumed transparent to active transactions

❌ Multi-AZ treated as backup

❌ Read replicas treated as immediately consistent

❌ OpenSearch failure allowed to break transactional APIs

❌ Email/SaaS dependency placed directly inside critical transaction

❌ Multi-region adopted for prestige

❌ Active/active claimed without conflict-resolution design

❌ Route 53 treated as instantaneous failover

❌ DR health check based only on load-balancer HTTP 200

❌ Automatic regional failover on every temporary error

❌ RPO/RTO defined by engineers without business input

❌ Same RPO/RTO assigned to every system

❌ Recovery order undefined

❌ DR runbook never executed

❌ Secondary infrastructure existing only as untested Terraform

❌ Failover designed but failback ignored

❌ Backups accessible through same compromised credentials

❌ Backups never restored

❌ Backup success treated as recovery proof

❌ Ransomware recovery assuming production credentials remain trusted

❌ Chaos engineering performed without bounded blast radius

❌ Game day judged successful because nothing broke

❌ Capacity testing only under healthy conditions

❌ Production used as first failure test
```

---

# 149. Final Mediverse Enterprise Resilience & DR Reference Architecture

```text
                              USERS
                                │
                                ▼
                         Route 53 / DNS
                                │
                                ▼
                         AWS EDGE / ALB
                                │
                                ▼
                       PRIMARY AWS REGION
                                │
               ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
               ▼                ▼                ▼
              AZ-A             AZ-B             AZ-C
               │                │                │
               ▼                ▼                ▼
             EKS              EKS              EKS
               │                │                │
```

# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                         | Decision                                    |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| Resilience model             | **Failure-aware + defense in depth**        |
| Production HA baseline       | **Multi-AZ**                                |
| Critical service replicas    | Multiple                                    |
| Pod distribution             | AZ/node aware                               |
| Critical capacity            | Failure-capable                             |
| Spot                         | Supplemental/fault-tolerant workloads       |
| Node model                   | Replaceable/immutable                       |
| Application state on nodes   | **Rejected**                                |
| Startup probe                | Workload-driven                             |
| Readiness                    | Traffic eligibility                         |
| Liveness                     | Restart-worthy failure only                 |
| PDB                          | Critical workloads where appropriate        |
| Graceful shutdown            | Required                                    |
| Remote-call timeout          | Required                                    |
| Deadline propagation         | Preferred                                   |
| Retries                      | Bounded + safe                              |
| Retry backoff                | Exponential                                 |
| Retry jitter                 | Required at scale                           |
| Retry ownership              | Explicit                                    |
| Circuit breaker              | Dependency-specific                         |
| Spring implementation        | Resilience4j preferred                      |
| Bulkheads                    | Critical dependency isolation               |
| Load shedding                | Required where overload threatens stability |
| Backpressure                 | Explicit                                    |
| Idempotency                  | Required for retryable side effects         |
| Hard dependency failure      | Fail safely                                 |
| Soft dependency failure      | Graceful degradation                        |
| Async side effects           | Decoupled                                   |
| Redis outage                 | Controlled DB fallback                      |
| Kafka failure                | Replication + idempotent recovery           |
| OpenSearch                   | Degradable/rebuildable                      |
| RDS                          | Multi-AZ + recovery                         |
| Multi-AZ                     | **HA, not DR backup**                       |
| Regional DR                  | Requirement-driven                          |
| Initial DR                   | **Backup/Restore**                          |
| Evolution                    | Pilot Light / Warm Standby                  |
| Active/passive               | Preferred before active/active              |
| Active/active                | Exceptional                                 |
| DNS failover                 | Route 53 where required                     |
| DR health                    | Critical-journey aware                      |
| Split brain                  | Must be prevented                           |
| RPO                          | Business/data-tier specific                 |
| RTO                          | Business/service-tier specific              |
| Recovery order               | Dependency-driven                           |
| IaC/GitOps recovery          | Required                                    |
| Failover runbook             | Required                                    |
| Failback runbook             | Required                                    |
| Backup isolation             | Required                                    |
| Immutable recovery points    | Critical data where justified               |
| Ransomware recovery          | Clean recovery architecture                 |
| Business continuity          | Required                                    |
| Chaos engineering            | Controlled/hypothesis-driven                |
| Game days                    | Required for critical platform              |
| DR exercises                 | Periodic                                    |
| Failure testing              | CI/CD where practical                       |
| Capacity testing             | Includes degraded scenarios                 |
| Resilience scorecards        | Required for critical services              |
| Operational readiness review | Required                                    |
| Status                       | **Accepted**                                |
| Priority                     | **Critical**                                |

---

# ADR-067 — Enterprise Application Architecture & Spring Boot Microservices Engineering Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Backward Compatibility**.

---

# 61. OpenAPI Contract Governance

Every externally consumed REST API should expose an OpenAPI specification.

```text
Spring Boot Service
       │
       ▼
    OpenAPI
       │
       ├── Paths
       ├── Schemas
       ├── Security
       ├── Errors
       └── Examples
```

OpenAPI is an API contract, not merely Swagger UI documentation.

---

# 62. API-First vs Code-First

Mediverse should not force one approach onto every service.

```text
API-first
→ useful for externally coordinated contracts

Code-first
→ efficient for team-owned/internal APIs
```

The important requirement is that implementation and published contract remain synchronized.

---

# 63. API-First

API-first should be preferred when:

```text
Frontend/backend teams work independently
External consumers exist
Multiple services depend on contract
SDK generation is required
Contract review is important
```

Design occurs before implementation.

---

# 64. Code-First

Code-first may remain appropriate for simpler internal services.

```text
Controller / DTO
       │
       ▼
Generated OpenAPI
       │
       ▼
Contract validation
```

Generated specifications must still be reviewed.

---

# 65. API Contract CI

CI should detect unintended contract changes.

```text
Previous OpenAPI
       │
       ▼
Compatibility Check
       ▲
       │
New OpenAPI
```

Breaking changes should fail or require explicit approval according to governance.

---

# 66. API Documentation

Documentation should explain more than endpoints.

Include:

```text
Authentication
Authorization
Rate limits
Pagination
Errors
Idempotency
Examples
Deprecation
Versioning
```

---

# 67. API Deprecation

Deprecated APIs require an explicit migration path.

```text
v1
 │
 ├── Deprecated
 │
 ▼
Migration Window
 │
 ▼
v2
 │
 ▼
v1 Removal
```

Removal dates must reflect consumer commitments.

---

# 68. Controller Responsibility

Controllers should remain thin.

```text
HTTP
 │
 ▼
Controller
 │
 ▼
Application Service
```

Controllers handle transport concerns—not core business workflows.

---

# 69. Fat Controller Anti-Pattern

Rejected:

```text
Controller
 ├── authorization logic
 ├── SQL
 ├── business rules
 ├── Kafka publishing
 ├── mapping
 └── transaction orchestration
```

This destroys separation and testability.

---

# 70. Command/Query Separation

Application use cases should distinguish state-changing commands from queries conceptually.

```text
Command
→ changes state

Query
→ reads state
```

This does not require a full CQRS architecture.

---

# 71. CQRS Evaluation

Full CQRS should be introduced only when read and write requirements genuinely diverge.

```text
Commands
   │
   ▼
Write Model

Queries
   │
   ▼
Read Model
```

CQRS adds synchronization and operational complexity.

---

# 72. CQRS Anti-Pattern

Do not create:

```text
CommandBus
QueryBus
20 handlers
15 abstractions
```

around five CRUD endpoints merely because CQRS is fashionable.

---

# 73. Application Use Cases

Application services should expose business-oriented operations.

Prefer:

```java
publishCourse()
enrollLearner()
submitAssessment()
```

rather than generic:

```java
save()
update()
process()
```

where meaningful domain semantics exist.

---

# 74. Repository Boundary

Repositories should model domain persistence needs.

```text
Domain
   │
   ▼
CourseRepository
   │
   ▼
Persistence Adapter
   │
   ▼
JPA
```

Domain code should not require knowledge of Hibernate internals.

---

# 75. Spring Data JPA

Spring Data JPA should remain the standard relational persistence abstraction for normal Mediverse services.

Native SQL or specialized access is allowed when measurement or query complexity justifies it.

---

# 76. JPA Entity Boundary

Persistence entities should remain inside the owning service.

Never expose them as:

```text
REST contracts
Kafka contracts
Shared-library contracts
Cross-service domain models
```

---

# 77. JPA Relationships

Relationships should be modeled conservatively.

A large object graph such as:

```text
Course
 └── Modules
      └── Lessons
           └── Resources
                └── Progress
```

should not automatically become a deeply navigable JPA graph.

---

# 78. Lazy Loading

Lazy loading should generally remain the default for potentially expensive relationships.

Required data should be fetched explicitly within valid transaction boundaries.

---

# 79. Open Session in View

Mediverse APIs should generally avoid depending on Open Session in View.

```text
Controller serialization
        │
        X
hidden DB query
```

Database access should be explicit in application/persistence layers.

---

# 80. Transaction Management

Transactions should normally begin at application-service/use-case boundaries.

```text
Controller
    │
    ▼
@Transactional
Application Use Case
    │
    ▼
Repositories
```

---

# 81. Transaction Scope

Transactions should be short.

Do not routinely perform:

```text
BEGIN
 ↓
Database update
 ↓
Call external API
 ↓
Wait 10 seconds
 ↓
Kafka request
 ↓
COMMIT
```

External operations should not hold database transactions open unnecessarily.

---

# 82. Read-Only Transactions

Read-only transaction hints may be used where useful.

They do not replace query optimization or correct database architecture.

---

# 83. Transaction Propagation

Spring transaction propagation should be used deliberately.

`REQUIRES_NEW` should not become a convenient mechanism for hiding poor transaction design.

---

# 84. DTO Mapping

Mapping between:

```text
API DTO
Application model
Domain model
Persistence model
```

should remain explicit enough that boundaries are visible.

---

# 85. MapStruct

MapStruct should be preferred for repetitive compile-time DTO mapping where manual mapping becomes noisy.

It provides:

```text
Compile-time generation
Type safety
Low runtime overhead
Explicit mapping configuration
```

---

# 86. Mapping Warning

Do not map every layer into an identical object merely to claim architectural purity.

If three objects contain identical fields and provide no meaningful boundary, reconsider the design.

---

# 87. Lombok Policy

Lombok may be used selectively for boilerplate reduction.

Acceptable examples:

```text
@Getter
@Builder
@RequiredArgsConstructor
```

Use cautiously on domain/JPA models.

---

# 88. Lombok @Data

`@Data` should generally be avoided on JPA entities.

Generated:

```text
equals()
hashCode()
toString()
setters
```

can interact badly with entity identity, lazy relationships and mutable state.

---

# 89. Constructor Injection

Dependencies should use constructor injection.

Preferred:

```java
public CourseService(CourseRepository repository) {
    this.repository = repository;
}
```

Field injection should be avoided.

---

# 90. Outbound HTTP Client

Spring services requiring synchronous HTTP calls should standardize on supported Spring HTTP clients rather than introducing arbitrary client libraries per service.

---

# 91. RestClient

For modern Spring Boot synchronous request/response workloads, `RestClient` should be preferred over legacy `RestTemplate` for new code.

```text
Service
  │
  ▼
RestClient
  │
  ▼
Remote API
```

---

# 92. WebClient

`WebClient` should be used when reactive/non-blocking behavior is actually required.

Using WebClient does not automatically make an application scalable.

---

# 93. RestTemplate

Existing `RestTemplate` applications may continue during controlled migration, but new services should not select it as the default.

---

# 94. HTTP Client Configuration

Every outbound client should explicitly define:

```text
Connection timeout
Request/read timeout
Connection pool
TLS
Authentication
Observability
Retry behavior
```

Defaults should not be trusted blindly.

---

# 95. Resilience Integration

Outbound calls should follow ADR-066.

```text
RestClient
    │
    ▼
Timeout
    │
    ▼
Bulkhead
    │
    ▼
Retry where safe
    │
    ▼
Circuit Breaker
```

Do not blindly apply every resilience pattern to every endpoint.

---

# 96. OAuth2 Resource Server

Protected Spring Boot APIs should normally operate as OAuth2/OIDC resource servers according to ADR-064.

```text
Access Token
     │
     ▼
Spring Security
     │
     ▼
JWT validation
     │
     ▼
SecurityContext
```

---

# 97. Token Validation

Services should validate:

```text
Signature
Issuer
Audience where required
Expiration
Relevant claims
```

A token being syntactically valid is insufficient.

---

# 98. Authorization

Authorization should exist close to protected operations.

```text
Authenticated Identity
        │
        ▼
Role / Scope / Permission
        │
        ▼
Business Authorization
        │
        ▼
Operation
```

---

# 99. Method Security

Spring method authorization may protect application-service operations.

Example:

```java
@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('course:publish')")
```

But complex business authorization should not become unreadable SpEL expressions.

---

# 100. Ownership Authorization

Resource ownership must be validated.

```text
User has COURSE_EDIT
        │
        ▼
Does user have permission
for THIS course?
```

Global roles alone may not answer this.

---

# 101. Kafka Producer

Kafka producers should publish governed domain events.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
Outbox
    │
    ▼
Publisher
    │
    ▼
Kafka
```

Direct publishing is acceptable only where dual-write consistency is irrelevant.

---

# 102. Producer Configuration

Production producer settings should explicitly consider:

```text
acks
Retries
Delivery timeout
Compression
Batching
Idempotence
Serialization
```

Configuration must follow durability and latency requirements.

---

# 103. Kafka Consumer

Consumers should implement a clear pipeline.

```text
Deserialize
    │
    ▼
Validate
    │
    ▼
Idempotency
    │
    ▼
Business Processing
    │
    ▼
Commit
```

---

# 104. Consumer Idempotency

Consumers must assume duplicate delivery unless stronger guarantees are proven.

Use appropriate:

```text
eventId
unique constraint
processed-event record
aggregate version
business key
```

---

# 105. Consumer Transactions

Database writes and offset handling require deliberate semantics.

Do not acknowledge a message before critical processing is safely completed.

---

# 106. Poison Events

Invalid messages should follow ADR-065 retry/DLQ policy.

A single bad message must not indefinitely block a partition.

---

# 107. Transactional Outbox

Business state and event intent should be persisted atomically.

```text
@Transactional
     │
     ├── Domain state
     └── Outbox event
             │
           COMMIT
             │
             ▼
          Publisher
             │
             ▼
            Kafka
```

---

# 108. Outbox Cleanup

Published outbox records require controlled lifecycle management.

Without cleanup:

```text
outbox
  │
  ▼
millions
  │
  ▼
billions
```

eventually becomes an operational problem.

---

# 109. Scheduled Jobs

Scheduled jobs should be used for inherently scheduled work—not as a substitute for proper event architecture.

Examples:

```text
Periodic cleanup
Retention enforcement
Scheduled publication
Reconciliation
```

---

# 110. Distributed Scheduling

In a multi-replica service:

```text
Pod A ─ scheduled job
Pod B ─ scheduled job
Pod C ─ scheduled job
```

may execute the same task three times.

Jobs must be:

```text
Idempotent
Leader-controlled
Externally scheduled
or appropriately locked
```

depending on semantics.

---

# 111. Kubernetes CronJob

Platform-level scheduled tasks should consider Kubernetes CronJobs when execution is naturally independent of a continuously running service.

---

# 112. Async Execution

Spring `@Async` should be used carefully.

It does not create durable asynchronous processing.

```text
Application crashes
      │
      ▼
In-memory async task
      X
```

Durable business work belongs in durable queues/events.

---

# 113. Executor Governance

Thread pools must be bounded.

Rejected:

```text
unlimited queue
+
unlimited workload
```

which simply converts overload into memory exhaustion and latency.

---

# 114. Virtual Threads

Java virtual threads should be evaluated for high-concurrency blocking-I/O services where the selected Java/Spring stack supports them appropriately.

```text
Request
   │
   ▼
Virtual Thread
   │
   ▼
Blocking I/O
```

They can reduce thread-management cost.

---

# 115. Virtual Threads Are Not Magic

Virtual threads do not increase:

```text
Database connections
CPU
Kafka partitions
Remote API capacity
Memory
```

A service can create 100,000 virtual threads and still have only 50 database connections.

Backpressure remains necessary.

---

# 116. Concurrency Safety

Singleton Spring beans may be accessed concurrently.

Mutable request-specific state must not be stored in singleton service fields.

---

# 117. Caching

Application caching should follow ADR-065.

```text
Application
   │
   ▼
Redis
   │ miss
   ▼
PostgreSQL
```

Cache behavior is part of application correctness.

---

# 118. Spring Cache Abstraction

Spring Cache may be used where its abstraction matches requirements.

Do not hide complex invalidation semantics behind annotations if correctness becomes unclear.

---

# 119. Feature Flags

Feature flags should separate deployment from release where useful.

```text
Deploy code
    │
    ▼
Flag OFF
    │
    ▼
Controlled enablement
```

---

# 120. Feature Flag Lifecycle

Flags require:

```text
Owner
Purpose
Default
Expiration/removal plan
Observability
```

Permanent forgotten flags create combinatorial complexity.

---

# 121. Database Migration

Flyway should be the default relational schema migration tool unless a service has an approved reason to use Liquibase.

```text
Git
 │
 ▼
Flyway Migration
 │
 ▼
Deployment
 │
 ▼
PostgreSQL
```

---

# 122. Migration Immutability

Applied migration files should not normally be edited.

Create a new migration.

Changing history destroys reproducibility between environments.

---

# 123. Zero-Downtime Migration

Follow ADR-065:

```text
EXPAND
   │
   ▼
DEPLOY COMPATIBLE CODE
   │
   ▼
BACKFILL
   │
   ▼
SWITCH
   │
   ▼
CONTRACT
```

Database and application versions must tolerate rolling deployment overlap.

---

# 124. Structured Logging

Application logs should be machine-readable in production.

Example conceptual fields:

```json
{
  "timestamp": "...",
  "level": "INFO",
  "service": "course-service",
  "traceId": "...",
  "message": "Course published",
  "courseId": "..."
}
```

Follow ADR-063 for observability governance.

---

# 125. Logging Policy

Do not log:

```text
Passwords
Access tokens
Refresh tokens
Secrets
Sensitive request bodies
Sensitive medical/personal information without explicit approved need
```

Security rules from ADR-064 apply.

---

# 126. Correlation and Trace Context

Services should propagate standard trace context across:

```text
HTTP
Kafka
Async workflows
```

Do not invent unrelated proprietary correlation mechanisms without need.

---

# 127. Micrometer

Spring Boot services should use Micrometer-based instrumentation for application metrics and tracing integration.

Common metrics include:

```text
Request latency
Request count
Error rate
JVM
Connection pools
Kafka
Cache
Business metrics
```

---

# 128. Business Metrics

Technical metrics alone are insufficient.

Useful business signals may include:

```text
Enrollments completed
Assessment submissions
Course publication failures
Upload processing failures
```

Avoid high-cardinality identifiers as metric labels.

---

# 129. Spring Boot Actuator

Actuator should provide operational endpoints required by the platform.

Typical endpoints:

```text
health
info
metrics
prometheus
```

Exposure should be explicitly configured.

---

# 130. Actuator Security

Do not expose all Actuator endpoints publicly.

Sensitive operational endpoints require network/security controls.

---

# 131. Health Indicators

Health should distinguish application state from dependency state.

Readiness may depend on hard dependencies.

Liveness should not restart applications merely because an external dependency is temporarily unavailable.

---

# 132. Testing Strategy

Mediverse adopts a layered testing strategy.

```text
              /\
             /  \
            / E2E\
           /------\
          /Contract\
         /----------\
        /Integration \
       /--------------\
      /   Unit Tests   \
     /__________________\
```

The objective is confidence—not maximizing one test category.

---

# 133. JUnit 5

JUnit 5 should remain the standard Java test framework.

Tests should describe behavior rather than implementation trivia.

---

# 134. AssertJ

AssertJ should be preferred for expressive assertions where useful.

Tests should remain readable enough that failures explain what behavior broke.

---

# 135. Mockito

Mockito should isolate collaborators in focused unit tests.

Do not mock everything.

A test containing:

```text
15 mocks
```

often signals excessive coupling or a test operating at the wrong level.

---

# 136. Spring Slice Tests

Use focused Spring tests where appropriate:

```text
@WebMvcTest
@DataJpaTest
@JsonTest
```

instead of booting the entire application for every test.

---

# 137. Testcontainers

Integration tests requiring infrastructure should prefer Testcontainers for realistic dependencies.

```text
JUnit
  │
  ├── PostgreSQL container
  ├── Kafka container
  └── Redis container
```

where justified.

This reduces divergence from production behavior compared with simplistic substitutes.

---

# 138. H2 Warning

H2 should not be relied upon as proof that PostgreSQL-specific persistence behavior works.

Differences exist in:

```text
SQL
Types
Locking
Sequences
Constraints
Query behavior
```

PostgreSQL integration tests should use PostgreSQL.

---

# 139. WireMock

WireMock or equivalent should simulate external HTTP dependencies for integration tests.

Tests should cover:

```text
Success
Timeout
5xx
Malformed response
Slow response
Retry behavior
```

not only happy paths.

---

# 140. Contract Testing

Consumer/provider contract testing should be considered when independently deployed services have important API dependencies.

```text
Consumer expectation
       │
       ▼
Contract
       │
       ▼
Provider verification
```

This detects integration breakage before deployment.

---

# 141. ArchUnit

ArchUnit should enforce important architectural boundaries where useful.

Examples:

```text
Domain must not depend on controller
Domain must not depend on JPA adapter
Controllers must not access repositories directly
```

Architecture rules become executable.

---

# 142. Mutation Testing

Mutation testing should be evaluated for high-value domain logic.

It asks:

> Would the test suite detect deliberately introduced logic defects?

Do not require it indiscriminately across trivial code.

---

# 143. Performance Testing

Critical APIs should have explicit performance tests.

Measure:

```text
Latency
Throughput
Error rate
Resource consumption
Database load
Connection saturation
```

under realistic concurrency.

---

# 144. Golden Path

The platform team should provide a standard Spring Boot service template.

```text
New Service
    │
    ▼
Golden Path Template
    │
    ├── Security
    ├── Observability
    ├── Testing
    ├── Docker
    ├── Kubernetes
    ├── CI/CD
    ├── OpenAPI
    └── Resilience
```

Teams should not rebuild platform plumbing for every service.

---

# 145. Template Governance

A service template should accelerate teams without permanently locking them to outdated dependencies.

Templates require:

```text
Versioning
Upgrade guidance
Ownership
Security maintenance
Documentation
```

---

# 146. Production Readiness

Before production, each service should prove:

```text
Owner identified
API/event contracts documented
Authorization implemented
Database migrations tested
Observability operational
Timeouts configured
Retries bounded
Health probes correct
Resources defined
SLO established
Runbook available
Rollback tested
Backup/recovery addressed
Load characteristics understood
```

---

# 147. Service Evolution

Services must evolve without assuming synchronized deployment of every consumer.

```text
Producer v2
   │
   ├── Consumer v1
   └── Consumer v2
```

Compatibility windows are normal in distributed systems.

---

# 148. Microservice Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ Microservices because "enterprise systems use microservices"
❌ Service per database table
❌ Service per entity
❌ Distributed monolith
❌ Shared database tables across service boundaries
❌ Shared JPA entity libraries
❌ Synchronous calls through five services for simple operations
❌ Circular service dependencies
❌ Universal enterprise domain object
❌ DDD abstractions around trivial CRUD
❌ Huge aggregates
❌ Business logic in controllers
❌ Controllers accessing repositories directly
❌ JPA entities serialized as APIs
❌ EAGER relationships everywhere
❌ Open Session in View hiding database access
❌ Transactions around external network calls
❌ Arbitrary REQUIRES_NEW usage
❌ @Data on every JPA entity
❌ Field injection
❌ RestTemplate selected for new applications without reason
❌ WebClient used only because "reactive is faster"
❌ HTTP calls without bounded timeouts
❌ Retry annotations copied onto every client
❌ Huge authorization expressions
❌ Kafka events published before database commit
❌ Consumers assuming exactly-once processing
❌ In-memory @Async used for durable business work
❌ Scheduled jobs duplicated across every replica
❌ Unbounded executors
❌ Virtual threads treated as infinite capacity
❌ Cache annotations hiding incorrect invalidation
❌ Permanent feature flags
❌ Editing already-applied Flyway migrations
❌ Breaking schema changes during rolling deployment
❌ Secrets/PII dumped into logs
❌ Public unrestricted Actuator endpoints
❌ H2 used as proof of PostgreSQL compatibility
❌ Mock-heavy tests with no integration coverage
❌ Full Spring context started for every unit test
❌ E2E tests used as the entire test strategy
❌ No contract compatibility checks
❌ New service built from scratch with different conventions
❌ Shared libraries becoming a distributed monolith
❌ Services deployed independently but unable to evolve independently
```

---

# 149. Final Mediverse Spring Boot Application Reference Architecture

```text
                              CLIENT
                                │
                                ▼
                         API GATEWAY / ALB
                                │
                                ▼
                     SPRING BOOT SERVICE
                                │
                    ┌───────────┴───────────┐
                    ▼                       ▼
                 INBOUND                  SECURITY
                    │                       │
          ┌─────────┼─────────┐             ▼

        REST      Kafka     Scheduler         │
```
