# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                       | Decision                                                |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| Architecture strategy      | Business-capability driven                              |
| Microservices              | Requirement-driven, not default                         |
| Early architecture         | Modular monolith acceptable/preferred where appropriate |
| Domain modeling            | DDD where complexity justifies it                       |
| Service boundary           | Bounded context/capability                              |
| Aggregate                  | Transactional invariant boundary                        |
| Architecture style         | Hexagonal/ports-and-adapters for complex services       |
| Simple CRUD                | Keep simple                                             |
| Package strategy           | Feature/domain oriented                                 |
| Java                       | Centrally governed modern LTS                           |
| Spring Boot                | Centrally governed supported release                    |
| Build                      | Maven                                                   |
| Shared entity libraries    | **Rejected**                                            |
| Configuration              | Externalized + typed                                    |
| Secrets                    | ADR-064                                                 |
| REST                       | Resource/business-capability oriented                   |
| DTOs                       | Required at external boundaries                         |
| JPA entity exposure        | **Rejected**                                            |
| Validation                 | Request + domain + DB                                   |
| Error standard             | RFC 9457 Problem Details                                |
| Pagination                 | Required for growing collections                        |
| API versioning             | Compatibility-driven                                    |
| OpenAPI                    | Required for consumed APIs                              |
| API-first                  | Contract-heavy APIs                                     |
| Code-first                 | Acceptable for simpler internal APIs                    |
| Contract compatibility CI  | Required                                                |
| Controllers                | Thin                                                    |
| CQRS                       | Requirement-driven                                      |
| Persistence                | Spring Data JPA                                         |
| OSIV dependence            | Generally **rejected**                                  |
| Transaction boundary       | Application use case                                    |
| Mapping                    | Explicit                                                |
| MapStruct                  | Preferred when mapping complexity warrants              |
| Lombok                     | Selective                                               |
| `@Data` on JPA             | Generally **rejected**                                  |
| DI                         | Constructor injection                                   |
| Synchronous HTTP           | RestClient preferred                                    |
| Reactive HTTP              | WebClient where genuinely required                      |
| RestTemplate               | Legacy/migration only                                   |
| Resilience                 | ADR-066                                                 |
| Authentication             | OAuth2/OIDC                                             |
| Authorization              | Scope/role + resource/business authorization            |
| Messaging                  | Kafka                                                   |
| Event delivery             | At least once assumption                                |
| Consumers                  | Idempotent                                              |
| Dual writes                | Transactional outbox                                    |
| Scheduled work             | Explicit distributed semantics                          |
| Durable async              | Kafka/queue, not `@Async`                               |
| Virtual threads            | Workload-driven evaluation                              |
| Cache                      | Redis / ADR-065                                         |
| Feature flags              | Governed + temporary                                    |
| DB migrations              | Flyway default                                          |
| Migration strategy         | Expand → migrate → contract                             |
| Logging                    | Structured                                              |
| Metrics/tracing            | Micrometer                                              |
| Operations endpoints       | Actuator                                                |
| Unit testing               | JUnit 5                                                 |
| Assertions                 | AssertJ                                                 |
| Mocking                    | Mockito selectively                                     |
| Slice tests                | Preferred where applicable                              |
| Integration infrastructure | Testcontainers                                          |
| PostgreSQL testing         | Real PostgreSQL                                         |
| HTTP dependency simulation | WireMock                                                |
| Contract testing           | Important independent-service boundaries                |
| Architecture enforcement   | ArchUnit                                                |
| Mutation testing           | Critical domain logic evaluation                        |
| Performance testing        | Critical APIs                                           |
| Service creation           | Golden-path template                                    |
| Production readiness       | Mandatory review                                        |
| Status                     | **Accepted**                                            |
| Priority                   | **Critical**                                            |

---

---

# ADR-068 — Enterprise Frontend Architecture, React Engineering & Web Platform Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Optimistic Update Safety**.

---

# 61. Authentication & OIDC Browser Architecture

Mediverse browser authentication should use standards-based OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect.

```text
Browser
   │
   ▼
Mediverse Web
   │
   ▼
Identity Provider
   │
   ▼
Authentication
   │
   ▼
Mediverse APIs
```

The frontend must not implement its own password/token protocol.

---

# 62. Authorization Code + PKCE

For browser-based public clients using OAuth directly, **Authorization Code Flow with PKCE** should be the baseline.

```text
Browser
   │
   ├── code_challenge
   ▼
Identity Provider
   │
   ▼
Authorization Code
   │
   ▼
Browser
   │
   ├── code_verifier
   ▼
Token Endpoint
```

Implicit Flow should not be used for new Mediverse applications.

---

# 63. PKCE Purpose

PKCE protects authorization-code exchange by binding the authorization request to the client that initiated it.

An intercepted authorization code alone should therefore be insufficient for token exchange.

---

# 64. BFF Evaluation

A **Backend for Frontend (BFF)** should be evaluated for the main authenticated Mediverse web application.

```text
Browser
   │
   │ Secure session cookie
   ▼
BFF
   │
   │ OAuth tokens
   ▼
Mediverse APIs
```

This can keep OAuth tokens outside browser JavaScript.

---

# 65. BFF Benefits

A BFF can provide:

```text
Token isolation
HttpOnly session cookies
API aggregation
Browser-specific contracts
Centralized CSRF protection
Simpler browser authentication
```

It also adds another deployable runtime and must therefore solve a real requirement.

---

# 66. BFF Is Not an API Gateway

These responsibilities should not be confused.

```text
BFF
→ frontend-specific backend behavior

API Gateway
→ platform/API ingress concerns
```

They may coexist.

---

# 67. Token Storage

Long-lived authentication tokens should not casually be stored in:

```text
localStorage
sessionStorage
IndexedDB
```

because JavaScript-accessible storage is exposed to successful XSS.

---

# 68. HttpOnly Cookies

When BFF/session architecture is adopted, session cookies should normally use appropriate:

```text
HttpOnly
Secure
SameSite
```

settings.

`HttpOnly` prevents ordinary JavaScript from directly reading the cookie.

---

# 69. Cookie Limitation

Cookies improve token isolation but introduce CSRF considerations because browsers attach cookies automatically.

Security architecture therefore changes rather than disappears.

---

# 70. CSRF

State-changing cookie-authenticated requests require appropriate CSRF defenses.

Potential controls include:

```text
SameSite policy
CSRF tokens
Origin validation
Request-method discipline
```

according to architecture.

---

# 71. XSS

XSS remains one of the most important browser threats.

Primary controls include:

```text
React escaping
Avoiding unsafe HTML injection
Input/output handling
CSP
Dependency governance
No arbitrary script execution
```

---

# 72. dangerouslySetInnerHTML

Use of:

```text
dangerouslySetInnerHTML
```

must be exceptional.

If rich HTML is required, content must pass through an approved sanitization architecture.

---

# 73. Content Security Policy

Mediverse should deploy a restrictive CSP.

Conceptually:

```text
default-src 'self'
script-src ...
style-src ...
img-src ...
connect-src ...
frame-src ...
object-src 'none'
```

Exact directives depend on production integrations.

---

# 74. CSP Rollout

For complex existing applications, CSP may first be deployed in report-only mode to identify legitimate dependencies before enforcement.

The target remains enforcement—not permanent report-only operation.

---

# 75. Third-Party Scripts

Every third-party browser script increases:

```text
Supply-chain risk
Privacy exposure
Performance cost
CSP complexity
Failure dependencies
```

Third-party JavaScript requires explicit justification.

---

# 76. Frontend Authorization UX

The UI may hide or disable actions the current user cannot perform.

```text
Permission
    │
    ▼
UI Capability
```

But this is usability—not security enforcement.

---

# 77. Backend Authorization Remains Mandatory

An attacker can bypass the React application and call APIs directly.

Therefore:

```text
Frontend permission check
        ≠
Authorization boundary
```

ADR-064 and ADR-067 remain authoritative.

---

# 78. Session Expiration

Expired authentication should produce controlled behavior.

```text
API
 │
 ▼
401
 │
 ▼
Auth handler
 │
 ▼
Renew session if valid
or
Re-authenticate
```

Do not create infinite token-refresh loops.

---

# 79. Concurrent Authentication Failure

If 50 API calls simultaneously receive authentication failure, the frontend should avoid initiating 50 independent refresh operations.

Authentication renewal should be coordinated.

---

# 80. Logout

Logout should clear application authentication state and invalidate server-side sessions/tokens where the selected architecture supports it.

Sensitive cached user-specific state should also be cleared.

---

# 81. TanStack Query Cache

Server-state cache policy should reflect data semantics.

```text
Query
 │
 ├── fresh
 │
 ├── stale
 │
 └── garbage collected
```

Do not assign identical freshness settings to every API.

---

# 82. Query Keys

Query keys should be deterministic and structured.

Example:

```text
['courses', courseId]
['courses', { category, page }]
```

Poor key design causes invalidation and cache-consistency bugs.

---

# 83. Cache Invalidation

After mutations, invalidate only relevant queries where practical.

```text
Update Course
     │
     ▼
Mutation Success
     │
     ├── course/{id}
     └── affected course lists
```

Globally invalidating every query wastes network and server capacity.

---

# 84. Prefetching

Likely next data may be prefetched when evidence shows UX benefit.

Examples:

```text
Next lesson
Course details
Adjacent page
```

Do not prefetch half the application speculatively.

---

# 85. Pagination

Frontend pagination must match backend semantics.

For stable administrative lists:

```text
page + size
```

may be sufficient.

For feeds/large changing datasets:

```text
cursor
```

may be preferable.

---

# 86. Infinite Scrolling

Infinite scrolling should be used only where the interaction model benefits from it.

It is often poor for:

```text
Administrative tables
Precise navigation
Accessibility-heavy workflows
Content users need to relocate
```

Pagination may be superior.

---

# 87. Offline Behavior

The frontend should explicitly distinguish:

```text
Online
Offline
Poor connection
Backend unavailable
```

rather than presenting every network failure as the same generic error.

---

# 88. File Upload Architecture

Large uploads should avoid unnecessarily passing file bytes through application servers.

```text
Browser
   │
   ▼
Mediverse API
   │ authorize
   ▼
Presigned Upload
   │
   ▼
S3
```

---

# 89. Upload Workflow

Recommended flow:

```text
1. Select file
       │
2. Client validation
       │
3. Request upload authorization
       │
4. Receive presigned destination
       │
5. Upload to S3
       │
6. Confirm completion
       │
7. Server-side validation/scanning
       │
8. Asset becomes available
```

Client validation does not replace server validation.

---

# 90. Upload Progress

Large uploads should provide meaningful progress.

```text
Uploading
████████░░ 80%
```

But the UI must distinguish:

```text
Upload completed
```

from:

```text
Asset validated and ready
```

---

# 91. Multipart Upload

Large educational videos and 3D assets should use multipart upload where appropriate.

This enables:

```text
Chunking
Retry of failed parts
Better large-file resilience
Potential resume behavior
```

---

# 92. Abandoned Multipart Uploads

Incomplete multipart uploads consume storage.

S3 lifecycle policies should clean abandoned uploads according to ADR-065.

---

# 93. Media Delivery

Public/authorized static media should normally be delivered through CDN architecture rather than Spring Boot streaming every byte.

```text
S3
 │
 ▼
CloudFront
 │
 ▼
Browser
```

---

# 94. Private Media

Private course assets require authorization-aware delivery.

Potential architecture:

```text
Browser
   │
   ▼
Authorization API
   │
   ▼
Signed URL / Cookie
   │
   ▼
CloudFront
   │
   ▼
S3
```

---

# 95. Video Architecture

Large educational video should use streaming-oriented delivery rather than treating every video as a giant downloadable object.

Adaptive streaming should be evaluated for serious production video workloads.

---

# 96. Real-Time Architecture

Real-time communication should be requirement-driven.

Options include:

```text
Polling
Long polling
SSE
WebSocket
```

Do not choose WebSockets merely because the feature is described as "real time."

---

# 97. Server-Sent Events

SSE is appropriate for primarily server-to-browser streams such as:

```text
Processing status
Notifications
Progress updates
AI generation status
```

where full bidirectional communication is unnecessary.

---

# 98. WebSockets

WebSockets should be used when persistent bidirectional communication is genuinely required.

Examples may include:

```text
Collaborative interaction
Live classroom features
Interactive presence
Bidirectional real-time sessions
```

---

# 99. Reconnection

Real-time clients must handle:

```text
Disconnect
Reconnect
Duplicate event
Missed event
Session expiration
Network change
```

A WebSocket connection should never be assumed permanent.

---

# 100. Real-Time State Reconciliation

After reconnect:

```text
Reconnect
   │
   ▼
Fetch authoritative state
   │
   ▼
Apply subsequent events
```

may be safer than assuming every event was received.

---

# 101. 3D Learning Architecture

Mediverse's 3D educational modules should be treated as a specialized rendering subsystem.

```text
React Application
       │
       ▼
React Three Fiber
       │
       ▼
Three.js
       │
       ▼
WebGL / GPU
       │
       ▼
3D Educational Scene
```

3D should remain isolated from ordinary application concerns.

---

# 102. React Three Fiber

React Three Fiber should be preferred for integrating Three.js scenes into the React application when React lifecycle/composition provides value.

Raw Three.js remains appropriate for lower-level capabilities when necessary.

---

# 103. Drei

`@react-three/drei` may provide reusable helpers for:

```text
Controls
Loaders
Environment
Text
Camera utilities
Performance helpers
```

Use helpers deliberately rather than treating Drei as the architecture.

---

# 104. 3D Feature Boundary

A 3D physiology module should have its own feature boundary.

```text
features/anatomy3d/
│
├── components/
├── scenes/
├── models/
├── interactions/
├── loaders/
├── annotations/
├── educational-content/
└── tests/
```

Do not scatter WebGL logic throughout ordinary React pages.

---

# 105. 3D Asset Format

**glTF/GLB** should be the default runtime delivery format for 3D web assets.

It supports web-oriented:

```text
Meshes
Materials
Textures
Animations
Scene hierarchy
```

---

# 106. Source vs Runtime Assets

Production runtime assets should be distinguished from authoring assets.

```text
Blender / Source
      │
      ▼
Optimization Pipeline
      │
      ▼
GLB Runtime Asset
      │
      ▼
CDN
```

Do not ship raw authoring assets directly to users.

---

# 107. Geometry Optimization

Models should be optimized for browser rendering.

Consider:

```text
Polygon count
Draw calls
Material count
Mesh count
Texture size
Animation complexity
```

A beautiful 4-million-polygon organ model that freezes mid-range phones is a failed web asset.

---

# 108. Draco and Meshopt

Geometry compression such as Draco or Meshopt should be evaluated according to asset characteristics.

Compression trades:

```text
Smaller transfer
        vs
Client decode cost
```

Measure on target devices.

---

# 109. Texture Optimization

Textures frequently dominate 3D payload size.

Optimize:

```text
Resolution
Compression
Texture count
Mipmaps
Color channels
Reuse
```

Modern GPU-friendly compressed texture formats should be evaluated.

---

# 110. Progressive 3D Loading

Users should not wait for an entire complex anatomical scene before receiving useful feedback.

```text
UI shell
   │
   ▼
Essential model
   │
   ▼
Annotations
   │
   ▼
High-detail assets
```

Progressive loading improves perceived performance.

---

# 111. Level of Detail

Complex scenes should evaluate LOD.

```text
Far
→ low-detail model

Near
→ higher-detail model
```

Rendering detail users cannot perceive wastes GPU resources.

---

# 112. Frustum Culling

Objects outside the visible camera region should not consume unnecessary rendering work where engine capabilities permit optimization.

Scene design should support efficient culling.

---

# 113. Draw Calls

3D performance is not determined only by polygon count.

Excessive:

```text
Objects
Materials
State changes
Draw calls
```

can severely reduce performance.

---

# 114. Instancing

Repeated objects should use GPU instancing where appropriate.

Example:

```text
Thousands of repeated structures
        │
        ▼
Instanced rendering
```

instead of thousands of independent draw calls.

---

# 115. Web Workers

CPU-heavy operations that do not require DOM access should be evaluated for Web Workers.

Examples:

```text
Data parsing
Complex calculations
Asset processing
Some simulation work
```

This can protect main-thread responsiveness.

---

# 116. Main Thread

The browser main thread is a finite resource shared by:

```text
React
Layout
Input
JavaScript
3D orchestration
Animation
```

Long tasks directly damage UX.

---

# 117. WebGL Capability Detection

The application should detect unsupported or severely constrained rendering environments.

```text
3D supported
     │
   ┌─┴─────┐
   ▼       ▼
  Yes      No
   │       │
   ▼       ▼
3D Mode  Accessible
         fallback
```

---

# 118. 3D Fallback

Fallbacks may include:

```text
2D anatomical diagrams
Images
Video
Interactive labelled illustrations
Structured text
```

Educational access must not depend entirely on GPU capability.

---

# 119. Educational Annotations

3D scenes should connect visual structures to learning content.

```text
3D Structure
    │
    ▼
Annotation
    │
    ├── Name
    ├── Description
    ├── Function
    ├── Clinical relevance
    └── Audio where appropriate
```

3D without instructional design is decoration.

---

# 120. Performance Budgets

Mediverse should define explicit frontend performance budgets.

Budgets should cover:

```text
Initial JavaScript
Route chunks
Images
Fonts
3D assets
Long tasks
Core Web Vitals
```

Exact thresholds should be measured against target devices and network conditions.

---

# 121. Core Web Vitals

Frontend performance monitoring should track current user-centric web performance metrics, including applicable Core Web Vitals.

These metrics should be collected from real users where privacy requirements permit.

---

# 122. Bundle Budget

CI should detect abnormal bundle growth.

```text
Build
 │
 ▼
Bundle Analysis
 │
 ├── within budget → pass
 └── excessive     → review/fail
```

Bundle size should not silently grow forever.

---

# 123. Tree Shaking

Libraries should be imported in ways that allow unused code elimination.

A 20 KB requirement should not introduce a 2 MB dependency bundle without scrutiny.

---

# 124. Dynamic Imports

Heavy features should load on demand.

```text
Student Dashboard
      │
      X
No need to load
3D anatomy engine immediately
```

The 3D runtime should be loaded when needed.

---

# 125. Image Optimization

Images should use appropriate:

```text
Dimensions
Compression
Responsive variants
Lazy loading
Modern formats
```

Serving desktop-resolution images to every mobile device wastes bandwidth.

---

# 126. Font Optimization

Fonts should be deliberately governed.

Avoid downloading numerous:

```text
Families
Weights
Styles
Scripts
```

that most users never need.

Use appropriate preload/subsetting/self-hosting strategies where justified.

---

# 127. PWA Evaluation

PWA capabilities should be requirement-driven.

Useful possibilities:

```text
Installability
Offline shell
Cached educational resources
Background capabilities where supported
```

But "make it a PWA" is not itself a product requirement.

---

# 128. Service Worker Risk

Service workers introduce another cache/lifecycle layer.

Poor update logic can leave users running stale application code after deployment.

Versioning and invalidation must be deliberate.

---

# 129. Offline Learning

If offline learning becomes a product requirement, architecture must explicitly solve:

```text
Content download
Storage quotas
Content versioning
Progress recording
Synchronization
Conflicts
Security
Expiry
Logout cleanup
```

This is substantially more complex than caching HTML.

---

# 130. Internationalization

User-facing strings should not be permanently embedded throughout components.

```text
Component
   │
   ▼
Translation Key
   │
   ▼
Locale Resource
```

The architecture should support future language expansion.

---

# 131. English and Marathi

Where Mediverse supports English and Marathi, educational terminology requires curated translations rather than blind machine substitution.

Medical meaning must remain authoritative.

---

# 132. Locale Formatting

Localization includes:

```text
Dates
Times
Numbers
Units
Pluralization
Relative time
```

not only translated strings.

---

# 133. RTL Readiness

Even if initial languages are LTR, shared design-system components should avoid assumptions that make future RTL support unnecessarily difficult.

Prefer logical layout concepts where practical.

---

# 134. Frontend Testing Strategy

Mediverse should use layered frontend testing.

```text
             /\
            /E2E\
           /----\
          /Visual\
         /------\
        /Integration\
       /----------\
      / Component  \
     /--------------\
    /   Unit Tests   \
   /__________________\
```

Tests should protect user behavior rather than implementation details.

---

# 135. Vitest

Vitest should be the default unit/component test runner for the Vite frontend unless future tooling requirements justify change.

---

# 136. React Testing Library

React Testing Library should test components from the user's perspective.

Prefer:

```text
Find button by accessible role
Click
Observe outcome
```

over testing internal component state.

---

# 137. MSW

Mock Service Worker should be preferred for realistic API mocking in frontend tests where appropriate.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
HTTP request
    │
    ▼
MSW
    │
    ▼
Controlled response
```

This tests the API boundary more realistically than mocking every hook.

---

# 138. Playwright

Playwright should be the primary browser E2E framework.

Critical journeys should include:

```text
Login
Course discovery
Enrollment
Lesson consumption
Assessment submission
File upload
Permission boundaries
```

---

# 139. Accessibility Testing

Automated accessibility testing should be integrated into component and/or browser testing.

Automation cannot prove full accessibility.

Manual keyboard and assistive-technology testing remains necessary for critical experiences.

---

# 140. Visual Regression

Visual regression testing should be used selectively for:

```text
Design-system components
Critical layouts
Complex learning visualizations
```

Do not create thousands of unstable screenshots with no ownership.

---

# 141. Error Boundaries

React Error Boundaries should isolate rendering failures where appropriate.

```text
3D Module crashes
       │
       ▼
Local Error Boundary
       │
       ▼
Rest of course remains usable
```

One component failure should not unnecessarily blank the whole application.

---

# 142. Frontend Observability

Production frontend telemetry should capture appropriate:

```text
JavaScript errors
Failed requests
Performance
Core Web Vitals
Route transitions
Feature failures
3D initialization failures
```

while respecting privacy requirements.

---

# 143. Source Maps

Production source maps may be made available securely to approved observability tooling.

They should not expose sensitive source/configuration unnecessarily.

---

# 144. Environment Configuration

Frontend builds must assume all shipped browser configuration is publicly inspectable.

Therefore:

```text
VITE_API_URL
→ acceptable configuration

VITE_DATABASE_PASSWORD
→ catastrophic design error
```

There are no secret frontend environment variables once bundled into browser code.

---

# 145. Package Management & Supply Chain

Mediverse should standardize one Node package-management workflow.

npm is acceptable; pnpm should be evaluated if workspace efficiency and strict dependency handling provide measurable value.

Regardless of tool:

```text
Lockfile
Reproducible install
Dependency scanning
Controlled upgrades
Registry governance
```

are required.

---

# 146. Frontend CI/CD

Frontend CI should execute approximately:

```text
Checkout
   │
   ▼
Locked Dependency Install
   │
   ▼
Type Check
   │
   ▼
Lint
   │
   ▼
Unit / Component Tests
   │
   ▼
Build
   │
   ▼
Bundle Budget
   │
   ▼
Security Checks
   │
   ▼
E2E / Required Quality Gates
   │
   ▼
Deploy Artifact
```

Build once; promote immutable artifacts where deployment architecture permits.

---

# 147. S3 + CloudFront Deployment

For SPA/static deployment:

```text
Git
 │
 ▼
CI
 │
 ▼
Vite Build
 │
 ▼
Immutable Assets
 │
 ▼
S3
 │
 ▼
CloudFront
 │
 ▼
Users
```

Hashed assets should receive long-lived caching.

The HTML shell should use a shorter caching strategy so deployments can reference new asset hashes.

---

# 148. Frontend Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ Plain JavaScript for new production application code without reason
❌ TypeScript with pervasive any
❌ Assuming TypeScript validates API data
❌ React state used for every state category
❌ Every API response copied into Redux
❌ Global Context used as a high-frequency state database
❌ One enormous components/ directory
❌ Circular feature dependencies
❌ Everything moved into shared/
❌ Business logic scattered through JSX
❌ Raw fetch/Axios calls in every component
❌ Hand-maintained duplicate API types when generated contracts are viable
❌ Client validation treated as security
❌ Frontend route guards treated as authorization
❌ OAuth tokens casually persisted in localStorage
❌ dangerouslySetInnerHTML with untrusted content
❌ Third-party scripts added without security/performance review
❌ CSP permanently disabled because integrations are inconvenient
❌ Every error displayed as "Something went wrong"
❌ Blank screens during loading
❌ Empty results treated as errors
❌ Optimistic success for irreversible operations
❌ Infinite scrolling everywhere
❌ Cache invalidation by refreshing the whole application
❌ Uploading multi-GB video through Spring Boot without reason
❌ Declaring S3 upload complete before security processing completes
❌ Spring Boot used as a static-media streaming server
❌ WebSockets selected for simple status updates
❌ Reconnect logic assuming no events were missed
❌ Raw unoptimized Blender assets shipped to browsers
❌ Multi-million-polygon models shipped to mobile devices
❌ 8K textures everywhere
❌ Loading Three.js on the login page
❌ 3D as the only representation of required educational content
❌ 3D visual spectacle without learning purpose
❌ No reduced-motion support
❌ Device-specific responsive breakpoints
❌ Clickable divs replacing buttons
❌ ARIA used instead of semantic HTML
❌ Accessibility postponed until release
❌ Bundle size allowed to grow without budgets
❌ Service worker caching without update strategy
❌ "Offline support" implemented as cache everything
❌ Strings hardcoded throughout UI
❌ Machine translation trusted for authoritative medical terminology
❌ Tests coupled to implementation details
❌ E2E tests used for every behavior
❌ Screenshot tests created without ownership
❌ Browser telemetry collecting sensitive content
❌ Secrets placed in VITE_* variables
❌ npm install without lockfile discipline in CI
❌ CDN invalidation used for every hashed asset
❌ Micro-frontends introduced because microservices exist
```

---

| Language                  | **TypeScript**                                 |
| Type safety               | Strict target                                  |
| Build tooling             | **Vite**                                       |
| Authenticated application | SPA                                            |
| Public SEO content        | SSR/SSG evaluation                             |
| Next.js                   | Requirement-driven                             |
| Source architecture       | Feature-oriented                               |
| Shared code               | Controlled                                     |
| UI architecture           | Design system                                  |
| Component documentation   | Storybook where justified                      |
| Styling                   | One governed primary strategy                  |
| Accessibility             | **WCAG 2.2 AA baseline**                       |
| Responsive model          | Mobile-first                                   |
| Routing                   | React Router                                   |
| Route loading             | Code split/lazy                                |
| Backend authorization     | Mandatory                                      |
| Server state              | **TanStack Query**                             |
| Global client state       | Redux Toolkit only when justified              |
| Local state               | React                                          |
| URL state                 | Router/search params                           |
| Forms                     | **React Hook Form**                            |
| Runtime schemas           | **Zod**                                        |
| API contracts             | OpenAPI                                        |
| API client                | Generated where viable                         |
| Errors                    | Problem Details aware                          |
| Authentication            | OIDC/OAuth                                     |
| Browser OAuth             | Authorization Code + PKCE                      |
| BFF                       | Preferred evaluation for authenticated app     |
| Token storage             | Avoid casual browser persistence               |

| XSS                       | Defense in depth                               |
| CSP                       | Required production control                    |
| Uploads                   | Presigned S3                                   |

| Real-time                 | Requirement-driven                             |
| SSE                       | Server→client streaming                        |

# ADR-069 — Enterprise AI/LLM, RAG, Intelligent Tutoring & Medical AI Architecture Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — AI Security Principle**.

---

# 61. Medical AI Output Safety & Factuality

Medical educational output must be treated as higher-risk than ordinary generative content.

The system should distinguish:

```text
Fluent answer
      ≠
Correct answer
      ≠
Grounded answer
      ≠
Educationally appropriate answer
```

Generation quality therefore requires multiple independent controls.

---

# 62. Medical Claim Grounding

Important factual medical claims should be grounded in approved Mediverse knowledge sources when the capability is operating in grounded tutoring mode.

```text
Question
   │
   ▼
Evidence Retrieval
   │
   ▼
Generation
   │
   ▼
Claim ↔ Evidence Check
   │
   ▼
Answer
```

The model's pretrained knowledge alone should not automatically be treated as authoritative course content.

---

# 63. Clinical Question Detection

The system should detect when a conversation moves from education toward patient-specific clinical decision-making.

Examples:

```text
"What causes tachycardia?"
→ educational

"My heart rate is 150 and I feel dizzy. What should I do?"
→ patient-specific / higher-risk
```

The second case crosses a materially different risk boundary.

---

# 64. Clinical Boundary Enforcement

Clinical-risk classification should influence system behavior.

```text
Request
   │
   ▼
Risk Classification
   │
   ├── Educational
   │      ▼
   │    Tutor
   │
   └── Clinical-risk
          ▼
      Restricted Policy
```

A prompt disclaimer alone is not sufficient enforcement.

---

# 65. Uncertainty

The AI must be permitted to express uncertainty.

Useful states include:

```text
Supported
Partially supported
Conflicting evidence
Insufficient evidence
Outside approved corpus
```

Forced confidence creates hallucinations.

---

# 66. Evidence Conflict

If authoritative sources disagree, the system should not silently select one answer.

```text
Source A ─┐
          ├──► Conflict Detection
Source B ─┘
                 │
                 ▼
        Explain disagreement
```

Edition, guideline date and source authority may matter.

---

# 67. Answer Verification

High-value generated answers should support a post-generation verification stage where practical.

```text
Draft Answer
     │
     ▼
Claims Extraction
     │
     ▼
Evidence Verification
     │
     ▼
Final Answer
```

Verification should not simply ask the same model, with the same context, whether it thinks its own answer is correct and treat that as proof.

---

# 68. Claim-Level Verification

Verification should operate at meaningful claim granularity.

Example:

```text
Answer
 ├── Claim 1 → Source A ✓
 ├── Claim 2 → Source B ✓
 └── Claim 3 → unsupported ✗
```

Unsupported material can then be removed, qualified or regenerated.

---

# 69. Moderation

Input/output moderation should be capability-specific.

It may need to detect:

```text
Abuse
Unsafe requests
Self-harm content
Sexual content
Violence
Prompt attacks
Privacy violations
Clinical-risk requests
```

Medical terminology itself must not be incorrectly blocked merely because it contains anatomically explicit terms.

---

# 70. Medical Context-Aware Safety

A medical learning platform necessarily discusses:

```text
Anatomy
Reproductive physiology
Disease
Injury
Drugs
Death
Clinical procedures
```

Safety systems therefore need context awareness.

Naive keyword blocking would make the platform unusable.

---

# 71. Multilingual Medical AI

Language translation must preserve medical meaning.

Architecture:

```text
Learner Language
      │
      ▼
Terminology Layer
      │
      ▼
Retrieval
      │
      ▼
Reasoning
      │
      ▼
Localized Explanation
```

---

# 72. Canonical Medical Terminology

Where possible, concepts should have language-independent identifiers.

Conceptually:

```text
Concept ID
   │
   ├── English term
   ├── Marathi term
   ├── Synonyms
   └── Abbreviations
```

This is more robust than treating translated strings as independent concepts.

---

# 73. Marathi Tutoring

For Marathi educational support, the system should preserve important English medical terminology where that improves academic usefulness.

Example style:

```text
हृदयाचे आकुंचन (cardiac contraction)
```

rather than forcing unnatural translations for every technical term.

---

# 74. Translation Validation

High-value medical terminology dictionaries should be reviewed by qualified subject/language experts.

LLM translation alone should not establish canonical terminology.

---

# 75. Cross-Lingual Retrieval

A Marathi question may need to retrieve English authoritative material.

```text
Marathi Query
     │
     ▼
Cross-Lingual Understanding
     │
     ▼
English Corpus
     │
     ▼
Evidence
     │
     ▼
Marathi Explanation
```

Retrieval quality must be explicitly evaluated for this scenario.

---

# 76. Multimodal AI

Mediverse AI should support multimodal educational interactions where they improve learning.

Potential inputs:

```text
Text
Diagram
Image
3D scene state
Audio
```

---

# 77. Image Understanding

Image-capable models may assist with educational diagrams.

```text
Diagram
   +
Question
   │
   ▼
Vision Model
   │
   ▼
Educational Explanation
```

The model should receive sufficient contextual information to know what educational material it is analyzing.

---

# 78. Image Grounding

Visual interpretation can hallucinate structures.

Where authoritative labels/metadata exist, use them.

```text
Image
   │
   ├── Visual model
   └── Authoritative metadata
            │
            ▼
       Explanation
```

---

# 79. 3D-Aware Tutor

The AI tutor should understand the current 3D learning context without requiring the model to infer everything from screenshots.

```text
3D Scene
   │
   ├── selectedStructure = mitralValve
   ├── lesson = cardiacCycle
   ├── animationPhase = ventricularSystole
   └── cameraContext
           │
           ▼
        AI Tutor
```

Structured scene state is superior to guessing scene semantics from pixels.

---

# 80. 3D Tool Integration

The tutor may invoke controlled frontend actions.

Example:

```text
Learner:
"Show me where the mitral valve is."

AI
 │
 ▼
Tool:
focusStructure("mitral-valve")
 │
 ▼
3D Engine
 │
 ▼
Highlight + Camera Focus
```

---

# 81. AI-to-3D Command Safety

The model should not emit arbitrary JavaScript.

Instead:

```text
LLM
 │
 ▼
Structured Tool Call
 │
 ▼
Schema Validation
 │
 ▼
Allowed Scene Command
```

---

# 82. 3D Tool Allowlist

Potential commands:

```text
focusStructure()
highlightStructure()
isolateStructure()
playAnimation()
pauseAnimation()
setLearningStep()
showAnnotation()
```

The scene engine remains authoritative over execution.

---

# 83. Scene State Feedback

After executing a tool, the frontend should return structured state.

```text
AI command
    │
    ▼
3D engine
    │
    ▼
Execution result
    │
    ▼
AI
```

This prevents the model from assuming an action succeeded.

---

# 84. Speech-to-Text

Voice input may improve accessibility and tutoring interaction.

```text
Learner Speech
      │
      ▼
Speech Recognition
      │
      ▼
Transcript
      │
      ▼
AI Tutor
```

Transcripts should remain visible/editable where practical.

---

# 85. Medical Speech Recognition

General speech recognition may perform poorly on:

```text
Drug names
Anatomical terminology
Latin-derived terms
Abbreviations
Mixed Marathi-English speech
```

Medical vocabulary accuracy requires evaluation.

---

# 86. Text-to-Speech

AI explanations may be converted to speech.

```text
Tutor Response
      │
      ▼
TTS
      │
      ▼
Audio
```

Text must remain available for accessibility and verification.

---

# 87. TTS Pronunciation

Medical terminology pronunciation should be tested.

A fluent voice that repeatedly mispronounces core terminology damages educational quality.

---

# 88. AI Quiz Generation

AI may generate draft questions from approved learning content.

```text
Learning Objective
      +
Approved Evidence
      │
      ▼
Question Generator
      │
      ▼
Validation
      │
      ▼
Question Bank
```

---

# 89. Quiz Structure

Generated questions should use structured contracts.

```json
{
  "question": "...",
  "type": "single_best_answer",
  "options": [],
  "correctOption": "...",
  "explanation": "...",
  "learningObjective": "...",
  "citations": []
}
```

---

# 90. Quiz Validation

A generated question is not automatically valid because an LLM produced it.

Validation should inspect:

```text
Correctness
Single best answer
Distractor quality
Ambiguity
Learning-objective alignment
Difficulty
Evidence support
Terminology
```

---

# 91. Assessment Boundary

High-stakes graded assessments should not be populated directly with uncontrolled real-time generated questions.

Prefer:

```text
AI Draft
   │
   ▼
Validation
   │
   ▼
Human Review where required
   │
   ▼
Approved Question Bank
```

---

# 92. Distractor Generation

Incorrect answer choices should be:

```text
Plausible
Clearly incorrect under the intended interpretation
Educationally meaningful
Non-trivial
```

Random nonsense makes MCQs easier without improving learning.

---

# 93. Explanation Generation

Question explanations should describe:

```text
Why the correct answer is correct
Why relevant distractors are incorrect
Underlying concept
Source evidence
```

This is more educationally useful than returning only an answer key.

---

# 94. Adaptive Difficulty

Difficulty may adapt based on learner performance.

```text
Performance
    │
    ▼
Learner Model
    │
    ▼
Difficulty Selection
    │
    ▼
Next Question
```

The adjustment mechanism should be measurable and explainable.

---

# 95. Difficulty Is Multidimensional

Difficulty is not merely:

```text
easy / medium / hard
```

It can depend on:

```text
Recall depth
Concept integration
Clinical application
Distractor similarity
Required reasoning steps
Prior knowledge
```

---

# 96. Learner Knowledge Model

Mediverse should maintain an authoritative learning-state model outside the LLM.

```text
Learner
   │
   ▼
Knowledge Model
   │
   ├── Topic mastery
   ├── Attempts
   ├── Accuracy
   ├── Recency
   └── Confidence estimate
```

The LLM may consume this state but should not be its sole source of truth.

---

# 97. Knowledge Graph

Curriculum concepts may be represented as dependencies.

```text
Cell Physiology
      │
      ▼
Membrane Potential
      │
      ▼
Action Potential
      │
      ▼
Cardiac Electrophysiology
```

This supports prerequisite-aware learning.

---

# 98. Knowledge Tracing

Knowledge tracing may estimate changing learner mastery over time.

Conceptually:

```text
Prior Mastery
     +
Question Result
     +
Difficulty
     +
Time
     │
     ▼
Updated Mastery
```

Sophisticated ML is not mandatory initially.

---

# 99. Start Simple

Do not jump immediately to deep-learning knowledge-tracing models.

A transparent model using:

```text
Attempts
Accuracy
Difficulty
Recency
Confidence
```

may provide more operational value initially.

Complexity should be earned through evidence.

---

# 100. Spaced Repetition

Review scheduling should incorporate forgetting and recall history.

```text
Successful Recall
      │
      ▼
Longer Interval

Failed Recall
      │
      ▼
Shorter Interval
```

AI may generate explanations, but scheduling should remain deterministic enough to test.

---

# 101. Recommendation Engine

Learning recommendations may combine:

```text
Curriculum requirements
Mastery
Prerequisites
Recent mistakes
Upcoming assessments
Learner goals
```

Recommendations should optimize learning outcomes—not raw screen time.

---

# 102. Recommendation Explainability

The system should be capable of explaining:

> "Why am I being asked to study this?"

Example:

```text
Recommended:
Cardiac Action Potentials

Because:
2 recent errors
+
prerequisite for ECG interpretation
```

---

# 103. AI-Generated Learning Paths

AI may propose learning paths.

But the curriculum graph and academic requirements remain authoritative.

```text
AI Proposal
    │
    ▼
Constraint Validation
    │
    ▼
Learning Path
```

---

# 104. Educator Oversight

Educators need governance controls for AI-generated learning material.

Potential states:

```text
Draft
Reviewed
Approved
Rejected
Archived
```

---

# 105. Human Review

Human review should be risk-based.

Not every low-risk AI explanation requires pre-publication review.

But reusable/high-impact content may.

Examples:

```text
Generated flashcard
→ automated checks may suffice

Official assessment question
→ stronger review

Canonical medical explanation
→ subject expert review
```

---

# 106. Content Provenance

Reusable AI-generated content should record:

```text
Model
Model version
Prompt version
Source documents
Generation time
Reviewer
Approval status
```

---

# 107. Evaluation Architecture

AI quality must be measured systematically.

```text
AI Change
   │
   ▼
Evaluation Suite
   │
   ├── Retrieval
   ├── Factuality
   ├── Grounding
   ├── Safety
   ├── Language
   └── User Experience
   │
   ▼
Release Decision
```

---

# 108. Golden Evaluation Dataset

Maintain curated evaluation cases representing real Mediverse tasks.

Examples:

```text
Basic physiology questions
Complex mechanism explanations
Ambiguous questions
Marathi questions
Diagram questions
3D-context questions
Insufficient-evidence cases
Adversarial prompts
```

---

# 109. Dataset Versioning

Evaluation datasets are production assets.

Record:

```text
Dataset version
Question
Expected properties
Reference answer
Source evidence
Risk category
Language
Difficulty
```

---

# 110. Factuality Evaluation

Factuality evaluation should ask whether medical claims are correct according to the approved reference set.

Fluency must not influence factual scoring.

---

# 111. Groundedness Evaluation

Groundedness asks:

```text
Does the answer follow
the provided evidence?
```

A fact may happen to be correct while still being unsupported by the retrieved sources.

Those are different metrics.

---

# 112. Retrieval Evaluation

RAG should be evaluated independently from generation.

Measure:

```text
Recall@K
Precision@K
MRR where useful
Relevant chunk ranking
Metadata filter correctness
```

If retrieval fails, prompt engineering will not reliably fix the system.

---

# 113. Retrieval Test Cases

Each important test query should identify expected relevant evidence.

```text
Question
   │
   ▼
Expected Source(s)
   │
   ▼
Retriever
   │
   ▼
Compare
```

---

# 114. Citation Correctness

Measure whether:

```text
Citation exists
        │
        ▼
Correct source?
        │
        ▼
Correct passage?
        │
        ▼
Actually supports claim?
```

Citation count is not a quality metric.

---

# 115. Hallucination Measurement

Track unsupported-claim rate rather than relying on subjective impressions that answers "look good."

A polished hallucination is still a failure.

---

# 116. LLM-as-Judge

LLMs may assist evaluation at scale.

They should not be treated as unquestionable ground truth.

Potential problems:

```text
Model bias
Position bias
Preference for verbosity
Self-preference
Prompt sensitivity
Inconsistent scoring
```

---

# 117. Expert Medical Evaluation

A representative subset of outputs should be evaluated by qualified medical educators/subject experts.

Human evaluation should focus on:

```text
Accuracy
Educational clarity
Omissions
Misleading simplification
Clinical nuance
Terminology
```

---

# 118. Inter-Rater Reliability

For subjective evaluations, multiple evaluators may disagree.

Evaluation design should measure agreement where important rather than pretending human labels are perfectly objective.

---

# 119. Prompt Regression Testing

Prompt changes require regression evaluation.

```text
Prompt v18
   │
   ▼
Evaluation Suite
   │
   ▼
Compare against v17
```

"Prompt looks better" is not an adequate production release criterion.

---

# 120. Model Upgrade Gate

A new model version should pass:

```text
Quality
Safety
Grounding
Latency
Cost
Multilingual
Tool-use
Structured-output
```

evaluation before broad rollout.

---

# 121. Adversarial Testing

AI red-team suites should test:

```text
Prompt injection
Indirect injection
Data extraction attempts
Authorization bypass
System prompt extraction
Corpus poisoning
Unsafe clinical requests
Tool misuse
Malformed structured output
Excessive resource consumption
```

---

# 122. Streaming Responses

Long tutoring answers should support token streaming where it improves perceived latency.

```text
Request
  │
  ▼
Model
  │
  ▼
Token Stream
  │
  ▼
Browser
```

Streaming does not reduce actual generation cost.

---

# 123. Streaming Safety

Some controls can only evaluate complete output.

Architecture must decide whether content can safely stream before all post-generation validation is complete.

Higher-risk workflows may require buffering or staged validation.

---

# 124. Latency Budget

AI requests should have explicit latency budgets.

Break latency down:

```text
Authentication
     +
Retrieval
     +
Reranking
     +
Model queue
     +
Generation
     +
Validation
```

Without decomposition, "AI is slow" is not actionable.

---

# 125. Parallelization

Independent work should run concurrently where safe.

```text
Question
   │
   ├── Retrieve knowledge
   ├── Fetch learner context
   └── Fetch scene context
           │
           ▼
         Merge
```

Sequential network chains create avoidable latency.

---

# 126. Token Budgets

Each AI capability should define token/context budgets.

```text
System instructions
+
Conversation
+
Retrieved evidence
+
Tool results
+
Output
```

All consume finite context and money.

---

# 127. Context Compression

Large conversations should use controlled compression.

Potential strategies:

```text
Relevant-turn selection
Conversation summarization
Structured memory
Retrieval over conversation history
```

Do not continuously append everything forever.

---

# 128. Context Relevance

More context is not necessarily better.

Irrelevant context can reduce:

```text
Accuracy
Attention
Latency
Cost efficiency
```

Context selection is an engineering problem.

---

# 129. Semantic Caching

Semantically similar low-risk requests may use cached answers where:

```text
Source corpus unchanged
Prompt/model policy compatible
Personalization irrelevant
Freshness acceptable
Security scope identical
```

This requires strict cache-key and authorization design.

---

# 130. Cache Safety

Never serve another user's private/personalized AI result because semantic similarity matched.

Cache boundaries must include authorization and personalization dimensions where applicable.

---

# 131. AI Rate Limiting

AI endpoints require stronger consumption controls than ordinary cheap APIs.

Limits may consider:

```text
User
Organization
Feature
Model
Token usage
Request cost
Time window
```

---

# 132. Cost Attribution

Every model invocation should be attributable to a meaningful dimension.

```text
Service
Feature
Model
Tenant/user class where appropriate
Environment
Token usage
```

This allows cost optimization.

---

# 133. Cost Per Learning Outcome

The useful metric is not merely:

```text
$ / 1M tokens
```

Mediverse should eventually understand:

```text
Cost per tutoring session
Cost per quiz generated
Cost per active learner
Cost per completed learning objective
```

---

# 134. Quotas

Free or bounded plans may require quotas.

Quota enforcement must happen before expensive model execution where possible.

---

# 135. Model Fallback

Fallback should be capability-aware.

```text
Primary Model
      │ failure
      ▼
Fallback Router
      │
      ▼
Compatible Model
```

A cheaper fallback that cannot perform required structured/tool/vision behavior is not actually compatible.

---

# 136. Provider Outage

The application should degrade deliberately.

Potential fallback:

```text
AI Tutor unavailable
        │
        ├── Existing course content ✓
        ├── Search ✓
        ├── Assessments ✓
        └── 3D learning ✓
```

An LLM outage should not make the entire learning platform unusable.

---

# 137. AI SLOs

AI capabilities need their own SLOs.

Possible indicators:

```text
Availability
Time to first token
End-to-end latency
Structured-output success
Retrieval success
Tool execution success
Grounded-answer rate
```

---

# 138. AI Observability

Every AI request should produce a trace across:

```text
Tutor API
   │
   ▼
Retrieval
   │
   ▼
Reranking
   │
   ▼
Model
   │
   ▼
Tools
   │
   ▼
Validation
```

This integrates with ADR-063.

---

# 139. AI Telemetry

Useful metadata may include:

```text
Request ID
Feature
Prompt version
Model/version
Retriever version
Embedding version
Retrieved document IDs
Token usage
Latency
Tool calls
Validation result
```

Subject to privacy rules.

---

# 140. Prompt Logging

Raw prompts and responses may contain sensitive or copyrighted content.

Do not indiscriminately log everything.

Prefer configurable:

```text
Metadata-only telemetry
Redaction
Sampling
Restricted diagnostic logging
Retention limits
```

---

# 141. AI Audit Trail

For high-value generated artifacts, retain enough provenance to reconstruct:

```text
What generated this?
Which model?
Which prompt?
Which sources?
Which tools?
Which validation?
Who approved it?
```

---

# 142. User Feedback

AI responses may support structured feedback.

```text
Helpful?
Accurate?
Citation problem?
Too difficult?
Too simple?
```

Feedback should feed evaluation—not automatically retrain or modify production behavior.

---

# 143. Feedback Poisoning

User feedback is untrusted data.

Attackers or noisy users can intentionally manipulate feedback.

Training/evaluation pipelines must validate and aggregate it appropriately.

---

# 144. Experimentation

AI changes should support controlled experiments.

```text
Model A
vs
Model B

Prompt A
vs
Prompt B

Retriever A
vs
Retriever B
```

Experiments must measure educational and safety outcomes, not only engagement.

---

# 145. Feature Flags

New AI capabilities should use controlled rollout.

```text
Internal
   │
   ▼
Medical reviewers
   │
   ▼
Small cohort
   │
   ▼
Expanded cohort
   │
   ▼
General availability
```

Rollback should be fast.

---

# 146. AI Incident Response

AI incidents require explicit operational procedures.

Examples:

```text
Systematic factual errors
Unsafe outputs
Data exposure
Prompt injection exploitation
Broken citations
Model-provider regression
Runaway costs
Retrieval corruption
```

Response may include:

```text
Disable feature
Switch model
Rollback prompt
Disable corpus
Block tool
Invalidate cache
Preserve evidence
Investigate
```

---

# 147. Production Readiness

Before an AI capability reaches production it should demonstrate:

```text
✓ Defined educational purpose
✓ Risk classification
✓ Approved data sources
✓ Source licensing understood
✓ Prompt versioned
✓ Model version governed
✓ Authorization enforced
✓ Prompt injection tested
✓ Retrieval evaluated
✓ Grounding evaluated
✓ Factuality evaluated
✓ Citation correctness evaluated
✓ Multilingual evaluation where relevant
✓ Medical expert review where required
✓ Latency budget
✓ Token/cost budget
✓ Rate limits
✓ Fallback behavior
✓ Observability
✓ Auditability
✓ Privacy review
✓ Incident runbook
✓ Feature flag / kill switch
```

---

# 148. AI Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ "Add ChatGPT" treated as an architecture
❌ One unrestricted AI endpoint for everything
❌ LLM used as authorization engine
❌ LLM allowed to execute arbitrary SQL
❌ LLM allowed to execute arbitrary JavaScript
❌ Provider SDK spread across every microservice
❌ Provider abstraction pretending all models are identical
❌ Model versions changing silently
❌ Prompts scattered as string literals
❌ Prompt changes deployed without evaluation
❌ Secrets embedded in system prompts
❌ Free-form text parsed with regex when schemas are available
❌ Tool calls executed without authorization
❌ RAG treated as hallucination elimination
❌ Entire textbook flattened into arbitrary chunks
❌ No source provenance
❌ Copyrighted content ingested without licensing review
❌ Vector search assumed superior to lexical search
❌ topK increased until answers "look better"
❌ Entire corpus dumped into model context
❌ Citations generated without verifying support
❌ Citation count treated as correctness
❌ Model pretrained knowledge treated as canonical curriculum
❌ Model forced to answer when evidence is missing
❌ Entire conversation resent forever
❌ Model-generated memory treated as authoritative learner state
❌ Retrieved documents trusted as instructions
❌ User-uploaded content inserted into trusted corpus automatically
❌ System prompts assumed secret
❌ One safety prompt treated as security
❌ Medical terminology blocked by naive moderation
❌ Machine translation trusted as canonical medical terminology
❌ Marathi queries evaluated only in English
❌ Screenshots used when structured 3D scene state exists
❌ AI emits arbitrary Three.js code
❌ AI assumes a 3D tool call succeeded
❌ Speech recognition deployed without medical vocabulary testing
❌ AI-generated questions directly inserted into high-stakes exams
❌ Incorrect MCQ distractors generated as obvious nonsense
❌ LLM owns learner mastery state
❌ Deep ML knowledge tracing introduced before basic measurement
❌ Recommendation engine optimizes screen time instead of learning
❌ LLM-as-judge treated as objective ground truth
❌ No medical expert evaluation
❌ Fluent answers mistaken for factual answers
❌ Prompt/model upgrades without regression gates
❌ Streaming unsafe content before applicable validation
❌ Unlimited token budgets
❌ Every query sent to the most expensive model
❌ Semantic cache leaking personalized responses
❌ No AI-specific rate limiting
❌ No cost attribution
❌ Provider outage breaks the whole platform
❌ Raw prompts/responses logged indefinitely
❌ User feedback automatically treated as training truth
❌ Experiments optimize engagement while ignoring correctness
❌ No feature kill switch
❌ No AI incident response process
```

---

# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                      | Decision                                                         |
| ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| AI role                   | Educational assistance                                           |
| Clinical decision support | Outside default Mediverse AI boundary                            |
| AI integration            | Central governed AI platform/gateway                             |
| Provider coupling         | Abstracted                                                       |
| Managed models            | Initial preference where requirements permit                     |
| Self-hosting              | Requirement-driven                                               |
| Model routing             | Capability/risk/cost aware                                       |
| Model upgrades            | Evaluated + controlled                                           |
| Prompts                   | Versioned production artifacts                                   |
| Structured output         | Preferred for machine consumption                                |
| Tool calling              | Allowlisted + authorized                                         |
| Arbitrary tool execution  | **Rejected**                                                     |
| RAG                       | Primary grounding mechanism where authoritative evidence matters |
| Knowledge sources         | Governed + licensed                                              |
| Provenance                | Mandatory                                                        |
| Chunking                  | Semantic/structure-aware                                         |
| Embeddings                | Version governed                                                 |
| Initial vector store      | **PostgreSQL + pgvector evaluation/preference**                  |
| Dedicated search          | Scale/search-requirement driven                                  |
| Retrieval                 | Hybrid evaluation                                                |
| Reranking                 | Evaluation-driven                                                |
| Citations                 | Claim-support oriented                                           |
| Unsupported answers       | Uncertainty permitted                                            |
| Conversation memory       | Scoped and controlled                                            |
| Learner state             | Deterministic application data                                   |
| Prompt injection          | Untrusted-input model                                            |
| Retrieved documents       | Data, not instructions                                           |
| AI authorization          | Never authoritative                                              |
| Medical safety            | Risk-based                                                       |
| Multilingual              | First-class architecture                                         |
| Marathi                   | Medical terminology-aware                                        |
| Multimodal                | Supported where educationally useful                             |
| 3D tutor                  | Structured scene-aware                                           |
| AI→3D commands            | Schema-controlled tools                                          |
| Speech                    | STT/TTS evaluation                                               |
| Quiz generation           | Draft + validation                                               |
| High-stakes assessments   | Controlled/approved question bank                                |
| Adaptive learning         | Learner-model driven                                             |
| Knowledge tracing         | Start interpretable/simple                                       |
| Spaced repetition         | Deterministic core                                               |
| Recommendations           | Learning-outcome optimized                                       |
| Human oversight           | Risk-based                                                       |
| AI provenance             | Required for reusable/high-value artifacts                       |
| Evaluation datasets       | Versioned                                                        |
| Retrieval evaluation      | Independent                                                      |
| Factuality                | Explicit metric                                                  |
| Groundedness              | Explicit metric                                                  |
| Citation correctness      | Explicit metric                                                  |
| LLM-as-judge              | Supporting tool only                                             |
| Expert medical review     | Required where risk warrants                                     |
| Prompt regression         | Required                                                         |
| Model upgrade gates       | Required                                                         |
| Red teaming               | Required                                                         |
| Streaming                 | UX/risk driven                                                   |
| Token budgets             | Per capability                                                   |
| Semantic caching          | Low-risk + authorization-safe only                               |
| Rate limiting             | AI-specific                                                      |
| Cost attribution          | Required                                                         |
| Provider fallback         | Capability-aware                                                 |
| AI outage                 | Core platform remains operational                                |
| AI SLOs                   | Dedicated                                                        |
| AI telemetry              | Version/provenance aware                                         |
| Raw prompt logging        | Restricted                                                       |
| Audit trail               | High-value artifacts                                             |
| Feedback                  | Evaluation input, not automatic truth                            |
| Experimentation           | Controlled                                                       |
| Kill switch               | Required                                                         |
| Incident response         | Required                                                         |
| Status                    | **Accepted**                                                     |
| Priority                  | **Critical**                                                     |

---
