# ADR-070 — Enterprise Testing, Quality Engineering, Verification & Release Confidence Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Soak Testing**.

---

# 61. Performance Test Architecture

Performance testing should model the complete request path.

```text
Virtual Users
     │
     ▼
Ingress / CDN
     │
     ▼
API Gateway
     │
     ▼
Application
     │
 ┌───┼───────────┐
 ▼   ▼           ▼
DB  Redis       Kafka
 │
 ▼
Dependencies
```

Testing a controller in isolation does not establish system capacity.

# 62. Load-Testing Tooling

Mediverse should standardize primarily on **k6** for API/platform load testing.

Gatling remains reasonable where JVM-native simulation or advanced workload modeling provides a concrete advantage.

Tool proliferation should be avoided.

# 63. Workload Modeling

Tests should reproduce realistic behavior rather than simply hammering one endpoint.

```text
1000 Learners
      │
      ├── 40% course browsing
      ├── 25% lesson activity
      ├── 15% assessments
      ├── 10% progress APIs
      └── 10% AI tutoring
```

Production telemetry should eventually inform these distributions.

# 64. Arrival Rate vs Concurrent Users

Performance tests should distinguish:

```text
Concurrent users
        ≠
Requests per second
```

A user may remain active while generating very few requests.

Workload models should therefore reflect actual traffic patterns.

# 65. Latency Percentiles

Average latency is insufficient.

Track at minimum useful percentiles such as:

```text
p50
p90
p95
p99
```

A healthy average can conceal a severe tail-latency problem.

# 66. Throughput

Capacity analysis should measure:

```text
Requests/sec
Transactions/sec
Events/sec
Messages/sec
Bytes/sec
```

according to subsystem.

# 67. Saturation

Performance tests must correlate latency with infrastructure saturation.

Observe:

```text
CPU
Memory
GC
Thread pools
DB connections
Kafka lag
Redis latency
Disk I/O
Network
```

# 68. Bottleneck Identification

When latency rises:

```text
Latency ↑
   │
   ├── CPU saturated?
   ├── DB pool exhausted?
   ├── locks?
   ├── dependency latency?
   ├── GC?
   ├── queue buildup?
   └── network?
```

Do not respond by blindly adding replicas.

# 69. Performance Regression Gates

Important services should maintain baseline performance results.

```text
Baseline
   │
   ▼
New Build
   │
   ▼
Comparison
   │
 ┌─┴────────┐
 ▼          ▼
Within     Regression
Budget       │
             ▼
           Review
```

# 70. Performance Gate Stability

Performance gates should run in sufficiently controlled environments.

Tiny latency differences from noisy shared infrastructure should not fail builds arbitrarily.

# 71. Database Performance Testing

Performance verification should include realistic:

```text
Dataset sizes
Indexes
Query patterns
Pagination
Concurrency
Connection pools
```

A query tested against 20 rows tells little about production behavior against millions.

# 72. N+1 Regression Testing

Critical ORM workflows should detect accidental N+1 behavior.

```text
GET /courses
     │
     ▼
1 course query
+
500 child queries
```

may pass functional tests while failing operationally.

# 73. Cache Performance

Caching tests should verify:

```text
Hit rate
Miss behavior
Stampede behavior
TTL
Invalidation
Dependency fallback
```

A cache is not automatically a performance improvement.

# 74. AI Performance Testing

AI workloads require separate modeling.

Measure:

```text
Time to first token
Tokens/sec
Total response time
Retrieval latency
Reranking latency
Tool latency
Provider throttling
Concurrent streams
```

# 75. AI Cost Under Load

AI load testing should estimate financial capacity as well as technical capacity.

```text
100 requests/sec
        │
        ▼
Token consumption
        │
        ▼
Model cost
        │
        ▼
Daily / Monthly projection
```

A technically scalable architecture can still be financially unsustainable.

# 76. SSE Testing

SSE testing should verify:

```text
Concurrent connections
Reconnect
Last-event behavior
Proxy timeout
Idle timeout
Authentication expiry
Resource consumption
```

# 77. WebSocket Testing

WebSocket workloads should test:

```text
Connection establishment
Concurrent connections
Message rate
Broadcast/fan-out
Disconnect
Reconnect
Backpressure
Node termination
```

# 78. Frontend Performance Testing

Browser performance tests should measure real rendering behavior.

```text
Network
  │
  ▼
JS Download
  │
  ▼
Parse / Execute
  │
  ▼
React Render
  │
  ▼
Interactive UI
```

Backend latency alone does not describe user experience.

# 79. 3D Performance Testing

Mediverse 3D modules require device-aware benchmarks.

Measure:

```text
Asset download
Decode time
Scene initialization
Frame rate
Frame time
Memory
GPU pressure
Interaction responsiveness
```

# 80. 3D Device Matrix

Test at least representative:

```text
Low/mid-range mobile
Modern mobile
Integrated-GPU laptop
Desktop
```

Optimizing only on developer workstations is unacceptable.

# 81. Frame-Time Budget

3D performance should reason primarily in frame time.

Approximately:

```text
60 FPS → ~16.7 ms/frame
30 FPS → ~33.3 ms/frame
```

Actual target depends on experience/device capability.

# 82. Graceful 3D Degradation

Tests should verify that constrained devices can reduce:

```text
Model detail
Texture quality
Effects
Animation complexity
```

or fall back to non-3D learning experiences.

# 83. Resilience Testing

Functional success under healthy conditions is insufficient.

Mediverse must verify behavior when dependencies fail.

```text
Application
    │
    ├── DB failure
    ├── Redis failure
    ├── Kafka failure
    ├── AI provider failure
    └── network latency
```

# 84. Fault Injection

Controlled fault injection may simulate:

```text
Latency
Connection failure
Timeout
HTTP errors
Pod termination
Resource pressure
Dependency unavailability
```

# 85. Chaos Engineering

Chaos engineering should be introduced only after basic resilience engineering exists.

Randomly killing infrastructure without hypotheses, observability and safeguards is not useful chaos engineering.

# 86. Chaos Hypothesis

A valid experiment starts with:

> "If dependency X fails, user capability Y should continue within boundary Z."

Then deliberately test it.

# 87. PostgreSQL Failure

Test application behavior during:

```text
Connection loss
Restart
Failover
Connection exhaustion
Slow queries
Deadlocks
```

where architecture supports those conditions.

# 88. Redis Failure

If Redis is unavailable, determine explicitly whether each capability should:

```text
Fail closed
Fail open
Use database fallback
Return degraded response
```

Do not discover this behavior during production incidents.

# 89. Kafka Failure

Test:

```text
Broker unavailable
Producer timeout
Consumer restart
Lag accumulation
Duplicate delivery
Retry
DLQ
Poison messages
```

# 90. Retry Verification

Retries must be tested against transient and permanent failures.

```text
Transient
   │
   ▼
Retry
   │
   ▼
Success

Permanent
   │
   ▼
Bounded retries
   │
   ▼
Fail
```

Infinite retry loops are failures.

# 91. Retry Storm Testing

During dependency outage:

```text
10,000 requests
      ×
3 retries
      =
30,000 dependency attempts
```

Retry policies can amplify incidents.

Load/resilience testing should expose this.

# 92. Timeout Testing

Every remote dependency should have defined timeout behavior.

Tests should verify:

```text
Connect timeout
Read timeout
Request timeout
End-to-end deadline
```

where relevant.

# 93. Circuit Breaker Verification

If circuit breakers are used, verify:

```text
Closed
   │
Failures
   ▼
Open
   │
Cooldown
   ▼
Half-open
   │
Recovery
   ▼
Closed
```

# 94. Kubernetes Disruption

Test application behavior during:

```text
Pod restart
Rolling deployment
Node drain
Replica loss
Autoscaling
Readiness failure
```

# 95. Pod Termination

Graceful shutdown tests should verify:

```text
SIGTERM
   │
   ▼
Stop accepting work
   │
   ▼
Finish/transfer work
   │
   ▼
Close resources
   │
   ▼
Exit
```

# 96. Backup Verification

A successful backup job does not prove recoverability.

```text
Backup created
      ≠
Backup restorable
```

Restore verification is mandatory.

# 97. Restore Testing

Regularly restore backups into isolated environments and verify:

```text
Database starts
Schema valid
Data readable
Application connects
Critical workflows operate
```

# 98. Backup Integrity

Tests should detect:

```text
Corruption
Missing objects
Incomplete backup
Wrong encryption keys
Permission failures
```

# 99. Disaster-Recovery Exercises

DR procedures should be exercised rather than merely documented.

```text
Primary unavailable
       │
       ▼
Declare disaster
       │
       ▼
Restore / fail over
       │
       ▼
Validate
       │
       ▼
Resume service
```

# 100. RPO Verification

Recovery Point Objective must be measured against actual recovery behavior.

If RPO is 15 minutes but restoration loses four hours of data, the architecture failed regardless of documentation.

# 101. RTO Verification

Recovery Time Objective should be measured from realistic disaster declaration to usable service restoration.

Automation that technically restores a database but requires six hours of manual debugging does not satisfy a one-hour RTO.

# 102. Observability Testing

Observability must itself be tested.

Verify that failures produce useful:

```text
Logs
Metrics
Traces
Events
Alerts
```

# 103. Trace Verification

Critical workflows should verify trace propagation across:

```text
Ingress
  │
  ▼
Service A
  │
  ▼
Kafka
  │
  ▼
Service B
  │
  ▼
Database
```

where tracing architecture supports it.

# 104. Alert Testing

Alerts should be deliberately triggered in controlled environments.

An alert rule that has never fired is an unverified assumption.

# 105. Alert Quality

Test for:

```text
Detection
Correct severity
Useful context
Routing
Deduplication
Recovery notification
```

# 106. Synthetic Monitoring

Production synthetic tests should periodically verify critical safe workflows.

Examples:

```text
Landing page
Authentication endpoint health
Course catalogue
Read-only API
```

Avoid synthetic tests that create uncontrolled production data.

# 107. Production Smoke Tests

Immediately after deployment, verify a small set of critical capabilities.

```text
Deployment
    │
    ▼
Smoke Tests
    │
 ┌──┴──┐
 ▼     ▼
Pass   Fail
 │      │
 ▼      ▼
Continue Rollback
```

# 108. Accessibility Testing

Accessibility quality requires:

```text
Static analysis
Component automation
Browser automation
Keyboard testing
Screen-reader testing
Human review
```

No single scanner proves WCAG compliance.

# 109. Automated Accessibility

Automated tools should detect common problems such as:

```text
Missing labels
Invalid ARIA
Contrast issues
Heading problems
Form accessibility
```

within their technical limitations.

# 110. Keyboard Verification

Critical workflows must be tested using keyboard-only interaction.

Especially:

```text
Navigation
Dialogs
Forms
Assessment
Media controls
3D controls/fallback
```

# 111. Screen-Reader Verification

Critical learning experiences should receive manual assistive-technology testing.

Automated DOM checks cannot prove understandable screen-reader behavior.

# 112. Visual Regression

Visual regression should protect stable high-value UI surfaces.

```text
Baseline Screenshot
        │
        ▼
New Screenshot
        │
        ▼
Diff
```

Differences require interpretation, not automatic panic.

# 113. Browser Matrix

Mediverse should define supported browser versions explicitly.

Testing should focus on supported browsers rather than attempting every browser ever released.

# 114. Device Matrix

Device testing should be risk-based.

Cover representative:

```text
Viewport sizes
Touch input
Pixel densities
Performance classes
Mobile browsers
Desktop browsers
```

# 115. 3D Educational Verification

3D testing must validate more than rendering.

Verify:

```text
Correct anatomical structure
Correct label
Correct animation
Correct interaction
Correct learning explanation
Correct fallback
```

A technically beautiful but anatomically incorrect model is a critical defect.

# 116. AI/RAG Quality Gates

ADR-069 evaluation should become part of release verification.

```text
AI Change
   │
   ▼
Golden Dataset
   │
   ├── Retrieval
   ├── Factuality
   ├── Grounding
   ├── Citation correctness
   ├── Safety
   └── Multilingual
   │
   ▼
Quality Gate
```

# 117. AI Regression

Model or prompt changes should be compared against the currently approved baseline.

A new model being newer or more expensive does not establish superiority.

# 118. AI Nondeterminism

AI tests must account for probabilistic output.

Avoid assertions such as:

```text
response ==
exact giant paragraph
```

Prefer evaluating:

```text
Required facts
Forbidden claims
Schema
Evidence
Safety
Semantic criteria
```

# 119. RAG Retrieval Tests

Retrieval should be testable without generation.

```text
Query
   │
   ▼
Retriever
   │
   ▼
Top-K
   │
   ▼
Expected evidence present?
```

This isolates retrieval failures from model failures.

# 120. Medical Expert Gate

High-risk reusable medical educational content should support subject-matter expert approval where ADR-069 requires it.

Automated tests cannot establish every medical nuance.

# 121. Test Data Management

Test data should be:

```text
Controlled
Repeatable
Representative
Non-sensitive
Versionable where useful
Easy to reset
```

# 122. Production Data

Copying raw production data into lower environments should not be the default testing strategy.

It introduces privacy and security risk.

# 123. Synthetic Data

Synthetic data should model realistic:

```text
Users
Courses
Assessments
Progress
Relationships
Edge cases
Scale
```

without reproducing sensitive user information.

# 124. Seed Data

Deterministic seed datasets should support integration and E2E environments.

Tests should know their starting state.

# 125. Test Isolation

Tests should not depend on execution order.

```text
Test A
   X
must not create state
required by Test B
```

Each test should own or reliably initialize required state.

# 126. Environment Strategy

Testing should span:

```text
Developer environment
      │
      ▼
CI isolated dependencies
      │
      ▼
Ephemeral integration environment
      │
      ▼
Shared staging where required
      │
      ▼
Production verification
```

# 127. Ephemeral Environments

Pull requests may receive short-lived environments when the cost is justified.

```text
Pull Request
     │
     ▼
Namespace / Environment
     │
     ▼
Deploy
     │
     ▼
Integration / E2E
     │
     ▼
Destroy
```

# 128. Shared Environment Problem

Shared QA environments commonly create:

```text
Data collisions
Unknown configuration
Test interference
Manual mutation
Flaky failures
```

Ephemeral environments reduce—but do not automatically eliminate—these problems.

# 129. Environment Parity

Lower environments should match production behavior where differences matter.

Not necessarily production scale.

Prioritize parity for:

```text
Database engine
Runtime
Container
Configuration model
Networking behavior
Security controls
Deployment mechanism
```

# 130. Flaky-Test Governance

A flaky test is a defect.

```text
Same code
Same test
Different result
```

destroys trust in CI.

# 131. Flaky-Test Tracking

Track:

```text
Test
Failure frequency
Owner
First observed
Root cause
Resolution
```

Do not normalize repeated reruns until green.

# 132. Quarantine Policy

Temporary quarantine may prevent one flaky test from blocking all engineering.

But quarantine requires:

```text
Owner
Ticket
Reason
Expiry
```

Otherwise quarantine becomes a graveyard.

# 133. Deterministic Testing

Control sources of nondeterminism:

```text
Time
Randomness
Network
Concurrency
External APIs
Shared state
Locale
Timezone
```

where possible.

# 134. Code Coverage

Coverage is a diagnostic metric—not proof of correctness.

```text
100% line coverage
        ≠
100% behavior correctness
```

# 135. Coverage Policy

Coverage thresholds may prevent catastrophic testing decline.

They should not incentivize meaningless assertions purely to increase percentages.

# 136. Mutation Testing

Mutation testing should be evaluated for high-value domain logic.

```text
Original:
score >= 50

Mutation:
score > 50
```

If tests still pass, the suite may not meaningfully protect that behavior.

# 137. CI Parallelization

Independent test stages should run concurrently where infrastructure allows.

```text
                 BUILD
                   │
       ┌───────────┼───────────┐
       ▼           ▼           ▼
     Unit       Security     Frontend
       │           │           │
       ▼           ▼           ▼
 Integration   IaC Scan      Browser
       └───────────┼───────────┘
                   ▼
                GATE
```

Fast feedback matters.

# 138. Test Selection

Large repositories may use change-aware test selection.

However, incorrect dependency analysis can skip necessary tests.

Critical release pipelines should retain broader verification stages.

# 139. Quality Gates

A production candidate should satisfy defined gates such as:

```text
✓ Compilation
✓ Static analysis
✓ Unit tests
✓ Integration tests
✓ Contract compatibility
✓ Security policy
✓ Migration validation
✓ Required E2E
✓ Performance thresholds where applicable
✓ Accessibility requirements
✓ AI evaluation where applicable
✓ Artifact integrity
```

# 140. Release Evidence

Each release should produce machine-readable evidence.

```text
Release
  │
  ├── Commit SHA
  ├── Artifact digest
  ├── Test results
  ├── Security results
  ├── Contract results
  ├── Migration status
  └── Deployment verification
```

# 141. Progressive Delivery Verification

Release confidence continues after CI.

```text
Artifact
   │
   ▼
Small Cohort
   │
   ▼
Observe
   │
 ┌─┴─────────┐
 ▼           ▼
Healthy    Regression
 │           │
 ▼           ▼
Expand     Rollback
```

# 142. Canary Analysis

Canary evaluation should compare meaningful signals.

Examples:

```text
Error rate
Latency
Saturation
Business failures
Authentication failures
AI failures
```

A pod merely being `Running` is not sufficient.

# 143. Rollback Testing

Rollback procedures must themselves be tested.

```text
Deploy N+1
    │
    ▼
Failure
    │
    ▼
Rollback N
    │
    ▼
Validate
```

Do not assume Helm rollback automatically solves database or event-contract incompatibility.

# 144. Defect Escape Metrics

Track defects discovered after release.

Classify by:

```text
Severity
Subsystem
Root cause
Detection gap
Test layer that should have caught it
```

The objective is improving the quality system, not assigning blame.

# 145. DORA + Quality Metrics

Delivery metrics should be interpreted together.

Useful measures include:

```text
Deployment frequency
Lead time for changes
Change failure rate
Failed deployment recovery time
```

alongside:

```text
Escaped defects
Flaky tests
Rollback frequency
SLO violations
Security findings
Performance regressions
```

Optimizing deployment frequency alone can produce fast delivery of bad software.

# 146. Quality Feedback Loop

```text
PRODUCTION INCIDENT
        │
        ▼
ROOT CAUSE
        │
        ▼
WHY WASN'T IT DETECTED?
        │
        ▼
ADD / IMPROVE CONTROL
        │
        ▼
TEST / MONITOR / POLICY
        │
        ▼
PREVENT RECURRENCE
```

Every significant escaped defect should improve the engineering system.

# 147. Release Confidence Model

Release confidence should be evidence-based.

```text
                RELEASE CONFIDENCE
                        │
       ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
       ▼                ▼                ▼
   CORRECTNESS       SECURITY        RELIABILITY
       │                │                │
       ├──────── PERFORMANCE ────────────┤
       │                │                │
       ├─────── ACCESSIBILITY ───────────┤
       │                │                │
       ├──────── COMPATIBILITY ──────────┤
       │                │                │
       └────────────────┼────────────────┘
                        ▼
                 RELEASE DECISION
```

# 148. Quality Engineering Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ "QA owns quality"
❌ Testing only after development completes
❌ Test count treated as quality
❌ 100% coverage treated as correctness
❌ Everything mocked
❌ Every test boots the full Spring application
❌ H2 treated as PostgreSQL
❌ Unit tests used to claim integration works
❌ No database constraint tests
❌ No transaction/concurrency testing
❌ Kafka mocked everywhere
❌ REST services released without contract compatibility checks
❌ Breaking OpenAPI changes discovered by consumers in production
❌ Event schema changes deployed without compatibility validation
❌ Database migrations tested only on empty databases
❌ Assuming application rollback means database rollback
❌ E2E tests used for every behavior
❌ Authorization tests checking only allowed paths
❌ Frontend route guards treated as security tests
❌ Security scanning postponed until release
❌ Vulnerability scanners treated as penetration tests
❌ Load tests hitting one endpoint unrealistically
❌ Average latency used as primary performance metric
❌ Performance testing against tiny datasets
❌ Adding replicas before identifying bottlenecks
❌ AI performance measured only by total latency
❌ Ignoring AI cost under load
❌ WebSockets tested only with one connection
❌ 3D tested only on high-end developer machines
❌ FPS ignored while optimizing 3D
❌ Chaos engineering before basic resilience
❌ Random pod killing without hypotheses
❌ Infinite retries
❌ Retry amplification ignored
❌ No dependency timeout tests
❌ Backup success treated as recovery proof
❌ DR documentation never exercised
❌ RPO/RTO existing only in PowerPoint
❌ Observability assumed to work without tests
❌ Alerts never deliberately triggered
❌ Automated accessibility scanner treated as WCAG certification
❌ 3D visual correctness assumed to imply anatomical correctness
❌ AI tests asserting exact generated paragraphs
❌ RAG evaluated only end-to-end
❌ LLM output fluency treated as medical correctness
❌ Raw production user data copied into QA
❌ Tests dependent on execution order
❌ Shared QA environment manually mutated forever
❌ Flaky tests rerun until green
❌ Quarantined tests with no owner or expiry
❌ Coverage increased using meaningless assertions
❌ Sequential CI when independent stages can parallelize
❌ Every test executed on every keystroke regardless of cost
❌ Production release based only on CI green status
❌ Canary judged only by Kubernetes pod health
❌ Rollback process never tested
❌ Deployment frequency optimized while quality collapses
❌ Escaped defects fixed without improving prevention/detection
```

# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                       | Decision                                |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Quality ownership          | Whole engineering organization          |
| Strategy                   | Risk-based                              |
| Verification               | Shift-left + shift-right                |
| Java tests                 | JUnit 5                                 |
| Assertions                 | AssertJ                                 |
| Mocking                    | Mockito selectively                     |
| Spring integration         | Spring Boot Test                        |
| Infrastructure integration | **Testcontainers**                      |
| Production DB testing      | PostgreSQL                              |
| H2                         | Limited/non-equivalent                  |
| Kafka testing              | Real integration where behavior matters |
| Redis testing              | Real integration where semantics matter |
| REST contracts             | OpenAPI compatibility                   |
| Event contracts            | Schema compatibility                    |
| DB migrations              | CI integration testing                  |
| Zero-downtime DB changes   | Expand/contract verification            |
| Frontend unit/component    | Vitest + RTL                            |
| Browser API mocking        | MSW                                     |
| E2E                        | Playwright                              |
| Authorization              | Positive + negative tests               |
| IDOR/BOLA                  | Explicit testing                        |
| SAST                       | CI                                      |
| SCA                        | CI                                      |
| Secret scanning            | Required                                |
| Container scanning         | Required                                |
| IaC scanning               | Required                                |
| DAST                       | Risk-based                              |
| Pen testing                | Risk/compliance based                   |
| Load testing               | **k6 default**                          |
| Performance metrics        | Percentiles + throughput + saturation   |
| Performance regression     | Baseline gates                          |
| AI performance             | Latency + TTFT + throughput + cost      |
| SSE/WebSocket              | Concurrency + recovery testing          |
| 3D                         | Device/GPU-aware testing                |
| Resilience                 | Explicit                                |
| Fault injection            | Controlled                              |
| Chaos                      | Hypothesis-driven                       |
| Retry testing              | Required                                |
| Timeout testing            | Required                                |
| Circuit breakers           | State-transition verified               |
| Kubernetes disruption      | Tested                                  |
| Backup                     | Restore-verified                        |
| DR                         | Exercised                               |
| RPO/RTO                    | Measured                                |
| Observability              | Tested                                  |
| Alerts                     | Tested                                  |
| Synthetic monitoring       | Production-safe                         |
| Accessibility              | Automated + manual                      |
| WCAG confidence            | Never scanner-only                      |
| Visual regression          | Selective                               |
| Browser/device matrix      | Explicit                                |
| Anatomical 3D correctness  | Domain validated                        |
| AI/RAG                     | Evaluation gates                        |
| Medical AI                 | Expert validation where risk warrants   |
| Test data                  | Synthetic/non-sensitive preferred       |
| Test isolation             | Required                                |
| Environments               | Ephemeral where valuable                |
| Flaky tests                | Defects                                 |
| Quarantine                 | Temporary + owned                       |
| Coverage                   | Diagnostic/gate, not quality proof      |
| Mutation testing           | High-value logic evaluation             |
| CI                         | Parallelized                            |
| Release evidence           | Machine-readable                        |
| Progressive delivery       | Verified                                |
| Canary                     | Application + business signals          |
| Rollback                   | Tested                                  |
| Defect escape              | Measured                                |
| Quality feedback           | Continuous                              |
| Status                     | **Accepted**                            |
| Priority                   | **Critical**                            |

---

---

# Part VII — Reliability, SRE & Observability Architecture

# ADR-071 — Enterprise Developer Platform, Internal Developer Portal, Golden Paths & Engineering Productivity Standard

## Part 3 — Sections 101–150

Continuing directly from **Section 100 — Developer Productivity**.

---

# 101. DORA & Engineering Productivity Measurement

Platform effectiveness should be evaluated using delivery outcomes rather than platform activity.

Core DORA-oriented measures include:

```text
Deployment Frequency
Lead Time for Changes
Change Failure Rate
Failed Deployment Recovery Time
```

The platform should improve these metrics without incentivizing teams to game them.

---

# 102. Metrics Must Be Interpreted Together

Optimizing one metric independently can create destructive incentives.

```text
Deployment Frequency ↑
        │
        X
does not automatically mean
        │
        ▼
Engineering Productivity ↑
```

If change failure rate simultaneously increases, delivery capability may actually be deteriorating.

---

# 103. SPACE Framework

Developer productivity should also consider the broader SPACE dimensions:

```text
S → Satisfaction & well-being
P → Performance
A → Activity
C → Communication & collaboration
E → Efficiency & flow
```

No single metric accurately represents developer productivity.

---

# 104. Activity Metrics

Metrics such as:

```text
Commits
Pull requests
Lines of code
Tickets closed
Hours online
```

must not be used as individual productivity scores.

They measure activity—not engineering value.

---

# 105. Cognitive Load

One of the IDP's primary responsibilities is reducing unnecessary cognitive load.

Without a platform:

```text
Developer
   │
   ├── Spring configuration
   ├── Maven configuration
   ├── Docker
   ├── Kubernetes
   ├── Helm
   ├── Terraform
   ├── IAM
   ├── Argo CD
   ├── Prometheus
   ├── OpenTelemetry
   ├── security scanners
   ├── CI
   └── cloud networking
```

With a good platform:

```text
Developer
   │
   ▼
"I need a production-ready
Spring Boot service."
   │
   ▼
Golden Path
```

Abstraction should remove repetitive infrastructure decisions without hiding operationally important behavior.

---

# 106. Cognitive Load Categories

Platform design should distinguish:

```text
Intrinsic Load
    │
    └── complexity inherent to business/domain problem

Extraneous Load
    │
    └── unnecessary tooling/process complexity

Germane Load
    │
    └── knowledge useful for solving the problem
```

The platform should primarily attack **extraneous cognitive load**.

---

# 107. Developer Surveys

Quantitative telemetry cannot measure every developer experience problem.

Periodic surveys should evaluate:

```text
Onboarding difficulty
CI frustration
Environment reliability
Documentation quality
Platform discoverability
Deployment confidence
Tooling satisfaction
```

---

# 108. Platform Adoption

Track adoption by capability.

```text
Spring Golden Path       85%
Observability Defaults   92%
Platform CI              78%
Self-Service DB          61%
Preview Environments     43%
```

Low adoption should trigger investigation—not immediate enforcement.

---

# 109. Adoption Diagnosis

Low adoption may mean:

```text
Poor documentation
Missing capability
Bad UX
Migration cost
Performance problems
Platform unreliability
Golden path too restrictive
Teams unaware of capability
```

Do not automatically conclude that developers are "resisting standards."

---

# 110. Golden-Path Adoption

Golden-path usage should be observable.

The important question is:

> Are teams voluntarily choosing the paved road because it is genuinely easier?

Mandatory adoption can conceal a bad developer experience.

---

# 111. Platform Product Analytics

The IDP should understand usage such as:

```text
Service creations
Environment requests
Provisioning failures
Template usage
CLI usage
Portal usage
Documentation searches
Failed workflows
```

Telemetry should respect privacy and should not become developer surveillance.

---

# 112. Time to First Production

A useful platform metric is:

```text
Repository Created
       │
       ▼
First Working Commit
       │
       ▼
First Successful CI
       │
       ▼
First Non-Prod Deployment
       │
       ▼
First Production Deployment
```

Measure where time is actually being lost.

---

# 113. PR Cycle Time

PR cycle time may reveal friction across:

```text
CI duration
Review delay
Environment availability
Test instability
Security approval
Deployment process
```

The platform should target systemic bottlenecks.

---

# 114. CI Feedback Time

Developers should receive high-value feedback quickly.

Preferred progression:

```text
SECONDS
 └── formatting / linting

MINUTES
 └── unit / component / security

LATER
 └── integration / E2E / expensive verification
```

Do not force developers to wait 45 minutes to discover a formatting error.

---

# 115. Environment Provisioning Time

Self-service environments should have measurable provisioning objectives.

```text
Request
   │
   ▼
Provisioning
   │
   ▼
Ready
```

If "self-service" takes two hours, developer experience remains poor.

---

# 116. Developer Toil

Track repetitive work that can reasonably be automated.

Examples:

```text
Manual certificate requests
Manual namespace creation
Repeated pipeline setup
Manual dashboard setup
Secret rotation tickets
Manual DNS changes
Environment cleanup
```

High-frequency toil should feed the platform roadmap.

---

# 117. Platform Team Topology

The platform team should own the internal platform as a product.

```text
APPLICATION TEAMS
       │
       ▼
 PLATFORM TEAM
       │
       ├── Developer Platform
       ├── Golden Paths
       ├── Platform APIs
       ├── Self-Service
       └── Shared Capabilities
```

It should not become a ticket-processing infrastructure team.

---

# 118. Platform-as-Product

The platform requires:

```text
Users
User research
Roadmap
Prioritization
Documentation
Support
SLOs
Versioning
Feedback
```

Internal software still needs product management.

---

# 119. Platform Product Manager

At sufficient organizational scale, a platform product-management function should coordinate:

```text
Developer needs
Platform priorities
Adoption
Roadmap
Success metrics
Cross-team requirements
```

The role should not dictate architecture independently of engineering.

---

# 120. Platform Roadmap

Platform investment should prioritize high-frequency/high-friction engineering problems.

Conceptually:

```text
                     HIGH FREQUENCY

                          │
              Automate    │    PRIORITIZE
                          │
LOW FRICTION ─────────────┼──────────── HIGH FRICTION
                          │
                Ignore    │    Investigate
                          │
```

Do not build features merely because they make impressive portal demos.

---

# 121. Support Model

Platform support should have explicit channels.

```text
Documentation
     │
     ▼
Self-Service Diagnostics
     │
     ▼
Developer Community
     │
     ▼
Platform Support
     │
     ▼
Incident Escalation
```

---

# 122. Platform Doctor

The CLI should provide diagnostic capability where practical.

Conceptually:

```text
mediverse doctor
```

could validate:

```text
Git credentials
Cloud identity
Kubernetes connectivity
Required CLI versions
Repository metadata
Platform connectivity
Local container runtime
```

Diagnostics should identify actionable failures.

---

# 123. Documentation Ownership

Every platform capability requires an explicit documentation owner.

```text
Platform Feature
      │
      ├── Code Owner
      ├── Operational Owner
      └── Documentation Owner
```

Documentation without ownership becomes stale quickly.

---

# 124. Platform Versioning

Platform capabilities require controlled versioning.

Versioned surfaces include:

```text
Templates
Maven parent
BOM
Helm libraries
Terraform modules
CI workflows
Platform APIs
CLI
```

---

# 125. Backward Compatibility

Platform upgrades should minimize forced synchronized migrations.

```text
Platform v1
     │
     ├── Service A
     ├── Service B
     └── Service C

Platform v2 released

Services migrate
independently where possible.
```

---

# 126. Template Versioning

A generated repository must record which template/version created it.

Example:

```yaml
platform:
  template: spring-service
  version: 4.2.0
```

Otherwise the platform cannot reliably understand repository lineage.

---

# 127. Template Upgrade Problem

Scaffolding solves repository creation.

It does **not** solve future upgrades.

```text
Template v1
    │
    ▼
Generate Service
    │
    ▼
Service evolves independently
    │
    X
Template v2 cannot simply
overwrite repository
```

Upgrade strategy must therefore be designed separately.

---

# 128. Automated Template Evolution

Where possible, common behavior should live in versioned shared components rather than copied template code.

Examples:

```text
Maven parent
BOM
Shared CI workflows
Helm library
Terraform modules
Internal libraries
```

This reduces mass-copy migration requirements.

---

# 129. Dependency Automation

Dependency-update automation should propose controlled upgrades.

```text
Dependency Update
      │
      ▼
Automated PR
      │
      ▼
CI / Security / Tests
      │
      ▼
Review
```

Blind automatic production upgrades are inappropriate for critical dependencies.

---

# 130. Service Migration Campaigns

Major platform upgrades may require structured migration campaigns.

```text
Identify affected services
          │
          ▼
Provide migration tooling
          │
          ▼
Automated PRs
          │
          ▼
Team validation
          │
          ▼
Track completion
```

Manual wiki instructions for hundreds of repositories do not scale.

---

# 131. Deprecation Policy

Platform capabilities should have lifecycle states.

```text
Experimental
    │
    ▼
Supported
    │
    ▼
Deprecated
    │
    ▼
End of Support
    │
    ▼
Removed
```

Transitions require communication and migration paths.

---

# 132. Breaking Platform Changes

Breaking changes require:

```text
Impact analysis
Migration guide
Compatibility window
Automation where practical
Explicit deadline
Support
```

Platform teams should not unexpectedly break application teams through central updates.

---

# 133. Federated Platform Contribution

Application teams should be able to contribute improvements.

```text
Application Team
      │
      ▼
Platform Contribution
      │
      ▼
Review
      │
      ▼
Reusable Capability
```

This prevents the platform team from becoming the sole bottleneck.

---

# 134. InnerSource

Shared platform components may use an InnerSource model.

Required controls include:

```text
Contribution guidelines
Maintainers
CODEOWNERS
Review policy
Testing
Release process
```

"Everyone can edit everything" is not InnerSource governance.

---

# 135. Plugin Governance

Portal plugins introduce code, dependencies and privileges.

Every plugin should have:

```text
Owner
Purpose
Security review
Dependency policy
Permission scope
Maintenance plan
```

---

# 136. Backstage Plugin Security

If Backstage is adopted, plugins must not automatically receive broad infrastructure access.

```text
Backstage Plugin
       │
       ▼
Platform API
       │
       ▼
Authorization
       │
       ▼
Capability
```

Prefer this over:

```text
Plugin
   │
   ▼
Administrator Cloud Credentials
```

---

# 137. Platform API Lifecycle

Platform APIs should follow explicit lifecycle management.

```text
Design
  │
  ▼
Review
  │
  ▼
Version
  │
  ▼
Release
  │
  ▼
Observe
  │
  ▼
Deprecate
```

The internal nature of an API does not justify careless breaking changes.

---

# 138. Platform Security Threat Model

The IDP is security-sensitive because it may influence:

```text
Source repositories
CI/CD
Cloud infrastructure
Kubernetes
Secrets
DNS
Databases
Production deployments
```

Compromise can have organization-wide blast radius.

---

# 139. Platform Identity

Platform actions should use strong identity.

```text
Human
  │
  ▼
Enterprise Identity

Workload
  │
  ▼
Workload Identity
```

Long-lived shared administrative credentials should be eliminated where possible.

---

# 140. Privileged Operations

High-risk operations may require stronger controls.

Examples:

```text
Production database deletion
Production environment destruction
IAM privilege escalation
Secret-system administration
Critical DNS modification
```

Controls may include:

```text
Explicit authorization
Approval
Step-up authentication
Audit logging
Break-glass procedures
```

according to risk.

---

# 141. Platform Disaster Recovery

The platform requires recovery planning for critical state such as:

```text
Catalog metadata
Platform configuration
Git repositories
Artifact metadata
Terraform state
Secrets infrastructure
CI configuration
```

But the IDP should avoid becoming the only copy of authoritative desired state.

---

# 142. Platform Control-Plane Failure

Architecture should support:

```text
Portal unavailable
       │
       ▼
Existing production workloads
       │
       ▼
CONTINUE RUNNING
```

Where possible, GitOps reconciliation and existing runtime services should not depend continuously on portal availability.

---

# 143. FinOps Integration

Self-service infrastructure must expose cost implications.

```text
Developer Request
       │
       ▼
Estimated Cost
       │
       ▼
Policy / Budget
       │
       ▼
Provision
       │
       ▼
Actual Cost Attribution
```

"Self-service" without cost controls can become self-service cloud waste.

---

# 144. Cost Attribution

Platform-created resources should automatically receive attribution metadata.

Examples:

```text
team
service
environment
cost-center
owner
lifecycle
```

Cost allocation should not depend on manually reconstructing ownership months later.

---

# 145. Platform Capacity Planning

The platform must plan capacity for shared systems such as:

```text
CI runners
Artifact registry
Kubernetes
Observability
Kafka
Shared databases where applicable
Build caches
```

A successful developer platform can create its own scaling bottlenecks.

---

# 146. CI Runner Strategy

CI runners should be segmented by workload and trust level where necessary.

```text
CI Control Plane
      │
      ├── Standard Builds
      ├── Integration Tests
      ├── Privileged/Special Builds
      └── Production Deployment
```

Untrusted pull-request workloads should not automatically share privileged execution environments.

---

# 147. Build Caching

CI should use safe caching for:

```text
Maven dependencies
Node dependencies
Build outputs where deterministic
Container layers
```

Cache keys must prevent stale or incompatible artifacts from contaminating builds.

---

# 148. Architecture Conformance

The platform should automatically detect important architectural drift.

Examples:

```text
Missing ownership
Unsupported Java version
Deprecated parent POM
Old Helm library
Missing security scan
Missing SLO
Privileged container
Unsupported API version
```

Conformance should distinguish:

```text
Violation
Warning
Recommendation
```

rather than treating every deviation as equally severe.

---

# 149. Platform Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ Calling Kubernetes the "developer platform"
❌ Calling Backstage alone the "developer platform"
❌ Portal-first architecture without stable platform APIs
❌ Building a portal before understanding developer problems
❌ Platform team acting as ticket queue
❌ Every service starting from an empty repository
❌ Copying old repositories as templates
❌ Supporting Maven and Gradle equally without need
❌ Uncontrolled dependency versions
❌ CI depending on random agent tool versions
❌ Dockerfiles handcrafted differently for every service
❌ Rebuilding artifacts separately per environment
❌ Kubernetes workloads without resource expectations
❌ Helm boilerplate copied across hundreds of repositories
❌ Central Helm updates silently modifying all services
❌ Terraform modules exposing hundreds of irrelevant inputs
❌ Breaking Terraform module updates automatically consumed
❌ Portal becoming a competing desired-state database
❌ Production infrastructure provisioned manually by default
❌ Self-service without guardrails
❌ Temporary environments without TTL
❌ Databases without owners
❌ Kafka topics without ownership/schema governance
❌ Manual certificate renewal
❌ Production secrets manually distributed
❌ Observability added after incidents
❌ Security added after service creation
❌ Policy enforced only at production admission
❌ Every recommendation made mandatory
❌ No exception mechanism
❌ Permanent architecture exceptions
❌ Documentation with no owner
❌ API/event interfaces undiscoverable
❌ Scorecards used as meaningless gamification
❌ Ticket-based provisioning for routine resources
❌ Portal plugins containing hidden infrastructure logic
❌ CLI and portal implementing different business rules
❌ Developer onboarding requiring dozens of undocumented steps
❌ IDP outage breaking running production workloads
❌ Platform telemetry used for developer surveillance
❌ Commit count treated as productivity
❌ Lines of code treated as productivity
❌ Low platform adoption blamed automatically on developers
❌ Optimizing DORA metrics individually
❌ Platform roadmap driven by impressive demos
❌ Template generation with no upgrade strategy
❌ Shared configuration copied instead of versioned
❌ Breaking platform changes without migration tooling
❌ Platform team as sole contribution bottleneck
❌ Backstage plugins with administrator cloud credentials
❌ Long-lived shared platform credentials
❌ Production destructive actions without stronger controls
❌ Self-service infrastructure without FinOps visibility
❌ Untrusted CI workloads sharing privileged runners
❌ Architecture conformance treating warnings and critical violations identically
```

---

# ADR-072 — Enterprise Architecture Governance, Standards Enforcement, Technical Debt & Evolution Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Infrastructure Debt**.

---

# 61. Security Debt

Security debt includes known weaknesses intentionally or accidentally left unresolved.

```text
Security Debt
     │
     ├── Unsupported crypto
     ├── Excessive IAM permissions
     ├── Long-lived credentials
     ├── Missing authorization controls
     ├── Unpatched dependencies
     └── Legacy authentication
```

Security debt must be risk-ranked rather than treated like ordinary refactoring backlog.

# 62. Security Debt Escalation

Critical security debt may override ordinary product prioritization.

```text
Finding
   │
   ▼
Risk Assessment
   │
   ├── Low ─────► Backlog
   ├── Medium ──► Planned remediation
   ├── High ────► Priority remediation
   └── Critical ► Immediate action
```

# 63. Data Debt

Data debt includes:

```text
Poor data quality
Unknown ownership
Duplicate sources of truth
Missing lineage
Weak schemas
Uncontrolled PII
Inconsistent identifiers
Unmaintained migrations
```

Data debt frequently survives application rewrites because the underlying data remains.

# 64. Schema Debt

Examples include:

```text
Ambiguous columns
Missing constraints
Incorrect data types
Unbounded JSON usage
Duplicated fields
Legacy nullable fields
```

Database schema quality is part of architecture quality.

# 65. Testing Debt

Testing debt includes:

```text
Missing critical tests
Flaky tests
Slow pipelines
Over-mocking
Weak integration coverage
Missing contract tests
Unmaintained E2E suites
```

High test count does not imply low testing debt.

# 66. Observability Debt

Observability debt includes:

```text
Unstructured logs
Missing metrics
Missing traces
Unknown service ownership
No SLOs
No useful dashboards
No actionable alerts
```

It often becomes visible only during incidents—when remediation is most expensive.

# 67. Documentation Debt

Documentation debt exists when operational or architectural knowledge diverges from reality.

```text
Documentation
      │
      X
Actual System
```

Stale documentation can be worse than absent documentation because it creates false confidence.

# 68. AI Debt

AI systems introduce additional debt categories.

```text
AI Debt
 ├── Prompt debt
 ├── Model-version debt
 ├── Evaluation debt
 ├── Dataset debt
 ├── Retrieval debt
 ├── Embedding debt
 ├── Safety-policy debt
 └── Observability debt
```

# 69. Prompt Debt

Prompts should not evolve into unexplained production strings.

Significant prompts need:

```text
Version
Owner
Purpose
Evaluation
Model compatibility
Change history
```

# 70. Evaluation Debt

AI capabilities without maintained evaluation datasets accumulate evaluation debt.

Without regression evidence:

```text
Prompt Change
     +
Model Change
     +
RAG Change
     =
Unknown Quality Change
```

# 71. Retrieval Debt

RAG systems can accumulate:

```text
Stale embeddings
Obsolete documents
Duplicate chunks
Weak metadata
Bad chunking
Poor retrieval configuration
```

A stronger LLM does not automatically repair poor retrieval architecture.

# 72. Debt Remediation Economics

Debt should be treated as an economic decision.

```text
Cost of Remediation
       vs
Expected Cost of Retention
```

Retention cost includes delivery friction, incidents, risk, operational toil and future migration difficulty.

# 73. Remediate vs Retain

Immediate remediation is justified when:

```text
Risk is unacceptable
Interest is high
Change frequency is high
Security exposure is serious
Migration window is closing
Dependency reaches EOL
```

Some low-interest debt can rationally remain.

# 74. Debt Trend

Track debt direction, not merely total count.

```text
Debt
 ^
 |          /
 |        /
 |      /
 |_____/____________> Time

BAD: debt accumulating faster
than remediation.
```

# 75. Debt Aging

Age can be useful but should not dominate prioritization.

A two-week-old critical security weakness may matter more than a three-year-old harmless code smell.

# 76. Debt Hotspots

Combine debt with change frequency.

```text
HIGH CHANGE + HIGH DEBT
        │
        ▼
Priority Hotspot

LOW CHANGE + LOW RISK
        │
        ▼
Potentially Leave Alone
```

# 77. Architectural Runway

Architecture should provide enough runway for foreseeable product development.

```text
Current Capability
       │
       ▼
Near-Term Product Needs
       │
       ▼
Architectural Runway
```

Do not build five years of speculative infrastructure.

# 78. Runway Planning

Runway should be based on evidence such as:

```text
Product roadmap
Capacity projections
Compliance deadlines
Dependency EOL
Known scaling limits
Upcoming integrations
```

# 79. Evolutionary Architecture

Mediverse should favor architectures capable of controlled change.

```text
Architecture N
      │
      ▼
Small Safe Change
      │
      ▼
Architecture N+1
```

Evolution is preferable to repeated large rewrites.

# 80. Changeability

Important architecture qualities include:

```text
Replaceability
Deployability
Testability
Observability
Modularity
Compatibility
Reversibility
```

A system that works today but cannot safely change is accumulating strategic risk.

# 81. Reversible Decisions

Many decisions are relatively reversible.

Examples:

```text
Internal library
UI component library
Logging format
Local implementation pattern
```

These generally deserve lighter governance.

# 82. Irreversible Decisions

Some decisions have high reversal cost.

Examples:

```text
Public API contract
Persistent data model
Major cloud commitment
Identity architecture
Organization-wide platform
Large vendor contract
```

These deserve stronger evidence and review.

# 83. Two-Way vs One-Way Doors

Use the heuristic:

```text
TWO-WAY DOOR
Change cheaply
    │
    ▼
Decide quickly

ONE-WAY DOOR
Expensive reversal
    │
    ▼
Investigate deeply
```

Do not apply heavyweight governance to every two-way-door decision.

# 84. Experimentation

Uncertainty should often be resolved through controlled experimentation rather than argument.

```text
Question
   │
   ▼
Hypothesis
   │
   ▼
Experiment
   │
   ▼
Evidence
   │
   ▼
Decision
```

# 85. Experiment Boundaries

Experiments need:

```text
Scope
Owner
Timebox
Success criteria
Cost boundary
Security boundary
Cleanup plan
```

Otherwise experiments become permanent shadow architecture.

# 86. Technology Radar

Mediverse should maintain a technology radar.

Suggested categories:

```text
ADOPT
TRIAL
ASSESS
HOLD
```

# 87. Adopt

`ADOPT` means:

> Technology is approved and supported for appropriate production use.

It does not mean every team must use it.

# 88. Trial

`TRIAL` means:

> Technology has demonstrated potential and may be used in controlled production contexts with appropriate ownership.

# 89. Assess

`ASSESS` means:

> Technology is being investigated but should not yet become a production dependency without explicit approval.

# 90. Hold

`HOLD` means:

> Avoid for new development.

Reasons may include:

```text
Security
Operational complexity
Poor ecosystem
Strategic mismatch
Licensing
Cost
Better replacement
End of life
```

# 91. Technology Evaluation

Emerging technology should be evaluated against concrete criteria.

```text
Functional fit
Security
Reliability
Performance
Operability
Ecosystem
Skills
Cost
Licensing
Exit strategy
Integration
Maturity
```

# 92. Hype Resistance

Architecture should reject:

```text
Technology is popular
        ↓
Therefore Mediverse needs it
```

Technology adoption requires a problem worth solving.

# 93. Build-vs-Buy Framework

Evaluate:

```text
Strategic differentiation
Requirements fit
Build cost
Operating cost
Vendor cost
Integration
Security
Compliance
Customization
Exit cost
```

# 94. Build When

Building is more defensible when capability:

```text
Creates strategic differentiation
Requires unusual domain behavior
Needs deep integration
Cannot be safely sourced externally
```

# 95. Buy When

Buying is more defensible when capability is commodity and mature external solutions provide better economics.

Examples may include generic infrastructure capabilities rather than core educational differentiation.

# 96. Hidden Build Cost

Building includes:

```text
Development
Testing
Security
Documentation
Operations
Upgrades
On-call
Compliance
Maintenance
```

"Open source" and "free to download" do not mean free to operate.

# 97. Hidden Buy Cost

Buying includes:

```text
Subscription
Integration
Migration
Training
Customization
Vendor management
Exit cost
Data portability
```

# 98. Vendor Lock-In

Vendor dependence is not automatically bad.

The relevant question is:

> Does the value received justify the switching cost and strategic risk?

# 99. Lock-In Assessment

Evaluate:

```text
Proprietary APIs
Data gravity
Contract restrictions
Migration complexity
Skills dependency
Operational coupling
Pricing leverage
```

# 100. Exit Strategy

Critical vendor decisions should document:

```text
Export mechanism
Data format
Replacement options
Migration estimate
Contract termination
Fallback strategy
```

Not every vendor requires an elaborate exit implementation, but critical dependencies require an understood path.

# 101. Technology Lifecycle

Technologies should move through controlled lifecycle states.

```text
Assess
  │
  ▼
Trial
  │
  ▼
Adopt
  │
  ▼
Maintain
  │
  ▼
Deprecate
  │
  ▼
Retire
```

# 102. Deprecation Trigger

Triggers include:

```text
Vendor EOL
Security risk
Unsupported runtime
Low adoption
Better standard
Operational burden
Strategic change
```

# 103. Deprecation Is Not Removal

Deprecation means:

```text
No new adoption
Migration planning
Support window
Replacement guidance
```

Immediate removal may be unsafe.

# 104. Migration Program

Large migrations require programmatic management.

```text
Inventory
   │
   ▼
Classify
   │
   ▼
Prioritize
   │
   ▼
Automate
   │
   ▼
Migrate
   │
   ▼
Validate
   │
   ▼
Retire
```

# 105. Migration Inventory

Before migration, identify:

```text
Systems
Owners
Dependencies
Data
Traffic
Criticality
Versions
Consumers
```

Migrating what you have not inventoried is guesswork.

# 106. Migration Waves

Large migrations should usually occur in waves.

```text
Pilot
  │
  ▼
Low-Risk Cohort
  │
  ▼
General Migration
  │
  ▼
Complex Exceptions
  │
  ▼
Retirement
```

# 107. Automated Migration

Where repetitive changes exist, provide:

```text
Codemods
Automated PRs
Configuration transforms
Migration scripts
Validation tools
```

Humans should review meaningful changes, not manually repeat mechanical edits hundreds of times.

# 108. Strangler Modernization

Legacy systems should often be replaced incrementally.

```text
                 ROUTER
                /      \
               ▼        ▼
          LEGACY      NEW
             │          │
             └────┬─────┘
                  │
        Capability moves gradually
                  │
                  ▼
              NEW SYSTEM
```

# 109. Strangler Boundary

Choose seams such as:

```text
API
Domain capability
Workflow
User segment
Event
Data ownership
```

A poor boundary can create more coupling than the legacy architecture.

# 110. Big-Bang Rewrite

Mediverse should treat complete rewrites skeptically.

They frequently underestimate:

```text
Hidden behavior
Edge cases
Migration
Operational knowledge
Integration complexity
Timeline
```

A rewrite may still be justified, but requires strong evidence.

# 111. Legacy Stabilization

Before modernization, it may be rational to add:

```text
Tests
Observability
API façade
Dependency mapping
Data validation
```

to the legacy system.

Understanding the existing system reduces migration risk.

# 112. Service Retirement

Creating services is easy.

Deleting them is part of architecture.

```text
Candidate Service
      │
      ▼
No Consumers?
      │
      ▼
No Required Data?
      │
      ▼
Traffic Removed
      │
      ▼
Archive
      │
      ▼
Delete
```

# 113. Retirement Checklist

Verify:

```text
Consumers removed
Traffic zero
Jobs disabled
Topics handled
DNS removed
Secrets removed
Infrastructure destroyed
Alerts removed
Documentation updated
Ownership closed
```

# 114. Zombie Services

A service with no known owner and uncertain consumers should be treated as architectural risk.

Do not leave it running forever because nobody is confident enough to delete it.

# 115. Data Migration Governance

Data migration requires explicit controls around:

```text
Source
Target
Mapping
Validation
Consistency
Rollback
Privacy
Retention
Audit
```

# 116. Migration Validation

Validate:

```text
Record counts
Constraints
Relationships
Checksums where useful
Business invariants
Sample correctness
Application behavior
```

Record count alone does not prove semantic correctness.

# 117. Dual Write Risk

Dual writing introduces consistency risk.

```text
Application
   ├────► Old DB
   └────► New DB
```

One write may succeed while the other fails.

Prefer architectures that explicitly handle consistency rather than assuming dual writes are atomic.

# 118. Backfill

Large backfills should be:

```text
Restartable
Observable
Rate-limited
Idempotent where possible
Auditable
```

They must not unexpectedly destroy production capacity.

# 119. Data Cutover

Cutover plans should define:

```text
Preconditions
Traffic switch
Validation
Rollback window
Ownership
Communication
```

# 120. Architecture Documentation Freshness

Architecture documentation needs lifecycle management.

```text
System Changes
      │
      ▼
Docs Updated?
   ┌──┴──┐
   ▼     ▼
 Yes     No
          │
          ▼
      Documentation Drift
```

# 121. Documentation Freshness Metadata

Important documents should include:

```text
Owner
Last reviewed
Scope
Status
Related ADRs
```

# 122. C4 Synchronization

C4 diagrams should reflect significant architecture changes.

```text
ADR
 │
 ▼
Implementation
 │
 ▼
C4 Model
```

Architecture diagrams that describe a system from two years ago should not be treated as authoritative.

# 123. Documentation Source of Truth

Avoid maintaining the same architecture facts manually in five places.

Prefer generating views from structured metadata where feasible.

# 124. ADR Discovery

With 72+ decisions, plain folder browsing becomes insufficient.

Engineers should be able to search by:

```text
Technology
Domain
Service
Owner
Status
Requirement strength
Related ADR
```

# 125. Architecture Knowledge Graph

Structured architecture metadata may create relationships such as:

```text
TEAM
 │ owns
 ▼
SERVICE
 │ implements
 ▼
ADR
 │ depends on
 ▼
PLATFORM
 │ deployed to
 ▼
KUBERNETES
```

This can support impact analysis and discovery.

# 126. Knowledge Graph Boundary

Do not build a complex graph platform merely because the concept is attractive.

Start from concrete discovery and impact-analysis problems.

# 127. Governance Automation

The ideal path is:

```text
Architecture Decision
        │
        ▼
Structured Metadata
        │
        ▼
Policy / Fitness Function
        │
        ▼
Platform Enforcement
        │
        ▼
Evidence
```

This turns architecture from static documentation into executable governance.

# 128. Decision Lead Time

Measure time from significant proposal to decision.

```text
RFC Open
   │
   ▼
Review
   │
   ▼
Decision
```

Long lead time may indicate governance bottlenecks.

# 129. Review SLA

Architecture review should have service expectations.

Teams cannot wait indefinitely for governance responses.

Urgency and decision risk should determine response targets.

# 130. Exception Rate

Track exceptions by standard.

```text
Standard A → 2 exceptions
Standard B → 37 exceptions
```

Standard B deserves investigation.

# 131. Drift Rate

Track meaningful drift over time.

```text
New violations
Resolved violations
Outstanding violations
Age
Severity
```

Raw violation count alone can mislead as the system grows.

# 132. Debt Trend Metrics

Track by:

```text
Category
Severity
Owner
Age
Interest
Creation rate
Remediation rate
```

# 133. Governance Effectiveness

Good governance should result in:

```text
Fewer preventable incidents
Lower architecture drift
Faster safe decisions
Reduced unsupported technology
Controlled exceptions
Improved migration readiness
Higher standard adoption
```

# 134. Governance Cost

Governance itself has cost.

Measure:

```text
Review waiting time
Manual approvals
Exception processing
Required meetings
Documentation burden
Developer friction
```

A control whose cost exceeds the risk reduction should be challenged.

# 135. Team Autonomy

Teams should retain autonomy inside architectural guardrails.

```text
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│      ENTERPRISE GUARDRAILS  │
│                             │
│   ┌─────────────────────┐   │
│   │   TEAM AUTONOMY     │   │
│   │                     │   │
│   │ Implementation      │   │
│   │ Local design        │   │
│   │ Experimentation     │   │
│   └─────────────────────┘   │
└─────────────────────────────┘
```

# 136. Autonomy Requires Accountability

Teams choosing local solutions remain responsible for:

```text
Security
Reliability
Operability
Cost
Compatibility
Supportability
```

Autonomy is not exemption from engineering outcomes.

# 137. Architecture Community of Practice

A cross-team community should share:

```text
Patterns
Failures
Experiments
Migration lessons
New technologies
Architecture proposals
```

Architecture knowledge should not exist only inside the EAB.

# 138. Architecture Office Hours

Optional office hours can provide early feedback before teams invest heavily in questionable designs.

This is more useful than discovering architectural problems at final approval.

# 139. Architecture Champions

Larger teams may nominate architecture champions.

```text
EAB
 │
 ▼
Architecture Community
 │
 ▼
Team Champions
 │
 ▼
Engineering Teams
```

They facilitate communication rather than acting as local architecture police.

# 140. Governance Operating Model

```text
                   ENTERPRISE ARCHITECTURE BOARD
                              │
                 Strategic Standards / Risk
                              │
              ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
              ▼               ▼               ▼
          PLATFORM         SECURITY         DATA/AI
              │               │               │
              └───────────────┼───────────────┘
                              ▼
                 ARCHITECTURE COMMUNITY
                              │
                              ▼
                      ENGINEERING TEAMS
                              │
                              ▼
                    LOCAL DECISION MAKING
```

# 141. Governance Feedback Loop

```text
STANDARD
   │
   ▼
IMPLEMENT
   │
   ▼
MEASURE
   │
   ▼
INCIDENTS / EXCEPTIONS / FRICTION
   │
   ▼
LEARN
   │
   ▼
CHANGE STANDARD
   │
   └────────────► IMPLEMENT
```

Governance itself must evolve.

# 142. Architecture Health Review

Periodic reviews should focus on trends rather than manually inspecting every service.

Review:

```text
Critical debt
Unsupported technology
Architecture drift
Exception hotspots
Major migrations
Security risk
Reliability trends
Platform adoption
```

# 143. Governance Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ Every technical decision requiring EAB approval
❌ Architects becoming implementation gatekeepers
❌ Architecture review only through meetings
❌ ADR for every minor coding choice
❌ ADRs without scope or owners
❌ Accepted ADRs silently rewritten
❌ Superseded ADRs deleted
❌ "Must" used for every recommendation
❌ Architecture documents treated as eternally correct
❌ Policies enforced only through documentation
❌ Standards with no machine-verifiable controls where feasible
❌ Every violation blocking production regardless of severity
❌ Drift automatically assumed to mean implementation is wrong
❌ Exceptions handled through private messages
❌ Permanent exceptions without review
❌ Security exceptions approved by unauthorized individuals
❌ Technical debt reduced to TODO count
❌ Every imperfection registered as formal debt
❌ Debt prioritized only by age
❌ Fixed universal debt percentage regardless of risk
❌ Unsupported dependencies ignored until emergency migration
❌ AI prompts changed without versioning/evaluation
❌ RAG debt assumed solvable by larger models
❌ Architecture built years ahead of demonstrated need
❌ Heavy review for reversible decisions
❌ Experiments without timeboxes or cleanup
❌ PoCs quietly becoming production systems
❌ Technology adopted because competitors use it
❌ Technology radar treated as a popularity chart
❌ Open source assumed to have zero cost
❌ SaaS assumed cheaper without exit-cost analysis
❌ Vendor lock-in automatically treated as unacceptable
❌ Critical vendor dependency without exit understanding
❌ Deprecated technology immediately removed without migration window
❌ Migration programs without inventories
❌ Hundreds of identical migrations performed manually
❌ Big-bang rewrite assumed easier than incremental modernization
❌ Legacy system rewritten before its hidden behavior is understood
❌ Services created forever but never retired
❌ Zombie services with unknown ownership
❌ Data migration validated only by row counts
❌ Unsafe dual writes assumed consistent
❌ Backfills with no throttling or restartability
❌ Architecture diagrams never updated
❌ Same architecture metadata manually duplicated everywhere
❌ Building a knowledge graph without a concrete use case
❌ Architecture review with indefinite response times
❌ Governance success measured by number of reviews
❌ Governance cost ignored
❌ Team autonomy without accountability
❌ Central architects disconnected from engineering reality
```

# 144. Architecture Governance Maturity Model

```text
LEVEL 1 — REACTIVE
Architecture knowledge lives in people.

LEVEL 2 — DOCUMENTED
Standards and ADRs exist.

LEVEL 3 — STANDARDIZED
Golden paths and explicit governance exist.

LEVEL 4 — AUTOMATED
Policies and fitness functions enforce key standards.

LEVEL 5 — EVOLUTIONARY
Architecture continuously adapts using operational evidence.
```

Mediverse should target **Level 4 with selective Level 5 capabilities**, not pursue maturity for its own sake.

```text
                     NEW DECISION
                          │
                          ▼
                 ARCHITECTURALLY

                              ▼      ▼

                           REVIEW   REVIEW

                              DECISION

                                 │

                      PASS             DRIFT
                         │               │

                      OPERATE     ▼      ▼      ▼

```

```text
                     DISCOVER DEBT
```
