# 149. ADR-072 Decision Outcome

| Area                       | Decision                                      |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Governance philosophy      | Central principles + distributed decisions    |
| Decision locality          | Lowest responsible level                      |
| Governance intensity       | Proportional to blast radius/reversibility    |
| Significant decisions      | ADR                                           |
| Exploration                | RFC                                           |
| ADR history                | Preserved                                     |
| ADR states                 | Proposed / Accepted / Deprecated / Superseded |
| ADR ownership              | Mandatory                                     |
| ADR scope                  | Explicit                                      |
| Requirement strength       | MUST / SHOULD / MAY                           |
| EAB                        | Strategic/high-impact decisions               |
| Ordinary review            | Lightweight/asynchronous                      |
| High-risk decisions        | Deeper review                                 |
| PoCs                       | Hypothesis-driven + timeboxed                 |
| Conformance                | Automated where practical                     |
| Evolutionary controls      | Fitness functions                             |
| Policy                     | Policy as code                                |
| Enforcement                | Earliest practical stage                      |
| Findings                   | Severity differentiated                       |
| Drift                      | Detect + evaluate                             |
| Exceptions                 | Explicit, owned, risk-assessed                |
| Exception expiry           | Default                                       |
| Technical debt             | Classified and owned                          |
| Debt prioritization        | Risk + interest + impact + cost               |
| Fixed debt percentage      | Rejected                                      |
| Security debt              | Risk-prioritized                              |
| Data debt                  | Governed                                      |
| Testing debt               | Governed                                      |
| Observability debt         | Governed                                      |
| AI debt                    | Explicit category                             |
| Architectural runway       | Evidence-driven                               |
| Architecture style         | Evolutionary                                  |
| Reversible decisions       | Lightweight governance                        |
| Irreversible decisions     | Stronger evidence                             |
| Experiments                | Bounded                                       |
| Technology radar           | Adopt / Trial / Assess / Hold                 |
| Technology adoption        | Problem/evidence driven                       |
| Build vs buy               | Full lifecycle economics                      |
| Vendor lock-in             | Explicit trade-off                            |
| Critical vendors           | Exit strategy understood                      |
| Technology lifecycle       | Governed                                      |
| Deprecation                | Migration window                              |
| Large migrations           | Programmatic                                  |
| Automation                 | Preferred for repetitive migration            |
| Legacy modernization       | Incremental preferred                         |
| Big-bang rewrite           | Exceptional                                   |
| Service retirement         | Required lifecycle capability                 |
| Data migrations            | Explicit validation                           |
| Architecture docs          | Owned + reviewed                              |
| C4                         | Synchronize with significant changes          |
| ADR discovery              | Searchable                                    |
| Architecture metadata      | Structured                                    |
| Knowledge graph            | Use-case driven                               |
| Decision lead time         | Measured                                      |
| Exception rate             | Measured                                      |
| Drift rate                 | Measured                                      |
| Debt trends                | Measured                                      |
| Governance cost            | Measured                                      |
| Team autonomy              | Within guardrails                             |
| Accountability             | Required                                      |
| Community of practice      | Established                                   |
| Governance maturity target | Level 4 + selective Level 5                   |
| Status                     | **Accepted**                                  |
| Priority                   | **Critical**                                  |

# 150. Governing Invariant

The final ADR-072 architecture can be reduced to one feedback system:

```text
             INTENT
               │
               ▼
            DECISION
               │
               ▼
            STANDARD
               │
               ▼
          GOLDEN PATH
               │
               ▼
         IMPLEMENTATION
               │
               ▼
          CONFORMANCE
               │
               ▼
           PRODUCTION
               │
               ▼
            EVIDENCE
               │
      ┌────────┼────────┐
      ▼        ▼        ▼
    DRIFT     DEBT   EXCEPTIONS
      │        │        │
      └────────┼────────┘
               ▼
             LEARN
               │
               ▼
             EVOLVE
               │
               └────────────► INTENT
```

> **Architecture governance must preserve intent without freezing implementation. Standards exist because they reduce meaningful organizational risk, not because consistency is inherently valuable. Teams should be autonomous inside explicit guardrails, exceptions should be visible and temporary, technical debt should be managed economically, and production evidence must be allowed to prove that an existing architectural decision needs to change.**

---

---

# ADR-073 — Enterprise FinOps, Cloud Cost Governance, Capacity Economics & Unit Economics Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Poor Spot Candidates**.

---

# 61. On-Demand Capacity

On-Demand capacity provides maximum flexibility but generally carries a higher unit price than committed capacity.

Best suited for:

```text
Unknown demand
New workloads
Short-lived workloads
Burst capacity
Migration periods
Uncertain architecture
```

Do not purchase long-term commitments merely because a workload currently exists.

---

# 62. Commitment Economics

Stable baseline workloads may benefit from commitment-based pricing.

Conceptually:

```text
Total Demand
     │
     │                 /\      Burst
     │       /\       /  \
     │──────/──\─────/────\────
     │==========================
     │     Stable Baseline
     └──────────────────────────► Time

Stable baseline → Commitment candidate
Variable demand → Flexible capacity
```

---

# 63. Savings Plans / Reserved Capacity

Commitments should be based on measured baseline utilization.

Avoid:

```text
Forecast says we may need 100
        │
        ▼
Commit to 100 immediately
```

Prefer:

```text
Measured stable baseline
        │
        ▼
Conservative commitment
        │
        ▼
Flexible capacity for remainder
```

---

# 64. Commitment Coverage

Track:

```text
Eligible Spend
Committed Spend
Commitment Coverage
Commitment Utilization
Effective Savings
```

High coverage with poor utilization is not optimization.

---

# 65. Commitment Utilization

If committed capacity is purchased but unused:

```text
Discounted Resource
       +
No Utilization
       =
Waste
```

Discount percentage is irrelevant if the resource was unnecessary.

---

# 66. Commitment Laddering

Large commitments should be introduced progressively where uncertainty exists.

```text
Observed Baseline
      │
      ▼
Commitment 1
      │
      ▼
Observe Growth
      │
      ▼
Commitment 2
```

This reduces forecasting risk.

---

# 67. Workload Predictability

Classify workloads:

```text
Predictable
Seasonal
Bursty
Batch
Event-driven
Experimental
```

Capacity strategy should differ by class.

---

# 68. Seasonal Demand

Mediverse may experience predictable educational peaks:

```text
Exam periods
Course launches
Academic deadlines
Live learning events
```

Capacity forecasts should incorporate these patterns rather than extrapolating simple monthly averages.

---

# 69. PostgreSQL Economics

Database cost includes:

```text
Compute
Storage
IO
Backups
Replication
Network
Licensing where applicable
Operations
```

Database optimization must consider workload behavior, not instance price alone.

---

# 70. Database Rightsizing

Measure:

```text
CPU
Memory
Connections
IOPS
Storage growth
Query latency
Cache hit ratio
Replication behavior
```

before changing database capacity.

---

# 71. Oversized Database

A common failure pattern:

```text
Performance Incident
      │
      ▼
Increase DB Size
      │
      ▼
Incident disappears
      │
      ▼
Never investigate query
      │
      ▼
Permanent Cost Increase
```

Scaling hardware can hide application or query defects.

---

# 72. Query Optimization Economics

Before scaling vertically, investigate:

```text
Slow queries
Missing indexes
N+1 queries
Poor joins
Excessive result sets
Connection misuse
Unnecessary database calls
```

A ₹0 query optimization can outperform a permanent infrastructure upgrade.

---

# 73. Read Replica Economics

Read replicas should solve measured problems.

```text
Primary
  │
  ├── Writes
  │
  └── Read Replica
          │
          └── Read-heavy workload
```

Replicas increase:

```text
Compute cost
Storage cost
Replication cost
Operational complexity
```

They are not free scaling.

---

# 74. Database Connection Economics

Uncontrolled connection pools can force larger database infrastructure.

```text
50 Pods
 ×
50 Connections
 =
2,500 Potential Connections
```

Connection-pool sizing is therefore an infrastructure economics concern.

---

# 75. Database Autoscaling Caution

Database capacity is harder to scale elastically than stateless application workloads.

Capacity planning must account for:

```text
Connection behavior
Cache warming
Replication
Storage
Failover
Resize duration
```

---

# 76. Storage Economics

Storage cost depends on more than capacity.

```text
Storage Cost
    =
Capacity
+
IO
+
Requests
+
Replication
+
Backup
+
Retrieval
```

---

# 77. Storage Classification

Data should be classified by access pattern.

```text
HOT
 │
 ▼
Frequently accessed

WARM
 │
 ▼
Occasionally accessed

COLD
 │
 ▼
Rarely accessed

ARCHIVE
 │
 ▼
Retention only
```

---

# 78. Storage Lifecycle

Lifecycle automation should move eligible data between appropriate tiers.

```text
HOT
 │
 ▼
WARM
 │
 ▼
COLD
 │
 ▼
ARCHIVE
 │
 ▼
DELETE
```

subject to retention requirements.

---

# 79. S3 Lifecycle

Potential candidates include:

```text
Old application exports
Historical reports
Archived learning assets
Old logs
Backup artifacts
Unused asset versions
```

Lifecycle rules must respect compliance and recovery requirements.

---

# 80. Orphaned Object Cleanup

Object storage can accumulate:

```text
Abandoned multipart uploads
Old generated assets
Unused versions
Temporary exports
Expired preview assets
```

These should have explicit cleanup policies.

---

# 81. Backup Economics

Backups have value because they reduce recovery risk.

Optimization should consider:

```text
Retention
Frequency
Replication
Storage tier
Restore requirement
Compliance
```

Deleting backups simply to reduce storage cost is not FinOps.

---

# 82. RPO Economics

Lower RPO generally requires more protection.

```text
Lower acceptable data loss
          │
          ▼
More frequent replication / backup
          │
          ▼
Higher Cost
```

Business criticality must justify the target.

---

# 83. RTO Economics

Lower RTO often requires:

```text
Warm capacity
Replication
Automation
Standby infrastructure
Pre-provisioned dependencies
```

which increases cost.

---

# 84. Redis Economics

Redis cost is primarily memory economics.

Track:

```text
Dataset size
Memory utilization
TTL behavior
Eviction
Replication
Persistence
Hit rate
```

---

# 85. Cache Value

Caching is economically useful when:

```text
Cost avoided by cache hits
        >
Cost of operating cache
```

Adding Redis to every service by default is not optimization.

---

# 86. Cache TTL Economics

Excessively long TTLs may waste memory.

Excessively short TTLs may eliminate useful cache benefits.

TTL should reflect:

```text
Freshness requirements
Request frequency
Recomputation cost
Memory pressure
```

---

# 87. Cache Hit Ratio

A large expensive cache with a very low hit ratio should be challenged.

```text
Cache Requests: 1,000,000
Hits:             50,000

Hit Ratio = 5%
```

The workload may not justify the cache.

---

# 88. Kafka Economics

Kafka cost includes:

```text
Broker compute
Storage
Replication
Network
Partitions
Retention
Observability
Operations
```

Topic creation is not economically free.

---

# 89. Kafka Partition Economics

Excessive partitions increase:

```text
Broker overhead
Metadata
File handles
Replication work
Operational complexity
```

Partition count should reflect throughput and parallelism requirements.

---

# 90. Kafka Retention Economics

```text
High throughput
      ×
Long retention
      ×
Replication factor
      =
Large storage requirement
```

Retention should be driven by business and recovery requirements.

---

# 91. Event Payload Economics

Large Kafka messages increase:

```text
Network
Storage
Replication
Consumer processing
```

Events should carry appropriate domain information without becoming uncontrolled document transport.

---

# 92. 3D Asset Economics

Mediverse's immersive content can create substantial delivery cost.

```text
3D Model
Textures
Audio
Animation
Video
       │
       ▼
Asset Size
       │
       ▼
CDN / Network Cost
```

Asset optimization is therefore part of application architecture.

---

# 93. 3D Model Optimization

Consider:

```text
Mesh simplification
LOD
Geometry compression
Texture compression
Texture resizing
Lazy loading
Asset reuse
```

without damaging required visual quality.

---

# 94. Level of Detail

LOD can reduce rendering and transfer requirements.

```text
Near Camera
   │
   ▼
High Detail

Medium Distance
   │
   ▼
Medium Detail

Far Distance
   │
   ▼
Low Detail
```

---

# 95. Asset Compression

Large uncompressed 3D assets should not be distributed casually.

Compression strategy should consider browser/device compatibility and decompression cost.

---

# 96. Texture Economics

A visually simple scene can still become expensive if every asset carries oversized textures.

Track:

```text
Resolution
Compression
Format
Mipmaps
Reuse
Device target
```

---

# 97. CDN Architecture

Static learning assets should generally be delivered through CDN/cache infrastructure rather than repeatedly from application servers.

```text
User
 │
 ▼
CDN Edge
 │
 ├── HIT ─────► Asset
 │
 └── MISS
      │
      ▼
    Origin
```

---

# 98. CDN Cache Hit Ratio

Higher useful cache hit ratios reduce origin load and often reduce latency.

But cache policies must preserve content correctness and invalidation behavior.

---

# 99. Immutable Asset Versioning

Prefer content/version-based asset URLs.

```text
model-v17.glb
```

or equivalent immutable identifiers.

This enables long-lived caching without ambiguous invalidation.

---

# 100. Video Economics

Video delivery may dominate network cost.

Control through:

```text
Adaptive bitrate
Appropriate resolution
Compression
CDN
Caching
Device-aware playback
```

Do not send 4K media to a device displaying a small embedded educational panel unless needed.

---

# 101. Network Egress

Cloud network transfer can become a major cost driver.

Track:

```text
Internet egress
Cross-region traffic
Cross-AZ traffic
NAT traffic
CDN origin traffic
Inter-service traffic
```

---

# 102. Data Gravity

Large datasets should not move repeatedly without reason.

```text
DATA
 │
 └── 50 TB

Repeated cross-region transfer
        │
        ▼
High cost + latency
```

Move computation closer to data where architecture permits.

---

# 103. Cross-AZ Traffic

High-frequency service communication across availability zones can create material transfer cost.

Do not eliminate multi-AZ resilience merely to avoid that cost.

Instead understand and optimize unnecessary traffic.

---

# 104. Cross-Region Traffic

Cross-region architectures should explicitly justify:

```text
Replication
User latency
DR
Regulation
Availability
```

because cross-region data movement has both cost and complexity.

---

# 105. NAT Economics

NAT infrastructure can become a hidden cost center when workloads generate substantial outbound traffic.

Analyze:

```text
Traffic source
Destination
Volume
Need for internet path
Private endpoint availability
```

---

# 106. Private Endpoints

Private/service endpoints may reduce NAT dependence for suitable cloud services.

But endpoint costs themselves must be included.

"Private" does not mean "free."

---

# 107. Chatty Microservices

Architecture can create network cost.

```text
Request
  │
  ▼
Service A
  │
  ▼
Service B
  │
  ▼
Service C
  │
  ▼
Service D
```

Thousands of unnecessary remote calls affect both latency and cost.

---

# 108. Observability Economics

Observability has a non-trivial cost.

```text
Logs
Metrics
Traces
Profiles
Events
        │
        ▼
Ingestion
Storage
Indexing
Query
Retention
```

More telemetry is not automatically better observability.

---

# 109. Logging Economics

Logging cost roughly follows:

```text
Event Volume
   ×
Event Size
   ×
Retention
   ×
Indexing Cost
```

Debug-level production logging should not remain enabled indiscriminately.

---

# 110. Structured Logging

Structured logging improves queryability but does not remove the need for volume control.

Avoid repeatedly logging enormous payloads.

---

# 111. Sensitive Logging

Sensitive information should not be logged merely because storage is available.

This is both:

```text
Security risk
Privacy risk
Compliance risk
Cost waste
```

---

# 112. Log Retention Tiers

Different logs may require different retention.

```text
Operational logs
Security/audit logs
Debug logs
Compliance logs
```

Retention must follow purpose rather than one global number.

---

# 113. Metrics Cardinality

High-cardinality labels can cause explosive monitoring cost.

Dangerous examples include:

```text
user_id
request_id
session_id
email
random identifiers
```

These generally belong in logs/traces rather than metric labels.

---

# 114. Metric Value Review

A metric should exist because someone uses it for:

```text
SLO
Alerting
Capacity
Debugging
Product understanding
```

Unused metrics should be candidates for removal.

---

# 115. Trace Economics

Recording every span for every request indefinitely can become expensive.

Tracing strategy should consider:

```text
Traffic
Incident needs
Criticality
Sampling
Retention
Span volume
```

---

# 116. Trace Sampling

Possible strategies:

```text
Head sampling
Tail sampling
Error-biased sampling
Latency-biased sampling
Adaptive sampling
```

Sampling must preserve useful incident evidence.

---

# 117. Error Trace Retention

High-value traces such as:

```text
Errors
Very slow requests
Critical transactions
```

may deserve higher retention probability than routine successful traffic.

---

# 118. CI/CD Economics

CI consumes:

```text
Runner compute
Storage
Network
Artifact storage
Security scanning
Test environments
Engineering waiting time
```

A slow pipeline has both cloud cost and developer productivity cost.

---

# 119. Runner Utilization

Track:

```text
Busy time
Idle time
Queue time
Job duration
Runner type
Cost per build
```

---

# 120. Ephemeral CI Runners

Ephemeral runners can improve isolation and elasticity.

```text
Job
 │
 ▼
Create Runner
 │
 ▼
Execute
 │
 ▼
Destroy Runner
```

Startup latency and image-pull cost must still be considered.

---

# 121. Build Caching Economics

Effective caching reduces:

```text
Compilation time
Dependency downloads
Container builds
Runner consumption
Developer waiting
```

But caches require storage and invalidation discipline.

---

# 122. Test Economics

Tests have different cost/value profiles.

```text
Unit
  │ cheap / fast

Integration
  │ moderate

E2E
  │ expensive / slower
```

Do not repeatedly execute every expensive test when a cheaper signal can safely determine that it is unnecessary.

---

# 123. Artifact Economics

Registries accumulate:

```text
Container images
Maven artifacts
npm packages
SBOMs
Build outputs
```

Retention policies are required.

---

# 124. Image Retention

Do not delete:

```text
Currently deployed images
Rollback candidates
Required audit artifacts
```

But thousands of obsolete unreferenced development images need not live forever.

---

# 125. Preview Environment Economics

Preview environments create enormous DX value but can create uncontrolled cost.

```text
PR Open
   │
   ▼
Environment Created
   │
   ▼
PR Closed
   │
   ▼
Environment Destroyed
```

Destruction must be automated.

---

# 126. Preview TTL

Every temporary environment should have:

```text
Owner
Creation time
Expiry
Associated PR/task
Cleanup controller
```

No owner + no TTL = predictable waste.

---

# 127. Development Environment Scheduling

Non-production environments that are unused overnight/weekends may be candidates for scheduled scale-down.

Only apply this when it does not disrupt required testing or geographically distributed teams.

---

# 128. UAT Economics

Do not assume UAT must duplicate full production capacity continuously.

UAT should reproduce relevant architecture and behavior while capacity can often be smaller.

---

# 129. Production Parity

Production parity means:

```text
Architecture / configuration behavior
```

not necessarily:

```text
Identical expensive capacity
```

---

# 130. Multi-Region Economics

Multi-region architecture can approximately duplicate major infrastructure categories.

```text
Region A
   +
Region B
   +
Replication
   +
Networking
   +
Operations
```

This must be justified by availability, latency, regulatory, or recovery requirements.

---

# 131. DR Economics

Disaster recovery strategy should align cost with business requirement.

```text
Backup & Restore
      ↓
Pilot Light
      ↓
Warm Standby
      ↓
Active/Passive
      ↓
Active/Active

Increasing readiness
Increasing cost
```

---

# 132. RTO/RPO Cost Frontier

```text
Cost
 ^
 |                         ● Active/Active
 |                 ● Warm Standby
 |          ● Pilot Light
 |    ● Backup/Restore
 |
 +------------------------------------>
              Recovery Capability
```

The strongest DR architecture is not automatically the correct architecture.

---

# 133. Capacity Forecasting

Forecast capacity for:

```text
CPU
Memory
Database
Storage
Kafka
Network
AI tokens
Vector storage
GPU
Observability
CI
```

---

# 134. Capacity Headroom

Production systems require deliberate headroom.

```text
Expected Peak
     +
Failure Headroom
     +
Growth Headroom
     =
Required Capacity
```

100% utilization is not a healthy target.

---

# 135. Performance-Cost Frontier

Every major workload has a trade-off curve.

```text
Performance
    ^
    |                       ●
    |                 ●
    |            ●
    |       ●
    |  ●
    +----------------------------> Cost
```

Beyond some point, large cost increases produce tiny performance improvements.

Architecture should identify that point.

---

# 136. Cost-Aware Architecture Review

Significant ADRs should answer:

```text
What are the major cost drivers?
How does cost scale with traffic?
What is fixed vs variable?
What happens at 10× demand?
What creates egress?
What requires replication?
What are expected unit economics?
What is the exit cost?
```

---

# 137. Developer Self-Service Cost Estimation

ADR-071 self-service workflows should expose estimated economics before provisioning.

```text
Developer
   │
   ▼
"Create PostgreSQL"
   │
   ▼
Configuration
   │
   ▼
Estimated Monthly Cost
   │
   ▼
Policy
   │
   ▼
Provision
```

---

# 138. Cost Guardrails

Examples:

```text
Maximum preview environment size
Maximum default DB class
Maximum non-prod retention
Required TTL
GPU approval threshold
High-cost resource approval
```

Guardrails should target material risk rather than create approval bureaucracy for trivial resources.

---

# 139. FinOps Policy as Code

Where practical:

```text
Infrastructure Request
       │
       ▼
Cost Policy
       │
 ┌─────┴─────┐
 ▼           ▼
Allow      Review
```

Examples may include:

```text
Missing cost tags
Oversized non-prod resources
No TTL
Unexpected public egress
Unapproved GPU class
```

---

# 140. Optimization Backlog

Optimization opportunities should be managed like engineering work.

```text
Opportunity
    │
    ▼
Expected Saving
    │
    +
Engineering Cost
    │
    +
Risk
    │
    ▼
Priority
```

Do not spend ₹500,000 of engineering effort to save ₹20,000 annually.

---

# 141. Optimization ROI

Conceptually:

```text
Annual Savings - Implementation Cost - Added Operating Cost
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Implementation Investment
```

Precise financial methodology may vary, but opportunity cost must be considered.

---

# 142. Sustainability & Resource Efficiency

Resource efficiency often aligns with both FinOps and environmental efficiency.

Examples:

```text
Higher utilization
Reduced idle compute
Efficient storage
Reduced unnecessary transfer
Appropriate model selection
Efficient software
```

Do not use sustainability claims as justification for compromising required reliability.

---

# 143. FinOps Metrics

Mediverse should track a focused set of metrics:

```text
Total cloud spend
Forecast accuracy
Budget variance
Cost attribution coverage
Idle resource cost
Commitment utilization
Cost anomalies
Cost per active learner
Cost per learning session
Cost per AI interaction
Kubernetes utilization efficiency
Observability cost
Non-prod cost
Optimization savings
```

---

# 144. FinOps Maturity Model

```text
LEVEL 1 — REACTIVE
Bills reviewed after they arrive.

LEVEL 2 — VISIBLE
Costs attributed and dashboards available.

LEVEL 3 — CONTROLLED
Budgets, anomalies and guardrails exist.

LEVEL 4 — OPTIMIZED
Unit economics and automated optimization drive decisions.

LEVEL 5 — ECONOMIC ARCHITECTURE
Cost becomes a continuous architectural fitness dimension.
```

Mediverse should target **Level 4**, with selective Level 5 capabilities where economics materially affect architecture.

---

# 145. FinOps Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ "Cloud cost belongs to Finance"
❌ Optimizing only total monthly spend
❌ Cloud resources without owners
❌ Manual tagging as primary attribution
❌ Shared costs hidden or arbitrarily allocated
❌ Chargeback before teams have trustworthy showback
❌ Killing production because budget crossed 100%
❌ Cost alerts without owner/context
❌ Treating every cost increase as waste
❌ Ignoring unit economics
❌ Using request count alone for AI economics
❌ Sending every AI request to the strongest model
❌ Sending every AI request to the cheapest model
❌ Unlimited AI output tokens
❌ Entire conversation history sent blindly to LLMs
❌ Re-embedding entire corpus after tiny changes
❌ Huge RAG context injected without relevance
❌ Self-hosted AI assumed cheaper than APIs
❌ GPU allocation without utilization measurement
❌ Kubernetes requests copied blindly
❌ Rightsizing to average utilization
❌ Zero headroom as optimization target
❌ Autoscaling without maximum boundaries
❌ Stateful critical workloads forced entirely onto Spot
❌ Commitments purchased from optimistic forecasts
❌ Discount percentage treated as savings despite low utilization
❌ Database scaling used to hide bad queries
❌ Read replicas added without measured need
❌ Unlimited application connection pools
❌ Storage retained forever
❌ Backups deleted purely for cost reduction
❌ Redis added to every service by default
❌ Huge caches with poor hit ratios
❌ Kafka partitions created "just in case"
❌ Infinite Kafka retention without requirement
❌ Unoptimized 3D assets delivered directly from application servers
❌ 4K media delivered where lower resolution satisfies UX
❌ Cross-region traffic ignored
❌ NAT cost ignored
❌ Chatty microservices treated as financially free
❌ Debug logs permanently enabled in production
❌ User IDs used as metric labels
❌ Every trace retained forever
❌ CI cost measured without developer waiting time
❌ Build caching ignored
❌ Artifact registries with infinite retention
❌ Preview environments without TTL
❌ Non-production infrastructure running permanently without need
❌ Production parity interpreted as identical capacity
❌ Multi-region deployed because "enterprise systems should have it"
❌ Active/active DR without business justification
❌ 100% infrastructure utilization targeted
❌ Architecture reviews ignoring economics
❌ Self-service hiding cost from developers
❌ Every expensive resource requiring the same approval process
❌ Cost optimization without ROI analysis
❌ Spending more engineering money than optimization can reasonably save
```

---

# 146. FinOps Decision Flow

```text
                    NEW RESOURCE / CHANGE
                             │
                             ▼
                      BUSINESS NEED
                             │
                             ▼
                       COST ESTIMATE
                             │
               ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
               ▼             ▼             ▼
             FIXED        VARIABLE       SHARED
               │             │             │
               └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                             ▼
                        UNIT ECONOMICS
                             │
                             ▼
                         GUARDRAILS
                             │
                    ┌────────┴────────┐
                    ▼                 ▼
                  PASS              REVIEW
                    │                 │
                    └────────┬────────┘
                             ▼
                          DEPLOY
                             │
                             ▼
                          MEASURE
                             │
              ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
              ▼              ▼              ▼
          UTILIZATION       COST         SLO/QUALITY
              │              │              │
              └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                             ▼
                         OPTIMIZE
```

---

# 147. Cost Feedback Architecture

```text
AWS Billing / Usage
        │
        ├──────── Kubernetes Allocation
        ├──────── AI Usage
        ├──────── Database Usage
        ├──────── Network Usage
        └──────── Platform Usage
        │
        ▼
   COST DATA MODEL
        │
        ├── Team
        ├── Service
        ├── Environment
        ├── Product
        └── Capability
        │
        ▼
   FINOPS ANALYTICS
        │
   ┌────┼─────┬────────┐
   ▼    ▼     ▼        ▼
Budget Unit  Forecast Anomaly
       Cost
   │    │     │        │
   └────┴─────┼────────┘
              ▼
       ENGINEERING ACTION
              │
       ┌──────┼───────┐
       ▼      ▼       ▼
   Rightsize Scale  Redesign
       │      │       │
       └──────┼───────┘
              ▼
       ARCHITECTURE FEEDBACK
```

---

# 148. FinOps Governance Integration

ADR-073 integrates directly with the preceding architecture:

```text
ADR-071
Developer Platform
      │
      ▼
Self-Service Cost Visibility
      │
      ▼
ADR-072
Architecture Governance
      │
      ▼
Cost-Aware Decisions
      │
      ▼
ADR-073
FinOps
      │
      ▼
Economic Evidence
      │
      └──────────────► Architecture Evolution
```

FinOps therefore becomes an architectural feedback mechanism rather than a monthly billing exercise.

---

---

# ADR-074 — Enterprise Sustainability Engineering, Green Software, Carbon-Aware Computing & Resource Efficiency Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Hidden 3D Work**.

---

# 61. AI/LLM Sustainability

AI introduces a distinct resource-consumption profile.

```text
AI Capability
     │
     ├── Prompt processing
     ├── Inference
     ├── Retrieval
     ├── Embeddings
     ├── Vector search
     ├── Evaluation
     └── Training / fine-tuning
             │
             ▼
       COMPUTE / ENERGY
```

AI features must therefore justify not only their functional value but also their computational intensity.

---

# 62. AI Value per Computation

The goal is not to minimize AI usage indiscriminately.

Measure useful outcome relative to resource consumption.

```text
Learning Value
────────────────
AI Resource Cost
```

A more expensive inference may be justified when it materially improves an important educational outcome.

---

# 63. Model Size

Larger models generally require greater computational resources.

Therefore:

```text
Task Complexity
      │
      ▼
Required Capability
      │
      ▼
Appropriate Model
```

not:

```text
Every Request
      │
      ▼
Largest Available Model
```

---

# 64. Model Routing

ADR-073's economic model-routing strategy also becomes a sustainability control.

```text
Request
   │
   ▼
Classify
   │
   ├── Simple ─────► Small Model
   ├── Standard ───► Standard Model
   └── Complex ────► High-Capability Model
```

Routing must preserve required quality and safety.

---

# 65. AI Quality-Efficiency Frontier

Model selection should evaluate:

```text
Quality
Latency
Cost
Energy/resource intensity
Safety
```

Conceptually:

```text
Quality
  ^
  |                         ● Large
  |                  ● Medium
  |           ● Small
  |
  +--------------------------------> Resource Use
```

The largest model is justified only when the additional capability matters.

---

# 66. Token Efficiency

Unnecessary tokens create unnecessary computation.

Potential waste includes:

```text
Repeated system instructions
Irrelevant conversation history
Redundant RAG context
Verbose tool outputs
Unnecessary generated text
```

---

# 67. Context Window Governance

Context should contain what the model actually needs.

```text
Available Context
      │
      ▼
Relevance Selection
      │
      ▼
Required Context
      │
      ▼
Model
```

Large context windows should not become an excuse for poor context management.

---

# 68. Conversation Compression

Long-running AI sessions may use:

```text
Recent messages
       +
Structured state
       +
Relevant retrieved history
       +
Summarized older context
```

instead of replaying the entire history indefinitely.

---

# 69. Output Efficiency

Generated responses should be bounded according to product requirements.

```text
Task
 │
 ▼
Required Information
 │
 ▼
Appropriate Output Budget
```

Generating 4,000 tokens where 300 satisfy the learning objective wastes latency and computation.

---

# 70. RAG Efficiency

RAG should retrieve the minimum context required to achieve the target answer quality.

```text
Query
  │
  ▼
Candidate Retrieval
  │
  ▼
Reranking
  │
  ▼
Relevant Context
  │
  ▼
LLM
```

---

# 71. Retrieval Top-K

Large `top-k` values should not be selected blindly.

Increasing retrieval count can increase:

```text
Vector work
Reranking work
Prompt size
Inference work
Latency
```

while potentially reducing answer quality through irrelevant context.

---

# 72. Chunk Efficiency

Chunking should balance:

```text
Retrieval precision
Embedding count
Storage
Prompt size
Semantic completeness
```

Neither extremely small nor extremely large chunks are universally optimal.

---

# 73. Embedding Lifecycle

Embeddings require lifecycle management.

```text
Document Created
      │
      ▼
Embed
      │
      ▼
Document Changed
      │
      ▼
Re-embed Changed Content
      │
      ▼
Document Deleted
      │
      ▼
Delete Embeddings
```

Deleted source content should not leave permanent orphaned vectors.

---

# 74. Incremental Embedding

Prefer changed-content processing over full-corpus re-embedding where technically appropriate.

```text
1 changed chapter
       │
       X
Re-embed 5 million chunks
```

is obvious computational waste.

---

# 75. Vector Storage Efficiency

Track:

```text
Vector count
Dimensions
Indexes
Replicas
Metadata
Retention
Unused collections
```

Vector databases require the same lifecycle discipline as other persistent systems.

---

# 76. AI Caching

Reusable AI results may be cached when correctness, personalization and privacy permit.

```text
Request
  │
  ▼
Reusable Result?
  │
 ┌┴───────┐
 ▼        ▼
YES       NO
 │         │
Cache     Infer
```

---

# 77. Cache Correctness

Sustainability cannot justify stale or incorrect AI output.

Cache keys and invalidation may need to incorporate:

```text
Model version
Prompt version
Knowledge version
User context
Policy version
```

depending on the feature.

---

# 78. AI Batching

Suitable asynchronous AI workloads may batch requests to improve hardware utilization.

Candidates include:

```text
Embedding generation
Offline evaluation
Content classification
Bulk summarization
Dataset processing
```

Interactive tutoring requests generally have different latency constraints.

---

# 79. Quantization

Self-hosted models may use quantization when evaluation demonstrates acceptable quality.

```text
Model
 │
 ▼
Reduced Precision
 │
 ├── Memory ↓
 ├── Compute ↓
 └── Possible Quality Change
```

Quality regression must be measured rather than assumed absent.

---

# 80. GPU Utilization

GPU allocation should expose:

```text
GPU utilization
Memory utilization
Queue depth
Batch efficiency
Idle time
Throughput
```

Expensive accelerators sitting idle represent both financial and resource inefficiency.

---

# 81. GPU Sharing

Where workload isolation and technology permit, GPU sharing may improve utilization.

However, sharing must not introduce unacceptable:

```text
Performance interference
Security risk
Memory contention
Operational complexity
```

---

# 82. GPU Scale-Down

Elastic AI infrastructure should release GPU capacity when sustained demand disappears where architecture permits.

Permanent GPU allocation for occasional experimentation is rejected.

---

# 83. Training vs Fine-Tuning

Before training or fine-tuning, ask whether the problem can be solved through:

```text
Prompting
RAG
Tools
Structured workflows
Smaller adaptation
Existing model
```

Training is not the default solution to every AI product requirement.

---

# 84. Fine-Tuning Justification

Fine-tuning should define:

```text
Quality target
Baseline
Dataset
Expected improvement
Training cost
Inference impact
Evaluation
Lifecycle
```

Without measurable benefit, repeated training cycles are waste.

---

# 85. Experiment Tracking

AI experiments should record enough metadata to avoid repeating failed expensive experiments.

```text
Model
Dataset
Parameters
Prompt
Evaluation
Resource usage
Outcome
```

---

# 86. AI Evaluation Efficiency

Evaluation suites should be representative.

Running every expensive model against every historical example on every tiny change may be unnecessary.

Use layered evaluation:

```text
Small smoke set
      │
      ▼
Regression set
      │
      ▼
Full evaluation
      │
      ▼
Specialized / safety evaluation
```

according to change risk.

---

# 87. Observability Footprint

Observability itself consumes infrastructure.

```text
Application
   │
   ├── Logs
   ├── Metrics
   └── Traces
        │
        ▼
 Collection
 Processing
 Storage
 Query
```

Telemetry must provide operational value.

---

# 88. Log Efficiency

Avoid:

```text
Duplicate logs
Huge payload logging
Permanent debug logging
Repeated stack traces
High-frequency useless events
```

Logging less is acceptable when the removed data had no operational value.

---

# 89. Metric Efficiency

Metrics should use bounded dimensions.

```text
GOOD
service
endpoint
status_class

DANGEROUS
user_id
request_id
email
session_id
```

Unbounded cardinality wastes resources and can destabilize monitoring systems.

---

# 90. Trace Efficiency

Tracing strategy should preserve useful evidence while controlling volume.

Use appropriate:

```text
Sampling
Tail-based retention
Error prioritization
Latency prioritization
Service-specific policies
```

---

# 91. Telemetry Retention

Different telemetry classes require different retention.

```text
High-value audit
      │
      ▼
Longer retention

Temporary debugging
      │
      ▼
Short retention
```

One universal retention period is rejected.

---

# 92. CI/CD Sustainability

Software delivery consumes:

```text
Runner CPU
Memory
Storage
Network
Test infrastructure
Container builds
Security scans
```

Pipeline efficiency is therefore part of sustainable engineering.

---

# 93. Build Caching

Reuse safe deterministic build work.

Examples:

```text
Maven dependencies
Node dependencies
Container layers
Compilation outputs where safe
```

Avoid repeatedly downloading and rebuilding identical inputs.

---

# 94. Incremental Builds

Where tooling supports trustworthy incremental execution:

```text
Changed Code
     │
     ▼
Affected Build Work
```

should be preferred over rebuilding unrelated components.

---

# 95. Test Selection

Testing strategy should maximize defect-detection value per execution cost.

```text
Change
  │
  ▼
Risk Analysis
  │
  ▼
Required Tests
```

This does not justify skipping critical regression or security verification.

---

# 96. Flaky Tests

Flaky tests waste:

```text
Runner resources
Developer time
Repeated execution
Investigation effort
```

Flakiness is therefore quality debt, productivity debt, cost debt and sustainability debt simultaneously.

---

# 97. CI Retry Governance

Blind retry loops are rejected.

```text
Test Failed
   │
   ▼
Retry 10 times
```

can conceal defects while multiplying compute.

Retries should exist only for understood transient failure modes.

---

# 98. Developer Environments

Local and remote development environments should avoid permanently allocated unused infrastructure.

Potential controls:

```text
Auto-stop
Hibernate
TTL
Scale-down
Shared services
On-demand startup
```

---

# 99. Remote Development

Cloud development environments should expose utilization and lifecycle.

```text
Developer starts workspace
        │
        ▼
Workspace active
        │
        ▼
Idle threshold
        │
        ▼
Suspend
```

---

# 100. Database Efficiency

Database sustainability starts with application behavior.

```text
Application
   │
   ├── Query design
   ├── Indexing
   ├── Connection usage
   ├── Result size
   └── Transaction design
```

Hardware scaling should not substitute for basic database engineering.

---

# 101. Query Efficiency

Measure:

```text
Execution time
Rows scanned
Rows returned
IO
CPU
Locking
Frequency
```

A query executed one million times deserves different attention from an equally slow query executed once per month.

---

# 102. Index Efficiency

Indexes trade:

```text
Read Performance ↑
        vs
Storage ↑
Write Work ↑
Maintenance ↑
```

Unused or redundant indexes should be detectable.

---

# 103. N+1 Query Waste

```text
1 request
   │
   ├── Query 1
   ├── Query 2
   ├── Query 3
   ├── ...
   └── Query 500
```

can waste application, database and network resources.

N+1 problems should be detected during performance engineering.

---

# 104. Connection Pool Efficiency

Oversized pools can increase:

```text
Database memory
Connection overhead
Contention
Infrastructure requirements
```

Pool size should be based on measured concurrency rather than arbitrary defaults.

---

# 105. Redis Efficiency

Redis should have a measurable purpose.

```text
Cache
Session
Rate limiting
Coordination
```

Do not introduce an always-on Redis cluster merely because a framework makes it convenient.

---

# 106. Redis Memory Lifecycle

Use:

```text
TTL
Eviction policy
Memory monitoring
Key-size monitoring
Unused-key cleanup
```

where appropriate.

---

# 107. Kafka Efficiency

Kafka sustainability depends on:

```text
Partition count
Replication
Retention
Message size
Compression
Traffic
Consumer behavior
```

---

# 108. Event Compression

Compression can reduce storage and network use for suitable event workloads.

But compression introduces CPU cost.

The correct configuration depends on the workload.

---

# 109. Kafka Retention

Retain events according to business and recovery requirements.

```text
High Throughput
      ×
Long Retention
      ×
Replication
```

can create substantial resource demand.

---

# 110. Dead Consumers

Unused consumers, abandoned consumer groups and obsolete topics should be discoverable and removed through controlled lifecycle management.

---

# 111. Resilience Resource Trade-Off

Reliability often requires redundancy.

```text
Replica 1
Replica 2
Replica 3
```

uses more resources than a singleton.

This is not automatically waste.

---

# 112. Sustainability vs Reliability

Never optimize:

```text
3 replicas → 1 replica
```

without evaluating:

```text
Availability
Failure tolerance
Maintenance
Traffic
Recovery
```

Required resilience has legitimate resource cost.

---

# 113. Redundancy Right-Sizing

The goal is:

```text
Minimum redundancy
that satisfies
required reliability
```

not maximum redundancy everywhere.

---

# 114. Multi-AZ Footprint

Multi-AZ infrastructure may be required for availability.

Optimize unnecessary replication and traffic without eliminating required fault tolerance.

---

# 115. Multi-Region Footprint

Multi-region architectures multiply:

```text
Compute
Storage
Replication
Network
Operational systems
```

They therefore require explicit business justification.

---

# 116. Disaster Recovery Sustainability

DR strategy should align with required RTO/RPO.

```text
Backup/Restore
      │
Pilot Light
      │
Warm Standby
      │
Active/Passive
      │
Active/Active

Resource requirement ↑
```

Do not maintain active/active infrastructure merely for architectural prestige.

---

# 117. Recovery Testing

An apparently efficient backup-only DR architecture that cannot actually recover is not sustainable engineering.

Recovery capability must be tested.

---

# 118. Embodied Carbon

Software ultimately runs on physical hardware whose manufacturing has environmental impact.

Conceptually:

```text
Hardware Footprint
       =
Operational Energy
       +
Embodied Impact
```

Exact allocation may be difficult in public cloud environments.

---

# 119. Hardware Efficiency

Higher useful utilization can reduce the amount of hardware capacity required to deliver equivalent work.

```text
10 poorly utilized servers
          │
          ▼
5 efficiently utilized servers
```

may reduce both operational and embodied resource demand, subject to resilience requirements.

---

# 120. Hardware Lifetime

Software requirements can indirectly shorten device/server usefulness.

Avoid unnecessary:

```text
Memory inflation
CPU inflation
GPU requirements
Bundle growth
Asset growth
```

that provide little user value.

This is especially important for student devices.

---

# 121. Backward Device Support

Efficient Mediverse applications should remain usable on reasonable older hardware where product requirements permit.

This improves both accessibility and device longevity.

---

# 122. Carbon Telemetry

Where reliable data is available, the platform may ingest:

```text
Cloud usage
Energy estimates
Region carbon intensity
Resource utilization
Functional workload volume
```

to derive sustainability metrics.

---

# 123. Carbon Data Pipeline

```text
Cloud / Platform Usage
          │
          ▼
Resource Consumption
          │
          +
Carbon Intensity
          │
          ▼
Estimated Emissions
          │
          +
Functional Units
          │
          ▼
SCI / Intensity Metrics
```

---

# 124. Carbon Signal Reliability

Carbon-aware automation should account for data:

```text
Freshness
Geographic resolution
Temporal resolution
Methodology
Availability
Confidence
```

Do not move production workloads based on unreliable signals.

---

# 125. Sustainability Metadata

Workloads may declare characteristics such as:

```yaml
sustainability:
  workloadClass: batch
  deferrable: true
  maxDelay: 6h
  locationFlexible: false
```

This enables platform-level scheduling decisions.

---

# 126. Carbon-Aware Platform API

Conceptually:

```text
submit-job
    │
    ├── deadline
    ├── region constraints
    ├── resource requirements
    └── carbon flexibility
          │
          ▼
      Scheduler
```

The application should not implement carbon-scheduling logic independently.

---

# 127. Developer Portal Integration

ADR-071's portal should expose useful sustainability information alongside cost.

Example:

```text
Service: ai-tutor

CPU efficiency        78%
Idle capacity         12%
AI tokens/session     4,200
Estimated SCI trend   ↓ 9%
Storage growth        ↑ 14%
```

Avoid meaningless green badges.

---

# 128. Sustainability Scorecard

Potential checks:

```text
✓ Resource requests reviewed
✓ Temporary environments have TTL
✓ Storage lifecycle configured
✓ Observability cardinality controlled
⚠ AI token/session increasing
✗ Orphaned preview environments
```

---

# 129. Sustainability Fitness Functions

Machine-verifiable examples include:

```text
Temporary environment MUST have TTL
Non-prod GPU MUST have owner
Container MUST define resource requests
Large static assets MUST meet delivery budget
Logs MUST respect retention policy
```

Not every sustainability objective can be enforced automatically.

---

# 130. Resource Budgets

Teams may define budgets for:

```text
Frontend bundle size
3D asset size
API payload
AI tokens
Build duration
Storage growth
Log ingestion
```

These are engineering budgets, not merely financial budgets.

---

# 131. Budget Regression

Example:

```text
Frontend JS budget = 500 KB

PR result = 740 KB
```

The pipeline should surface the regression.

Whether it blocks deployment depends on policy severity.

---

# 132. AI Token Budget

AI capabilities should establish expected token envelopes.

```text
Feature
  │
  ├── Expected input
  ├── Expected output
  ├── RAG context
  └── Maximum
```

Unexpected growth becomes observable.

---

# 133. Architecture Review

Significant ADRs should answer:

```text
What work is performed?
What can be avoided?
What is always-on?
What scales with demand?
What data is retained?
What network movement occurs?
What accelerator resources are required?
Can work shift in time/location?
What is the reliability trade-off?
```

---

# 134. Sustainability Review Scope

Heavy sustainability review should be reserved for material workloads such as:

```text
Large AI systems
Large-scale data processing
High-bandwidth media
3D delivery
Multi-region systems
GPU infrastructure
High-volume telemetry
```

Do not create bureaucracy for trivial application changes.

---

# 135. Sustainability Optimization Backlog

Opportunities should include:

```text
Resource saving
Estimated carbon/resource impact
Financial saving
Engineering cost
Reliability risk
User impact
Confidence
```

---

# 136. Optimization Priority

Prioritize high-impact, low-risk opportunities first.

```text
                     HIGH IMPACT
                         │
             PLAN        │      PRIORITIZE
                         │
HIGH EFFORT ─────────────┼──────────── LOW EFFORT
                         │
             AVOID       │      QUICK WIN
                         │
```

Impact estimates should not pretend to be more precise than available data allows.

---

# 137. FinOps Integration

ADR-073 and ADR-074 should share telemetry.

```text
Resource Usage
     │
     ├────► COST
     │       ADR-073
     │
     └────► RESOURCE/CARBON
             ADR-074
```

Separate duplicate measurement systems would create unnecessary complexity.

---

# 138. Joint Optimization

Prefer improvements that simultaneously reduce:

```text
Cost
Resource use
Latency
Operational complexity
```

Examples may include:

```text
Removing unused infrastructure
Query optimization
Asset compression
Build caching
Rightsizing
```

These are high-value engineering improvements.

---

# 139. Trade-Off Governance

When goals conflict:

```text
Security
Reliability
Performance
Accessibility
Cost
Sustainability
```

the trade-off should be explicit.

Sustainability does not automatically outrank safety or reliability.

---

# 140. Sustainability Governance

Ownership should be distributed.

```text
Enterprise Architecture
        │
        ├── Principles
        │
Platform Engineering
        │
        ├── Controls / telemetry
        │
FinOps
        │
        ├── Shared economics
        │
Engineering Teams
        │
        └── Workload efficiency
```

A central sustainability team cannot optimize application code it does not own.

---

# 141. Sustainability Metrics

Mediverse should prefer a focused set:

```text
SCI / functional-unit trend where measurable
Compute utilization
Idle-resource rate
Storage growth
Network transfer
AI tokens/session
GPU utilization
Observability ingestion
Frontend transfer size
3D asset transfer
CI compute time
Temporary-resource waste
```

---

# 142. Metric Interpretation

Metrics must be interpreted alongside product demand.

Example:

```text
Total AI compute ↑ 50%
AI tutoring sessions ↑ 200%
```

may represent improved efficiency rather than deterioration.

Intensity metrics prevent simplistic conclusions.

---

# 143. Sustainability Maturity Model

```text
LEVEL 1 — UNAWARE
Resource consumption largely invisible.

LEVEL 2 — VISIBLE
Major workloads and waste measured.

LEVEL 3 — EFFICIENT
Rightsizing, lifecycle and resource budgets standardized.

LEVEL 4 — OPTIMIZED
Sustainability integrated into platform and architecture.

LEVEL 5 — CARBON-AWARE
Flexible workloads respond intelligently to reliable carbon signals.
```

Mediverse should target **Level 4**, adopting Level 5 selectively where it provides measurable benefit.

---

# 144. Sustainability Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ Calling ordinary cost reduction "green" without evidence
❌ Carbon claims with false precision
❌ Optimizing carbon while violating security
❌ Optimizing carbon while violating SLOs
❌ Assuming cheaper automatically means greener
❌ Assuming cloud automatically means sustainable
❌ Moving workloads without considering data transfer
❌ Carbon-aware scheduling for latency-critical requests
❌ Maximum Kubernetes utilization as target
❌ Removing resilience headroom
❌ Oversized Kubernetes requests left indefinitely
❌ Non-production infrastructure running forever
❌ Temporary environments without TTL
❌ Serverless automatically considered sustainable
❌ Data retained forever
❌ Duplicate datasets without purpose
❌ Huge API payloads
❌ Unbounded API collections
❌ Aggressive polling without need
❌ Massive frontend bundles
❌ Third-party scripts without value review
❌ Entire 3D worlds downloaded at startup
❌ 4K textures on tiny objects
❌ Rendering hidden scenes continuously
❌ Largest LLM used for every task
❌ Huge context windows filled because capacity exists
❌ Excessive RAG top-k
❌ Full corpus re-embedded after tiny changes
❌ Orphaned vectors retained forever
❌ GPUs permanently allocated to occasional experiments
❌ Fine-tuning without measurable quality objective
❌ Repeating AI experiments without tracking results
❌ Every AI evaluation executed for every trivial change
❌ Unlimited observability ingestion
❌ High-cardinality metric labels
❌ Debug telemetry retained indefinitely
❌ CI repeatedly rebuilding identical dependencies
❌ Blind test retries
❌ Cloud developer workspaces never suspended
❌ Scaling databases instead of fixing obvious query defects
❌ Redis introduced without measurable value
❌ Kafka retention set indefinitely by default
❌ Reliability redundancy classified automatically as waste
❌ Active/active multi-region architecture without requirement
❌ Sustainability scorecards reduced to green badges
❌ Sustainability review required for every tiny code change
❌ Separate FinOps and sustainability telemetry stacks collecting identical data
```

| Primary optimization      | Useful value per resource           |
| First optimization step   | Eliminate unnecessary work          |

| SCI                       | Supported where measurable          |

| FinOps telemetry          | Reused                              |

| Reliability headroom      | Required                            |
