# 150. Governing Invariant

The entire ADR reduces to:

```text
                        USER VALUE
                            │
                            ▼
                      REQUIRED WORK
                            │
                            ▼
                 CAN WORK BE AVOIDED?
                     ┌──────┴──────┐
                     ▼             ▼
                    YES            NO
                     │             │
                   REMOVE          ▼
                            CAN IT BE REDUCED?
                              ┌────┴────┐
                              ▼         ▼
                             YES        NO
                              │         │
                           OPTIMIZE      ▼
                                  CAN IT BE SHIFTED?
                                    ┌───┴───┐
                                    ▼       ▼
                                   YES      NO
                                    │       │
                                  SHIFT     RUN
                                    │       │
                                    └───┬───┘
                                        ▼
                                VERIFY QUALITY
                                        │
                     ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐
                     ▼                  ▼                  ▼
                  SECURITY          RELIABILITY            UX
                     │                  │                  │
                     └──────────────────┼──────────────────┘
                                        ▼
                                     MEASURE
                                        │
                                        ▼
                                     IMPROVE
```

> **Mediverse will not treat sustainability as a branding exercise or pursue lower resource consumption at the expense of security, reliability, accessibility or learning quality. The architecture must first eliminate unnecessary computation, then reduce unavoidable work, improve hardware utilization, and only then apply temporal or spatial carbon-aware execution where trustworthy signals and workload flexibility make it technically justified.**

---

---

# ADR-075 — Enterprise Business Continuity, Disaster Recovery, Cyber Resilience & Operational Resilience Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Identity Provider Failure**.

---

# 61. Identity Continuity

Identity is part of the recovery control plane.

```text
Application healthy
Database healthy
Kubernetes healthy
Network healthy
        │
        ▼
Identity unavailable
        │
        ▼
Users cannot authenticate
        │
        ▼
Business service unavailable
```

Identity continuity must therefore be designed according to business criticality.

---

# 62. Emergency Authentication

Recovery personnel must retain a controlled path into critical infrastructure when normal identity systems are unavailable.

```text
Normal Access
     │
     ▼
Enterprise IdP
     │
     X
Unavailable
     │
     ▼
Break-Glass Path
```

This path must not become an everyday authentication shortcut.

---

# 63. Break-Glass Accounts

Break-glass access should be:

```text
Rarely used
Strongly protected
Independent of failed identity dependencies
Audited
Alerted
Periodically tested
Credential-rotated
Time-bounded where possible
```

A break-glass account whose credentials nobody can retrieve during an emergency provides no resilience.

---

# 64. Break-Glass Governance

Use should trigger immediate security visibility.

```text
Break-Glass Login
       │
       ├── Alert
       ├── Audit
       ├── Incident record
       ├── Session monitoring
       └── Post-use credential rotation
```

---

# 65. Secrets Management Failure

Applications may depend on secrets infrastructure for:

```text
Database credentials
API credentials
TLS material
Signing keys
Service credentials
Third-party tokens
```

Loss of the secrets control plane must have defined runtime and recovery behavior.

---

# 66. Runtime Secret Independence

Where technically safe, an already-running application should not necessarily fail instantly because the secret-management control plane becomes temporarily unavailable.

```text
Secrets Manager unavailable
          │
          ├── Existing workload continues
          │
          └── New workload may fail startup
```

The exact behavior depends on credential rotation and security requirements.

---

# 67. KMS Failure

Encryption creates a critical recovery dependency.

```text
Backup exists
   │
   ▼
Encryption Key unavailable
   │
   ▼
Backup unusable
```

Backing up encrypted data without protecting recovery access to the required keys is incomplete.

---

# 68. Key Recovery

Critical encryption keys require appropriately protected recovery mechanisms consistent with the security architecture.

Recovery must consider:

```text
Deletion
Disablement
Permission loss
Account compromise
Region loss
Operator error
```

---

# 69. Credential Compromise

A disaster can be caused by security compromise rather than infrastructure destruction.

```text
Credential Compromised
        │
        ▼
Contain
        │
        ▼
Revoke
        │
        ▼
Rotate
        │
        ▼
Assess Impact
        │
        ▼
Recover Trusted State
```

---

# 70. Credential Rotation During Recovery

Recovery procedures should identify dependent credentials rather than rotate randomly.

```text
Compromised Root
      │
      ▼
Dependency Graph
      │
      ├── Cloud credentials
      ├── Database credentials
      ├── Git credentials
      ├── CI/CD credentials
      ├── Registry credentials
      └── Third-party tokens
```

---

# 71. Observability Outage

Monitoring infrastructure itself can fail.

```text
Production
   │
   ▼
Observability ✗
   │
   ▼
System state uncertain
```

Absence of alerts during a monitoring outage does not mean the platform is healthy.

---

# 72. Monitoring the Monitoring

Critical observability components should have independent health signals where justified.

```text
Prometheus
Grafana
Log platform
Alerting
      │
      ▼
External / independent health check
```

---

# 73. Observability Degraded Mode

During telemetry failure, operators may rely temporarily on:

```text
Cloud-native health
Kubernetes status
Load-balancer health
Synthetic probes
Application health endpoints
Database health
Direct logs
```

Recovery runbooks should identify these alternate signals.

---

# 74. Region Failure

Region loss is materially different from an AZ failure.

```text
REGION A
   │
   X
Unavailable
   │
   ▼
Can critical Mediverse capabilities
operate elsewhere?
```

The answer must be determined before the incident.

---

# 75. Multi-Region Is Not Automatically Required

Mediverse rejects:

```text
"Enterprise platform"
       │
       ▼
"Therefore active-active multi-region"
```

Multi-region architecture must be justified by:

```text
BIA
RTO
RPO
Availability requirement
Regulation
User geography
DR economics
```

---

# 76. DR Strategy Spectrum

```text
Backup & Restore
       │
       ▼
Pilot Light
       │
       ▼
Warm Standby
       │
       ▼
Active / Passive
       │
       ▼
Active / Active
```

Moving downward generally increases readiness, complexity and cost.

---

# 77. Backup-and-Restore DR

```text
PRIMARY REGION
     │
     ▼
Backups
     │
     ▼
Protected Storage

Disaster
     │
     ▼
Create Infrastructure
     │
     ▼
Restore Data
     │
     ▼
Start Services
```

Suitable where longer RTO is acceptable.

---

# 78. Pilot-Light DR

Maintain only essential foundations in the recovery region.

```text
Recovery Region

Networking       ✓
Critical data    ✓
Core security    ✓
Minimal platform ✓
Full compute     ✗
```

During disaster, remaining capacity is provisioned.

---

# 79. Warm Standby

```text
Primary Region
   │
   ▼
Full Production Capacity

Recovery Region
   │
   ▼
Reduced Running Capacity
```

During failover:

```text
Scale recovery region
        │
        ▼
Redirect traffic
```

This reduces RTO at increased steady-state cost.

---

# 80. Active/Passive

A passive environment is maintained ready for promotion.

```text
Region A
 ACTIVE
   │
   ├──── replication ────► Region B
   │                       PASSIVE
```

Failover procedures must address data consistency and traffic switching.

---

# 81. Active/Active

```text
Users
  │
  ├────────► Region A
  │
  └────────► Region B
```

Both regions serve production traffic.

This introduces difficult problems around:

```text
Data consistency
Conflict resolution
Routing
Sessions
Replication
Split brain
Operational complexity
Testing
```

---

# 82. DR Economics

Recovery architecture should satisfy:

```text
Required Recovery Capability
────────────────────────────
Sustainable Cost + Complexity
```

The strongest possible DR architecture is not automatically the correct one.

---

# 83. Recovery Cost Curve

```text
Cost
 ^
 |                         ● Active/Active
 |                  ● Active/Passive
 |             ● Warm Standby
 |        ● Pilot Light
 |   ● Backup/Restore
 |
 +--------------------------------------> Recovery Speed
```

ADR-073 FinOps governance applies directly.

---

# 84. Data Replication Strategy

Replication should define:

```text
Source
Target
Direction
Latency
Consistency
Failure behavior
Recovery authority
```

"Replicated" alone is insufficient documentation.

---

# 85. Synchronous Replication

Synchronous replication can reduce data loss but may increase:

```text
Write latency
Failure coupling
Network dependency
```

It must match actual RPO requirements.

---

# 86. Asynchronous Replication

Asynchronous replication can reduce runtime coupling but introduces a replication gap.

```text
Primary
  │
  ├── Transaction T1
  ├── Transaction T2
  ├── Transaction T3
  │
  X Disaster
  │
Replica has only T1/T2
```

The potential gap must fit the agreed RPO.

---

# 87. Backup Strategy

Critical data should define:

```text
Backup frequency
Retention
Encryption
Isolation
Immutability
Location
Restore procedure
Validation
Ownership
```

A backup job returning `SUCCESS` proves only that the job completed.

---

# 88. Immutable Backups

Critical backups should be protected against modification/deletion for an appropriate period where supported.

```text
Attacker
   │
   ├── Encrypt production
   └── Delete backups
             │
             X
        Immutable Copy
```

This is particularly important for cyber recovery.

---

# 89. Backup Isolation

Backup access should not share unrestricted administrative paths with production.

```text
Production Admin Compromised
            │
            X
     Backup Security Boundary
            │
            ▼
      Recovery Copy Survives
```

---

# 90. Backup Account Separation

For sufficiently critical workloads, backups may require stronger isolation through separate:

```text
Accounts
Credentials
Roles
Policies
Administrative boundaries
```

according to the threat model.

---

# 91. Backup Geographic Diversity

A regional disaster should not destroy both production and its only recovery copy.

Backup placement must match the disaster scenarios the architecture claims to survive.

---

# 92. Backup Retention

Retention should support:

```text
Operational recovery
Delayed corruption discovery
Security incidents
Compliance
Forensics
```

while ADR-073 and ADR-074 govern unnecessary storage.

---

# 93. Ransomware Recovery

Ransomware changes the recovery problem.

```text
Normal DR:
Infrastructure failed

Cyber DR:
Infrastructure may exist
but cannot be trusted
```

Recovery must restore **trusted state**, not merely available state.

---

# 94. Cyber Recovery

Cyber recovery requires determining:

```text
What was compromised?
When did compromise begin?
Which identities are trusted?
Which artifacts are trusted?
Which backups are clean?
Which infrastructure can be reused?
```

---

# 95. Clean-Room Recovery

For severe compromise:

```text
Compromised Environment
          │
          X
    Security Boundary
          │
          ▼
      CLEAN ROOM
          │
          ├── Trusted identity
          ├── Trusted tooling
          ├── Trusted artifacts
          ├── Clean backups
          └── Controlled networking
```

Recovery should not automatically reuse potentially compromised control planes.

---

# 96. Trusted Recovery Artifacts

Critical recovery inputs include:

```text
Source repositories
Container images
Helm charts
Terraform modules
OS/base images
Dependencies
Backups
SBOMs
Signatures
Configuration
```

Recovery requires confidence in their provenance.

---

# 97. Artifact Integrity

Where ADR security controls provide signatures or attestations:

```text
Artifact
   │
   ▼
Verify provenance
   │
 ┌─┴──────┐
 ▼        ▼
Valid   Unknown
 │        │
Use     Investigate
```

Unknown provenance should not silently enter clean-room recovery.

---

# 98. Recovery Dependency Order

Systems cannot be restored randomly.

Example:

```text
1. Network / DNS foundations
        │
2. Identity / KMS / Secrets
        │
3. Kubernetes / Platform
        │
4. Databases / Persistent State
        │
5. Messaging / Cache
        │
6. Core Application Services
        │
7. Frontend
        │
8. Secondary Capabilities
        │
9. AI / Analytics
```

Actual order must follow the dependency graph.

---

# 99. Recovery Orchestration

Recovery should combine automation and explicit gates.

```text
Automated Step
      │
      ▼
Validation
      │
      ▼
Next Step
      │
      ▼
Validation
```

Blind automation can rapidly reproduce corruption or misconfiguration.

---

# 100. Degraded Operating Modes

Resilience is not binary.

```text
100% Capability
      │
      ▼
Core Capability
      │
      ▼
Read-Only Capability
      │
      ▼
Emergency Information
      │
      ▼
Unavailable
```

Mediverse should intentionally design useful intermediate states.

---

# 101. Read-Only Mode

If writes cannot be safely accepted:

```text
Courses              ✓
Existing content      ✓
Historical progress   ✓

New progress writes   ✗
Assessment submission ✗
Administrative writes ✗
```

A clearly communicated read-only mode may be safer than accepting writes that cannot be preserved.

---

# 102. AI-Disabled Mode

AI should be removable from the critical request path where business requirements allow.

```text
Core Learning
      │
      ├── Course access ✓
      ├── Assessment ✓
      ├── Progress ✓
      └── AI Tutor ✗
```

This prevents an AI-provider outage from unnecessarily becoming a platform outage.

---

# 103. Feature Shedding

During extreme load or partial failure:

```text
Critical
  ├── Authentication
  ├── Course access
  └── Assessment

Optional
  ├── Recommendations
  ├── Analytics
  ├── Rich personalization
  └── AI enrichment
```

Optional work may be disabled to preserve critical capacity.

---

# 104. Graceful Degradation

Applications should define fallback behavior for dependencies.

```text
Recommendation Service ✗
        │
        ▼
Course page still loads
without recommendations
```

A non-critical dependency should not automatically become a critical failure.

---

# 105. Traffic Management

Recovery may require:

```text
DNS changes
Global load balancing
CDN configuration
Ingress changes
Traffic weighting
Maintenance responses
```

Traffic control must itself be recoverable.

---

# 106. Failover

Failover means transferring service responsibility to a recovery environment.

```text
PRIMARY
   │
   X
   │
   ▼
FAILOVER
   │
   ▼
RECOVERY
```

It must not be treated as simply changing DNS.

---

# 107. Failover Preconditions

Before failover, establish where possible:

```text
Failure scope
Data state
Replication state
Recovery environment health
Dependency health
Traffic readiness
Security status
```

---

# 108. Split-Brain Risk

A dangerous scenario:

```text
Region A
accepting writes
     │
     │
     X Network partition
     │
     │
Region B
also accepting writes
```

Both sides may believe they are authoritative.

---

# 109. Single-Writer Authority

Where the data model requires a single writer, failover must explicitly transfer authority.

```text
Writer A
   │
   ▼
Fence A
   │
   ▼
Promote B
   │
   ▼
Writer B
```

Promotion without fencing can corrupt state.

---

# 110. Data Reconciliation

After partial failures, data may diverge.

Recovery may require:

```text
Compare
Detect missing transactions
Detect duplicates
Resolve conflicts
Replay events
Repair derived state
Validate business invariants
```

---

# 111. Idempotent Recovery

Recovery workflows should be safely repeatable where possible.

```text
Run recovery step
       │
       X interrupted
       │
       ▼
Run again safely
```

Idempotency reduces operator fear and recovery complexity.

---

# 112. Failover Validation

After failover, verify more than HTTP `200`.

Validate:

```text
Authentication
Critical reads
Critical writes
Database integrity
Messaging
Object access
User workflows
Security controls
Observability
Capacity
```

---

# 113. Synthetic Recovery Transactions

Controlled synthetic transactions can validate end-to-end capability.

```text
Synthetic User
     │
     ▼
Login
     │
     ▼
Open Course
     │
     ▼
Perform Test Operation
     │
     ▼
Validate Persistence
```

---

# 114. Failback

Failback is a separate operation.

```text
Recovery Region
      │
      ▼
Stable
      │
      ▼
Original Region Restored
      │
      ▼
Synchronize
      │
      ▼
Validate
      │
      ▼
Controlled Failback
```

Never assume returning home is easier than failing over.

---

# 115. Failback Criteria

Failback should require:

```text
Root cause addressed
Original environment trusted
Data synchronized
Dependencies healthy
Capacity ready
Security validated
Rollback path available
```

---

# 116. Disaster Declaration

A major outage does not automatically require DR activation.

Decision authority should be explicit.

```text
Incident
   │
   ▼
Assess
   │
   ▼
Normal recovery viable?
 ┌─┴─────┐
 ▼       ▼
YES      NO
 │        │
Continue  Consider disaster declaration
```

---

# 117. Disaster Declaration Authority

Roles should define who can authorize:

```text
Region failover
Emergency access
Recovery environment activation
Data restoration
Traffic migration
Failback
```

Ambiguity during crisis increases downtime.

---

# 118. Incident Command

Major recovery requires clear command structure.

```text
Incident Commander
        │
        ├── Technical Recovery
        ├── Security
        ├── Communications
        ├── Business/Product
        └── Vendor Coordination
```

One person should not attempt to execute every role.

---

# 119. Recovery Communication

Communication should cover:

```text
What happened
Known impact
Current operating mode
Recovery progress
User actions if any
Next update
```

Do not publish speculative root causes during active recovery.

---

# 120. Internal Communication

Engineering communication should distinguish:

```text
Facts
Hypotheses
Decisions
Actions
Owners
Timestamps
```

This reduces confusion during long-running incidents.

---

# 121. Recovery Runbooks

Critical services require executable recovery documentation.

A runbook should contain:

```text
Trigger
Prerequisites
Access requirements
Commands/actions
Expected output
Validation
Rollback
Escalation
Owner
```

---

# 122. Runbook Quality

This is not sufficient:

```text
"Restore PostgreSQL."
```

A useful runbook answers:

```text
From which backup?
To where?
Using which credentials?
What recovery point?
How is integrity checked?
Who approves promotion?
```

---

# 123. Runbook Versioning

Runbooks should be:

```text
Version controlled
Reviewed
Tested
Updated after exercises/incidents
Accessible during primary-tool outage
```

A runbook stored only inside the failed system is poorly designed.

---

# 124. Recovery Automation

Automate deterministic repetitive operations.

Candidates:

```text
Infrastructure provisioning
Cluster bootstrap
Backup restoration
DNS preparation
Validation probes
Configuration reconciliation
```

---

# 125. Human Gates

Retain human approval around high-risk irreversible operations such as:

```text
Promoting database authority
Destroying corrupted environments
Changing global traffic
Executing destructive restoration
Failback
```

where risk warrants it.

---

# 126. Restore Drills

Restore testing must occur before a disaster.

```text
Select Backup
     │
     ▼
Restore
     │
     ▼
Start Application
     │
     ▼
Validate
     │
     ▼
Measure Recovery Time
```

---

# 127. Tabletop Exercises

Tabletops test decision-making without necessarily disrupting infrastructure.

Scenario:

```text
"Primary AWS region unavailable.
Identity provider degraded.
Last confirmed replication point:
7 minutes ago."
```

Teams then execute the decision process.

---

# 128. Game Days

Game days test operational behavior using controlled technical failure.

Potential scenarios:

```text
Node loss
AZ loss
Database failover
Redis loss
Kafka broker loss
AI provider outage
DNS misconfiguration
Observability failure
```

---

# 129. Chaos Engineering Integration

Chaos engineering validates assumptions about expected failures.

```text
Hypothesis
   │
   ▼
Controlled Failure
   │
   ▼
Observe
   │
   ▼
Verify SLO / Recovery
   │
   ▼
Improve
```

Chaos is not random destruction.

---

# 130. DR Exercises vs Chaos Engineering

```text
CHAOS ENGINEERING
Tests resilience to controlled failure.

DR EXERCISE
Tests recovery after normal resilience
boundaries are exceeded.
```

Both are needed for different questions.

---

# 131. Recovery Exercise Scope

Exercises should eventually test combinations.

Real disasters rarely respect architecture diagrams.

Example:

```text
Region outage
    +
Expired recovery credential
    +
Delayed replication
    +
Monitoring degradation
```

Single-failure tests alone create false confidence.

---

# 132. Exercise Safety

Exercises require:

```text
Scope
Abort criteria
Owner
Communication
Blast-radius controls
Rollback
Observation
```

Testing resilience should not casually create a real disaster.

---

# 133. Recovery Evidence

Every material exercise should record:

```text
Scenario
Expected behavior
Actual behavior
RTO achieved
RPO achieved
Failures
Manual steps
Unexpected dependencies
Follow-up actions
```

---

# 134. Recovery Metrics

Mediverse should track:

```text
Restore success rate
Restore duration
Failover duration
Failback duration
Backup success
Backup age
Recovery-point gap
Runbook success
Exercise frequency
RTO compliance
RPO compliance
```

---

# 135. Recovery Time Measurement

Do not stop the clock when infrastructure boots.

```text
Disaster
   │
   ▼
Infrastructure restored
   │
   X
Not necessarily recovered
   │
   ▼
Critical business capability validated
   │
   ▼
RTO achieved
```

Business capability restoration is the meaningful endpoint.

---

# 136. Recovery Scorecard

Example:

| Capability     | Tier | RTO | RPO | Last Restore Test | Result                 |
| -------------- | ---: | --: | --: | ----------------- | ---------------------- |
| Authentication |    1 | 30m | N/A | Current quarter   | PASS                   |
| Course API     |    1 |  1h | 15m | Current quarter   | PASS                   |
| Progress DB    |    1 |  1h |  5m | Current quarter   | PASS                   |
| AI Tutor       |    2 |  4h | N/A | Current quarter   | DEGRADED MODE VERIFIED |
| Analytics      |    3 | 24h | 12h | Current half      | PASS                   |

Targets shown here are illustrative; actual values must come from BIA.

---

# 137. Operational-Resilience Fitness Functions

Machine-verifiable controls may include:

```text
Critical DB MUST have tested backup
Critical service MUST declare recovery tier
Tier 1 service MUST declare RTO/RPO
Temporary DR credentials MUST expire
Critical backups MUST meet maximum-age policy
Recovery repository MUST be accessible
Critical workloads MUST satisfy topology policy
```

---

# 138. Recovery Readiness Gate

A Tier 1 service should not be considered production-ready merely because its deployment succeeds.

```text
Deployment Ready
      +
Monitoring Ready
      +
Security Ready
      +
Recovery Ready
      =
Production Ready
```

---

# 139. Architecture Review Integration

Significant architecture reviews should ask:

```text
What happens if this dependency disappears?
What state can be rebuilt?
What state must be restored?
What is the failure domain?
What is the RTO?
What is the RPO?
How is recovery tested?
What happens during partial recovery?
How is failback performed?
```

---

# 140. DR Change Management

Changes affecting:

```text
Replication
Backups
DNS
Identity
KMS
Database topology
Regions
Recovery automation
Network routing
```

should evaluate impact on recovery capability.

---

# 141. Cyber-Resilience Integration

Operational resilience and cybersecurity intersect at:

```text
Identity
Backups
Artifact integrity
Secrets
Supply chain
Recovery access
Forensics
Clean-room recovery
```

Security architecture that prevents attacks but cannot recover from one is incomplete.

---

# 142. FinOps Integration

ADR-073 applies to DR decisions.

Track:

```text
Steady-state DR cost
Recovery capacity cost
Replication cost
Backup cost
Exercise cost
Expected downtime exposure
```

The cheapest DR architecture may create unacceptable business risk.

---

# 143. Sustainability Integration

ADR-074 applies as well.

Idle standby capacity should be justified by recovery objectives.

```text
Recovery requirement
      │
      ▼
Required standby capacity
```

Not:

```text
"More replicas feel safer."
```

---

# 144. Operational Resilience Maturity Model

```text
LEVEL 1 — BACKUP EXISTS
Recovery largely assumed.

LEVEL 2 — DOCUMENTED
RTO/RPO and runbooks exist.

LEVEL 3 — TESTED
Restores and failovers exercised.

LEVEL 4 — ENGINEERED
Recovery integrated into platform,
architecture and delivery.

LEVEL 5 — ADAPTIVE
Recovery is continuously validated,
measured and improved.
```

Mediverse should target **Level 4**, progressing selected Tier 0/1 capabilities toward Level 5.

---

# 145. Operational Resilience Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ "We have backups, therefore we have DR"
❌ Replication treated as backup
❌ Backup success treated as restore proof
❌ RTO/RPO invented by infrastructure teams
❌ Every service assigned identical recovery targets
❌ Active/active because it looks enterprise-grade
❌ Multi-region without BIA justification
❌ Application multi-AZ while critical DB remains single-AZ
❌ Recovery dependent on manual console knowledge
❌ Terraform state without recovery protection
❌ GitOps recovery assuming Git can never fail
❌ Runtime depending on CI availability
❌ Search indexes treated as irreplaceable when reproducible
❌ Redis cache treated like authoritative data
❌ Kafka replay without idempotency
❌ AI outage causing complete learning-platform outage unnecessarily
❌ Unlimited retries during dependency failure
❌ DNS omitted from dependency analysis
❌ Identity omitted from DR
❌ Break-glass credentials never tested
❌ Backups encrypted with unrecoverable keys
❌ Production admins able to delete every recovery copy
❌ Backups stored only in the failed region
❌ Cyber recovery performed inside an untrusted control plane
❌ Unsigned/unverified artifacts used in clean-room recovery
❌ Services restored in arbitrary order
❌ Recovery automation without validation gates
❌ DR architecture with no degraded mode
❌ Read-only capability never designed
❌ Optional features consuming resources during critical recovery
❌ Failover treated as a DNS change
❌ Both regions accepting conflicting writes
❌ Failback performed immediately after infrastructure returns
❌ Disaster declaration authority undefined
❌ One engineer acting as commander, operator and communicator
❌ Runbooks stored only in the unavailable platform
❌ Runbooks consisting of vague statements
❌ Recovery exercises never performed
❌ Chaos engineering confused with random failure injection
❌ RTO measured only until servers start
❌ Recovery findings not converted into engineering work
```

---

```text
                         DISRUPTION
                             │
                             ▼
                       DETECT / ASSESS
                             │
                  ┌──────────┴──────────┐
                  ▼                     ▼
             NORMAL FAILURE       DISASTER-SCALE
                  │                     │
                  ▼                     ▼

                  │              │             │

                  │                            ▼

                  │           INFRA          DATA        IDENTITY
                  │              │             │             │

                  │                            ▼

                  │                            │

                                          FAILBACK?

```

---

# 147. Cyber Recovery Reference Flow

```text
                      SECURITY INCIDENT
                             │
                             ▼
                         CONTAIN
                             │
                             ▼
                    COMPROMISE BOUNDARY
                             │
              ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
              ▼              ▼              ▼
           IDENTITY        SYSTEMS         DATA
              │              │              │
              └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                             ▼
                       TRUST DECISION
                             │
                  ┌──────────┴──────────┐
                  ▼                     ▼
              REUSABLE             UNTRUSTED
                  │                     │
                  │                     ▼
                  │                CLEAN ROOM
                  │                     │
                  └──────────┬──────────┘
                             ▼
                      TRUSTED ARTIFACTS
                             │
                             ▼
                        CLEAN BACKUP
                             │
                             ▼
                     REBUILD PLATFORM
                             │
                             ▼
                      ROTATE SECRETS
                             │
                             ▼
                       RESTORE DATA
                             │
                             ▼
                    SECURITY VALIDATION
                             │
                             ▼
                     BUSINESS VALIDATION
                             │
                             ▼
                         RESTORE
```

---

# 148. Enterprise Recovery Control Plane

```text
                    MEDIVERSE RECOVERY CONTROL PLANE
                                  │
       ┌──────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┐
       ▼                          ▼                          ▼
    PEOPLE                     PROCESS                    PLATFORM
       │                          │                          │
       ├─ Incident Cmd            ├─ BIA                     ├─ IaC
       ├─ SRE                     ├─ RTO/RPO                 ├─ GitOps
       ├─ Security                ├─ Runbooks                ├─ Backups
       ├─ Platform                ├─ Exercises               ├─ Replication
       └─ Product                 └─ Communication           └─ Automation
       │                          │                          │
       └──────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┘
                                  ▼
                           RECOVERY EVIDENCE
                                  │

          RESTORE              FAILOVER              CYBER
           TEST                 TEST                RECOVERY
             │                    │                    │
             └────────────────────┼────────────────────┘
                                  ▼

                                  │
```

# 149. ADR-075 Decision Outcome

| Area                       | Decision                                  |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| Resilience basis           | Business capability                       |
| BIA                        | Required for critical capabilities        |
| MTD                        | Defined where applicable                  |
| RTO/RPO                    | Business-driven                           |
| Recovery tiers             | Tier 0–3                                  |
| Dependency mapping         | Mandatory for critical services           |
| HA vs DR                   | Explicitly separated                      |
| AZ failure                 | HA where tier requires                    |
| Cluster loss               | IaC + GitOps rebuild                      |
| Manual cloud configuration | Recovery debt                             |
| Git repositories           | Recovery protected                        |
| CI outage                  | Runtime independent                       |
| Terraform state            | Protected and recoverable                 |
| PostgreSQL                 | Backup + PITR + restore tests             |
| Replication                | Not considered backup                     |
| Redis                      | Recovery based on role                    |
| Kafka                      | Replay/idempotency aware                  |
| Object storage             | Version/lifecycle/recovery governed       |
| Search                     | Rebuildable where derived                 |
| Vector indexes             | Rebuildable where appropriate             |
| AI outage                  | Degraded mode preferred where possible    |
| Third-party dependencies   | Failure behavior defined                  |
| DNS                        | Critical dependency                       |
| Identity                   | Explicit continuity requirement           |
| Break-glass                | Protected, audited, tested                |
| Secrets/KMS                | Recovery dependency                       |
| Observability outage       | Alternate signals required                |
| Multi-region               | BIA/RTO/RPO justified                     |
| DR strategy                | Tier-specific                             |
| Active/active              | Exceptional, not default                  |
| Immutable backups          | Critical-data requirement where justified |
| Backup isolation           | Required for cyber resilience             |
| Cyber recovery             | Trusted-state recovery                    |
| Clean room                 | Severe compromise scenario                |
| Artifact integrity         | Verified                                  |
| Recovery ordering          | Dependency driven                         |
| Degraded modes             | Explicitly designed                       |
| Read-only mode             | Supported where useful                    |
| Feature shedding           | Supported                                 |
| Split brain                | Explicitly prevented                      |
| Failover                   | Controlled and validated                  |
| Failback                   | Separate controlled operation             |
| Disaster declaration       | Authority defined                         |
| Incident command           | Required                                  |
| Runbooks                   | Executable and tested                     |
| Restore drills             | Required                                  |
| Tabletop exercises         | Required                                  |
| Game days                  | Required for critical systems             |
| Chaos integration          | Controlled                                |
| Recovery evidence          | Retained                                  |
| Fitness functions          | Automated where meaningful                |
| FinOps integration         | Required                                  |
| Sustainability integration | Required                                  |
| Maturity target            | Level 4; Tier 0/1 toward Level 5          |
| Status                     | **Accepted**                              |
| Priority                   | **Critical**                              |

```text
          VALIDATION             INTEGRITY                WORKFLOWS
            │                        │                        │
            └────────────────────────┼────────────────────────┘
                                     ▼
                           SERVICE RESTORATION
                                     │
                                     ▼
                           DATA RECONCILIATION
                                     │
                                     ▼
                              SAFE FAILBACK
                                     │
                                     ▼
                           RECOVERY EVIDENCE
                                     │
             ┌───────────────────────┼───────────────────────┐
             ▼                       ▼                       ▼
           RTO/RPO               RUNBOOKS               EXERCISES
             │                       │                       │
             └───────────────────────┼───────────────────────┘
                                     ▼
                          RESILIENCE SCORECARD
                                     │
                                     ▼
                                  ADR-072
                         EVOLUTIONARY GOVERNANCE
```

---

---

# ADR-076 — Enterprise Data Governance, Data Architecture, Data Quality, Lineage, Metadata & Data Lifecycle Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Master and Reference Data**.

---

# 61. Enterprise Identifier Strategy

Identifiers must be stable, unambiguous and appropriate to their domain.

```text
Business Entity
      │
      ▼
Stable Identifier
      │
      ├── APIs
      ├── Events
      ├── Databases
      ├── Analytics
      └── AI/Data Products
```

Changing a display name, email address or other mutable business attribute must not unexpectedly change entity identity.

---

# 62. Natural vs Surrogate Identifiers

Natural identifiers originate from business attributes.

Examples:

```text
email
registration_number
external_course_code
```

Surrogate identifiers are system-generated.

```text
learner_id
course_id
assessment_id
```

Mutable business attributes should generally not become permanent technical identity.

---

# 63. Globally Unique Identifiers

Distributed systems may benefit from identifiers that can be generated independently.

Possible approaches include:

```text
UUID
ULID
Provider-generated identifiers
Domain-specific identifiers
```

The choice should consider:

```text
Uniqueness
Ordering
Storage
Index behavior
Exposure
Interoperability
```

No identifier format is universally superior.

---

# 64. Identifier Immutability

Once externally referenced, identifiers should normally remain stable.

```text
Learner ID
    │
    ├── Enrollment
    ├── Progress
    ├── Assessment
    ├── Events
    └── Analytics
```

Reassigning identifiers can corrupt lineage and reconciliation.

---

# 65. External Identifiers

External identifiers should be distinguished from internal identity.

```text
Mediverse Learner ID
        │
        ├── University ID
        ├── LMS ID
        └── Identity Provider ID
```

Mappings require explicit ownership.

---

# 66. Reference Data Governance

Shared reference datasets should define:

```text
Owner
Authoritative source
Allowed values
Version
Effective dates
Change process
Consumers
```

Hard-coded copies across services create uncontrolled divergence.

---

# 67. PostgreSQL Governance

PostgreSQL remains an important operational system of record for Mediverse.

Governance must cover:

```text
Database ownership
Schema ownership
Migration ownership
Access
Indexing
Retention
Backup
Classification
Observability
```

---

# 68. Database Ownership

Every production database must have an accountable owning service/team.

```text
progress-db
     │
     ▼
Progress Domain
```

"Shared database owned by everyone" usually means owned by nobody.

---

# 69. Schema Ownership

Schemas should correspond to clear ownership boundaries where practical.

A service must not modify another service's schema simply because network connectivity exists.

---

# 70. Cross-Service Database Access

Mediverse rejects routine direct database coupling:

```text
Service A
   │
   └──────── SQL ───────► Service B Database
```

Prefer:

```text
Service A
   │
   ├── API
   └── Event
         │
         ▼
     Service B
```

Exceptions require architectural justification.

---

# 71. Why Direct Database Coupling Is Dangerous

It bypasses:

```text
Domain rules
API contracts
Authorization logic
Compatibility boundaries
Observability
Ownership
```

and makes independent evolution substantially harder.

---

# 72. Database Migration Governance

Schema migrations require:

```text
Versioning
Review
Backward compatibility
Deployment sequencing
Rollback/forward-fix strategy
Observability
Recovery awareness
```

ADR-075 applies to destructive migration failure.

---

# 73. Expand-and-Contract Migration

Prefer staged migration for breaking schema evolution.

```text
EXPAND
  │
  ├── Add new structure
  │
  ▼
MIGRATE
  │
  ├── Applications transition
  │
  ▼
CONTRACT
  │
  └── Remove obsolete structure
```

This reduces deployment coupling.

---

# 74. Change Data Capture

CDC can propagate operational changes without repeatedly querying entire tables.

```text
PostgreSQL
    │
    ▼
Transaction Log
    │
    ▼
CDC
    │
    ▼
Kafka / Data Platform
```

CDC is infrastructure, not business semantics by itself.

---

# 75. CDC Governance

CDC pipelines must define:

```text
Source
Captured tables
Schema evolution
Ordering
Replay
Retention
Sensitive fields
Consumers
Failure handling
```

Blindly publishing every database column is rejected.

---

# 76. Transactional Outbox

Where reliable state change plus event publication is required:

```text
Business Transaction
       │
       ├── Update Domain State
       └── Insert Outbox Event
                │
                ▼
             COMMIT
                │
                ▼
          Event Publisher
                │
                ▼
              Kafka
```

This avoids unsafe dual-write patterns.

---

# 77. Dual-Write Anti-Pattern

```text
Update PostgreSQL ✓
Publish Kafka Event ✗
```

can leave inconsistent systems.

Likewise:

```text
Publish Event ✓
Database Commit ✗
```

can publish facts that never became authoritative state.

---

# 78. Kafka Data Governance

Kafka topics are governed data interfaces.

Each important topic should define:

```text
Owner
Purpose
Schema
Classification
Retention
Partition strategy
Consumers
Compatibility
SLO
```

---

# 79. Topic Naming

Topic names should communicate domain and purpose rather than implementation accident.

Conceptually:

```text
assessment.submitted
enrollment.changed
course.completed
```

Naming conventions should be standardized platform-wide.

---

# 80. Event Lineage

Lineage should follow events through downstream processing.

```text
Assessment DB
      │
      ▼
AssessmentSubmitted
      │
      ▼
Kafka
      │
      ├── Progress Processor
      ├── Analytics
      └── Notification
```

This makes downstream impact visible.

---

# 81. Event Retention

Kafka retention should reflect:

```text
Replay requirements
Recovery
Audit needs
Consumer lag
Storage economics
Compliance
```

Infinite retention is not a default.

---

# 82. Event Replay Governance

Before replay:

```text
Replay Window
     │
     ▼
Affected Consumers
     │
     ▼
Idempotency
     │
     ▼
Side Effects
     │
     ▼
Approval / Execution
```

Replay is a controlled data operation.

---

# 83. Redis Data Authority

Redis should normally contain:

```text
Cached
Ephemeral
Derived
Short-lived coordination state
```

rather than irreplaceable authoritative business data.

---

# 84. Cache Provenance

A cache entry should conceptually have an upstream authority.

```text
PostgreSQL
    │
    ▼
Application
    │
    ▼
Redis
```

When Redis and PostgreSQL disagree, authority must already be known.

---

# 85. Cache Lifecycle

Cache governance should define:

```text
TTL
Invalidation
Eviction
Maximum size
Serialization version
Sensitive-data rules
```

---

# 86. Elasticsearch/Search Governance

Search indexes are generally derived data products.

```text
Authoritative Data
       │
       ▼
Index Pipeline
       │
       ▼
Elasticsearch
       │
       ▼
Search API
```

The source of truth remains upstream.

---

# 87. Search Schema

Search mappings require governance around:

```text
Field types
Analyzers
Language
Index versions
Aliases
Sensitive fields
Re-index strategy
```

---

# 88. Reindexing

Large schema changes may require:

```text
Index v1
   │
   ▼
Create Index v2
   │
   ▼
Backfill
   │
   ▼
Validate
   │
   ▼
Switch Alias
   │
   ▼
Retire v1
```

This enables controlled migration.

---

# 89. Object Storage Governance

Object storage may contain:

```text
Course media
Documents
Exports
Datasets
Backups
AI knowledge sources
3D assets
```

Each object class requires ownership and lifecycle policy.

---

# 90. Object Metadata

Important objects should carry or be associated with metadata such as:

```text
Owner
Classification
Content type
Created time
Source
Retention class
Checksum
Version
```

---

# 91. Data Lake Decision

Mediverse should not create a data lake merely because large organizations commonly have one.

A lake is justified when requirements exist for:

```text
Large-scale analytics
Raw historical data
Multiple analytical consumers
ML datasets
Cross-domain analysis
```

---

# 92. Data Lakehouse Decision

A lakehouse architecture may be considered when Mediverse requires combined:

```text
Object storage economics
Table semantics
Schema management
Transactional capabilities
Analytical interoperability
```

It is not automatically superior to a warehouse or simpler analytical platform.

---

# 93. Data Swamp Prevention

```text
DATA LAKE
   │
   ▼
No ownership
No catalogue
No quality
No lifecycle
No semantics
   │
   ▼
DATA SWAMP
```

Cheap storage does not justify uncontrolled accumulation.

---

# 94. ETL vs ELT

Both patterns are permitted.

```text
ETL

Extract → Transform → Load

ELT

Extract → Load → Transform
```

Selection depends on:

```text
Platform capability
Security
Data volume
Latency
Transformation complexity
Governance
```

---

# 95. Batch Processing

Batch workloads should define:

```text
Input
Schedule
Expected volume
Freshness
Retry behavior
Idempotency
Output
SLO
```

A batch job completing successfully does not prove its output is correct.

---

# 96. Stream Processing

Streaming systems should define:

```text
Ordering
Event time
Processing time
Windows
State
Checkpoints
Late events
Duplicates
Recovery
```

---

# 97. Event Time vs Processing Time

```text
Event occurred: 10:00
Event received: 10:07
Event processed: 10:08
```

These timestamps represent different concepts and must not be conflated.

---

# 98. Late Data

Streaming pipelines should explicitly define how late events are handled.

Possible strategies:

```text
Accept within window
Update previous result
Route to correction stream
Quarantine
Reject
```

---

# 99. Out-of-Order Events

```text
Expected:
A → B → C

Received:
A → C → B
```

Consumers requiring ordering must define how this is resolved.

---

# 100. Data Pipeline Idempotency

Reprocessing the same input should not accidentally multiply business results.

```text
Input X
  │
  ├── Process
  │
  X failure
  │
  └── Process again
```

Idempotency is both a data-quality and recovery property.

---

# 101. Vector Database Governance

Vector stores require governance equivalent to other enterprise data platforms.

Track:

```text
Collection owner
Source corpus
Embedding model
Dimensions
Metadata schema
Classification
Retention
Index configuration
```

---

# 102. Embedding Provenance

Every governed embedding set should be traceable to:

```text
Source document
Source version
Chunking strategy
Embedding model
Model version
Creation time
Pipeline version
```

---

# 103. Embeddings Are Derived Data

Conceptually:

```text
Source Content
     │
     ▼
Chunking
     │
     ▼
Embedding Model
     │
     ▼
Vectors
```

The vector is not the authoritative source document.

---

# 104. Embedding Model Change

Changing embedding models may invalidate compatibility with existing vectors.

```text
Embedding Model A
       │
       ▼
Vector Space A

Embedding Model B
       │
       ▼
Vector Space B
```

Mixing incompatible embeddings without deliberate design is rejected.

---

# 105. RAG Knowledge Governance

RAG introduces a governed knowledge pipeline.

```text
Knowledge Source
      │
      ▼
Validation
      │
      ▼
Classification
      │
      ▼
Chunking
      │
      ▼
Embedding
      │
      ▼
Retrieval
      │
      ▼
LLM
```

---

# 106. RAG Source Authority

The system must know whether retrieved content is:

```text
Authoritative
Approved
Draft
Historical
User-generated
External
```

Retrieval relevance does not prove authority.

---

# 107. RAG Freshness

Knowledge sources should expose:

```text
Published time
Effective time
Last updated
Version
Expiry where applicable
```

Stale content can produce confidently wrong AI responses.

---

# 108. RAG Deletion Propagation

```text
Source deleted
      │
      ▼
Chunk deleted
      │
      ▼
Embedding deleted
      │
      ▼
Search/vector index updated
      │
      ▼
Cache invalidated
```

Deletion must propagate through derived AI systems.

---

# 109. AI Dataset Governance

Datasets used for:

```text
Training
Fine-tuning
Evaluation
RAG
Prompt testing
Safety testing
```

require ownership, provenance and permitted-use metadata.

---

# 110. AI Dataset Versioning

An experiment should identify exactly which dataset version was used.

```text
Model Version
      +
Dataset Version
      +
Configuration
      =
Reproducible Evaluation
```

---

# 111. AI Evaluation Data Separation

Evaluation datasets should be protected from accidental contamination by training/fine-tuning data where the evaluation methodology requires independence.

Otherwise reported quality can become misleading.

---

# 112. Synthetic Data

Synthetic data may be used for:

```text
Development
Testing
Performance testing
Demonstrations
AI experimentation
```

where it adequately represents required characteristics.

---

# 113. Synthetic Does Not Mean Safe Automatically

Synthetic datasets should be assessed for:

```text
Re-identification risk
Source leakage
Realistic distributions
Bias
Coverage
Utility
```

A copied production record with the name changed is not genuinely synthetic.

---

# 114. Production Data in Non-Production

Default:

```text
Production Sensitive Data
          │
          X
     DEV / TEST
```

unless an explicitly approved and controlled requirement exists.

---

# 115. Non-Production Data Controls

Prefer:

```text
Synthetic data
Masked datasets
Tokenized datasets
Purpose-built fixtures
```

over unrestricted production clones.

---

# 116. Data Masking

Masking should remove or transform sensitive values while preserving required testing utility.

```text
Original
ganesh@example.com

Masked
user_18492@example.test
```

Masking rules must consider relationships between fields.

---

# 117. Tokenization

Tokenization may replace sensitive values with controlled tokens.

```text
Sensitive Value
      │
      ▼
Tokenization Service
      │
      ▼
Opaque Token
```

The token vault becomes a security-critical dependency.

---

# 118. Access Governance

Data access must follow:

```text
Identity
Purpose
Role
Classification
Least privilege
Auditability
```

Database connectivity alone does not authorize unrestricted data use.

---

# 119. Row-Level Controls

Where justified, access may be restricted by row.

Example:

```text
Educator A
    │
    ▼
Students assigned to A
```

rather than all learners in the platform.

---

# 120. Column-Level Controls

Sensitive attributes may require stronger access than ordinary fields.

```text
Course title       → normal authorized access
Sensitive identity → restricted access
```

Controls should follow classification.

---

# 121. Data Residency

Some data may be constrained to approved geographic locations.

Residency requirements must propagate to:

```text
Primary database
Replicas
Backups
Analytics
Logs
Search
AI providers
Vector stores
```

Moving only the primary database is insufficient.

---

# 122. Data Sovereignty Dependency

Before using an external processor:

```text
Dataset
   │
   ▼
Classification
   │
   ▼
Residency Requirement
   │
   ▼
Provider / Region Eligibility
```

This is especially important for AI and analytics services.

---

# 123. Encryption at Rest

Sensitive persistent data should use appropriate encryption.

This includes where applicable:

```text
Databases
Object storage
Backups
Analytics
Search
Vector stores
```

Encryption keys themselves require ADR-075 recovery planning.

---

# 124. Encryption in Transit

Data moving across:

```text
Client → Platform
Service → Service
Platform → Database
Platform → External Provider
Region → Region
```

should use appropriate transport protection.

---

# 125. Retention Governance

Retention must be explicit by data category.

```text
Dataset
   │
   ▼
Purpose
   │
   ▼
Retention Requirement
   │
   ▼
Archive / Delete
```

"Keep everything indefinitely" is rejected.

---

# 126. Retention Metadata

Important datasets should identify:

```text
Retention class
Retention start event
Retention duration
Deletion action
Archive requirement
Legal hold behavior
```

---

# 127. Archival

Archival is appropriate when data must remain available but no longer requires expensive operational storage.

```text
HOT
 │
 ▼
WARM
 │
 ▼
COLD / ARCHIVE
 │
 ▼
DELETE
```

---

# 128. Deletion

Deletion must propagate through relevant copies.

```text
Authoritative DB
      │
      ├── Cache
      ├── Search
      ├── Analytics
      ├── Object storage
      ├── Vector DB
      └── Derived datasets
```

A deletion API that removes one row while leaving five governed copies is incomplete.

---

# 129. Deletion Verification

For critical deletion workflows:

```text
Deletion Requested
       │
       ▼
Delete
       │
       ▼
Propagation
       │
       ▼
Verification
       │
       ▼
Evidence
```

---

# 130. Legal Hold

Where legally applicable, legal hold can override ordinary deletion schedules.

```text
Normal Retention Expired
        │
        ▼
Legal Hold Active?
    ┌───┴───┐
    ▼       ▼
   YES      NO
    │        │
Retain     Delete
```

Legal requirements must be defined by appropriate legal/privacy authority, not guessed by engineering.

---

# 131. Backup Lifecycle

Backups are copies of governed data and therefore inherit relevant:

```text
Classification
Encryption
Residency
Retention
Access
Deletion constraints
```

Backup systems are not outside data governance.

---

# 132. Backup vs Deletion

Immediate removal of an individual record from immutable backups may be technically impossible or conflict with recovery requirements.

Therefore deletion architecture must explicitly define backup handling rather than pretending backup copies do not exist.

---

# 133. Data Observability

Data systems require operational visibility across:

```text
Freshness
Volume
Schema
Quality
Distribution
Pipeline health
Lineage
```

Application infrastructure monitoring alone is insufficient.

---

# 134. Freshness Monitoring

```text
Expected update:
every 5 minutes

Last successful update:
47 minutes ago
```

should generate a meaningful data-health signal.

---

# 135. Volume Anomalies

Detect unexpected:

```text
Record count drops
Record explosions
Missing partitions
Empty batches
Unusual event rates
```

according to expected behavior.

---

# 136. Schema Anomalies

Detect unexpected:

```text
Column removal
Type changes
Nullability changes
Unknown event versions
Unexpected fields
```

before they silently corrupt downstream systems.

---

# 137. Distribution Anomalies

Some failures preserve schema and row counts while corrupting values.

Example:

```text
Typical score mean: 72
Current score mean: 3
```

Distribution monitoring can expose these failures.

---

# 138. Data Incidents

A data incident may occur even when infrastructure is fully healthy.

Examples:

```text
Stale analytics
Missing events
Incorrect transformation
Duplicate records
Broken lineage
Corrupted embeddings
Wrong reference data
```

Data incidents require ownership and incident processes.

---

# 139. Lineage-Aware Incident Analysis

```text
Bad Source Data
      │
      ▼
Lineage Graph
      │
      ├── Analytics
      ├── Search
      ├── Recommendations
      └── AI/RAG
```

Lineage allows responders to identify affected consumers quickly.

---

# 140. Data SLOs

Critical data products may define SLOs for:

```text
Freshness
Completeness
Availability
Quality
Delivery latency
```

Example:

```text
99.9% of progress events
available analytically
within 10 minutes
```

Targets must follow actual product requirements.

---

# 141. Data Product Scorecard

Example:

| Dimension          | Status |
| ------------------ | ------ |
| Owner              | ✓      |
| Contract           | ✓      |
| Classification     | ✓      |
| Lineage            | ✓      |
| Freshness SLO      | ✓      |
| Quality rules      | ✓      |
| Retention          | ✓      |
| Recovery tested    | ✓      |
| Consumer inventory | ⚠      |
| Cost allocation    | ✓      |

A scorecard exposes governance debt rather than hiding it in documentation.

---

# 142. Data Policy as Code

Machine-verifiable rules should be automated where useful.

Examples:

```text
Restricted dataset MUST have owner
Production dataset MUST declare classification
Kafka topic MUST declare retention
Data product MUST declare authoritative source
Temporary dataset MUST have expiry
AI vector collection MUST identify embedding model
```

---

# 143. Data Fitness Functions

Architecture pipelines may validate:

```text
Schema compatibility
Required metadata
Retention configuration
Sensitive-data controls
Quality thresholds
Lineage registration
Recovery requirements
```

Governance should move left without turning every change into bureaucracy.

---

# 144. FinOps and Storage Economics

ADR-073 applies throughout the data lifecycle.

Track:

```text
Database storage
Replicas
Backups
Kafka retention
Object storage
Analytics
Search indexes
Vector indexes
Data transfer
```

Data without lifecycle governance becomes permanent cost.

---

# 145. Sustainability Integration

ADR-074 applies equally.

Prefer eliminating:

```text
Unused copies
Obsolete datasets
Unnecessary replication
Repeated full processing
Orphaned vectors
Infinite telemetry/data retention
```

before optimizing the infrastructure storing them.

---

# 146. Disaster Recovery Integration

ADR-075 and ADR-076 must share state classification.

```text
AUTHORITATIVE
     │
     └── Backup / replication / PITR

DERIVED
     │
     └── Rebuild where feasible

EPHEMERAL
     │
     └── Recreate / discard
```

Recovery investment should follow data value and rebuildability.

---

# 147. Data Governance Maturity Model

```text
LEVEL 1 — FRAGMENTED

Data exists across systems with
unclear ownership and semantics.


LEVEL 2 — CATALOGUED

Important data is classified,
owned and discoverable.


LEVEL 3 — GOVERNED

Contracts, quality, lifecycle
and lineage are standardized.


LEVEL 4 — PRODUCTIZED

Data products expose measurable
quality, SLOs and platform controls.


LEVEL 5 — INTELLIGENT

Governance is increasingly automated,
lineage-aware and integrated into
applications, analytics and AI.
```

Mediverse should target **Level 4**, selectively adopting Level 5 capabilities where automation produces real operational value.

---

# 148. Data Governance Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ "The database is the documentation"
❌ Tables without owners
❌ Shared databases owned by everyone
❌ Multiple uncontrolled sources of truth
❌ Analytics systems treated as transactional authority
❌ Search indexes treated as authoritative state
❌ Redis caches treated as authoritative business records
❌ Vector databases treated as original knowledge
❌ Direct cross-service database coupling by default
❌ Breaking migrations without transition strategy
❌ Database CDC exposed as enterprise semantics automatically
❌ Database + Kafka unsafe dual writes
❌ Kafka topics without owners
❌ Events without schemas
❌ Events exposing arbitrary database internals
❌ Semantic changes hidden behind compatible data types
❌ Infinite Kafka retention by default
❌ Replay without idempotency analysis
❌ Data lakes without ownership/catalogue/lifecycle
❌ ETL success treated as data-quality proof
❌ Streaming without late-event strategy
❌ Streaming without duplicate strategy
❌ Embeddings without source provenance
❌ Mixing incompatible embedding spaces
❌ RAG retrieval treated as proof of authority
❌ Deleted documents remaining indefinitely in vector stores
❌ AI datasets without versions
❌ Evaluation data contaminated by training data
❌ Production databases cloned freely into development
❌ Calling lightly modified production records "synthetic"
❌ Sensitive data available because network connectivity exists
❌ Residency applied only to the primary database
❌ Backups excluded from classification governance
❌ Retention = forever
❌ Deletion only from the primary table
❌ Legal requirements invented by engineers
❌ Quality defined only as "pipeline succeeded"
❌ Monitoring only infrastructure and ignoring data freshness
❌ Schema monitoring without semantic governance
❌ Data incidents without owners
❌ Lineage existing only as a static architecture diagram
❌ Governance requiring manual approval for every trivial dataset
❌ Policy documents without automated controls where automation is practical
❌ Storage optimization while retaining useless data forever
```

---

# 149. ADR-076 Decision Outcome

| Area                              | Decision                                       |
| --------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| Governance model                  | Federated ownership + central standards        |
| Data organization                 | Business domains                               |
| Domain owner                      | Required                                       |
| Data steward                      | Required for governed critical domains         |
| Data products                     | Standard for important shared datasets         |
| Authoritative source              | Explicit                                       |
| System of record                  | Explicit by business concept                   |
| Operational/analytical separation | Preferred                                      |
| Derived data                      | Upstream authority required                    |
| Classification                    | Mandatory for significant data                 |
| Schema ownership                  | Explicit                                       |
| Canonical models                  | Selective, not universal                       |
| Business glossary                 | Required for critical concepts                 |
| Metadata catalogue                | Enterprise capability                          |
| Lineage                           | Required for critical data flows               |
| Column lineage                    | Risk/value based                               |
| Provenance                        | Required where material                        |
| Data contracts                    | Required for important shared interfaces       |
| Semantic compatibility            | Governed                                       |
| Event schemas                     | Governed                                       |
| Quality dimensions                | Multi-dimensional                              |
| Quality validation                | Automated where practical                      |
| Quarantine                        | Supported                                      |
| Reconciliation                    | Required where consistency matters             |
| Identifier strategy               | Domain-governed                                |
| PostgreSQL ownership              | Service/domain aligned                         |
| Cross-service SQL                 | Rejected by default                            |
| Database migrations               | Versioned and recovery-aware                   |
| CDC                               | Supported, governed                            |
| Transactional outbox              | Preferred for reliable state/event publication |
| Kafka topics                      | Governed data interfaces                       |
| Redis                             | Derived/ephemeral by default                   |
| Search indexes                    | Derived                                        |
| Object storage                    | Lifecycle governed                             |
| Data lake                         | Requirement-driven                             |
| Lakehouse                         | Requirement-driven                             |
| Batch/stream                      | Explicit semantics                             |
| Late/out-of-order data            | Explicitly handled                             |
| Vector DB                         | Governed                                       |
| Embedding provenance              | Required                                       |
| RAG source authority              | Required                                       |
| AI datasets                       | Versioned and provenance-aware                 |
| Synthetic data                    | Preferred for non-prod where suitable          |
| Production data in non-prod       | Restricted by default                          |
| Access                            | Least privilege + purpose                      |
| Residency                         | End-to-end                                     |
| Encryption                        | Classification driven                          |
| Retention                         | Explicit                                       |
| Archival                          | Lifecycle based                                |
| Deletion                          | Propagated and verifiable                      |
| Legal hold                        | Overrides ordinary deletion where applicable   |
| Backups                           | Governed data copies                           |
| Data observability                | Required for critical products                 |
| Data SLOs                         | Required where business-critical               |
| Policy-as-code                    | Preferred where measurable                     |
| FinOps                            | Integrated                                     |
| Sustainability                    | Integrated                                     |
| DR                                | Authority/rebuildability aligned               |
| Maturity target                   | Level 4                                        |
| Status                            | **Accepted**                                   |
| Priority                          | **Critical**                                   |

---
