---

# ADR-077 — Enterprise AI Governance, Responsible AI, LLMOps, Model Risk & AI Safety Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing from **Section 60 — Agent Identity**.

---

# 61. AI Evaluation Framework

No AI capability reaches production merely because its outputs "look good."

Evaluation must answer:

```text
Does it solve the intended task?
        │
        ├── Correctly?
        ├── Reliably?
        ├── Safely?
        ├── Fairly?
        ├── Within latency targets?
        ├── Within cost limits?
        └── Under adversarial conditions?
```

Evaluation requirements scale with the AI risk tier.

---

# 62. Evaluation Dimensions

Mediverse AI evaluation should consider:

```text
Task Quality
Groundedness
Factuality
Safety
Robustness
Consistency
Latency
Cost
Accessibility
Fairness
Tool Accuracy
Retrieval Quality
User Experience
```

A single aggregate score is insufficient for important systems.

---

# 63. Task-Specific Metrics

Metrics must reflect the actual task.

```text
Classification
    └── Precision / Recall / F1

Retrieval
    └── Recall@K / Precision@K / ranking

Generation
    └── Groundedness / correctness / relevance

Agent
    └── Task success / tool correctness / policy compliance
```

Using the wrong metric can make a bad system appear good.

---

# 64. Golden Evaluation Datasets

Critical AI capabilities should maintain representative evaluation datasets.

```text
Golden Dataset
      │
      ├── Normal cases
      ├── Difficult cases
      ├── Edge cases
      ├── Safety cases
      ├── Adversarial cases
      └── Historical regressions
```

---

# 65. Golden Dataset Governance

ADR-076 applies.

Evaluation datasets require:

```text
Owner
Version
Provenance
Classification
Expected outputs/criteria
Coverage
Retention
```

A random spreadsheet of prompts is not an enterprise evaluation framework.

---

# 66. Evaluation Dataset Independence

Where methodology requires independent evaluation:

```text
Training / Tuning Data
          │
          X
    Golden Evaluation
```

Contamination can produce misleading performance results.

---

# 67. Offline Evaluation

Before deployment:

```text
Candidate AI System
        │
        ▼
Evaluation Suite
        │
        ▼
Quality + Safety + Cost
        │
        ▼
Release Gate
```

Offline evaluation becomes part of AI CI/CD.

---

# 68. Evaluation Baselines

New versions should be compared against:

```text
Current production version
Previous approved version
Deterministic baseline
Human baseline where meaningful
```

A model improvement claim requires a meaningful reference point.

---

# 69. Regression Testing

Changes to any of these can cause AI regressions:

```text
Model
Prompt
RAG corpus
Chunking
Embedding model
Retriever
Tool definitions
Temperature
Context policy
Post-processing
```

Therefore AI regression testing must cover the system, not just the model.

---

# 70. LLM-as-Judge

LLMs may assist evaluation, especially at scale.

But:

```text
LLM judges LLM
      │
      ▼
Potential bias
Position bias
Model preference
Prompt sensitivity
Inconsistency
```

LLM-as-judge results must not automatically be treated as ground truth.

---

# 71. Human Evaluation

Human evaluation remains important for:

```text
Nuance
Pedagogical usefulness
Domain correctness
Ambiguous cases
Safety
User experience
```

especially for higher-risk educational and medical content.

---

# 72. Human Evaluator Guidance

Evaluators require explicit rubrics.

```text
Bad:

"Is this response good?"

Better:

Accuracy
Relevance
Groundedness
Completeness
Safety
Clarity
```

Otherwise evaluator disagreement becomes meaningless noise.

---

# 73. Inter-Rater Agreement

For subjective evaluations, Mediverse should measure evaluator consistency where appropriate.

Large disagreement may indicate:

```text
Poor rubric
Ambiguous task
Insufficient expertise
Subjective requirement
```

rather than merely "bad evaluators."

---

# 74. Hallucination Evaluation

Test whether generated claims are:

```text
Supported
Unsupported
Contradicted
Unverifiable
```

according to the task's evidence requirements.

---

# 75. Groundedness Evaluation

For RAG:

```text
Generated Claim
      │
      ▼
Retrieved Evidence
      │
 ┌────┼────┐
 ▼    ▼    ▼
Yes Partial No
```

A relevant document does not guarantee that every generated claim is grounded in it.

---

# 76. Retrieval Evaluation

RAG evaluation should separate:

```text
RETRIEVAL FAILURE

Correct evidence never retrieved

from

GENERATION FAILURE

Correct evidence retrieved
but model answered incorrectly
```

Without this separation, teams optimize the wrong component.

---

# 77. RAG Evaluation Pipeline

```text
Question
   │
   ▼
Expected Evidence
   │
   ▼
Retriever
   │
   ├── Recall@K
   ├── Ranking
   ├── Authority
   └── Freshness
          │
          ▼
         LLM
          │
          ├── Correctness
          ├── Groundedness
          └── Citation accuracy
```

---

# 78. Agent Evaluation

Agents require more than answer-quality testing.

Evaluate:

```text
Task completion
Planning behavior
Tool selection
Argument correctness
Authorization compliance
Step count
Recovery behavior
Cost
Side effects
```

---

# 79. Tool-Use Testing

For each tool:

```text
Should tool be called?
        │
        ▼
Correct tool?
        │
        ▼
Correct arguments?
        │
        ▼
Authorized?
        │
        ▼
Result interpreted correctly?
```

---

# 80. Agent Failure Scenarios

Test:

```text
Tool timeout
Tool returns malformed data
Permission denied
Partial success
Duplicate response
Network failure
Conflicting tool results
Malicious tool output
```

Agents must not assume tool success.

---

# 81. Adversarial Testing

AI systems should be tested against intentional attempts to cause failure.

Examples:

```text
Prompt injection
Jailbreak
Context poisoning
Data extraction
Tool abuse
Role confusion
Malformed inputs
Resource exhaustion
```

---

# 82. AI Red Teaming

Higher-risk capabilities require structured red-team exercises.

```text
Threat Model
     │
     ▼
Attack Scenarios
     │
     ▼
Execute
     │
     ▼
Observe Failure
     │
     ▼
Mitigate
     │
     ▼
Retest
```

---

# 83. Red-Team Findings

Findings should enter normal engineering governance:

```text
Finding
   │
   ▼
Severity
   │
   ▼
Owner
   │
   ▼
Remediation
   │
   ▼
Verification
```

A red-team report sitting in a document repository provides little protection.

---

# 84. Bias and Fairness Evaluation

Where user impact warrants it, evaluate whether system quality materially differs across relevant populations or contexts.

Metrics must be selected according to the use case.

Fairness cannot be reduced to one universal number.

---

# 85. Multilingual Evaluation

Mediverse must not assume:

```text
English quality
      =
Marathi quality
      =
Hindi quality
      =
Other language quality
```

Each supported language requires representative evaluation where AI behavior matters.

---

# 86. Translation Risk

AI-generated translation can alter:

```text
Meaning
Terminology
Medical concepts
Assessment intent
Safety information
```

Critical educational content may require domain-aware validation.

---

# 87. Accessibility Evaluation

AI-generated interfaces/content should be assessed for compatibility with accessibility requirements.

AI should not create a second, less-accessible user experience.

---

# 88. Uncertainty

Probabilistic systems inherently contain uncertainty.

The application should not convert uncertainty into false certainty through UI design.

```text
Model uncertain
      │
      ▼
UI displays:
"Definitely correct"
      │
      ▼
Bad system design
```

---

# 89. Confidence Scores

Raw model probabilities or self-reported confidence must not automatically be interpreted as calibrated real-world confidence.

Calibration must be demonstrated where confidence drives decisions.

---

# 90. Abstention

AI systems should be capable of declining when evidence or confidence is inadequate.

```text
Question
   │
   ▼
Sufficient evidence?
 ┌─┴─────┐
 ▼       ▼
YES      NO
 │        │
Answer   Abstain / escalate
```

A forced answer is often worse than no answer.

---

# 91. Content Safety

Safety controls may cover:

```text
Harmful instructions
Harassment
Sexual content
Self-harm
Violence
Illegal activity
Sensitive content
```

according to product requirements and applicable policies.

Safety controls must be tested, not merely configured.

---

# 92. Safety Layering

Do not rely on one safety mechanism.

```text
Input Controls
      │
      ▼
System Instructions
      │
      ▼
Model Safety
      │
      ▼
Output Controls
      │
      ▼
Application Rules
```

Defense in depth applies to AI.

---

# 93. AI Security Threat Model

AI threat modeling should include:

```text
Prompt injection
Model extraction
Data exfiltration
Training-data leakage
RAG poisoning
Tool abuse
Supply-chain compromise
Credential exposure
Denial-of-wallet
Resource exhaustion
```

---

# 94. Denial-of-Wallet

AI introduces a failure mode where attackers may generate excessive cost.

```text
Attacker
   │
   ▼
Expensive Requests
   │
   ▼
Tokens / GPUs / Tools
   │
   ▼
Cost Explosion
```

Rate limits and budgets become security controls as well as FinOps controls.

---

# 95. AI Supply Chain

The AI supply chain may include:

```text
Models
Tokenizers
Libraries
Containers
CUDA/runtime
Prompt packages
Embedding models
Datasets
Evaluation frameworks
```

Each dependency introduces provenance and vulnerability considerations.

---

# 96. Open-Source Model Governance

Before adopting an open-source/open-weight model, evaluate:

```text
License
Source
Provenance
Model card
Security
Known limitations
Runtime requirements
Maintenance
Community/support
```

"Free weights" does not mean free operationally or legally.

---

# 97. Model Artifact Integrity

Self-hosted model artifacts should be verified before deployment.

```text
Approved Model
     │
     ▼
Checksum / Signature
     │
     ▼
Verification
     │
     ▼
Deployment
```

---

# 98. Self-Hosted Model Governance

Self-hosting transfers responsibility to Mediverse for:

```text
Capacity
GPU infrastructure
Scaling
Patching
Security
Availability
Serving
Monitoring
Model lifecycle
```

It should not be selected solely to avoid API charges.

---

# 99. GPU Capacity Governance

GPU workloads should define:

```text
Model size
Memory requirements
Concurrency
Batching
Latency
Utilization
Scaling
Recovery
Cost
```

Idle GPU capacity can become substantial waste.

---

# 100. Model Serving

The serving layer should expose operational signals such as:

```text
Request rate
Queue depth
Time to first token
Generation latency
Tokens/sec
GPU utilization
Errors
OOM events
```

---

# 101. Fine-Tuning Governance

Fine-tuning requires explicit justification.

```text
Problem
   │
   ├── Prompt engineering enough?
   ├── RAG enough?
   ├── Tooling enough?
   │
   ▼
Fine-tuning justified?
```

Fine-tuning is not the default solution to every quality problem.

---

# 102. Training-Data Provenance

Fine-tuning datasets must identify:

```text
Origin
Ownership
License/permission
Classification
Processing
Version
Quality
```

ADR-076 governs the dataset.

---

# 103. Fine-Tuning Reproducibility

Record:

```text
Base model
Dataset version
Hyperparameters
Training code
Environment
Random seed where relevant
Resulting artifact
Evaluation results
```

---

# 104. Fine-Tuned Model Evaluation

A successful training job is not evidence of improvement.

```text
Base Model
     │
     ▼
Baseline Evaluation

Fine-Tuned Model
     │
     ▼
Same Evaluation
     │
     ▼
Compare
```

Safety regressions must be evaluated alongside quality improvements.

---

# 105. Research-to-Production Boundary

Experimentation environments may move quickly.

Production cannot inherit that looseness automatically.

```text
Research
   │
   ▼
Candidate
   │
   ▼
Evaluation
   │
   ▼
Security Review
   │
   ▼
Governance Gate
   │
   ▼
Production
```

---

# 106. Production Readiness Gate

Production AI requires, according to risk:

```text
Owner
Risk classification
Approved model
Approved data use
Evaluation evidence
Security controls
Observability
Cost limits
Rollback
Incident process
```

---

# 107. AI Release Unit

The actual AI release unit may be:

```text
Application version
+
Model version
+
Prompt version
+
Retriever version
+
Embedding version
+
Knowledge version
+
Tool configuration
```

This combination defines behavior.

---

# 108. Shadow Deployment

Candidate AI may receive production-like requests without controlling user-visible behavior.

```text
Request
   │
   ├────► Production AI ───► User
   │
   └────► Candidate AI ────► Evaluation
```

Sensitive-data policies still apply.

---

# 109. Canary Deployment

```text
Traffic
  │
  ├── 95% Current
  └──  5% Candidate
```

Observe quality, safety, latency and cost before expansion.

---

# 110. AI A/B Testing

A/B tests should have:

```text
Hypothesis
Success metric
Guardrail metrics
Population definition
Duration
Stopping criteria
```

User experimentation must respect applicable privacy and product governance.

---

# 111. Online Evaluation

Production evaluation should monitor real-world behavior that offline datasets may miss.

Signals may include:

```text
User corrections
Abandonment
Regeneration
Escalation
Tool failures
Citation failures
Safety events
```

---

# 112. Feedback Is Not Ground Truth

```text
Thumbs Up
```

does not necessarily mean:

```text
Factually Correct
```

User feedback is one signal among several.

---

# 113. Model Drift

AI quality may change because of:

```text
User behavior
Data distribution
Knowledge corpus
Provider model changes
Prompt changes
Tool changes
External world changes
```

Drift monitoring should therefore be system-aware.

---

# 114. Knowledge Drift

For educational knowledge:

```text
Source changes
      │
      ▼
RAG corpus stale
      │
      ▼
AI answers stale
```

ADR-076 freshness controls must propagate into AI observability.

---

# 115. AI Observability

AI telemetry should include appropriate:

```text
Request metadata
Model
Prompt version
Token usage
Latency
Retrieval
Tool calls
Errors
Safety events
Evaluation signals
Cost
```

without violating privacy/data-minimization requirements.

---

# 116. AI Trace

A trace may conceptually show:

```text
User Request
     │
     ▼
Prompt Build
     │
     ▼
Retrieval
     │
     ▼
Model Call
     │
     ▼
Tool Call
     │
     ▼
Model Call
     │
     ▼
Response
```

This is essential for debugging agentic systems.

---

# 117. Sensitive Trace Data

AI observability can accidentally become a secondary sensitive-data store.

Logs/traces must therefore apply:

```text
Redaction
Classification
Access controls
Retention
Encryption
```

ADR-076 applies.

---

# 118. Token Telemetry

Track:

```text
Input tokens
Output tokens
Cached tokens where relevant
Context utilization
Tokens by model
Tokens by capability
```

This supports performance and cost analysis.

---

# 119. AI Cost Attribution

ADR-073 requires attribution where practical.

```text
AI Cost
  │
  ├── Product
  ├── Feature
  ├── Environment
  ├── Model
  └── Tenant/use case
```

Without attribution, optimization becomes guesswork.

---

# 120. AI Unit Economics

Useful metrics may include:

```text
Cost per tutoring session
Cost per generated assessment
Cost per successful agent task
Cost per 1,000 AI interactions
```

Raw monthly API cost is insufficient.

---

# 121. Latency Budget

AI requests should define latency budgets.

```text
Total UX Budget
      │
      ├── Retrieval
      ├── Model queue
      ├── Time to first token
      ├── Generation
      └── Tools
```

Optimize the bottleneck rather than blindly switching models.

---

# 122. Quality–Latency–Cost Triangle

```text
                 QUALITY
                   /\
                  /  \
                 /    \
                /      \
               /________\
            COST       LATENCY
```

Model selection and routing require explicit trade-offs.

---

# 123. AI Incident Definition

AI incidents may include:

```text
Unsafe outputs
Systematic hallucinations
Data leakage
Prompt injection
Unauthorized tool actions
Severe quality regression
Unexpected provider behavior
Runaway cost
RAG poisoning
```

Infrastructure can remain perfectly healthy during an AI incident.

---

# 124. AI Incident Response

```text
Detect
  │
  ▼
Assess
  │
  ▼
Contain
  │
  ▼
Disable / Degrade / Rollback
  │
  ▼
Investigate
  │
  ▼
Correct
  │
  ▼
Re-evaluate
```

---

# 125. AI Kill Switch

Critical AI capabilities require a fast path to disable risky behavior.

```text
AI Feature
   │
   ▼
Kill Switch
 ┌─┴─────┐
 ▼       ▼
ON      OFF
```

This should not require an emergency code deployment where avoidable.

---

# 126. Granular Kill Switches

Prefer disabling:

```text
Specific model
Specific tool
Specific agent
Specific feature
Specific tenant
Specific data source
```

rather than unnecessarily shutting down the entire platform.

---

# 127. AI Rollback

Rollback may require restoring:

```text
Model
Prompt
Retriever
Embedding model
Knowledge index
Tool definitions
Routing configuration
```

Application-code rollback alone may not restore previous AI behavior.

---

# 128. Provider Outage

ADR-075 governs continuity.

Possible behavior:

```text
Primary AI unavailable
        │
        ├── Approved fallback
        ├── Smaller/local model
        └── AI-disabled mode
```

Selection depends on risk and data restrictions.

---

# 129. Provider Model Deprecation

Providers may retire models.

Therefore Mediverse needs:

```text
Deprecation monitoring
Replacement evaluation
Migration plan
Regression testing
Cutover
Rollback where possible
```

Do not wait until the provider's shutdown date.

---

# 130. LLMOps Control Plane

```text
                        LLMOps
                          │
       ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐
       ▼                  ▼                  ▼
     BUILD              RELEASE            OPERATE
       │                  │                  │
       ├─ Prompts          ├─ Evaluation      ├─ Traces
       ├─ RAG              ├─ Approval        ├─ Quality
       ├─ Models           ├─ Canary          ├─ Safety
       └─ Agents           └─ Rollback        └─ Cost
```

---

# 131. Model and Prompt Registry

Mediverse should maintain discoverable records of production:

```text
Models
Prompts
Embedding models
RAG configurations
Agent configurations
Evaluation results
```

---

# 132. Reproducibility

For a material AI response or regression investigation, teams should be able to determine as far as technically possible:

```text
Which model?
Which prompt?
Which context?
Which retrieval configuration?
Which knowledge version?
Which tools?
Which application version?
```

Perfect output reproducibility may not always be possible with external probabilistic services, but configuration provenance is still mandatory.

---

# 133. Developer Golden Path

Platform engineering should provide reusable AI patterns for:

```text
Model access
Authentication
RAG
Prompt registry
Evaluation
Tracing
Cost telemetry
Safety controls
Tool authorization
Deployment
```

This reduces teams building incompatible AI infrastructure independently.

---

# 134. AI Policy as Code

Machine-verifiable rules may include:

```text
Production AI MUST have owner
Production AI MUST declare risk tier
External model MUST be approved
Agent tool MUST declare authorization
AI capability MUST have evaluation suite
High-risk AI MUST have oversight
Production prompt MUST be versioned
AI feature MUST declare fallback behavior
```

---

# 135. AI Fitness Functions

Architecture pipelines can verify:

```text
Evaluation thresholds
Prompt version presence
Approved model list
Data-policy compatibility
Token limits
Agent step limits
Tool allowlists
Kill-switch configuration
Observability
```

---

# 136. AI Scorecard

Example:

| Control                 | Status |
| ----------------------- | ------ |
| Business owner          | ✓      |
| Risk tier               | ✓      |
| Model approved          | ✓      |
| Data use approved       | ✓      |
| Prompt versioned        | ✓      |
| Golden dataset          | ✓      |
| RAG provenance          | ✓      |
| Security testing        | ✓      |
| Cost telemetry          | ✓      |
| Kill switch             | ✓      |
| Fallback                | ✓      |
| Latest regression suite | ⚠      |

This makes AI governance debt visible.

---

# 137. AI FinOps Integration

ADR-073 applies directly.

Optimization hierarchy:

```text
Remove unnecessary AI call
        │
        ▼
Reduce context
        │
        ▼
Cache safely
        │
        ▼
Use smaller suitable model
        │
        ▼
Batch where appropriate
        │
        ▼
Optimize infrastructure
```

Do not start with GPU tuning when the application makes unnecessary model calls.

---

# 138. AI Sustainability Integration

ADR-074 applies.

Efficiency strategies include:

```text
Right-size models
Reduce redundant generation
Reduce unnecessary context
Cache appropriate outputs
Batch workloads
Avoid idle GPU capacity
Retire unused models/indexes
```

Quality and safety requirements remain primary constraints.

---

# 139. AI Disaster-Recovery Integration

ADR-075 governs:

```text
Provider outage
Model-serving outage
Vector DB loss
Embedding-index recovery
Prompt registry loss
AI configuration loss
GPU cluster loss
```

Core learning should remain available without AI where the business model permits.

---

# 140. Data-Governance Integration

ADR-076 governs:

```text
Training data
Evaluation data
Prompt data
RAG sources
Embeddings
Agent memory
AI logs
Feedback
Generated artifacts
```

AI does not create an exemption from enterprise data governance.

---

# 141. AI Governance Operating Model

```text
Enterprise Architecture
        │
        ├── Standards
        │
AI Governance
        │
        ├── Risk
        ├── Policy
        └── Approval
        │
Domain/Product
        │
        ├── Business accountability
        │
AI Platform
        │
        ├── Golden paths
        ├── Evaluation
        └── Observability
        │
Engineering
        │
        └── Implementation
```

Governance should be federated rather than centralized into a bottleneck.

---

# 142. Risk-Based Governance

Do not require the same approval process for:

```text
AI-generated UI label
```

and:

```text
AI-generated high-impact learner decision
```

Over-governance of trivial AI encourages teams to bypass governance entirely.

---

# 143. AI Governance Maturity

```text
LEVEL 1 — EXPERIMENTAL

Teams independently call models.


LEVEL 2 — INVENTORIED

Models and AI capabilities are known.


LEVEL 3 — CONTROLLED

Risk, evaluation, security and
release standards exist.


LEVEL 4 — PLATFORMIZED

LLMOps, evaluation, observability
and policy controls are standardized.


LEVEL 5 — CONTINUOUSLY ASSURED

Production behavior continuously feeds
evaluation, risk and governance.
```

Mediverse should target **Level 4**, selectively progressing high-value capabilities toward Level 5.

---

# 144. AI Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ "Use AI because the product needs AI"
❌ Using LLMs for deterministic rules
❌ Largest model by default
❌ API availability treated as model approval
❌ Model-only evaluation
❌ Prompts stored as uncontrolled strings
❌ Production prompts changed without versioning
❌ Provider "latest" aliases without change awareness
❌ Retrieved text treated as trusted instructions
❌ RAG relevance treated as authority
❌ More context assumed to mean better answers
❌ Hallucination solved by adding RAG and doing no evaluation
❌ Fabricated citations
❌ Tool request treated as authorization
❌ Agent permissions exceeding user permissions
❌ Unbounded agent loops
❌ Permanent agent memory without lifecycle governance
❌ AI self-reported confidence treated as calibrated confidence
❌ Forced answers when evidence is inadequate
❌ One safety filter treated as sufficient
❌ Red-team findings without remediation
❌ English evaluation assumed to cover every language
❌ LLM-as-judge treated as unquestionable ground truth
❌ Fine-tuning before defining the actual problem
❌ Successful fine-tuning job treated as improvement
❌ Open-weight models assumed to be free
❌ Self-hosting assumed cheaper
❌ GPU clusters without utilization governance
❌ Production release without golden evaluation
❌ Application rollback assumed to roll back AI behavior
❌ User thumbs-up treated as factual correctness
❌ Logging complete prompts regardless of sensitivity
❌ No token/cost attribution
❌ No kill switch
❌ Fallback to an unapproved provider
❌ AI provider outage taking down core learning unnecessarily
❌ AI governance applied only before launch
```

---

# 148. Cross-ADR AI Control Model

ADR-077 does not stand alone.

```text
                         ADR-077
                     AI GOVERNANCE
                           │
          ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
          ▼                ▼                ▼
       ADR-076          ADR-075          ADR-073
         DATA          RESILIENCE         FINOPS
          │                │                │
          └────────────────┼────────────────┘
                           ▼
                        ADR-074
                    SUSTAINABILITY
                           │
                           ▼
                        ADR-072
                EVOLUTIONARY GOVERNANCE
```

Therefore:

```text
AI quality without data governance
            = unreliable knowledge

AI without resilience
            = fragile capability

AI without FinOps
            = uncontrolled economics

AI without sustainability
            = unnecessary resource consumption

AI without evolutionary governance
            = architecture drift
```

| Model approval            | Required                                      |

# ADR-078 — Enterprise Developer Platform, Internal Developer Platform, Platform Engineering & Golden Path Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Kafka Self-Service**.

---

# 61. Redis & Cache Self-Service

Teams should request caching as a governed capability rather than manually creating unmanaged Redis infrastructure.

```text
Service
   │
   ▼
Cache Requirement
   │
   ▼
Platform
   │
   ├── Provision
   ├── Credentials
   ├── Network access
   ├── Monitoring
   ├── Backup where required
   └── Catalogue registration
```

ADR-076 remains authoritative: Redis is normally derived or ephemeral state, not the system of record.

---

# 62. Cache Profiles

The platform may expose profiles such as:

```text
cache-small
cache-standard
cache-high-throughput
cache-ha
```

rather than exposing every infrastructure parameter.

Advanced configuration remains available through controlled escape hatches.

---

# 63. Object Storage Self-Service

Applications requiring object storage should declare:

```text
Purpose
Classification
Expected size
Retention
Access pattern
Public/private requirement
Recovery requirement
```

The platform translates this into governed storage.

---

# 64. Object Storage Lifecycle

Provisioning should automatically attach appropriate:

```text
Encryption
Access policy
Versioning
Lifecycle
Retention
Monitoring
Cost attribution
Ownership metadata
```

Creating a bucket is the easy part. Governing it for years is the actual platform responsibility.

---

# 65. DNS Self-Service

Applications should request DNS through a controlled interface.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
DNS Request
    │
    ▼
Ownership Validation
    │
    ▼
DNS Automation
    │
    ▼
Record
```

Manual production DNS changes should be exceptional.

---

# 66. Certificate Automation

TLS certificate lifecycle should be automated.

```text
Domain
  │
  ▼
Certificate Request
  │
  ▼
Validation
  │
  ▼
Issue
  │
  ▼
Deploy
  │
  ▼
Renew Automatically
```

Certificate expiry should not depend on calendar reminders.

---

# 67. Secrets Self-Service

Developers should reference secrets rather than manually distribute them.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
Secret Reference
    │
    ▼
Secrets Platform
    │
    ▼
Runtime Injection
```

Secrets must not be embedded in:

```text
Git
Docker images
Helm values committed in plaintext
Application logs
CI output
```

---

# 68. Secret Ownership

Every important secret should have:

```text
Owner
Purpose
Consumers
Rotation policy
Environment
Classification
```

Anonymous credentials inevitably become permanent credentials.

---

# 69. Secret Rotation

The platform should automate rotation where practical.

```text
Current Credential
       │
       ▼
Create New
       │
       ▼
Distribute
       │
       ▼
Validate
       │
       ▼
Revoke Old
```

Applications should tolerate credential rotation without unnecessary downtime.

---

# 70. Configuration Management

Configuration and secrets must remain conceptually separate.

```text
CONFIGURATION

LOG_LEVEL=INFO
FEATURE_X=true

SECRETS

DB_PASSWORD=...
API_TOKEN=...
```

Both require lifecycle management, but their security properties differ.

---

# 71. Configuration Versioning

Production configuration should be traceable.

For material incidents, teams should be able to answer:

```text
What configuration was active?
Who changed it?
When?
Through which deployment?
```

---

# 72. Observability by Default

Every golden-path workload should automatically receive baseline observability.

```text
Service
  │
  ├── Logs
  ├── Metrics
  ├── Traces
  ├── Health
  └── Runtime metadata
```

Observability should not be an optional task developers remember three days before production.

---

# 73. OpenTelemetry Golden Path

OpenTelemetry should provide standardized instrumentation where appropriate.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
OpenTelemetry
    │
    ├── Traces
    ├── Metrics
    └── Context propagation
```

Application teams should not independently invent telemetry conventions.

---

# 74. Trace Context Propagation

Distributed requests should preserve trace context.

```text
Frontend
   │
   ▼
Gateway
   │
   ▼
Service A
   │
   ▼
Kafka
   │
   ▼
Service B
```

Without correlation, distributed debugging becomes substantially harder.

---

# 75. Structured Logging

Golden paths should provide structured logging.

Conceptually:

```json
{
  "service": "assessment-service",
  "environment": "uat1",
  "traceId": "...",
  "level": "ERROR",
  "event": "assessment_submission_failed"
}
```

Sensitive information must not be logged merely because structured logging makes it convenient.

---

# 76. Standard Service Metrics

Services should automatically expose baseline signals such as:

```text
Request rate
Error rate
Latency
CPU
Memory
Restarts
Dependency failures
JVM/runtime health
```

Domain-specific metrics remain the responsibility of the product team.

---

# 77. Dashboard Provisioning

A new service should receive a baseline dashboard automatically.

```text
Service Created
      │
      ▼
Telemetry Registered
      │
      ▼
Dashboard Generated
```

Developers then extend it with business-specific observability.

---

# 78. Alerting Templates

Golden paths should provide sensible alerts for:

```text
Availability
Error rate
Latency
Crash loops
Resource saturation
Dependency failure
SLO burn
```

but avoid generating hundreds of low-value alerts automatically.

---

# 79. Alert Quality

A platform that automatically creates noisy alerts is not helping.

An alert should generally indicate:

```text
User impact
Imminent user impact
Actionable infrastructure risk
SLO threat
```

not merely that a metric crossed an arbitrary threshold.

---

# 80. SLO Templates

Services should declare service criticality.

```text
Service Tier
     │
     ▼
Suggested SLO Profile
     │
     ├── Availability
     ├── Latency
     └── Error budget
```

Teams refine targets according to business requirements.

---

# 81. Runbook Integration

Operational alerts should link to relevant:

```text
Runbook
Dashboard
Logs
Traces
Service owner
Dependency information
```

An alert without diagnostic context unnecessarily increases MTTR.

---

# 82. Security by Default

Golden paths must automatically embed baseline security controls.

```text
Repository
   │
   ├── Dependency scanning
   ├── Secret scanning
   ├── SAST
   └── Branch protection

Artifact
   │
   ├── Vulnerability scanning
   ├── SBOM
   └── Signing

Runtime
   │
   ├── Non-root
   ├── RBAC
   ├── Network controls
   └── Policy
```

---

# 83. Policy as Code

Architecture/security policies that are machine-verifiable should be automated.

Examples:

```text
Container MUST NOT run privileged
Production workload MUST declare owner
Production workload MUST define resources
Public service MUST use approved ingress
Image MUST come from approved registry
```

---

# 84. Policy Enforcement Layers

Policies may operate at:

```text
IDE / local
      │
      ▼
Pull Request
      │
      ▼
CI
      │
      ▼
GitOps
      │
      ▼
Admission Control
      │
      ▼
Runtime
```

Earlier feedback is preferable to late rejection.

---

# 85. Terraform Module Catalogue

Infrastructure teams should publish supported modules.

Examples:

```text
PostgreSQL
Redis
Object Storage
DNS
Network
Kubernetes
Observability
IAM
```

Modules should encode organizational defaults.

---

# 86. Terraform Module Versioning

Infrastructure modules require semantic lifecycle management.

```text
postgres-module
      │
      ├── v1
      ├── v2
      └── v3
```

Consumers must not be forced into uncontrolled breaking upgrades.

---

# 87. Self-Service Infrastructure

Platform workflows should invoke approved infrastructure modules.

```text
Developer Intent
      │
      ▼
Platform API
      │
      ▼
Policy
      │
      ▼
Terraform
      │
      ▼
Cloud Infrastructure
```

Developers consume a capability rather than becoming infrastructure specialists for routine needs.

---

# 88. Crossplane / Operator Decision

Kubernetes-native provisioning technologies such as Crossplane or custom operators should be adopted only where their reconciliation model creates clear value.

```text
Need continuous reconciliation?
          │
      ┌───┴───┐
      ▼       ▼
     YES      NO
      │        │
Operator/    Terraform may
Crossplane   remain simpler
```

Adding another control plane without a concrete need is rejected.

---

# 89. Platform Resource API

The IDP may expose higher-level resources such as:

```yaml
apiVersion: platform.mediverse.io/v1
kind: Database
metadata:
  name: assessment-db

spec:
  engine: postgres
  profile: standard
  criticality: high
```

The platform determines implementation details.

---

# 90. Ephemeral Environments

Short-lived environments can support:

```text
Pull requests
Integration testing
Demonstrations
Experiments
```

when their value justifies their infrastructure cost.

---

# 91. Preview Environment

```text
Pull Request
    │
    ▼
Build
    │
    ▼
Preview Environment
    │
    ▼
Test / Review
    │
    ▼
PR Closed
    │
    ▼
Destroy
```

Lifecycle automation is mandatory.

---

# 92. Environment TTL

Ephemeral environments should have expiration.

```text
Created
   │
   ▼
TTL
   │
   ▼
Still required?
 ┌─┴───┐
 ▼     ▼
YES    NO
 │      │
Extend Destroy
```

Otherwise "ephemeral" environments become permanent cost.

---

# 93. Developer Sandbox

A sandbox should provide freedom within controlled boundaries.

```text
Developer
    │
    ▼
Sandbox
    │
    ├── Quotas
    ├── Restricted data
    ├── Restricted network
    ├── TTL
    └── Cost limits
```

---

# 94. Test Data Integration

ADR-076 should be integrated into platform workflows.

Non-production environments should default toward:

```text
Synthetic data
Masked data
Generated fixtures
Approved test datasets
```

rather than unrestricted production copies.

---

# 95. API Catalogue

The developer portal should expose discoverable APIs.

For each API:

```text
Owner
Purpose
Version
OpenAPI definition
Authentication
Consumers
Lifecycle
Documentation
```

---

# 96. API Discovery

Instead of:

```text
Developer
   │
   ▼
Ask Slack:
"Does anyone know the enrollment API?"
```

prefer:

```text
Developer Portal
      │
      ▼
Search "Enrollment"
      │
      ▼
API + Docs + Owner
```

---

# 97. Event Catalogue

Kafka events should also be discoverable.

```text
Topic
Event schema
Producer
Consumers
Owner
Retention
Classification
Documentation
```

ADR-076 event governance becomes visible to developers.

---

# 98. Data Product Catalogue

Governed data products should appear alongside software components.

```text
Software
APIs
Events
Datasets
```

should be navigable through a coherent developer experience.

---

# 99. AI Capability Catalogue

ADR-077 capabilities should be registered.

The catalogue may expose:

```text
AI capability
Owner
Risk tier
Model
RAG source
Evaluation status
Deployment
Documentation
```

---

# 100. Unified Catalogue

The long-term goal is not five disconnected catalogues.

```text
                     DOMAIN
                        │
                        ▼
                      SYSTEM
                        │
       ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
       ▼                ▼                ▼
    SERVICES           DATA              AI
       │                │                │
       ├── APIs          ├── Products     ├── Models
       └── Events        └── Stores       └── Agents
```

---

# 101. TechDocs

Documentation should live close to engineering ownership and be rendered through the platform where useful.

```text
Repository
    │
    ▼
Docs as Code
    │
    ▼
Developer Portal
```

---

# 102. Documentation Ownership

Documentation without ownership becomes stale.

Important documentation should inherit component ownership wherever possible.

---

# 103. ADR Discovery

Architecture decisions should be discoverable from relevant components.

```text
assessment-service
      │
      ├── ADR-076 Data Governance
      ├── ADR-077 AI Governance
      └── ADR-078 Platform Standard
```

Developers should not need to search an unrelated document repository manually.

---

# 104. Dependency Graph

The catalogue should increasingly expose relationships.

```text
Frontend
   │
   ▼
Gateway
   │
   ▼
Assessment Service
   │
   ├── PostgreSQL
   ├── Kafka
   └── Redis
          │
          ▼
     Progress Service
```

---

# 105. Dependency Impact

Dependency visibility supports questions such as:

```text
"If Kafka cluster X fails,
which systems are affected?"

"If assessment-service changes,
who consumes it?"
```

This materially improves incident response and change planning.

---

# 106. On-Call Integration

Production components should link to operational ownership.

```text
Service
  │
  ▼
Owning Team
  │
  ▼
On-call / Escalation
```

The catalogue should not stop at repository ownership.

---

# 107. Service Scorecards

The platform should evaluate baseline engineering health.

Potential dimensions:

```text
Owner
Documentation
CI
Security
Observability
SLO
Runbook
Dependencies
Recovery
Cost allocation
```

---

# 108. Scorecards Are Not Vanity Rankings

Scorecards should identify actionable engineering debt.

They must not become simplistic team leaderboards that incentivize gaming metrics.

---

# 109. Production Readiness Scorecard

Before production:

| Control             |      Required |
| ------------------- | ------------: |
| Owner               |             ✓ |
| CI/CD               |             ✓ |
| Security scans      |             ✓ |
| Resource limits     |             ✓ |
| Health probes       |             ✓ |
| Logs                |             ✓ |
| Metrics             |             ✓ |
| Dashboard           |             ✓ |
| Alerts              |             ✓ |
| SLO                 |    Risk-based |
| Runbook             |             ✓ |
| Backup/recovery     |   If stateful |
| Data classification | If applicable |
| Cost ownership      |             ✓ |

---

# 110. Cost Visibility

ADR-073 should surface directly in developer workflows.

Developers should be able to see:

```text
Service cost
Environment cost
Database cost
Storage cost
AI cost
Cost trend
```

without becoming cloud-billing experts.

---

# 111. Cost Before Provisioning

Self-service should expose approximate economic consequences.

```text
Request:
High-availability PostgreSQL

Estimated profile:
$$$$

Alternative:
Standard PostgreSQL
$$
```

Developers should make informed choices before infrastructure exists.

---

# 112. Sustainability Visibility

ADR-074 should expose relevant resource-efficiency signals.

Potential examples:

```text
Idle environments
Low-utilization workloads
Oversized requests
Unused storage
Idle GPU capacity
```

The objective is actionable efficiency, not decorative carbon dashboards.

---

# 113. DORA Metrics

The platform should help measure:

```text
Deployment frequency
Lead time for changes
Change failure rate
Recovery time
```

but metrics must be interpreted in context.

---

# 114. DORA Metrics Are Not Individual KPIs

Using delivery metrics to rank individual developers creates bad incentives and corrupts the data.

They should primarily support system and team-level improvement.

---

# 115. Developer Experience Metrics

Platform success should also measure:

```text
Time to first commit
Time to first deployment
Environment provisioning time
CI duration
Deployment duration
Developer satisfaction
Documentation discoverability
Platform support demand
```

---

# 116. Platform Telemetry

The platform itself requires product analytics.

```text
Which golden paths are used?
Where do workflows fail?
Which steps are slow?
Which templates are avoided?
Which escape hatches are common?
```

Escape-hatch frequency is particularly valuable architectural feedback.

---

# 117. Platform SLOs

The IDP should define SLOs for critical capabilities.

Examples:

```text
Service creation availability
Deployment pipeline availability
Provisioning latency
Portal availability
GitOps reconciliation
Artifact availability
```

A platform that product teams depend on is itself a production system.

---

# 118. Portal, CLI and API

No single interface should become mandatory for every workflow.

```text
                 PLATFORM API
                     │
          ┌──────────┼──────────┐
          ▼          ▼          ▼
        PORTAL      CLI       AUTOMATION
```

The API/control plane should provide the durable foundation.

---

# 119. Developer Portal

The portal is optimized for:

```text
Discovery
Service creation
Documentation
Status
Ownership
Scorecards
Common self-service
```

---

# 120. Platform CLI

The CLI is useful for:

```text
Developer automation
Local workflows
Bootstrap
Diagnostics
Advanced operations
```

It should use the same platform capabilities rather than implementing a second platform.

---

# 121. Platform API

A stable platform API enables:

```text
Portal
CLI
GitOps
CI/CD
Automation
External integrations
```

This reduces UI-specific coupling.

---

# 122. Backstage Decision Framework

[Backstage](https://backstage.io/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) is a strong candidate when Mediverse requires an extensible developer portal with a software catalogue, templates, documentation and plugin ecosystem.

But adopting Backstage does **not** automatically create an IDP.

```text
Backstage
    =
Portal Framework

Backstage
    ≠
Complete Platform
```

The underlying automation, APIs, ownership model and platform product still have to exist.

---

# 123. Backstage Adoption Decision

Adopt it if:

```text
Catalogue requirements are substantial
Plugin ecosystem provides leverage
TechDocs is useful
Templates align with workflows
Team can operate/customize it
```

Do not adopt it merely because "platform engineering uses Backstage."

---

# 124. GitOps as Platform Interface

Some advanced users may interact through declarative Git.

```text
Platform Resource
      │
      ▼
Git
      │
      ▼
Review
      │
      ▼
Reconciliation
```

Portal and GitOps interfaces should converge on the same underlying control model.

---

# 125. Escape Hatches

Golden paths must support legitimate exceptions.

```text
Golden Path
    │
    ▼
Requirement unsupported?
   ┌─┴────┐
   ▼      ▼
  NO     YES
   │      │
Use      Escape Hatch
Path       │
           ▼
       Document Reason
```

---

# 126. Exception Governance

Exceptions should record:

```text
Reason
Owner
Risk
Scope
Approver where required
Expiry/review date
Migration possibility
```

Permanent undocumented exceptions become shadow architecture.

---

# 127. Escape-Hatch Feedback Loop

Repeated exceptions indicate a platform problem.

```text
Same Escape Hatch
used 20 times
      │
      ▼
Not exceptional anymore
      │
      ▼
Platform capability candidate
```

---

# 128. Platform Versioning

Platform interfaces require versioning.

This includes:

```text
Templates
APIs
Terraform modules
Helm charts
CI workflows
Policies
Custom resources
```

---

# 129. Compatibility

Platform teams must consider backward compatibility for existing consumers.

A centralized platform can create a very large blast radius if it makes uncontrolled breaking changes.

---

# 130. Template Migration

When a template improves:

```text
Template v3
    │
    ▼
Existing v1 Services
    │
    ▼
Automated Analysis
    │
    ▼
Migration PR
```

The objective is continuous convergence, not permanent generation-time divergence.

---

# 131. Platform Deprecation

Deprecated capabilities require:

```text
Announcement
Replacement
Migration guidance
Timeline
Telemetry
Support
Retirement
```

Silent removal is unacceptable.

---

# 132. Breaking Platform Changes

Breaking changes require stronger rollout discipline because hundreds of services may depend on the platform.

Prefer:

```text
Introduce new version
      │
      ▼
Canary consumers
      │
      ▼
Migration
      │
      ▼
Measure
      │
      ▼
Retire old version
```

---

# 133. Platform Security Boundary

The IDP may hold substantial privilege.

It may be capable of creating:

```text
Repositories
Infrastructure
Credentials
Deployments
DNS
Databases
Permissions
```

Therefore compromise of the platform can have enterprise-wide consequences.

---

# 134. Platform Least Privilege

The platform should not operate as one universal administrator identity.

Prefer scoped identities for:

```text
Provisioning
Deployment
DNS
Secrets
Repository automation
Catalogue
```

with explicit authorization boundaries.

---

# 135. Platform Auditability

Sensitive platform actions should answer:

```text
Who requested it?
Which workflow?
Which identity executed it?
What changed?
When?
Was approval required?
```

---

# 136. Multi-Cluster Abstraction

Product teams should generally consume:

```text
Environment / workload capability
```

rather than hard-coding unnecessary cluster-specific assumptions.

The platform may map workloads to clusters according to policy.

---

# 137. Multi-Cloud Abstraction

Do not promise perfect cloud portability.

```text
"One abstraction hides every cloud"
```

usually degenerates into the lowest common denominator.

Abstract stable organizational capabilities, not every provider-specific feature.

---

# 138. Platform Team Topology

A possible model:

```text
                    PLATFORM ORGANIZATION
                            │
          ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
          ▼                 ▼                 ▼
     Developer          Runtime           Infrastructure
     Experience         Platform            Platform
          │                 │                 │
          └─────────────────┼─────────────────┘
                            ▼
                       Product Teams
```

Exact topology should follow organizational scale.

---

# 139. Enabling Teams

Specialists may temporarily help teams adopt:

```text
Kubernetes
Observability
Security
Data
AI
Platform capabilities
```

The objective is capability transfer, not permanent dependency.

---

# 140. Platform Product Management

The platform backlog should be prioritized using:

```text
Developer pain
Business impact
Adoption
Risk reduction
Support volume
Delivery friction
Cost
Strategic architecture
```

Platform roadmaps should not be driven only by what platform engineers find technically interesting.

---

# 141. Platform Adoption

Mandating platform usage before it is useful is a bad strategy.

The preferred path should win because it provides:

```text
Faster delivery
Less boilerplate
Better reliability
Better security
Better visibility
Less operational work
```

---

# 142. Measuring Platform Success

A successful platform should improve outcomes such as:

```text
↓ onboarding time
↓ provisioning time
↓ deployment friction
↓ duplicated infrastructure code
↓ security misconfiguration
↓ support tickets
↓ cognitive load

↑ deployment frequency
↑ standard compliance
↑ service ownership visibility
↑ developer satisfaction
↑ operational consistency
```

---

# 143. Platform Maturity Model

```text
LEVEL 1 — MANUAL

Teams manually assemble
infrastructure and pipelines.


LEVEL 2 — STANDARDIZED

Templates, modules and
documentation exist.


LEVEL 3 — SELF-SERVICE

Common capabilities are
automated behind golden paths.


LEVEL 4 — PRODUCTIZED

Portal, API, catalogue, scorecards,
SLOs and platform product management
operate coherently.


LEVEL 5 — ADAPTIVE

Platform telemetry, policy,
automated migrations and developer
feedback continuously evolve
the paved roads.
```

Mediverse should target **Level 4**, selectively progressing toward Level 5.

---

# 144. Platform Engineering Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ Platform engineering = renamed DevOps team
❌ IDP = Kubernetes dashboard
❌ IDP = Backstage installation
❌ Platform team as ticket queue
❌ Self-service requiring manual approval everywhere
❌ Developers writing identical Kubernetes YAML repeatedly
❌ 100 copied Jenkinsfiles
❌ 100 independently maintained Helm charts
❌ Infrastructure modules without owners
❌ Golden paths that cannot be escaped
❌ Escape hatches without governance
❌ Hiding infrastructure so completely developers cannot debug it
❌ Requiring every developer to become a Kubernetes expert
❌ Requiring no developer to understand Kubernetes at all
❌ Service creation without ownership metadata
❌ Repositories without CODEOWNERS
❌ Production components absent from the catalogue
❌ Manual observability onboarding
❌ Dashboards without useful signals
❌ Alert generation without alert quality
❌ Secrets in Git
❌ Permanent credentials by default
❌ Manual certificate renewal
❌ Uncontrolled production DNS
❌ Production data copied freely into preview environments
❌ Ephemeral environments without TTL
❌ Self-service infrastructure without cost visibility
❌ DORA metrics used to rank developers
❌ Scorecards used as vanity leaderboards
❌ Portal as the only platform interface
❌ Platform UI containing business logic unavailable through APIs
❌ Perfect multi-cloud abstraction promises
❌ Template scaffolding with no migration strategy
❌ Platform breaking changes without consumer migration
❌ Platform administrator identity with unlimited privileges
❌ Platform roadmap driven entirely by technical novelty
❌ Mandating a bad platform to improve "adoption"
```

---

# 148. Cross-ADR Platform Control Model

ADR-078 operationalizes previous architecture decisions.

```text
                         ADR-078
                    DEVELOPER PLATFORM
                           │
       ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐
       ▼                   ▼                   ▼
    GOLDEN PATH        SELF-SERVICE         CATALOGUE
       │                   │                   │
       └───────────────────┼───────────────────┘
                           ▼
                      GUARDRAILS
                           │
       ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐
       ▼                   ▼                   ▼
    ADR-077             ADR-076             ADR-075
       AI                 DATA             RESILIENCE
       │                   │                   │
       └───────────────────┼───────────────────┘
                           ▼
                       ADR-073
                        FINOPS
                           │
                           ▼
                       ADR-074
                   SUSTAINABILITY
                           │
                           ▼
                       ADR-072
               EVOLUTIONARY GOVERNANCE
```

The important architectural shift is:

```text
BEFORE

Architecture Document
       │
       ▼
Developer reads it
       │
       ▼
Developer manually implements it


AFTER

Architecture Decision
       │
       ▼
Platform Capability
       │
       ▼
Golden Path
       │
       ▼
Automated Guardrail
       │
       ▼
Developer consumes it
```

That is the difference between documented architecture and **executable architecture**.

# 150. Final Mediverse Internal Developer Platform Reference Architecture

```text
                              MEDIVERSE ENGINEERS
                                      │
                 ┌────────────────────┼────────────────────┐
                 ▼                    ▼                    ▼
           DEVELOPER PORTAL          CLI                 GIT
                 │                    │                    │
```

---

# ADR-079 — Enterprise Testing Architecture, Quality Engineering, Test Automation & Continuous Verification Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing from **Section 60 — Performance Regression**.

---

# 61. Capacity Validation

Performance testing must determine not merely whether Mediverse is "fast," but how much workload the system can safely sustain.

```text
Increasing Load
      │
      ▼
Application
      │
      ▼
Throughput
      │
      ├── Healthy
      ├── Saturating
      └── Failure
```

Capacity testing should establish:

```text
Maximum sustainable throughput
Concurrency limits
Resource saturation point
Database limits
Queue limits
External dependency limits
Recovery characteristics
```

---

# 62. Capacity Is End-to-End

A service capable of processing:

```text
10,000 requests/sec
```

is irrelevant if its database safely handles only:

```text
1,500 requests/sec
```

Capacity must consider the entire critical request path.

---

# 63. Capacity Headroom

Production should not normally operate continuously at its demonstrated maximum.

```text
Tested Capacity
      │
      ├────────────── 100%
      │
Safe Operating Range
      ├────────────── 60–80%
      │
Expected Load
```

Exact headroom depends on workload volatility and scaling behavior.

---

# 64. Autoscaling Verification

Autoscaling configuration must be tested.

```text
Load ↑
  │
  ▼
Metric ↑
  │
  ▼
Autoscaler
  │
  ▼
Replicas ↑
  │
  ▼
Capacity ↑
```

A configured HPA is not evidence that scaling works correctly.

---

# 65. Scale-Up Testing

Verify:

```text
Trigger threshold
Scale-up delay
Pod startup
Readiness
Load distribution
Dependency capacity
Stabilization
```

Fast application scaling can simply move the bottleneck to PostgreSQL, Kafka or another dependency.

---

# 66. Scale-Down Testing

Scale-down can introduce failures through:

```text
In-flight request termination
Consumer rebalancing
Connection churn
Cache loss
Long-running job interruption
```

Therefore scaling down requires verification as well.

---

# 67. Resource-Limit Testing

Kubernetes resource requests and limits should be validated against realistic workload.

```text
Too Low
  │
  ├── CPU throttling
  ├── OOMKilled
  └── instability

Too High
  │
  ├── poor utilization
  └── unnecessary cost
```

---

# 68. Memory Pressure Testing

Applications should be tested under realistic memory pressure.

Observe:

```text
Heap
GC behavior
Native memory
Container memory
OOM behavior
Recovery
```

JVM heap size alone does not represent complete container memory usage.

---

# 69. CPU Saturation Testing

Verify behavior when CPU approaches saturation.

```text
CPU ↑
 │
 ▼
Latency ↑
 │
 ▼
Timeouts ↑
 │
 ▼
Retries ↑
 │
 ▼
Potential cascading failure
```

---

# 70. Stress Testing

Stress tests intentionally exceed normal operating capacity.

Their purpose is to discover:

```text
Failure boundary
Failure mode
Blast radius
Protection behavior
Recovery behavior
```

---

# 71. Graceful Degradation

When overloaded, the system should preferably:

```text
Reject controlled work
Throttle
Queue within bounds
Disable optional features
Return explicit errors
```

rather than fail unpredictably.

---

# 72. Load Shedding Verification

If load shedding exists:

```text
Incoming Traffic
       │
       ▼
Capacity Guard
    ┌──┴───┐
    ▼      ▼
 ACCEPT   REJECT
```

tests should verify which traffic is rejected and whether critical operations remain protected.

---

# 73. Spike Testing

Sudden demand must be tested separately from gradual load.

```text
Traffic
   │
   │             █████████
   │             █████████
   │    ███      █████████
   └──────────────────────► Time
```

Autoscaling may react too slowly to abrupt spikes.

---

# 74. Soak Testing

Soak tests run representative workload for extended periods.

They detect:

```text
Memory leaks
Connection leaks
Thread leaks
Queue growth
Disk growth
Cache degradation
Performance drift
```

Short load tests frequently miss these failures.

---

# 75. Resilience Testing

Resilience testing verifies system behavior when dependencies fail.

```text
Service A
   │
   ▼
Service B
   │
   X
Failure
```

The important question becomes:

> What does Service A do next?

---

# 76. Dependency Failure Testing

Test scenarios should include:

```text
Connection refused
Timeout
Slow dependency
HTTP 5xx
Malformed response
Partial response
Authentication failure
Rate limiting
Network interruption
```

---

# 77. Timeout Verification

Every remote dependency should have intentional timeout behavior.

```text
Request
   │
   ▼
Dependency
   │
   X
No Response
   │
   ▼
Timeout
```

Tests should verify that requests do not wait indefinitely.

---

# 78. Retry Verification

Retries should be tested for:

```text
Retryable failures
Non-retryable failures
Backoff
Jitter
Maximum attempts
Idempotency
```

Uncontrolled retries amplify incidents.

---

# 79. Retry Storm

```text
Dependency slows
      │
      ▼
Requests timeout
      │
      ▼
Every caller retries
      │
      ▼
Traffic multiplies
      │
      ▼
Dependency collapses
```

Resilience tests must verify retry amplification risk.

---

# 80. Circuit-Breaker Verification

Where circuit breakers are used:

```text
Failures
   │
   ▼
Threshold
   │
   ▼
OPEN
   │
   ▼
Reject quickly
   │
   ▼
HALF OPEN
   │
   ▼
Probe
   │
   ▼
CLOSE / OPEN
```

Every transition should be testable and observable.

---

# 81. Bulkhead Verification

Critical workloads may require isolation.

```text
Workload A ──► Pool A

Workload B ──► Pool B
```

Failure or saturation in one workload should not unnecessarily exhaust all resources.

---

# 82. Chaos Engineering

Chaos engineering introduces controlled failure to validate resilience assumptions.

```text
Hypothesis
    │
    ▼
Inject Failure
    │
    ▼
Observe
    │
    ▼
Steady State Maintained?
```

Chaos is experimentation, not random destruction.

---

# 83. Chaos Preconditions

Chaos experiments require:

```text
Clear hypothesis
Defined blast radius
Observability
Abort criteria
Responsible owner
Recovery path
```

Running random pod deletions and calling it chaos engineering is rejected.

---

# 84. Kubernetes Failure Testing

Useful scenarios may include:

```text
Pod termination
Node loss
Network interruption
DNS failure
Resource pressure
Persistent-volume issue
Ingress disruption
```

according to system criticality.

---

# 85. Disaster-Recovery Testing

ADR-075 recovery assumptions must be exercised.

```text
Failure
   │
   ▼
Recovery Procedure
   │
   ▼
Restore
   │
   ▼
Validate
   │
   ▼
RTO/RPO achieved?
```

A backup that has never been restored is not demonstrated recovery capability.

---

# 86. Security Testing Strategy

Security verification must span the lifecycle.

```text
CODE
 │
 ├── SAST
 ├── Secret scanning
 └── SCA
 │
 ▼
ARTIFACT
 │
 └── Container scanning
 │
 ▼
RUNNING SYSTEM
 │
 ├── DAST
 ├── API testing
 └── Penetration testing
```

---

# 87. SAST

Static Application Security Testing identifies relevant code-level weaknesses before runtime.

It should be integrated into CI with risk-based severity handling.

---

# 88. SAST Noise

Blocking every finding regardless of context creates alert fatigue.

Findings should consider:

```text
Severity
Exploitability
Reachability
Context
Compensating controls
```

where tooling and process permit.

---

# 89. Software Composition Analysis

SCA should identify vulnerable third-party dependencies.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
Dependencies
    │
    ▼
Known Vulnerabilities
```

ADR-078's SBOM capability strengthens this process.

---

# 90. Dependency Update Verification

Updating a vulnerable dependency can itself introduce regressions.

Therefore:

```text
Security Update
      │
      ▼
Build
      │
      ▼
Regression Suite
      │
      ▼
Release
```

---

# 91. Secret Scanning

Repositories and CI should detect likely exposed credentials.

Detection must be paired with remediation.

If a real secret was committed, deleting the line is insufficient—the credential may need rotation.

---

# 92. Container Security Testing

Container verification should cover:

```text
Known vulnerabilities
Approved base image
User privileges
Unexpected packages
Secrets
Artifact provenance
Configuration
```

---

# 93. DAST

Dynamic Application Security Testing can probe running applications for runtime weaknesses.

It complements rather than replaces SAST.

---

# 94. API Security Testing

APIs require explicit verification of:

```text
Authentication
Authorization
Object-level authorization
Input validation
Rate limits
Sensitive-data exposure
Mass assignment
Error leakage
```

---

# 95. Authorization Matrix Testing

Security-sensitive APIs should test roles against operations.

| Role     | Read |  Create |  Update |  Delete |
| -------- | ---: | ------: | ------: | ------: |
| Student  |    ✓ | Limited | Limited |       ✗ |
| Lecturer |    ✓ |       ✓ |       ✓ | Limited |
| Admin    |    ✓ |       ✓ |       ✓ |       ✓ |

The actual matrix is domain-specific and should be encoded in automated tests.

---

# 96. Negative Security Tests

Do not test only:

```text
Authorized user succeeds.
```

Also test:

```text
Anonymous user fails.
Wrong role fails.
Cross-tenant access fails.
Expired token fails.
Tampered token fails.
```

---

# 97. Penetration Testing

Risk-appropriate systems should receive human-led penetration testing.

Automated scanners cannot replace adversarial reasoning.

---

# 98. Infrastructure Testing

Infrastructure code is production code.

Terraform verification should include appropriate:

```text
Formatting
Validation
Static analysis
Policy checks
Plan inspection
Module tests
Integration tests
```

---

# 99. Terraform Plan Verification

CI should make infrastructure changes visible before application.

```text
Terraform Change
      │
      ▼
Plan
      │
      ▼
Policy / Review
      │
      ▼
Apply
```

---

# 100. Helm Testing

Helm charts should verify:

```text
Template rendering
Required values
Schema validation
Golden defaults
Upgrade behavior
Policy compliance
```

---

# 101. Kubernetes Manifest Testing

Rendered manifests should be checked for required organizational controls.

Examples:

```text
Resource requests
Resource limits
Probes
Security context
Labels
Ownership
Approved image
```

---

# 102. Policy Tests

ADR-078 policy-as-code rules themselves require tests.

```text
Policy
  │
  ├── Allowed fixture → PASS
  └── Forbidden fixture → FAIL
```

A broken policy engine can either block everything or protect nothing.

---

# 103. GitOps Verification

GitOps tests should verify:

```text
Repository structure
Manifest validity
Environment overlays
Policy compliance
Argo CD rendering
Dependency references
```

before merge where practical.

---

# 104. Post-Deployment Verification

A successful Argo CD sync is not equivalent to a healthy application.

```text
Git Sync
   │
   ▼
Resources Created
   │
   ▼
Application Ready?
   │
   ▼
Critical Function Works?
```

---

# 105. Data Quality Testing

ADR-076 data quality rules should become executable tests.

Dimensions may include:

```text
Completeness
Validity
Uniqueness
Consistency
Freshness
Referential integrity
```

---

# 106. Data Contract Testing

Data producers and consumers should validate agreed schemas and semantics.

```text
Producer
   │
   ▼
Data Contract
   │
   ▼
Consumer
```

Schema compatibility alone does not guarantee semantic compatibility.

---

# 107. Pipeline Testing

Data pipelines should test:

```text
Input assumptions
Transformation logic
Schema evolution
Late data
Duplicate data
Missing data
Failure recovery
Replay
```

---

# 108. AI Quality Integration

ADR-077 AI evaluation becomes part of ADR-079's quality architecture.

AI testing includes:

```text
Golden datasets
Regression evaluation
Groundedness
Safety
RAG retrieval
Agent behavior
Tool authorization
Adversarial testing
```

---

# 109. AI Tests Are Probabilistic

Traditional assertion:

```text
expected == actual
```

may not always apply to generative AI.

Evaluation may instead use:

```text
Thresholds
Rubrics
Groundedness
Semantic criteria
Safety constraints
Statistical behavior
```

---

# 110. AI Regression Testing

Every material change to:

```text
Model
Prompt
Retriever
Embedding
Knowledge corpus
Tool definition
Routing
```

should trigger appropriate evaluation.

---

# 111. RAG Regression Testing

Test both:

```text
Question
   │
   ▼
Correct evidence retrieved?
```

and:

```text
Retrieved evidence
      │
      ▼
Correct grounded answer?
```

Do not collapse retrieval and generation quality into one score.

---

# 112. RAG Corpus Tests

Knowledge ingestion should verify:

```text
Document parsing
Chunk creation
Metadata
Authority
Freshness
Embedding
Indexing
Deletion
```

---

# 113. Agent Testing

Agent verification should cover:

```text
Task success
Planning
Tool choice
Arguments
Authorization
Maximum steps
Failure recovery
Side effects
```

---

# 114. Agent Tool Safety Tests

Explicitly verify:

```text
Unauthorized tool call → blocked

Malformed arguments → rejected

High-impact action → confirmation

Tool timeout → controlled recovery
```

The LLM must never be the authorization mechanism.

---

# 115. Test Data Management

Tests require intentional data lifecycle management.

```text
Generate
   │
   ▼
Provision
   │
   ▼
Use
   │
   ▼
Reset
   │
   ▼
Destroy
```

---

# 116. Synthetic Test Data

Synthetic data should be preferred where it provides sufficient realism.

Advantages include:

```text
Privacy
Repeatability
Scenario control
Easy reset
Scale generation
```

---

# 117. Production Data in Testing

Production data should not be copied casually into non-production environments.

ADR-076 controls apply.

Where realistic production-derived data is necessary, approved masking or transformation processes are required.

---

# 118. Test Data Builders

Code-level builders/fixtures should make scenarios explicit.

```text
Student
  ├── active
  ├── suspended
  ├── completed-course
  └── no-enrollment
```

Readable test data improves test intent.

---

# 119. Environment Strategy

Tests should execute at the smallest suitable environment.

```text
Local
  │
  ▼
CI disposable dependencies
  │
  ▼
Ephemeral environment
  │
  ▼
Shared integration/UAT
  │
  ▼
Production verification
```

---

# 120. Ephemeral Test Environments

ADR-078 preview environments can provide realistic system testing without permanent environment proliferation.

```text
PR
 │
 ▼
Ephemeral Environment
 │
 ▼
Integration/E2E
 │
 ▼
Destroy
```

---

# 121. Test Isolation

Tests should not depend unnecessarily on execution order.

Bad:

```text
Test 1 creates student
Test 2 assumes student exists
Test 3 deletes student
```

Each test should establish its own required state where practical.

---

# 122. Deterministic Testing

The same test under the same controlled conditions should produce the same outcome.

Sources of nondeterminism include:

```text
Time
Randomness
Concurrency
External APIs
Shared state
Network timing
Async processing
```

Control these deliberately.

---

# 123. Time Testing

Inject controllable clocks rather than relying directly on current system time for domain logic.

This makes scenarios such as expiry and scheduling deterministic.

---

# 124. Flaky Tests

A flaky test is a defect in the engineering system.

```text
Same code
   │
   ├── PASS
   ├── FAIL
   └── PASS
```

It destroys trust in CI.

---

# 125. Flaky-Test Governance

Flaky tests should be:

```text
Detected
Tracked
Owned
Diagnosed
Fixed
```

not permanently ignored.

---

# 126. Test Retries

Retries may help diagnose transient infrastructure noise.

They must not become a mechanism for hiding flaky tests.

```text
Fails first attempt
Passes retry
      │
      ▼
Still investigate
```

---

# 127. Test Quarantine

Severely flaky tests may be temporarily quarantined when they block delivery disproportionately.

But quarantine requires:

```text
Owner
Reason
Issue
Expiry
Repair plan
```

Otherwise quarantine becomes deletion without admitting it.

---

# 128. Parallelization

Independent tests should execute in parallel where safe.

```text
Test Suite
   │
 ┌─┼─┬─┐
 ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼
T1 T2 T3 T4
```

But shared state must not introduce nondeterminism.

---

# 129. Feedback Speed

Developers should receive fast feedback first.

```text
SECONDS
Static + unit

MINUTES
Component + integration

LATER
E2E + expensive performance/security
```

A 90-minute mandatory pipeline for every small commit is poor engineering.

---

# 130. Test Selection

Not every test must necessarily run for every change.

Risk-aware selection may use:

```text
Changed files
Dependencies
Affected components
Test history
Risk classification
```

Full suites still run at appropriate lifecycle points.

---

# 131. Test Impact Analysis

The platform may map:

```text
Code Change
    │
    ▼
Dependency Graph
    │
    ▼
Affected Tests
```

This can reduce feedback time while preserving confidence.

It must be conservative enough not to silently omit important verification.

---

# 132. Mutation Testing

Mutation testing evaluates whether tests detect deliberately introduced code defects.

```text
Original:
amount > 0

Mutation:
amount >= 0
```

If the suite still passes, it may not meaningfully verify that behavior.

---

# 133. Mutation Testing Scope

Mutation testing can be computationally expensive.

Use it selectively for important domain logic rather than blindly across every line.

---

# 134. Code Coverage

Coverage provides useful information.

It does **not** prove correctness.

```text
100% line coverage
        ≠
100% behavior verified
```

---

# 135. Coverage Governance

Coverage should identify suspiciously untested areas, not become a target developers game with meaningless assertions.

Avoid treating one universal percentage as enterprise quality.

---

# 136. Quality Gates

Release gates should combine evidence.

```text
Build
 │
 ├── Tests
 ├── Security
 ├── Contracts
 ├── Policy
 ├── Quality
 └── Risk
 │
 ▼
Release Decision
```

---

# 137. Risk-Based Gates

A typo in documentation and a payment/security/clinical-impact change should not require identical verification.

Test rigor should scale with:

```text
Impact
Complexity
Change scope
Criticality
Reversibility
Historical risk
```

---

# 138. Release Confidence

Mediverse should reason about confidence from multiple signals:

```text
Automated tests
Static analysis
Security evidence
Performance evidence
Change size
Canary health
Observability
Historical reliability
```

No single metric should become the universal release score.

---

# 139. Progressive Delivery Verification

Deployment should continue testing assumptions.

```text
Candidate
   │
   ▼
Canary
   │
   ▼
Observe
   │
 ┌─┴────┐
 ▼      ▼
Good    Bad
 │       │
Expand  Rollback
```

---

# 140. Canary Analysis

Compare candidate and baseline using appropriate:

```text
Error rate
Latency
Saturation
Business metrics
Security signals
AI quality signals
```

A pod being `Ready` is insufficient evidence for promotion.

---

# 141. Production Synthetic Monitoring

Synthetic transactions should continuously verify critical journeys.

```text
Synthetic User
      │
      ▼
Login
      │
      ▼
Critical Operation
      │
      ▼
Expected Result
```

Synthetic monitoring complements infrastructure health checks.

---

# 142. Observability-Driven Verification

ADR-078 telemetry becomes testing evidence.

```text
Deployment
    │
    ▼
Logs + Metrics + Traces
    │
    ▼
Expected Behavior?
```

Testing and observability should reinforce each other.

---

# 143. Defect Escape Analysis

Production defects should feed the testing strategy.

Ask:

```text
Why did this defect occur?
Why was it not detected earlier?
Which test/control should have detected it?
Would adding that test provide useful future protection?
```

Do not mechanically add an E2E test for every incident.

---

# 144. Quality Metrics

Useful signals may include:

```text
Escaped defects
Flaky-test rate
Pipeline duration
Test failure distribution
Change failure rate
Rollback rate
Mean detection time
Regression recurrence
```

Metrics should drive improvement, not punishment.

---

# 145. Test Economics

Testing has cost.

```text
Test Value
    =
Risk Reduction
    ─────────────
Build + Runtime + Maintenance Cost
```

This is conceptual, not a literal universal formula.

A test that costs hours to maintain while detecting negligible risk may be worse than no test.

---

# 146. Quality Scorecard

A service scorecard may include:

| Capability            | Status |
| --------------------- | ------ |
| Unit tests            | ✓      |
| Component tests       | ✓      |
| API verification      | ✓      |
| Contract tests        | ✓      |
| DB migration tests    | ✓      |
| Event tests           | ✓      |
| E2E critical journeys | ✓      |
| Accessibility         | ✓      |
| Security testing      | ✓      |
| Performance baseline  | ⚠      |
| Resilience tests      | ✓      |
| Flaky tests           | 2 ⚠    |
| Production synthetic  | ✓      |

Scorecards expose debt; they do not replace engineering judgment.

---

# 147. Testing Golden Path

ADR-078 should provide standardized test capabilities.

```text
Service Template
      │
      ▼
Testing Toolkit
      │
      ├── JUnit
      ├── Testcontainers
      ├── API testing
      ├── Contract testing
      ├── Playwright
      ├── Security scanning
      ├── Performance framework
      └── Observability
```

Product teams extend the baseline according to domain risk.

---

# 148. Quality Maturity Model

```text
LEVEL 1 — REACTIVE

Testing occurs primarily
after implementation.


LEVEL 2 — AUTOMATED

CI runs repeatable automated
verification.


LEVEL 3 — ENGINEERED

Testing strategy covers contracts,
data, security and performance.


LEVEL 4 — CONTINUOUS

Progressive delivery, production
verification and quality telemetry
close the lifecycle.


LEVEL 5 — ADAPTIVE

Risk, production evidence,
dependency graphs and historical
failure dynamically influence
verification strategy.
```

Mediverse should target **Level 4**, selectively introducing Level 5 capabilities where the economics justify them.

---

# 149. Quality Engineering Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ QA owns quality
❌ Testing begins after development
❌ Every test is @SpringBootTest
❌ H2 treated as PostgreSQL
❌ Everything mocked
❌ Every scenario implemented as E2E
❌ Fixed sleeps for asynchronous tests
❌ Shared test state without isolation
❌ Flaky tests accepted as normal
❌ Retry-until-green pipelines
❌ Permanent test quarantine
❌ 100% coverage treated as proof of correctness
❌ Coverage targets gamed with meaningless assertions
❌ Testing framework internals
❌ Tests tightly coupled to implementation
❌ Contract changes without compatibility verification
❌ Database migrations tested only on empty databases
❌ Kafka tests verifying only that send() was called
❌ Duplicate event delivery ignored
❌ Retry behavior untested
❌ Performance testing only before launch
❌ /health endpoint used as workload model
❌ HPA configuration assumed to work
❌ Resource limits selected without workload evidence
❌ Chaos engineering as random failure injection
❌ Backups trusted without restore tests
❌ SAST treated as complete security testing
❌ Security scanners blocking everything regardless of context
❌ Secret detection without credential rotation
❌ Production data casually copied into test environments
❌ Ephemeral environments without destruction
❌ AI evaluated only through exact-string assertions
❌ RAG evaluation ignoring retrieval
❌ Agent testing ignoring authorization
❌ Every test executed on every keystroke
❌ 90-minute feedback loops accepted as normal
❌ DORA/quality metrics used to rank individuals
❌ Argo CD "Synced" treated as proof of application health
❌ Canary promotion based only on Kubernetes readiness
❌ Test count treated as quality
```

---
